events.title: emu: boot pre-1.04 TOS from a generated AUTO-folder floppy
events.message:
emu: boot pre-1.04 TOS from a generated AUTO-folder floppy

GEMDOS HD does not exist below TOS 1.04 (Hatari refuses it), so the run
path used to refuse those ROMs outright. Every TOS executes AUTO/*.PRG
from the boot floppy, so write a per-session 720 KiB FAT12 image with
AUTO/PROG.PRG (src/build/FloppyImage.cpp, geometry pinned against a real
mkfs.vfat image in tst_parsers) and boot it via --disk-a with no
positional and no -d.

On this path --debug must accompany --debug-except: the autostart
deferral arms the exception mask only on INF load, which a floppy boot
never performs, so without the startup toggle the mask stays zero and
faulting programs never break in.

Verified live against TOS 1.02: the entry breakpoint fires (program
loads at 0xCC04 rather than the GEMDOS-HD 0x12596) and an illegal
instruction breaks in with a CPU exception. Unverifiable ROMs whose
warning the user accepts take the same path. Resolves PLAN.md 9.4.

events.title: Ignore UDP connection resets so a departed spectator cannot fail the players
events.message:
Ignore UDP connection resets so a departed spectator cannot fail the players

Windows reports an ICMP port-unreachable for an earlier send as
WSAECONNRESET on the UDP socket's next receive or send. On the host's
shared socket that reset arrived as soon as a spectator left, and the
players' link failed with error 10054 (both Windows unit-test jobs). A
reset on a datagram socket is a destination that went away, not a broken
link: the transport now treats it as no packet on receive and as a sent
packet on send, leaving the protocol's own timeouts to drop the dead
link, as they do on every other platform.

events.title: release: add deb, rpm, dmg and msi installers
events.message:
release: add deb, rpm, dmg and msi installers

The installers are built with CPack from the same staged trees the
archives carry (the AppDir for deb/rpm, bundle/ for dmg/msi), so an
installer and its archive are byte-identical content: binary, bundled Qt
runtime, vasm, the hrdb-main Hatari, EmuTOS, licences and notices.
CPACK_INSTALL_CMAKE_PROJECTS="" suppresses the project's own install
rules, which otherwise doubles the payload with both trees; the binary's
rpath is $ORIGIN/../lib so a package resolves its bundled Qt from any
install prefix (verified from a sandbox extraction).

- Linux job builds deb + rpm after the AppImage and self-verifies the
  deb with --diagnose under xvfb.
- macOS job builds a dmg and asserts its contents (app bundle, ROM,
  notices).
- Windows job builds an MSI via WIX (installed if absent) and asserts it
  exists. Upload and release-attach steps now carry all assets, archives
  included.
- DEB/RPM declare no shared-library dependencies: the packages are
  self-contained by design, and a distro Qt may be below the 6.5 floor.

deb and rpm verified end to end locally: metadata, contents layout, and
the packaged pist --diagnose resolving its bundled tools and ROM.

events.title: ui: fix memory/stack interactions and add the debug console
events.message:
ui: fix memory/stack interactions and add the debug console

Memory editing fixes, from a user report ('the value returns'):

- applyDump rewrote every cell with signals live, so each setText fired a
  phantom memoryEdited → debugger write + pane refresh → new dump → an
  unbounded write/refresh storm that closed the in-progress editor and
  reinstated the dumped value. Programmatic rewrites are now
  signal-blocked; clear() and the invalid-commit restore path compose
  correctly under an outer blocker.
- A plain double-click on a cell whose 4-byte window looked like an
  address navigated instead of editing — roughly half of memory. Double-
  click now always edits; pointer-following moved to Alt+double-click
  (Ctrl is macOS's secondary-click gesture).
- Dumps whose first row is not the view's base are discarded as stale
  (navigation while a dump is in flight), so display, status text and
  edit-write addresses stay consistent; goToAddress blanks the stale
  region instead of showing old bytes under a new base.
- The table is focusable while editing, so F2 and the in-place editor
  actually receive keys; editing a second memory pane refreshes that
  pane, not the first.

Stack → memory navigation, previously unimplemented: StackView gains an
addressActivated signal — a pointer-looking value follows to its target
(return addresses), any other row follows the slot's own address — wired
into the first memory pane, which now raises itself out of the bottom
tab group on navigation (watchpoint activation too).

Debug console: the build/debug console gains an input line. Typed
commands go through IDebugBackend::consoleCommand(); the ack appears
exactly once on both transports (HRDB emits console-originated acks;
native streams stderr). The command translation table is factored into
translateCommand() shared by typed and internal commands.

Also: MainWindow swaps backends at launch from the project's
debugBackend setting (SettingsDialog gains the transport combo), all
capability gates use the launched binary's probe (launchedCaps), and the
dead pre-connect that printed a nullptr warning per test run is gone.
docs (PLAN/FUTURE/ARCHITECTURE/AGENTS/README) brought up to date:
Phase 2/3 statuses, the HRDB ledger entries, fork provenance, the
first-run and notices delivery notes, and the new test inventory.

events.title: release: bundle the hrdb-main Hatari fork as the AppImage emulator
events.message:
release: bundle the hrdb-main Hatari fork as the AppImage emulator

The Linux AppImage's only emulator is now the hrdb-main fork (upstream
2.6.1 plus the remote-debug listener), pinned by commit (21aa4cb) and
tarball checksum and installed as 'hatari'. PiST's content probe selects
HRDB for it automatically; stock Hatari keeps the native backend, so a
fresh install gets typed framing, pause-while-running and one transport
everywhere with no per-project switching.

- build-hatari action gains variant (upstream|hrdb) and binary-name
  inputs, so CI builds the fork side-by-side (hatari-hrdb, exercising the
  tst_hrdb and transport-swap suites) while the release builds it as the
  bundled 'hatari'.
- The AppImage verification asserts the diagnose output reports
  'transport: hrdb', so an upstream binary shipped by mistake fails the
  release.
- collect-notices.py detects the fork in a bundle by the same probe and
  emits a pinned-commit source offer (an upstream-tarball link cannot
  satisfy GPLv2 for a patched binary); NOTICE matches.
- macOS and Windows archives are unchanged: no emulator is bundled
  there today.

The fork is never patched: it is built unmodified and driven as a
subprocess by command-line arguments, exactly like upstream.

events.message:
packaging: derive dependency notices from artifact contents

packaging/collect-notices.py assembles each archive's licence set from
what is actually inside it — the binaries present, the libraries the
bundled emulator links (ldd/otool), and every staged shared library —
rather than from a static list. Whether Hatari links Capstone depends on
the build host, so its BSD text ships exactly when Capstone does; the
local CI build proves the fork doesn't link it.

- Canonical texts committed under packaging/notices/ (GPL-2.0/3.0,

- vasm's licence section is extracted from the pinned source tarball's

- A bundled hrdb-main fork is detected by the same content probe PiST
  uses and gets a pinned-commit source offer, since an upstream-tarball
  link cannot satisfy GPLv2 for a patched binary.
- THIRD-PARTY.txt manifest generated per artifact; the release workflow

Verified by building a real AppImage locally with linuxdeploy and

events.title: debug: add IDebugBackend with native and HRDB implementations
events.message:
debug: add IDebugBackend with native and HRDB implementations

Extract the debug-transport contract from EmulatorHost and implement it
twice: the native stdin/prompt transport (stock Hatari) and HrdbBackend
over the tattlemuss hrdb-main fork's typed TCP protocol (56001, 0x100a).

- IDebugBackend covers start/stop, stepping, breakpoints, memory dumps,
  state snapshots, pause, and the shared signal set. EmulatorHost is the
  native implementation.
- HrdbBackend: entry stop via the bootstrap parse file (airtight; a
  socket-armed entry bp races TOS boot), registers and live TEXT/DATA/BSS
  bases from typed regs, uuencoded mem payloads rendered as upstream 'm'
  text, BreakCond breakpoints and watchpoints, step, client-synthesized
  step-over, pause-while-running, console commands via the fork's stderr.
- HatariProbe gains a content probe (hasHrdb): the fork is
  version-identical to upstream and adds no CLI option, so only the
  listener banner string distinguishes it. Backend selection defaults to
  auto (probe decides); forced native/hrdb mismatches are refused at
  launch with the reason named.
- EmbedSocket shares the control-socket server (embed size reports,
  hatari-debug lines) between both backends.
- Native pause works via 'hatari-debug b pc ! 0 :once' over the control
  socket; hatari-stop alone only halts the VBL loop. This exposed a real
  race: a stdout prompt outrunning the stderr entry banner left
  m_awaitingEntryPrompt stale, swallowing the next stop's prompt. Fixed
  in handleStderrLine and pinned by tst_emulatorhost.

tst_hrdb (12 live tests, gated on $PIST_HRDB_HATARI) covers entry,
registers/bases, mem read/write, stepping, step-over, breakpoints, pause
and the embed-size seam, and honours PIST_REQUIRE_EMULATOR like the
upstream emulator suite.

events.title: Settle checkpoints before same-frame disk changes and keep feeds flowing
events.message:
Settle checkpoints before same-frame disk changes and keep feeds flowing

Review findings on spectator mode, each with a regression test:

- A disk change that lands on a 60-frame checkpoint boundary was applied
  by the browser wrapper before the checkpoint was compared, so the
  host's pre-change digest met a post-change machine and the spectator
  failed. Spectator::verify_frame now reports whether the boundary is
  settled, and both frontends apply a due change only once it is. The
  core test records a change on frame 120 and the web wrapper test
  performs one at a held boundary.
- The host page sent a whole disk image (up to 16 MiB) in one pump after
  a single buffer check. RtcWatchPeer keeps the taken buffer and an
  offset and sends one chunk at a time while the channel's buffer stays
  within FEED_BUFFER, with a bounded number of chunks per pump for a
  channel that never reports its buffer.
- The room service deleted a spectator's answer as it was fetched, so a
  response lost in transit left the spectator unable to retry. A fetched
  answer now frees the place but stays readable for a minute.
- The desktop flush serviced spectator links without reading the host
  socket, so direct-UDP acknowledgements never reached their slots and a
  long feed could be cut off at the timeout. Session::spectators_delivered
  polls the host's control link first; the flush loops on it.

events.title: Serve netplay spectators from the browser page and room service
events.message:
Serve netplay spectators from the browser page and room service

The room service gains watch rooms: a host that admits spectators
creates a second room with its own 22-character capability, so a
spectator link never reaches a player room. Signaling runs the other
way round from player rooms: each spectator reserves a place and
offers, the host polls for offers (which keeps the room alive) and
answers them, and a fetched answer frees the place. Entries are stored
per spectator, role mismatches answer 403, and stale offers and
answers are pruned.

The page moves the shared WebRTC plumbing and connection codes into
netplay-rtc.js and adds netplay-watch.js: RtcWatch (the spectator's
offering link), RtcWatchPeer (the host's answering peer) and
SpectatorHub, which polls the watch room while the host machine runs,
serves the host media once described, requires a matching machine
fingerprint, and streams the feed in 16 KiB messages under bounded
buffering, dropping a spectator that never drains. The Advanced block
gets a Spectators count and the host a separate spectator invitation
with copy and share; a #watch= link offers Watch game.

WebEmu gains netplay_enable_spectators, netplay_identity and
spectator_feed_open/take/close for the host, and start_spectating,
spectate_receive and spectate_status for a spectator whose run loop
paces like a player or replays a backlog in bounded bursts with its
audio discarded. Every mutation and input entry point now checks a
session_active flag that covers spectating. The WASM harnesses run
two late spectators and a spectator that follows every disk change.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Add netplay spectators with a confirmed-only feed
events.message:
Add netplay spectators with a confirmed-only feed

A host can admit up to eight spectators, who follow the game without
owning a controller port and may join while it is in progress. Only the
host serves them: the guest and the CLNP input protocol are unchanged.

The host's Rollback logs each frame's inputs as they become confirmed,
and Connection::enable_feed keeps that history, the checkpoint digests
and every disk change (with the digests measured before and after it)
in a spectate::Feed. A spectator receives the same cold-boot bundle a
guest gets, replays the feed from frame zero unpaced until it is level
with the players, and then executes confirmed frames a few frames
behind them, verifying every 60-frame checkpoint and failing closed on
a mismatch. No remote emulator checkpoint is ever deserialized.

Session now serves host, guest and spectator roles. The feed rides the
reliable control channel as kind byte 4; Control checks a local/peer
role pair, holds chunks in its receive window instead of failing once
four messages are queued, shares Arc bundle parts between links, and
merges small messages with the length prefix. Direct UDP spectators
share the host's socket, demultiplexed by source address into a capped
slot table; Internet mode keeps the iroh endpoint accepting after the
player joins and admits each connection by capability, with a separate
CLNS1. spectator invitation that cannot claim the player slot. Each
connection is pumped by its own task, so a spectator's failure lands
only in its queues, and the host drops a silent link after ten seconds.

The launcher gains a Watch role, a Spectators row and a spectator-code
copy action; the CLI gains --netplay-spectators, --netplay-spectator-
invite and --netplay-watch. A spectator's window sends no input to the
machine, catch-up runs unpaced with live audio muted like a warp gate,
headless captures keep one frame per pass, and a headless host flushes
its feed to connected spectators before exiting. check-netplay.py can
launch late-joining spectator processes and requires identical PNGs.

Owner's request for a gamepad-only setup (a Steam Deck in Game Mode has
no keyboard, and the suggested controller template has nothing bound to
a numbered key or a Ctrl chord): "Can the first menu support a highlight
bar... so the player can still highlight and select a choice hitting the
A key?"

This screen actually had exactly that once, and it was removed on
purpose: D-018 (live-confirmed) found the real disk's screen polls only
for the literal Ctrl+1/Ctrl+2 chord, no cursor, no fire-select at all, and
an earlier pass deleted the invented cursor to match (FV-1c1/FV-1c2).
Reintroducing it needed the owner's own call given that history, not a
silent reversal.

GameFlow.selection_row (new) tracks the highlight; _on_selection moves it
on UP/DOWN and resolves FIRE to whichever SELECT_* event that row
represents, gated the whole time on `not is_original(...)` - the same
test the mouse already uses (options.pointer_allowed). render/frontend.py
draws it through the screen's existing mouse-hover highlight, no new
visual language needed.

A follow-up question - should ORIGINAL get the same exception
specifically on a Deck with no keyboard at all - was declined by the
owner, citing the standing ruling on the mouse: ORIGINAL means the
original machine too, and does not bend for whatever hardware happens to

events.title: Alien (1984): a Python remake
events.message:
Alien (1984): a Python remake

A playable reimplementation of Alien (Mind Games / Argus Press Software,
1984) for the Commodore 64, rebuilt in Python by reading the original
disk's 6502 code and copying what it actually does.

Two ways to play: ORIGINAL matches the 1984 disk exactly - same rules,
same odds, same screens, no additions. UPDATED adds an optional analog
CRT look, sound effects, mouse control, a quicker boot chain, feedback
the original never gave you (a notice when an attack on the Alien lands,
for one), and true randomness for the opening death and the hidden
android where the disk always drew from a short fixed list. Everything
added is off under ORIGINAL and toggleable from the options screen.

No game data is distributed here - you supply your own disk image, and
the first run decodes the graphics, sprites, text and music out of it.
docs/re/ carries the decompilation itself: the annotated disassembly, the
memory map, the discoveries log, and the faithfulness report, so the
reverse-engineering behind the remake can be checked independently of the
remake's own code.

See the README for how to install and play, on Windows, Linux, or a
Steam Deck.

events.title: The pack loop's includes are clean's, not distclean's (#18)
events.message:
The pack loop's includes are clean's, not distclean's (#18)

hexwab, issue #18: 2fa5213 FTBFS for him, debug and release, with
`ASSERT spr_end <= SWRAM_BASE + &4000`. `make clean` did not help;
`make distclean` did. His previous build was 044b42c.

DIAGNOSED, AND IT IS A REAL FRAGILITY RATHER THAN A DOC GAP.
src/data/brfimg.asm, lowimg.asm and krimg.asm are the pack loop's own
output: gitignored, different between a DEV and a -Release build, and
- the part that bites - THEY SURVIVE A BRANCH SWITCH. --ensure only
creates them when MISSING; it never asks whether the ones on disc
belong to this tree, so the first assembly reads whatever is there.
#20 changed keyredef, so his krimg.asm was ~161 bytes wrong for bank
5.

THE LOOP CANNOT CLIMB OUT OF THAT. Its whole premise is assemble ->
pack -> assemble again, and when a stale stream overflows a bank the
assembly stops BEFORE pack_overlays runs to regenerate it. The one
state it cannot repair is the one that stops it.

The same trap cost me an hour during the rebase of this branch, and I
reported it and did not fix it. Fixed now, in both pipelines:

  make clean          removes the three includes (they leave distclean)
  ./build.ps1 -Clean  new - the same, plus build/ and the loose SAVEs.
                      build.ps1 had NO clean target at all, so Windows
                      had no recovery but deleting them by hand
  first failed pass   build.ps1 names the likely cause and the fix
                      instead of just re-throwing beebasm's error

Documented in CLAUDE.md's build block and a new section of
docs/build.md, including the part that should stop anyone worrying
about what has already shipped: A BUILD THAT COMPLETES HAS CONVERGED.
If a stale stream still fits, pack_overlays regenerates it from that
assembly's own output, sees the difference and exits 10 for another
pass. Only the failing case is dangerous, and only because it is
confusing.

Verified: ./build.ps1 -Clean empties all three, a plain build then
stubs and converges from cold ("stubbed brfimg/lowimg/krimg ...
assembling again"), and -Clean -Release chains. A pristine clone of
23a4267 also builds -Release to the same 86,016 -> 55,808 image, which
is what says the COMMIT was always sound and only hexwab's working
tree was stale.

events.title: Merge issue #18: OSBYTE 140, one *RUN boot, and the zero page it opens
events.message:
Merge issue #18: OSBYTE 140, one *RUN boot, and the zero page it opens

hexwab's contract correction, and what it paid for.

THE CONTRACT (layer-13 DECISION 4). There are two problems with two
different answers and the port gave the loader's answer to the game. A
LOADER still needs to load, so it borrows the filing system's workspace
and must own the machine to do it. A GAME that has finished loading
calls OSBYTE 140 and has the filing system detach, hand its hooks back
and stand its NMI hardware down - and only then is the workspace ours.
We were the second case behaving as the first while making OS calls
anyway. Acorn's DFS does not hook them, which is the only reason it
ever ran; hexwab's Opus 1770 with DDOS 3.45 hung at the deck plan.

EVERY DISC BOOTS BY *RUN NOW, which is not tidying but the
precondition: the game runs inside DFS's workspace at &1100-&1900, and
*EXEC writes there - as does closing an exec file, which is an implicit
*EXEC. The dev disc's *EXEC !BOOT had DFS scribble over the very
instructions executing OSBYTE 140.

THE ZERO PAGE (DECISION 5). Every absolute-mode data reference in the
build was counted per operand and attributed to the bank making it.
abs -> zp saves a byte per reference always and a cycle only when not
indexed, so scalars pay and arrays do not: drIdx is 45 references in one
byte where drEnergy is 51 in fourteen. Three tiers, 27 bytes of zero
page:

  main RAM   39 ->  91 B      bank 6  260 -> 303 B
  bank 4     64 -> 129 B      bank 7   86 ->  90 B, pad 5 -> 236
  bank 5    148 -> 149 B

405 bytes across five regions. &D0-&E6 was measured free on top of that
- the VDU driver's workspace, which OSBYTE 140 does NOT free, but which
nothing touches while the game owns IRQ and issues no VDU call.

ONE REGRESSION, FOUND BY KC AND FIXED IN b36d73a: score is not loaded
any more, and &CC-&CF is DFS's old workspace, so the briefing panel
showed 24001300. Zeroed once at boot. The reasoning that let it through
- "SKIP 4 means CombatInit is its only initialiser" - was wrong, because
SKIP inside a SAVEd block emits zeros into the disc file, and it is
corrected everywhere it was written down. The other 22 moved variables
were then audited against the same fault with read breakpoints across
the OSBYTE 140 -> ZpSeed window, and are clean.

Docs re-read from a fresh label dump rather than adjusted, which turned
up three main-RAM rows that were WRONG rather than stale (keyTab and
DECK_DONE were listed above code_end) and two figures on main that were
already stale before this branch touched them.

Release Candidate #8 (zero page) built and smoke-tested from the
shipping 204,800-byte image: autoboot, stamp with no DEBUG line, probe,
intro, title, briefing with the score at 0, and into play.

NOT DONE, and both are cheap for someone with a POSIX box and a few
minutes of play: `make check-ps1` has not run since both build pipelines
changed, and Tier 2's transfer minigame board and lift side view were
never driven.

Issue #18's &0D9F question and hexwab's warning that filing-system
workspace need not stop at &1900 are both still open.

events.title: Fix: score showed DFS leftovers in the briefing panel (#18)
events.message:
Fix: score showed DFS leftovers in the briefing panel (#18)

KC: "on boot, the briefing shows a very large number in the panel".
It read 24001300, and &CC-&CF read `24 00 13 00`. Reproduced, fixed
and the rest of the moved variables audited for the same fault.

MY BUG, AND MY STATED REASONING FOR IT WAS WRONG. Tier 1's note said
score needed no seeding because it "was SKIP 4, never an EQUB, so
CombatInit has always been its only initialiser". SKIP inside a SAVEd
block emits zeros into the disc file - so score was LOADED as zero and
stayed zero from boot until CombatInit, and the panel drew 0 on the
title and the briefing, both of which come long before any CombatInit.
Zero page is not loaded, and &CC-&CF is inside &B0-&CF, which is DFS's
own zero-page workspace, so after the boot loads it holds DFS's
leftovers.

FIXED by zeroing score once in .start, beside OSBYTE 140 - nine bytes,
reproducing exactly what loading the image used to do. NOT in ZpSeed:
that runs on every route into play and GoTitle reaches TitleSeq, so
seeding it there would tie it to HsEntry still being ordered BEFORE
ts_loads, and a future reordering would silently wipe the score out
from under the high-score entry. Zeroing at boot has no ordering to
break.

THE OTHER TWENTY-TWO ARE CLEAN, and that was measured rather than
argued. The exposure window is OSBYTE 140 to the first ZpSeed, and
InfoCall and FillPanel both run inside it - they are ts_loads calls
that precede ZpSeed, and infoscr.asm and panel.asm do reference the
moved names. Read breakpoints on sndFx1, moveMode, dbCap, pnTmp and
pnCol across that window ALL lost the race to ZpSeed's execute
breakpoint, twice over: nothing reads a seeded byte before it is
seeded. InstallIrq is the last call in ts_loads, well after ZpSeed, so
the sound tick cannot reach sndFx1/2, snCvH or snTm2 early either.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2), both directions: a cold boot now shows
0 in the briefing panel where it showed 24001300, and a game played
with CTRL+C scored 1305 (&CC-&CF = 00 00 13 05), so the boot zeroing
does not touch a live score.

  main RAM  100 -> 91 B  (code_end &2F9C -> &2FA5)

The wrong reasoning is corrected everywhere it was written down -
main.asm's zero-page map, combat.asm, droid.asm's ZpSeed header,
CLAUDE.md, memory-map.md and layer-13 DECISION 5, which now carries
the whole story including the audit.

events.title: Size the libretro state envelope from the machine it was built for
events.message:
Size the libretro state envelope from the machine it was built for

retro_serialize_size() reported a flat 64 MiB for every session, while
a stock A500 with one floppy writes 4.3 MiB of state. The frontend
takes that number at face value: RetroArch allocates it for every
rollback slot and, with netplay's per-frame check, checksums a whole
buffer each frame. Measured on this core, that checksum alone cost
1.43 ms a frame against the 2.7 ms it takes to emulate the frame.

The bound is computable, because what a checkpoint holds is: each RAM
bank and ROM image once, chip RAM twice more (the BUS chunk carries
current_frame_chip_ram and last_frame_chip_ram, whole copies, which is
the entire size difference between an OCS and an AGA machine), the
drive's disk image, this core's own copy of every disk slot, and the
chipset scratch -- registers, the Copper and blitter, and the per-line
beam events the renderer replays. Only the last of those is measured
rather than derived; across nine OCS and AGA titles it stayed under a
megabyte, and 4 MiB is reserved for it. WHDLoad's hard-disk overlays go
on top as they did before.

An A500 with one floppy now reserves 14.0 MiB, an A1200 18.0 MiB and a
CD32 11.2 MiB, and the same nine titles peak at between a third and a
half of their envelope over 2,500 frames each. The per-frame checksum
falls to 0.31 ms, and RetroArch's rollback ring shrinks with it.

Two things follow from paying per disk slot. A floppy session reserves
its playlist and two spares, because each slot costs a whole image in
every checkpoint, and add() now refuses past that naming the session's
limit; a CD session, whose slots hold a reference rather than an image,
keeps all sixteen. And retro_unserialize can no longer insist the
buffer be no larger than this session reserves, or state files written
when every session reserved 64 MiB would stop loading: they are mostly
trailing zeros, and the payload length in their own header is what has
to fit.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Judge the netplay check by the workload, not RetroArch's exit
events.message:
Judge the netplay check by the workload, not RetroArch's exit

The Libretro job failed 12 of its last 76 completed runs, always in the
same step and always with "netplay test timed out". In every one of
those runs the client's log already said

    Content ran for a total of: 00 hours, 00 minutes, 24 seconds

which is the 1,200 frames it was asked for at 49.92 fps: the whole
workload, every per-frame CRC exchanged and every one agreed. Eleven of
the twelve never reached the monitor-refresh line that ends the log of
every passing run, so the client had wedged in RetroArch 1.18's driver
teardown and never exited, and the harness sat on client.poll() until
its 600 second budget ran out. The check has never once failed on a CRC
mismatch.

That teardown is the frontend's business, not the core's, and this file
already made the same allowance for the host, which stops answering
quit requests once its peer disconnects. Make it for the client too:
wait for the completion marker, compare the emulated seconds it reports
against the frames that were asked for, so a run cut short still fails,
and then allow --exit-grace for the process to leave before cleanup
stops it like the Xvfb servers. A timeout now prints the tail of both
peer logs, which is what the log artifacts were being fetched for.

The two subsystems the run never uses are switched off in the generated
configuration while here; MIDI was failing to initialise on every run
and saying so.

events.title: Tier 1: the hot scalars into the reclaimed zero page (#18)
events.message:
Tier 1: the hot scalars into the reclaimed zero page (#18)

OSBYTE 140 made the second half of the zero page legitimately ours
(61500a8, hexwab's contract). This spends thirteen bytes of it on the
measured top of the reference list.

MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. Every absolute-mode data reference in the build
was counted per operand and attributed to the bank of the code making
it. abs -> zp saves ONE BYTE PER REFERENCE always, and one cycle only
when the reference is not indexed - abs,X and zp,X are both 4 cycles.
So scalars pay and arrays do not: drEnergy is 51 refs but 14 zp bytes
(3.6:1) where drIdx is 45 refs in one byte (45:1). Arrays are left
where they are, deliberately.

  sndFx1 &A9  sndFx2 &AA  joyYDir &AB  numDoors &AC  moveMode &AD
  drIdx  &AE  drCount &AF snCvH   &B0  snTm2    &B1  score    &B2-&B5

ZERO PAGE IS NOT LOADABLE, and it does not survive the front end, so
every EQUB initial value these carried in the code image had to be
re-established at run time. SprSeedYcol already did exactly that for
drYcol0-2, so it is now ZpSeed and the nine seeded scalars are simply
an extension of its table: eighteen bytes, one run, one loop, and the
count is ASSERTed against the last symbol. moveMode's MM_MOBILE is the
only non-zero seed and the reason this is a table, not a fill.

SCORE IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED, and that is a correctness point
rather than an oversight. It was SKIP 4, never an EQUB, so CombatInit
has always been its only initialiser. ZpSeed runs once per route into
play and the briefing's fire exit is one of those routes, so seeding
score there would be a silent wipe. It sits one byte past the run.

FONTCODE_BYTES 201 -> 185: DoScore is in the PARAFNT block and lost 16
bytes to zero page. The ASSERT caught it, which is what it is for.

  main RAM   30 ->  100 B   (code_end &2FE2 -> &2F9C)   +70
  bank 4     25 ->  129 B   (ends &BFE7 -> &BF7F)      +104
  bank 5    342 ->  345 B                                +3
  bank 6    254 ->  263 B                                +8
  bank 7     84 ->   88 B                                +4
  PARAFNT                                                +16

193 bytes of the five tight regions for thirteen of zero page, and
~180 cycles a pass off the non-indexed reads.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2), and the seeding was tested the way
beeb-bss-bugs says to rather than trusting an emulator that zeroes
RAM: &A0-&B5 was filled with &A5 at the title, then fire through the
briefing into play. Zero page read back 00 10 20 08 18 28 10 20 30 -
drYcol exact - with numDoors 3, moveMode &80 (MM_MOBILE, and the panel
reads "Mobile"), score 0000, and the &A5 gone entirely. A CTRL+]
deck hop then loaded a new deck with its doors and droids correct.
DEBUG_POS assembles again, which it did not before the space came back.

events.title: OSBYTE 140 when loading is done, and one *RUN boot (#18)
events.message:
OSBYTE 140 when loading is done, and one *RUN boot (#18)

hexwab's contract correction. There are two problems with two different
answers, and the port gave the loader's answer to the game:

  a LOADER still needs to load, so it borrows the filing system's
  workspace and must OWN THE MACHINE to do it - claim the NMI, let no
  OS code run, because regaining control is the only way the filing
  system can find out;

  a GAME that has finished loading calls OSBYTE 140 and has the filing
  system detach, hand its hooks back and stand its NMI hardware down.
  Only then is the workspace ours - &B0-&CF in the zero page, and
  &0E00 up to OSHWM, where the low overlay lives.

We were the second case behaving as the first while making OS calls
anyway: OSBYTE 229 per game start, &0F at the game over, 19 at every
rupture align, all after PageLowIn has buried the workspace. Acorn's
DFS does not hook those, which is the only reason it ever ran; hexwab's
Opus 1770 with DDOS 3.45 hung at the deck plan. 044b42c blamed the
memory map - that change stands, the deck plan's pointers cost nothing
where they are, but its reasoning does not and the note is corrected.

The call goes after the PARXFER load, the last load on any path, and
before the OSBYTE 143 that was already there. The NMI claim stays:
hexwab calls it belt-and-braces, and it is eight bytes against an
unrecoverable jump through stale 6502.

AND EVERY DISC BOOTS BY *RUN NOW, which is not tidying - it is what
makes the above possible. THE GAME RUNS INSIDE DFS's WORKSPACE:
&1100-&1900 is the random-access file buffer area, and living there
works only because *LOAD, and *RUN which is *LOAD plus a jump, never
touch it. *EXEC does. So does CLOSING an exec file, which is an
implicit *EXEC: a first attempt put OSBYTE 119 in front to close it
politely and hung identically, the close being itself a write into the
region it was meant to make safe. The dev disc's *EXEC !BOOT therefore
had DFS scribble over the instructions executing the call - boot
reached *RUN PARA, went black, and jsbeeb found the CPU inside the
DNFS ROM at &ACB1 with ROMSEL 14.

The dev build loses nothing: the stamp it used to *TYPE from INFO the
stub prints itself, from the same BuildStamp macro, DEBUG_ line and
all, and INFO is still a disc file for *TYPE INFO at a prompt. Both
pipelines pass -opt 2 unconditionally now, make_disc.py knows one
!BOOT shape, and BOOT_RUN and the text branch are gone.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2): release disc *RUN !BOOT -> intro ->
title; dev disc SHIFT+BREAK -> stamp with its DEBUG: line -> probe ->
title -> briefing -> play. &A9-&CF seeded with &A5 in play and read
back untouched after 800 frames. Without the call the title draws at
frame 745; with it and an *EXEC boot it never appears.

code_end &2FD9 -> &2FE2, 30 B free. Bank 4 unchanged at 25 B.

NOT DONE, and noted in the layer doc: &0D9F is the MOS's extended
vector table, not the filing system's, so OSBYTE 140 does not make it
ours and lowcode2 still lands on it. Nor is there a guard for hexwab's
broader point that filing system workspace need not stop at &1900.

events.title: Put away the console window a desktop launch opens
events.message:
Put away the console window a desktop launch opens

Starting Copperline from Explorer, the Start menu or the Store package
left a console window sitting behind the emulator.

The obvious answer -- windows_subsystem = "windows" -- is the wrong one.
copperline.exe is one binary doing two jobs, and the console subsystem
is what the command-line half needs: a shell waits for a
console-subsystem process and its output lands in the terminal, where a
GUI-subsystem one hands the prompt straight back and prints nowhere
anybody is looking. Every scripted --screenshot-after run, and the
functional-coverage CI jobs, would read their results before the run
they asked for had finished.

So the subsystem stays as it is and the window goes instead, and only
when it is ours to take away: GetConsoleProcessList reporting this
process alone means Windows made that console for this launch, where a
shell -- or cargo run -- would still be attached to it and keeps every
byte Copperline writes. The standard handles are pointed at NUL before
FreeConsole, because Rust fetches them per write and println! panics
when the write fails.

The window can still flash: Windows puts it on screen before any of this
code runs, and hiding it first is the earliest that can be cut short.

events.title: Give copperline.exe the Copperline icon
events.message:
Give copperline.exe the Copperline icon

winit's with_window_icon dresses the window at runtime, but says nothing
about the file on disk, so Explorer, the taskbar, the Start menu and the
Store package all drew the generic default executable icon.

Link the icon in as a Win32 resource instead. Resource id 1 is what the
shell draws -- the lowest icon id in a binary wins -- and it names the
same multi-size .ico the window already loads, so the executable and the
window it opens agree. The script sits beside the icon it names, which
is where the resource compiler looks first; build.rs passes the
directory as an include path as well, for the toolchains that do not.

Scoped to the one binary that is the app: copperline-ctl and
copperline-import-uae ship beside it but are not Copperline. A toolchain
with no resource compiler is not fatal either -- it warns and builds an
emulator with the default icon.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Run native file pickers on a thread of their own
events.message:
Run native file pickers on a thread of their own

On Windows the file dialog opened from the disk button could sit on
"Working on it..." forever, in every folder, while staying responsive to
clicks -- and then work perfectly the next time it was opened.

A blocking rfd picker runs the shell's own modal loop on the calling
thread, and Copperline calls it from inside the winit event callback.
winit's WM_PAINT arm sets redraw_requested to should_buffer() and, once
DefWindowProcW has validated the window, re-arms an internal paint with
RedrawWindow(RDW_INTERNALPAINT) if that flag is set, so a redraw asked
for while events were being buffered is not lost. should_buffer() is
"the runner is not holding an event handler", which is true for as long
as one of our callbacks is on the stack -- so every paint the dialog's
modal loop dispatches immediately arms the next one, GetMessage always
has a message to hand back, and the queue never goes idle. The shell
fills its item view on idle, so the list never arrives.

Whether it bit at all came down to an internal paint being pending when
the click was handled: a running machine arms one every frame through
request_redraw, a machine sitting in the launcher does not, which is why
it looked like it struck at random and why the launcher's own dialogs
never showed it.

So the picker gets a thread of its own, whose queue is quiet, and the
event-loop thread pumps its own messages while it waits -- a thread that
stops pumping is ghosted as "Not Responding" after about five seconds.
WM_PAINT is validated rather than dispatched, since dispatching it is
the re-arm above; nothing is lost, as the emulator is stopped for the
duration, and the windows are invalidated again on the way out.

Every blocking picker goes through the new helper: floppies, CD, PCMCIA,
save states, Kickstart ROMs, the debugger's dumps, the SoundFont and
MT-32 pickers, and the launcher's nine. The netplay path already used
rfd's async picker, which spawns a thread of its own, and is unchanged.
Other platforms keep calling the picker on the main thread, which is
what AppKit and GTK require, with the same Send bounds everywhere so a
capture that could not make the move fails to build on every platform.

Volba `stopy vozidel` je pusti i mimo pasmo. Drzi se STRANOU SIMULACE:
seznam zije na `state`, ne na `g`, takze se nedostane do `netStateHash`
ani nesahne na RNG a dva hraci po siti muzou mit kazdy jine nastaveni.
Snimek se voli puvodnim vzorcem `((uhel + 16) & 0xE0) >> 5 & 3`, jen
uhel neni z veze, ale ze smeru pohybu. Vozidla: tank, flattank, juntank
a jeep; stopa po kazdych sedmi ujetych pixelech, strop 3000.

Pri tom se doplnil orez dekalu podle viditelnosti v obou vykreslovacich
cestach - dekaly maji `life: Infinity`, takze jich za dlouhou hru muzou
byt tisice. Plati to i pro puvodni kratery a stopy min.

OPRAVA REGRESE Z 7af7527: prvni verze podpixelove cesty si drzela
zvetseninu u kazdeho platna spritu. `smoothSpriteCanvas` ale zaklada
nove platno pro kazdou kombinaci sprite + operace + paleta a u
maskovanych spritu je v klici jeste poloha, takze vznika nove kazdy
snimek - do pameti se sypala dve platna na maskovany sprite a snimek.
V dlouhem behu to vyslo na 425 ms na snimek misto jedne milisekundy.
V `smoothSpriteCanvas` je na presne tuhle past varovani uz z drivejska;
slapl jsem do ni o patro vys. Opraveno jednim sdilenym platnem.

Zmereno, ze podpixelova cesta sama regrese NENI: tataz scena s ni
189 ms, bez ni 194 ms, a po dlouhem behu 142 vs 144 ms.

Nalez k dalsimu kroku (zatim NEUDELANO): nejdrazsi vec v obraze jsou
mekke stiny - tataz scena se 17 stiny stoji 28 ms bez nich a 192 ms
s nimi, tedy ~9,6 ms na stin, protoze `ctx.filter` se vola na kazdy
zvlast. Da se predrozostrit a zakesovat.

events.title: Podpixelove sprity: objekty uz po zemi nepodkluzuji
events.message:
Podpixelove sprity: objekty uz po zemi nepodkluzuji

Hrac hlasil, ze pohyb objektu pusobi trhane oproti scrollu pozadi.
Nebylo to rychlosti, ale rozdilem mrizek. Krok mezi snimky pri 60 Hz:

    zoom 4x:  pozadi -0,208 px plynule,  objekt 0,25 / 0,5 px
    zoom 6x:  pozadi -0,208 px plynule,  objekt 0,333 / 0,5 px

Teren se pri zapnutem prolnuti kresli na ZLOMKOVOU polohu, sprity se ale
kvantovaly na cely bod displeje - objekty proto po plynule jedouci zemi
podkluzovaly.

A tady konecne dava prevzorkovani smysl. Zvetseni nejblizsim sousedem
samo o sobe nemeni nic (0 rozdilnych bodu ze 147 456, zmereno minule),
ale ve dvojici s VYHLAZOVANIM ano: sprite se zvetsi na rozliseni
displeje a teprve pak klade na zlomkovou polohu, takze se michaji body
displeje, ne herni pixely. Vnitrek spritu zustane tvrdy, rozmaze se jen
okraj o jeden bod.

Zmereno po zavedeni - rozkmit kroku spritu mezi snimky:

    zoom 4x:  0,25  px -> 0
    zoom 6x:  0,167 px -> 0

Pozadi ma rozkmit 0 v obou pripadech, sprity se mu tedy vyrovnaly.

Vedlejsi ucinek: naklon je konecne videt. Posuny 1 / 4 / -1,5 px se pri
kvantovani na cely bod displeje zaokrouhlovaly skoro k nule.

Hloubka ostrosti se pro sprity presunula do souradnic displeje. Cena
celkem 10,24 -> 10,31 ms na snimek pri sedmi pozemnich objektech.

`smoothtest` bezi nove v tom, co se nasazuje (podpixelove sprity
zapnute): mimo obdelniky spritu je rozdil proti klasickemu snimku porad
0 bodu, uvnitr vzrostl ze 364 na 925 - presne ten mekky okraj.

Vsech sedm kontraktu OK.

events.title: Naklon jako uklon a hloubka ostrosti i pro objekty na zemi
events.message:
Naklon jako uklon a hloubka ostrosti i pro objekty na zemi

Dve hlaseni od hrace.

1) Natoceni spritu bylo videt, ale cetlo se jako ZATACENI, ne jako
naklon. Otoceni je pryc. Z pohledu shora je videt horni strana stroje,
takze se pri uklonu kazdy bod posune do strany o svou vysku nad podelnou
osou krat sin(uhel). Rozdil mezi castmi je to, co oko cte jako uklon:

    rotor (nejvys)   +4   px pri plnem vychylu
    trup             +1   px
    stin             -1,5 px

Trup se od sve skutecne polohy vzdali nejvys o JEDINY pixel - podle
spritu trupu hrac miri a uhyba, takze je to zamer. Rozpeti mezi rotorem
a stinem je pritom 5,5 px.

Posun stinu na opacnou stranu je vedoma STYLIZACE: fyzikalne by se stin
kazde casti posunul stejne jako ta cast. Ciste fyzikalni varianta ale
dava jen rozdil rotor - trup (3 px) a ten se utopi ve vlastni animaci
rotoru, jak uz bylo zmereno minule.

Naklon dopredu a dozadu je tyz kod v ose y.

2) "Objekty lezici nebo vznikajici na zemi jsou ostre jako puvodne" -
rozostril se teren a objekty na nem zustaly ostre. Kamera je zaostrena
na rovinu, ve ktere leti hrac (z = 32), takze mekkost je 1 - |z| / 32.
Primy odecet po BOB zaznamech:

    tank-hull, trilo        z= 0   mekkost 1,00
    tank-turret             z= 1   mekkost 0,97
    player, mama, air-fod   z=32   mekkost 0,00
    stiny                          mekkost 0,00 (maji vlastni podle vysky)

Cena pri sedmi pozemnich objektech na scene: 10,37 -> 10,42 ms na snimek
v headless Chromiu, tedy pul procenta.

Prah v kontraktu prepocitan na zmerene hodnoty: faze bez rotoru hnou
96 body, s rotorem 120 az 155, prah je 80. Od nuly (blikani mezi
naklonenym a rovnym telem) to bezpecne oddeli.

events.title: Naklon vrtulniku: natoceni tela, protoze rotor sam nebyl videt
events.message:
Naklon vrtulniku: natoceni tela, protoze rotor sam nebyl videt

Hrac nahlasil, ze naklon nevidi. Zmereno pri zvetseni 4x, kolik bodu
displeje se zmeni:

  naklon rotoru (plny vychyl)            2 544
  vlastni zmena faze rotoru mezi tiky    7 904 az 9 536
  zmizeni rotoru (faze bez nej)          5 152

Efekt se utopil ve vlastni animaci: rotor se kazdy tik promeni tri az
ctyrikrat vic, nez cim ho naklon posune, a pulku tiku se nekresli vubec.
Stabilni plocha, na ktere je zmena videt, je TELO - to se mezi tiky
nemeni.

Telo se proto jeste natoci v rovine obrazovky o 8 stupnu. Roll ani pitch
to byt nemuzou (0,26 a 0,5 px, pod rozlisenim spritu); viditelne je az
otoceni, kde spicka ujede 16 * sin(uhel) = 2,2 px. Je to vylozene
stylizace, ne fyzika. Po pridani se naklon hne 8 633 body misto 2 544.

PREVZORKOVANI POTREBA NENI - merenim vyvraceno. Rotace spritu 1:1
a rotace jeho ctyrnasobne zvetseniny nejblizsim sousedem daji pixel po
pixelu TOTEZ: 0 rozdilnych bodu ze 147 456 pri 0, 3, 8 i 15 stupnich.
Platno vzorkuje az v rozliseni displeje, takze zvetsovat predem nema co
pridat. Zmenu prinese teprve chytry zvetsovac nebo vyhlazovani (8 %
plochy) - to by ale dalo vrtulnik z jine hry nez zbytek obrazu.

Pri praci se naslo, ze `heliTiltParts` vracelo null ve ctyrech fazich
z osmi (ty bez rotoru), takze se telo pulku tiku kreslilo rovne a stroj
by pri letu do strany blikal. Kontrakt ted meri vsech osm fazi; overeno
negativni kontrolou, ktera spadne na [0, 370, 0, 345, 0, 268, 0, 284].

Plynulost pohybu: neni co zlepsit. Zmereno na kroku nakreslene polohy
mezi snimky - na 60 Hz je od dvojnasobneho zvetseni rozptyl 0 px
(rovnomernych 2,5 px), na 120 a 144 Hz zbyva 0,17 az 0,5 px a je to
principialni: kvantum 1/S px je presne jeden bod displeje. Netrhane
nepusobi poloha, ale to, ze stroj nema zrychleni - `+356` se nastavi na
768 naraz (0x9476), coz je chovani originalu.

Vsech sedm kontraktu OK.

events.title: Vylepseno: naklon vrtulniku rozkladem na telo a rotor
events.message:
Vylepseno: naklon vrtulniku rozkladem na telo a rotor

Hrac se ptal, jestli by slo sprite prevzorkovat a tim umoznit animaci
naklonu. Slo by, ale na tenhle efekt to potreba neni: `JEEPHELI.LIN` uz
telo a rotor obsahuje zvlast.

Nejdriv oprava vlastniho cisla z minule uvahy - pletly se tri ruzne
naklony. Na spritu 17x32 pri 10 stupnich:

  roll (naklon do strany)         17 * (1-cos 10) = 0,26 px
  pitch (nos dolu)                32 * (1-cos 10) = 0,50 px
  otoceni v rovine obrazovky      16 * sin 10     = 2,80 px

Prvni dva jsou pod rozlisenim spritu, treti ne - takze "neviditelne"
platilo jen pro dva z nich.

Zmereno v datech: `#0` je cele telo (306 pixelu, sedm barev), `#5`..`#8`
samotne listy rotoru - cely snimek ma jediny index 7, protoze se kresli
sekundarni cestou 0x0B0A, ktera barvu zdroje ignoruje a zapisuje barvu 0.
Slozeni "telo + rotor s pevnym posunem" da puvodni snimek:

  #1 = #0 + #5 (+1,+1)   1 chybny pixel ze 448
  #2 = #0 + #6 (+1,+1)   0 ze 429
  #3 = #0 + #7 ( 0, 0)   0 ze 406
  #4 = #0 + #8 (+2,+2)   0 ze 403

Na hotovem obraze je rozklad pri nulovem naklonu bez ztraty: 0 zmenenych
pixelu v sedmi fazich animace z osmi, ve fazi 1 dva (telo a jeho stin).

Naklani se JEN rotorovy disk. Je to jednobarevna plocha, takze na nem
neni zadna kresba, kterou by preskalovani poskodilo, a telo zustava
pixel po pixelu nedotcene. Disk lezi nad podelnou osou, takze se hub
vychyli o HUB * sin(uhel) = 1,1 px a disk zkrati na cos(uhel) = 0,8 px
na 32 px sirky. Uhel 13 stupnu; pri 22 uz to vypada, ze se rotor
odpojil.

Uhel se bere z vlastniho pohybu hrace po obrazovce, ne z posuvu mapy
(jinak by stroj trvale visel nosem dopredu), a nabira se s konstantou
ctyri tiky. Krokuje se po TICICH, ne po snimcich, aby nezavisel na
frekvenci monitoru - zmereno pri drzene klavese 0 -> 0,25 -> 0,44 ->
... -> 0,98 za ctrnact tiku, po pusteni zpet pod 0,02.

Je to ciste zobrazovaci stav na `state`, ne na `g`: do simulace ani do
`netStateHash` se nedostane, lockstep i sitovy kontrakt zustavaji
nedotcene.

Kontrakt v uitest.py meri obe strany - pri nulovem naklonu nejvyse 2
zmenene pixely, pri plnem aspon 100. Overeno negativni kontrolou: po
vynulovani posunu v HELI_ROTOR_PART spadne na [0, 73, 0, 70, 0, 0, 0,
83], tedy presne na trech fazich, ktere posun potrebuji.

Vsech sedm kontraktu OK.

events.title: make the dock "Move to" menu work on tabs, and let drags cross the video
events.message:
make the dock "Move to" menu work on tabs, and let drags cross the video

Two reported problems with rearranging panels:

1. The right-click "Move to" menu only appeared in a stray spot. It keyed off a
   "within 30px of the dock's top" heuristic, which is wrong for tabbed docks:
   those have no title bar, and their tab belongs to a QMainWindowTabBar in the
   dock *area*, not to the dock, so walking up from the tab never found a dock.
   The filter now resolves the target two ways: a tab is matched to its dock by
   title (a tab bar with no matching dock title is a content tab widget and is
   ignored), and a painted title bar is recognised as a press inside a dock but
   outside its content (the default title bar is drawn by the dock, so there is
   no title-bar child widget to find). Right-click on any tab or title bar now
   offers "Move to left / right / bottom / Float".

2. Native drag-and-drop did not work. The Qt mechanism itself is fine (verified
   by driving a title-bar drag through QApplication::notify), but the embedded
   emulator's SDL window is a foreign, reparented window that consumes the
   pointer events over it, so a drag crossing the video stops tracking. While a
   title-bar/tab press is held, the video's child window is now given an empty
   input region via the X Shape extension, letting drag events fall through to
   Qt; the region is restored on release so the emulator accepts input again.

Tests: right-click on a tab moves that dock; right-click on a painted title bar
moves that dock; a title-bar left-press is not consumed by the filter (so drag
can start). A full synthetic drag is not testable offscreen — a cross-area
drag's transient floating window crashes the offscreen platform's backing-store
teardown regardless of this change — so the X11 shape mechanics are verified
with a direct Xlib probe and drag-over-video needs a real-display check.

events.title: Validate the packaged identity, and fix the docs link and XML escaping
events.message:
Validate the packaged identity, and fix the docs link and XML escaping

The docs build was failing on the Store listing link:

  guide/getting-started.md:86 Link for
  "https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9MW1L1PVNXSG" did not resolve.
  (410, Gone)

An unpublished listing answers 410, so the link comes out until the app is
live, and the release checklist now says to put it back at first
publication.

From the review:

- The CI step claimed to check the package identity but only printed it, so
  a wrong-but-well-formed Name or Publisher would have packed cleanly and
  been refused at upload instead. It now compares Name, Publisher and
  PublisherDisplayName against identity.psd1 and the version against the
  bundle's own file name, case-sensitively, as Partner Center does.
- Identity values are escaped into the manifest. They are free text from
  Partner Center, and a publisher display name containing an ampersand
  would otherwise produce a manifest that is not well-formed.
- The command-line tools table overstated the limitation: a packaged app
  can alias several executables, through an Application entry each. The
  reason this package does not is that hiding those entries needs a waiver.

add a right-click "Move to" menu to dock title bars

Rearranging panels worked only by finding the drag gesture, which is not
discoverable — and in a tab group it is not obvious how to move a single tab out.
Every dock title bar now offers a right-click "Move to left / right / bottom /
Float" menu, so moving a panel between areas is a menu choice rather than a
hidden gesture. Qt's native drag still works alongside it.

The menu pops up non-modally from an app-level event filter that catches a
right-click in a dock's title-bar strip (walking up from the clicked widget to
its dock, since a right-click inside the content is consumed by the view and
never reaches the dock). Verified by a QTest that synthesizes the title-bar
right-click through QApplication::notify and asserts the chosen area changes.

events.title: Drop the command-line aliases from the Store package
events.message:
Drop the command-line aliases from the Store package

Partner Center refuses the package outright:

  Package acceptance validation error: The package file Copperline-x64.msix
  specifies a headless app. You don't have permission to create a headless
  app. Please update AppListEntry="none" in the AppxManifest file and also
  ensure you have the waiver "HeadlessAppBypass" associated to this app.

An Application may declare one execution alias, so aliasing the companions
needs an Application element each, and hiding those is what the Store calls
a headless app. Listing them visibly instead would put two console tools in
the Start menu, where clicking one flashes a window and exits -- a worse
result than not aliasing them, and a certification risk of its own. The
package now declares the emulator alone; the portable zip stays the way to
get the command-line tooling, which the install docs now say.

events.message:
fix the embedded display positioning: fit to the container's real size

The video sat small and top-left in a large dock instead of centred or filling.
The cause: the aspect-preserved fit was computed against the widget's Qt
geometry, which for a native dock widget can be stale and smaller than the real
on-screen window. Measured against a large dock, Qt reported 426x230 while the
actual X11 window was 728x324, so the fit (and its centring) was computed for a
region the video does not occupy, leaving it small and off to one side.

The fit now queries the container's real size from the X server
(embeddedContainerSize) and centres the aspect-preserved video within that,
falling back to Qt geometry only when X11 is unavailable. The video now fills or
letterboxes correctly regardless of how large the dock is.

events.title: Package Copperline for the Microsoft Store
events.message:
Package Copperline for the Microsoft Store

Adds an MSIX bundle alongside the portable zip: one submission that serves
both x64 and ARM64 machines, signed by the Store rather than by a
certificate of our own.

The package payload is the zip payload. stage-payload.ps1 now holds the one
definition of what a Windows release contains, and build-zip.ps1 and
build-msix.ps1 each wrap the same staged directory, so the bundled AROS,
FMV, A2091, A4091, LIDE and HRTMon ROMs and the WHDLoad archives sit beside
the executable in the package exactly as romsearch.rs expects to find them.
The CI job packs the payloads the release zips were built from, so the bytes
that go through the Store are the bytes the zip boot smoke test booted, then
unbundles the result and checks both architectures, the package identity and
the emulator itself are really inside.

Execution aliases keep the command line usable: a package installs under
WindowsApps, which nobody has on PATH, and copperline-ctl and
copperline-import-uae are only useful from a prompt.

The Store reserves the fourth version component and forbids a leading zero,
so the package version shifts the major up by one and 0.20.0 ships as
1.20.0.0. Three things a packaged install cannot do are documented rather
than worked around: file type associations wait on a positional path being
dispatched by file type instead of being read as a Kickstart ROM, raw
floppy and hard-disk device access needs an elevation a packaged app cannot
perform, and portable mode needs a writable install directory.

events.title: debug surface: register/memory editing, memory panes, PC history, pause hint
events.message:
debug surface: register/memory editing, memory panes, PC history, pause hint

Four additions to the debug surface, plus a regression fix found while building them.

REGISTER EDITING: D/A/PC/SR cells are editable when stopped; a commit sends
`r <reg>=<value>` (Hatari's mandatory `=` form, silent on success) and refreshes.
USP/ISP stay read-only — Hatari cannot set them by name (its own todo notes SP/SSP
register names are unimplemented). Also exposed as the `setreg` remote command.

MEMORY EDITING: byte cells are editable when stopped (type-to-edit; a double-click
still follows address values, and edits non-address ones). A commit sends
`w b <addr> <value>` and refreshes. Also the `setmem` remote command.

MULTIPLE MEMORY PANES: a "+" button on the memory pane opens another, each in its
own tabbed dock with its own dump-routing tag, so two regions can be watched at
once without dumps bleeding between panes. The tag travels with each queued dump
command, and responses route back to the pane that asked. Pinned by
tst_gui::memoryPanesAreIndependent.

PC HISTORY: a new view showing the recent execution path from Hatari's `history`
command (enabled in the bootstrap with `history cpu`), refreshed on each stop —
"how did I get here" as a list of recent PCs and their instructions.

REGRESSION FIX (found while building this): a plain step produced no refresh at
all — moving the refresh into onDebuggerStopped only fired on running->stopped
*transitions*, and a step-from-stopped is not a transition, so nothing updated
(registers, disassembly, editor). step()/stepOver() now refresh explicitly.

STEP-BACK: attempted via statesave/stateload and removed. Verified against 2.6.1
that stateload restores by resetting the machine into a *running* state and
completing the restore on the next CPU instruction — after it, the machine runs
forward and never returns to a debugger prompt, which is incompatible with this
debugger's prompt-framed transport. Documented in FUTURE.md rather than shipped
broken; real step-back needs an upstream non-destructive restore or record/replay.

Also: a `cmd` remote command to run an arbitrary debugger command, for agents.
Full suite green (8 suites).

events.message:
aga: -DFRUA_PALTEST — a one-photo colour-path test for a real machine

Paints all 256 palette entries as a 32x8 grid (row = AGA bank) with ramps
whose low nibbles matter, through the game's own copper list, and holds
it 12 s after the display comes up. A photo then separates "the art's
colours" from "the machine's colour path": groups of identical swatches =
LOCT low nibbles ignored, a dead row = a bank's writes lost, a wrong hue =
a channel wired wrong. Built for the A1200 + IceDrake report that a
module's bright yellow came out pale where amiberry shows it right.
Verified in amiberry: every row a smooth ramp.

events.title: panels: Photoshop-style tabs and movable, persistent layouts
events.message:
panels: Photoshop-style tabs and movable, persistent layouts

Every dock is now movable, floatable and closable, docks nest and tab within an
area, and the whole arrangement persists across runs via QSettings
saveState/restoreState. Panels can be dragged between docks, torn off into
floating windows, tabbed onto one another, or closed and re-shown from the View
menu — the management model the user asked for, rather than a fixed set of dock
widgets.

The default arrangement is a sane starting point rather than nine scattered
docks: the debug views (Registers, Disassembly, Stack, Hardware, Breakpoints)
are tabbed into one panel with the Emulator display prominent above it, and
Output/Memory are tabbed at the bottom. The View menu lists every dock for
show/hide and has a Reset layout action that returns to that default.

Two things make it robust rather than decorative: every dock carries a stable
objectName, which is what saveState keys the arrangement on; and the
embedded-display toggle keeps authority over the Emulator dock's visibility even
after a layout is restored, so restoring an old layout can't silently re-show a
display the user has turned off. The persistence round-trip is pinned by
tst_gui::dockLayoutPersistsAcrossRestart — hide a dock in one window, and a
fresh window restores it hidden.

events.title: code review P1–P3 fixes, and an emulator display that resizes properly
events.message:
code review P1–P3 fixes, and an emulator display that resizes properly

Two bodies of work, both verified end to end.

CODE REVIEW (docs/code-review-glm-001.md), the headline being a real break in the
core debug loop, reproduced by a failing test before any fix and passing after:

- P1: breakpoints set before Run never armed, and the editor never followed the
  PC. Three chained causes, all fixed: arm when the live bases actually arrive
  (not on a zero-delay timer that always lost the race to the basepage response);
  hand those bases to the program map via setLiveBases so any line resolves and
  locationFromPc works at all; and refresh on every stop, so the editor follows
  on a breakpoint hit and not only on a step. A fourth surfaced while testing:
  resume() left a queued command in flight, and the next stop's prompt completed
  it with a stale response instead of the stop being detected — resume() now
  discards stale commands. tst_gui::breakpointSetBeforeRunFiresAndEditorFollows
  pins the whole loop: it failed before, passes after.
- P2 (transport): start() resets every per-session framing field via
  resetTransport(); stop() emits stopped/running changes so the UI and remote
  clients learn the session ended; stateUpdated is emitted once per refresh
  batch, not once per parsed response.
- P3: vlink warnings no longer recorded as errors (severity regex captured the
  numeric group); the stack view's return-address heuristic uses the real text
  extent rather than requiring a data section; tst_remotecontrol added to the
  Windows console fix-up; and the nits (duplicate includes, duplicated CMake
  source entries, an unused member, and several small robustness items).
- Watchpoint firing is now verified end to end against a live Hatari — it fires
  on a change and not on a same-value write, with negative controls.

EMULATOR DISPLAY: resizing no longer pushes the video out or leaves ghost
trails. The fit now preserves the video's aspect ratio and centres it with a
black letterbox instead of squashing it into the dock. Two underlying causes are
worth recording: the container's X11 window can hold a stale size that disagrees
with the widget's Qt geometry, so the fit is taken from Qt geometry; and Hatari
does not pump SDL events while stopped in the debugger, so a stopped session
only rescales on the next run — the letterbox keeps that looking intentional
rather than broken. Verified: grow and shrink both re-fit cleanly.

events.title: debug views: watchpoints, a stack view, and hardware registers
events.message:
debug views: watchpoints, a stack view, and hardware registers

Three additions to the debug surface, each the kind of thing an assembly
developer reaches for.

WATCHPOINTS break when a memory value changes. Hatari has no data watchpoints
(upstream's `w` command is compiled out), so a watch is armed as a conditional
breakpoint using self-inequality — `b ($addr).w ! ($addr).w` — which the
debugger's change tracking evaluates as "fire when the value differs". That
caveat is honest and worth knowing: a write of the same value, or a read, does
not fire. Set from Run ▸ Add watchpoint or the `watchpoint` remote command, shown
in the breakpoints panel, and double-clicking one navigates memory to the
address. Verified live: a watch on the 200Hz counter at $4BA fires the moment it
ticks. The exact self-inequality format is pinned by tests, because a drift in
it would silently stop watchpoints working.

STACK VIEW shows the 32-bit values at the stack pointer, refreshed on every stop,
with values inside the program's text segment marked as likely return addresses
— the fastest way to see who called the current routine, since a jsr/bsr pushes
the return address as a long. It needs its own dump channel: the routing travels
with each queued command (EmulatorHost's Pending), so a stack dump and a memory
dump back-to-back reach stackDumpReady and memoryDumpReady respectively instead
of clobbering each other. That routing is pinned by an integration test.

HARDWARE REGISTERS shows the ST's hardware state — shifter/video, MFP, ACIA/IKBD,
sound, blitter, DMA — from Hatari's `info` commands, which is the useful view
because the I/O registers have read side effects or only make sense interpreted.
Refreshed on each stop, with a selectable subject.

Full suite green (8 suites); README documents all three.

events.title: embedded display: fill the dock instead of sitting small in it
events.message:
embedded display: fill the dock instead of sitting small in it

The embedded video used to stay at its native resolution (640x436) in the
top-left of the dock with dead black space around it, which read as broken
rather than letterboxed. Two things made it hard to fix, and both are worth
recording.

First, the video does not render at all while the debugger is stopped — Hatari
renders frames only while the emulation runs, so a stopped session shows a black
panel, which looked like a broken embed until the difference was understood.

Second, and the actual fix: the SDL window now resizes to fill the container, and
Hatari rescales its renderer to fit — exactly what it does for a hand-resized
window (SDL_WINDOWEVENT_SIZE_CHANGED -> Screen_SetTextureScale). The subtlety is
*when* and *from what* to take the container's size. The container is a native
window in a dock, and its Qt size() provably lags the size the dock gives the
underlying X11 window: fitEmbedded saw 320x200 while the X11 window was already
463x290, and resizeEvent never fired on the growth. Fitting from that stale Qt
size is what left the video small. The fit now reads the X server's own
attributes for the container (ground truth), and a short settle timer re-fits
over the first moments after launch while the dock's layout is still settling.

Verified over the control socket: the ST desktop now scales to fill the Emulator
dock at 463x290, tracking the dock, with no dead space.

events.title: Title and briefing UX: transfer to the briefing, live keys, quieter chatter (#20)
events.message:
Title and briefing UX: transfer to the briefing, live keys, quieter chatter (#20)

hexwab's issue #20, four parts, three taken and one declined by KC.

[11f DECISION 20] TRANSFER at the title asks for the briefing. Both keys
TiWait read started the game and skipped the briefing, so the one thing a
confused player does was what denied them the controls, and the only
route to the briefing was to sit out the timeout. FIRE keeps $2907's
behaviour; TRANSFER branches to the timeout's own exit. The timeout is
back to one 16-bit lap - tiPage gone, 5.5 s against 10.9, the order of
the C64's own 256 frames - which is safe to shorten now that nobody has
to wait it out. The dwell is seeded on this path too, which the
timeout's arm never could be: a timeout arrives at a fixed count.
Title overlay 386 -> 384 bytes.
OPEN END, recorded at the decision: nothing on the title SAYS so. Its
thirty-six glyphs are block letters and panels, so a prompt would have
to come from textfont through FontCell.

[11f DECISION 21] The briefing names the keys that are actually bound.
DECISION 7's mechanism for the keys instead of the scores: BmPatchKeys
runs from BmRowScan on every depack of BR_KEY_PAGE. Each key line is two
records now - label at column 8, name at column 22, where the hand-tuned
spacing already put it - so the patch writes a fixed field at a known
offset and the alignment is the record's own. make_briefing.py pads a
keyN-labelled record to KEY_FIELD = 9 and emits BR_KEY0..5, BR_KEY_PAGE
and BR_KEY_FIELD.
WHAT IT COST: the redefine screen is a ZX0 stream that depacks over
BR_RECS, so its name machinery cannot be reached while a page is up and
sits in the arena the key records live in. BmKrAscii, bmKeyChar,
BmKrChar, bmKrNames and the dispatch factored out of BmKrShow as
BmKrNameCtl are resident in briefman.asm now. Bank 5: 194 bytes,
spr_end &BEAA -> &BF6C (342 free -> 148); XKR shrank 1,014 -> 591 raw
and 774 -> 462 packed, paying back most of the 423 that moved.

events.title: embedded display, remote control, and a memory view you can follow
events.message:
embedded display, remote control, and a memory view you can follow

Three features, one theme: making the IDE observable and controllable instead of
a black box you poke with a mouse.

MEMORY VIEW — follow pointers, and stay fresh.
A memory pane that goes stale the moment you step is broken, and one where you
can see a pointer but not follow it is frustrating. Double-click a byte cell and,
if the 32-bit big-endian value there looks like an address (non-zero, even, and
within the ST's 24-bit bus), the view jumps to it. And the pane now re-reads on
every state change, not just when you navigate. Double-click rather than single:
a single click has to stay free to select a cell.

EMBEDDED DISPLAY — the emulator can live in a panel now.
On Linux, View ▸ Embed emulator display runs Hatari's video inside the IDE
rather than in a separate window, via X11 reparenting: Hatari attaches its SDL
window into a container PiST names with PARENT_WIN_ID. This surfaced three
things that only show up when you actually run it:

  - PiST has to be an X11 client to have a window ID to hand out, so on Wayland
    it now runs under XWayland (the plan always said to).
  - Hatari creates the reparented window SDL_WINDOW_HIDDEN and never maps it, so
    the panel stayed black until PiST mapped the child itself (src/ui/EmbedX11).
  - The video-size report arrives with NO trailing newline — control.c's own
    comment claims one and its sprintf writes none — so parsing that waited for
    a line terminator never fired, and the panel never learned its size.

Separate-window mode is the default and the only mode where reparenting cannot
work (Wayland without XWayland, and for now macOS and Windows).

REMOTE CONTROL — hooks for scripts and AI agents.
The IDE now exposes the same kind of control socket the emulator does, because
driving a GUI by faking keyboard input is brittle and reading the screen is
worse. --control-port (or PIST_CONTROL_PORT) opens a localhost-only,
off-by-default line protocol: open / build / run / stop / step / stepover /
continue / breakpoint / screenshot / console / state / help / quit. Build and
run answer only once the work is genuinely done, so a script never has to poll.
The screenshot goes through XGetImage because QScreen::grabWindow returns black
under XWayland — and it captures the embedded display too.

Verified end to end over the socket itself: run, screenshot, and console all
driven without touching the keyboard, showing the ST screen embedded in the
panel. The new tst_remotecontrol suite pins the framing and the synchronous
responses; it pumps a real event loop because QTcpSocket::waitForReadyRead only
watches the client socket's notifier, which would leave a same-process server
unanswered. Full suite green (8 suites). README documents the protocol.

events.title: ci: fix the AppImage verification, not the build
events.message:
ci: fix the AppImage verification, not the build

Two more failures from the release workflow, both in the check I wrote rather
than the artifact — the AppImage itself was correct, which is the frustrating
kind of bug because the workflow said the build was broken.

1. The bundled-ROM assertion matched a leading version number
   (`^ 1.02\t/tmp/.mount_...`), but EmuTOS does not render as one: it prints
   `EmuTOS (TOS 2.06)\t/tmp/.mount_.../usr/share/emutos/etos1024k.img`. So a
   genuinely-correct AppImage, with its ROM found from its own mount, failed the
   gate. Matched by path instead, and the autostart check now looks at the EmuTOS
   line specifically so a system 1.02 ROM (which always carries that warning)
   cannot cause a false failure.

2. The copy of the bundled Hatari into the AppDir was gated on the matrix flag,
   but the linuxdeploy `-e` that makes it follow Hatari's libraries was not — a
   leftover from an earlier rewrite that reintroduced the inconsistency it was
   meant to remove. One flag now drives both, via an argument array, so a
   no-emulator build is just a smaller AppImage rather than a confusing failure.

Both verified against the real diagnose output shape and with `bash -n`. The
lesson taken: three of the four CI failures in this work were in the verification
logic, not the product, so this pass re-read the whole step as the runner
executes it rather than patching the reported line.

correct banner and then exits 1, because it reports the version and goes on to

emulator whose libraries are missing dies in the dynamic linker and prints no

directions verified — real output passes, a simulated missing-library error fails.

is also the only way this was going to surface: the same command appears to work
when its exit status is read through a pipe, where `$?` reports the pipe's last
command rather than Hatari's.

events.title: bundle the emulator, and fix the ROM our archives already shipped
events.message:
bundle the emulator, and fix the ROM our archives already shipped

The Linux AppImage now carries Hatari 2.6.1 alongside the assembler and the ROM,
so a fresh download runs and debugs with nothing else installed. Two things made
that necessary and one thing nearly made it useless.

WHY BUNDLE. No distribution package is a usable version: Ubuntu 22.04 ships
2.3.1 and 24.04 ships 2.4.1, while the project is developed and verified against
2.6.1. 2.4.1 returns truncated debugger responses that break source-line
debugging, so the previous advice — "install it with your package manager" — was
recommending a configuration that does not work. Hatari is GPL-2.0-or-later and
is redistributed unmodified from a checksum-pinned upstream tarball; it is never
patched and never committed to this repository, exactly as vasm is handled.
NOTICE gains the redistribution basis, the source pointer, and an entry for the
GNU Readline that the bundled build links — readline matters because with it
Hatari prints its debugger prompt to stdout and without it to stderr, and PiST
speaks the former.

THE BUG. Every release archive already carried an EmuTOS ROM in share/emutos and
nothing looked there: the string did not appear in tosSearchPaths() at all. So on
any machine without the hatari package the bundled ROM was invisible and Run and
debug were dead on first launch — the exact thing bundling it was meant to
prevent. It survived release checking because the verification step sets
PIST_TOS_DIR, which short-circuits the discovery logic a user depends on; a check
that configures its way past the code under test cannot fail.

Discovery now walks up from the executable looking for share/emutos and
share/hatari, covering all three archive layouts (bin/, usr/bin/ inside an
AppImage, Contents/MacOS inside a macOS bundle), and deliberately precedes the
system locations without overriding an explicit choice. The walk is exposed as
paths::bundledDataSearchPaths() so it can be tested at all, since tosSearchPaths()
always starts from the running executable. Verified by reverting the fix: the new
test fails with "share/emutos beside the executable was not searched", and passes
when restored.

Two packaging faults found by testing the built AppImage in a clean container
rather than on the machine that built it:

  - naming only `pist` with -e meant linuxdeploy never followed Hatari's
    libraries, so the bundled emulator arrived without SDL2, readline or libpng
    and could not start. Both executables are now named.
  - the reverse mistake was nearly committed: forcing in every library ldd
    reported as missing copies glibc-coupled libraries from the build host, and a
    libtinfo taken from a development machine demanded GLIBC_2.42 on a 2.39
    system. The excluded X11/Wayland/ALSA set is linuxdeploy's deliberate
    decision, correct because every desktop has them, and it is left alone.

The release verification now runs the bundled emulator and asserts the
non-universal libraries are present, and checks the AppImage's ROM discovery with
PIST_TOS_DIR pointedly unset.

Verified: the shipped Hatari binary and its shipped libraries pass all 12
emulator debug-session tests (breakpoints, stepping, registers, memory); the full
suite is green; and inside the built AppImage, `pist --diagnose` resolves the
bundled assembler, emulator and ROM from the mount with no environment help.

The emulator build itself moves into a composite action shared by CI and release,
because three separate bugs had already been fixed in the one inline copy and a
second copy would have drifted the same way.

events.title: ci: test against the Hatari we support, not the distribution's
events.message:
ci: test against the Hatari we support, not the distribution's

The emulator suite failed in CI on four tests, and the captured dialogue gave the
answer immediately:

    INFO : Hatari v2.4.1, compiled on: Apr 1 2024, 05:56:46

Ubuntu 24.04 packages 2.4.1. Everything in this project was designed and verified
against 2.6.1. Register dumps come back from 2.4.1 as a single line with `SR=`
missing, so registers never become valid and every test that reads them fails —
none of which reproduces on 2.6.1, with the same ROM, locally.

CI now builds 2.6.1 from a checksum-pinned source tarball. Testing a version no
user will have is worse than not testing: the failures are noise that hides real
ones, and the passes mean nothing. Ubuntu 22.04 ships 2.3.1 and 24.04 ships 2.4.1,
so no distribution package is usable — the same conclusion the release packaging
reached for vasm, and an argument for bundling Hatari rather than trusting the
user's copy.

`libreadline-dev` is now installed as part of the test environment because it
determines the transport: with readline the debugger prompt goes to stdout, without
it the fallback prints to stderr. Those are different code paths in our host, so
leaving it to chance would have meant testing one and shipping the other.
