events.title: Take block structure from m68k-parser
events.message:
Take block structure from m68k-parser

scanBlocks walked the directives itself, keeping three parallel stacks and
its own copies of the opener, alternative and terminator lists. m68k-parser
1.6.0 derives the nesting, so this becomes a reshaping of that tree into the
flat views the analyses want: a flow region per line, terminated REPT bodies,
and conditionals with their arms.

isBlockBoundary now asks blockRole rather than matching against local lists,
which is what kept those lists here in the first place. The BlockStructure
and ConditionalBlock shapes are unchanged, so cfg, symbols, project-symbols
and context are untouched.

118 lines to 95, with the parts that were easy to get subtly wrong - pairing
terminators through nesting, and which blocks count as terminated - now
shared with the other consumers rather than reimplemented.

One behavioural difference in malformed input: the old scan tracked macros,
repeats and conditionals independently, so any ENDM closed a macro even with
a REPT still open inside it. The parser matches each terminator to a block it
can actually close, leaving the inner one unterminated. Both are defensible;
the new one is consistent with what the other consumers now see.

Verified beyond the 608 tests by diffing CLI output over 20 real sources
before and after, holding the parser version constant: byte for byte
identical.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.7.0 for blockRole, which is not published yet.

events.title: Let the keyboard pane float free of the layout
events.message:
Let the keyboard pane float free of the layout

The keyboard sits under the screen in the main column, which is a poor place
for something far wider than it is tall — and its scale is set by the width it
is given, so where it sits decides how big it is. Drag its title bar and it
tears out where it stands and follows the pointer; the title bar also carries a
toggle to send it back. A floating pane resizes from its bottom-right corner,
horizontally: the height is a consequence of the width, so there is no second
axis to drag.

Position and width persist per pane, and a pane whose stored position falls
outside a window that has since shrunk is pulled back into view on mount and on
resize. Floating is a per-pane opt-in — only the keyboards ask for it, and
sidebar panes keep the HTML5 drag-and-drop reordering they had.

events.title: Keyboards were DPR times too big on a high-DPI screen
events.message:
Keyboards were DPR times too big on a high-DPI screen

The display-scale setting counts physical pixels — one emulator pixel maps to
exactly that many, which is what keeps the picture pixel-perfect — so both
renderers divide by the DPR when they size the canvas's CSS box. The variable
the on-screen keyboards size themselves from carried the raw setting instead,
and CSS is what lays them out. The two only agree at 1x: on a Retina Mac the
canvas halved and the keyboards did not, so every cap and legend came out twice
the size relative to the screen, and the scene's own width clamp then pinned
the keyboard to the pane. Windows at 125% had the same fault at a quarter the
size, small enough to pass for right.

--display-scale now carries scale / dpr. The DPR signal moves out of Screen.tsx
into state, since two places need it and it has to re-run the CSS variable when
the window moves between displays; Screen.tsx reads the same signal it always
did. A test pins the invariant the regression broke: the CSS scale handed to
the keyboards is the one the canvas measures itself in.

events.title: Report vasm diagnostics for include files
events.message:
Report vasm diagnostics for include files

An include is excluded from assembly by default, because assembling one on
its own reports errors that exist only out of context: it depends on whatever
pulls it in. The effect was that `.i` files got no vasm diagnostics at all.

vasm names the file each message belongs to, and the include trace that
reached it, so one run describes the same error from the point of view of
every file in the chain. That was being discarded: the filename was captured
by the pattern and never read, and every message was re-pointed to the
outermost file, which is right only when that is the file being reported on.

parseVasmOutput now parses messages into their location and trace, and places
each one against a given file: at its own line when that file has the
problem, at the include statement when the file is further up the chain, and
not at all when the message belongs elsewhere. Without a target it uses the
outermost position, which is what it always did.

Saving an include therefore assembles a program that includes it and reports
what belongs to it. Saving a program is unchanged: an error in one of its
includes still appears on the include statement, with the path to the problem
in the message.

Only one program is assembled, the first that includes the file, so saving a
widely shared header does not assemble every part of a demo. Which one is
arbitrary where several qualify, and a file no program includes is still not
assembled.

events.title: Discover entry points, and offer the nearest definition first
events.message:
Discover entry points, and offer the nearest definition first

getEntryPoints reads the include graph for files that are assembled rather
than included: roots that pull in at least one other file. The second
condition matters, since a workspace holds plenty of files nothing includes -
vendored headers, unused data - and those are orphans rather than programs.
getEntryPointsFor names the programs a given file belongs to, which for a
shared header is all of them.

There is no formal marker for an entry point in assembly, so this is a
reading of the include graph rather than a fact about the project. Measured
against local projects it lines up: chonk and desire-sitm give two each,
plasma three, and tte-vaporous one per demo part.

Definitions are now returned nearest first, by steps through the include
graph, rather than in whatever order files happened to be indexed. Where a
name is defined more than once in a unit the closest one is the one a reader
most likely means, and the order was previously arbitrary.

Per-unit vasm diagnostics is the obvious next use and is not done here. vasm
does name the file each message belongs to, but the output is currently
attributed wholesale to the file that was assembled, with an included file's
errors deliberately re-pointed to the include statement. Assembling an entry
point on behalf of an include would mean publishing diagnostics to files
other than the one saved, and clearing them again, which is a larger change
than it looks.

events.title: Index the workspace on startup
events.message:
Index the workspace on startup

Symbol resolution was only as complete as the set of files that happened to
be loaded, which was whatever had been opened plus what those included. Find
references and rename therefore missed uses in files the editor had not been
shown, and results changed as tabs were opened.

The workspace is now indexed in the background once the connection is up.
Indexing keeps symbols and include edges and discards syntax trees, which is
what makes covering a whole workspace affordable: 923 files in 838ms, against
the couple of hundred megabytes retaining their parses would have cost.

Build output and dependency directories are skipped. A build directory
usually holds a copy of every source, which would otherwise show up as a
second definition of every symbol; in one local project that is 25 of 89
files. `m68k.exclude` adds further patterns.

Indexing runs after initialize rather than during it, so the first request is
not held up. Requests arriving while it is still going see what has been
indexed so far, which is no worse than the lazily populated store they saw
before.

Scoping is unaffected: with both entry points of a two-part workspace now
indexed, which is exactly the condition that used to leak, a label private to
one still resolves and renames only within its own unit, while a symbol in a
shared include is found in every part - including parts that were never
opened, which is the point.

events.title: Separate indexed files from open ones in the store
events.message:
Separate indexed files from open ones in the store

Groundwork for indexing the whole workspace. Resolution needs every file's
symbols and include edges, but only the file a request names needs its syntax
tree, and keeping trees for everything is what makes a full index too
expensive: measured over a 970 file project, retaining parse output costs
245MB against 15MB for symbols and includes alone.

IndexedDocument holds what crosses file boundaries. ProcessedDocument extends
it with the document, its parse and its block structure, and is what an open
file gets. The store holds either, and isProcessed distinguishes them.

Every site that needed the tree turned out to be working on the document the
request names, which is open by definition, so each is a guard rather than a
change in behaviour. The exception was hover, which read the declaration line
out of the defining file's text: that file is usually not the open one, so
the line is now captured when the symbol is recorded. This also fixes hover
for a definition in a file that happens not to be loaded.

Nothing indexes the workspace yet; included files are indexed instead of
processed, which is the only behavioural change here.

events.title: Scope symbol lookup to the assembly unit
events.message:
Scope symbol lookup to the assembly unit

getDependencies walked the include graph in both directions at once, so from
any file it reached everything sharing any include. Two entry points that
both include a hardware definitions file were treated as one namespace.

The effect on rename was destructive rather than merely noisy. Renaming a
label in one entry point edited the call sites of the same-named label in an
unrelated one, but not its definition - getDefinitions returned early from
the current document while getReferences walked the whole component - so the
other file was left calling a label that no longer existed.

An assembler splices includes into the file that pulls them in, so the unit
of naming is that tree, not the workspace. getUnitFiles finds the trees a
document belongs to by looking at what includes it, and the rest of each tree
by looking at what those files include. Only the document itself is followed
upwards: climbing up from a file reached on the way down is what crossed from
one tree into another.

Inclusion being textual, the scope has to run downwards as well as up. A
symbol defined in a file can be referenced by a file it includes, which an
existing test covers, so this is not simply the reverse of the old direction.

Also scopes incdir to the files a document can see. Pooling them across the
whole store let an incdir in one part of a workspace change how an unrelated
part resolved its includes.

Behaviour, checked over stdio as well as in tests: a label private to one
entry point no longer leaks into a sibling and rename touches only its own
file, while a symbol in a shared include still finds its uses in every unit
that includes it, and rename updates all of them.

Workspace symbol search is left alone. It is a search across the workspace
rather than a resolution question.

events.title: Memotech MTX keyboard addition
events.message:
Memotech MTX keyboard addition

The MTX500, MTX512 and RS128 share one deck, so there is one face and only the
badge's model name changes with the model. Everything sits on a 1u pitch and
no cap is under it: the typing block staggers 0.5u / 0.25u / 0.5u behind 1.5u
modifiers, the number, Q and A rows finish flush at 15u with BS, LINE FEED and
RET, and the numeric keypad and two-column function block stand off to the
right in their own recessed wells, their four rows on the main block's row
lines. The MEMOTECH rule runs across the top.

Every cap and both its legends come from MTX BASIC's own key tables — one entry
per matrix cell at 0x1729 unshifted and 0x177A shifted — which settles the caps
the host key map never named: LINE FEED is [3,6], the keypad's 8/EOL is [1,7]
and its 9/BRK is [0,8], and ENT/CLS is [7,7]. The two unlabelled caps flanking
the space bar are the one guess: the ROM gives the spare cells on their sense
line no character at all, so they are presented as further space bars.

events.title: Parse float literals
events.message:
Parse float literals

`dc.s`, `dc.d`, `dc.x`, `dc.p` and `fequ` take floating point values in
vasm's mot syntax, but a decimal point ended the number: `dc.s 1.5` came back
as 1 with the fraction dropped, and `fequ 3.14` as 3. A silently wrong value
is worse than a reported error, since nothing downstream can tell.

A dot between two runs of digits now reads as a float, with an exponent if
one follows. Digits are required on both sides, so `1.w` stays a word-sized
absolute address and a leading dot still begins a local label. A bare `1e3`
is left as a decimal followed by a symbol rather than guessed at, and there
is no use of exponent notation anywhere in the corpus to suggest otherwise.

NumberFormat gains "float". Whether a float is meaningful where it appears
is left to the caller: `dc.b 1.5` parses as a float but is not valid data for
a byte, which is a linting question rather than a parsing one.

The corpus has exactly one real occurrence, `COUNT 6.666666666666667`, which
previously fell back to a raw macro argument because the expression stopped
short of the text.

Version left alone: bumping it here is what pushed the last two releases past
1.5.0 and 1.7.0.

events.title: Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat one character left of the text
events.message:
Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat one character left of the text

MOS 2.1 sets the V9938's R18 display adjust to 0x0A, which shifts the whole
picture six source pixels right — a full character cell in the 6-pixel MOS
font. The renderer honours it, as the hardware does; the overlay and the cell
blanking did not, because both positioned themselves against the border origin
alone. So the transcribed text read correctly but sat a character to the left
of the glyphs it was covering.

The V9938 now exposes the adjust it is already applying, and the Einstein's
field box adds it. Blanking takes its x from that same box, so the two cannot
drift apart again.

events.title: Einstein 256 keyboard: sizes, tones and a working ALPHA LOCK lamp
events.message:
Einstein 256 keyboard: sizes, tones and a working ALPHA LOCK lamp

Sizing: ESC and GRAPH become 1u, and each left-hand modifier grows to meet its
own row's first key (CTRL 1.5u, ALPHA LOCK 1.75u, SHIFT 2.25u) instead of
stopping a quarter unit short; BREAK widens to 1.5u to meet the double-bar cap.
The legend card is cut to the span of the eight function caps rather than
overrunning F7, and its eight cells now divide evenly whatever their text — the
long RST:BCOL4 was stretching its own cell. The cursor cluster comes up and in.

Tones: the caps are the machine's beige rather than white, the function strip
with them; the modifiers are darker and nearly flat; and every gradient is
vertical, with the top-left sheens gone. The case now fills the pane instead of
stopping at the scene box. The POWER lamp and label are dropped.

The cursor wedges print outline arrows, and the ALPHA LOCK lamp moves onto its
own cap, so it lights with the latch and travels with the key.

events.title: Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat over the wrong box
events.message:
Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat over the wrong box

The overlay stretches the transcribed grid across the descriptor's active area,
which holds for every machine whose text fills it. The 256's does not: MOS 2.1
runs GRAPHIC 2, so a 42x24 grid of 12x8 buffer cells is 504x192 centred in a
512x212 window. The overlay was starting ten lines high and stretching 212/192
too tall, so it drifted further off the text with every row down the screen.

A transcribe driver can now report the field its grid actually occupies, in
buffer pixels, and the overlay sits over that when given; machines whose text
fills the active area say nothing and are unaffected. The Einstein reports the
same box blankCells paints into, so the two cannot drift apart.

events.title: Overeni dekodovani ADF proti pameti originalu a mereni period 0x553a
events.message:
Overeni dekodovani ADF proti pameti originalu a mereni period 0x553a

Diky bazi A6 jde porovnat, co z ADF rozbalime, s tim, co ma original v chip
RAM. Produkcni cesta unpackC(adf, off+4, size) sedi bajt po bajtu:
BIGEXPL.SND (8486 B) na 0x4cb38 a SMART.SND (8280 B) na 0x4ec60. Vzorek
vybuchu u smrti bosse je tedy spravny. AMTITUNE.MOD se za behu hry nenajde,
protoze titulni hudba se pri nacteni hernich dat zahodi.

Prvni cista nahravka 0x553a z originalu (spustena prepsanim displacementu
volani 0x8aa4 na 0x553a, aby efekt sel nativni cestou vcetne zastaveni DMA)
dava jako nejkratsi skutecne zahrane periody 114, 116, 119, 120, 125, 126.
Teoreticky limit jednoho kanalu je 227/2 = 113,5, takze nas
PAULA_PAL_MIN_DMA_PERIOD = 123 je asi o 130 centu moc vysoko. vAmiga zadny
pevny clamp nema, StateMachine.cpp implementuje skutecny automat.

Prah zatim nemenim: 0x553a posila obe vrstvy pres oba selektory a druha
muze po rejectu propadnout do teze dvojice, takze se v jednom kanale sectou
dva tony (200 a 202) a odhad frekvence z prechodu nulou prestane platit.

events.title: Einstein 256 display was drawn twice as wide as it should be
events.message:
Einstein 256 display was drawn twice as wide as it should be

The V9938 buffer is 512 pixels across the active window because the chip has
genuine 512-pixel modes; the 256-pixel modes — including the GRAPHIC 2 the MOS
boots in — double into it, the same trick the CPC's gate array and the SAM use.
Those machines then set pixelAspectX to 0.5 to present the buffer at its true
width. The Einstein 256 was left at 1, so every 256-mode screen reached the
canvas stretched to twice its width, its 6-pixel MOS glyphs 12 wide.

events.title: Take block structure from the parser
events.message:
Take block structure from the parser

m68k-parser 1.6.0 derives macro, repeat and conditional nesting, so the two
places that worked it out here no longer need to: folding walks the block
tree instead of scanning directives with its own stack, and a macro
definition's extent comes from its block rather than a forward search for
`endm`. The opener and terminator tables go with them, since they belong
next to the parser that reads the directives.

The structure is computed once per document alongside the parse and kept on
ProcessedDocument, rather than per request.

Folding also gets more correct as a side effect. It used to treat any
terminator as closing the innermost open block, so `macro / ifeq / endm`
closed the conditional; the parser matches each terminator to a block it can
actually close, leaves the inner one unterminated, and closes the macro.

New diagnostics come with it: unterminated blocks and terminators that match
nothing were invisible before. Measured over 3,598 local sources, 15,838
blocks produce exactly one report, and it is a real bug - a macro that opens
IFLT and reaches ENDM without an ENDC.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.6.0, which is not published yet, so `npm ci` will
fail until it is.

events.title: Add a block structure layer
events.message:
Add a block structure layer

Lines are parsed independently, which is what keeps the parser usable on
half-written and macro-templated code, but it leaves every caller to recover
nesting for itself. m68k-lsp derives it twice, for folding ranges and for the
extent of a macro definition, and m68k-lint has its own module for it.

parseBlocks walks a ParsedFile once and pairs each opener with its
terminator, returning macro, repeat and conditional blocks with their
children, the arms of each conditional, and the name of each macro. blockAt
and enclosingBlocks look up what contains a line. Indices are positions in
ParsedFile.lines rather than one-based Location.line, which the doc comments
say explicitly, since mixing the two has been a recurring source of
off-by-one bugs.

Kept as a separate entry point rather than a second parse mode. There is one
line parser, so a fix cannot land in one mode and not the other, callers who
do not need nesting pay nothing, and a file that does not balance still
parses - which matters in an editor, where an unterminated block is the
normal state while typing rather than an error.

This also makes a class of real errors detectable that nothing reported
before: unterminated blocks, terminators matching nothing, and crossed
nesting such as `macro / ifeq / endm`, where the inner block is reported and
the outer one still closes.

Checked over 3,598 local m68k sources: 15,838 blocks, and exactly one file
reports an error - a macro that opens IFLT and reaches ENDM without an ENDC,
which is a genuine bug in that source.

events.title: Disassemble Knight Lore from a map someone had already drawn
events.message:
Disassemble Knight Lore from a map someone had already drawn

The other builds discover which bytes are instructions by playing the game and
recording what runs. That approach stalled here: the title screen reads the
keyboard hardware directly rather than through the ROM, and the mapped code
never got past it -- 140 addresses out of 30699 bytes.

It did not need discovering. tcdev disassembled and annotated Knight Lore in
2017 and Michael R. Cook converted that to SkoolKit form in 2019, and the map
is right: assembling their disassembly and diffing $6108-$D8F2 against the
snapshot matches on 30697 of 30699 bytes. The two that differ are the operand
of LD HL,$F100 at $D6B8, where the snapshot is right and SkoolKit's own
skool2bin is wrong -- it clamps an operand pointing past the end of the binary
it is writing.

So the map comes from there, extracted with skool2ctl -w abs: block
boundaries, the code/data split, sub-block lengths and labels, and nothing
else. Neither work carries a licence, so none of their prose is reproduced;
the commentary in knightlore_annotations.ctl and knightlore.ref is written
from the code in this build. Same posture as pobtastic's Atic Atac names --
use the facts, credit the person, write your own words.

Borrowed facts still get checked. 40696 bytes reassemble byte for byte, and
the snapshot the build writes is compared with the snapshot it read: identical
in all 49179 bytes. That second check is not redundant. The round trip only
sees the game block and is blind to the registers, and this snapshot is taken
mid-frame rather than at a cold start, so a machine resumed without its IX, IY
and alternates does not carry on playing. It caught both: the registers were
being dropped, and SP was two out, because the .sna header holds SP after PC
has been pushed while write_sna() wants the value from before.

Two build checks come out of getting this wrong first:

- check_alignment() -- an instruction comment is written "$ADDR,N" where N is
  a byte count, and SkoolKit does not complain when N stops mid-instruction.
  It resumes decoding from wherever the count ran out and carries on. Writing
  $B028,6 over a seven-byte run invented an LD B,$47, and everything above
  $B02F moved. The round trip caught it 9000 lines away, as an sjasmplus error
  about writing past 65536.
- check_coverage() -- the map's blocks must run in order from $6108, because a
  hole becomes zeros in the output rather than an error.

Two things about the game came out of writing the annotations. The object
table is forty records of thirty-two bytes at $5C08, which is LAST-K: Knight
Lore puts its own data straight over the ROM's system variables, because it
never calls the ROM once running and reads the keyboard itself at $B5F7. And
all 103 sprites share one format -- a width, a height, then a mask byte and a
bitmap byte per cell -- proved by arithmetic rather than by eye, since for
every one of them the gap to the next label is exactly
2 + 2 * (width AND $7F) * height.

events.title: Keep macro template names out of the symbol table

Keep macro template names out of the symbol table

m68k-parser 1.5.2 marks a symbol or label whose name embeds a placeholder,
so `.loop\@` and `BLTEN_\1` are recognised as templates resolved per macro
expansion rather than names that exist as written.

Definitions previously did this by looking for a backslash in the name, which
is now the parser's job to report. References did not do it at all, so every
use of an interpolated name was recorded as a reference to a symbol that
could never be defined, and turned up in find-references.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.5.2, which is not published yet, so `npm ci` will
fail until it is.

events.title: Represent macro arguments and interpolated names honestly
events.message:
Represent macro arguments and interpolated names honestly

Three related changes, all additive to the AST.

Macro arguments that are not expressions
----------------------------------------
Arguments are substituted textually, so they need not be valid operands.
`BITDEF MEM,24BITDMA,9` passes `24BITDMA`, which cannot be an identifier
because it starts with a digit; it was silently truncated to the number 24
with the rest dropped.

A new MacroArgumentNode keeps the raw text, used only where the expression
stopped short of the argument's end. Arguments that parse in full keep their
structure, so `MyMacro d0,d1` still gives registers. 36 arguments across the
corpus take this path, including a float literal that was truncating to its
integer part.

Interpolated names
------------------
`BLTEN_\1`, `.loop\@` and `PUSHM_\@` were reported as ordinary symbols and
labels, so the tree claimed a symbol existed where the name is really a
template resolved at expansion. SymbolNode and LabelNode now carry
`interpolated` for these, which is a fact about the name rather than
something each consumer should rediscover by looking for backslashes. 832
symbols and 956 labels in the corpus are marked.

Macro parameter locations inside expressions
--------------------------------------------
A parameter used inside an expression, as in `CopOffs+\1`, had a location one
character short, because the tokenizer strips the leading backslash from the
token value and the length was taken from it. Slicing the source at the node
gave `\` rather than `\1`, which would misplace an editor highlight.

Found because the under-coverage check above misfired on it, sending four
perfectly good expressions down the raw-text path.

events.title: Read a C style comment after an operand as a comment
events.message:
Read a C style comment after an operand as a comment

`ASHIFTSHIFT = 12  /* bits to right align */` was parsed with `12 /* bits`
as the operand and `to right align */` as the comment, because `/` reads as
division and continues the operand across the whitespace. The comment text
was wrong in the tree, which matters wherever it is surfaced - the language
server shows it as documentation on hover.

Motorola syntax ends the operand field at whitespace and treats the rest of
the line as a comment, which is how these comments work in the NDK headers
in the first place. Whitespace followed by `/*` now ends the operand, while
a spaced-out division such as `12 / 4` still parses as an expression, since
requiring the asterisk is what separates the two.

Found by instrumenting the parser to report tokens left over after a
complete expression and running it over 3,598 local m68k sources: this was
130 of the 175 hits.

events.title: Tatung Einstein 256 keyboard addition
events.message:
Tatung Einstein 256 keyboard addition

A second Einstein deck, picked by model the way the CPC picks between its
three. The 256 is a squarer, charcoal machine: the four left-hand modifiers
share a margin and grow rather than stepping (ESC 0.75u, CTRL 1.25u, ALPHA
LOCK 1.5u, SHIFT 2u) while the typing block staggers by the usual
0.5u/0.25u/0.5u and every row finishes flush; the function keys are their own
1.25u strip under the printed BASIC legend card; ENTER is an L across two
rows; and the cursor keys are four wedges on a detached pad out past the deck.
The POWER lamp, the ALPHA LOCK lamp and the cursor well come with it.

The cursor pad needed its wiring settled. MOS 2.1 decodes shifted [1,5] and
[2,5] to the same codes as unshifted, so the TC-01's trick of reaching the
upper legend through SHIFT gives down and right again, not up and left.
Sweeping every cell and modifier against the real ROM found left on [0,1] —
the cell MAME marks unused, and which the TC-01 has no key for — and no single
cell for up at all, so up goes through CONTROL+K, the only route to 0x0B in
either MOS. Host arrow keys follow the same per-model chords.

Caps now press a chord rather than one cell, since neither deck's cursor keys
are one switch apiece, and both faces share one layout, one geometry module and
one controller.

events.title: Fix operand splitting, parenthesised displacements and at-sign symbols
events.message:
Fix operand splitting, parenthesised displacements and at-sign symbols

Found by parsing 3,598 m68k sources (~867k lines) from local projects. Error
count over that corpus drops from 472 to 79, with the remainder all in a
GNU/MIT syntax file and vendored toolchain headers using Aztec-style `/1`
macro parameters.

Angle brackets in operand splitting
-----------------------------------
`<` began a lookahead for a matching `>` that stopped only at whitespace, so
in `dc.w 1,((W+16)>>4)|(24<<6),0,((W+16)>>4)|(24<<6)` it found the `>` in a
later operand and swallowed `<6),0,((W+` as a string literal. The list came
back with two operands instead of four.

An angle-quoted string is a whole argument, as in `MyMacro <a,b>`, so it is
now only recognised where the operand has not started yet. A `<` further in
is a comparison or shift operator.

Parenthesised displacements
---------------------------
`lea (WIDTH+32)/8(a0,d0.w),a2` was rejected: the indexed-addressing test
required the displacement to contain no parens, so it fell through to the
plain displacement branch, whose register group accepts commas and so read
`a0,d0.w` as a register name.

The displacement may now contain parens, and the register group is taken
from the final parenthesised group. Two location bugs went with it - the base
register was positioned from the first `(` in the text rather than the one it
came from, so hover and go-to-definition would have pointed into the
displacement.

Also accepts a macro parameter or alias as the register in `(vposr+1,\1)`,
but only where the first part is a compound expression and so cannot itself
be a register. `(sin,x)` stays base-plus-index, since with two bare names
there is nothing to tell the two forms apart.

At-sign symbols
---------------
vasm's mot syntax defines ISIDSTART as '.', '@', '_' or a letter, so
`@palette` is an ordinary symbol. The tokenizers accepted neither, producing
UNKNOWN_CHARACTER; several operand regexes already allowed `@`, so this was
inconsistent as well as wrong. `@` before an octal digit is still an octal
literal, and a lone `@` is still rejected, matching ISBADID.

Positional comments after a complete operand
--------------------------------------------
A digit following whitespace continued the operand, so the trailing `0` in
`dc.w bplcon1,$08 0` was parsed as expression rather than as the positional
comment Motorola syntax makes it. Digits now use the same completeness check
as letters.

Not changed: the expression parser still drops tokens left over after a
complete expression, so `#5 foo` parses as `5`. Reporting those turned out
to flag `/* ... */` comments in the standard NDK headers, because operand
splitting is deliberately lenient about spaces for vasm's -spaces mode.
Distinguishing the two needs a syntax mode rather than a heuristic.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Accept register aliases as index registers, and keep unknown size qualifiers
events.message:
Accept register aliases as index registers, and keep unknown size qualifiers

Two gaps found while moving m68k-lsp off tree-sitter onto this parser.

Register aliases in the index position
--------------------------------------
`equr` binds a register to a name, so `(sin,x)` is ordinary indexed
addressing once the names resolve. The base position already accepted a
symbol and fell back to one for any valid identifier, but the index position
rejected anything that was not a literal register or macro parameter, even
though its return type declared SymbolNode and the node was built correctly
regardless. The result was a MALFORMED_INDEXED_ADDRESSING error alongside a
perfectly good node.

The index position now mirrors the base position: a valid identifier becomes
a symbol for the caller to resolve, and only something that cannot be a name
at all - `(a0,#5)`, `(a0,123)`, `(a0,$ff)` - is still reported.

Measured over 199 assembly files (~42k lines): 55 false errors removed, all
of them this pattern.

Unknown size qualifiers
-----------------------
A dot not followed by a recognised size produced no qualifier node. For
`move.` the dot was still being typed; for `move.z` the text was consumed and
then dropped, so it was absent from the tree entirely.

Both now yield an `unknown` qualifier spanning the text after the dot, empty
in the first case. This makes the tree faithful to the source, and lets an
editor tell that the cursor is on a size while one is being typed - without
it, completion after `move.` cannot know to offer b/w/l.

QualifierNode accordingly gains UnknownNode, which is additive to the union
but worth noting for any exhaustive switch over it.

Nothing reads the tree-sitter tree any more, so the parser, its grammar and
the plumbing around it all come out:

Also drops the commented-out incremental reparse in TextDocumentSyncProvider
and the changeToEdit helper that only served it. It had been disabled for
being order dependent under neovim, and m68k-parser has no incremental API,
so it had no future.

The .vsix goes from 15 files / 513KB to 13 files / 385KB, and the only wasm
it still carries is vasm itself. createContext no longer loads anything, so
starting the server is just process startup.

Fixes a regression from the hover commit that the unit tests missed and the
end-to-end check caught: hovering a label definition returned nothing. A
label was a `symbol` node under the grammar and is its own node type in
m68k-parser, so it needs routing to the symbol table lookup too. Now tested.

events.title: Move hover and folding onto the m68k-parser AST
events.message:
Move hover and folding onto the m68k-parser AST

Hover swaps descendantForPosition for nodeAtPosition and reads values off
the nodes instead of their source text: SizeNode.size, SymbolNode.name,
NumericLiteralNode.raw, SpecialRegisterNode.register. Include paths come from
StringLiteralNode.content, which is already unquoted, so hover no longer
needs processPath. An unrecognised mnemonic parses as a macro call, and some
of those are directives the parser does not know but the docs do, so a doc
lookup is still attempted rather than labelling them macros.

Folding is the one piece that needed rebuilding rather than translating. The
grammar exposed block bodies as nested element_list nodes; a line-oriented
tree has to track the nesting, so blocks are found by scanning directives
with a stack. else/elseif close the section above and open the next, empty
bodies produce nothing, and a closer only pops when it matches the innermost
open block, so the guard conditionals that wrap includes cannot swallow the
rest of a file.

Label folding was already running off the symbol table and is untouched.

The old suite only covered `ifeq`, so this adds tests for macro bodies,
conditional branches, nesting and unbalanced blocks.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Build the symbol table from the m68k-parser AST
events.message:
Build the symbol table from the m68k-parser AST

processSymbols was the largest tree-sitter consumer, and feeds definitions,
references, rename, folding and workspace symbols. The Symbols structure is
unchanged, so every consumer of it is untouched and the existing tests carry
the contract.

Where the grammar distinguished definitions by node type, the directive now
does: equ/fequ/= give a constant, set a variable, rs an offset, equr/fequr a
register, equrl/fequrl/reg/freg a register list, macro a macro. section and
xref/nref name their symbol in an operand rather than a label, so those are
read from operands. Lists mirror the tree-sitter grammar rather than being
guessed.

Two things the old query got for free needed rebuilding:

- A definition's range covered its whole grammar node, which for a macro runs
  to `endm`. Line-oriented parsing means scanning forward for the matching
  directive.
- Documentation comments came from sibling walking. Same-line comment first,
  else the run of comment-only lines above, now read off the line array.

Reference collection also gets more precise: the old query captured every
symbol node and worked out which were definitions from their parent, so
register names in `equr` operands and section names were swept up as
references to symbols that do not exist. Those directives are now excluded.

Verified end to end over stdio as well as by unit tests: cross-file
definition lookup through an include, local labels nested under their parent,
reference search, and doc comments on hover.

events.title: Move the formatters onto the m68k-parser AST
events.message:
Move the formatters onto the m68k-parser AST

Replaces the last four tree-sitter queries outside symbols and folding.
Formatters now take a FormatContext holding the parsed file and the source
text, so the three that only ever wanted `tree.rootNode.text` (align, trim,
end-of-line) no longer need a syntax tree at all, and DocumentFormatter no
longer needs a Language to construct.

Two formatters get simpler because the AST carries what they were deriving:
LabelColonFormatter reads LabelNode.scope instead of matching the name
against a local-label pattern, and CaseFormatter reads
NumericLiteralNode.format instead of a hexadecimal_literal query.

Two places needed care, both now covered by tests:

- m68k-parser classifies assembly-flow directives (ifeq/endc, rept/endr,
  macro/endm) as plain directives, but the formatter exposes a separate
  `case.control` option. syntax.ts gains a control mnemonic set mirroring
  `control_mnemonic` in the tree-sitter grammar.

- `section name,bss` yields a section-type node but `section bss` does not,
  since with one operand the parser cannot tell a type from a section name.
  CaseFormatter recognises the single-operand form against the known section
  types so `case.sectionType` keeps working.

Fixes a bug this surfaced: an external label written `foo::` was having both
colons stripped under labelColon "off". The old label query never matched
those at all, the grammar giving them their own node type. They are now
skipped on LabelNode.scope, since the colons carry meaning there rather than
being a style choice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Generate diagnostics from the m68k-parser AST
events.message:
Generate diagnostics from the m68k-parser AST

Replaces the two tree-sitter queries in DiagnosticProcessor. Syntax errors
came from `(ERROR)` nodes and were all reported as the bare string "Parser
error"; they now carry m68k-parser's typed code, its hint where there is one,
and a location that points at the offending text rather than a whole
subtree. The unsupported-processor check moves from an
`(instruction_mnemonic)` query to walking parsed lines.

Checked against 199 real assembly files (~42k lines) from local projects
before wiring it up. 198 parse clean. The exception is a GNU/MIT syntax file
(`sp@(4)`, `movew`, C comments), a dialect this extension does not target and
vasm would reject too.

That sweep did turn up one false-positive class worth 55 errors in a single
file: m68k-parser reports MALFORMED_INDEXED_ADDRESSING for `(sin,x)` where
both names are `equr` register aliases. It builds the correct node and
accepts a symbol as the base, so this looks like an upstream bug -
indexRegister is already typed to allow a SymbolNode. Suppressed here for an
index shaped like a name, which leaves `(a0,#5)` and `(a0,$ff)` reported.

Note the processor check inherits an existing limitation: instruction docs
record support per mnemonic rather than per size, so `muls.l` on a 68000 is
not flagged. Unchanged by this commit, but it caught out a test.

events.title: Replace the line-parsing regex with m68k-parser
events.message:
Replace the line-parsing regex with m68k-parser

src/parse.ts was built around a single ~800-character regex carrying twenty
lines of ASCII-art documentation. It now delegates to m68k-parser and just
flattens the AST into the position-oriented view its consumers want, so the
interface is unchanged and the existing 47 parse tests validate the swap
directly. 46 of them passed on the swap alone.

The one behavioural gap: m68k-parser emits a qualifier node only for a size
it recognises, so a half-typed "move." or an invalid "move.z" produces none.
Completion reads the size component to know it should offer b/w/l, and
without it would have fallen through to offering operands instead. parseLine
synthesises the component from the text after the dot to preserve that.

parseSignature moves to src/signature.ts. It parses the documented syntax of
a mnemonic (`move.[bwl] <ea>,<ea>`) rather than assembly source, so it has no
business going through an assembly parser and stays hand-rolled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Add m68k-parser AST layer alongside the tree-sitter tree
events.message:
Add m68k-parser AST layer alongside the tree-sitter tree

Groundwork for moving the server onto m68k-parser. Nothing reads the new
tree yet; consumers migrate one at a time in following commits.

src/ast.ts provides the primitive tree-sitter gave us for free and
m68k-parser does not: locating the innermost node at a position, plus the
traversal helpers built on it.

Traversal is structural rather than a switch over the node union. The parser
exports around forty node interfaces sharing no base beyond `type` and
`loc`, and that set grows with each release, so walking own properties for
values that look like nodes means an upstream addition needs no change here.

Two conversions worth noting, both covered by tests:
- `Location.line` is one-based, and absent entirely on locations from
  `parseLine`; language-server positions are zero-based. locationAsRange
  handles both and takes an explicit line for the single-line case.
- Columns need no adjustment: both are zero-based and end-exclusive.

`containsColumn` treats the end as inclusive so a cursor sitting just after
a token still resolves to it, matching what the regex parser did for
completion and signature help. Where that makes two adjacent nodes match,
the earlier one wins.

events.title: Tatung Einstein TC-01 keyboard
events.message:
Tatung Einstein TC-01 keyboard

An on-screen key deck traced from a UK TC-01: the eight function caps, the
deeply stepped typing rows whose leading modifier widens with each step, the
twin-arrow cursor caps, the red ENTER and the offset space bar. Cap legends
are the machine's own glyphs, not the ASCII behind them — the codes MAME
labels [, backslash, ], ^, backtick, {, |, } and ~ draw as left arrow, half,
right arrow, up arrow, pound, quarter, double bar, three-quarters and division
sign in the MOS font, and the caps are printed accordingly. Front-face
block-graphic legends are omitted.

MOS 1.2's key-decode table (0x10C5) also settles what MAME's matrix guesses
at. There are only two cursor caps, each carrying two arrows: [2,5] decodes
to cursor-right unshifted and left (0x08) shifted, [1,5] to down (0x0A) and
up (0x0B). The cells MAME calls LEFT, RIGHT and UP are the arrow *character*
caps, and its TAB cell is the cursor cap — the deck has no TAB key. Host
arrows now land on the right cells, with the two upper legends asserting
SHIFT while held.

SHIFT, CONTROL and GRAPH are not scanned rows, so the keyboard exposes them
as a ninth synthetic line carrying the status byte's own bits, letting the
pane press them as ordinary cells.

events.title: Restructure as npm workspaces and modernise tooling
events.message:
Restructure as npm workspaces and modernise tooling

Move client/ and server/ under packages/ and drive them as npm workspaces.
The manual postinstall that ran `npm install` in each sub-package is gone,
along with the two extra lockfiles and the hand-maintained version pin
between the client and server packages.

Packaging changes as a consequence: with workspaces the server resolves to
a symlink in the root node_modules, which vsce cannot follow. The build now
bundles the server and copies it next to the client instead, so the .vsix is
self-contained and ships no node_modules. web-tree-sitter is bundled rather
than external, with its runtime tree-sitter.wasm copied beside each bundle
because the emscripten glue resolves it as `__dirname + "/tree-sitter.wasm"`.

Tooling:
- esbuild one-liner -> scripts/build.mjs (build, watch, asset copying)
- .eslintrc.js -> flat eslint.config.js
- tsc output moved to .tsbuild so out/ belongs solely to esbuild
- engines: node >=20, vscode ^1.85
- CI: node 14 -> 20/22/24 matrix, checkout@v5, setup-node@v6

Dependency upgrades: typescript 4.6 -> 5.9, eslint 7 -> 9, jest 27 -> 30,
esbuild 0.14 -> 0.25, prettier 2 -> 3, husky 7 -> 9, vscode-languageserver
7 -> 9, vscode-languageclient 7 -> 9, minimatch 5 -> 10, which 2 -> 4.
Drops the unused `nan` dependency.

Fixes surfaced by the upgrades:
- minimatch 10 is a named export
- fs.watch passes a nullable filename (@types/node 24 types this correctly)
- jest 30 removed the toBeCalled* matcher aliases

events.title: Build the macOS dmg slices on separate runners and move neutral CI jobs to Linux
events.message:
Build the macOS dmg slices on separate runners and move neutral CI jobs to Linux

The dmg job compiled the aarch64 and x86_64 release binaries back to back
on one 3-core macos-latest runner. The shipping profile is fat LTO with one
codegen unit, so each build is essentially single-threaded (12.5 + 11.2
minutes on a full cache hit, 40-48 minutes without one), and the second
gained nothing from the idle cores. Split the build into a per-target
matrix and a package job that lipo-joins the downloaded slices through a
new PREBUILT_DIR knob in build-dmg.sh: same runner minutes, half the wall
time. A single multi-target cargo invocation was measured and rejected
because two concurrent copperline compiles peak near 14 GB of resident
memory, beyond the 7 GB hosted runner.

Every push also queued ten macOS jobs against the five concurrent macOS
jobs the plan allows, so the short test jobs waited 7-9 minutes for a
runner after their build finished. Move the platform-neutral work off
macOS: fmt/clippy and the player checks become one Linux job with one
cache entry, the docs build (and docs release) run on Linux with
setup-typst instead of brew, and the gdb-remote job goes away because the
RSP suite already runs inside the prebuilt unit-lib binary (gdb is a
default feature). The MSRV job keeps only its registry cache. The Actions
cache pool sits above the 10 GB cap and evicts entries within the hour,
which is what turned warm dmg builds into cold ones; this removes about
3 GB of demand, the rest is a follow-up.

events.title: Nalezena baze A6: 0x17dc v chip RAM, AMPROG.OBJ na 0xefc0
events.message:
Nalezena baze A6: 0x17dc v chip RAM, AMPROG.OBJ na 0xefc0

A6 nese globaly (fp@(N)) i skokovou tabulku na zapornych offsetech a
nastavuje jej zavadec jeste pred vstupem do AMPROG.OBJ (0xc72 uz ho pouziva
prvni instrukci), takze v disassembly videt neni.

Metoda: fp@(3530) je mapova pozice 16.16, kterou scroll task 0x3cd4 snizuje
presne o fp@(3526) = 0x4000 za VBL. Dva otisky chip RAM N snimku od sebe ->
jediny long, ktery klesl o N*0x4000 a ma pred sebou 0x4000. Baze AMPROG se
najde podle bajtu rutiny 0x5556. Dva behy s ruznou delkou hry daly stejne
hodnoty; skokova tabulka na zapornych offsetech obsahuje BRA.W po ctyrech
bajtech, jak se cekalo. Konstanty i oba vyhledavaci skripty jsou ulozene v
tools/survey/vacmp.py, aby sly pri jine sestave premerit.

Dve otevrene veci tim padly:
- fp@(12490) ("Tokens picked up") je na originalu v obou behach nula, presne
  jak rikala disassembly - statisticka obrazovka to drzi spravne;
- fp@(3530) bylo po 20 s hry 0xE7E5 a po 50 s 0xE66E, tedy 359 radku za 30 s
  = 12,0 px/s; zpetna extrapolace sedi na 0xE9C0, cimz je potvrzena
  konstanta ve vzorci na procenta, drive jen odvozena ze vzorce.

Zvuk 0x553a: instalace pozadavku primo do hlasove struktury zafunguje, ale
zacatek vyjde potichu, protoze se preskoci zastaveni DMA z 0x4bca. Ciste to
jde prepsanim displacementu volani 0x8aa4 na 0x553a - jeden vystrel pak
spusti synth nativni cestou. Prvni trasa ukazuje periody kolem 130-150 tam,
kde nas render clampuje na 123; pozadovanych 74 nehraje ani jeden.

events.title: 3d: a picture's colour-cycle range no longer outlives the picture — the ground stops cycling (#21)
events.message:
3d: a picture's colour-cycle range no longer outlives the picture — the ground stops cycling (#21)

A1200 report on v0.9.25, Curse of the Fire Dragon outdoors at night:
"color cycling is happening on the ground". Not the backdrop's doing — its
loader installs no cycle records. Five base-game pictures carry a cycle
record over CLUT 144..175, the backdrop band (BIGPIC entry 3: 144+8, PICB
27: 160+16, PICC 25: 144+16 and 160+16, PICE: 86+65), and jt993 -> jt1069
installs them when the picture shows. On the Mac they die when the walk's
palette comes back, because that install goes through jt1069 too and its
Phase 3a frees every range the request overlaps. The port's wall, backdrop
and UI bands are DIRECT installs (port_clut_install*), so nothing freed
them: jt1067 kept rotating slots 144..175 — by then the backdrop's mirrored
colours — and committing them every 11 ticks.

port_cycle_free_overlap does Phase 3a's bookkeeping (mark the slots used,
empty the entry, raise its -3162 flag) in both direct installers. The wall
sets' own fire cycles are freed with their band and re-armed by
dungeon_cycle_ensure before the next jt1067, exactly as after a picture.

Proved on the Falcon (Hatari), machine-independent since l6e58 writes
through qd_set_palette on every backend: mk_bigpic_design.py --picture 242
(id 240+k is BIGPIC entry k+1; entry 3 holds the 144+8 range), beginplay,
Return, eight stills standing still. v0.9.25: six of seven frames differ
from the first inside the view hole. This build: all identical, and the
FRUA_CYCTRACE log shows "direct install frees range base=144" at the
backdrop install. The plain fixed build's menu is byte-identical to the
release's.

events.title: Stream save-state chunks instead of buffering the whole machine
events.message:
Stream save-state chunks instead of buffering the whole machine

Write each Bus chunk as a run of length-prefixed blocks straight into the
zlib encoder as its fields arrive, opening a chunk on its first field and
closing it when a field of another chunk follows, so only the catch-all
chunk is buffered and a save holds at most one block beyond the machine.
Read Bus chunks straight from the stream under the decoder's nesting
limit, buffering only the descriptor, the value chunks and payloads a
migration rewrites, so a load holds at most one block beyond what it has
decoded. Memory-backed disk images of any size therefore save and load
with the footprint the flat format had.

Require the END marker to be empty and version 0 and to be followed by
the end of the compressed stream, in the loader and in inspect, so data
after the marker and a corrupt zlib trailer are refused. Order the chunk
table as the Bus fields fall, retire the stale bincode and wasmtime
versioning notes and the fuzz target's description, and extend the tests
and documentation accordingly.

docs/no-load.md: the founding ledger was wrong in both directions

Revisiting why the branch cannot proceed. The answer is not the wall in
S4b; it is that S1's table was never re-derived after the branch learnt
what the streams actually are. New S1a.

"Loads come off one at a time, each costing its packed size resident,
forever" is wrong twice, and the errors partly cancel, which is why it
survived four steps.

A RESTORATION COSTS NOTHING RESIDENT. PARASPR is the blitter, already
resident in bank 5; its 3,512 is the price of putting it back after the
briefing evicts it. PARAFNT is the font, already resident at &3000. Both
need their DESTROYER removed, not a home -- which is what steps 3 and 5
do. S1 called them "the expensive part" when they are the free part.
Overstated by 5,459.

CODE COSTS ITS UNPACKED SIZE, AND CONTENT READ IN PLACE CANNOT BE PACKED
AT ALL. PARMAN's 1,485 of briefman/keyredef/sndchat runs during the
briefing: 4,290 not 3,595. PARTITL's artwork is read in place by TiPaint
with no arena at title time, and its high-score screen is code: measured
by building it, 2,262 not 1,597. Understated by 1,360 between them.

Corrected total: 8,051 resident, not 12,151, of which 5,789 is still to
find.

AND THE SUPPLY WAS TOTALLED AS A POOL. "Free SWRAM was 1,237 B" adds four
banks together; nothing can span a bank, and S1 states that constraint
one sentence later. Today 2,201 is "free" but the largest block is 759
and keyredef is 776 packed, 1,014 unpacked. It fits nowhere.

Supply against demand, added up for the first time: 1,237 at branch start
+ 3,295 (step 2) + 217 (bank 4 pass) + 2,100 (SCANSTEP tail folding, the
one big reserve) = 6,849, against 8,051. The branch falls ~1,200 short of
its goal even after spending the reserve it hoped not to need. Steps 6
and 7 do not help: step 6's ~500 is main-RAM low workspace and step 7's
~140 is code image, and bank content can live in neither.

Nobody ever added the two columns together. S1 showed 12,151 against
1,237 -- a ten-to-one gap that reads as "needs work" rather than "compute
whether this is possible" -- and step 2 then delivered 3,295, which felt
like progress against a target no one had quantified.

What it changes: the goal is ~1,200 bytes out of reach rather than
hopeless, so one concession closes it (dropping PARBRF, 769, leaves ~430
to find); SCANSTEP tail folding is no longer optional, being 2,100 of the
6,849 and the only thing that gives banks 5 or 6 a block big enough for
keyredef; and keyredef could be depacked into the briefing's own 3,196
byte arena and run there, an idea the plan never considered, which drops
it from 1,014 unpacked to 776 packed.

events.title: Bank 4: the rotor rows were stored 56 times and are 28 pictures
events.message:
Bank 4: the rotor rows were stored 56 times and are 28 pictures

The bank 4 pass. Bank 4 had eight bytes free; it has 225.

THE FINDING THAT MATTERS IS NEGATIVE: bank 4 cannot be packed. Bank 7's
3,295 bytes came from streams read once, on a modal screen, with the tile
map free as an arena to depack into. Bank 4 is the resting bank during
play and everything in it is read while the game runs, so there is
nowhere to depack to -- and the disc already ZX0s the whole bank
(16,376 -> 10,780), so packing a block inside it buys nothing there
either. Measured every block anyway; docs/no-load.md S4c has the table.
levels.asm is the trap in it: the biggest data block in the bank, and
already ZX0 (BuildLevel is pointer setup in front of Zx0Unpack), so a
second pass recovers 4%.

What paid was redundancy, which is step 2's own lesson. drSprData stores
249 rows of seven bytes and 173 are distinct. The rotor's 40 rows are 26
pictures and its 16 end rows are 2 -- the bottom half of the rotor is the
top half in reverse row order and the ends alternate -- and
build_rotor_code has always known that, its docstring says "28 distinct
rotor rows". The flattening that builds drSprData did not, and stored all
56. Interning them: 249 rows -> 218, 217 bytes.

Only half the table can be interned and the split is the blitter's.
drOfs is an explicit byte offset per (phase, row), so duplicates share
one copy. drDigit is a BASE the blitter adds (row-6)*7 to, so a type's
eight digit rows stay contiguous -- interning them would break the
arithmetic and would not pay: 45 duplicate digit rows, 315 bytes, against
384 for the offset table needed to reach them.

Verified. export_droids.py now re-derives the expected picture from the
listing and asserts it against what drOfs and drDigit point at, all 168
(phase, row) and 192 (type, digit row) pairs, every run. Offline: the old
and new tables were followed through both indexes and compared -- 360
reachable rows, zero mismatches, every offset in bounds. Only two readers
exist and both are drSprData + table[index], with no linear walk and no
size assumption. In jsbeeb: 900 frames scrolling right and 700 down,
which crosses the buffer wrap repeatedly and is what drives SprFetchRow;
droids render clean.

COSTED AND REJECTED, recorded so they are not re-run: colourMap dedup
(16 deck rows, only 7 distinct) was BUILT and measured +1 byte, because
tiledefs.asm opens with its own ALIGN &100 and swallows everything
colourMap gives up -- CLAUDE.md's "the next ALIGN pads by the same
amount", exactly. Reverted. The first attempt also put cmapBase in front
of colours.asm's ALIGN and overflowed the bank by 30, which is the other
half of the same rule. Also rejected: 2-bit colourMap packing, tiledefs
row indexing.

The pass does not unblock anything: 225 B is short of keyredef's 1,014
and of the ~650 door.asm wants. Banked because bank 4 had eight bytes.

events.title: Store save states as versioned per-subsystem chunks
events.message:
Store save states as versioned per-subsystem chunks

Replace the flat positional bincode state file, which every serialized
struct change invalidated (nine version bumps inside each of the last
two releases), with a chunk container: an uncompressed DESC chunk, then
a zlib stream of tagged, individually versioned chunks per component and
Bus subsystem, ending in an END marker. Payloads are self-describing
MessagePack, so structs gain and lose fields between releases without a
version change; a chunk version moves only for a change no default can
express, and a migration then rewrites the older payload on load.

Keep Bus as one derived serde struct: a splitting Serializer files each
field into the chunk that claims it (unclaimed fields land in BUS) and a
joining Deserializer feeds the chunks back to the derived visitor as one
map. In-process snapshots for reverse debugging, run-ahead and netplay
rollback stay positional bincode; the netplay handshake carries a schema
fingerprint instead of the state version.

Refuse flat-format files with a message naming the layout, walk every
payload for shape and nesting before decoding, and grow chunk buffers
only as far as the stream holds. Add container, routing, tolerance,
migration and hostile-input tests, regenerate the fuzz seed, and update
the save-state, board and guide documentation.

events.title: Label scrbufA in Ghidra, and record that its base looks one byte off
events.message:
Label scrbufA in Ghidra, and record that its base looks one byte off

verify is now ok=694 mismatched=0 no_symbol=0: every port symbol the
generated list names has a symbol in Ghidra carrying that name.

The label goes at 0x2c867, which is the PORT'S model rather than a fact
recovered from the image -- scrbufA is referenced only at +511 through
the align-up constant, that constant sits inside a relocated longword,
and `base+0x1FF` and `base-1+0x200` store the same value.  That is
reloc_audit category E, and it stays open.

Labelling it turned up evidence that the port's reading is the wrong one
of the two.  Three independent indications point at base 0x1c866:

  * all 282 other symbols in the reference BSS layout sit at EVEN
    addresses -- under +0x1FF, scrbufA is the only odd one;
  * in_evrt, the cell below it, is a BOOL16 at 0x1c864 and so ends
    exactly at 0x1c866, which is dense packing as everywhere else;
  * the two sibling align-up sites (stpScrB 0x65ae, fillTopR 0x6880)
    both `addl #512` then `andl #-512`, so +0x200 is this program's
    idiom.  Only the scrbufA site bakes the constant in, which is why
    it is the one that cannot be read directly.

Not acted on: it is a claim about the 1985 source, it moves the spec
row, and it wants the regenerate-and-review cycle.  Recorded in
CLAUDE.md instead, together with the circularity to avoid -- "the
original does not even align them, scrbufA lands on an odd address" is
a restatement of the +0x1FF assumption, not evidence for it.

docs/no-load.md: the wall, measured

Steps 4, 5 and 6 are all blocked on the same thing and it is worth
writing down once rather than re-deriving. New S4b.

Free bank space is 8 / 665 / 552 / 759 and cannot be pooled -- one bank
is visible at a time, so a stream fits in one or in none.

Step 4 has one candidate left. PARALOW packs to 730 against bank 7's
759; its depack stub eats most of the 29 that leaves, so the machine
would end with about four spare bytes in its last flexible bank to
remove the second-smallest of five loads. PARBRF packs to 769 and
misses bank 7 by ten. Left for KC rather than taken.

Step 5's posted figure did not count the half that has to move. If bank
5 is never evicted then PARMAN cannot land in it, so both halves need
permanent homes: 2,805 of page streams PLUS keyredef 1,014 + briefman
456 + sndchat 15. That is 4,290 against 1,976, and keyredef alone
exceeds the largest free block, so step 5 does not even start.

SCANSTEP tail folding, the one big held reserve, is ~1,050 B in each of
banks 5 and 6 -- 4,076 available, still ~214 short before fragmentation,
for ~1% of the blit window and a change the listing diff cannot check.
Step 6's ~500 B are main-RAM low workspace and cannot hold bank content.

Five options recorded, none obviously right: spend bank 7 on PARALOW;
SCANSTEP folding; make keyredef its own on-demand overlay (it is the
single biggest obstacle and CTRL+R is the rarest screen in the game);
another packing pass, this time on bank 4, which nobody has asked "is
this generatable?" of; or stop.

Measured, not estimated: the PARMAN split comes from the symbol dump and
the packed sizes from bin/zx0.exe on the shipped files.

events.title: The title overlay stops being a disc file
events.message:
The title overlay stops being a disc file

no-load step 4, first item. Step 3 left PARTITL at 397 bytes -- the
cheapest of the six post-boot streams by a factor of two -- so it is the
first one to go resident. The image lives in bank 7 at titlImg,
TiResident copies it down, and there is no title file on the disc.

It is still ASSEMBLED at &0900, because it runs there and is not
position-independent. beebasm's COPYBLOCK moves the assembled bytes into
the bank, which is what makes "assembled at one address, kept at another"
possible in a single pass. Two things follow and both are load bearing:
SAVE "PARXFER" moved BELOW the PARTITL block so it writes the bank after
the COPYBLOCK has filled it, and TITL_BYTES is hand-maintained with an
ASSERT, because the bank reserves the space long before the overlay is
assembled and beebasm resolves constants in file order -- the same
arrangement CON_STR_BYTES and FONTCODE_BYTES already use.

TiResident copies exactly TITL_BYTES, one full page then a tail, not two
whole pages: a page-granular copy would read past the image, and at the
tail of a bank that is the MOS ROM. It ends in main RAM's PgData, whose
RTS is TitleSeq's -- a PAGEBANK executed in the bank would swap the RTS
out from under itself.

Measured:

  main-RAM code image  0 B free -> 14 B      code_end &2FF2
  bank 7               1181 -> 759           397 image + 25 TiResident
  post-boot loads      6 -> 5
  disc files           12 -> 11
  disc image, packed   46848 -> 46592

The 14 bytes of code image are the point and they were the surprise.
LDX/LDY/JSR OSCLI (7) became JSR PgXfer / JSR TiResident (6), and
loadtitl's EQUS "LOAD PARTITL" + CR (13) went entirely. docs/no-load.md
S10 said step 3 would find the bytes BUGS.md #23 needs and was wrong;
this is what paid, and #23 wants three of the fourteen. The pattern
generalises: every remaining stream carries its own filename and call
site, and going resident reclaims those too.

Verified. Offline: the 397 bytes COPYBLOCK placed in the bank were
extracted from the raw SSD and compared against beebasm's own listing of
&0900-&0A8D -- identical across the 383 bytes the listing renders as
code. Against the previous build's PARTITL file they differ in exactly
eight bytes, and all eight are 16-bit operands into the code image, each
moved down by 13 or 14 -- the shift loadtitl's deletion caused, not
corruption. In jsbeeb: cold boot title (first copy), game, ESCAPE, game
over, high-score entry, title again (SECOND copy, from the game-over
path -- which is why TitleSeq pages SWRAM_XFER explicitly rather than
relying on the bank it arrives on; boot arrives with it up, the
game-over seam does not), briefing timeout, briefing, fire exit, game.
-Release assembles and builds its disc.

NOT verified: the -Release image was not booted this time, only built.

make_disc.py's LAYOUT loses PARTITL. That list doubles as the
required-file check, which caught the first build of this change exactly
as it should have.

psg_epp, g_unus3, g_rphs and psg_vrg are DATA cells nothing in the image

already carried rows for 0x3d23c and 0x3f8b0 under the TRUNCATED names,

events.title: Generate the Ghidra verify list from the repo instead of by hand
events.message:
Generate the Ghidra verify list from the repo instead of by hand

LcpVerifyNames.java read ~/ghidra_scripts/lcp_verify.tsv, a file kept by
hand outside version control.  Renaming a port symbol therefore made
`sync_ghidra_names.sh verify` report a false mismatch until someone
remembered to edit that file too -- dg_petok -> pat_ok did exactly that,
with Ghidra being the correct side.  A checker whose expectations have to
be maintained alongside the thing they check will drift, and one that
cries wolf gets ignored.

tools/gen_ghidra_verify.py builds the list instead, from the two sources
the build already trusts: lcp_sym.68k for segments and addresses, and
tools/stx_bss_layout.tsv for BSS, where lcp_sym.68k carries lo68's
placement rather than the reference's.  `verify` regenerates it every
run and passes it to the script as an argument.

Two decisions in the generator, both about keeping real drift visible:

  * It expands the 8-char truncated linkage names against the names the
    port declares at file scope, and only where the expansion is unique.
    Comments, string literals and K&R parameter lists are kept out of
    that pool -- prose supplies "controlled" and "controller" for
    _control, and `short index;` at column 0 between sf_sl's header and
    its brace is a LOCAL, which made the libc symbol _index resolve to
    it and assert a name the repo never owned.
  * It omits the 98 DRI libc and GEM-binding symbols, which have no
    declaration in this tree.  Ghidra's names for them follow no
    reproducible rule (___pname, but _afreebase, _iob, _ctype), the hand
    file guessed, and those guesses were 14 of its 15 permanent
    mismatches.

The first generated run found four survivors of an earlier sync that had
pushed lcp_sym.68k's truncated names verbatim -- the same error as
lcp_pat for lcp_path: body_sh, body_pt, evnt_ti and form_al.  Fixed in
the database, which is committed here.  verify is now ok=689
mismatched=0; the remaining no_symbol=5 are addresses Ghidra has no
label at (four unreferenced BSS globals, plus scrbufA, whose base is
inferred).

lcp_sync.tsv moves into the repo as tools/ghidra/lcp_sync.tsv for the
same reason.  It stays curated rather than generated: the generated list
names all 694 port symbols, and pushing every one would overwrite the
descriptive names Ghidra's analysis carries for the globals the map has
never covered.

events.title: The title comes off &3000, and hsGlyphs dies with the move
events.message:
The title comes off &3000, and hsGlyphs dies with the move

no-load step 3. PARTITL was assembled over PARAFNT's ground, so the
high-score screen carried 72 glyphs of its own -- and all 72 were
byte-identical to glyphs already in textfont, permuted rather than
contiguous, which is why a block diff never found them. Move the overlay
and the duplication goes with it.

Split three ways, because the plan's address does not exist. docs/no-load.md
S6 put the code at &07F4-&0C90; &0800-&08FF in the middle of that is the
MOS's sound workspace, and the MOS owns IRQ1V through every load the title
makes -- main.asm's PARBRF block records the BRK that cost. PARBRF keeps
&0400-&0800, the title gets &0900-&0C90, and the 912 bytes that leaves hold
the driver only:

  PARTITL, &0900   397 B  title.asm + HsEntry
  bank 7          1140 B  titleGlyphs + titleRLE, raw, read in place
  bank 7            72 B  hsRemap, replacing 1152 B of glyphs
  bank 7           139 B  the three strings and everything below .HsRun

HsEntry stays in the overlay because TitleSeq calls it from main RAM and
its PAGEBANK pair must not execute from a bank it is about to swap out.
Everything below it needed no trampoline at all: HsEntry has always paged
SWRAM_XFER around the whole screen for hstable.asm, so HsRun runs with the
bank it always ran with and reaches FontCell, keydown, score and textfont
out in main RAM. Not one byte of code image.

The invariant that replaces the private alphabet, and no ASSERT can check
it: PARAFNT must be resident whenever HsRun runs. It is -- only a finished
game sets hsArmed, and GoTitle reaches TitleSeq through SetupPlain, which
exists precisely so that SetupMode's VDU 22 does not clear &3000-&7FFF.

Measured: bank 7 free 3021 -> 1181, PARTITL raw 3307 -> 397, disc image
48896 -> 46848 packed, code image unchanged at 0 B free.

Verified. tools/export_hsremap.py re-derives both tables from the C64
listing and compares all 1152 bytes against the COMMITTED textfont.asm on
every run. Both builds' listings reduced to a (mnemonic, addressing class,
length) stream: across HsRun..hsTmp2, 279 entries, and the only difference
is HsGlyph's two new instructions -- so the move dropped and reordered
nothing; TiShow differs by exactly its two JSRs and HsEntry is identical.
In jsbeeb: boot, title, game, ESCAPE, game over, high-score entry (walked
A-J and back to capital I, the one irregular remap entry, then committed
three initials), title, briefing timeout, briefing, fire exit, game. And
after a full title dwell &0900-&0A8D read back byte-for-byte identical to
the PARTITL file on disc but for tiRun/tiLo/tiHi/tiPage, the overlay's own
counters -- which is the measurement that says &0900 is safe where &0800
is not. -Release booted through to the title as well.

NOT verified: no cross-build A/B of the high-score screen against main --
identical glyph bytes and an identical instruction stream were reasoned
from, not measured. &0A8D-&0C90 is untested because nothing reaches it.

Step 3 frees no code image, so BUGS.md #23 and #24 are still unfunded; S10
said it would find them and was wrong. Corrected there.

events.title: Initial commit
events.message:
Initial commit

A language server and VS Code extension for m68k-lint.

The server is deliberately narrow: textDocumentSync, code actions and
diagnostics, and nothing else. It is meant to run alongside m68k-lsp, and
any provider it declares that the other also provides would surface to the
user as a formatter prompt or a definition picker. The two sets of
diagnostics complement each other -- m68k-lsp reports what vasm says will
not assemble, this reports what assembles fine but is wrong or slow.

Quick fixes go through the library's own applyOnce rather than splicing
suggestion.replacement directly, so eligibility and the annotate rewrite
cannot drift from what m68k-lint --fix does. Only the changed run is
extracted, keeping the edit local.

Tests drive the built server over stdio as a separate process. The bugs
worth catching live in the protocol surface -- declared capabilities,
subscribed notifications, and initialize ordering -- and none of those are
reachable from a unit test. One test guards that no provider is declared
that a full 68k language server also provides.

branch). XferEnter4 copies palXfer into palPlay and the IRQ makes that
live at the next fire 1; XfStart then draws the board. Putting an
876-byte depack at the top of XfStart -- ~34k cycles, near enough a
whole field -- opened that gap wide enough for the IRQ to land in it,
so the palette went live over a screen that was still the old one.

The same mechanism as the exit flash two commits into this branch, in
the other direction, and the same lesson: a depack is a field of work
and must not sit between a palette change and the redraw that
justifies it.

So the depack is its own routine, XfBoardIn, and XferEnter calls it
BEFORE XferEnter4 -- while the information screen is up and staying up,
and the arena is not on display. XfStart is back to what it was. Costs
three paging calls; nothing between the depack and XfStart writes the
tile map (XferEnter4 touches the palette, the speeds and the CRTC).

THE CODE IMAGE IS NOW EXACTLY FULL: code_end == FONT_ADDR == &3000, no
bytes free. It has been here before (loader-compression.md) and the
GUARD is what will catch the next byte.

events.title: The portrait pool ships packed, eight images to a chunk
events.message:
The portrait pool ships packed, eight images to a chunk

4,032 bytes -- 63 images of 64 -- become eight ZX0 streams plus a
16-byte offset table, 2,371 in all. PoImgPtr depacks the chunk it needs
into the tile map; it is the only place the pool's address was ever
computed, so nothing downstream changed.

EIGHT PER CHUNK makes the indexing free: chunk = slot >> 3, offset =
(slot AND 7) * 64, which is the shift work the flat pool already did.
A chunk is 512 bytes, half the arena. Measured alternatives in total
packed bytes: 63/chunk 2,130 but wants a 4,032 arena that does not
exist; 21 2,215; 9 2,339; 3 2,477; 1 2,742.

Two bugs of mine on the way, both worth the comments they now carry:

(slot AND 7) * 64 is a NINE BIT number and the ROR chain leaves its top
bit in carry. The flat pool never met that -- it took the page from
slot DIV 4 separately, so its CLC threw away a carry that carried
nothing. Here the carry is the ninth bit. PO_BASE is asserted page
aligned so the low byte is the offset alone.

And X IS THE CALLER'S. The old PoImgPtr was three shifts and two adds
and touched no index register, so pod_ybase keeps its loop counter in X
across the call; Zx0Unpack destroys X and Y. That ran the loop on a
garbage counter and presented as the whole game hanging on a black
screen for fifty seconds -- it was not hanging, it was depacking over
and over. poXsv saves X across the depack; Y needs nothing, both
callers reload it.

Verified: all eight chunks decompress byte-identically to the old flat
pool (checked against git HEAD), and the 001 information screen draws
correctly at normal speed.

NOT verified: a type whose four slots straddle a chunk boundary. Types
12 (slots 15,37,38,39), 13 (55,56,57,58) and 17 (7,8,11,9,10) are the
ones that do; the droid database shows them and I could not drive the
navigation to reach it. Same code path as the single-chunk case plus
the X fix, but it wants an eyeball.

Bank 7: 1,485 bytes free -> 3,021.

events.message:
The plan page rebuilds the map it reads

Going to the console ship page and then the deck plan showed garbage
(KC). ConDeck7 walks the tile map IN PLACE and is the only screen that
does; the ship page now depacks the lift artwork into that same map,
and two console pages in a row never pass through RedrawAll, because
the console does not return to the deck until it closes. So the plan
read the lift screen.

ct_trydeck rebuilds before it hands over to bank 7. Both console pages
are one-shot -- conDeckReq 1 -> 2 -- so it is once per visit, ~40k
cycles, and it goes ahead of PgXfer because BuildLevel is bank 4s and
bank 4 is still the resting bank at that point.

THE READER ENSURES THE MAP, rather than each screen cleaning up after
itself. Cleaning up would work today and rot the moment something else
takes the arena; this is one rule that holds however many users it
gains. screen.asm's header carries it, next to the rebuild that covers
the other direction -- LEAVING a modal screen.

Assembles; the deck plays. The repro itself is KC's to re-run.

events.title: The transfer board ships packed, into the tile map
events.message:
The transfer board ships packed, into the tile map

876 bytes of board -- glyph pool, slot table, the five rows and the
code list -- become a 288-byte ZX0 stream. XfStart depacks it into the
tile map at &4600 before XfBuildGlyphOf reads the first byte of it.

The arena is the one the previous commit opened up: the map is a pure
function of the deck, nothing writes it while a modal screen is up, and
RedrawAll rebuilds it on the way out. XB_UNPACKED is 876 of the 1,024.

NOT GENERATABLE, which was the first thing tried. poLut collapsed
because both its tables were one function of one nibble; this does not,
because the three glyph sets use logicals {0,3}, {0,1,3} and {0,2,3} --
the recolour is PARTIAL, shared frame characters staying neutral while
only some logical-3 pixels take the owner's colour. That subset is
artwork, not a rule, so the pool has to be carried.

No read site changed. The exporter emits XB_O_* offsets and rebinds
xbCode/xbPool/xbSlot/xbTop/xbMid/xbBottom to XB_BASE + offset, so every
LDA in the renderer is untouched. XB_BASE is declared in main.asm, not
in the generated file: which arena this uses is a decision, not a
detail. xferboard.asm is now INCLUDEd BEFORE xfer.asm because beebasm
resolves constants in file order -- the trap console.asm's header
describes -- and both sit before plandata.asm's ALIGN either way, so
the padding is unmoved.

Verified: the depacked image is byte-identical to the data the old file
held, at every one of the six offsets (checked against git HEAD). In
jsbeeb, a real transfer against a 329 Messenger -- the board draws
correctly through the whole minigame with all three glyph sets live,
&4600 reads back as xbCode then the pool exactly, and the losing exit
runs on through death and game over without a hitch.

gauge because it collected the 233 the last commit left in the pad.
