events.title: poLut: two tables of 256 were one of 16
events.message:
poLut: two tables of 256 were one of 16

The portrait blitter expands a multicolour byte through poLutL and
poLutR, 512 bytes of bank 7. It never needed them. One mc byte is four
2-bit pixels drawn double-wide: the left MODE 1 byte is pixels 0,0,1,1
and the right 2,2,3,3, so each half is a function of ONE NIBBLE of the
source, and both halves take the same sixteen values --

  left = poLut[b >> 4]      right = poLut[b AND 15]

-- which the two tables were writing out longhand, 256 entries each to
carry 16 bytes of information. export_portraits.py now emits the one
table and ASSERTS the identity over all 256 inputs every time it runs,
so the claim cannot rot. portrait.asm extracts the nibble: ~10 cycles a
source byte on a draw that happens once per screen, never per frame.

489 bytes of bank 7 content. The bank gauge shows +256 because
plandata.asm's ALIGN swallowed the remaining 233 -- the pad rule in
CLAUDE.md, working the other way for once. The next saving assembled
before that ALIGN collects those 233 for nothing.

Bank 7: 7 bytes free -> 263. Portrait verified in jsbeeb on the 001
screen; 61 of the 63 images take the multicolour path this touches.

events.title: The tile map becomes an arena
events.message:
The tile map becomes an arena

RedrawAll rebuilds the map from the deck number before it draws, so
&4600-&4A00 is scratch for the whole of any modal screen. The map is a
pure function of the deck: door.asm gives each open door a private copy
of its tile definition rather than patching the map, and nothing else
writes there after BuildLevel.

That is 1,024 contiguous bytes of arena on every screen that is not the
deck -- the first step of issue #2's no-load plan, which spends it on
the transfer board, the lift side view and the droid portrait pool.

It goes below PalBlack, not in ReframeView. In ReframeView first, and
the transfer exit flashed the board in the deck's palette for a frame:
xferExit4 restores palPlay before it jumps, SetPalette waits for the
next fire 1, and a BuildLevel ahead of PalBlack is ~40k cycles, about
one field. Below PalBlack the play area is already black. The rebuild
belongs with the reader of the map, not the caller.

Verified in jsbeeb: &4600-&4A00 filled with &AA while the 001 screen
was up, then dismissed through InfoCall's IS_ACT_GAME arm -- the map
came back byte-for-byte and the deck drew clean. 5 bytes of bank 4.

events.message:
bubbleghost perf wave 4: the GEM door and tick entry — 486K/frame, x1.04; the rest is structural

Measured: 489.1K cycles/frame (16.40 fps) -> 485.6K (16.52); the
orchestrator's gate run on this tree read 483.8K / 16.58. The original is
466.9K / 17.18. The 0.3% instrument spread is close to the wave's 0.7%, so
the objdump counts are the durable numbers.

Harness (atari/)
- bubble_backend.c: the raster copy is one noinline routine whose four saved
  longwords live in d2-d5/a2-a4 instead of a flag-guarded struct GCC kept
  in the frame (15 stack accesses around the jsr): 1,184 -> 971 cycles per
  door call. The parameter block is staged by five spelt-out stores;
  machine_address translates against the mem it is handed. A review-caught
  regression reverted: v_opnvwk traps with ptsin = 0 (A_vdi_pblock is
  all-zero in the post-init image) and the sentinel must stay.
- bubble_os.s / bubble_main.c: bg_timer_c_entry is the whole tick outside
  the ISR (12 instructions, ~296 cycles, was 428 across three routines);
  tick 2,434 -> 2,297 cycles.
- build.sh: the $484 conterm pin folded into the two-language loop; the
  mirror gate anchored to bg_timer_c_entry's body. Four asm-visible operand
  widths pinned with _Static_assert.
- smoke.py `game`: a second breakpoint on the room-frame PC (`:2 :once`)
  dumps the framebuffer after one whole frame has been drawn through the
  door, byte-identical to the original's (entry and drawn captures each
  0 of 32,000 differ; entry vs drawn differs by 361 bytes on each side).
  Deleting the source raster translation now reds it (414 bytes differ);
  deleting the destination's is a bus error. Both had survived the
  first-arrival capture. The MFDB restores are equivalent mutants: every
  vro_cpyfm site rewrites both fd_addr slots before the call.

What is left and why (STATUS.md "Performance"): the door's translation
(~8.4K/frame) has no counterpart — the cores' pointers are image offsets by
construction; the tick's C body vs hand asm (~6K) and its entry (~1.2K);
the fp package +2.3K. The copy runs and the object tier are at parity; the
collision probe is 1.6K ahead.

Verification: make test 1895 green from a clean build/; build.sh title +
smoke.py title OK; build.sh play + smoke.py game OK; profile.py ours +
compare. Mutations red: CONTERM moved, the mirror deleted or relocated,
bg_in_timer_c widened, VDI_POINTER_LONGS 4, the tick counter dropped.

517.4K cycles/frame -> 489.1K, 15.50 -> 16.40 fps, x1.05 the original's
466.9K / 17.18. The waves compose: 517.4 - 20.9 - 7.9 predicted 488.5.

Reconstruction
- src/clib.c: fp_div's 32-step divisor halving is one uint64_t shift —
  written as two 32-bit halves it compiled to a 70-cycle register shift per
  step; now the original's own lsr.l/roxr.l (20). fp_pack_double's
  normalise loop tests the top bit and takes the tail's +1 before the loop:
  40 -> 22 cycles a pass against the original's 24. fp_dispatch 8,959 ->
  5,368 cycles/call (x2.26 -> x1.36); the whole fp package 22.6K -> 14.6K
  cycles/frame (original 11.4K); game_frame_update x1.49 -> x1.24.
- test/test_clib.py: two deep-normalise vectors (23 and 15 passes) added to
  the direct pack test, which had none past one; three rewrites brute-
  forced equivalent by the review's finders (2-4M cases each).
- src/sound.c: comments only — the ISR cursor's field displacement is added
  to the pointer, so a corrupted base is tellable apart from the wrapped
  address form and no case seeds one; recorded as the 7th sound residual.

Harness (atari/)
- bubble_backend.c: the GEM door's contrl accesses are d16(An) behind a
  CURSOR_BARRIER in the VDI arm (A_vdi_contrl is past a word displacement,
  so each slot cost a 32-bit immediate + indexed access).
- build.sh: the PSG port gate pinned each store line WHOLE (its scrape
  swallowed the value expression, so `& 15` passed it green), plus a check
  that the trapped gate still carries its andi.l #PSG_REG_MASK.
- shim_include/psg.h: the inline ISR write stays unmasked like the
  original's five bare port pairs (0x14682..0x1487c); the trap handler
  alone masks (and.b #$f @ 0x1495c). The old "16 selects register 0"
  hardware claim is withdrawn, not inverted.

Finding: the three sprite routines' x1.09 was never the VDI — ~18K/frame
of Timer C tick was nested in their inclusive totals; halving the tick took
them to x1.05 with no sprite work at all.

Docs: STATUS.md / atari/README.md "Performance" carry waves 3a and 3b with
measured rows, the merged headline, the levers left (the GEM door's ~800
cycles of spills per call, fp_float_to_double's two-half spelling off the
room loop, a codegen scan to pin the fp rewrites) and the unpinned pins.

flyingshark: bootstrap — Gamex unpack, 244/248 named, harness, assets, audio

Flying Shark (Firebird 1988, Prime Software / Images Design), from a Gamex
hard-disk release. The real game is the Gamex-LZ payload inside FILES/FSLA;
FILES/FRD is the original disks' files concatenated, indexed by a 16-byte
directory in the FSLA stub. Target = that program (50,358 B, 1563 relocs);
the Gamex wrapper/GOS is documented, not reconstructed.

Bootstrap
- tools/unpack_dist.py (+ test): depacks the three wrappers, splits FRD into
  bin/disk/A/ and places FLYSHARK.PRG under bin/disk/AUTO/ (sha pinned).
- tools/boot_shots.py: the unmodified original boots under TOS 1.04 from the
  AUTO folder to title, credits and hall of fame over a live scrolling
  level 1. Started from the desktop it crashes: Setscreen(0x70000,0x78000)
  pins the 0x1f900-byte screen ring at 0x58800, so the program must load
  below 0xd922 (notes/loader.md, "Where the screen lives").
- Ghidra bootstrap (1563 relocs) + a second project for MODULE.BAK at
  0x58944; names.txt 244 fn / 281 var / 163 cmt / 13 proto merged from three
  naming slices (notes/frontend.md, gameplay.md, assets_survey.md,
  sound_engine.md).

Recreate harness (recreate/, kit binding)
- project.toml with the tos_malloc_unused byte-scan evidence; post_load_image
  fixture = the ORIGINAL boot chain replayed under the oracle in three
  staged slices (the replay caught a store a hand transcription missed);
  post_new_game_image adds init_new_game. Pins: file relocation, ring
  arithmetic (aligned + unaligned Physbase), the 9-byte MODULE.BAK /
  entity-arena overlap, staging-window arithmetic. 47 passed, 4 loud skips.

Assets and audio
- tools/extract_assets.py: 218 masked sprites, 13 tile banks, 5 rendered
  level maps, palettes (out/assets, gitignored); formats refused on any
  inconsistency.
- tools/extract_audio.py: oracle-driven capture of the MODULE.BAK driver —
  5 tunes (2 one-shot, 3 proven loops) + 13 effects as YM6/WAV + manifest,
  reproducibility and audibility refusals, channel-C pre-emption pinned.
- tools/ym_capture.py: channel_sounds/audible_frames gain an explicit
  envelope_is_level policy (default unchanged); gate_open exported.

Docs
- docs/packed-executables.md: Gamex hard-disk installs (stub-served
  container) and the load-address-vs-buffer-arithmetic rule.

Deferred (recorded in recreate/STATUS.md): kit hoist of the per-project
heap-guard / register-stub / collector copies; bootable .ST needs
st_build.py to write two subdirectories; TILE_BANK_TILES define.

  length of the tick and cleared last.

events.title: Limit notes to what has to be checked
events.message:
Limit notes to what has to be checked

Notes were carrying three different kinds of thing. Conditions, which a
reader has to act on. Restatements of the measurement, which the impact
line already gives. And explanations of how the rewrite works, which the
before-and-after already shows.

Only the first is worth a note, and the other two were applied
inconsistently anyway -- some rules explained their encoding, most did
not. Seventy-one notes removed: the impact restatements, and the
narration of what an instruction does or why an encoding is shorter.

Across the audit corpus that takes notes shown from 170 to 99, and leaves
about half the diagnostics with none. A safe MOVEQ rewrite now shows the
finding, the change and the measurement, and stops.

What stays says something to check or something that was relied on:
flags that differ, a register proven dead, a stack depth the callee must
not depend on, a label that must survive, a constant the replacement no
longer mentions. Justifications of equivalence went with the
explanations -- `safe` already says the rewrite is equivalent, and
repeating the proof underneath it is the same noise in a different voice.

events.title: Explain the CLR.B in the stack-scratch shifts
events.message:
Explain the CLR.B in the stack-scratch shifts

`move.b dN,-(sp)` reserves a word and writes only its high byte, so
reading the word back brings the low byte out of whatever was already in
that slot. The CLR.B clears that, not anything belonging to the register
-- which means a slot that is already zero does not need it, and zeroing
one once serves every shift after it.

Not offered as a rewrite. Nothing here can know what is in memory below
SP, and an interrupt or exception pushes its frame exactly there, so a
zero left below SP holds only while nothing interrupts. That makes it a
technique for someone who knows their interrupt state rather than a
substitution to apply, and the note says so.

Only the sequences that actually emit a CLR.B carry it. The LSR and ASR
forms reach the same result by clearing the register first and have
nothing to say about the slot.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Let one condition have several consumers
events.message:
Let one condition have several consumers

    move.l  d0,dosHandle
    sne     isOS2
    bne.s   .dosOk

was reported, because the instruction before the branch writes no flags
and so looked like something the condition had merely survived. It is an
Scc: it reads the same condition the branch does. Nothing says the flags
are meant more clearly than another instruction already testing them.

Branches were exempt for the wrong reason -- they do not fall through, so
an earlier check happened to catch them -- while Scc and the other
conditionals that do fall through were not. Reading the condition codes
is now the test, which covers all of them and chains of them.

The rule still reports what it is for: a condition surviving across an
instruction that has no interest in it. That includes an Scc in that
position, since the exemption is for the instruction in between rather
than for Scc itself.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Stop treating vasm as the only assembler
events.message:
Stop treating vasm as the only assembler

The note pinned the whole question on vasm's optimisation setting. vasm
is much the most common choice, but not the only one, and an assembler
that does not fold the operand emits the extension word whatever its
settings say.

So the condition is whether the extension word survives, and vasm's
default optimisations are the common reason it does not, rather than the
definition of the answer.

events.title: Say when the zero-displacement saving is real
events.message:
Say when the zero-displacement saving is real

The previous commit said vasm encodes both spellings identically, full
stop. It does so under its default optimisations. Assembling with those
disabled emits the extension word, and the two bytes are then genuinely
there -- which is precisely when someone would want this rule on.

Off by default is still right, since the default build drops it anyway,
but the note now tells a reader with optimisations disabled that the rule
is worth enabling rather than implying it never pays.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Turn redundant-zero-displacement off by default
events.message:
Turn redundant-zero-displacement off by default

vasm and other optimising assemblers encode 0(a0) and (a0) the same way,
so there is nothing to save in the output. The audit measures two bytes
and four cycles because it measures what is written, not what comes out
of the assembler, and the rule's own note claimed the extension word cost
something. Both now say what is actually being compared.

What remains is a preference about how the source reads, which is what
the `style` preset is for. A zero displacement is sometimes written on
purpose so a line matches the non-zero cases around it, and rewriting
that away costs the reader more than it saves anyone.

Kept in the audit and in the tests: the rewrite still has to be correct
for anyone who turns it on.

events.title: Model DIVU and DIVS as reading a long dividend
events.message:
Model DIVU and DIVS as reading a long dividend

    move.w  #100,d0
    divu.w  #4,d0

is the classic way to get a wrong answer, and nothing reported it. DIVU
and DIVS take a 32-bit dividend; the `.w` names the divisor and the
quotient, not the operand read out of the register. The read was modelled
at the operand's width, so the upper half looked unused and every rule
reasoning about it was working from the wrong picture.

MULU and MULS are the other way round -- low word in, long out -- and
were already right. Setting only the low word before one of those is
correct and still says nothing. The asymmetry is now covered by tests
either way round, since it is the kind of thing that gets "tidied" into
symmetry later.

The rule needed a second fix to benefit. Its exemption asked whether the
routine writes the register whole anywhere, and a divide does -- so the
instruction whose bug this is was excusing it. An instruction that reads
the register no longer counts as establishing it.

SWAP is the exception and keeps counting. It reads what it writes, but it
is how the upper half is addressed at all: move.w / swap / move.w defines
all 32 bits, the unknown half having been rotated down and overwritten.
Seeing that from the second write would take a backward bit analysis, and
the presence of the SWAP is the same answer for far less.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Report partial writes only where nothing establishes the upper bits
events.message:
Report partial writes only where nothing establishes the upper bits

Writing the halves of a register separately is ordinary: a word into the
low half, a SWAP, a word into the other. Every write in that sequence is
partial, so each one looked like it had inherited whatever was above it,
and the rule fired throughout real source.

The question is not whether a single write is narrow but whether the
routine ever takes charge of the register at all. A MOVE.L, CLR.L, MOVEQ
or SWAP anywhere between the surrounding non-local labels means both
halves are accounted for and there is nothing to say. Local labels are
branch targets inside a routine, so they do not bound it.

What is left is the case the rule was written for: upper bits that are
read but never established anywhere in the routine, and so hold whatever
happened to be in the register on entry.

The constant-seed exemption is now a special case of this and could be
dropped, but it states the zero-extension idiom plainly and costs
nothing, so it stays.

One test changes sides. `move.l d5,d2` followed by `move.b (a2),d2` was
held up as a narrow write over bits of unknown provenance; it is the
author putting d5 there and then replacing the low byte, which is the
pattern being reported as noise. It now asserts the opposite, with a
companion that keeps the genuine case covered.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Space findings from different files apart
events.message:
Space findings from different files apart

Each file was printed with its own console.log, so findings within a file
were separated by a blank line and findings either side of a file
boundary by a single newline -- least space exactly where most was
wanted, since that is where the reader's attention has to move furthest.

All the blocks are now emitted together: one blank line between findings,
two between files.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add N, and describe the answers by what they actually do
events.message:
Add N, and describe the answers by what they actually do

Y was documented as the counterpart to d, which it is not. Y lasts for
this run; d is written into the config and lasts for good. Calling them
opposites implied a symmetry that does not exist, and reading the matrix
out properly showed a gap: there was no way to stop being asked about a
rule for this run without turning it off permanently.

N fills it. Two things vary, and now both vary freely:

    this occurrence   this rule
    y / n             Y / N        for this run
    a (a comment)     d (config)   written down

Y and N leave nothing behind, which is the whole difference from d: the
next run asks again. Someone deferring forty findings today has not
decided the rule is unwanted.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add Y, to accept a whole rule at once
events.message:
Add Y, to accept a whole rule at once

Answering forty near-identical findings one at a time is how a review
stops being read. Y settles a rule for the rest of the session and is the
counterpart to d: one says always, the other never, and both stop the
session asking again.

Case is significant, so the answer is no longer folded before matching.

A finding of an accepted rule that has no rewrite is still put to the
reader. The standing answer is "apply", and there is nothing there to
apply, so it cannot reach that case -- prefer-link-sequence offers a
rewrite for a clean frame setup and declines for one with a label inside
it, and only the first is settled by Y.

events.title: Replace acknowledge and ignore with a choice of scope
events.message:
Replace acknowledge and ignore with a choice of scope

"Acknowledge" read as a claim that the code is intentional, but equally
as "I have applied this by hand" -- which is not a suppression at all,
since a finding you have actually fixed stops being reported on its own.
And the difference it drew from "ignore" was one of sentiment, recorded
in a comment nobody would act on differently.

The distinction that does matter is scope. `a` allows this occurrence and
writes a directive beside it. `d` says the rule does not suit this
project and turns it off in m68k-lint.json, where one entry replaces a
comment on every occurrence. Once disabled, the session stops asking
about that rule rather than putting each remaining case to the reader.

The config is read and re-emitted rather than rewritten from a template,
so keys this version does not know about survive. Where no config exists
one is created in the project root.

events.title: bubbleghost atari: BUBBLE.PRG from the verified cores boots to the menu under Hatari
events.message:
bubbleghost atari: BUBBLE.PRG from the verified cores boots to the menu under Hatari

recreate/atari/ builds the game from the 132 verified cores, UNMODIFIED
(build.sh refuses a dirty or untracked core: git diff on src/include),
with the m68k-elf toolchain: the OS is real on target — trap #2 for the
VDI/AES (the game's own parameter blocks, pointers translated at the
seam), GEMDOS/XBIOS/BIOS wrappers in bubble_os.s (file I/O first, the
handle-0 note), the Timer C ISR and the trap #9 PSG gate installed for
real, GHOST.LOA executed for the speech with its sample pointer
translated, Mshrink to a 664 KiB image (75 KB spare on a 1 MB machine).

smoke.py judges the boot on the surfaces of docs/on-target-execution.md:
exit status + log, the trap ledger (call for call, lengths compared),
the hardware-state vector (pens, rez, video base), the displayed
framebuffer against a savebin of the SHIPPED binary anchored at the same
PC (all 32,000 bytes identical), the rendered capture, the program's own
43-field record (every field asserted), timelines reported. Three
negative controls (a moved pen, a poked word, an ISR that does not
chain) each redden exactly their surfaces; `floppy` boots disk/BUBBLE.ST
to the desktop.

Defects only the target could show, all fixed and written up: the trap
#9 gate installed one instruction late (bombs); no Mshrink, so TOS's VDI
got handle 0 and drew nothing while every self-check stayed green; the
conterm mirror was a no-op (0x7 at the anchor); the floppy opens no A:\
window (TOS 1.04 ignores the shipped DESKTOP.INF's #W and #Z lines — the
game is two double-clicks away, as the original's disk is).

Unpinned, stated in atari/README.md: play is unjudged (mouse-driven; the
headless protocol has no mouse motion), nothing on iron, the XBIOS group
has no seam under xbios_trap_call (Setcolor/Vsync not reissued), the

events.title: Add an interactive review
events.message:
Add an interactive review

--fix takes every eligible rewrite at once, which is the wrong shape for
a suggestion resting on an assumption a person has to check. -i shows
each finding as it would be reported, with what applying it would do, and
asks.

Five answers: apply, skip, acknowledge, ignore, stop. The middle two both
write a m68k-lint-disable-next-line directive and differ only in the
reason recorded, which is the point rather than an accident.
"reviewed: intentional" and "ignored" are different claims, and someone
reading the file later can tell which was meant.

They are also the useful answers for a finding with no rewrite. Roughly
half the suspicious rules ask whether code is intentional rather than
proposing a change, and until now there was nothing to do about one
except keep seeing it. Those findings offer acknowledge and ignore
without apply.

Questions come in file order, because that is how a person reads. Edits
are made afterwards from the bottom up, because that is the only order in
which line numbers stay valid, and separating the two means no decision
is ever taken against text that has already shifted under it.

The session logic takes the answers through a callback, so the ordering
rules are tested without a terminal; only the prompting itself needs one.

events.title: Apply only what is measurably worth applying
events.message:
Apply only what is measurably worth applying

--fix filtered on applicability alone, which answers whether a rewrite
means the same thing, not whether it is worth making. Four of the
suggestions it would apply unattended were not improvements: a safe
trade-off costing two bytes to save thirty-two cycles, and three neutral
rewrites with no measured gain at all.

Improvements are applied by default. A trade-off is equivalent but
spends one resource to buy another, which is a choice about what the
code is for; it becomes applicable under --goal speed or --goal size,
where the filtering has already dropped the ones that hurt the chosen
resource, so what remains genuinely helps the axis asked for. Under
balanced it is a coin-flip and is left alone. No new flag: saying which
resource matters is the decision, and --goal already says it.

Neutral rewrites are never applied. Changing a file for no measured gain
is churn, and the neutral cases are a clarity rule that would be better
placed in `style` than treated as an optimisation.

A suggestion with no measurement stays eligible. A dead write is a defect
to remove whatever the timings say, and impact is only measured for
optimization rules on a 68000 at all.

events.title: Add --fix-annotate
events.message:
Add --fix-annotate

    ; was:
    ; asr.w #8,d0
    ;------------------------------
    move.w  d0,-(sp)
    move.b  (sp)+,d0
    ext.w   d0
    ;------------------------------

The idioms these rules produce are opaque. A multiply becoming five
instructions, or a shift becoming a stack trick, is unreadable without
the thing it replaced, and once that is gone nothing in the file says
what the sequence was for.

Two signals decide whether a rewrite needs it, both measured rather than
declared. The replacement having more lines than it replaces catches the
expansions. A name dropped from the result catches the rest: `divu.w
#SCALE,d0` becoming `lsr.l #3,d0` does not grow, but the reason for the
3 has gone. That second signal reuses the symbol comparison already
made when the diagnostic was built, now recorded as data rather than
only described in prose, so there is one implementation of it.

An ordinary one-for-one rewrite is left plain; annotating `moveq #100,d0`
would be noise.

`;` rather than `*`, because the block is indented to match the code and
a `*` comment is only a comment in column zero. The indent follows the
instruction rather than the line, so a block under a label lines up with
the code and not with the label. A label sharing the replaced line stays
live on the replacement: only a copy of it appears in the comment.

Off unless asked for. --fix should do the predictable thing, and writing
comment blocks into someone's source is a preference rather than a
default.

events.title: Add --fix
events.message:
Add --fix

Applying a suggestion is a splice: `span` says which lines it stands for
and `replacement` is what goes there. Everything that makes that safe was
built before this -- the replacement carries the indentation, operand
column, label and comments of the lines it replaces, and a rule declines
to offer one wherever a faithful rewrite is impossible.

--fix applies `safe` suggestions and rewrites the file.
--fix-conditional also applies `conditional` ones, which rest on an
assumption stated in their notes; that is a decision for a person, so it
is a separate flag rather than a degree of the same one. --fix-dry-run
reports what would change and writes nothing.

Fixes go in from the bottom of the file up so the line numbers of those
still to come stay valid. Two suggestions covering the same lines cannot
both be spliced, so the lower is taken and the other left for the next
round, where it is recomputed against the text that now exists. Rounds
repeat because one rewrite exposes another: removing a dead write and
then shortening what remains settles in two.

Two backstops. A pass limit, because a rule and its inverse can never
both be live so a cycle should be impossible, and a limit turns a bug
into a stopped run rather than one that never ends. And a verify hook,
used by the CLI to reparse the result: a round that would leave the file
less parseable than it found it is rolled back. Rules matching across an
ENDC produced exactly that before it was fixed, and a fixer writing to
disk should not assume every such bug has been found.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Write out two more derivations that would otherwise lose a name
events.message:
Write out two more derivations that would otherwise lose a name

Surveying every rule with a symbolic operand found seven that drop a
name. The question for each is whether the derivation can be written in
assembly at all.

Three can. The bit mask was done in the previous commit; the other two
are a sum and an exact halving:

    addq.l #SMALL,d0 / addq.l #2,d0   ->  addq.l #SMALL+2,d0
    move.l #BYTES,d0                  ->  moveq #BYTES/2,d0 / add.b d0,d0

Both are exact rather than approximations: the total is the sum of the
two immediates, and the halving is guarded on the value being even.

Only where there is a name to keep. `#3+2` preserves nothing and reads
worse than `#5`, so two literals are still folded. That is the opposite
judgement from the bit mask, where `1<<2` says which bit is meant and is
worth writing even for a literal.

Four cannot and keep the note instead. Three are a shift count derived
by log2 from a multiplier or divisor, and no assembler has a log2
operator; the fourth constructs a byte complement whose expression form
would be both unreadable and constrained by MOVEQ's range.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Write bit masks as a shift of the bit number
events.message:
Write bit masks as a shift of the bit number

    bset #2,d3   ->   or.w #$0004,d3

said which bits were set but not which bit was meant, and where the bit
number was a symbol it threw the name away: `bset #SPRITE_ON,d3` became
`or.w #$0100,d3`, which no longer tracks the constant it came from.

Written as `or.w #1<<2,d3` the mask says what it is, and
`or.w #1<<SPRITE_ON,d3` keeps the name. BCLR takes the complement of the
same shift, `and.w #~(1<<SPRITE_ON),d3`.

A compound bit number is parenthesised: `1<<BASE+1` would depend on the
assembler agreeing with C that `+` binds tighter than `<<`, and
`1<<(BASE+1)` does not.

The measurements are unchanged, which was worth checking rather than
assuming, since the operand is now an expression rather than a literal:
68kcounter sizes both forms identically, and the constant folding added
for symbolic operands resolves the shift before measuring.

events.title: Stop rules matching across block directives
events.message:
Stop rules matching across block directives

    ifne    LIGHTS
    bsr     UpdateLightSpritePosition
    endc
    rts

The tail-call rule paired the BSR with the RTS and offered a BRA
spanning all three lines. Applying it deletes the ENDC and the file stops
assembling.

The scan for an adjacent instruction was purely lexical. It already
stopped at a macro invocation; it now stops at a conditional, REPT or
macro boundary too, which covers every rule that looks for a sequence
rather than just the one that was reported.

A worse case falls out of the same fix. With the RTS in an ELSE arm
instead, the two instructions never both execute, and the rule was
pairing them anyway -- a wrong rewrite rather than a broken one.

A span containing any directive is now refused outright as well. That is
redundant for rules using the adjacent-instruction search, but it catches
a rule that builds a span some other way, and it covers directives that
are not block boundaries: `neg.l d0 / even / sub.l d0,d1` would have
collapsed the alignment away.

The optimisation survives where it is genuinely a sequence: a pair wholly
inside one arm still matches, as does an adjacent pair with no directive
between.

events.title: Let a goal keep what is free on the axis it cares about
events.message:
Let a goal keep what is free on the axis it cares about

The measurement filter had this right -- it excludes on `delta > 0`, so
a rewrite that is neutral on one axis and better on the other survives
both goals. The `serves` gate added on top did not: it turned the whole
rule off under the opposing goal, before any figures were consulted.

Cost is a property of the instance, not the rule. `muls.w #2` and
`muls.w #10` go through muls-word-selected-constants and only the second
costs bytes; the first saves 34 cycles for nothing and was being hidden
from every size-focused run. Two rules measured deltas of both 0 and 2,
so this was not hypothetical.

So the declaration now applies only where there are no figures to
consult, which is what it was for: 68kcounter covers the 68000 alone, and
measurement can be turned off. Inverse pairs are gated either way,
measured or not, because exclusivity is not a preference -- both halves
running would let each recreate the other's input.

Finding both halves of a pair needs the rule list, since the rule
declaring `inverseOf` knows it is one half but the rule it names does
not. That set now defaults from the built-in rules rather than to empty,
so a caller that omits it does not silently lose exclusivity. The
existing pair test caught exactly that when the default was empty.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Carry trailing comments into replacements
events.message:
Carry trailing comments into replacements

    move.l  #100,d0     ; how many faces
    ->  moveq #100,d0

lost the only record of what the value was for. Unlike a dropped label
this breaks nothing, which is why it was the lesser half of the problem,
but it is still the author's work being thrown away by a rewrite that
never meant to touch it.

The comment is carried across with the spacing it had, so where the
replacement is the same width it stays in its column. Where one
instruction becomes several it goes on the first line, since that is the
operation it described.

Comments further into a collapsing match have no line left to sit
beside. They are kept on their own rather than dropped -- a comment is
usually the only explanation of why the code is as it is -- and indented
to match the code they came from, since a comment in column zero beside
indented instructions reads as a banner rather than an aside.

Deleting an instruction keeps its comment too, next to the label if there
is one, so `start: move.w #100,d0 ; unused` leaves `start: ; unused`
rather than removing a branch target and an explanation together.

Measurement is unaffected: comments contribute no bytes and no cycles,
checked rather than assumed.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Stop replacements from deleting labels
events.message:
Stop replacements from deleting labels

    start:  move.l #100,d0     ->   moveq #100,d0

marked `safe`. Applying it deletes `start:` and every branch to it stops
assembling. A replacement stands in for whole lines, so everything on
them that is not the instruction goes with them; a label is the case
that breaks a build rather than merely losing information.

A label on the first matched line still points at the same instruction
after the rewrite, so it is carried across, and deleting a labelled
instruction leaves the label behind on its own line rather than removing
the branch target with the dead code.

A label further into the match is different: three lines collapsing to
one leaves nowhere for a label that pointed at the second. There is no
rewrite to offer, so the finding becomes manual. That is what
prefer-link-sequence and the tail-call rules already did by hand, and it
now holds for every rule whether or not the author thought of it. No
current rule rewrites N lines into N, so nothing is refused that could
have been kept; a rule that did would want finer treatment.

Done where the diagnostic is built, next to the indentation and operand
alignment, since all three are the same question of where the
replacement is going and what is already there.

events.title: Say when a replacement works out a value instead of carrying it
events.message:
Say when a replacement works out a value instead of carrying it

Keeping the source's symbols covered the rules that copy a value
through. It cannot cover the ones that derive a value: a shift count
from a multiplier, the sum of two ADDQs. There the name simply
disappears.

    muls.w #SCALE,d0   ->   ext.l d0 / asl.l #3,d0
    divu.w #SCALE,d0   ->   lsr.l #3,d0
    addq.l #SMALL,d0
    addq.l #2,d0       ->   addq.l #5,d0

The 3 is log2 of SCALE and the 5 is SMALL plus two, but nothing in the
result records that. Change SCALE to 16 and the code is quietly wrong,
with no diagnostic and nothing to grep for. That is worse than a
replacement that merely grows: a longer one is visible, this is not.

So each diagnostic now compares the names in the code it replaces against
the names in the replacement, and reports any that did not survive. It
reuses the already-parsed file for the original and parses only the
replacement. A replacement that deletes code drops every name in it by
design and is not reported.

Nothing fires across the audit corpus, whose fixtures use literals, so
the note only appears where a real constant was actually lost.

events.title: Let rules declare the goal they serve, and add the first inverse pair
events.message:
Let rules declare the goal they serve, and add the first inverse pair

Converting two consecutive ADDs back into a shift is a real size
optimisation, but it exactly undoes shift-two-adds: applying one
recreates the other's input. Both can be `safe` when the flags are dead,
so a fixer applying safe rewrites to a fixpoint would not terminate.

Rules can now declare `serves: "speed" | "size"` when a rewrite trades
one resource for the other, and `inverseOf` when it undoes another. A
rule that serves a goal is off under the other goal; an inverse is off in
balanced runs, leaving the rule that does not declare itself an inverse
as the canonical direction. So at most one of a pair is ever live, by
construction rather than by getting a filter right.

This is a declaration rather than a tag, and it gates whether the rule
runs at all, which is why it sits beside `platforms` and
`enabledByDefault` rather than in `tags`. It replaces
`speed-size-tradeoff`, which did the same job for one goal only and was
checked against nothing. It is needed because impact is measured only for
68000 targets and only when measurement is on; where numbers exist they
still decide.

Tests derive the truth from the audit: a rule measured as costing bytes
must serve speed, one costing cycles must serve size, one costing neither
must declare no goal, and an inverse must serve the opposite goal to the
rule it names. The no-two-live check asks effectiveSeverity rather than
restating its logic, so the two cannot drift.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Drop the speed and size tags, keep the one that does work
events.message:
Drop the speed and size tags, keep the one that does work

--goal speed and --goal size already filter on measured impact. The
`speed` and `size` tags were read by nothing and disagreed with the
measurements in 49 places: 41 rules save cycles without a `speed` tag,
five tagged `speed` save none, and three tagged `size` save no bytes.
Removed, 106 of them across 60 files.

`speed-size-tradeoff` is a different thing and stays. Impact is measured
only for 68000 targets and only when measurement is enabled, so it is the
fallback that keeps a size-costing suggestion out of a size-focused run
when there are no numbers to consult. It matters most for the 68020+
rules that can never be measured at all.

That fallback was quietly broken in two ways. Six rules spelled it
`size-tradeoff`, which the filter never matched -- harmless in practice,
since all six are 68000-only and therefore always measured, but it meant
the tag did nothing it appeared to do. And seven rules that measurably
cost bytes carried no tag at all, so with measurement disabled they
passed a size-focused run.

Both fixed, and a test now derives the answer from the audit: every rule
the corpus measures as costing bytes must carry the tag, and no rule that
saves or keeps bytes may. The hand-written tag is now checked against
measurement rather than trusted alongside it.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Record the 68kcounter discrepancies found while auditing impact
events.message:
Record the 68kcounter discrepancies found while auditing impact

Three measurement differences against yacht.txt, with reproductions, so
they can be fixed in the counter rather than lived with here.

A redundant size on a bit instruction adds an extension word that the
encoding does not have: bset.l #3,d0 measures 6 bytes where bset #3,d0
measures 4, and bclr.l measures 4, so the two spellings disagree with
each other as well as with the reference.

An immediate bit number always bills the slower branch. yacht.txt splits
BSET, BCHG and BCLR on whether the bit number is under 16, which is a
literal in the instruction; the counter reports the higher figure for
both. BTST has no such split and is correct. This one is not worked
around: it understates savings by 2 cycles, which errs safe, and
patching a cycle table from outside the tool is worse than fixing it
inside.

A compound displacement is mis-detected as a wider addressing mode.
`lea (200*2)(a3),a3` measures 6 bytes and 12 cycles where the identical
`lea 1610(a3),a3` measures 4 and 8. Symbols alone are fine, so it is the
expression shape rather than the unresolved name, and it is what turned
address-add-to-lea into a reported regression on ordinary source.

Also checked and found correct: BTST #data,Dn at 10 cycles, which I had
initially misread against the BTST Dn,Dm row.

events.title: Fix two measurements found by auditing speed/size tags against impact
events.message:
Fix two measurements found by auditing speed/size tags against impact

Checking the hand-written speed and size tags against what the audit
actually measures turned up 49 disagreements. Most are loose tagging, but
two were real.

A rotate by a register has the same base-plus-multiplier-times-n timing
as a shift, and like the shift rules it fires only once the count is
proven. It records that count as `rotateCount` where the range resolver
looked only for `shiftCount`, so known-register-rotate measured as an
unresolved range and its saving never appeared. It saves 20 cycles.

prefer-bset reported saving no bytes. BSET on a data register operates on
all 32 bits whatever size is written, so the `.l` the rule emits adds
nothing the encoding does not already fix; yacht.txt gives `#<data>,Dn
.L` as 10(2/0), two word fetches, four bytes. 68kcounter bills the
spelled-out form an extra extension word, and inconsistently -- it sizes
`bclr.l` correctly. The measurement copy now drops a redundant size on a
bit instruction, the same kind of normalisation as the indentation it
already applies. The suggestion keeps the spelling the rule chose.

events.title: Give diagnostics a first-class span, and stop reporting syntax
events.message:
Give diagnostics a first-class span, and stop reporting syntax

A finding covers a run of lines, and a suggestion's replacement stands in
for all of it: BSR followed by RTS becomes one BRA. That extent was
reconstructed inside the impact module by sniffing `data` key names --
sourceEndIndex, or anything ending InstructionIndex -- so it existed only
where measurement had run, and any rule storing an unrelated key ending
that way would have silently widened it. Anything applying a replacement
needs the extent unconditionally, so it is computed once when the
diagnostic is reported and carried on it. Measurement falls back to
computing it, so a diagnostic built by hand still measures.

The CLI now shows every line of a match instead of only the first, which
had hidden half of what a suggestion was about to replace. The caret is
gone: all but one rule points at a mnemonic, so the underline never said
more than "this instruction", and under a multi-line match it marked one
line as though the rest were context.

Syntax errors are no longer reported, counted, or treated as a failed
run. Two reasons. The project's stated line is that the assembler owns
validation, and this parser is deliberately more permissive than any one
assembler, so a line it cannot read may be perfectly valid to yours --
failing a build over that is worse than silence. And the parser is built
to recover so analysis can continue mid-edit, which is exactly when
transient syntax errors would flood an editor.

Going silent has its own risk: an empty result on a file that was never
fully read. So a file that does not parse cleanly is noted once, saying
findings may be incomplete, and the detail stays in --format json for
tooling that wants it.

Labels and comments on replaced lines are still discarded, which is the
next thing to fix before anything applies these automatically.

events.title: Offer a rewrite wherever one exists
events.message:
Offer a rewrite wherever one exists

optimization/bsr-rts-tail-call described the replacement in prose and
then withheld it, marked "manual". The rewrite is BRA to the same target:
entirely mechanical, and the reason for caution -- the callee sees one
fewer return address on the stack -- is a condition that can be stated,
which is what `conditional` is for.

Several rules were worse than that: they produced replacement text and
marked it "manual" anyway, so the CLI printed a rewrite on one line while
the line above declared none existed. The adjacent CLR and MOVE
combinations, jsr-jmp-tail-dispatch, the memory form of the
logical-identity TST rules, and DIVU power-of-two with an unproven
remainder all did this.

The line is now that "manual" means there is no single rewrite to write
down: a label inside the matched code that other code may branch to, or a
finding that asks about intent rather than proposing a substitution. A
test over the audit corpus holds it, so the two cannot drift apart again.

Two things fell out of this. The tail-call rules can now be measured,
having been exempt from the impact audit for having nothing to measure,
and they save 2 bytes and 24 cycles apiece. And their label check turned
out to catch only a label sharing the RTS line, missing the more common
one on its own line above it, which marks the same entry point.

events.title: Record CMPA as setting the condition codes
events.message:
Record CMPA as setting the condition codes

    move.l  #CopBlitEnd,d1
    cmpa.l  a2,a0
    beq.s   .noFaces        <- "BEQ relies on CCR preserved across CMPA"

CMPA sat in the list of address-register operations that deliberately
leave CCR alone, alongside MOVEA, ADDA, SUBA, PEA, EXG, LINK and UNLK.
Those belong there. CMPA does not: it stores nothing, and like every
compare it sets N, Z, V and C from the subtraction while preserving X.
The name is the only thing it shares with them.

So an ordinary compare-and-branch was read as a branch consuming a
condition no instruction had produced, which is precisely what the rule
exists to catch, reported against the one case where the producer is
right there on the line above.

The interpreter agrees, and the calibration set now says so: CMPA sets Z
on equal and N with C on less.

The rule still earns its keep. ADDA really does preserve CCR, and a
branch after one is still reported.

events.title: Treat conditional assembly arms as alternatives
events.message:
Treat conditional assembly arms as alternatives

Exactly one arm of an IF/ELSE/ENDC is assembled, but the directives were
skipped like any other non-instruction line, so the arms ran into each
other and a write in the first looked overwritten by the second:

    ifne    SHADOW_ON
    moveq   #7-1,d7     <- reported dead by dead-register-write
    else
    moveq   #8-1,d7
    endc

I had noted this shape when macros were fixed and called it conservative
on the grounds that both arms' reads are counted. That was only half the
picture: counting both arms' *writes* on one path invents a kill that no
assembly of the file performs.

The code above a block now reaches the first executable line of every
arm, and every arm reaches the code below, with no arm reaching another.
A block with no ELSE also reaches the code below directly, since the
condition may be false and the arm not assembled at all. Nesting works by
construction, and ELSEIF and ENDIF are recognised alongside ELSE and
ENDC.

Precision is kept: a write dead within a single arm is still reported, as
is one that every arm overwrites.

events.title: Report MOVEA.W sign extension only where it is observed
events.message:
Report MOVEA.W sign extension only where it is observed

Flagging every word load into an address register is too noisy to be
useful: using a spare address register to hold a 16-bit value when data
registers run short is ordinary, and reading it back with MOVE.W is
completely unaffected by the extension.

The extension writes the upper half, so it matters exactly when that half
is read again. Using the register as a base address reads all 32 bits and
is reported; reading it back as a word reads none of them and is not.
Neither is a register overwritten in full before any use, or never used
again.

The rule also stopped depending on how the instruction is spelled. It
fired only on the generic `move.w <ea>,An` and ignored an explicit
`movea.w`, which is the same instruction; source normalised to `movea.w`
was never checked at all.

Answering this needed the bit-level liveness walk to cover address
registers, which it declined to do. Two things were needed beyond the
operand shapes. A base-address operand reads the whole register whatever
width it transfers. And arithmetic that reads an address register and
writes it back passes the question through rather than answering it: a
first attempt called it a full read, which reported a value only ever
read back as a word, and treating the write as a kill would have lost the
case that is read as a long. The upper half of an ADDA result comes from
the upper half that went in, and its low half cannot depend on the half
above it.

events.title: Measure operand expressions by value, not by spelling
events.message:
Measure operand expressions by value, not by spelling

Keeping the source's symbols in a replacement made rules report false
regressions. 68kcounter reads the written form to decide an addressing
mode, and a compound displacement defeats it:

    lea SCREEN_BW/2+(SCREEN_H/2*SCREEN_BW)(a3),a3   6 bytes, 12 cycles
    lea 1610(a3),a3                                 4 bytes,  8 cycles

so address-add-to-lea, which saves 4 cycles at no cost in size, was
measured as +2 bytes and reported as a regression.

The symbols are not the cause. A simple `lea SCREEN_BW(a3),a3` measures
correctly, and a purely numeric `lea (200*2)(a3),a3` does not, so
substituting symbol for symbol would not have helped: the expression has
to collapse to its value. Both sides of the comparison are collapsed, so
originals written with a compound displacement are now measured properly
too, which they never were.

The suggestion itself is untouched and still shows what the author wrote,
which is the point of keeping symbols in the first place.

Immediates and displacements only. Substituting an absolute address would
change which absolute form is chosen, and a branch target is an address
the measurement has no business rewriting. Anything that does not
evaluate is left as written, so this can only sharpen a measurement,
never invent one.

events.title: Measure shift timing when the count is proven
events.message:
Measure shift timing when the count is proven

optimization/stack-known-register-shift carried the note "Measured on
68000 as a resource regression rather than an improvement" while actually
saving 36 cycles. Its cycles were never measured: a shift by a register
has a timing range, 68kcounter reports the range rather than a figure,
and the assessment then saw only the size, which is worse.

The range exists because the count is unknown in general. 68kcounter
records the calculation behind it -- base plus multiplier times n, over n
in 0..63 -- and these rules fire only once constant propagation has
proven the count, which they already record. Substituting it is the same
arithmetic 68kcounter does for a literal count, not an estimate.

Four rules move from unmeasured to measured, all trade-offs saving
between 2 and 36 cycles at a cost in bytes: stack-known-register-shift,
known-register-asr-long-high, known-register-asr-word-low-only and
known-register-shift-reduction. The audit now reports no partial rows.

A conditional branch is a range too, but not because of a count: its
timing depends on whether it is taken, and no count makes that
determinate. An earlier draft of this fell through to the first of the
two values and would have reported the taken path as the measurement.
Those stay unmeasured, which is what the rules with a branch in their
replacement still show.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Stop narrow writes from ending a register's life
events.message:
Stop narrow writes from ending a register's life

suspicious/dead-register-write fired on instructions whose result was
still in use, reported from real source:

    swap    d7
    move.w  d4,d7
    swap    d7

Two independent faults, both in the semantics rather than the rule.

EXT and EXTB were grouped with CLR as instructions that write their
operand without reading it. CLR does; EXT sign-extends the value already
there, so whatever produced it is live. That alone explained the second
report, a word load feeding an ext.l.

The larger one: liveness treated every write as ending the register's
life. A byte or word operation on a data register leaves the bits above
it in place, so the first SWAP above is exactly what the preserved upper
half carries. Narrow writes are now recorded as partial, and a partial
write passes liveness through rather than killing it. MOVEA, MOVEM.W and
the word multiplies and divides are excluded: they write the whole
register despite a narrow size.

That alone would have lost the true positives, since a register written
narrowly twice stays live throughout while the first write is plainly
dead. The bit-level walk that already existed gave up at any write it
could not prove was full width; it now subtracts the bits a narrower
write covers and continues, which is the question it existed to answer.
The rule consults it when its own write is partial.

One knock-on. deadScratch asked for a wholly dead register, and got one
before only because a word write wrongly killed it. The low-word multiply
recipes only ever touch the scratch with word operations, so they now ask
for a register whose low word is dead; the full-result recipes copy a
long into it and still ask for the whole register.

events.title: Add run_all.sh: the whole suite in the order that works
events.message:
Add run_all.sh: the whole suite in the order that works

Everything in it was run by hand before, and the ORDERING is why it
exists.  The byte-identity checks need the SHIPPED build; the runtime
tests need a GATED one, because the copy protection never passes under
an emulator here; and leaving the wrong one in build/alcyon makes the
next run lie.  Both failure modes bit me today: a gated binary can
never pass prg_diff, and a shipped binary parks the resident in
cs_mvIn's wave loop so every runtime test fails 0/11 with no hint why.
run_all.sh restores the shipped build on exit, including on failure.

Measured 14/14 in 210 seconds -- not the ~20 minutes I first guessed,
because the gated configuration is built ONCE and the four runtime
tests reuse it through NO_REBUILD instead of each doing its own Alcyon
build.  The docs now say 3.5 min.

  shipped build, byte identity, prg_diff, reloc_audit, stx_check,
  ppbalance, host build, host linktest, 10 host unit tests, gated
  build, test_keyboard 11/11, test_actions 33/33, test_saveload 7/7,
  test_longrun_stable STABLE

--quick drops the emulator phase and runs in about ten seconds, which
is the one to use while editing.

Two bugs found by running it, both mine, both in parsing other tools'
output: reloc_audit's category D ends "0 of 283" so a ': 0$' test
called a passing audit a failure, and the unit-test count only saw the
three tests that print "name: PASS".  Also gave test_longrun_stable.sh
a PATH shim -- it invokes a bare `hatari`, and there is none on PATH
here.

CLAUDE.md's opening still claimed only the TEXT segment matched and
that "data and bss layout are the remaining work".  That has been out
of date since 2026-09-03; it now states the whole binary matches, with
the MD5.

events.title: recreate_kit: model the VDI/AES, console reads, Fseek, IKBD and console ledgers
events.message:
recreate_kit: model the VDI/AES, console reads, Fseek, IKBD and console ledgers

Bubble Ghost is a GEM application — every string, bar and sprite goes
through trap #2 — and reads keys with Cconis/Crawcin/Cnecin, so nothing
that draws could be differentially verified. The deterministic model now
covers it, identically on both sides (src/gem.c + src/raster.c are the
first stateless kit sources linked into liboracle.so AND every candidate;
the workstation state lives in the image so the byte diff owns it).

Model
- VDI (17 opcodes): v_opnvwk (honours work_in; zeroes all 45+6 outputs),
  v_clsvwk, v_clrwk, vst_*/vsf_*/vswr_mode, vr_recfl (hollow = colour 0,
  solid = fill colour, patterned refused), vro_cpyfm (ST device format,
  1-8 planes, all 16 logic ops, direction chosen on overlap, clipping only
  when fd_addr == 0 — the VDI's own rule), v_gtext through a synthetic 8x8
  font (pixel fidelity to TOS is an on-target matter, said so), vq_mouse /
  vq_key_s from the poke block, vs_clip, cursor calls. AES: appl_init,
  appl_exit, graf_handle, graf_mouse. Anything else refuses by opcode.
- GEMDOS Cconis/Crawcin/Cnecin over a queue of staged keys
  (harness.console_keys, 8 deep; refuse when empty — never block, never
  fabricate), Fseek modes 0/1/2 over the staged-file cursor, Crawio write,
  Cconws (returns the count), BIOS Bconout(4) as IKBD bytes.
- One ordered OFF-IMAGE EVENT LEDGER (CONOUT, IKBD, GEM_MOUSE, VDI_CURSOR)
  compared per run like the Dosound/PSG ledgers, armed for the poison
  re-run too (the attribution pass used to skip every new model).
- os_malloc: the candidate-side arena (base and limit installed, Malloc(-1)
  answers the free size, refuses past the ceiling); harness compares the
  two bump pointers per run.
- Parameter-block pointers bounded before wrapping; the raster core's
  per-pixel addressing hoisted (7x at identical semantics).

Tests: kit 631 -> 730 — an independent Python raster reference over all
16 ops incl. overlap, every modeled opcode driven through BOTH doors
(trap #2 vs os_vdi) with ledgers compared, refusal paths, 20 mutants
caught (one first-pass survivor, an unterminated Cconws, closed). Joust,
Zynaps, Wonder Boy, BuggyBoy, Bubble Ghost suites unchanged/green.

Docs: TRAP_MODEL phases 11-13 (with "reached by" per opcode and measured
mutation lines), README (eight groups, console keys, the poke-block
widening rule), docs/tos-os-calls.md pointer; Wonder Boy's poke-block
waiver rewritten for the widened block (0x600..0x65f).

events.title: Align replacement operands with the column the source uses
events.message:
Align replacement operands with the column the source uses

Matching the indent still left a replacement out of line with its
neighbours, because rules emit a single space between the mnemonic and
its operands where source almost always uses a tab.

The operand column is taken from the parsed line rather than by scanning
text, so a label or a size qualifier cannot confuse where the mnemonic
ends. Where the source separates with tabs the replacement is padded with
tabs, which keeps the columns together whatever width tabs are rendered
at, since both land on the same stop; where the source aligns with
spaces, the column is matched in spaces.

A single space is deliberately left alone. Treating it as a column to
match pads a shorter mnemonic out to it and turns `moveq #100,d0` into
`moveq  #100,d0` from source that never lined anything up. That was the
first attempt, and it moved 69 tests.

Alignment through tabs is not unconditional: a tab narrow enough that the
two mnemonics fall in different cells separates them. That is equally
true of tab-aligned source written by hand, and the test says so rather
than asserting more than holds.

Highlighting tests now build their expectations from the exported
palette instead of hard-coding colour codes, so retuning a colour is not
a test failure -- as it was when mnemonic and size were given the same
blue.

events.title: Take highlighting structure from the parser
events.message:
Take highlighting structure from the parser

The highlighter re-derived line structure with a regex, which meant
reimplementing rules the parser already gets right -- where a label may
appear, whether a dot is a size qualifier or part of a name, whether a
semicolon opens a comment or sits inside a string. It got the first of
those wrong: with no constraint tying the label to column zero, an
indented mnemonic was matched as a label and never coloured.

Now the parser supplies the spans -- label, mnemonic, size qualifier,
each operand, comment -- and only the inside of an operand is tokenised
here, which is the one split the parser does not provide: it gives an
operand's extent, not the division between registers, numbers and
punctuation within it.

That removes the whole class of bug rather than the one instance. `.loop`
as a branch target is a symbol while `.loop:` in column zero is a label;
`bsr.s` splits but `dbf` does not; a semicolon inside dc.b "a;b" is not a
comment. None of these needed code, and each has a test.

Behaviour is unchanged: the thirteen existing highlighting tests passed
against the rewrite untouched, stripping the colour back out still
reproduces --no-color byte for byte, and the caret stays aligned.

events.title: Highlight assembly in terminal output
events.message:
Highlight assembly in terminal output

Colours the source line a diagnostic points at and the replacement it
suggests: mnemonics and their size qualifiers, registers, literals in
any base, strings, punctuation and comments. Symbols and labels are left
plain, so the names carrying the meaning stay the most readable thing on
the line rather than competing with the syntax around them.

A small tokeniser rather than a reuse of the parser. The lines being
coloured are already known to be assembly, mis-colouring is cosmetic
rather than harmful, and it has to run over replacement snippets that are
not parseable files on their own.

Reading the line positionally, the way an assembler does, matters more
than it looks. A first attempt matched an optional label before the
mnemonic without requiring column zero, so on an indented line the
mnemonic itself was taken for a label and never coloured -- and in
`lea SCREEN_BW/2(a3),a3` the symbol was coloured as the operation. A
label only exists in column zero.

Escape sequences occupy no columns, which the caret underlining a
diagnostic depends on: it is positioned from the uncoloured text.
Verified by stripping the colour back out of a coloured run and getting
the --no-color output byte for byte.

Also updates format.test.ts, which still asserted the two-space prefix
that the previous commit removed from formatImpact.

events.title: xbin_diff: establish the baseline; other Activision titles unreachable
events.message:
xbin_diff: establish the baseline; other Activision titles unreachable

Ran the tool against every Activision ST title on this machine, which
turns out to be one -- and against the period Alcyon toolchain's own
binaries, which is the more useful result.

The baseline answers the question a reader should ask first, "is 10%
sharing just the common toolchain?":

    C168.PRG      4347 shared, but only  68 below 0x1733a
    CP68.PRG      4177 shared, but only  68 below
    DOODLE.PRG     219 shared,            0 below
    COMMAND.PRG      0 shared,            0 below
    AUDIO.PRG    10055 shared,         8614 below   <-- Music Studio

An unrelated Alcyon program shares 0-68 bytes of non-library code, and
every C168 match is libc (__doprt, _malloc, __flsbuf, _free).  Music
Studio's 8614 is ~125x that, so the relationship is real rather than an
artifact of shared tooling.  Recorded in CLAUDE.md and in the tool's
own --help, since it is the key to reading its output.

The other Activision ST titles are NOT reachable here, and that is
worth writing down so nobody repeats the search: PaintWorks,
Ghostbusters II, Fighting Soccer and Hacker II exist only as
GreaseWeazle FLUX dumps (.scp inside .7z), and neither converter
installed will run headlessly -- `gw convert` dies with
'bitarray.bitarray' object has no attribute 'itersearch' (bitarray 3.x
dropped it), and HxCFloppyEmulator / UnifiedFloppyTool are GUI only.
Pinning an older bitarray would fix gw, but that is the maintainer's
environment to change, not mine.

Also corrected the tool's header, which still carried the vague "1043
bytes in the MIDI sequencer" instead of the per-function figures.

events.title: Indent suggested replacements to match the code they replace
events.message:
Indent suggested replacements to match the code they replace

Rules emit compact replacement text starting in column zero. That is not
valid assembly: a token in column zero is a label, so a multi-line
replacement pasted as written defines a label per line and assembles
nothing like the intent. Single-line replacements had the same problem
less visibly.

Indentation is applied centrally when the diagnostic is created, so no
rule has to think about it. It is taken from the line the diagnostic sits
on, which means tabs or spaces are matched as the file uses them, at
whatever width. Where a label occupies column zero, the instruction's own
indentation is the gap between the label and the mnemonic, and that is
what is adopted. Deletions stay empty rather than becoming a line of
whitespace.

Impact measurement was unaffected: it already normalised snippets to
assembler columns before handing them to 68kcounter, which is the same
problem solved locally.

Two consumers assumed unindented text and needed updating. The CLI
printed a replacement inline after its label, which put every line after
the first at the left margin; multi-line replacements now print as a
block. The differential checker matched anchored patterns against
replacement lines, so its syntax adaptation and its skip detection both
stopped firing -- the latter silently reintroduced the known A7 byte-push
divergence as an unexplained difference. Both now normalise on the way
in.

Test expectations were updated mechanically. Three that assert a
four-space fixture keep four spaces rather than gaining a tab, which is
the feature working.

events.title: music: decode, convert and render the .SNG/.ORG songs
events.message:
music: decode, convert and render the .SNG/.ORG songs

Documents the Activision Music Studio song format from the playback code
itself (mq_parh, mq_pacm, mq_pars, mq_rdur, mq_qnne, mq_bust, mq_dise,
psg_upE, mq_tick) and adds tools that act on it.

  music/SNG_FORMAT.md   the container, the event bytecode, the ADSR
                        records, the timing model and the lyric block
  music/midi/           format-1 MIDI, one named track per voice
  music/psg/*.regs.txt.gz  YM2149 register traces, 960 Hz timestamps
  music/sng_report.txt  structure dump of all 16 DATA songs

  source/tools/sngdump.py        decoder + MIDI export
  source/tools/psgrender.py      tick-accurate PSG engine + audio
  source/tools/render_psg_all.py batch driver, one common gain
  source/tools/midicheck.py      independent MIDI re-parse
  source/tools/prg.py            GEMDOS PRG reader

Findings worth recording:

- Header command 0x80 is the key signature, not a channel count.  Its
  operand indexes g_msmk, and decoding the masks reproduces the circle
  of fifths exactly (1=C, 2..8 sharps, 9..15 flats).  Notes with
  accidental mode 00 store staff position; the key is applied at play
  time by mq_bust.
- The sequencer runs at 960 Hz, not 200 Hz: mq_inti installs Timer A
  with Xbtimer(0, 5, 0x28, mq_tick), and psg_upE runs every 4th tick.
  One duration unit is 1/24 quarter note = 2400/tempo ticks, which
  makes the tempo byte literally BPM.  Bar markers confirm it -
  STARSPAN is 32 bars over 96.0 quarters, i.e. 3/4.
- The trailing 0x02 of the \xCD Mstudio \xCD signature is a file-type
  byte, not fixed magic; STANDARD.SND on the Music Studio disk is 01.
- MIDI OUT and PSG transpose differently (channel-map nibble vs
  envelope nibble), so the two exports are not the same performance.

Rendered WAV under music/psg/ is gitignored: it is derived, and
render_psg_all.py regenerates it bit-for-bit from the sources.

events.title: Negate compound expressions instead of falling back to a number
events.message:
Negate compound expressions instead of falling back to a number

The previous commit kept symbols only where negation was unnecessary or
the expression was a bare symbol, because an operand opening with `-(`
is also how predecrement is written and I could not confirm an assembler
would read `-(EXPR)(a3)` as a displacement. Confirmed that it does, so
the last case that dropped to a magic number no longer needs to.

A compound expression is now wrapped rather than prefixed:
`suba.w #SCREEN_BW/2+(SCREEN_H/2*SCREEN_BW),a3` gives
`lea -(SCREEN_BW/2+(SCREEN_H/2*SCREEN_BW))(a3),a3`. The parentheses are
required, not stylistic -- unary minus binds tighter than the operators
inside, so `-SCREEN_BW/2` is not the negation of `SCREEN_BW/2`.

events.title: DEBUG_TRCHK: the tranche split, put on trial and acquitted
events.message:
DEBUG_TRCHK: the tranche split, put on trial and acquitted

KC reports sprite pixels occasionally left on the deck in a firefight,
no repro. The split was the first suspect: within a pass the order is
restore A, draw A, ... restore B, draw B, so a tranche-B sprite drawn
over a tranche-A one saves A's pixels into its background and stamps
them back at its old position next pass. SprAssignTr prevents that by
forcing overlapping sprites into one tranche, and SprOverlapXY pads
its test by 2 units and 8 scanlines on the stated grounds that 8 px is
the most a sprite's view position can shift in a pass. That is false
of bullets: cbDisp is $F4/$00/$0C, so the player's moves 12 world px a
pass in each axis.

SprTrCheck (bank 6, behind DEBUG_TRCHK, off by default and costing
nothing off - code_end and spr2_end are unchanged) keeps each slot's
last-drawn position and counts pairs in opposite tranches whose UNION
of this pass's and last pass's footprints intersect. Exact, no pad,
because the pad is what is on trial. Three hex bytes at the top left
of the panel: the count and the last offending pair.

Harness validated by flipping one branch to count SAME-tranche
overlaps instead: 1D within seconds. The real test then stayed at 00
through minutes of a contrived worst case - droid types poked to class
16, shipLevel 31, the player armed so his 12 px/pass bullets were in
the air, INVULN on to survive it. The padding shortfall is real
arithmetic and does not produce a violated invariant in play. The
split is not the cause; BUGS.md #22 records what is ruled out and
where to look next.

events.title: Keep the source's symbols in suggested replacements
events.message:
Keep the source's symbols in suggested replacements

A replacement that carries a value through unchanged was writing the
number the expression evaluates to, so

    adda.w  #SCREEN_BW/2+(SCREEN_H/2*SCREEN_BW),a3

suggested `lea 1610(a3),a3`. That is a correct instruction and a bad
edit: it throws away the name that says what the value means, and
freezes a number that was meant to track the constant when it changes.
Replacements now reuse the operand's own source text, recovered from the
node's location, and the base a literal was written in survives too, so a
$3f mask stays hexadecimal rather than becoming 63.

Applied to the fifteen rules that copy a value rather than compute one.
Rules emitting a derived number -- a shift count from a multiplier, the
sum of two ADDQs, 16 minus a rotate count -- still write a number,
because there is no symbol left to keep.

Two normalisations are needed to make recovered text safe in an operand
field, neither of which changes meaning. Whitespace is stripped, since an
assembler ends the operand at the first space and `SCREEN_BW / 2 + 10`
would otherwise truncate to `SCREEN_BW`. Redundant enclosing parentheses
are dropped, since a displacement opening with `(` reads like an
addressing mode.

Negation, needed where SUB becomes LEA or a negative LEA displacement
becomes SUBQ, is only done in the text for a bare symbol or number.
Anything compound would need `-(...)`, and an operand opening with `-(`
is how predecrement is written, so those keep the evaluated number rather
than emit something an assembler may misread. Negating an existing minus
cancels, so `lea -SMALL(a0),a0` gives `subq.w #SMALL,a0`.

Impact audit unchanged at 0 regressions and 0 unmeasured, so 68kcounter
still sizes every replacement; differential checker unchanged.

events.title: Resolve constants across the project, without guessing
events.message:
Resolve constants across the project, without guessing

Files are linted one at a time, so a constant defined in an include was
simply unknown, and 67 of 88 rule files depend on resolving constants.
Rebuilding the real include hierarchy would need the program's entry
point and the assembler's include paths, neither of which is in the
source. Indexing every assembly and header file under the project
sidesteps that.

The index is monotonic by construction: it answers only for a name every
file that defines it agrees on. Where two files disagree -- a debug and a
release configuration, per-machine hardware headers -- the name stays
unknown and the dependent rules stay silent, exactly as before. So it can
turn "unknown" into "known" but never "known" into "wrong", which matters
because a misresolved constant makes rules fire at full confidence.

That property only holds on an honest foundation, and the existing
single-file table was not one. It resolved two different definitions of a
name to whichever came last, though which is in force depends on assembly
order and conditional arms we cannot evaluate; it now reports unknown. A
definition repeated identically is still not a conflict, since headers
get included twice. Definitions inside macro bodies are no longer file
constants: they belong to an expansion, may not exist until the macro is
invoked, and may differ between invocations.

The obvious next rule -- that a definition inside a conditional is
uncertain -- is deliberately absent. The include-guard idiom puts most
real constants inside one, so it would gut resolution. The genuinely
dangerous case, arms of an if/else that disagree, is already a conflict.

Diagnostics name the file a borrowed value came from. A constant taken
from a header the linter merely found is the likeliest thing to be wrong
about a report, and provenance turns a confident, inexplicable diagnostic
into one the reader can check.

Also fixes the CLI indexing the working directory rather than the
directory being linted when no config file marks the project root.

events.title: Make macros and REPT visible to the dataflow analysis
events.message:
Make macros and REPT visible to the dataflow analysis

The parser gives a macro call `mnemonic.type === "macro"`. Every layer
filtered on `type === "instruction"`, so a call was not a CFG node, was
skipped by the liveness fixpoint, and reported no register semantics at
all. A macro invocation was therefore modelled as a no-op that reads
nothing, which is the most dangerous possible default.

Reported symptom: dead-register-write flagged writes that the macro
went on to read. The same root cause was worse elsewhere. Because
nextInstruction stepped over macro lines, sequence rules matched runs of
instructions straddling a call, and their replacements span the matched
run -- prefer-link-sequence would collapse a frame setup around an
intervening macro and emit a LINK that deleted it.

A call is now opaque: operands count as reads, everything else is
unknown, all five condition codes become untrustworthy, and the
adjacent-instruction search stops rather than stepping over it.

Two related block-structure faults surfaced while testing this.

Macro definition bodies were analysed as ordinary straight-line code, so
flow ran from above a definition, through its body, and out below it --
a path that never executes. Definitions are now their own flow region
that nothing enters or leaves. The body is still analysed, because a
write its own body overwrites before reading is dead in every expansion,
but its last line escapes rather than reading as the end of the program.

REPT bodies had no back edge, so a value written late in an iteration
and read early in the next looked dead. The identical shape written as a
DBF loop was correctly quiet, which is what gave it away.

Precision is kept throughout: dead writes inside macro bodies and inside
REPT bodies are still reported, and a write spanning a macro definition
is still dead, since the definition emits nothing there.
