events.title: Add a differential semantic checker, and fix three rules it found
events.message:
Add a differential semantic checker, and fix three rules it found

The impact audit proved a replacement was cheaper. Nothing proved it was
equivalent: every rule's semantics rested on hand-reasoning in a comment.
`npm run verify:semantics` runs each audit case and its replacement on an
m68k interpreter from a seeded state and compares all sixteen registers
and the five condition-code bits.

It is a bug finder, not a prover, and does not gate CI. The interpreter
is a teaching tool whose own documentation disclaims full accuracy, so it
is calibrated against 29 documented 68000 behaviours first and a
difference is reported as a rule and an interpreter disagreeing. Two of
the first calibration failures were errors in the expectations rather
than the interpreter.

Results are bucketed by applicability, because a rule declaring itself
`conditional` has said it changes the condition codes and fires only
where they are dead; a flag difference there is the rule working as
documented. A register difference is excused by nothing.

Three real defects, now fixed and covered by unit tests:

- prefer-link-sequence claimed `safe` with no flag check. LINK sets no
  condition codes; the MOVE.L a6,-(SP) it replaces sets N and Z and
  clears V and C.
- quick-negative claimed `safe` with no flag check. ADD sets C on a carry
  out where SUB sets it on a borrow.
- negate-add-power-of-two-to-eor was off by one. XOR by a mask m maps x
  to m-x, so the identity pairs with ADD #m, not the next power of two:
  neg/add #8 of 3 is 5 where eor #7 of 3 is 4. Renamed to
  negate-add-mask-to-eor and now matches the mask.

Two things had to be handled to get coverage at all. The interpreter
panics after roughly 250 instantiations with no way to dispose one, so
the run is sharded across child processes; without that only 14 of 80
cases ran. And its assembler does not select the address form of
MOVE/ADD/SUB/CMP for an address-register destination, so it invented
flags for every rule touching SP until the address form was written out
explicitly.

80 cases now run: 57 identical, 23 differing only in declared flags,
0 unexplained.

events.title: Make the cross-binary comparison a tool, and it sharpens the finding
events.message:
Make the cross-binary comparison a tool, and it sharpens the finding

source/tools/xbin_diff.py replaces the throwaway script I ran three
times.  It takes a PRG or a whole .stx (running stx_extract.py itself)
and reports shared bytes, coverage PER REFERENCE FUNCTION using
lcp_sym.68k, and the longest runs.  Attribution comes from the symbol
table at run time rather than a hardcoded region map, so it follows the
build instead of going stale.

Documented in it, because it is the trap: relocated longwords hold
absolute addresses that two binaries never agree on, so a shared
function is chopped into one run per relocation site.  Judge by the
coverage column, never by run length.  Matches at or above 0x1733a are
DRI library and expected; matches below it are the finding.

Writing it properly immediately produced a sharper result than the
inline version had.  "1043 bytes somewhere in mq_*" resolves to
specific functions:

      _cp_main    7290 / 7500   97.2%
      _mq_bust     344 /  466   73.8%
      _mq_dise     556 / 1258   44.2%
      _mq_pars      45 /  662    6.8%
      _psg_wr       78 bytes
      _sf_irqp       0 /  456    NOTHING

So the descent from Music Studio's player is concentrated exactly where
it should be: mq_bust, the scale-table builder, is three-quarters
identical, and mq_dise, the MIDI-out dispatcher, nearly half.  CLAUDE.md
now carries the per-function table in both places that discuss it.

events.title: The bottom edge's blank was 3 cycles from the wrap
events.message:
The bottom edge's blank was 3 cycles from the wrap

A scanline is 128 CPU cycles, the display is cycles 0-79 and blanking
is 80-127, so fire 3's R8 write has to land in that window. Measured
in jsbeeb in gameplay - the phase of rt_drawok's STA CRTC_DATA against
a frame-paint anchor - it was starting at 121, 117 and 119 on three
consecutive frames, so the write landed at 120-124: three to seven
cycles of margin. The IRQ's own latency swings further than that (the
6502 finishes its instruction first, and SetCRTCStart's SEI window is
17 cycles), so the frames that overran put a character of the row
below the view in the bottom-left corner of the play area. KC saw it.

T1_TUNE -22 -> -32: 10 us, which moves every fire 20 cycles earlier
and centres fires 2 and 3 in blanking - fire 3's write measured at ~99
after, twice. Nothing crosses a line boundary, so no edge moves: the
same 120 scanlines are displayed. Fire 1's window is 16 SCANLINES wide
and does not care.

The old constant came from the T1_PROBE calibration recorded beside
it; reality had drifted ~6 us later than that arithmetic since, the
phase being a property of the whole IRQ path. docs/raster-timing.md
has the numbers and the measurement method, which is cheaper than
T1_PROBE and gives a number rather than a step to eyeball.

events.title: The cleared-deck stipple takes $240C's character filter
events.message:
The cleared-deck stipple takes $240C's character filter

LvClearedMark marked every cell of the deck's rectangle, and that
rectangle is not the deck's shape: lift_DeckWidth is 26 and 24 for the
two bottom decks - the whole hull at those rows, straight through the
middle engine decks - and the tall decks' rectangles overhang to the
right of a hull that steps in. So a cleared bottom deck stippled a
strip across the whole character row, and a cleared engine deck
stippled a solid rectangle over its neighbours.

The C64 gets away with the same table because lift_HighlightDeck
($240C) filters every cell by its CHARACTER before swapping it, and
that filter is what says which cells are the deck's. The walk now
reads the character shadow - the colour shadow's own pointer less
XS_COFF, borrowed and put back, so it still needs one zero-page pair -
and applies both arms, transliterated as LvHighlight already is.

112 B of bank 6 (664 free -> 552); nothing else moved.

Verified in jsbeeb on the console's ship page against a model of
$240C's filter run over the decoded side view: with 11/14/15 cleared
the shadow matches cell for cell, deck 14's row being cols 1-5, 7-9,
23, 25, 26 rather than a solid 26; with 10/12/13 cleared deck 10 marks
8, 10 and 11 cells on its three rows, stepping with the hull.

events.title: Music Studio cannot settle g_sfDoB -- but cp_main is 97% shared with it
events.message:
Music Studio cannot settle g_sfDoB -- but cp_main is 97% shared with it

Went looking for external evidence on the g_sfDoB size question.  The
Activision Music Studio ST disk is on this machine, and LCP's sequencer
descends from its player, so it was the obvious source.  Extracted it
with the project's own stx_extract.py and diffed AUDIO.PRG's text
against LCP_STX's by hashing 32-byte windows.

It does not settle the question.  10 063 bytes are shared, but
sf_irqp -- the function that copies into g_sfDoB -- shares ZERO of its
456 bytes, and the whole 0x400c-0x1733a game span shares nothing at
all.  That buffer's code is LCP's own, so Music Studio's layout says
nothing about it.  STANDARD.SND turns out to be an instrument-NAME
table (signature version 0x01), not Dosound data.  Avenue closed.

What the comparison DID find is worth more than the question that
prompted it:

  cp_main is Activision's, not LCP's.  Of cp_asm's 7 499 bytes, 7 289
  are byte-identical to Music Studio -- 97.2% -- and the largest single
  run is 6 904 bytes at LCP_STX 0x02514-0x0400C, ending exactly where
  cp_asm stops and stx_u1 begins.  The 210 bytes that differ sit in
  five islands, one of them 89 bytes, about the size of the
  self-decrypting block cp_main is documented to carry.  So this is a
  shared Activision protection routine with per-title constants, which
  independently corroborates that the region is hand assembly and not
  compiled C -- a second binary agreeing with a conclusion previously
  resting on the maintainer's word plus a relocation argument.

  The MIDI sequencer really does share code: 1 043 of mq_*'s 5 212
  bytes, plus 78 around mq_tick.  That is the player lineage the shared
  .SNG format already implied, now byte-confirmed.

Everything else shared is DRI library, expected of two Alcyon builds.

Docs only; shipped build still MD5 eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10.

events.title: copperhf: key the DMA-coherency latch on actual writes; consume it on read hits
events.message:
copperhf: key the DMA-coherency latch on actual writes; consume it on read hits

Address both findings from the PR #654 Copilot review:

1. Bus::devices_wrote_memory was latched from DeviceHost::touched_memory,
   which memory_mut() sets on ANY access -- and the A2091 ticks
   memory_mut() unconditionally (WASM boards likewise), so every timed-
   device flush would have cleared the whole data cache and disabled the
   model in practice on such machines. The latch is now keyed on actual
   DMA writes only: DeviceHost gains wrote_memory, set by its
   dma_write_word/dma_write helpers (copperhf and the WASM plugin host
   route through them already) and by note_wrote_memory() for boards that
   pump DMA through the free helpers -- the A2091 gets the same private
   write latch the SDMAC got, forwarded from its tick wrapper. The CDTV
   DMAC tick never touches guest memory (its sector DMA rides the
   synchronous register-access path), so it needs nothing. The
   synchronous access path keeps its conservative touched_memory clear,
   unchanged pre-existing behaviour.

2. The instruction-boundary coherent flush alone left the JIT batch path
   exposed: a slow MMIO access mid-batch flushes timed devices (whose
   tick can DMA), and later instructions in the same up-to-64-instruction
   batch could still hit the stale line -- a polling driver (the boot
   mounter's chf_do_io shape) reads a completion register and then the
   DMA'd bytes without passing a boundary. read_sized now consumes the
   latch and drops the data cache before serving any data-read cache
   hit, closing the window for JIT and interpreter alike.

The regression test now pins all three properties: boundary-flush
coherence, read-hit latch consumption with no intervening boundary, and
that idle device ticks do not latch (the precision half of finding 1).
Verified the 68040 [cpu] dcache repro boots with and without --jit.

events.title: Map the remaining globals; fix four wrong rows found doing it
events.message:
Map the remaining globals; fix four wrong rows found doing it

The coverage figure was the first thing wrong.  "~366/397, remaining
~93" came from comparing lcp_sym.68k's 8-char TRUNCATED linkage names
against this file's full names, so lcp_watr, introSeq, date_day and
dozens more counted as unmapped when they were not -- the exact trap
the file's own instructions warn about.  Expanding the truncations and
dropping DRI libc and the AES library's gl_apid leaves THIRTEEN port
globals, not ninety-three.

Those thirteen now have a table of their own with what each one does,
derived from use sites: the three action tables, g_trel, g_rphs, the
four graf_handle metrics, psg_epp/psg_ovol/psg_vrg, and g_unus3 (= -1,
referenced by nothing -- same class as mi_sig and cmd_num).  They are
NOT given invented Ghidra names: at those addresses Ghidra has either a
PTR_ARRAY_xxx placeholder or the port's own name from the address-keyed
sync, so there is no 1985 name left to recover and manufacturing one
would fake the provenance this table exists to record.

Checking them turned up four wrong rows, three of which the file itself
had flagged as unverified ("assignment ... is by role"):

  The action tables are g_atact / g_atmod / g_atrel, each [16] and
  indexed rndRng(0,15) in airandom.c by the resident's activity level.
  They were paired with g_obala / g_obcla / g_obpha, which are OBJECT
  ANIMATION frame lists fed to od_draw -- and which this same file
  pairs, correctly, with object_alarm/clock/phone_animation further
  down.  g_obala appeared twice with contradictory meanings.  Settled
  by address: g_obala is Ghidra 0x2b92a and dat_u3a.c's own comment
  reads "alarm_animation @ 0x2B92A".

  triggered_event_list is g_trel, not pst_arr.  g_trel is Ghidra
  0x2b6da -- exactly the address globals.c cited for that name, in a
  comment sitting above pst_arr's declaration by mistake.  g_trel is
  the FIFO putEv appends to; pst_arr is a scratch buffer for player
  STATES and has no descriptive name.  That comment is corrected too.

Coverage re-measured after the edits: 417 port globals, 0 undocumented.

Comments and docs only.  prg_diff BYTE-IDENTICAL, MD5
eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10, reloc_audit clean (E=1 scrbufA).

events.title: Record prior art and what is worth borrowing from it
events.message:
Record prior art and what is worth borrowing from it

Several rules here turn out to be textbook compiler analyses arrived at
independently: dead-register-write is dead store elimination, known-zero-clear
is constant propagation, the multiply rules are strength reduction. Worth
knowing what the established tools do about the same problems.

Three findings that bear on decisions already taken or pending:

Clippy publishes definitions for correctness and suspicious that match the
distinction reached here by argument, which settles whether keeping both is
reasonable. It also has a nursery category for lints that are plausible but not
yet trusted, which this project has no equivalent for.

Massalin's 1987 superoptimizer paper did exhaustive peephole search on the
68000 specifically. Every optimization rule here was transcribed from a
document, so it is limited to what someone wrote down; search scored by
68kcounter would find peepholes no document lists.

The audit proves a replacement is cheaper and nothing proves it is equivalent.
Alive2 does that for LLVM with SMT; the 68000 does not need SMT, since
differential testing over an interpreter would do. The audit already holds 110
before/after pairs, so the missing piece is an execution engine.

events.title: Extend dead-register-write to loads, and move it to suspicious
events.message:
Extend dead-register-write to loads, and move it to suspicious

A dead write is almost always a typo, where the write was meant for a different
register, rather than an intentional waste of two bytes. Reporting it as a
missed optimization frames it as a saving when the useful message is that it
looks wrong, so the rule is now suspicious. It loses the measured saving line
and its audit case; neither was carrying the point.

A dead load from memory is now reported too. That was excluded before because
removing it could drop an access to a register that changes state when read.
Withholding the diagnostic was the wrong response to that: the concern is
whether removal is safe, not whether the dead write is worth knowing about. So
a load is reported with no replacement and manual applicability, with a note
about the possible side effect, while the register and immediate cases keep the
plain safe removal.

The extension is only sound because of the preceding commit. Postincrement and
predecrement now write their address register, so the single-register check
excludes them; before that fix they looked like ordinary reads and would have
been offered for removal, silently stopping the pointer advancing.

Dead stores to memory remain out of scope, needing alias analysis.

events.title: Record that postincrement and predecrement write their address register
events.message:
Record that postincrement and predecrement write their address register

An addEaSideEffectWrite helper existed and was correct, but was only called
from the MOVEM branch of getRegisterSemantics. Every other instruction reported
(a2)+ as reading a2 and not writing it, so the value analysis carried the
pre-increment constant forward: after lea $1000,a2 / move.w (a2)+,d1 it
believed a2 was still $1000 rather than unknown.

That is a soundness problem for anything resolving an address register from a
propagated constant, the Amiga custom-register checks included, where a
stepped pointer would name the wrong register.

Applied once centrally rather than in each of the branches, since every one of
them would otherwise have to remember. Liveness is unaffected: the register is
read as well as written, and reads already take precedence there.

Found while checking whether the dead-register-write rule could safely be
extended to memory operands - it could not have been, because the postincrement
would have looked like a pure read.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add optimization/dead-register-write
events.message:
Add optimization/dead-register-write

Flags a register write whose value is overwritten before anything reads it.
Often a typo rather than dead weight - the write was meant for a different
register - so the diagnostic says that as well as offering the removal.

Deliberately narrow, because removing an instruction is only sound when nothing
else depended on it:

- exactly one register written, so MOVEM and the like are out;
- that register provably dead, not merely unknown, so a value surviving to a
  return is left alone;
- every flag the instruction writes or leaves undefined also dead. This is what
  keeps `add.l d0,d1` before a `moveq` into the same register: ADD sets X, MOVEQ
  does not overwrite it, so X escapes and the ADD stays;
- register and immediate operands only. A load may be from a location that
  changes state when read, so removing it would change behaviour rather than
  save time. LEA is the exception, since it computes an address without
  dereferencing and its source must be a control addressing mode.

Measures -2 bytes and -4 cycles on the representative case.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Do not flag a narrow load over a known seed value
events.message:
Do not flag a narrow load over a known seed value

moveq #0,d2 followed by move.b 0(a2,d1.w),d2 is the ordinary way to zero-extend
a narrow load. The preserved upper bits are the whole point, and the rule was
reporting them as though they were leftovers.

The test is whether the register holds a known constant beforehand, not whether
a particular instruction precedes it. Constant propagation supplies that, so the
seed can be any distance away with unrelated work in between, and CLR or a
non-zero seed count just as much as MOVEQ #0. Where the upper bits genuinely
come from somewhere unknown, the rule still fires.

events.title: Move stale-condition-code to suspicious; lay rule files out by category
events.message:
Move stale-condition-code to suspicious; lay rule files out by category

The rule fires precisely when no concrete definition of the tested flag can be
shown to reach the conditional. In practice that usually means the producer is
in another file, or the routine is entered from elsewhere: an analysis
limitation rather than a proven fault. Relying on the CCR surviving across
address arithmetic is a deliberate technique too, as the EAB thread describes.

Its sibling suspicious/condition-after-preserved-ccr fires when a definition
can be shown to reach across a preserving instruction, so the less certain of
the two was carrying the stronger category. Recorded in
docs/rule-id-migrations.md for anyone with an override.

Rule files now sit under <category>/<platform>/ rather than a separate
platform/ tree, so the path mirrors the rule ID:
correctness/amiga-tas-unsupported lives in
correctness/amiga/tas-unsupported.ts. The layout guard follows, still allowing
a platform subdirectory to carry the platform name rather than repeating it in
the filename.

events.title: Mine the remaining sources: two rules, one target gate, one conflict settled
events.message:
Mine the remaining sources: two rules, one target gate, one conflict settled

carry-to-mask-via-subx, from the EAB thread: scs/ext.w/ext.l spreading the
carry across a register is a single subx.l dn,dn. The catch is that SCS reads C
while SUBX reads X, and CMP sets C without touching X, so after a comparison
the substitution would use a stale flag. It fires only when one instruction is
the reaching definition of both, which is exactly when they agree; a test pins
the CMP case as rejected.

arithmetic-immediate-via-scratch, from Optimizing 680x0 Applications: a long
immediate in the MOVEQ range costs two extension words, so routing it through a
dead scratch register is shorter and quicker. Measures -2 bytes and -4 cycles.
Leaves 1..8 to ADDQ and SUBQ, and is not offered for the 68040, which prefers
the immediate form.

The same document reverses the indexed-addressing preference by target: the
68000 family and 68060 favour the indexed mode, the 68020 and 68040 favour
precomputing the address. fold-index-into-effective-address, added earlier
today with no gating, is now restricted to the targets where it is a win.

One cross-source conflict settled by measurement rather than by picking a side.
The 680x0 performance guide says "and's and or's (even immediate versions) are
very often faster than bit sets/clears", which would contradict prefer-bset and
prefer-bclr. For the long-immediate forms those rules match, exact auditing
measures the bit instructions as cheaper, so they stand. Recorded in
docs/source-review.md rather than left to be re-litigated.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Drop the ADDQ/SUBQ address word-size rules; add three from the EAB thread
events.message:
Drop the ADDQ/SUBQ address word-size rules; add three from the EAB thread

Yacht settles the ADDQ question. M68000UM lists ADDQ.W #<data>,An as 4(1/0),
and Yacht records that as an error: the same microwords drive it as ADDQ.L
#<data>,An, patent USP4325121 gives 8 cycles, real-hardware evaluation confirms
8, and 8 makes ADDQ and SUBQ coherent. The EAB thread reaches the same
conclusion independently by measurement, and since 68kcounter is built on
Yacht, our own audit already measured zero difference. There is no size
difference either, so both rules did nothing. Removed, and their ASP68K rows
marked rejected rather than implemented.

Three rules added from the thread:

- mask-via-moveq: a load followed by a MOVEQ-sized mask is shorter the other
  way round, seeding the register with MOVEQ and ANDing the source in. Measures
  -4 bytes, -10 cycles.
- data-register-sign-bit-to-tas: bset #7,dn and ori.b #$80,dn are a single TAS.
  Separate from the memory-form rule and on by default, because a
  data-register operand performs no memory access and so carries none of the
  read-modify-write risk. Each form proves a different set of flags dead, since
  BSET and ORI differ from TAS in different ways.
- fold-index-into-effective-address: an index added to an address register
  purely to dereference it is what the indexed mode already does. Requires the
  base to be provably dead, since the fold leaves it unchanged.

A fourth was written and dropped. Replacing move.w/ext.l with movem.w to get
the sign extension free measures as a regression on one register: same size,
four cycles and one read worse. The thread says so in passing - MOVEM only
breaks even at three registers - which I had skimmed past; the audit caught it.
Recorded in docs/source-review.md along with the two claims that did not
survive measurement.

events.title: copperhf: make host-DMA coherent with the modelled 030/040/060 data cache
events.message:
copperhf: make host-DMA coherent with the modelled 030/040/060 data cache

A 68040 guest reading PFS3 volumes through copperhf.device got corrupted
file data ("version: file is not executable" straight out of the
startup-sequence) while the same image worked on an EC020 or through the
PIO-based IDE path. Root cause: copperhf drains completed reads on the
bus TICK path -- the host writes the payload and io_Actual/io_Error into
guest fast RAM asynchronously -- and the tick loop never consulted
DeviceHost::touched_memory, so the CPU's modelled data cache (which exec
40.10 enables at coldstart on an 040) kept serving stale lines over the
DMA'd bytes. The synchronous device-access path already dropped the
dcache on touched_memory; the asynchronous half was missing.

Fix both sides of the contract:

Host: Bus::devices_wrote_memory latches any device-tick DMA into guest
memory (the Zorro device loop, the CDTV DMAC, and the A3000 SDMAC's
pump_dma, which had the same latent bug for fast-RAM SCSI buffers), and
CpuBus::flush_timed_devices_dcache_coherent consumes it at every
instruction-boundary flush, dropping the dcache. Regression test
device_tick_dma_invalidates_dcache_at_coherent_flush pins the failure
and the fix.

Guest: the driver now performs exec's busmaster DMA cache maintenance
(V37+; no-op on Kickstart 1.3, which has neither the vectors nor cached
CPUs): CachePreDMA over the request block and data buffers in BeginIO
before the doorbell, and chf_post_dma -- called from int_handler.s
before each ReplyMsg, and from the mounter's polled chf_do_io --
CachePostDMA's the request block first (so the host-written fields it
then reads are fresh) and then the read/geometry/SCSICmd buffers. This
also makes the driver correct on genuinely cached silicon, not just
under the emulator's cache model. ROM rebuilt: 4472 -> 5212 bytes.

Verified: the full copperhf kickstart matrix (1.3/3.1/3.2/AROS incl.
both PFS3->4GiB axes), the whole default suite, and a real 9.6GB PFS3
disk image booting and running WHDLoad games on a 68040 with
[cpu] dcache = true.

events.title: Fix two false positives found in the EAB thread
events.message:
Fix two false positives found in the EAB thread

The saved EAB "68000 code optimisations" thread turned up two rules reporting
correct code, both confirmed against the linter before changing anything.

TAS on a data register is safe on Amiga, and the thread is emphatic about it:
"TAS Dx is perfectly safe, it does not do any memory accesses." What the custom
chip DMA cannot arbitrate is the locked read-modify-write cycle TAS uses to
reach memory. The rule flagged every TAS, including TAS Dn, at error severity.

Deferring stack cleanup across several TOS calls and removing all the
parameters with one adjustment is a documented idiom, shown in the thread as
two traps followed by a single addq.l #4,sp. The rule compared each call
against the next instruction, so it reported every call but the last. Pushes
are now accumulated across calls and compared against the adjustment that
eventually follows, which also catches the case where the batched total is
wrong.

sources/ is ignored by git and prettier. It holds third-party reference
material - forum dumps and copyrighted documents - kept locally for mining
rather than redistributed. Say if you would rather it were committed.

events.title: Add suspicious/movem-restore-mismatch
events.message:
Add suspicious/movem-restore-mismatch

A MOVEM save and its matching restore have to move the same register list, and
the two are edited separately so they drift apart. When the counts differ the
stack pointer is left unbalanced and the routine returns to garbage; when the
counts match but the registers do not, the stack survives and registers quietly
take each other's values, which is the harder version to find by hand.

Pairing is a linear scan keeping a stack of pending saves per base register.
Being wrong about which save a restore belongs to would produce confident
nonsense, so it stays quiet whenever pairing is not knowable:

- nothing pending, which is normal for a routine with more than one exit, since
  the first exit consumed the save;
- a restore matching a deeper pending save rather than the top, meaning the
  nesting cannot be resolved by a linear scan;
- anything still pending at RTS/RTE/RTR/RTD is discarded, so one routine's
  leftovers are never blamed on the next.

The message names which registers are saved but not restored and vice versa,
covers a size mismatch where the lists agree, and points at the line of the
matching save. Register sets are printed back in the d0-d3/a0 spelling rather
than expanded. Stacks held in an address register other than A7 are handled, as
is the single-register MOVEM spelling.

action-ID table had gone stale on top of that -- it listed ACTION_HELLO
as 18 where enums.h says 24.

Rewritten to test the shipped code with no gate at all.  New shared
harness tools/hatari_probe.sh runs the gated build headless with
--cmd-fifo, injects real keystrokes through the IKBD, and reads the
game's own globals out of memory, so every assertion is against the
variable the code actually writes.

test_keyboard.sh checks all ten deal_kc paths: lcp_watr for Ctrl-W,
putEv entry for the five event keys, value-change breakpoints for the
transient alarm_p and g_ptdoa, g_aliss for Return, and g_cdibp for the
erase key from BOTH Backspace and the cursor-left arrow.  Ctrl-P's
dg_petok guard is forced from the debugger because no typed command
reaches a_calld.  11/11.

test_actions.sh types every command the parser can accept and checks
the action against what the tables say it should be.  The expectations
are DERIVED from vocab data at run time rather than hard-coded, so
they cannot go stale the way the old ID list did; what is under test is
chk_encm agreeing with the tables it reads.  It also asserts that the
two rows which can never fire produce nothing.  33/33.

Four things the harness had to get right, each of which first showed up
as a plausible-looking failure in the thing under test:

  * The load base is DISCOVERED, by hunting bm32or's 1,2,4,8,16 longs
    and deriving the base from where they actually are.  It differs by
    launch path and a wrong one reads plausible garbage rather than
    failing.
  * Debugger replies are matched by the ADDRESS they print.  The FIFO
    is one-way with no request ids, so a late reply was being read as
    the answer to the next question -- which returns the PREVIOUS value
    and looks exactly like an off-by-one in the parser.
  * Keystrokes are injected far faster than the game consumes them (one
    per tick), so a fixed sleep after a 24-character command reads the
    previous command's result.  The script polls g_aliss instead.
  * g_aliss is reset before each command.  The queue is 10 deep and
    prsCmd silently drops the rest, so 33 commands cannot just be
    poured in.

Also: hatari-event takes a single alphanumeric character OR a NUMBER,
and a number is an ST scancode, not ASCII -- so Ctrl combinations hold
scancode 29 and space/Return/Backspace/left go in as 57/28/14/75.

events.title: Detect init source globs from files, not directory names
events.message:
Detect init source globs from files, not directory names

Sources in the project root are a common m68k layout, and the previous
detection guessed from directory names (src, asm and similar), so it suggested
src/** whenever such a directory existed and fell back to ** only when none
did. A project with sources in the root got a glob that silently missed them.

Detection now looks for assembly files:

  sources in the root              -> **
  sources only in subdirectories   -> those subdirectories
  sources in both                  -> **, since a narrower glob would miss some
  none found                       -> **

Build output, dot directories and node_modules are skipped, and the search is
depth-limited. A directory is suggested because it holds assembly files, not
because of what it is called.

events.title: Add m68k-lint --init to write a project config interactively
events.message:
Add m68k-lint --init to write a project config interactively

Asks for platform, processors, optimization goal and the style preset, then
writes m68k-lint.json.

Details that make the output better than a template:

- Source globs are suggested from directories that actually exist (src, asm and
  similar), rather than guessing.
- Only answers differing from the defaults are written. A config restating the
  defaults is noise, and it silently pins behaviour the user never chose.
- An ignore entry naming a bare directory gets the trailing /** it needs. Any
  pattern without it matches nothing, and does so silently, which is the trap
  most likely to catch someone writing their first config.
- Unknown processors are rejected rather than written out.
- The file is shown before writing, and an existing config is not overwritten
  without asking.

No dependencies: node:readline/promises, keeping the CLI dependency-free.
Without a TTY it exits 2 with a pointer to the schema instead of hanging.

The prompt logic lives in src/cli/init.ts behind a small Prompt interface, so
the whole flow is driven by tests without a terminal; the readline wrapper is
tested against a fake. src/cli coverage rises from 32% to 38%.

events.title: mi_pgtab: Ghidra's midi_channel_volume is wrong, and so is one more
events.message:
mi_pgtab: Ghidra's midi_channel_volume is wrong, and so is one more

The port is right and Ghidra's descriptive name is not.  mq_sepc
builds `g_meve[0] = (mi_chmap[index] & 0xf) | 0xc0` -- 0xC0 is the MIDI
Program Change status byte -- and the following `g_meve[1] =
mi_pgmap[index]` is therefore a program NUMBER, cached per physical
channel in g_mcpro.  mq_pacm confirms the shape: it loads two parallel
15-entry tables out of the song header, the channel map from bytes
0..14 and the program map from 15..29.  Volume never enters it, and
the initialiser {0,0,1,2,...,13,0x11} reads as default programs, not
as volumes (a default of 0 on channel 1 would be silence).

Auditing the rest of the address-keyed batch for the same failure
turned up a second: `midi_dma_start_lo` sits on pk_pscore, the
poker/blackjack PLAYER SCORE that games.c compares against pk_cscore
throughout.  Nothing MIDI touches it.

Both are the same mistake -- naming an unlabelled cell from its
neighbourhood rather than its use -- so the section now says plainly
that co-location is not agreement, marks the two rows `(Ghidra
WRONG)`, and tells the reader to check use sites before adopting any
Ghidra name.  The database itself is already correct: the sync renamed
both cells to the port names, so this table was the only place the bad
names survived.

Also fixed the file's own instructions, which still told the reader to
run apply_ghidra_renames.sh -- the dead HTTP pipeline whose endpoint
does not answer and whose scripts are not installed.  It now documents
sync_ghidra_names.sh, the Ghidra-must-be-closed rule, and the three
address/truncation traps.

events.title: Test every typed command; two rows can never fire
events.message:
Test every typed command; two rows can never fire

Enumerated the parser's whole surface from the tables rather than
guessing at phrasings: each word ORs bm_lo[g_ew2b[w]] into
g_ewb[ew2pos[w]], each g_ew2a row is a 10-byte mask plus action and
priority, and a row fires when its mask is a subset of the accumulated
bits, first match winning.  PLAY GAME -> row 22 -> action 16 validates
the model against behaviour already observed.

33 rows, 31 reachable, and all 31 verified in the emulator against
g_aqueu/g_aliss -- one command per row, from MAKE LOG to WHAT IN
NIGHTSTAND.

Two rows can never fire, and the byte-identical tables say so, meaning
these are the original's quirks and not port bugs.  Both predictions
were then confirmed by typing them: neither queued anything.

  Row 0, ACTION_HELLO, needs byte 9 bits 0x01|0x02, but all five words
  that reach byte 9 -- EXCUSE, PARDON, HELLO, ATTENTION, HEY -- carry
  0x02 and nothing supplies 0x01.  The greeting is unreachable from
  the keyboard.

  Row 6, the MESSY IS HOME phrasing of ACTION_CLEAN_UP, needs byte 4
  bit 0x08, supplied only by IS at vwd_tab index 84 -- a duplicate that
  chk_vwd can never return, since it takes the first spelling match at
  index 26.  The action still has row 5, TIDY UP OUGHT.

That duplicate is one of four dead vocabulary entries: START (35),
LIKE (71) and IS (84) are shadowed by earlier copies, and PLEASE at
index 0 is dead because chk_encm reads chk_vwd's 0 as "unrecognised" --
so the politeness word cannot contribute its bit and instead draws the
+4 priority penalty unknown words get.

events.title: Retract the KEY_CURSOR_LEFT misnomer claim -- the name is correct
events.message:
Retract the KEY_CURSOR_LEFT misnomer claim -- the name is correct

Testing the rename turned up that there was nothing to rename.  getKey
has `case 0x4b: return 8;` and 0x4b IS the cursor-left scancode,
reached because the arrow's ASCII byte is zero; Backspace independently
IS ASCII 8.  The two keys are aliases and both erase a character.
Measured: the ARROW takes g_cdibp 5 -> 4 and nulls g_cdinb[4].

The claim in 1870690 came from a test run with turbo on, where the
arrow appeared dead.  It was the tx_sctm confound documented in the
same section: key code 8 is not in tick.c's exempt list, so a key
arriving after tx_sctm has expired hits `g_cdibp = 0` first and the
erase then finds an empty buffer.  I had already found that confound
for plain typing and failed to apply it to the arrow result before
writing it down.

is NOT 0x12596 under the MCP -- run_program puts text at 0x12492, and
a wrong base reads plausible garbage instead of failing, so derive it
at run time (the longs 1,2,4,8,16 are bm32or and pin it in one read).
An earlier session's introSeq/dg_init numbers used the wrong base;
re-verified correctly, both are 0 and the conclusion stands, but only
the screenshots had ever really supported it.  Memory can be read
while the machine RUNS, which avoids pause/resume round trips eating
emulated time.  And with turbo on, tx_sctm's 160 ticks expire between
two MCP calls, so transient state must be caught with a value-change
breakpoint -- ($addr).w ! ($addr).w -- not by polling.

events.title: Analyse mi_lstk's 488-byte hole; the BSS accounting closes
events.message:
Analyse mi_lstk's 488-byte hole; the BSS accounting closes

Chased the second unexplained hole.  It is open like g_sfDoB's, but
weaker and harmless, and the work turned up an invariant worth keeping.

The invariant: lo68 gives the port 185892 bytes of BSS where the
reference has 187450 -- bss_remap only patches the header -- so the
reference holds 1558 bytes no port symbol claims.  Summing the gap
between each remapped symbol and its declared size accounts for 1556
of them, the missing 2 being the last symbol's tail.  So every other
byte of the reference's BSS is claimed and the port's sizes are right
everywhere a gap does not show.  27 gaps exist; 24 are <= 20 bytes of
alignment slop.  The three real ones are scrbufA (533, category E and
undecidable), mi_lstk (488) and g_sfDoB (340) -- i.e. exactly the
symbols whose size the image cannot report.

On mi_lstk itself, two things make it weaker than g_sfDoB.  Nothing is
referenced inside the gap, so unlike g_sfDoB there is no forced struct
reading: "bigger array" and "200 plus a dead ~488-byte global" are both
unforced, and dead declarations are known here (mi_sig, cmd_num).  And
the size has no behavioural consequence: mq_pshl guards mi_evcn < 49
and mq_popl reads [mi_evcn-2], so the highest byte touched is 49*4+3 =
199 of 200 and no overrun is possible at any size >= 200.

Also recorded: the empty sentinel is mi_evcn == 9 and mq_zero seeds 9,
so indices 0..8 are dead at the front as well -- only [9..49] is ever
touched, a 164-byte window in a 688-byte allocation.  And one avenue is
closed: the 1985 linker's .comm order is not source order, so
declaration order cannot place a hypothetical dead global.

events.title: instdisk: a backslash in a typed destination is not a separator on the Amiga — make it one
events.message:
instdisk: a backslash in a typed destination is not a separator on the Amiga — make it one

Field report, A1200, 2026-09-05: "I typed the path of Personal:Games\OpenUA\
but I didn't see it anywhere". AmigaDOS separates with '/' and treats '\' as
an ordinary filename character, so that destination was ONE component: the
module went into a drawer literally named "Games\OpenUA\" at the root of
Personal: — present, and invisible unless you knew to look for a drawer with
backslashes in its name.

Nobody means a backslash in an Amiga path. The console installer now turns
each one into '/', strips a trailing separator, and prints the path it will
actually use before doing anything. Atari builds are untouched: there '\' IS
the separator and '/' is accepted too. The Workbench Install icon route never
types a path at all (askdir), so it was never exposed.

Test: a destination typed as "<tmp>\Games\OpenUA\" lands in <tmp>/Games/OpenUA,
no directory with a backslash in its name is created, and the final line names
the normalised path. The Curse disk set on the stick was rebuilt so its disk 1
carries this instdisk.

A1200 report, 2026-09-05: the Curse of the Azure Bonds disk set "is using the
older one that is text based and I have no clue where it put the files". Both
halves were real.

WHERE IT WENT. The set was built as plain OpenUA-Data-N disks, so disk 1
carried the console installer (instdisk) and that is what got run. Its
default destination is DH0:OpenUA, taken on a bare RETURN — and CREATED if
absent, so on a machine whose real OpenUA drawer lives elsewhere the module
lands in a brand-new drawer on DH0: that looks empty. The destination was
printed once, at the top, before five disks of file names scrolled it away.
instdisk now ENDS with two lines that cannot be missed: the design's final
path ("The design Curse.dsn is now in <dest>/Curse.dsn - pick it with SELECT
A DESIGN"), and, when the destination had to be created, a NOTE saying so and
what to do about it. The design is taken from the FIRST manifest path only,
so a base-game set (root files first) never calls its bundled HEIRS a design.

THE OLDER ONE. mkdatadisks.sh grows MODULE=<Name>: volumes are labelled
<Name>-Data-N (instdisk matches disks by the DISK.LST header, never by volume
name, so nothing else changes — and the set can no longer be mistaken for the
base game's), the manifest is titled "<Name> module", and disk 1 carries a
Workbench Install icon like the engine disk's: IconX opens a console that
says this installs a module INTO an existing OpenUA drawer, then the OS
Installer asks the one question that matters — "Where is your OpenUA drawer?"
(default DH0:OpenUA, warns if there is no frua there) — copies the module into
it, and exits naming the destination. Workbench 3.1 has no Installer, so the
same icon falls back to instdisk, as the engine disk does.

instdisk also had no host test until now, and its first run under one was
KILLED mid-spin: the "insert an engine disk (s to skip)" prompt re-prompted
forever on a stdin that could never answer. EOF is now "s".
tests/test_instdisk.py pins the design line, the created-destination note as
the LAST thing printed, and the base-game control.

Rebuilt the Curse set with MODULE=Curse (Curse-Data-1..5, 5 disks, Install on
disk 1, disk 4 still carries the module's own MUSIC.SLB) and put it on the
Gotek stick with a README that matches; the instdisk on disk 1 is the one
built here.

events.title: 3d: the sky/floor flash was the PALETTE landing before the pixels (#20, the visible half)
events.message:
3d: the sky/floor flash was the PALETTE landing before the pixels (#20, the visible half)

The v0.9.22 fix memoised load_backdrop's 160 KB re-read (7 loads -> 2 on a
walk). It did not fix the report: the user still saw the flash on 0.9.23,
crossing outside <-> inside. Two reasons, and the second is the whole story:
a one-entry memo cannot help alternating between two zones, and the disk
read was never the VISIBLE part.

On a live-palette backend (AGA, TT: hw_palette) qd_set_palette lands in the
hardware CLUT immediately — aga_set_palette writes the copper words and "the
copper replays both every frame". So the instant load_backdrop installed the
NEW zone's band, the display, still showing the OLD backdrop's pixels,
rendered them through the new colours for the whole render until the
present. That is the flash: exactly the sky/floor region, one render long,
longer on a stock A1200. Same family as the ECS titles (#165), where the fix
was "planes and palette change together at the flip".

qd_set_palette_deferred: on a hw_palette backend the band is queued and
installed right after the backend present, so pixels and palette change
together; on quantiser and true-colour backends it installs immediately (the
ECS cut needs the palette before it runs). The clean-present skip will not
swallow a pending band. Only load_backdrop uses it — colour cycling and
every other palette write are untouched.

Proof in both directions, in amiberry, using the stretch-the-race trick from
FRUA_SLOWPRESENT: -DFRUA_BACKFLASH=40 holds the engine for 40 ticks right
after the band is queued, so what the display shows in that window can be
screenshotted. BEFORE: the sky pixels wearing the indoor band, held still
(frame f10). AFTER, the same sky -> indoor transition (zone 19 -> 8,
confirmed in DBG.LOG): no such frame — the sky keeps its own colours through
the hold and the indoor view appears whole. The probe stays under #ifdef.
Falcon (immediate arm) and TT (deferred arm) boot and walk in Hatari; all
four targets build; 557 host tests pass.

events.title: Take ownership of diagnostic notes instead of citing sources
events.message:
Take ownership of diagnostic notes instead of citing sources

Notes read as the linter's own findings and explain the mechanism, rather than
repeating what a document says:

  before: ASP68K records a 4-byte size saving for this form.
  after:  MOVEQ encodes the value in the instruction word, so no extension
          words are needed.

A reader fixing their code has no way to check what ASP68K said, and a claim we
repeat is a claim we own. Explaining why also avoids restating the measured
line, which now reports size and cycles directly.

Roughly 60 note, message and suggestion strings across 63 rule files. Where a
note was purely a size or speed claim it now gives the reason instead, since
the measurement is authoritative and displayed.

The CLI's "source size claim" line is gone. It named the source outright and
was pure provenance; the claim stays in JSON output, where the audit can still
use it. The measurement notes no longer name 68kcounter either.

Provenance is untouched where it belongs: docs.source, docs.note, the ASP68K
and Flamewing coverage manifests, and code comments. The generated rule
documentation still shows a Source column for all 105 attributed rules.

A new test guards emitted messages, notes and suggestions against attribution
creeping back. It caught one rule both of my sweeps had missed.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Merge prefer-lea-for-address-symbol into movea-immediate-to-lea
events.message:
Merge prefer-lea-for-address-symbol into movea-immediate-to-lea

The two rules never both fired - evaluate().known made them mutually exclusive -
but the split was on the wrong axis, and it rested on a claim the project's own
audit disproves.

Both measured neutral: size 0, cpu 0, r 0, w 0. So ASP68K's 68000/68010 speed
win for MOVEA #n,An -> LEA is not borne out, and that claim was the only thing
separating the rules. Both are really about clarity and letting the assembler
relax the operand to PC-relative.

Splitting on "does the immediate fold to a constant?" produced three problems.
An equ-defined address such as `SCREEN equ $10000` is a symbolic address load,
but folded, so it went to the ASP68K branch and got `lea SCREEN.l,a0` - the
forced suffix pinning it to absolute long and defeating the relaxation. On
68020+ that case got no diagnostic at all, because the CPU gate existed only to
serve the disproven speed claim. And a code label was handled while an
equ-defined address was not, which is arbitrary from the outside.

The merged rule covers both, on all targets, since anything loaded into an
address register is an address. `.L` emits no size suffix so the assembler can
relax; `.W` keeps its suffix, because MOVEA.W sign-extends and without it
#$8000 could assemble as $00008000 rather than $FFFF8000.

The ASP68K provenance and coverage row are kept, with the note corrected to
record that measurement contradicts the source. This follows the precedent set
in v0.39.8 for combine-consecutive-addq.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Condense CLI impact output to one line
events.message:
Condense CLI impact output to one line

Five lines of measurement became one, in the cycles(reads,writes) shape the 68k
manuals and 68kcounter use:

  saves: 4 bytes, 8(2,0) cycles

Numbers read as savings rather than raw deltas, so positive means cheaper than
before and a cost appears as a negative saving. With colour, savings are green,
costs red and no change grey. The separate size, assessment and per-metric cycle
lines are gone; the assessment is still in JSON output and drives
--impact-summary.

The suggestion heading is now "fix:". It previously read "suggestion:" directly
beneath the "suggestion" severity column, which looked like a bug.

Added --color to force colours on when stdout is not a TTY, which is also what
makes the colouring testable.

The formatting helpers moved to src/cli/format.ts because main.ts runs the CLI
on import and so cannot be imported by a test. The sign inversion is easy to get
backwards later, so it now has direct tests.

events.title: Clarify the NOP-before-RTE exemption: labels yes, instructions no
events.message:
Clarify the NOP-before-RTE exemption: labels yes, instructions no

Tightens what "immediately" means. A label between the NOP and the RTE is
unusual but harmless, since the NOP still falls through to the return. An
intervening instruction breaks the exemption, because the delay then no longer
sits against the return.

RTR stays out of scope.

events.title: uaconv: build MUSIC.SLB for hand-copied installs too — root and each .DSN
events.message:
uaconv: build MUSIC.SLB for hand-copied installs too — root and each .DSN

The last gap in design-first music. uainst converts a module's music when it
installs from a ZIP (v0.9.23); a module — or a whole DOS install — copied by
hand had no path to a bank at all and played the base game's soundtrack, or
nothing. uaconv already walks the OpenUA drawer and every .DSN under it for
the art pass, so the music pass rides the same walk: per directory, classify
the .XMI present, prefer Tandy > PC > Roland > AdLib > DQK, build the bank
with the shared core (byte-identical to the Python by test) and write
<dir>/MUSIC.SLB.

★ AN EXISTING MUSIC.SLB IS NEVER OVERWRITTEN. The Mac release's root bank
holds EIGHT songs; a DOS conversion holds three. Replacing one with the other
would silently lose five songs on every Mac-sourced install that ran uaconv,
so the tool reports "already there, kept" and moves on. The root scan is also
non-recursive, so a module's soundtrack cannot become the base game's — the
same trap stage_dos needed --skip-designs for.

uaconv had NO TESTS before this, despite its header calling the convert path
host-testable. tests/test_uaconv.py builds it with the host compiler and pins
six behaviours: the art pass still converts a .tlb (touched, so pinned), root
and design banks match the reference byte for byte, design music does not
leak into the root, an existing bank is kept byte for byte, driver preference
and the Q1..Q3 filter, and the no-XMI control (no bank, no "music:" line).

Verified ON AN EMULATED A1200 against an isolated tree (never the real
drawer — -d deletes .tlb originals after converting): the Amiga uaconv wrote
a root bank from TYDQ1..3 that is byte-identical to the host build AND to the
MUSIC.SLB stage_dos stages from the same files (5024 bytes, Tandy 3 of 3),
and a design bank from curse's Dqk*.xmi identical to the host (4878 bytes,
DQK 2 of 3, reported partial). The drawer README's uaconv line now says so.

events.title: Exempt NOP before RTE from suspicious/nop
events.message:
Exempt NOP before RTE from suspicious/nop

A NOP directly before RTE is a deliberate synchronisation delay, not leftover
padding: the interrupt-request clear has to reach the chipset before the return,
or a fast CPU returns while the level is still asserted and the interrupt fires
again. A contiguous run counts, since some handlers use more than one.

Not gated on --platform amiga. The idiom turns up in Amiga sources that are
linted without a platform selected, which is exactly where the false positive
would be most annoying, and a NOP placed immediately before an interrupt return
is deliberate on any target.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add correctness/amiga-bit-mask-constant
events.message:
Add correctness/amiga-bit-mask-constant

DMAB_*/INTB_* are bit numbers for BTST/BSET/BCLR/BCHG; DMAF_*/INTF_* are the
masks written to DMACON, INTENA and INTREQ. The names differ by one letter, so
an editor completion picks the wrong one easily, and the result is a silently
wrong value rather than an assembler error.

Classification is by symbol name alone, so the rule works without the include
files being visible - which matters, since there is no inter-file analysis.

What it decides on, in order of confidence:

- BTST/BSET/BCLR/BCHG take a bit number, so an F form there is always wrong.
- A value written to one of these registers is a mask, so a B form is always
  wrong. The target is resolved through absolute addresses and the CUSTOM base
  convention, including byte spellings like intreqr+1(a6), where an address one
  past a register still names it.
- Otherwise the majority within the expression decides, which catches a single
  slip in an ORed list without needing to resolve anything.

Both `!` and `|` are handled. A corrected line is offered when the constants
merely have the wrong letter, and withheld for a cross-family mistake, which has
no mechanical correction. `moveq #DMAB_COPPER,d0` is left alone: loading a bit
number for a later BTST is legitimate.

The address resolver is now shared with amiga-custom-register-access rather than
duplicated, so both agree on what counts as a hardware register.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Record that g_sfDoB's 56 is inferred, not measured
events.message:
Record that g_sfDoB's 56 is inferred, not measured

The maintainer's question is a fair one and the previous commit
overstated the case: g_sfDoB[56] came only from the distance to the
next referenced cell, and a declared array size never reaches the
codegen, so the image cannot report it.

g_sfDoB..g_srlgb is exactly 400 bytes.  So the original may instead
have had ONE 400-byte object with g_sfdos/g_sfdoc as fields at +56/+58
-- in which case there is no overrun and the port has mis-split one
object into three.

What IS settled: a 400-byte array plus two separate shorts is
impossible.  .comm packs densely here (0x3fe2a/0x3fe2e/0x3fe46), so a
400-byte buffer would put g_sfdos at +400, not +56.  If the buffer is
400 those cells must be struct fields.

What is not, and cannot be settled from the image: 56+2+2 needs an
unreferenced ~340-byte global at 0x3fe84, which is not exotic in this
source (mi_sig is declared and referenced by nothing, cmd_num has no
caller in the image, and mi_lstk leaves a second unexplained hole of
+488); the struct reading needs a 340-byte unused tail.  400 is round
and so is 340.  Both models are behaviourally identical -- under
either, any effect over 56 bytes writes those two write-only cells --
and the shipped binary is byte-identical either way.

A tempting false lead, checked and dropped: 0xff then 0 is the Dosound
terminator, which would make the cells sound data.  The reference
emits move.w/clr.w, so the bytes are 00 FF 00 00, not FF 00.

No code change; comments only.  Shipped build still
MD5 eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10.

events.title: installer: a module's music now converts ON THE MACHINE — xmi2slb ported to C
events.message:
installer: a module's music now converts ON THE MACHINE — xmi2slb ported to C

Yesterday's design-first MUSIC.SLB work left one gap it named itself: the
XMI -> SLB conversion was host-side Python, so a module installed by uainst on
the Amiga or Atari still played the BASE game's soundtrack — working audio,
wrong music. This is the port.

src/convert/xmi2slb.c mirrors tools/xmi2slb.py the way artconv.c mirrors
art_convert.py: the Python stays the byte-exact REFERENCE, and
tests/test_xmi2slb_c.py holds the C to IDENTICAL bytes — ten synthetic files
chosen for the tie rules a "close enough" port gets wrong (two notes on one
tick, channel-count ties broken by FIRST APPEARANCE, more than three channels,
percussion on 9, rest gaps, a note long enough to need tied grid codes, a
non-default tempo, a half-even period), full and partial sets, plus every
module in the corpus and the retail Tandy set. 30 checks, all identical. The
one 64-bit operation (tempo -> period) is done as an exact rational with
half-to-even rounding so it cannot disagree with Python's float by a unit.

uainst runs a third pass over the ZIP listing: classify every .XMI (the
retail ??DQ<n> naming, and the fan modules' dqkQ<n> / Dqk<n> shapes), prefer
Tandy > PC > Roland > AdLib > DQK, read Q1..Q3 from the design folder, build
the bank into <design>/MUSIC.SLB with the arena it already has for art. A
partial set converts what exists and says so on the console.

★ THE FIRST CUT FAILED ON THE TWO ROLAND MODULES, and the failure was worth
having: a fixed quarter-arena note cap read 4096 on a 68000 but 2730 on a
host with 8-byte longs, and alliance/wiz1pc carry 3591 note-ons. The 68000
build would have scraped through by luck. The arena is now carved
adaptively (notes up to half, the per-channel copy sized from the busiest
channel after parsing), and a new test proves a too-small arena fails with
ERR_SPACE rather than writing a truncated bank that looks valid.

Verified ON AN EMULATED A1200, not just on the host: the Amiga uainst,
handed a module carrying curse's eight Dqk*.xmi, printed
    music: DQK arrangement, 2 of 3 songs... MUSIC.SLB (4878 bytes)
and the file it wrote is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the host-built bank for the same
inputs. Both cross installers build (uainst_amiga 96480, UAINST.PRG 190472);
the Atari binary is built but not run — its remaining variable is TOS file
I/O, which the art pass already exercises. 551 host tests pass.

Not done here: uaconv's per-design pass (for a module copied by hand rather
than installed), and curse's six extra songs beyond Q1..Q3.

events.title: Add suspicious/atari-trap-stack-cleanup
events.message:
Add suspicious/atari-trap-stack-cleanup

GEMDOS, BIOS and XBIOS are caller-cleans-stack, and forgetting to remove the
parameters corrupts the stack in a way that surfaces far from the cause.

The rule compares the contiguous run of pushes before a trap against the
adjustment immediately after. That deliberately avoids a table of TOS function
signatures: the calling convention is invariant, whereas the function set varies
by TOS version, which we cannot know from source.

Details that matter:

- A byte push to -(sp) counts as two, because A7 is special-cased to stay
  word-aligned. The rule would be wrong for exactly the reason that makes the
  A7 byte shift trick work.
- TRAP #2 is excluded: GEM passes a parameter block in registers.
- Pterm0, Pterm and Ptermres never return, so their parameters are never
  removed. Detected from the opcode word pushed last.
- ADDQ keeps its own mnemonic while ADD to an address register normalizes to
  ADDA, and stack cleanup is written both ways, so both are matched along with
  LEA n(sp),sp.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Diagnose the four-minute exit: sf_irqp's g_sfDoB overrun
events.message:
Diagnose the four-minute exit: sf_irqp's g_sfDoB overrun

A -DSKIP_COPYPROT run died at VBL 16983, reproducible to the frame: a
bus error reading $ffffffa8 inside TOS's VDI at $fd23da, then TOS
looping on Pterm(-1) and the program exiting.  At 60 Hz that is 4.7
emulated minutes -- the "exits after four minutes" report.

--trace vdi named the call (VDI 0x6D, vro_cpyfm).  Piping debugger
commands to Hatari's stdin at the fault gave contrl[0]=109, a source
MFDB of g_obtmt+0x118 (stride 20 -> object 14, valid) and a pxy of
0,0,15,0x8003 / 271,92,286,0x805F.  Through od_draw, sy2 is
g_obtah[14]-1, so g_obtah[14] was 0x8004.  g_obtaw was intact and
g_obtah held SOUNDS.LCP block 17's payload[56:] byte for byte: sf_irqp
running off the end of g_sfDoB[56].

SOUNDS.LCP has 23 effects and three exceed 56 bytes -- blocks 8
(SFX_HEAD_NOD) and 17 (SFX_TOILET_REFILL) at 148, block 19 at 60 -- so
the worst overrun is 92 bytes.

The shipped build does not care.  bss_remap puts g_sfDoB at 0x3fe48
followed by g_sfdos (+56) and g_sfdoc (+58), both write-only -- set by
sf_so(), read nowhere in C or asm -- and then 342 bytes no symbol
claims (next is g_srlgb at +400).  The overrun dies in that hole, which
is why 1985 shipped it.  A gated build skips bss_remap and lo68 puts
g_obtah, the 56-entry object HEIGHT table, at exactly +56.

So globals.c pads g_sfDoB to 400 in test builds only.  The shipped
build keeps the original's 56: widening it there would change the BSS
size in the header.  Verified both ways -- shipped is still
MD5 eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10 with prg_diff BYTE-IDENTICAL and
reloc_audit unchanged (E=1 scrbufA); the gated build now runs 40000
VBLs with no bus error and no exit.

Two harness fixes fell out of it.  test_longrun_stable.sh ran to 15000
VBLs -- 1983 short of the bug -- and scored STABLE; the default is now
30000/25000.  And this Hatari wants "--avirecord on", the bare flag
having started to eat the next argument, which is why the script
reported "didn't produce an AVI" while swallowing --auto.

events.title: Complete the Amiga custom-register direction table
events.message:
Complete the Amiga custom-register direction table

The table held 24 of ~200 registers: the read-only set was complete at 16, but
the write-only side was a token sample of 8, so reading COLOR00 or SPR0POS
produced no diagnostic.

Now 200 registers from the Hardware Reference Manual appendix. The repetitive
families - audio channels, bitplane pointers and data, sprite pointers and
POS/CTL/DATA/DATB, COLOR00-31 - are generated rather than transcribed, since
that is exactly where a slip would hide unnoticed.

$1C0-$1FE is deliberately omitted. It mixes directions (HHPOSR at $1DA is
readable) and its availability varies by chipset. Omission is safe and
commission is not: a missing register produces no diagnostic, while a wrong
direction produces a confident false error. A test pins that the block stays
silent rather than guessing.

The symbol resolver derives from the same table, so CUSTOM-relative spellings
such as COLOR00(a6) now resolve too.

events.title: Drop the supervisor-mode rule; make MOVE SR key on use, not mode
events.message:
Drop the supervisor-mode rule; make MOVE SR key on use, not mode

A source file is one translation unit and nothing in it establishes the
privilege mode: the entry point may be elsewhere, a routine may be documented
"call via Supexec", and interrupt handlers run supervisor without calling
anything. There is no inter-file analysis, so every version of the rule warns
about correct code.

The same assumption had crept into portability/move-from-sr-privileged, which
claimed user-mode code starts trapping on the 68010. It now keys on something
local instead: MOVE SR is word-sized, so if only the low byte is observed the
code wants the condition codes and MOVE CCR is unprivileged everywhere - a
strict improvement whatever the privilege mode. If the system byte is observed,
the code needs SR and must already be supervisor, so stay quiet.
dataRegisterBitsUseAfter answers this with no new analysis.

events.title: Map the remaining globals: 758 of 784 now verified in Ghidra by address
events.message:
Map the remaining globals: 758 of 784 now verified in Ghidra by address

The 79 left after the last sync were not simply "unmapped".  Listing
them by address showed chains -- Ghidra holding a port name at an
address the port has since given to something else:

    0x2a1d0  port g_atact    ghidra g_obala
    0x2b92a  port g_obala    ghidra object_alarm_animation
    0x2a0f8  port pex_name   ghidra pex_ptr
    0x4d2da  port pex_ptr    ghidra pex_name      <- swapped
    0x3ca48  port pk_wcs     ghidra pk_cscore
    0x501a8  port pk_cscore  ghidra poker_display_x_offset

Ten of those, plus the g_mnhi/g_mnlo pair fixed earlier, are old port
labels stranded at the wrong cells by earlier name-keyed syncs.  Going
by name would have chased them further around; every row here went by
ADDRESS, which is authoritative -- DATA and TEXT are byte-identical and
BSS comes from stx_bss_layout.tsv.

Pushed 82 rows, 0 failures.  Verification over every port symbol:

    VERIFY ok=758 mismatched=15 no_symbol=11     (was 676 / 97 / 11)

All 15 remaining are DRI libc internals -- _chvec, _ctype, __cpmrv,
_fds, strchr -- where Ghidra's names are better than ours and are
deliberately left alone.

The map gains 62 rows, coverage ~304/397 -> ~366/397.  Only pairs whose
Ghidra side is a real descriptive name are recorded; the 10 stale port
labels and 9 Ghidra placeholders (SHORT_ARRAY_0005..., PTR_ARRAY_...)
are pushed but not written down as correspondences, because neither is
a name the original analysis chose.

Also fixed sync_ghidra_names.sh: "${extra[@]}" on an empty array trips
`set -u` under the bash 3.2 macOS ships, so the sync path failed while
verify worked.

Shipped build untouched -- cmp clean against DATA/LCP_STX.PRG.

events.title: Drop the atariste platform; one identifier covers the Atari family
events.message:
Drop the atariste platform; one identifier covers the Atari family

atariste was behaviourally identical to atarist - same ranges, differing only
in the display label - and per-model identifiers do not pay for themselves
here:

- The address heuristic gets worse, not better, with finer platforms. A
  narrower map produces false positives on code targeting a range of machines,
  while a wider one only risks missing a missing-# typo in I/O space.
- Platform gating is an exact match against a flat list, so each new model must
  be added to every rule's `platforms` array. Forgetting one silently disables
  the rule for that model rather than erroring.
- The 68030 in the TT and Falcon is already expressible as --cpu mc68030, so
  encoding it in the platform name too would duplicate an existing axis.

The STE and Mega STE hardware stays covered - DMA sound, blitter and the second
MFP sit inside the existing blocks - and a test pins that.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Widen the Atari expected-address ranges to the full hardware map
events.message:
Widen the Atari expected-address ranges to the full hardware map

The supplied range stopped at $FFFA23, which is MFP TCDR rather than a hardware
boundary: the 68901 register file continues to $FFFA2F, and $FFFA25 is TDDR,
behind the 200Hz system timer. The keyboard and MIDI ACIAs and the memory
controller were outside it too, so idiomatic ST code was warned about.

Now covered:

- $FF8000-$FFFA3F  memory controller, video, DMA, PSG, blitter, MFP
- $FFFA80-$FFFABF  second MFP (Mega STE and TT)
- $FFFC00-$FFFC07  keyboard and MIDI ACIAs

The first is one span rather than a block-by-block map, deliberately covering
the gaps between peripherals. This is a heuristic for a missing '#', and no
plausible intended immediate constant lands in Atari I/O space.

Tests walk fourteen real register addresses across the map, and pin that values
which could plausibly be an intended immediate are still flagged.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Finish the Ghidra name sync, headless
events.message:
Finish the Ghidra name sync, headless

The documented pipeline cannot run: apply_ghidra_renames.sh POSTs to a
server on :8089 and needs RenameLcpGlobals.java, list_data_symbols.java
and /tmp/ghidra_syms.txt, none of which exist.  Replaced with
tools/sync_ghidra_names.sh driving analyzeHeadless and two scripts kept
in tools/ghidra/ -- no server, no GUI, works on a closed project, and
`verify` re-runs the whole check read-only.

Pushed: 334 mapped globals (326 were already in place), 8 more by
ADDRESS because the port had renamed them since the last sync, and 148
function labels.  0 failures.

Three traps this turned up, all now written down in CLAUDE.md:

  * lcp_sym.68k's BSS addresses are lo68's, not the reference's.  BSS
    rows have to come from stx_bss_layout.tsv, which is where the remap
    puts the symbol.  DATA and TEXT are byte-identical so their link
    addresses are already right.
  * lcp_sym.68k carries 8-char TRUNCATED linkage names, and an earlier
    sync pushed those -- Ghidra held lcp_pat for lcp_path, aes_ini for
    aes_init, and 34 more.  Expanded against include/*.h and re-pushed.
    My own first pass repeated the mistake before I caught it.
  * Renaming by name breaks on a swap.  g_mnhi/g_mnlo had to go by
    address, and doing so showed GHIDRA had them right all along:
    midi_note_hi_limit sits on the 0x60 cell.  The port had them
    backwards, which I fixed earlier in the session, and my first edit
    to the map propagated the error before the address pass caught it.
    The map now reads hi->g_mnhi, lo->g_mnlo.

Nine stale map rows corrected to the names the port uses now: mi_tpb,
psg_racc, psg_rdel, g_mnhi, g_mnlo, lasthz, body_ptr, pex_ptr, sch_tab.

Verification is by address over every port symbol, not by trusting the
push: 676 of 784 in place, 0 failures.  Of the 97 that differ, 14 are
DRI libc internals, 4 are Ghidra placeholders with no name, and 79 are
globals the map has never covered -- its own note says ~93 remain.
Extending it is research rather than a mechanical push.

The library is deliberately left alone: Ghidra's strchr is a better
name than our index.

Shipped build untouched -- cmp clean against DATA/LCP_STX.PRG.

events.title: Add Atari ST and STE platform modes
events.message:
Add Atari ST and STE platform modes

suspicious/unexpected-absolute-address now applies to the Atari map as well as
the Amiga one. The rule had hardcoded "amiga" in both the range lookup and its
message text; it now resolves the platform from config, and the notes are built
from the range table rather than restated in prose.

Atari hardware registers are conventionally written as a sign-extended absolute
short. $FFFF8240.W, $FF8240 and the negative word -32192 all name the same
register, because the 68000 address bus is 24 bits and ignores A24-A31, so
expectedAbsoluteAddressRange now tests both the unsigned value and its 24-bit
truncation. All three spellings are covered by tests.

Expected regions are $FF8201-$FFFA23 as supplied, plus $000000-$0005FF for the
exception vectors and system variables. That second range is an addition: it is
the analogue of the existing Amiga vector entry, and without it idiomatic ST
code such as `move.l $44e,a0` for the screen base would be flagged on every
file.

ST and STE share one range, since the STE's DMA sound and blitter registers sit
inside the same block. They are separate platforms because finer-grained STE
rules will need to tell them apart.

Amiga behaviour is unchanged, with tests pinning that.

events.title: Ghidra project: the five function renames
events.message:
Ghidra project: the five function renames

unScn -> scn_dec, fLoad -> al_loal, lcp_load -> lc_load, al_lost ->
ldSpr, sp_reglp -> sp_regs.  These were LCP_ORG-era labels still
attached to LCP_STX functions -- the very thing that made me
misidentify the program in e10f13a and put a wrong claim in CLAUDE.md.

Ghidra was shut down before committing, and the database was verified
to reopen cleanly rather than being trusted on the shape of the files:

    analyzeHeadless . LCP -process -noanalysis -readOnly \
        -postScript CheckNames.java

    Processing read-only project file: /LCP.PRG.1.1
    VERIFY 0x152ca = scn_dec
    VERIFY 0x16428 = al_loal
    VERIFY 0x15ac8 = lc_load
    VERIFY 0x1528a = ldSpr
    VERIFY 0x15bdc = sp_regs
    VERIFY 0x15546 = main

That also settles which image the project holds: one program,
LCP.PRG.1.1, which CLAUDE.md identifies as LCP_STX.

db.4.gbf -> db.5.gbf is the checkpoint carrying the renames; the two
~journal.dat files go away because the transaction committed.  The
untracked LCP.lock and LCP.lock~ were left behind by the SIGTERM and
removed once no Ghidra process was running.

The globals half of the sync is still not runnable: apply_ghidra_renames.sh
needs an HTTP server on :8089 plus RenameLcpGlobals.java and
list_data_symbols.java, and none of those are present.

events.title: Correct the record: the Ghidra project IS LCP_STX, only its labels were stale
events.message:
Correct the record: the Ghidra project IS LCP_STX, only its labels were stale

e10f13a claimed the open Ghidra program was the LCP_ORG image, on the
strength of main decompiling with calls to unScn, fLoad and lcp_load --
none of which LCP_STX has as functions.  That inference was wrong.  The
disassembly at 0x15546 matches our byte-identical build at text 0x5546
instruction for instruction, down to the link #-42 and the two jsr
targets.  It is LCP_STX; what misled me was LCP_ORG-era NAMES still
attached to its functions.

The scn_cmn deletion stands and is better supported than the reason I
gave for it.  Ghidra's main builds the 30-byte read as
`move.l #0x2c6ce,(SP) / move.l #0x1e,-(SP) / bsr fr_read`, and 0x2c6ce
is link-time 0x1c6ce, which is scn_dic.  The `@ 0x4cf7c` in the port's
old comment was simply a wrong address -- 0x3cf7c sits two bytes inside
scn_buf and would run over mf_scrp, g_inpmd and g_ltscb.  One object,
two names.

Synced the five stale function labels through the MCP (Ghidra address =
link + 0x10000): unScn -> scn_dec, fLoad -> al_loal, lcp_load ->
lc_load, al_lost -> ldSpr, sp_reglp -> sp_regs.  Verified by
decompiling two of them back.  Note the decompiler serves a cache: main
still prints the old names until it is re-analysed.

The globals half cannot run: apply_ghidra_renames.sh needs a Ghidra
HTTP server on :8089 plus RenameLcpGlobals.java, list_data_symbols.java
and a fresh /tmp/ghidra_syms.txt, and all three scripts are missing
while the endpoint does not answer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Add optimization/prefer-lea-for-address-symbol
events.message:
Add optimization/prefer-lea-for-address-symbol

`move.l #label,a0` had no rule. The existing movea-immediate-to-lea only fires
when the immediate folds to a known constant, so a relocatable label matched
nothing at all.

It could not simply be extended, for three reasons: it is gated to 68000/68010
on an ASP68K cycle claim that does not apply here, its justification is a speed
win rather than assembler relaxation, and its replacement appends an explicit
size suffix. That last one matters most - `lea label.l,a0` pins the operand to
absolute long and defeats the PC-relative relaxation this rule exists to
enable, so the new rule emits a bare `lea label,a0`.

The two stay disjoint: a foldable immediate is a value rather than an address
and is left to the existing rule.

The impact audit measures the replacement as neutral, size 0 and cpu 0, which
independently confirms the two forms are identical as written. The benefit is
realised by the assembler, and docs/impact-measurement.md already records that
68kcounter measures source and cannot account for assembler optimizations.

Restricted to .L: MOVEA.W sign-extends, and matching it would force absolute
short and rule out PC-relative anyway. That case is already covered by
suspicious/movea-word-sign-extension.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: scn_cmn was never real: it is scn_dic, seen through the wrong Ghidra program
events.message:
scn_cmn was never real: it is scn_dic, seen through the wrong Ghidra program

The last unverifiable symbol in the relocation audit.  scn_cmn was a
30-byte BSS array nothing referenced, carried from the map entry
`scene_common_data` @ 0x4cf7c, with a comment crediting an unScn helper
in assets.c for filling it.

That helper does not exist.  LCP_STX inlines the .SCN file handling in
main and st_titl, and each does exactly one 30-byte dictionary read --
into scn_dic.  Decompiling main in the open Ghidra project shows why
the second name appeared: that project is the LCP_ORG image, whose main
really does call unScn, fLoad and lcp_load, none of which LCP_STX has.
scn_cmn is that revision's name for the same 30 bytes.

The reference's own BSS is decisive.  0x3cf7c is two bytes INSIDE
scn_buf, and a 30-byte object there would run over mf_scrp (0x3cf7e,
20 bytes), g_inpmd (0x3cf92) and the start of g_ltscb (0x3cf94) --
every one of them a symbol real relocations point at.  There is no hole
for it.  scn_dic's own address is 0x1c6ce, nowhere near.

Deleted, and the rename map now says so.  reloc_audit:

    A merges          0
    B aliases         0
    C split symbols   0
    D unverifiable    0        (was 1)
    E inferred bases  1        scrbufA
    F over-declared   0

E is the only one left and cannot be closed from the binary: scrbufA is
referenced solely at +511 through the align-up, and that constant sits
inside a relocated longword, so +0x1FF with base 0x1a7 and +0x200 with
base 0x1a6 are indistinguishable.

Still byte-identical: cmp clean against DATA/LCP_STX.PRG, MD5
eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10, 337 matched / 0 divergent, all ten
host tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: sarnau

events.title: last_hz and mi_lasT are one cell: express it with a union
events.message:
last_hz and mi_lasT are one cell: express it with a union

The relocation audit's only remaining alias.  The original keeps one
cell that the compositor reads and writes as a word (sc_ren8's frame
gate, sp_imfs's reset) and the sequencer as a byte (mq_pars, mq_qnne),
a byte write landing on the word's high half.  The port carried two
symbols and let the BSS spec map both onto the one address.

A cast macro cannot express it -- `#define mi_lasT (*(char *) &last_hz)`
makes Alcyon take the width from &last_hz and emit move.w where the
original has move.b, which I measured earlier and backed out.  A union
does: `union LASTHZ { unsigned short w; char b; }` with `last_hz` and
`mi_lasT` as macros over its two members.  Every use site is unchanged,
Alcyon emits the original's access widths, and the two symbols become
one.

The layout spec drops from 417 rows to 416 and no longer carries an
alias.  reloc_audit now reports:

    A merges          0
    B aliases         0        (was 1)
    C split symbols   0
    D unverifiable    1        scn_cmn
    E inferred bases  1        scrbufA
    F over-declared   0        (was 1 -- it WAS the B alias)

D and E are not defects and cannot be closed from the binary at all:
nothing relocates against scn_cmn, so neither its size nor its
existence is observable, and scrbufA is referenced only at +511 through
the align-up constant, so its base rests on assuming the original wrote
`scrbufA + 0x1FF`.

Still byte-identical from a clean tree: 123352 bytes, MD5
eae52d14023b51d7ac459a90d37eed10, cmp clean against DATA/LCP_STX.PRG,
337 matched / 0 divergent, and all ten host tests pass.
