events.title: Audit the unreferenced globals: two were real, one was missing
events.message:
Audit the unreferenced globals: two were real, one was missing

Following the _vbclock finding, audited every global the linked program
never relocates against.

DELETED as port artefacts -- nothing references them, and the code they
were meant to serve reaches the data directly:
  (already done last commit: _vbclock $0462, g_hzhi/g_hzlo $04BA/$04BC)

FOUND MISSING.  The audit cuts both ways: LCP_STX's data segment has
three pointers at 0x184/0x188/0x18c, 14 bytes apart, aiming at
psg_env[0..2] -- sizeof(PSG_ENVELOPE).  Nothing references that table
in either binary, but Alcyon emits an unreferenced initialized global
just the same, so the port now carries it as psg_epp[3].  Its three
pointers are the first three DATA relocations and they now agree with
LCP_STX's exactly.

SIZES corrected from the newly aligned head of the segment:
  mi_ndt  [32] -> [22].  LCP_STX's gap is 44 bytes.  mq_pars indexes it
          with a 5-bit field, so 22..31 read past the end -- the .SNG
          data never produces them.  (Same shape as g_sfDoB.)
  g_msmk  [16] -> [32].  The port had only the first half; the rest is
          0,0,1,2,...,0x0d,0x11.

KEPT, with the reasoning recorded: g_cotbl, g_unus1, g_unus2, env_val,
g_mccha, g_dsb, g_obtmp and scn_cmn are unreferenced but are ordinary
dead 1985 data as far as the evidence goes -- unlike the ST system
variables, none of them is a mistake about where a value lives, and
Alcyon allocates an unreferenced global regardless.

The data segment now agrees with LCP_STX byte for byte from 0x000
through 0x414 (was 0x191), and 3 of the 402 data relocations line up.

STRUCTURAL FINDING at 0x418, which is where the agreement now stops:
LCP_STX has mi_pgmap's pointer, then mq_parh's switch jump table (7
case longs + 12 text addresses -- the 0x1246/0x1264/0x129c/0x12a4/
0x132c targets CLAUDE.md already records as living inside mq_parh),
then main_pa and vdi_colt.  Alcyon emits a switch table into the .data
of the object that holds the function, and data from separate objects
cannot interleave -- so the globals and midi_seq's code are ONE object
in LCP_STX, exactly as the code unity units already model for text.

events.title: Merge all initialized data into one object; DATA order effectively done
events.message:
Merge all initialized data into one object; DATA order effectively done

The five remaining order inversions were all at FILE boundaries, and
they could not be fixed by reordering: LCP_STX's data segment
INTERLEAVES what the port had split across nine files, and data from
separate objects cannot interleave.  So the 1985 source kept every
initialized global in one object, and now so does the port -- all 146
data definitions live in globals.c, sorted by the LCP_STX offset the
relocation pairing gives.  psgfreq.c, sprglobs.c, sprload.c, tables.c,
tick_tables.c, vocab.c, calendar.c and events.c keep their BSS
declarations and code; their data moved out.

The block scanner now refuses to move anything whose text has a brace
before the '=', which is the guard the earlier attempt lacked -- that
one swept calendar.c's daily_rs into globals.c and broke main.

One inversion is left and it is an artefact, not a defect: _vbclock is
the last NAMED data symbol, so the ~4.5 KB of anonymous string
literals that follow it all get attributed to it and its "target" is
just wherever the first of those strings lives in LCP_STX.

Also removed `long _stksize = 65536L` from main.c.  That global is the
ATARI DK gemstart's memory-model hook; alcyon2's GEMSTART.O -- the
startup LCP_STX actually links -- contains no reference to it, and
neither does its GEMLIB.  Nothing in the linked program relocated
against it.  It was four dead bytes sitting ahead of psg_rot, and
removing them makes the port's data segment agree with LCP_STX's from
0x000 through 0x190 exactly.

DATA: 51 -> 1 inversions (the artefact), longest monotone run 10 -> 114.
data -56, bss -1268, text still 104156 == 104156 with zero differing
bytes.

Next two sizes the head of the segment now pins down: psg_rot has 16
bytes of room where the port declares 4, and mi_ndt 44 where the port
declares 64 (its index is masked & 0x1f, so 32 shorts is the port's
safe reading -- the same shape as the g_sfDoB contradiction).

events.title: Show datasheet stall per instruction in the profiler
events.message:
Show datasheet stall per instruction in the profiler

The 68kcounter comparison was reachable only from the export CLI. It is most
useful where you are already looking at the code, so the Disassembly view now
carries it: a per-instruction column showing cycles that execution spent
blocked rather than working, with the measured/datasheet/bus-access breakdown
on hover.

Computed host-side in attachDisassembly, next to where file/line is already
re-derived, and deliberately NOT stored in the .puaeprofile. The document holds
the raw capture rather than conclusions drawn from it — that is what lets an
older file pick up later improvements on load — and a stored timing figure
would be frozen against future corrections. It is recomputed from the
instruction text, which the document does store.

That also keeps the dependency out of the webview: profilerViewer.js is
unchanged at 5.7M with no 68kcounter in it, receiving computed values in the
model. Only the extension bundle grows, 940K -> 1.1M.

The applicability decision moves into theoreticalTimings.datasheetApplicability
so the CLI report and the UI cannot disagree about whether the comparison is
meaningful. Where it says no, the column is absent rather than showing a figure
that would be fiction — both captures on hand are 68020 and correctly show
nothing.

Also fixes DBcc going untimed: the counter register sits between mnemonic and
target ("dbf.w d7,-16(pc)"), which the branch-rewrite regex didn't allow. Since
a DBcc loop is about the most common shape in hand-written Amiga code, that was
every untimed instruction across both captures — coverage goes 98% -> 100%.

events.title: DATA ordering: reorder the initialized globals; 51 -> 5 inversions
events.message:
DATA ordering: reorder the initialized globals; 51 -> 5 inversions

The relocation pairing gives LCP_STX's data offset for every global, so
the target order is known exactly.  Sorting each file's initialized
definitions by it takes the port from 51 order inversions among 147
mapped data symbols to 5, and the longest monotone run from 10 to 70.

globals.c, sprglobs.c, tables.c, tick_tables.c and vocab.c reordered;
their BSS declarations are left where they are, since Alcyon emits a
.comm and the LINKER picks the bss order.

Two 8-char linkage collisions surfaced, one deliberate and one a bug:

  mi_pgmap / mi_pgmapb both truncate to _mi_pgma -- which is the point,
  the pointer is meant to live over the array's first four bytes -- but
  as68 only accepts that with the .comm ahead of the .data definition,
  so mi_pgmapb now sits immediately before mi_pgmap with a comment
  saying why it must.

  psg_rmpD / psg_rmpA also truncated to _psg_rmp, silently MERGING two
  distinct arrays into one 6-byte block.  LCP_STX has them at two
  addresses (bss 0x13030 and 0x23aee) -- which is what the relocation
  pairing had been reporting as an "ambiguous" symbol with two implied
  bases.  Renamed to psg_rdel / psg_racc; bss grows the 6 bytes the
  second array should always have had.

The 5 remaining inversions are all at FILE boundaries: LCP_STX's data
segment interleaves what the port split across globals.c, psgfreq.c,
sprglobs.c, sprload.c, tables.c, tick_tables.c, vocab.c, calendar.c and
events.c -- and data from separate objects cannot interleave, so the
1985 source kept these in one object.  Closing those needs the
definitions merged into a single translation unit.

CAUTION for that merge: a `;`-terminated block scan swallows the
FUNCTION above a declaration and moves it too (it cost a broken build
here -- daily_rs ended up inside globals.c).  /tmp-style scratch
parsers must recognise a `{` that follows a parameter list rather than
an `=`.

events.title: Add `dump --stalls`: measured cost vs 68000 datasheet timings
events.message:
Add `dump --stalls`: measured cost vs 68000 datasheet timings

A profile can say an instruction cost 40 color clocks but not whether that's
because it does a lot of work or because the CPU sat waiting while the blitter
and bitplane DMA had the bus. Those call for opposite fixes, and nothing in the
capture distinguished them.

68kcounter gives the datasheet cost assuming the CPU never waits, so the excess
over it is contention. `dump --stalls` reports that per function alongside the
bus accesses those executions demand — what the contention is competing for. A
high stall% says "blocked, look at the bus"; a low one says "genuinely this
expensive, look at the algorithm".

Two conversions the comparison depends on, both easy to get silently wrong:
68kcounter reports CPU clock cycles where timeDeltas are color clocks (half),
and a disassembler renders branch targets as pc-relative displacements, which
aren't source syntax and parse as no instruction at all — dropping every
branch, in exactly the tight loops this is most wanted for. Where an
instruction has several timings the slowest is taken, so the figure being
subtracted is conservative and a taken branch can't manufacture stall.

It refuses rather than misleads, via two guards. 68kcounter models the 68000
only, so a capture containing sub-color-clock samples (the 020+ cycle-exact
path) is rejected. That alone wasn't enough: a 68020 capture predating the
cycleDelta fix stores no zeros to give itself away, and the first run against
one produced a nonsensical -137.7% stall. So the second guard is that
contention can only ever add cycles — measured coming in below datasheet proves
the code isn't running 68000 timings, whatever the samples look like. Both
captures on hand now correctly refuse; the arithmetic and both guards are
covered by unit tests, since neither is a positive case.

Suggested by the library's author.

events.title: Calibrate check's thresholds against measured data
events.message:
Calibrate check's thresholds against measured data

Two of the thresholds were picked by eye when the checks were first written.
Both now have numbers behind them.

WIDTH_DIVERGENCE_PP keeps its value but gains the justification: sweeping
columns.ts's CODE_MATCH_WINDOW put a healthy layout at 0.2pp worst-case and a
deliberately mis-tuned one at 6.8pp, so 3pp sits well clear of noise while
still catching the failure the check exists for.

LOW_ANCHOR_RATE was measuring the wrong thing. Anchored-against-samples is
capped by instruction-cache behaviour nobody controls — a real 68020 frame has
10,028 fetch cells for 31,078 samples — so it read "low" on healthy captures
and fired on all four frames of a good one. It now counts against the fetch
cells actually available: of the positions the grid could confirm, how many did
we use? The same frame went from 7.9% (blind forward search) to 59.4%
(cycle-predicted), so half is a fair line, and a healthy capture is quiet again
while genuinely struggling frames (6-16%) still report.

Also records the measured getProfileRegs transfer cost next to the register cap
it justifies: ~94 ms at the 64k cap versus 26 ms at the old 16k one, against a
30 s timeout — so that cap is bounded by memory and document size, not
transfer. Comment only; no behaviour change, binary unaffected.

events.title: Predict the fetch-cell search position from the cycle clock
events.message:
Predict the fetch-cell search position from the cycle clock

buildSampleSlots searched blindly forward from the last match within a fixed
window, which strands the cursor behind the raster the moment anything runs
longer than that window without emitting a fetch cell — and then fails
permanently, since every later sample looks unmatchable too. A cached spin loop
does exactly this. On a real 68020 capture matching died at sample 1,907 of
31,078 and never recovered: 2.5% of samples anchored to an observed position,
the rest riding on extrapolation.

A grid slot is one color clock and timeDeltas are color clocks, so cycles
elapsed since the last confirmed match convert straight into slots travelled.
The search now looks around that predicted position rather than wherever the
cursor was left, so an unmatchable stretch no longer strands it.

That also turns the window into a tolerance on how far the grid may disagree
with the cycle clock, rather than a search budget — and it has to be tight.
Widening it starts matching the wrong lap of a loop: the same PC, a different
iteration. A wrong match is worse than no match, pinning a sample to a position
it never occupied and desynchronising everything after it. Swept against the
width-vs-cycles invariant, 512 matched FEWER samples than 128 (3452 vs 5959)
and pushed worst divergence to 6.8pp; 128 sits at the plateau at 0.2pp. The
table is in the comment.

Measured on frame 0 of a real capture: samples anchored 791 -> 5959 (2.5% ->
19.2%, against a 32% ceiling set by how many fetch cells exist at all), and the
instruction the Disassembly view shows at a known fetch cell is now right 58.2%
of the time versus 23.9%. Slot error p50/p90 unchanged at 2/5.

guest: bump the amiga-gcc image to gcc-v16.2

The 16.2 image regenerated every NDK inline header with sfdc 1.12, which
changes two things the guest sources relied on:

- The ...Tags varargs wrappers are now file-scope static functions that
  name DOS_BASE_NAME directly, so the function-local base idiom
  (#define DOS_BASE_NAME _dosbase) no longer compiles. Define
  __NOLIBBASE__ before the inline includes in the seven sources using
  it; the wrappers then take the base as an explicit argument at the
  call site, where the local is in scope.
- inline/exec.h no longer reaches dos/dos.h through inline/macros.h and
  inline/stubs.h, so BPTR users include <dos/dos.h> themselves (the FMV
  ROM sources and the MHI library header).

All thirteen consumers of toolchain.mk build; the ROM relocation,
data/bss and size checks, the MHI library check, and the a2091-rom and
fmv-rom Python suites pass. The committed guest probes and the copperhf
and services ROMs are rebuilt with the new compiler (the hostsocket ROM
is byte-identical); the unstripped probes only grew by the new linker's
__debug_* symbols, their code sections are unchanged. The a2091 and FMV
ROM assets are not rebundled here.

Verified with the unit suite and the integration tests that load the
rebuilt artifacts (a2091 boot, FMV, Video CD, copperhf, modem, zz9k,
hostfs and uaelib probes).

events.title: stx_strides.py: read 2-D array row strides out of the disassembly
events.message:
stx_strides.py: read 2-D array row strides out of the disassembly

Maintainer's point: a two-dimensional array is detectable at the
disassembly level.  It is -- Alcyon indexes `T a[N][M]` as
`base + i * sizeof(T[M])` and emits that scale as a literal
`muls.w #K,Dn` (or a shift when it is a power of two), so every array's
ROW STRIDE is written down in the text segment and can be read back
without reference to any source.

That is the other half of the layout evidence.  The relocation gaps say
how many BYTES LCP_STX gives a symbol; the stride says how big one row
is; N = gap / K.  Run over the whole binary it independently confirms
three sizes that were each derived a different way earlier:

    g_obtmt   stride 20   gap 1120  -> [56]      (main's `i < 56` loop)
    wp_ans    stride 12   gap 60    -> [5][12]   (WORDPZ.TXT has <= 5 '@')
    g_semfi   stride 20   gap 160   -> [8]       (SPRITE_HW_SLOTS)
    g_semfm   stride 20   gap 160   -> [8]

and checks the rest outright -- body_ptr[120][168], hd_shp[66][84],
pex_ptr[66][168], crd_mfdb[54], psg_env[3] (14-byte struct),
ctrl_cnt[121][3] and __fds[16] all come out exactly as declared.  Two
it disagrees with are known library/anonymous-data cases: __iob wants
32 entries of 14 (448) where the port's gemlib gives 440, and days_pm's
extent is inflated by the string literals Alcyon emits without symbols.

Caveat worth knowing: a `muls.w #10` sitting next to a reference to a
char buffer is decimal arithmetic (stEnter's `d[1]*10 + d[2]`), not
indexing -- in_str is 1-D despite the tool pairing them.

events.title: Fix the clock fallback using CPU cycles where color clocks are meant
events.message:
Fix the clock fallback using CPU cycles where color clocks are meant

IProfileModel.cyclesPerMicroSecond is the divisor for every display-unit
conversion (µs, rasterlines, % of frame), and the values it divides —
timeDeltas — are color clocks: the emulator reports costs as
get_cycles()/CYCLE_UNIT, one DMA-grid slot is one color clock, and a PAL frame
is DMA_HPOS*DMA_VPOS = 71051 of them.

The measured path was right: frameCycles/frameUs lands on ~3.55 color clocks
per µs. The fallback used when the emulator reports no frame length was
7.09379 — the CPU clock, which is master/4 against the color clock's master/8,
so exactly twice too large. On that path a full frame read as 10016 µs / 50.1%
of a frame / 156.5 rasterlines instead of 19951 / 99.8% / 311.7. The doc
comments on the field and on display.ts's Timing both described it as the CPU
clock too, which is presumably how the constant got there.

Adds PAL_COLOR_CLOCKS_PER_US / NTSC_COLOR_CLOCKS_PER_US next to the DMA
geometry they derive from, and picks between them by isPAL rather than
assuming PAL, so an NTSC capture with no reported frame length is right too.

Only the fallback path changes behaviour; captures that report a frame length
were already correct and are untouched. The scattered 7.09379 literals in

events.title: Prove the eight disputed bss block sizes
events.message:
Prove the eight disputed bss block sizes

Each one settled against evidence outside the port's own source -- the
relocation gap (what LCP_STX's layout allows), the code's own bound
(what it must hold), and where possible the shipped DATA file.

PROVEN AND APPLIED
  g_ltlp   2048 -> 1440 (360 char*).  fl_ltpl's loop is a literal
           `for (linecount = 0; linecount < 360; linecount++)`; the
           port's own comment already reasoned 360 from a_writl's
           4 sections x 96; the decoded LETTER.TXT yields 361 line
           segments; and LCP_STX's gap is exactly 1440.  Four
           independent agreements.
  in_str    256 -> 80.  Gap is exactly 80, with g_obtah immediately
           after.  Floor ~20 (a_writl's sprintf "%s %d, %4d") and the
           literal-word loop caps at in_str[15].
  wp_ans   [10][12] -> [5][12].  Decoding WORDPZ.TXT through fr_reac's
           nibble/token scheme gives 67 lines with at most FIVE '@'
           markers on any of them; gap is exactly 60.
  mi_ntLp    64 -> 25 pointers.  SOUNDS.LCP holds 23 blocks before the
           size-0 sentinel that ends sf_sl's loop; the gap is 100
           bytes and mi_nlp0 sits at +100, so 25 slots with 2 spare.
           sf_sl's `index < 500` is a loop limit, not the array size.
  pk_dpile   52 -> 13 shorts.  pk_disc is reset per hand and bumped at
           most 5+5 times, plus the explicit pk_dpile[10] write, so 11
           is the floor; gap is 26.
  mi_nOS   DELETED (128 bytes).  It and mi_noSt are one array -- the
           note-on/off handler writes one, mq_stop reads the other,
           and both map to the SAME LCP_STX address, bss 0x27738.

PROVEN CORRECT AS-IS
  mi_lstk  stays at 50 longs.  mq_pshl guards with `if (mi_evcn < 49)`
           and then writes [mi_evcn] and [mi_evcn+1], so 50 is exactly
           right.  Its 688-byte gap is NOT its size: 488 of those bytes
           are globals the port does not have.
  scrbufA  stays at 32512 (32000 + the 512 the align-up can shift).
           Its 33045-byte gap likewise carries 533 bytes of something
           else.

CONTRADICTED -- LEFT ALONE, FLAGGED
  g_sfDoB  the gap says 56 bytes (g_sfdos sits at +56), but SOUNDS.LCP
           contains two 148-byte effects and sf_irqp copies `size`
           bytes into it.  So either LCP_STX overruns this buffer by
           ~92 bytes on every large effect -- clobbering g_sfdos and
           g_sfdoc, and running into the 340 unexplained bytes past
           them -- or one of those three symbols is not what the port
           thinks.  Shrinking it now, while the bss ORDER is still
           wrong, would aim that overrun at whatever the port's linker
           happens to place after it.  Left at 256 until the order is
           reproduced.

The accounting now closes: bss is -1274, and after removing the 268
bytes of remaining excess it would be exactly 1542 short -- which is
the total of the unexplained gap bytes (1572) less scn_cmn (30, the
port's one bss symbol no relocation references).  Every remaining byte
is a global LCP_STX has and the port never touches.

events.title: Array sizes from the code's own loop bounds: bss -580 -> -68
events.message:
Array sizes from the code's own loop bounds: bss -580 -> -68

Two array families, both settled without guessing.

g_obtmt / g_obtaw / g_obtah: 64 entries -> 56.  main's OBJECTS walk is
a literal `for (i = 0; i < 56; i++)` that fills all three, and LCP_STX's
relocation gaps for all three agree exactly (1120 = 56 MFDBs, 112, 112).
The old "sized to comfortably cover the 50 or so records" comment was a
guess; the loop is the authority.

LCP_BODY_DEST_WORDS: 168 -> 256 shorts.  sp_lcpf's two call sites both
pass width=2, height=21 and it writes 4 shorts per (x,y), so only 168
are ever touched -- but all four buffers it writes into (g_lsimg,
g_lsmas, g_hsbuf, g_hsmas) measure 512 bytes in LCP_STX, so the
original declares a round 256 and uses two thirds of it.  Four
independent gaps agreeing is what makes this safe: growing a buffer
cannot overrun, and the code proves 168 is the floor.

bss 187382 vs 187450.  Remaining leads, all still ambiguous because a
gap absorbs any LCP_STX symbol the port lacks: mi_lstk (200 vs 688),
g_sfdoc (2 vs 342), scrbufA (32512 vs 33045 of room), g_ltlp (2048 vs
1440 -- its fill loop only indexes 66), g_sfDoB (256 vs 56), in_str
(256 vs 80), mi_ntLp (256 vs 102 -- sf_sl's `index < 500` is a loop
limit, not the array size), wp_ans (120 vs 60, i.e. [5][12] not
[10][12]).  Settling those needs the ORDER, which makes every gap
exact.

events.title: Stop profile recording at the final frame's true boundary
events.message:
Stop profile recording at the final frame's true boundary

Every capture's last frame overran by ~680 color clocks (~3 scanlines, a
consistent ~1%). retro_run() returns a few scanlines past the boundary it was
going to stop at, and unlike every earlier frame — bounded on both sides by
inter-frame markers — nothing marked where the last frame really ended, so
recording ran on into a tail that belonged to no requested frame.

wasm_profile_on_frame_boundary already knew when this happened: it's the
boundary reached once every requested frame has been marked off, where it
previously did nothing. It now stops recording there.

Two things follow from having an exact end:

- wasm_profile_finish measures frameCycles to that boundary rather than to
  whenever retro_run() happened to return, so the reported figure is the frame
  length instead of overstating it by the tail. It now comes back as exactly
  71051 (227 x 313) on PAL rather than 71733.

- the last sample's cycleDelta can be finalized properly instead of being left
  at the "1 = unknown" placeholder, since its cost is the time from its hook to
  the boundary, truncated at the frame edge. Inter-frame markers still drop
  theirs — one fabricated color clock per frame, well below anything
  measurable.

Verified across five capture start phases, one and two frames, whole and
narrow address ranges, running vs paused, and 68000 vs 68020 cycle-exact:
every frame now lands within 5 cycles of 71051, where the last frame
previously sat at 71728-71731. samples == inRange still holds exactly, and
test:wasm passes.

events.title: Screen buffers: 32512, the minimum this code's alignment needs
events.message:
Screen buffers: 32512, the minimum this code's alignment needs

Maintainer: the buffers need not be a round 32768 -- 32255 would do.
That is right for a 256-byte-aligned base, which is all the ST
hardware asks for.  This program aligns to 512, though, and that is
not an inference -- all three align-up sites are in the binary:

    sprites.c  0x15110  push scrbufA+0x1ff ; andi.l #-512,(sp)
    stpScrB    0x65ae   addl #512,d0 ; andl #-512,d0
    fillTopR   0x6880   addl #512,d0 ; andl #-512,d0

So the base can move up by 511 (the +0x1ff form) or a full 512 (the
+512 forms), and 32255 would let the screen run up to 256 bytes past
the end.  32000 + 512 = 32512 is the smallest size that cannot.

Both buffers now carry it, and both still fit LCP_STX's room for them
-- scrbufA has 33045 bytes before mi_dptr, scrbufB 32600 before
pk_quit -- with 533 and 88 bytes over for globals the port does not
have.  bss is back to -580 from -324; the round 32768 on scrbufA had
been covering for other arrays that are still too small (mi_lstk 200
vs 688, the four sprite dest buffers 336 vs 512), which is a better
place for those bytes to be accounted.

events.title: Fix "Follow" landing on the wrong instruction in the Disassembly view
events.message:
Fix "Follow" landing on the wrong instruction in the Disassembly view

Regression from the flame-graph alignment fix. Once column positions became
cycle-weighted, instructions the 68020 measures at zero color clocks (its
lumped accounting defers cycles onto whichever instruction next touches
memory) collapsed onto the same x as the neighbour that carried the lump: 55%
of columns in a real capture are now zero-width.

The shared cursor is an integer DMA slot, so those samples became
unaddressable. Every one of those 17,213 columns round-tripped
(columnIndexToSlot -> columnIndexAtX) to a *different* PC, which broke
everything that navigates by picking a sample and letting the CPU tab
re-derive it: jump to next execution, "View in context", the register panel's
jump-to-write, the step buttons, and the editor's source-line jump.
Single-stepping skipped 27% of instructions and could stick entirely.

No slot-based mapping can fix this — two samples at the same x are
indistinguishable by construction. So the cursor now carries the sample index
alongside the slot. Navigation that knows its target passes it through;
scrubbing the flame graph passes none and leaves the slot authoritative, and
every arbitrary-slot setter goes through one selectSlot helper so a stale
index cannot outlive the slot it came from.

Jump accuracy 89.3% -> 100%, stepping exact by construction. Scrubbing still
resolves only to slot granularity (44.6% of samples) — inherent, and the
reason step/jump exist.

events.title: Add `profile dump`/`profile check` CLI for .puaeprofile captures
events.message:
Add `profile dump`/`profile check` CLI for .puaeprofile captures

Investigating a suspect capture has meant hand-reimplementing the container
parse and sample decode in throwaway JS each time — laborious, and free to
drift from what the extension actually does. This adds an offline CLI that
goes through the real path (loadProfile -> buildFramesFromCaptures ->
buildColumns), so a report cannot disagree with the viewer.

`dump` is the read side: per-frame cost tables (self cycles, flame-graph
width, DMA bus census) plus a manifest summary, with --json/--frame/--functions
for programmatic use.

`check` is the more useful half. Raw per-function numbers are easy to
rationalise — a busy-wait at 76% of a frame looks plausible until you notice
the frame's samples sum to 157% of the color clocks a PAL frame physically
contains. Each check encodes one such invariant, and each corresponds to a bug
that shipped: frame-over-budget (the cycleDelta floor), width-vs-cycles
(flame-graph runs spread by sample index), registers-truncated and frame-short
(the profile/register buffer caps). It exits non-zero on an error-level
finding, so it also works as a gate.

Run against the captures from the recent profiler work, `check` reproduces the
whole three-bug investigation in one command.

Wired as a subcommand of the existing puae-debugger binary, dispatched before
any DAP/HTTP/emulator machinery loads. Also narrows the blanket `.claude`
ignore so project skills are tracked while local state stays untracked.

events.title: debugger: classify posted-write drain waits by their own arbitration; list CPUWAIT in help
events.message:
debugger: classify posted-write drain waits by their own arbitration; list CPUWAIT in help

Review follow-ups for the CPU wait attribution.

A posted 020+ chip write drains through the ordinary arbitration, in
which a busy nice blitter keeps every access cycle: the blitter-slowdown
yield that frees a synchronous grant after three misses does not apply
to the drain. Classifying the drain's waits from the CPU's view therefore
reported the slot as free (port turnaround) from the fourth miss on while
the blitter still held it. The classifier now takes the arbitration view
the waiting access is subject to: the CPU's view for a synchronous grant
(fence and yield included), the ordinary view for a drain. A 020 test
posts a write against a four-word source-only blit and checks every
drained clock stays the blitter's.

The scanline strip in the CPU wait view overlays the denied slots on the
dimmed owner pattern, as the raster does, instead of dropping the
owners.

CPUWAIT joins the console's HELP inspect list, with a test covering the
help entry, the no-trace message, and the traced-frame summary.

events.title: Screen buffers: the ST round-allocation pattern, where it fits
events.message:
Screen buffers: the ST round-allocation pattern, where it fits

Maintainer: an ST screen buffer is allocated as a round `char
buf[32768]` with the base aligned up inside it (the hardware wants
256-byte alignment; this code aligns to 512 via
`(base + 0x200) & ~0x1FF`).

scrbufA takes it: LCP_STX has 33045 bytes of room there, so 32768
fits with 277 to spare.  That alone moved bss from -580 to -68.

scrbufB does NOT fit the round size and stays at 32512.  The
relocation pairing puts pk_quit 32600 bytes after scrbufB's base --
25 sites agree on that address, against scrbufB's own single site --
so 32768 would swallow it.  32512 is 32000 plus the 512 the align-up
can shift, and leaves 88 bytes for globals the port does not have.
Flagging rather than forcing it: if scrbufB really is 32768 in the
1985 source, then one of those two relocation targets is not the
symbol the port thinks it is, and that is worth knowing.

data -44, bss -324, text still 104156 == 104156 with zero differing
bytes.

events.title: debugger: attribute CPU chip-bus waits in the Frame Analyzer and profile export
events.message:
debugger: attribute CPU chip-bus waits in the Frame Analyzer and profile export

The bus trace recorded who won each colour clock but not that the CPU was
waiting for it, so a coder could see the DMA pattern of a frame but not
which of those slots cost the 68000 time, nor which instruction paid.

Every colour clock the CPU asks for the chip bus and is denied is now
attributed, from the CPU's own view of the arbitration, to the class that
held it: fixed DMA (refresh, bitplane, sprite, disk, audio), the Copper's
access clock, the blitter with BLTPRI clear (the nice hold before the
slowdown counter yields), the blitter with BLTPRI set including its
warm-up fence (where the slot's recorded owner is idle because the
blitter's own cycle needs no bus), and the 020+ chip port's two-clock
turnaround, which is a wait on the CPU's own bus unit rather than a
denial. The sample carries the pending access kind and the instruction's
start PC. It is taken only while the frame analyzer is armed, on the cold
bus-observer path, so the timeline is untouched: the new bus tests pin
the same colour-clock cost as the unarmed scenarios, and two 40-second
control-protocol runs of a demo, one profiled from boot, stop at the same
clock with identical screen digests.

FrameBusTrace gains a per-slot wait grid parallel to the owner grid,
totals by class and by access kind, and a capped PC histogram that is
only read out sorted. The Frame Analyzer's Beam tab gains a "CPU wait"
checkbox (key W) that flips the raster, scanline strip, legend and
counters column to the wait view (denied slots in the denier's colour,
everything else dimmed; waited share, breakdown, top stalled PCs), plus
an always-drawn per-line stall gutter beside the raster. The console
gains CPUWAIT, profile.jsonl gains a cpu record and a cpu_wait grid
under slots, and profile.json lists the wait classes.

Opcode prefetches count under the read kind: the 68k core issues them as
plain word reads, so the fetch kind only covers immediate and extension
words read outside the prefetch queue. Documented as such.

events.title: Segment placement and sizes: data +3008 -> -44, bss +53884 -> -580
events.message:
Segment placement and sizes: data +3008 -> -44, bss +53884 -> -580

Acting on the relocation-pairing analysis.  Every referenced global now
sits in the same SEGMENT as LCP_STX's, and the two segments are within
a few hundred bytes instead of 57 KB.

Placement (data <-> bss), all evidence-driven:
  - Dropped the initializer from 155 globals.  Alcyon puts an
    explicitly zeroed global in .data; LCP_STX writes `short x;` and
    gets a .comm.  20 of them were NOT zero (g_pcmon/g_ppmon 400,
    mi_nlp0/mi_nxTk/mi_lpTk/g_mtdiv 100, psg_cvol 15, mi_evcn 9,
    lcp_watr 7, g_spdc/g_aprio 5, lcp_food 4, lcp_bwlS/g_aggun/
    scr_scal 1, lastAct/g_msmap/g_lcieo -1, and vdipb's five
    pointers) -- LCP_STX initialises none of them, and every one has
    a run-time writer.  vdipb works out because v_opnvwk assigns all
    five entries before its first trap.
  - Gave the eight that go the other way their real contents, read
    out of LCP_STX's data segment: bm32or/bm32and (LCP_STX ships the
    32 shift/mask longs rather than building them at run time),
    g_mstr, g_mcpro, mi_chmap, g_sepef, moff_f, and g_ew2a.

g_ew2a is now a real table (408 bytes, byte-exact).  Alcyon rejects
the NESTED form `{ {..}, a, p }` with "mismatched curly braces" -- but
it takes the FLATTENED list, which is how LCP_STX ships it.  The
port's host-side rows had action and priority the wrong way round in
33 of 34 rows: chk_encm returns the byte at +10 and adds the byte at
+11 to g_aprio, and LCP_STX's row 0 is (24, 15), not (15, 24).

g_mstr's static content is 0..99 then 110..127 then zeros -- the row
100..109 is simply missing from the 1985 table.  Preserved; mq_bust
rewrites all 132 entries before anything reads them.

Sizes:
  - scrbufA 65536 -> 32512 and scrbufB 33280 -> 32512.  Each holds ONE
    aligned screen; the "two screens, alt at +0x8000" reading came
    from the `&scrbufA[0x8000]` bug fixed in the previous commit.
  - dsb_stor 34816 -> 12832 bytes, which is what fillTopR can actually
    write: its largest caller is mg_stp's fillTopR(0x4d) = 77 rows of
    160, plus the 512 the align-up can shift.  LCP_STX's own gap there
    is 12836.
  - SPRITE_HW_SLOTS_ALLOC back to 8.  The port had widened these
    arrays to 10 so a stray slot-9 write stayed in bounds regardless
    of link order; LCP_STX tolerates it because the write lands in the
    adjacent array (g_sepey[9] == g_seacw[1]).  That safety now rests
    on reproducing the original's adjacency, which is the point.
  - Deleted workin/work_out and g_setmt/g_setaw/g_setah: duplicates of
    work_in/wk_out and the g_obt* trio, referenced by nothing.

What is left is ordering: 49 inversions among the data symbols and 61
among the bss ones, plus the -44/-580 that the derived gaps cannot
resolve while the order is wrong (each gap is only an upper bound --
it absorbs any unreferenced symbol that follows).  Text stays
104156 == 104156 with zero differing bytes.

events.title: Fix the alternate compositing buffer pointer (relocation analysis)
events.message:
Fix the alternate compositing buffer pointer (relocation analysis)

Pairing the relocation streams of the two binaries -- the text is
byte-identical, so the 6429 text relocation SITES are identical and
each one gives a port-address -> LCP_STX-address pair -- turned up two
sites where the port pointed somewhere else entirely.

  1. sc_ren8's alternate buffer.  `(long) &scrbufA[0x8000] & ~0x1FF`
     does NOT do what the port's comment claimed: Alcyon's int is
     16-bit, so 0x8000 is -32768 and c168 emitted
     `move.l #-32768+_scrbufA` -- the alt screen base was
     scrbufA - 32768, a pointer into the TEXT segment.  LCP_STX stores
     `scrbufA + 0x1FF` there, i.e. the SAME aligned buffer sp_iniM
     uses, which is also what the surrounding comment describes.
     Fixed to `((long) scrbufA + 0x1FFL) & ~0x1FFL`.

  2. mq_tick.s had g_msmsa and psg_ntAc the wrong way round: LCP_STX
     has psg_ntAc at 0x2270 and g_msmsa at 0x2271.  Seven text
     relocations pointed at the wrong byte.

Neither showed up before because verify_bytes AND stx_txtdiff both
wildcard relocated longwords -- a function can match byte for byte
while the address it loads is wrong.  With both fixed, all 6429 text
relocations now resolve to the same segment as LCP_STX's and every
text->text one to the identical address; text stays 104156 == 104156
with zero differing bytes.

events.title: Remove everything LCP_ORG-related
events.message:
Remove everything LCP_ORG-related

Maintainer directive: forget LCP_ORG.PRG.  It was a cracked dump used
as a temporary reference; DATA/LCP_STX.PRG is the shipped game and now
the port's only target.  Nothing about the old reference survives in
the tree.

Sources
  - Every `#ifdef FAITHFUL` / `#ifndef FAITHFUL` conditional resolved
    with FAITHFUL undefined (169 files).  A dropped `#endif` can carry
    an unterminated comment onto the next line, so the pass swallows
    those continuations too -- without that, six files ended up with
    an orphaned `*/` that cp68 happily passed through and c068 choked
    on.
  - Deleted the files that were left holding nothing but gated
    includes: aleisure.c, asimple.c, adoors.c, delivery.c, afood.c,
    aidle.c, abathrm.c, ahouse.c, aletter.c.  Their bodies already
    live in source/parts/ and stx_u2.c includes them in LCP_STX order.
  - Deleted vdiown.c, vdilib.c, vdiown_a.s, vdilib_a.s (superseded by
    vdistx.c + vdistx_a.s) and gemstart.s (the Atari DK startup --
    LCP_STX links alcyon2's GEMSTART.O verbatim).

Tools
  - verify_bytes.py and prg_diff.py default to DATA/LCP_STX.PRG, and
    verify_bytes' whole KEPT classification is gone: it existed only
    to excuse functions the cracked dump lacked, and against LCP_STX
    everything must match.  stx_check.sh no longer has to disable it.
  - alcyon_build.sh and alcyon_link.sh lost their FAITHFUL branches,
    the vdi_go injection, the Atari DK library set and the BSS remap
    step.  rom_map.py -> stx_map.py.
  - Deleted bss_remap.py, rom_bss_layout.tsv, rom_data_map.txt,
    rom_link_order.txt, rom_midi_engine.asm -- all LCP_ORG layout
    artefacts.  The bss work ahead needs an LCP_STX spec, not these.

Docs
  - CLAUDE.md rewritten around the single reference (1314 -> 1080
    lines).  The source-shape rule table keeps both columns, relabeled
    `wrong shape vs what LCP_STX actually has`, because the contrast
    is what makes each rule usable.
  - Makefile SOURCES regenerated from the real file set (31 files);
    STATUS.md flagged stale, since its file column predates parts/.

Verified: a clean rebuild (build/alcyon deleted first) still gives
text 104156 == 104156 with zero differing bytes, 337 matched /
0 divergent.  data +3008 and bss +53884 remain.

events.title: campaign2: TEXT is byte-identical to LCP_STX (104156 == 104156)
events.message:
campaign2: TEXT is byte-identical to LCP_STX (104156 == 104156)

The whole text segment now matches DATA/LCP_STX.PRG byte for byte
modulo relocations -- same size, zero differing bytes anywhere.

The last +44 was the VDI binding module.  LCP_STX has ONE trap
dispatcher and ONE parameter block where the port carried three
copies of the same 22-byte routine: vdiown_a.s's vdi_go on vdipb,
vdilib_a.s's vdi_go2 on vdipb2, and VDIBIND's own gsx1 on its private
pblock.  And its module is one object, in this order:

    vswr_mode 0x1733a < v_bar < v_gtext < v_opnvwk 0x17426 < v_pline
    < vqt_attributes 0x174e4 < vro_cpyfm 0x1753a < vsf_color
    < vsf_interior < vsf_style < vsl_color < vst_color
    < vst_height 0x176b8 < wr_src < wr_dst < gsx1 0x1772e

vqt_attributes and vst_height sitting BETWEEN Activision's own
bindings is the proof they are not linked from VDIBIND there -- the
1985 source copied the DRI bodies into the module, exactly as it did
with the rest of the binding layer.  v_opnvwk and vro_cpyfm live here
too rather than in a separate workstation object.

So the default build gets source/vdistx.c (the module in LCP_STX
order, the nine shared bindings included from parts/, the four
library-shaped bodies written out) plus source/vdistx_a.s
(wr_src, wr_dst and the single _gsx1 on _vdipb -- defining _gsx1
keeps VDIBIND's gsx1 member and its private pblock out of the link).
vdiown.h maps vdi_go and vdi_go2 onto gsx1 for this configuration;
tools/stx_units.txt skips vdiown.c and vdilib.c, and alcyon_link.sh
drops vdilib.o/vdilib_a.o from the default LIST.

Remaining: data +3008, bss +53884.

events.title: campaign2: the whole game code is code-identical to LCP_STX
events.message:
campaign2: the whole game code is code-identical to LCP_STX

stx_txtdiff reports ZERO differing bytes in 0x0..0x17340 -- every
instruction, branch displacement and immediate in LCP_STX's 94 736
bytes of game code now matches the port.  Only the relocated data and
bss longwords still differ, which is the next (and last) phase.

The step that got there was reproducing stx_u2's function ORDER.
LCP_STX did not lay that object out by source file -- aleisure's nine
functions alone run from 0xe338 to 0x12ca0 -- so 39 more bodies moved
into parts/ and stx_u2.c's include list IS the object's order now,
recovered by pairing every LCP_STX prologue span in 0xde36..0x148fe
against its byte-identical port counterpart.  adoors.c and asimple.c
handed their ungated a_gesff / p_sf* includes to stx_u2.c, and the
unit carries the union of the constituents' headers (they emit no
code, so layout is unaffected).

Three real recoveries fell out of the last three diffs:
  - The four SFX wrappers are ordered tvc, spe, hnd, grt -- the ids in
    the 0xf91e (SPEECH,3) and 0xf952 (GREETING,2) bodies settle it,
    against CLAUDE.md's earlier guess of tvc/grt/hnd/spe.
  - a_hello's random arm therefore plays SPEECH on the non-zero roll
    and GREETING on zero, not the other way round.
  - gameTick's `if (g_sepex[g_lcieo] < 0) g_sepex[g_lcieo] = 0;` clamp
    lives INSIDE the non-carrying arm; the port had it after the
    if/else, which is exactly what the 0x1570e end-of-then jump
    (0x157bc, not 0x1579a) was reporting.

Remaining text delta is +44 bytes, all of it in the VDI binding
module: LCP_STX has ONE trap dispatcher (the library's gsx1 at
0x1772e, with pblock as the single parameter block) where the port
carries vdi_go, vdi_go2 and a linked gsx1 -- 22 bytes each.

events.message:
campaign2: li_loor is the copy with the unused frame

LCP_STX carries the "stand and look" gesture TWICE -- 0x12c08 with
`link #-10` (three locals it never references) and 0x12c54 with
`link #-4` -- and the callers say which is which: a_lists/a_playp
reach 0x12c08, tt_on/tt_off reach 0x12c54.  So li_loor is the
three-local copy and it comes FIRST in the object; both now match
byte for byte.

Also checked off two suspected missing functions that turned out not
to be: 0xe310 is sc_sdtf (verify_bytes skips it for being under 48
bytes, which is why stx_unverified listed it), and its body is
identical to exitVdi's, which is what made the naive length+content
pairing report a duplicate.

With that, EVERY function in LCP_STX's game code is accounted for:
265 orig prologue spans against 265 port spans, one to one.  The 59
that still differ do so only in bsr displacements, because stx_u2's
intra-object function ORDER has not been reproduced yet -- e.g.
lcp_rgt's sole diff is `bsrw 0x1120a` where LCP_STX has
`bsrw 0x1203a`, the same sp_ssco at a different address.

events.title: campaign2: minigame object byte-identical (0x12a..0xd9ea)
events.message:
campaign2: minigame object byte-identical (0x12a..0xd9ea)

The whole first half of LCP_STX's game code -- the MIDI object,
cp_main, the 0x400c object and the entire minigame object -- now has
ZERO code differences against DATA/LCP_STX.PRG (only the relocated
data/bss longwords still differ, which is the next phase).

Recovered here:
  - pk_ante: the F10/quit arm ends with an explicit `return;` (its
    dead end-of-then jump is what gave it away) and the four money
    adjustments are ++/-- to memory, not `x = x + 1`.
  - pk_main: three more `else if` chains are separate `if`s in STX,
    each preceding arm closing with `goto next_round;`, and the
    round loop's trailing `goto next_round;` lives INSIDE the
    deepest block -- which is why every end-of-if jump in the
    function targets the epilogue rather than that goto.
  - pk_cdrw's redraw loop uses dm as the duplicate flag, n as the
    inner counter and card as the drawn card (the port had all
    three roles on the wrong frame slots).
  - pk_evhs declares i, c, j, dup in that order.
  - pk_chsc spells the face-card range `>= 8`, like pk_bjr.
  - cmd_num (0x17278, 112 bytes): a decimal string->number helper
    with the flag-save `while ((c = *p++) >= '0' && c <= '9')` shape.
    NOTHING in LCP_STX calls it -- Alcyon emits a static even when
    nothing references it -- and its 112 bytes were the last
    misalignment before blkcp_a, so lcp_upp, blkcp32 and the library
    now all sit at their exact STX addresses.

Text: port 104200 / orig 104156.  Code-identical 0x0..0xd9ea
(55 488 of the game's 94 736 bytes); the rest is stx_u2's function
order plus the data/bss layout.

events.message:
campaign2: eleven blackjack statics byte-exact

pk_ante, pk_evhs, pk_ddec, pk_cbet, pk_chsc, pk_bjr, pk_cnbj,
pk_dchd, pk_dbhi, pk_sbet and pk_bjwr now reproduce LCP_STX byte
for byte (residual diffs are bsr displacements from the games
object still sitting 0x20 bytes late).

Shapes recovered in this batch:
  - pk_bjr's hit/stand input uses the GLOBAL bj_key and pk_inph's
    255 idle sentinel, and its body is
    `if (forced) {...} else while (1) {...}` with `else if` chaining
    the F3/F1 arms; the ranks compare `<= 11 && >= 8`, not
    `< 12 && > 7`.
  - pk_cnbj carries a `result` local and an if/else-if ladder.
  - pk_dchd's dup scan is one short-circuit `||`, the seat loop is
    body-first with an explicit break, and the face-down test is
    `if (face_down)` (then arm = CARD_BACK).
  - pk_dbhi lays out char digits + `char str[4]` and uses the
    embedded-assignment form `str[0] = (hund = val / 100) + '0';`.
  - pk_sbet's countdowns are `while ((*bet_ptr)--)` / `while (n--)`
    with ++/-- on the money globals; two locals, no `cur`.
  - pk_bjwr indexes `pk_pwc[g_pchc * 4 + idx]` inline (no `off`
    local -- `arr[i + g * 4]` is what emits the addaw/addaw pair),
    sentinels the war piles with -1, reveals with `while (--idx)`,
    compares `(prank = ...) > (crank = ...)` in one expression, and
    keeps BOTH win paths inside the for(;;) with their own returns.

port text is 104120 bytes against LCP_STX's 104156 (delta -36).

events.title: Two leftovers from hexwab's inline-wrap patch: a dead store and a byte
events.message:
Two leftovers from hexwab's inline-wrap patch: a dead store and a byte

Both were left out of ecefec5 rather than folded in silently, and hexwab
has asked for them (issue #1).

RedrawAll's ra_row stored bufp+1 before the BPL and .ra_nowrap stores it
again unconditionally, so the first could never be observed. bufp is zero
page, so it is 2 bytes and 3 cycles, not 3 and 3 -- 48 cycles a redraw
across the 16 rows.

sTmp's low byte died with the same patch: SetCRTCStart shifts the low half
in A now, so only the high byte is live. EQUW -> EQUB, and the three
references move off sTmp+1.

  bank 4       $BFF5 -> $BFF3   2 B
  code image   $2FE8 -> $2FE7   1 B

Verified rather than inspected, since both touch address arithmetic:

  - Buffer oracle. Deck at scrollS = 48, line = 1, all three draw call
    sites NOPed, view settled, then a forced RedrawAll over the
    incrementally-scrolled buffer: 0 of 10,240 bytes differ. Both arms of
    ra_row's wrap run in that one test -- 16 rows at any scrollS > 0 span
    the end of the strip.
  - SetCRTCStart separately, because the buffer oracle is blind to it: a
    wrong start address moves the picture, not the buffer. crtcHi/crtcLo
    read back $0B06, which is ($5800 + 48) / 8.

events.title: akiko: gate transmitter-ready on the drive buffer having room
events.message:
akiko: gate transmitter-ready on the drive buffer having room

A PIO producer polls DRIVEXMIT before each command byte. With the drive's
receive buffer full, the PIO port dropped the byte but could re-assert the
latch straight away, since the ready condition only looked at the drive
being idle: the producer was told a byte was accepted when it had been
lost. Transmitter-ready now also requires room in the buffer, at the PIO
port, at the response-drain re-arm, and after a command that sends no
reply; a byte written while the latch is clear is an overrun and stays
dropped. Regression test covers the full-buffer case through the drain.

Also tightens the peripherals doc sentence that stated the checksum-error
outcome twice.

events.title: toccata: clear play/capture-active bits independently in write_reg9
events.message:
toccata: clear play/capture-active bits independently in write_reg9

write_reg9 only cleared self.active (and so play_active()) via
codec_stop() when both PEN and CEN dropped to zero together. A driver
that disables playback while leaving capture enabled (e.g. 0x03 ->
0x02) never took that path, so play_active() stayed stuck true and
the mixer fallback added in the previous commit would keep emitting
the final sample forever -- the same bug, reached a different way.

Clear each direction's bit in `active` independently as its own
enable bit clears, so play_active() reflects PEN alone regardless of
CEN's state. Flagged by Copilot's PR review.

events.title: akiko: keep the TX DMA draining the command ring during a lead-in dump
events.message:
akiko: keep the TX DMA draining the command ring during a lead-in dump

The TX DMA fetch was gated on the drive being idle (no command in its
turnaround, no reply undelivered), so while the drive streamed a TOC dump
the guest's command ring was consumed one byte per delivered packet.
Kickstart's cd.device queues a 3-byte LED packet for every TOC entry it
receives and an unpause right behind the request, which on a disc with
more than about 25 tracks laps the 256-byte ring; the lapped bytes then
parse as garbage after the dump, and the held unpause -- whose buffer the
deferral kept appending later bytes to -- fails its checksum as well. A
39-track disc (Pinball Illusions CD32) produced four checksum-error
replies at boot that the real drive never sends.

Model the drive side of the link explicitly: Akiko's DMA engine now
drains the ring into the drive's receive buffer (tx_fifo) regardless of
the drive's state, and the drive parses one command at a time out of that
buffer, still only between dumps, so the calibrated dump-exclusive hold
and the cold-boot timing are unchanged. PIO command bytes go through the
same buffer. command_deferred_for_toc is gone; STATE_VERSION 78.

Adds a regression test that replays Kickstart's LED-per-entry traffic on
a 42-point TOC and checks that the ring never lags by more than a packet,
that every LED packet and the unpause come out intact and in order, and
that the unpause is answered only after the last TOC entry.

events.title: campaign2: cp_main byte-exact -- ZERO divergent functions
events.message:
campaign2: cp_main byte-exact -- ZERO divergent functions

cp_main is hand-written assembly in LCP_STX (maintainer), so it is
recovered as source/cp_asm.s rather than C: 0x22c0-0x400b is one
self-contained object whose 21 relocations all point back inside
itself.  It saves d1-d7/a0-a5 into its own static block, goes
supervisor, sets TOS's flock byte, decrypts 96 bytes of itself in
place keyed by the drive number, drives the 1772 FDC directly through
$ff8604/$ff8606 and the DMA address registers to read the protected
track into a 6560-byte buffer that lives inside the text segment, then
re-encrypts itself and restores everything.  Its LONG return value is
assembled by six mutually recursive stubs that each add a constant.

Assembled with as68 -n: the original picks bsr.w where bsr.s would fit
(cpnxt's first call), so branch optimization has to be off and every
branch carries its own explicit size.  stx_check.sh's object list now
mirrors alcyon_link.sh's, or the symbol side-link disagrees with
LCP.PRG about the layout and every extent comes out wrong.

339 matched / 0 divergent, 90.0% of LCP_STX text.

events.title: toccata: silence the mixer fallback once the codec stops
events.message:
toccata: silence the mixer fallback once the codec stops

peek_last_sample() is the resampler's fallback in advance_mixer for
whenever the mixer's cadence outruns the codec's own causally-paced
production. advance_codec stops running entirely once play_active() is
false, so after codec_stop() the mixer took this fallback on every
tick and peek_last_sample() kept returning the last decoded DAC value
forever -- a permanent DC offset in the stem/mix instead of silence.

Gate the fallback on play_active() so it still holds the last sample
across a genuine underrun during active playback, but returns silence
once the codec is stopped.

events.title: dap: address the review findings
events.message:
dap: address the review findings

- The Debug Console's raw `!method` escape refuses the run-control
  verbs (continue, run_until, the steps, reverse_*, pause, shutdown): a
  raw `continue` blocked the adapter's only loop until a stop nothing
  the client could still send would cause, and a raw step moved the
  machine without a `stopped` event.
- A data breakpoint watches the words from its aligned start through
  its last byte, so an odd start no longer drops the final byte; the
  hit test uses half-open ranges, so an adjacent word no longer counts.
- A PC breakpoint whose address another of the session's breakpoints
  holds is shared only when the conditions agree (refused with a
  message otherwise), and removing the owner hands the machine
  breakpoint to the sharer instead of deleting it under it.
- Hit conditions keep the operator: `> 3` stops on the fourth hit,
  `>= 3` / `== 3` / `3` on the third.
- Array-form launch `args` are quoted for the AmigaDOS command line
  element by element (`*` escapes inside quotes).
- An explicit terminate, or disconnect with terminateDebuggee, shuts
  down an attached emulator too; a client vanishing, a restart, or the
  adapter's own exit stop only an emulator this session launched.
- HUNK_DREL16 / HUNK_DREL8 go back to the long relocation-table layout;
  only HUNK_DREL32 takes the short form in an executable.
- The end-to-end test asserts the source line after Step Back (the
  breakpoint's line) and after Step Out (the call site in scale).

events.title: romsearch: find a source build's assets from the executable's tree
events.message:
romsearch: find a source build's assets from the executable's tree

The bundled AROS ROM (and the FMV, HRTMon, A4091, A2091 and lide ROMs)
were looked for next to the executable, in the package's Resources or
share directories, and finally in `assets/` under the working directory,
which is how `cargo run` from the source tree finds them. A
`target/release/copperline` started from anywhere else -- an IDE's debug
adapter runs it from the IDE's own directory -- reported "the bundled
AROS ROM was not found" although the tree it was built in has it.

Fold the six copies of that search into one `asset_dirs` and add the
executable's ancestors (`target/release/../../assets/<sub>`, one level
more for a target directory nested in the tree) before the working-
directory fallback. Installed layouts are searched exactly as before.

events.title: debugger: add a Debug Adapter Protocol server, copperline-ctl --dap
events.message:
debugger: add a Debug Adapter Protocol server, copperline-ctl --dap

VS Code, nvim-dap and other DAP clients can debug a program in the
emulator with source-level breakpoints and stepping, registers, locals
and globals, memory, the custom chipset, reverse execution and a Debug
Console, without a GDB in between. The adapter is a control-protocol
client like the MCP mode: `launch` starts copperline --control-gui (or
--control for headless) --run PROG and rides the one-shot load stop to
relocate the program's debug information by segments.list, binds the
breakpoints set before the load, and runs to the entry point; `attach`
joins a session started with --control-info.

Stepping repeats step / step_over / step_out until the source line
changes, steps out of code without lines, and falls back to temporary
breakpoints on the function's other lines for a line that outgrows 64
single steps. Step Back repeats reverse_step the same way; the adapter
takes a reverse_anchor snapshot at every run stop, since the boot
volume --run stages is a host directory mount whose traffic a replay
from an older snapshot cannot reproduce, and pins --rtc-time to the
launch time so the guest clock replays too. Conditions are the
machine's own register/immediate/word compares; data breakpoints are
memory watches; exception filters are catch breakpoints. Serial output
(where KPrintF goes) is the Debug Console's stdout, and `!method {json}`
sends a raw control-protocol request.

tools/vscode-copperline is a declarative VS Code extension (plus a
40-line activator pointing at copperline-ctl) contributing the
`copperline` debug type; docs/debugger/dap.md documents the adapter,
its launch arguments and what each toolchain's debug information gives.
tests/dap_stdio.rs drives the adapter over stdio against the bundled
AROS ROM and the guest/dap-test probe, ignored like the other
process-spawning tests.

events.title: debuginfo: read symbols, LINE hunks and DWARF from Amiga executables
events.message:
debuginfo: read symbols, LINE hunks and DWARF from Amiga executables

A host-side reader for a guest program's debug information, behind the
new `dap` feature: the hunk table, HUNK_SYMBOL tables, vasm -linedebug
LINE debug hunks, and DWARF through gimli/object, either from the
trailing debug hunk amiga-gcc 6.5 -g writes or from an ELF the program
was converted from with elf2hunk. Line rows, functions with parameters
and locals (single-operation locations), globals, the common type DIEs
and .debug_frame come out addressed as hunk + offset, and DebugInfo
relocates them by the segment list the guest reports. unwind.rs walks
the stack by CFI where the DWARF covers the PC and otherwise by the
console STACK command's return-address scan.

The amiga linker resolves every cross-section reference inside the debug
hunk (abbreviation offset, stmt_list, strp, the FDEs' CIE pointers) as
an offset in the link address space, where the block follows the text,
data and bss hunks laid back to back from 0. Rather than rewrite the
DWARF, each section is handed to gimli behind that much padding, with
the bias measured from the first unit header's abbreviation offset.

Only amiga-gcc 6.5 with binutils 2.39 keeps the DWARF in hunk output;
the current amiga-gcc images (6.5 with binutils 2.46, and 13/15/16) drop
it, so the C fixture in guest/dap-test builds with the host-installed
toolchain, while the vasm fixture uses the shared docker image. Both
committed binaries are read by the unit tests.

events.title: control: report segments, anchor the reverse ring, stop at the --run load
events.message:
control: report segments, anchor the reverse ring, stop at the --run load

Three additions to the control protocol for a debugger client:

- `segments.list` returns the hunk segments of the program the scheduled
  process is running (the walk the console SEGMENTS command and the GDB
  stub's qOffsets already share) plus the programs an armed loadseg catch
  has recorded, so a client can relocate symbols at a `loadseg` stop.
- `reverse_anchor` snapshots the machine into the reverse-debug ring at
  the current position. Host-side state a restore cannot roll back (a
  directory mount's file handles, a disk image) makes a replay from an
  older frame boundary diverge: a reverse_step after a breakpoint in a
  `--run` session landed in ROM in another task. Replaying from a
  snapshot taken at the stop is exact.
- `--run PROG` with `--control` / `--control-gui` arms the one-shot
  loadseg stop `--gdb` has (control::Config::stop_on_load). The headless
  server installs it before the first resume; the windowed driver
  installs it before the first frame, so a client attaching after the
  warp boot cannot miss the load, and a stop that fired with no client
  attached is delivered as event.stopped on connect.

Bridge::send takes &self (the writer behind a mutex, ids atomic) so one
thread can block in wait() for an outstanding resume while another
sends pause; LaunchSpec gains windowed/noaudio so a bridge can start a
--control-gui session. MCP launches are unchanged.

events.title: Layer 9 DECISION 20: an energy bar, one pixel a point
events.message:
Layer 9 DECISION 20: an energy bar, one pixel a point

The C64 shows energy by flashing the player's sprite below eight and in
no other way, which is a threshold alarm and not a gauge: between 64 and
8 -- where a player decides whether to take a fight -- it says nothing.
Stew asked for a readout and KC took a single bar under the logo.

It costs the original's artwork nothing, because it goes where the
original draws nothing at all. panelframe's bottom-middle cells carry ink
on scanline 5 alone, so scanlines 0-4 of panel row 3 are blank INSIDE the
box; the bar takes scanline 2, centred in that band. No glyph moved and
no cell of the C64's status line was overdrawn. The colour was spare too
-- palPanel had logical 1 unused, so PN_PHYS_BAR is a fourth ink and the
paper, the logo, the score and the frame are where they were.

CB_ENERGY_FULL is $40 and a MODE 1 byte is four pixels, so a full bar is
sixteen bytes and the byte count IS the energy shifted right twice. No
scale factor, no multiply, and a four-entry table for the part-lit byte.
Centring on the nine-cell logo leaves 4 px either side, which puts the
left end on a byte boundary -- nothing is shifted or masked. Units are 8
bytes apart, so the draw is one STA abs,X with X stepping 8, gated on a
shadow byte like the score's.

pmEnergy is the fourth scalar in the bank-6 bridge, for the same reason
as the other three: drEnergy is entry 0 of the droid table, in bank 4,
and panel.asm cannot see it.

Verified against the buffer, not the screenshot: PnMirror's LDA drEnergy
patched to an immediate and the sixteen bytes read back at $527A+8n --
0 empty, 6 -> 0F 0C, 27 -> six 0F then 0E, 33 -> eight 0F then 08, 64 ->
sixteen 0F with the next address still 00. Scanline 5 read $FF and
scanlines 0/1/3/4 read $00 throughout, so the box's bottom edge is
untouched. Game over shows no bar (death leaves energy at zero) and the
briefing cannot show a stale one (PanelInit runs before PnBriefing).

Bank 6 -75 B (673 free), code image -7 B (24 free, code_end $2FE8).

events.title: zynaps atari: the trainer — hold Z+Y+N at the title; F1/F2/F3 cheats
events.message:
zynaps atari: the trainer — hold Z+Y+N at the title; F1/F2/F3 cheats

A deliberate, documented divergence, implemented ENTIRELY IN THE SHIM as
key-triggered pokes of bytes the game already honors (atari/zynaps_cheats.c
+ .h; no src/ include/ test/ file moved; the differential untouched at
4751 and the frame differential still ZERO bytes).

- ARM: hold Z+Y+N for ~2 s (100 VBLs) on the title/attract screen only —
  the window brackets attract_wait_for_start, releasing a key resets, the
  combo is refused in-game. Letters resolved AT RUNTIME from the game's
  own scancode->ASCII table @0x19a39 (a pure QWERTY map, no layout switch
  in the image), plus the AZERTY position for Z (0x11) so the user's
  French STE arms on the keys LABELED Z+Y+N; documented cost: W+Y+N also
  arms on QWERTY.
- F1 toggles the DORMANT invulnerability flag 0x19912 (the secrets hunt's
  find — three death-site reads, no writer in the shipped image);
  F2 lives -> 9 + the panel bit; F3 the five power-up commit arms at the
  game's own ceilings (power 4, shield 3 + HUD mirror, seeker, speed 1,
  timers, panel bits).
- FOUR ORPHANED SOUND EFFECTS RESURRECTED as feedback (35 = the arm
  fanfare with the fa 03 channel code no reachable stream uses; 19 / 37 /
  38 for F1/F2/F3), started through the verified sound_start.
- Inert by default and PROVEN so: every judged smoke mode asserts
  cheats_armed == 0 and zero fires (with the M1-modes' vacuousness stated,
  not hidden); smoke.py cheats is the positive control — arming + the
  fanfare stream on the PSG trace, six poked bytes read off the machine,
  and invulnerability AS BEHAVIOUR (survives to frame 400 where the
  control life ends at ~176; F1 again and the same ship dies at 464) —
  plus the wrong-key and in-game negatives. ZY_NOCHEATS=1 builds and
  smokes green with the ELF asked whether the watcher is in it.
- Pacing cost measured: ~800 cycles/frame = 0.2% (2.52 -> 2.53/2.54,
  ceiling 2.64). Mutations 4/4 killed (wrong-key reset, in-game refusal,
  a fire-count assertion, the dormancy gate).
- Review: the tap had been #ifdef'd inside a header every verified core
  includes (a core compiling differently between builds, invisible to the
  containment gate) — now unconditional, the purist build links an empty
  body; a tautological timer read-back deleted (the three timers honestly
  unpinned on target); a latent interrupt-context out-of-bounds fixed
  (g_fires sized by the wrong constant).

events.title: akiko: deliver subcode frames with a Q position during CD-DA play
events.message:
akiko: deliver subcode frames with a Q position during CD-DA play

The drive's pickup decodes P-W subcode for every frame it plays, and
Akiko DMAs each 96-byte frame into the misc page's subcode area and
raises the subcode interrupt. Copperline only did that from the data
read path, with a zeroed payload; an audio play streamed sectors into
the mixer without any subcode. The Kickstart 3.1 cd.device runs its
CD_ADDFRAMEINT servers and refreshes the CD_QCODE position from that
interrupt, so a title that starts a CD_PLAYTRACK and waits for its
first frame interrupt never got one (regression example: Liberation's
CD32 intro busy-waits on its frame-interrupt counter at 34s while the
audio keeps playing).

Deliver one subcode frame per streamed CD-DA sector through the same
sequence the read path uses (alternating 128-byte halves, $FFFF $0000
end marker, offset register advanced by 100, CDINT_SUBCODE), and fill
the Q channel from the TOC for both paths: an ADR 1 position packet
with control, track, index (index 0 counting down through a pregap),
track-relative and absolute MSF in BCD, and the inverted CRC-16-CCITT,
bit-interleaved with Q in bit 6. The SubQ drive command reports the
same position while a play runs or is paused, in WinUAE's cd_qcode
layout, instead of the all-zero packet. CdTrack::sector_count now has
a user, so its dead_code allowance goes.

No serialized struct changes; the state format stays at 77.

events.title: A42 soldé : l'élection de l'IRQ MFP voit enfin tout le lot de dispatch
events.message:
A42 soldé : l'élection de l'IRQ MFP voit enfin tout le lot de dispatch

Fin du dossier ouvert la veille. Le port de MFP_UpdateNeeded était PARTIEL : l'élection
ne voyait qu'une entrée à la fois, parce que Machine fait suivre chaque callback
d'ordonnanceur d'un cpu.updateIpl() — 18 sites — qui la déclenchait aussitôt. La règle
« seules les plus anciennes concourent » (pendingTime_ <= pendingTimeMin_) n'avait donc
jamais plus d'un candidat.

EXHIBITEUR D'ABORD, comme le TODO l'exigeait — mais en TABLE DE VÉRITÉ plutôt qu'en
étalon pixel : la règle se teste sur la puce nue en quatre lignes, là où un programme ST
aurait demandé deux handlers, un journal et un rendu pour une observation moins directe.
Ajouté à mfp-selftest (31 -> 35 contrôles) :
 · Timer D (priorité BASSE) arrive avant Timer A (HAUTE) -> c'est D qui est servi ;
 · l'ordre des raiseAt est indifférent, c'est la DATE qui tranche ;
 · à date ÉGALE, la priorité reprend ses droits ;
 · plus ancienne ET prioritaire -> pas de conflit.
Vérifié par mutation : NEOST_MFP_BATCH=0 fait échouer le premier cas (got=13, Timer A,
plus récent mais plus prioritaire, au lieu de want=4). C'est exactement le défaut que
corrige Hatari (2013/04/21, « fix Fuzion CD Menus 77, 78, 84 »).

LA REFONTE. Scheduler::setDispatchHooks borne le LOT — garde RAII et compteur de
profondeur, car runTo est ré-entrant (addStolenCycles du blitter). Machine y suspend
l'élection MFP pendant le lot et la tranche UNE FOIS à la fin, avant de relire l'IPL :
l'ordre d'Hatari (CycInt_Process, puis MFP_UpdateIRQ_All(0), puis IPL).

Les cpu.updateIpl() des callbacks sont LAISSÉS EN PLACE, contrairement à ce que le TODO
annonçait : le CPU est arrêté pendant le lot et Moira ne relit sa broche qu'à une
frontière d'instruction, donc les recalculs intermédiaires n'ont aucun effet observable —
les retirer aurait été une seconde refonte pour rien. Verrou d'A/B : NEOST_IPL_BATCH=0.

CE QUE ÇA CHANGE, MESURÉ : le groupement passe de 0 à 123 entrées groupées sur Super
Hang-On (sur 1 000 123) et 1 240 sur le bureau EmuTOS (sur 17,6 M) — environ 1 entrée sur
10 000. « Rarissime » comme l'inventaire l'annonçait, mais non nul, et désormais servi
dans le bon ordre.

⚠ EFFET DE BORD ASSUMÉ, regardé avant d'être classé. dmasnd_poll se décale de 288 px :
cet étalon arme la VBL (sr=$2300), donc l'instant de prise d'exception bouge d'un cheveu
et la phase du poll avec. L'écart est STRUCTURELLEMENT NUL — mêmes 61 valeurs distinctes,
même histogramme de deltas {6:47, 0:39, 8:12, 4:1}, une seule position à 2 octets près
(0038 -> 003A) ; la propriété contrainte (le compteur n'avance qu'au HBL) est intacte.
Référence re-posée. Sa note dit ce qui le justifie ET ce qui ne le justifie pas : c'est un
snapshot sans oracle (Hatari ne se reproduit pas dessus), il ne peut donc pas arbitrer
laquelle des deux phases est juste — ce qui la fait re-poser est que le nouvel ordre est
celui d'Hatari, pas une mesure pixel.

Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert (mfp-selftest 35/0, 25 étalons pixel,
MegaSTE 12/12).

events.title: campaign2: main recovered (310->315), and with it five helpers
events.message:
campaign2: main recovered (310->315), and with it five helpers

main (0x5546) is byte-identical.  It moves into stx_u1 and INLINES
five things the port had factored out, which is the whole reason it
is 1370 bytes against the port's 602:

 * ct_clrB -- the supervisor-mode conterm patch.
 * The .SCN file handling.  Only the nibble decoder is a function
   (parts/scn_dec.c, 0x52ca); the size, buffer and 15-word dictionary
   are globals, and the file handle is never closed.
 * al_locs -- body.lcp loads FIRST, then lcp_crnd for a new game,
   then the PEx filename is patched and loaded.  al_loal (0x6428)
   takes only (name, buffer): no size cap, no return value, and the
   header's second word IS the length.
 * al_loot/al_lost -- fixed 56- and 50-iteration walks with no
   zero-record or size checks.
 * sp_reglp -- its loop, calling sp_regs (0x5bdc) per sprite.

Also: STX calls `Dsetpath("data")` (the port's comment claimed there
was none); cp_main returns a LONG; the door draws are seven full
if/else pairs rather than ternaries in the argument, with only the
cabinet testing `== NO`; the dog bowl is three explicit state tests
with literal frame ids; and main ends at gameLoop with no Pterm.

sp_regs reads its four values back out of the tables instead of using
its parameters; sp_genma (0x408c) keeps the words-per-row division in
a local and walks with *p++.  pex_name is a `char *`, not an array.

deleted -- they do not exist in LCP_STX.

fix(tms9918a): inhibit 5S while F is still set and unread

Confirmed via the datasheet: the fifth-sprite status flag only updates
while F (the frame interrupt flag) is clear. An unread F from a
previous frame previously let 5S keep updating regardless, so a game
that fell behind on polling status could still see fresh 5S reports
it should not have gotten until it acknowledged F.

events.title: fix(vdp): update the VRAM address low byte on the first control byte
events.message:
fix(vdp): update the VRAM address low byte on the first control byte

Both the TMS9918A and V9938 control-port writers latched the first
byte without touching the address register at all, only combining
both bytes once the second byte arrived. Real hardware updates the
address registers low byte immediately on the first write. A data
port access sandwiched between the two control bytes (the second
never sent) previously used the fully stale address instead of the
new low byte combined with the old high byte.

events.title: fix(v9938): reset the palette write latch on R16, not R15
events.message:
fix(v9938): reset the palette write latch on R16, not R15

registerWrite() cleared paletteSecond when R15 (status register select)
was written -- unrelated to the palette port. R16 is the actual palette
index pointer, and writing it is what real hardware documents as
resetting the two-byte write latch so a fresh writePalette() sequence
starts clean.

Two failure modes from the swap: writing R15 mid-sequence wrongly
discarded a pending first byte, and writing R16 (e.g. to retarget the
index before a write) failed to reset the latch, so a stray leftover
first byte from before could combine with the next write into the
wrong entry.

events.title: zynaps atari: the 1 MB diet — 597,470 B against a measured 908,138 budget
events.message:
zynaps atari: the 1 MB diet — 597,470 B against a measured 908,138 budget

The target image shrinks to ZY_TARGET_IMAGE_BYTES = 0x80000 (the kit's
1 MiB OS_IMAGE_SIZE untouched off target). The census that warrants it:
the game shipped for a 512 KB ST and its hard-coded framebuffers end at
0x7fd00, 768 B under that machine's RAM top; program ends 0x6e96e with no
Malloc in the text; all 472 A_* addresses — 315 header #defines AND 157
.equs in the linked asm twins — are below 0x80000; no literal in the
shipped code falls in [0x80000, 0x100000); the upper half was harness-only.
Computed addresses get two WATCHED BANDS (the review caught the first
attempt's blind spot — a single band at 0x80000 sat 768 B above the
world's top): the tail [0x7fd00, 0x80000) checked zero and a 0xa5 guard
[0x80000, 0x81000), both clean after a 300-frame game run.

Budget MEASURED from GEMDOS's own basepage at --memsize 1 (TOS 1.04):
TPA 940,906 (floppy boot is cheaper, the GEMDOS figure is conservative);
minus a 32 KB stack reserve = 908,138; the play build is 597,470 —
310,668 B spare. 512 KB is out of reach, measured: TPA ~416,618 and
smoke.py title --memsize 0 never reaches the program.

Gates, all mutation-verified red: the census fails CLOSED (parsed vs
loose declaration counts); a 1 MB size gate (basepage+text+data+bss vs
the scraped budget); smoke.py check_the_memory (tail, guard, headroom, and
a TPA pin re-taking the build gate's measurement); a shim os_* scan (the
staging moved outside the array, so an os_fwrite from the shim would now
write .bss).

Matrix green at BOTH memsizes from clean builds: title 16 / titlefault 16
/ game 10 with the ZERO-byte frame differential / gamefault 9 / floppy 16,
plus floppy on TOS 1.02; pacing measured independent of memory size
(2.67-2.70 both, under the 2.81 ceiling). make test 4728 unchanged; no
src/ include/ test/ file touched.

Unpinned, recorded: os_in_image bounds at 512 KiB on target and 1 MiB off
it, so init.c's two slice guards stop at different addresses on the two
shores — both arms fail by NOT writing, the census argument holds it, and
pinning needs a refusal counter in src/ (not added).

events.title: fix(v9938): assert S2 HR (bit 5) instead of never setting it
events.message:
fix(v9938): assert S2 HR (bit 5) instead of never setting it

Real hardware toggles HR once per scanline (high during horizontal
blanking); this core has no sub-line T-state granularity to time that
precisely. It never set the bit at all, so any software polling HR
for a 0->1 edge would hang forever.

Synthesise a toggling pattern from the S2 read cadence instead — the
same technique already used for WD179x's INDEX pulse — so a polling
loop always eventually sees both states. Scoped to S2 reads only, so
the existing bit-masked S2 assertions elsewhere in the command-processor
tests (none of which check bit 5) are unaffected.

Recovered: frame -28 (twelve shorts, six untouched, clue_count ahead
of guess_count); the round prologue runs once per word with the
guess-count guard folded into a `while` condition and the "too many
guesses" tail inside the loop ending in `goto new_word`; the whole
key handling is a single `while (key_pressed != KEY_CTRL_M)` loop
(the port had three nested ones) with `if (...) { continue; }` arms;
`if (++index >= 10)`; `key_pressed += 0x20` with 'A'/'Z' bounds; the
letter store drops its (char) cast; the clue scan is a `for` with a
`break` and the swap search is `clue_count = g_agwol - 1` plus a
`for (;;)`; and the answer test calls ag_matc inline.

New codegen rule found by probe: a BRACED `if (c) { continue; }`
emits `beq over / bra Lcond` where the unbraced form folds into a
single conditional branch.  That is what the F1/clue guard needed.

Open: at +0x3dc the scan's second subscript uses an indexed EA
(`movea.l #base,a1 / tst.b (0,a0,a1.l)`).  Our c168 only emits that
shape when the base is a pointer VARIABLE or the index needs a
data-register computation; no spelling of the array access reproduces
it.  STX has the form exactly twice in the whole binary.

events.title: campaign2: gameTick recovered (293->294); LCP_ORG no longer the reference
events.message:
campaign2: gameTick recovered (293->294); LCP_ORG no longer the reference

Per the maintainer: LCP_ORG.PRG was a temporary hack, not the
original game.  New work is written directly in LCP_STX shape rather
than gated behind #ifdef FAITHFUL, and the LCP_ORG byte-identity
check is no longer run.  gameTick is the first function converted
outright -- its FAITHFUL arm is gone, and cy_yoff with it.

gameTick (0x156a6), four structural findings:
 * The carrying-mode arm comes FIRST and, crucially, is NOT an else:
   carrying falls straight through into the tick loop, which the
   port's if/else prevented.
 * cy_yoff is inlined as a `switch (g_lcieo)` with nine cases in
   source order 48, 3, 4, 49, 9, 22, 23, 50, 55 -- Alcyon SORTS the
   cmp.l value table but emits the bodies in source order, so the
   body layout is the evidence for case order (probe-confirmed).
 * The x clamp indexes g_sepex with g_lcieo, not with the slot, and
   there is no `slot` local at all; the redundant inner g_lcyof tests
   have two identical arms.
 * **getKey's no-key sentinel here is -1, not 0.**  The 2026-07-19
   incident's polarity belongs to this image after all.

Also: sc_ren8 (0x15138) and sp_lcha (0x16368 -- 740 bytes, the slot
