events.title: Layer 12 DECISION 6: the lift screen stipples cleared decks
events.message:
Layer 12 DECISION 6: the lift screen stipples cleared decks

Parked on 2026-08-31 because the marking walk would not fit bank 7 --
by about twenty bytes -- and nothing on ram-pass.md's reserve list
frees bank 7. That finding still stands: bank 7 measured 90 B free
today, TIGHTER than the 100-105 recorded in August, and neither of
hexwab's patches touched it.

What unparked it is the second option in that entry's own list, "put
the walk somewhere else". In August bank 6 had 7 B free and bank 5 had
6, so there was nowhere. hexwab's SCANSTEP deferred carry took bank 6
to 931 B and the code image from 3 B to 82. LvClearedMark is therefore
in console.asm, bank 6, and main RAM orchestrates the hop:

  LiftViewEnter  LvEnter4(4) -> LvStart7(7) -> LvClearedMark(6) -> LvStart7b(7)
  ConsoleTick    ConShipEnter4(4) -> LvShip7(7) -> LvClearedMark(6) -> LvRepaintAll(7)

Both bank-7 entries now stop short of LvRepaintAll, because the mark
has to reach the colour shadow between its being built and its being
painted. LvTick7 needs no second mark -- it repaints from the shadow.

THE STACK PAGE WAS NOT USED and stays an untouched reserve. It was the
August plan, but ram-pass.md lists the lift's deck-selection screen
among the paths its 128-byte measurement never exercised, and that is
the one screen this runs on. DECK_DONE is in the code image instead.

Two bank-7 dependencies had to be broken. The colour shadow is main
RAM so the walk can write it, but the deck rectangles are bank 7's:
export_sideview.py now also emits src/data/svdecks6.asm, the same four
tables under lvcDeck* names from the same listing in the same run, so
the copies cannot drift. sideview.asm came back byte-identical.
xsLineLo/Hi were not needed at all -- ten adds of 40, once a cleared
deck, on a screen drawn once.

  bank 6      931 B -> 748 B    (walk, 64 B of tables, 3 B scratch)
  bank 7       90 B ->  25 B    (the stipple in LvCellPaint)
  code image   82 B ->  31 B    (trampolines, DECK_DONE, its clear)
  bank 4       19 B ->  11 B    (exactly the 8 B August costed)

Verified in jsbeeb: CTRL+C on deck 5 sets DECK_DONE[5] and nothing
else; the walk marks 18 of deck 5's 18 cells and 18 in the whole
shadow, so nothing outside it; 16 of those paint chequered with the
halves aligned; the two that do not are char $A6, outside $80-$8F,
which has no lit partner and is left solid by design. A cleared deck
that is also the SELECTED deck paints solid, so clear one deck and
CTRL+] to another to see the effect at all.

events.title: fix(wd179x): WRITE SECTOR drops stale weak-sector copies
events.message:
fix(wd179x): WRITE SECTOR drops stale weak-sector copies

A write to a sector that had stored weak-bit copies (from an EDSK weak
sector) only updated sec.data; sec.copies was left in place, so a
subsequent read could still randomly hand back a pre-write variant via
readCopy(). A real write lays down one deterministic bit pattern,
destroying the weak-bit variation — clear copies on write, for both a
single WRITE SECTOR and each sector touched by a multi-sector write.

events.title: fix(wd179x): ignore a new command register write while BUSY
events.message:
fix(wd179x): ignore a new command register write while BUSY

Real hardware drops any command register write that arrives while a
command is still in progress, except Force Interrupt (0xD_), which
always aborts whatever is running. writeCommand() previously accepted
and dispatched a new command unconditionally, so a rogue write mid
Type II/III transfer would silently clobber the in-flight one instead
of being ignored.

Scoped to the BUSY-gating part of this review item; the I0-I3 Force
Interrupt condition bits are left unmodelled since they only matter
under a timing model this controller's instant-completion design
doesn't have.

events.title: fix(wd179x): READ TRACK reports RNF instead of undefined for a sector-less track
events.message:
fix(wd179x): READ TRACK reports RNF instead of undefined for a sector-less track

A track with no decoded sectors built a zero-length transfer buffer;
readData() indexed it anyway and handed the CPU JavaScript's
`undefined` in the A register instead of a byte. Report RECORD NOT
FOUND up front instead, matching readAddress's existing convention for
the same 'track present but nothing on it' case.

Scoped narrowly to this crash-adjacent bug — READ TRACK's broader
fidelity gaps (no IDAM/DAM/gap/CRC synthesis, fixed sector-count
termination) are a much larger feature addition, not a quick fix, and
are left for the WRITE TRACK item.

events.title: campaign2: drop LIBF from the default link -- LCP_STX has none
events.message:
campaign2: drop LIBF from the default link -- LCP_STX has none

The maintainer's observation that everything before mq_skip (0x12a)
and everything from vswr_mode (0x1733a) on is library code pinned the
one library difference: LCP_STX contains no float formatters at all.
Its __pftoa and __petoa call _ftoa and _etoa at address ZERO -- the
1985 link left both externals unresolved, since the %f/%e conversions
are unreachable in this program.

alcyon_link.sh now links gemlib without libf for the default build and
passes link68's UNDEFINED option so the two danglers resolve to 0
exactly as they do in LCP_STX; the port's __pftoa now calls 0 too.
That removes 2102 bytes the original never had and with them 17
divergent functions (ftoa, etoa and the fp*/ffp* set).  FAITHFUL is
unchanged -- LCP_ORG does contain LIBF.

Divergent: 103 -> 86.  The game's own code is 94 736 of the 104 156
text bytes, so the 41 206 proven bytes are 43.5% of what the port
actually has to reproduce.

events.title: fix(wd179x): READ ADDRESS rotates through ID fields instead of always sectors[0]
events.message:
fix(wd179x): READ ADDRESS rotates through ID fields instead of always sectors[0]

Real hardware returns whichever ID field the head next encounters as
the disk spins; repeated READ ADDRESS calls walk the track sequentially
and wrap at the index pulse. The emulator always returned the same
(first) sector, so software polling READ ADDRESS to enumerate a track's
sectors saw the same ID every time.

fix(wd179x): verify ID field cylinder/side against TR, add Type I verify

Confirmed against the WD1793/WD1772 datasheet (side-compare bit layout,
Track-Register comparison, V-bit verify semantics) before implementing,
since this is exactly the mechanism TR-DOS/G+DOS protections probe.

- Type II READ/WRITE SECTOR: a Sector Register (R) match in the sector
  map was accepted on its own. Real hardware also always compares the
  ID field's cylinder against the Track Register — this is how a disk
  can legitimately fail a read after a STEP without the 'u' flag
  desyncs the physical head position from TR, a documented protection
  technique. Added the cylinder check (findSector), plus the optional
  side-compare (command bits S/C) that was ignored entirely; both now
  apply to multi-sector continuation too.
- Type I RESTORE/SEEK/STEP: the V (verify) bit was read but never
  acted on. On V=1, compare the destination track's first ID field
  cylinder against the Track Register and set the seek-error bit
  (shares ST_RNF's bit, per the datasheet) on mismatch or a trackless
  destination.
- Left seek() itself alone: setting headTrack = trackReg = target on
  SEEK matches the datasheet definition of the command, not a bug.

Full suite (incl. every WD179x-based machine's boot tests) still
passes, so this doesn't regress the existing +D/Beta Disk/Einstein
disk paths.

Mirrors AY3891x's AYAntialiasMode (none/box/mute/lowpass): the MTX drives

  above Nyquist for the current sample rate (sample-rate-dependent
  threshold, recomputed on setSampleRate)

  each output sample
- 'lowpass' one-pole filters the mixed output at 14kHz

applies to whichever PSG the active machine carries.

fix(ay): make the 'mute' anti-alias threshold sample-rate dependent

'mute' only muted tone period <= 1 (~110kHz), a threshold sized for

them. The threshold is now computed from chipFreq and the current

period whose frequency is at or above Nyquist for the active output

events.title: Élection de l'exception MFP : la règle chronologique existait mais ne pouvait jamais s'appliquer — et les deux téléchargements du job Android n'avaient aucun filet
events.message:
Élection de l'exception MFP : la règle chronologique existait mais ne pouvait jamais s'appliquer — et les deux téléchargements du job Android n'avaient aucun filet

MFP — ÉLECTION GROUPÉE (port PARTIEL, assumé comme tel)

Mfp::raiseAt est un port ligne pour ligne de MFP_InputOnChannel (else compris). L'écart
était dans le QUAND. Hatari ne déclenche pas l'élection sur une entrée d'interruption :
il pose le bit pending et sa date, marque « à faire », et élit plus tard, une fois TOUTES
les entrées reçues — son commentaire (mfp.c:1084-1087) : « we must call MFP_UpdateIRQ()
only later in the main CPU loop, when all inputs were received, to choose the oldest
input's event time ». C'est ce qui rend opérant le test Pending_Time <= Pending_Time_Min
de MFP_InterruptRequest (2013/04/21, « fix Fuzion CD Menus 77, 78, 84 »).

NeoST avait pendingTime_[], pendingTimeMin_ et le test chronologique — mais il élisait
IMMÉDIATEMENT à chaque raiseAt, et updateIrq remet le minimum à l'infini en sortant. La
règle avait donc TOUJOURS un seul candidat et ne pouvait rien départager : une entrée
plus récente mais plus prioritaire l'emportait, là où le 68901 sert la plus ancienne.

Porté : raiseAt n'arme plus qu'irqUpdateNeeded_ ; flushIrqUpdate() élit au calcul d'IPL
(neostUpdateIpl, l'équivalent NeoST de la boucle CPU) et en fin de Mfp::updateTimers
(≙ mfp.c:689, avec l'horloge courante comme date de front, comme Hatari). Les entrées
multiples d'une MÊME fonction (TXERR→TXEMPTY, RXERR→RXFULL) sont désormais départagées.
Verrou d'A/B : NEOST_MFP_BATCH=0.

⚠ CE QUI RESTE, MESURÉ. Chez Hatari le flush est PAR INSTRUCTION (newcpu.c:3005, 5509) ;
chez NeoST il est PAR CALLBACK, car Machine fait suivre chaque callback d'ordonnanceur
d'un cpu.updateIpl() — 18 sites. Deux timers MFP échus dans le même runTo sont donc
encore élus séparément. Compté sur Super Hang-On : 0 groupement sur 1 000 000 d'entrées.
Conséquence honnête : ce port NE CHANGE AUCUNE IMAGE (A/B à 0 px sur Super Hang-On,
mfp_poll, blitter_timer, trace_odd). Ouvert en A42 dans TODO.md, avec les deux pièges à
connaître avant de s'y mettre : aucun exhibiteur connu (en poser un d'abord), et mfp_poll
NE PEUT PAS arbitrer ce chantier puisqu'il masque les IRQ.

make_mfp_poll_test.py : deux commentaires corrigés. (1) « avec IMRA=0 le bit de pending
ne se pose jamais » est FAUX — vérifié, une variante à IMRA=0 rend les 100 octets IPRA
ET TADR identiques ; le bit ne dépend que d'IER (MFP_InputOnChannel, mfp.c:1099), dont
raiseAt est le port 1:1. (2) La PORTÉE de l'étalon est maintenant écrite : masquer les
IRQ (SR=$2700) est un choix délibéré — on mesure les registres, pas le dispatch — mais il
le rend AVEUGLE à toute datation ou livraison d'interruption. C'est ce qui a fait rejeter
MFP_UpdateTimers à tort le matin même.

CI — LES DEUX TÉLÉCHARGEMENTS DU JOB ANDROID

Le workflow Artefacts a échoué le 2026-09-02 sur le seul job android : « Error on ZipFile
unknown archive » en préparant le NDK. Aléa confirmé (le même job repasse tel quel au push
suivant), mais publish dépend des huit paquets — un aléa réseau suffit donc à bloquer une
release, exactement comme l'apt-get install sans update qui avait empêché la 0.6.1 de
sortir. Audit : DEUX étapes réseau, aucune avec reprise.
 · sdkmanager --install : 3 tentatives, en PURGEANT le NDK partiellement installé entre
   deux (une extraction à moitié faite peut sinon être reprise telle quelle).
 · fetch_sdl.sh (clone SDL2) : même motif, avec purge d'extern/SDL2 — nécessaire ici car
   son garde d'entrée teste `-d extern/SDL2/.git` : un clone interrompu laisserait un
   arbre PARTIEL que le tour suivant prendrait pour valide.
Les deux échouent explicitement après 3 tentatives plutôt que de passer en silence.
Logique vérifiée dans les deux sens sous set -eu (succès après aléas ; code 1 après trois
échecs consécutifs).

Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert.

events.title: fix(ay): a non-zero upper nibble deselects the chip, not masks to 4 bits
events.message:
fix(ay): a non-zero upper nibble deselects the chip, not masks to 4 bits

Every machine's AY register-select port write did selectedReg = val &
0x0F, silently wrapping an out-of-range value down to a valid-looking
register. Real 8910/8912 silicon only latches a new register when the
whole byte's upper nibble is zero; anything else deselects the chip
instead, leaving whichever register was already selected active. This
matches FUSE's simplified masking, not real hardware.

Added a shared AY3891x.selectRegister() implementing the real contract
and switched every call site (Spectrum FFFD, CPC PPI-driven select,
MSX port 0xA0, Einstein) to use it. The .SNA selectedReg restore in
cpc-sna.ts is a snapshot field load, not a live bus cycle, so it's left
as a direct assignment.

events.title: fix(ay): R13 write also resets the envelope sub-step counter
events.message:
fix(ay): R13 write also resets the envelope sub-step counter

Writing the envelope shape register reset envStep (the 32-step position)
but left envCounter (the sub-step counter that counts up to envPeriod
before advancing envStep) at whatever value it held from before the
retrigger. Real hardware restarts the whole envelope generator on a
shape write, so the first step after a retrigger only ran for the
leftover fraction of envPeriod instead of the full period.

events.title: fix(ay): mask register read-back to each register's real bit width
events.message:
fix(ay): mask register read-back to each register's real bit width

readRegister() returned the raw stored byte for every register. Real
hardware has no physical latch for the unused high bits of the narrower
registers (R1/R3/R5/R13 are 4-bit, R6/R8-10 are 5-bit) -- they read back
0 regardless of what was last written, and chip-detect routines rely on
that. Masking only applies on read; writeRegister/getRegisters/snapshots
keep the raw byte exactly as written.

events.title: fix(audio): let the frame pacer catch up when the buffer runs low
events.message:
fix(audio): let the frame pacer catch up when the buffer runs low

Frame pacing was purely wall-clock driven (run a frame once framePeriod
has accumulated), throttled downward once the audio buffer was already
full but with no way to catch up when it wasn't. A real frame produces
slightly fewer samples than the worklet consumes per nominal 50Hz frame
(e.g. the 48K's true 50.08Hz vs the assumed flat 50Hz -- 958.47
samples/frame vs 960 consumed, about -0.16%), so that small steady drift
accumulated into periodic underruns: the worklet zero-fills, an audible
~10-sample gap roughly every 100ms.

Added a low-water mark (1 frame of buffered samples) below which a frame
now runs immediately regardless of accumulated wall-clock time, letting
the buffer catch back up before it actually runs dry.

events.title: fix(cpc): sign-extend ASIC sprite X/Y from their real 10/9-bit registers
events.message:
fix(cpc): sign-extend ASIC sprite X/Y from their real 10/9-bit registers

Sprite X/Y were sign-extended as full 16-bit values (<<16>>16), but the
real ASIC registers are only 10 bits (X) and 9 bits (Y) wide. That made
garbage in the unused high bits of xHi/yHi corrupt the coordinate as a
false sign flip, and put the actual sign bit at 15 instead of 9/8 --
e.g. a raw value of 0x200 is +512 under 16-bit sign-extension but -512
as the real 10-bit register would read it.

deps: bump m68k to 0.12.1 for the 68030/68040 timing models

m68k 0.12.0 lands the accelprobe-calibrated CPU timing work driven from
Copperline (m68k-rs #160): the 68030 now runs the MC68020UM section-8
tables, since its integer core is the 020's and the real 25 MHz 68030
board measures the same anchor figures the real A1200's 020 did, and the
68040 gets a single-issue pipeline model (timing_040.rs) in place of the
scaled-68000 approximation that real A3640 captures showed ~2-2.5x
pessimistic on plain execution. 0.12.1 adds decoded fast paths and
trace-JIT scheduling improvements. The public API change is additive
(new module and CYC_040_* constants), so no wrapper changes are needed.

All four lockfiles that carry m68k move together (root, cputest-runner,
copperline-player, copperline-web); the root lock also re-picks
tempfile's getrandom between two already-locked versions.

Re-running timing-test/accelprobe.adf against the real-hardware columns:
on tt-a4000-040.toml the move.w+dbra row is tick-exact, mulu.w and
cpushl within 7%, the bare dbra at the documented 3.0 vs 4.06 clocks;
on tt-a4000-030.toml the move.w, mulu.w and fast-stack trap rows land
within 1% and the bare dbra moves from 1.35x to 1.18x over. The trap,
call and movem rows, the CPU-slot bridge chip latency and per-region
fast-RAM billing are unchanged and remain the Copperline-side backlog.

docs/internals/cpu.md gains a 68040 timing section and the post-bump
probe figures; timing.md and timing-test/README.md follow the version.

events.title: fix(spectrum): mix the MIC bit into audible output (SAVE audio)
events.message:
fix(spectrum): mix the MIC bit into audible output (SAVE audio)

Port 0xFE writes discarded bit 3 (MIC) entirely, so tape SAVE and any
game that toggles MIC instead of EAR for an effect produced no sound at
all. Real hardware drives the speaker from both MIC (bit 3) and EAR
(bit 4) through their own resistor paths; approximated here as a simple
OR of the two bits, which is enough to make MIC-only output audible
without needing a full amplitude-weighted mix.

Deliberately left the Issue 2 vs Issue 3 board difference unmodelled
(bit 6 readback folding in MIC on Issue 2 boards) -- that needs a new
per-machine "ULA issue" setting and is a separate, larger feature; the
existing skipped test documents that gap already.

events.title: Les trois autres pistes « Super Hang-On » d'Hatari : deux étaient couvertes, la troisième manquait
events.message:
Les trois autres pistes « Super Hang-On » d'Hatari : deux étaient couvertes, la troisième manquait

Le nom du jeu apparaît QUATRE fois dans les sources d'Hatari. Après MFP_UpdateTimers, les
trois restantes ont été lues et confrontées à NeoST.

DÉJÀ PORTÉ — délai de 4 cycles sur la montée d'IRQ (mfp.c:107, 2013/03/01, « fix […]
Super Hang On, Super Monaco GP, Bolo ») : kIrqDelayToCpu, irqTime_, source
Scheduler::MFP_IRQ armée à irqTime_ + 4, et le cas « délai déjà écoulé » qui prend
l'exception à la frontière courante (verrou NEOST_MFP_EXACT bit1).

DÉJÀ CORRECT PAR CONSTRUCTION — bit pending posé deux fois avant l'IACK (video.c:320,
2013/05/03, « correct fix for Super Monaco GP, Super Hang On […] ») : NeoST modélise HBL
et VBL par des BOOLÉENS (Cpu68k.cpp:51-52, « ≙ pendingInterrupts = 0 »), effacés à
l'acquittement et lus comme un NIVEAU pour l'IPL. Deux poses du bit s'y confondent
naturellement en une interruption, là où Hatari a dû ajouter du code pour l'obtenir.

MANQUAIT, PORTÉ — cycles d'écriture dans MFP_IRQ_Time (mfp.c:113, 2013/03/14, « properly
fix Super Hang On »). Hatari date une écriture MMIO à currcycle + 4,
« the number of cycles when the write will be completed »
(Cycles_GetInternalCycleOnWriteAccess). NeoST datait ses IRQ nées d'une écriture registre
MFP à liveNow() — alors que sa PROPRE convention veut la fin d'accès à +2 (Moira facture
déjà le SYNC de tête ; c'est écrit dans Cpu68k::cyclesIntoInstr, et le Shifter l'applique
à ses écritures palette). Les IRQ étaient donc antidatées de 2 cycles, et comme la
visibilité CPU court depuis cet instant (irqTime_ + 4), l'exception partait 2 cycles trop
tôt. Corrigé sur les 9 sites via Mfp::writeEventTime.

⚠ AUCUN EFFET PIXEL DÉMONTRÉ À LA VALEUR JUSTE, et c'est dit plutôt qu'habillé : sur
Super Hang-On en jeu, +0 et +2 rendent la même trame au pixel près. Ce qui EST démontré,
c'est que le chemin pilote réellement l'émulation — NEOST_MFP_WRITE_END=40 déplace
24 773 px sur cette même trame. Port de FIDÉLITÉ adopté sur la lettre d'Hatari, pas sur
un pixel.

⚠ Et mfp_poll ne peut pas arbitrer ce point : son programme masque les IRQ (SR=$2700),
il reste à 0 px même avec 40 cycles de décalage. Utile à savoir — c'est ce même étalon
qui avait fait rejeter MFP_UpdateTimers à tort le matin même.

Verrou d'A/B : NEOST_MFP_WRITE_END (défaut 2 ; =0 restaure l'ancienne datation).
Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert, mfp_poll 0 px contre l'oracle.

events.title: copperhf: address independent-review and Copilot findings
events.message:
copperhf: address independent-review and Copilot findings

An independent multi-angle review (code-review ultra) found and this
fixes five confirmed issues:

- guest/copperhf/mounter.c: a corrupt LSEG hunk-size entry near
  0x3FFFFFFF made AllocMem(size + 8, ...) wrap ULONG to a tiny
  allocation while every later bounds check still trusted the huge
  unwrapped size -- a heap overflow from a crafted disk image. Capped
  at a new CHF_MAX_HUNK_BYTES (4 MiB, far above any real filesystem
  handler this device loads).
- src/control/exec.rs copperhf_attach: the CCP hot-attach path bypassed
  is_cd_image_path and volume_name_error, both enforced at
  [copperhf]-config-parse time. Added both checks.
- src/copperhf.rs dispatch_scsi: scsi_Length (raw guest field) was
  unbounded before a Vec::with_capacity allocation -- a multi-GB
  allocation DoS from a crafted HD_SCSICMD. Capped at SCSI_MAX_XFER
  (16 MiB), IOERR_BADLENGTH otherwise.
- write_scsi_sense: logs (does not change guest-visible behavior) when
  autosense can't be delivered to a bad sense pointer, for diagnosis.
- attach_unit/eject_unit: defensive debug_assert on unit < NUM_UNITS.

GitHub Copilot's own review then caught several more, independently:

- guest/copperhf/mounter.c (2 spots): a HUNK_RELOC32/RELOC32SHORT
  record's hunk number is the file's ABSOLUTE first_hunk..last_hunk
  numbering, not a 0-based index into this loader's local segs[]
  table -- normalized by first_hunk before indexing. Silent for every
  fixture tested so far since first_hunk is 0 for an ordinary linked
  executable; a correctness bug for any file that legitimately sets
  it otherwise.
- src/copperhf.rs HD_SCSICMD DataOut: a guest buffer shorter than the
  CDB's own transfer length was zero-padded and committed anyway
  (e.g. a two-sector WRITE with scsi_Length == 512 silently zeroed
  the second sector on disk). Now rejected with CHECK CONDITION /
  PARAMETER LIST LENGTH ERROR.
- src/scsi.rs rw_command (shared by every SCSI-backed board): READ/
  WRITE(12/16)'s 32-bit count reached a Vec allocation with no bound
  beyond the target's own total-sector check, and lba+count could
  wrap for a crafted 64-bit LBA. Added checked arithmetic and a
  64 MiB single-CDB transfer cap.
- src/copperhf.rs CMD_UPDATE: a failed flush() was logged but still
  reported to the guest as success. New WorkerResult::UpdateFailed
  surfaces IOERR_BADADDRESS instead.
- src/copperhf.rs dma_write_bytes: an odd-length transfer's trailing
  byte went through a 16-bit word write that also zeroed the
  *following* byte -- one past the guest's requested buffer. Read-
  modify-write preserves it.
- Six documentation/comment staleness fixes: two "later milestone"
  references to now-shipped docs/internals/copperhf.md, a stale

events.title: Super Hang-On : les bandes de couleur viennent du MFP, pas de l'affichage — et j'avais retiré le correctif le matin même
events.message:
Super Hang-On : les bandes de couleur viennent du MFP, pas de l'affichage — et j'avais retiré le correctif le matin même

Rapport utilisateur : « des bandes complètes sur toute la largeur, à n'importe quelle
hauteur, de temps en temps, souvent noires ou blanches », en jeu. Résolu par le port de
`MFP_UpdateTimers`, qu'Hatari documente NOMMÉMENT pour ce jeu (mfp.c:135, 2022/01/27) :
« fix the game Super Hang On, where `bclr #0,$fffffa0f` to clear Timer B ISR sometimes
happens at the same time that Timer C expires, which used the wrong ISR value and gave
FLICKERING RASTER COLORS ».

⚠ CORRECTION D'UN VERDICT QUE J'AVAIS ÉCRIT. Ce correctif avait été porté LE MATIN MÊME
puis retiré, avec la mention « RÉFUTÉ À LA MESURE, ne pas re-tenter » inscrite dans
l'inventaire des divergences. Le chiffre qui fondait ce rejet — l'étalon mfp_poll passant
de 80 à 88 px contre l'oracle — était un ARTEFACT : il était mesuré avant la correction
de l'échéance arrondie de readTimerData, le vrai défaut de cet étalon. Sur une base saine
le port est neutre : mfp_poll reste à 0 px contre l'oracle. CHANGELOG et
HATARI_DIVERGENCES portent la correction ; un faux verdict dans l'inventaire coûte plus
cher qu'une case vide.

Portée mesurée : 125 890 accès registre MFP sur 1,4 M (~9 %) trouvent un timer échu à
servir. Le dispatch reste CIBLÉ sur les quatre timers délai — un syncTo nu réactiverait
le modèle sync-driven réfuté (deadlock Enchanted Land). Verrou d'A/B :
NEOST_MFP_UPDTIMERS=0.

--- Autres chantiers de la même session -------------------------------------

FPU, décimal empaqueté (2 des 3 points de la puce TODO) : ±inf/NaN ne sortent plus en
BCD arbitraire — la libc rendait « +inf » au snprintf et le parseur en tirait des
chiffres — mais recopient le motif étendu (exposant $FFF, ≙ fp_from_pack) ; k > 17 arme
OPERR au lieu d'écrêter en silence. Banc porté de 12 à 14 tests, chacun vérifié par
mutation. INEX1 reste DÉLIBÉRÉMENT non posé : le drapeau appartient à la direction
décimal → étendu, que NeoST approxime par strtod — le poser à l'estime serait pire que
son absence.

Autozoom : deux défauts. (1) Le cadre s'élargissait aux bordures latérales sur le seul
signal « une bordure a bougé », qui est vrai aussi pour le haut ou le bas : Enchanted
Land était cadré sur 416 px pour une image de 320, soit un zoom 1,3x trop petit avec deux
bandes noires. La Glue compte désormais les lignes réellement élargies (Closure 272-275
sur 276 ; EL 4 sur 229 ; overscan_top 5 sur 229) et le seuil est posé au quart. (2) UNE
trame de transitoire suffisait à élargir le cadre pour 30 trames : l'hystérésis ne
protégeait que le retour. Il faut désormais 3 trames consécutives.

PSG : les écritures de registre étaient datées en échantillons HÔTE (20,8 us) au lieu de
la grille interne 250 kHz (4 us). Sur le digidrum 3 voies de Super Hang-On (groupes
R8/R9/R10 espacés de 524 cycles = 15,3 kHz), une période de 65,3 us quantifiée sur 20,8
donnait +/-30 % de gigue — le grésillement rapporté. Vérifié à l'oracle (audio extrait de
l'AVI d'Hatari) : NeoST rejoint Hatari dans les bandes où tombait le repliement
(10-16 kHz : 0,5 % -> 0,3 %, comme l'oracle).

Souris émulée : curseur de sensibilité (page Input, 0,05x a 4,00x, defaut 1,00x =
comportement d'avant), pour les souris hôtes à haute résolution — le ST compte les crans
d'une souris ~200 dpi. La règle d'accumulation vit dans util/MouseScale.hpp pour être
exerçable : selftest_logic vérifie la CONSERVATION (3000 px hôte à 0,3x -> 900 pas ST à
+/-1) et le traitement de NaN, dont int(NaN) figerait la souris pour la session.

« Machine gelée » : le bandeau nomme désormais la puce absente et le profil à choisir
(« $FF8900 is STE DMA sound - absent from the "st" profile »), et il est centré sur
l'ÉCRAN ST et non sur la fenêtre. Rapport Stardust : le halt est FIDÈLE (Hatari halte sur
la même instruction, même SSP impair), mais rien ne le disait à l'utilisateur.

Rééchantillonnage sans CRT : ImGui étirait la texture ST BRUTE en GL_NEAREST à une
échelle non entière (mesuré : 2,745 px/ligne, donc 149 lignes à 3 px et 51 à 2 px). La
passe d'effets sert désormais de rééchantillonneur même effets éteints — elle force
GL_LINEAR et interpole en Catmull-Rom. ⚠ Adoucit légèrement l'image : changement visible,
à arbitrer.

Instruments d'AFFICHAGE, qui manquaient entièrement : --shot-window (capture de la fenêtre
composée, glReadPixels avant le swap) et NEOST_WBAND_DIAG (bandes dans l'image affichée,
via une bande verticale de 16 px). Sans eux, tout ce qui se passe entre le framebuffer
émulé et l'écran était invisible au harnais. Plus NEOST_BAND_DIAG, NEOST_FRAMING_DIAG,
NEOST_SCALE_DIAG, NEOST_YMEV_DIAG.

📌 Leçon de méthode : CLAUDE.md prescrit de lire extern/hatari/src AVANT d'investiguer.
Sur ce dossier j'ai fait l'inverse — trois passes d'instrumentation sur l'affichage avant
de lire le journal d'Hatari, où le nom du jeu apparaît quatre fois. Un `grep -i 'hang.on'`
donnait la réponse en dix secondes.

Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert (399 auto-tests logique, 25 étalons pixel,
MegaSTE 12/12, mfp_poll 0 px contre l'oracle).

events.title: debugger: let --gdb-gui and --control-gui share one window
events.message:
debugger: let --gdb-gui and --control-gui share one window

A VS Code integration wants GDB for source-level debugging and the
control protocol for emulator control and observation at the same time.
Both windowed drivers were already frame-boundary drains on the same
session with disjoint state; the exclusion in main.rs stood in for two
contentions, which this change resolves instead:

- Stop routing and the pause state. A machine stop now answers every
  outstanding remote resume: surface_debug_stop lets both the control
  and the GDB hook consume a DebugStop and opens the local debugger
  panel only when neither did, and every host-side stop (a user or
  client pause, a run_until target, a GDB attach, interrupt or step,
  power off, a double fault) goes through one App primitive,
  complete_remote_resumes, so a control run_until ends with reason
  "pause" when GDB interrupts and a GDB continue ends with T05 (plus a
  console line naming the reason) when the control client pauses or
  its target lands. Repositioning verbs on either side (reverse steps,
  last-writer, the pointer servo, state.load) are refused while the
  other client's resume is outstanding.

- Warp holds. The single warp_hold slot becomes WarpHolds, one bit per
  programmatic source: each of the control client, the GDB client and
  the guest holds warp on its own, releases only its own (the reply or
  console line names any remaining holder), and the machine re-paces
  when the last hold goes; the manual toggle and power off clear them
  all. warp.get and event.warp gain a "holders" array, and event.warp
  can now name "gdb".

The headless forms keep owning the machine: --control still excludes
--gdb/--gdb-gui, --control-gui still excludes --gdb, and --benchmark-until
excludes all four.

Tests: a combined-mode drain suite (both pending answered by one
breakpoint with the panel closed, control pause and frame target ending
a GDB continue, GDB interrupt and attach ending a control run, reverse
refused under the other client's run, per-client warp holds incl. the
event.warp on release), the rewritten independent-holds warp test, and
the CLI acceptance/exclusions. Docs: gdb.md, control.md, run.md, ui.md.

events.title: fix(z80): mask portIn() to 8 bits, guarding IN r,(C)'s flags-table lookup
events.message:
fix(z80): mask portIn() to 8 bits, guarding IN r,(C)'s flags-table lookup

A port handler returning a value outside 0-255 flowed straight into
IN r,(C)'s SZP[val] lookup -- an out-of-range index on the 256-entry
table reads as undefined, which silently zeroed every flag but carry
instead of computing them from the low 8 bits. The Z80's data bus is
only ever 8 bits wide, so mask defensively at the single portIn() call
site rather than trusting every handler (and every consumer of its
return value) to do it themselves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: damieng

events.title: fix(z80): reset the Q register on interrupt/NMI acceptance
events.message:
fix(z80): reset the Q register on interrupt/NMI acceptance

interrupt() and nmi() never touched _qReg/_prevQ, so an ISR whose first
instruction is SCF/CCF would read whatever Q value the instruction right
before the interrupt left behind. Real hardware's INT/NMI acknowledge
cycle doesn't modify flags -- it's a "Q=0" step, same as any other
non-flag instruction -- so it should reset Q exactly like step() does
before every instruction, not leave it stale across the interrupt.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: damieng

events.title: fix(z80): resolve DD/FD prefix chains iteratively, not recursively
events.message:
fix(z80): resolve DD/FD prefix chains iteratively, not recursively

executeDD/executeFD recursed into themselves (and each other) for every
redundant prefix byte, so a long run of DD/FD bytes in RAM -- reachable
if execution runs off into filler data -- threw "Maximum call stack size
exceeded". Real hardware has no such limit; it's just re-running the same
M1 fetch each time.

Extracted the prefix-chain resolution into an iterative loop
(_resolveDdFdChain) that returns the final opcode and which register won,
leaving the large, timing-critical IX/IY instruction-decode bodies
untouched (renamed to _executeDDBody/_executeFDBody, taking the resolved
opcode as a parameter instead of fetching it themselves) -- a mechanical
split with no behavioural changes to the risky part of the code.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: damieng

events.title: fix(z80): NMI no longer copies IFF1 into IFF2
events.message:
fix(z80): NMI no longer copies IFF1 into IFF2

Real hardware's NMI sequence only clears IFF1; IFF2 is left untouched so
RETN's IFF1 <- IFF2 restores the pre-NMI state. Copying IFF1 into IFF2 on
entry happened to match hardware for a single NMI (IFF1/IFF2 already
track together outside NMI handling), but corrupts IFF2 on a nested NMI:
by the time a second NMI fires before the first's RETN, IFF1 is already
0 (cleared by the first), so the copy stomps IFF2's true pre-NMI value
with 0 -- permanently masking maskable interrupts once RETN eventually
runs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: damieng

events.title: fix(z80): EI;EI;X no longer lets an interrupt in before X
events.message:
fix(z80): EI;EI;X no longer lets an interrupt in before X

Every machine run loop cleared eiDelay after a step keyed off whether it
was already set *before* that step -- so EI;EI's second EI had its own
fresh re-arm wiped out by the first EI's already-consumed suppression,
letting an interrupt sneak in between the second EI and X.

Move the reset+re-arm entirely into Z80.step(): eiDelay resets to false
before every instruction (including a HALT re-fetch), and EI's own opcode
handler sets it back to true. Since nothing reads eiDelay mid-instruction,
this makes suppression correctly per-EI instead of "one instruction after
the first EI in a run." All six machine run loops' now-redundant (and
now actively harmful) eiBefore/clear bookkeeping is removed, except
Spectrum's HALT fast-path and instant tape-load trap, which bypass
step() entirely and still need their own one-shot clear.

translate exactly onto [copperhf] unitN instead of being approximated
onto a real IDE port (previously the only option, and a real
substitution -- it put the image behind the Kickstart IDE size limit
and modeled hardware the source config never had).

not already taken by an earlier drive); an out-of-range or colliding
number renumbers to the first free unit and is reported, since the
source's own numbering wasn't honored. Only once all seven [copperhf]
units are full does a drive fall back to [ide], keeping the prior
size-limit caveat for that last-resort case.

FS-UAE: its unnamed/uae-controller drives (previously routed to [ide]
or A3000 SCSI depending on machine profile -- machinery now dead and
removed) take successive [copperhf] units in encounter order; past
seven, a drive is flagged for manual placement on [scsi]/[lide].

Directory mounts (filesystem2/uaehf...dir) are untouched -- still
[[filesys]], as before.

fix(msx): put RAM in slot 2, not slot 3, matching the real HX-10

Per MAME's msx1.cpp and openMSX's Toshiba_HX-10.xml machine definition,
the HX-10's RAM lives in primary slot 2; slot 3 is the rear expansion
connector (unpopulated on a bare machine, not a second cartridge slot).
Our model had these swapped. This never affected boot or cartridges --
both use slot 1 correctly in either model, and the BIOS's runtime RAM
search just found RAM wherever it actually was -- but RAMAD0-3/EXPTBL and
a raw port 0xA8 readback would report a slot layout real HX-10 software
and other emulators wouldn't recognise.

events.title: fix(upd765a): apply the datasheet's End-of-Cylinder result rewrite (C+1, R=1)
events.message:
fix(upd765a): apply the datasheet's End-of-Cylinder result rewrite (C+1, R=1)

finishExecution() returned the last transferred sector's own C/R in the
result phase after a multi-sector read/write ran off the end of a normal
track. The real chip instead reports C+1/R=1 on a genuine (MT=0) search
exhaustion -- the standard "reissue with the returned CHRN to continue
onto the next cylinder" convention -- so software chaining across
cylinder boundaries got the wrong values back.

Scoped deliberately narrow to avoid the copy-protection path: a new
exNormalEOT flag is set only by advanceSector()'s genuine end-of-search
branch, never by the exSingleSector short-circuit (Alkatraz/Speedlock
mismatched-cylinder tracks) that stops after one sector without ever
searching. That path's result CHRN is a verified protection contract
(see the "single-sector protection mode" test, left untouched) and its
real-hardware EOT-result behaviour isn't verified here, so it keeps
reporting the sector actually read. Also left MT=1 alone, per the
datasheet note this only covers MT=0.

events.title: fix(v9938): line (FH) interrupt fires at the right border, not the start, of R19
events.message:
fix(v9938): line (FH) interrupt fires at the right border, not the start, of R19

advanceScanline(line) compared `line` directly against R19, so FH was set
the instant the matched line began -- before any of its own cycles had
even run. Real hardware asserts the line interrupt at the matched line's
right border, once it has finished. Since this is called once per line
before that line's cycles execute, "the line that just finished" is
line-1, so the comparison now uses that instead -- delaying the assert by
one advanceScanline call to land at the right border.

events.title: fix(cpc): decode the ASIC unlock sequence's 17th byte instead of toggling
events.message:
fix(cpc): decode the ASIC unlock sequence's 17th byte instead of toggling

pokeLockSequence toggled `locked` on the 16th byte of the unlock key
(or, if already unlocked, relocked immediately without even waiting for
a 17th byte), instead of examining the actual 17th byte value. Real
hardware decodes that byte directly: 0xEE unlocks, anything else locks
-- independent of the current state. The old toggle behaviour meant
re-sending the sequence while already unlocked always re-locked, even
when the following byte was 0xEE (which should leave it unlocked).

events.title: fix(wd179x): STEP OUT at track 0 stays at track 0, no 8-bit wrap
events.message:
fix(wd179x): STEP OUT at track 0 stays at track 0, no 8-bit wrap

STEP OUT unconditionally added -1 to the head position, so stepping out
at track 0 wrapped the 8-bit track counter to 255 instead of staying put.
Real hardware's TR00 input inhibits the pulse: the head never moves past
the physical track-0 stop. Also fixed the pinned test's stale comment,
which misread command byte 0x60 as having the 'u' (update track register)
flag set -- bit 4 is clear in 0x60, so only the physical position was
being checked, not trackReg (0x70 sets it).

events.title: fix(z80): reset selects IM 0, not IM 1
events.message:
fix(z80): reset selects IM 0, not IM 1

Real Z80 silicon resets to interrupt mode 0 (Zilog datasheet); RESET
never selects IM 1. ROMs that need IM 1 (e.g. the Spectrum 48K ROM)
select it explicitly during boot, so this only mattered for code that
reads cpu.im right after reset before any IM instruction runs.

events.title: fix(cpc): correct .SNA CPC-type byte values and Plus upper-ROM select restore
events.message:
fix(cpc): correct .SNA CPC-type byte values and Plus upper-ROM select restore

Two related .SNA compatibility bugs:

- The CPC-type byte at offset 0x6D used 3=6128Plus, 4=GX4000 -- the
  published CPCEMU/WinAPE format (cpcwiki SNA File Format) defines
  0=464, 1=664, 2=6128, 3=unknown, 4=6128 Plus, 5=464 Plus, 6=GX4000.
  WinAPE 6128 Plus snapshots (type 4) loaded here as GX4000 and vice versa.

- restorePaging() wrote .SNA byte 0x55 straight into the physical
  upper-ROM-page field, bypassing the logical->physical translation a live
  OUT &DFxx write goes through (selectUpperRom) -- so a Plus snapshot's raw
  firmware ROM number (e.g. 7 for AMSDOS) was misread as already being
  physical page 7 instead of resolving to page 3. Fixed by routing the
  restore through selectUpperRom() itself, and made saveCpcSna encode the
  physical page in the hardware-legit direct-physical (bit 7 set) form so
  our own snapshots round-trip exactly through the fixed loader.

events.title: fix(cpc): correct DCSR bit layout, DMA PAUSE prescaler, vscroll, and GA->ASIC palette mirroring
events.message:
fix(cpc): correct DCSR bit layout, DMA PAUSE prescaler, vscroll, and GA->ASIC palette mirroring

Four related CPC Plus / GX4000 ASIC bugs:

- DCSR (DMA Control/Status Register) built its interrupt-pending bits at
  bits 3-5 (ch0->5) instead of Arnold V's bits 4-6 (ch0->4), and never let
  a write clear the raster-pending bit (bit 7) at all -- the only ack
  mechanism IM1 code has, since it never calls consumeInterruptVector.

- DMA PAUSE ignored the channel's prescaler register entirely, waiting N
  ticks instead of N x (PPR+1) HSYNCs -- DMA soundtracks with PPR!=0 played
  at the wrong tempo.

- Vertical soft scroll (SSCR bits 4-6) added vscroll*0x0800 to the CRTC's
  MA, but the video address formula masks away MA bits 10-11 entirely, so
  vscroll=1 was silently dropped and vscroll>=2 hopped into the wrong 16K
  bank. Hardware actually offsets the computed *byte* address (vscroll<<11,
  letting the carry ripple naturally), not MA -- added a videoAddress()
  hook to GateArray for this.

- Classic FN_COLOUR (&7Fxx) writes never reached the ASIC's 12-bit palette
  once unlocked, so a game that unlocks for sprites/DMA but sets colours
  via the firmware rendered black. Added an onPenColourChanged() hook to
  mirror hardware colour writes into asicPalette (locked or not, matching
  real hardware), and fixed reset() to seed the palette with hardware
  colour 0's ASIC-native value instead of literal (transparent) black.

events.title: copperhf: fix SCSICmd sense-field offsets (m68k 2-byte alignment)
events.message:
copperhf: fix SCSICmd sense-field offsets (m68k 2-byte alignment)

Found by devsoak's -X HD_SCSICMD phase: the classic m68k ABI aligns
pointers to 2 bytes, so struct SCSICmd has NO padding between
scsi_Status (UBYTE at 21) and the scsi_SenseData pointer -- it sits at
22, the struct is 30 bytes, not 32. The M4 constants assumed 4-byte
pointer alignment (+2 on all three sense fields), so autosense read a
mangled sense pointer (the real pointer's low half spliced with
scsi_SenseLength), DMA'd the sense bytes to a wrong guest address, and
wrote scsi_SenseActual one byte past the caller's struct -- while the
caller read 0 at the real offset and saw no sense at all. This file's
own unit tests couldn't catch it: their fixture wrote through the same
wrong constants, self-consistent both ways.

The authority is now guest-side: chftest_m4.c _Static_asserts every
SCSICmd field offset (and sizeof == 30) against the real NDK header
with the real m68k compiler, so a constant drift fails the probe build
instead of corrupting guest memory, and a new e2e subtest issues an
unsupported opcode with SCSIF_AUTOSENSE and verifies HFERR_BadStatus,
CHECK CONDITION, scsi_SenseActual == 18, the ILLEGAL REQUEST sense
bytes at the real offsets, and that nothing was written past
scsi_SenseLength.

events.title: uaelib: draw the fn-88 overlay commands on the windowed presentation
events.message:
uaelib: draw the fn-88 overlay commands on the windowed presentation

The template's debug_clear/debug_rect/debug_filled_rect/debug_text
calls, accepted as no-ops until now, become a display list on the trap:
packed signed-short corners clamped into the 768x576 PAL hires space
Bartman's WinUAE fork composites, colours masked to 0x00RRGGBB, text
read from guest memory at call time (the caller's buffer may be reused
the moment the call returns), clear restarting the list, and a cap that
drops the newest command, counted. The list is guest state beside the
registry (save-state version 74), so run-ahead and rewind restore the
picture's annotations with the picture.

The window composites it in the presentation seam, after the frame
capture copy: the 768x576 space is stretched over the display sub-rect
the viewer sees (overlay_anchor, so autocrop and per-axis scaling are
tracked for free), filled rects and four-sided outlines through the
status bar's fill_rect, text through the 8x8 font at the nearest whole
glyph scale. It sits directly on the picture under every piece of host
chrome, and -- like everything drawn there -- can never appear in
screenshots, frame dumps, recordings or control-protocol captures,
which a digest-parity test pins.

The uaelib guest probe grows the template's overlay helpers and draws a
boxed caption, for windowed sessions; its recorded results are
unchanged.

events.title: review: cache the overlay raster, clip to the anchor, survive RTG
events.message:
review: cache the overlay raster, clip to the anchor, survive RTG

Four review findings on the overlay compositor:

- The display list was replayed in full on every redraw, so a large
  legal list -- even one the guest had stopped touching -- could stall
  the window indefinitely. The overlay now rasterizes into an
  anchor-sized RGBA buffer only when the list or destination geometry
  changes (keyed by a hash), and each redraw pays one bounded
  alpha-tested composite. A rasterization work budget (32 anchor-fulls
  of filled pixels) bounds the replay itself, dropping trailing
  commands like the trap's own list cap does.
- Rasterizing into the anchor-sized buffer also clips text glyphs to
  the anchor exactly like the rectangles, so a cropped sub-rect
  presentation no longer leaks overlay pixels into the letterbox.
- The glyph scale rounds to the nearest whole step instead of flooring:
  on HiDPI windows the ratio sits just under the next whole scale, and
  flooring rendered the text half-sized against its rectangles.
- The GPU RTG pass overdraws the display region after the CPU canvas is
  composited, which made the overlay invisible on RTG screens; a
  nonempty guest overlay now takes the same CPU-present fallback the UI
  overlays do.

Regression tests: budget drops the tail (last landed fill wins), the
cache replays only on a changed list, a 2x glyph escapes the 1x cell,
and no overlay pixel escapes a sub-rect anchor.

events.title: fix(einstein): stop halving the CTC timer-mode prescaler clock
events.message:
fix(einstein): stop halving the CTC timer-mode prescaler clock

EinsteinMachine set Z80Ctc.inputClockDivide = 2, believing the CTC's own
device clock was 2MHz (4MHz CPU / 2). MAME's XTAL/2 wiring is actually
the frequency on channels 0-2's external CLK/TRG pins (counter mode) —
the CTC device clock driving the timer-mode prescaler is the full
undivided 4MHz CPU clock. Since nothing here drives those external pins
(the Einstein never uses CTC counter mode), the divide only ever hit the
timer path, doubling every timer-based interrupt period (channel 3's
periodic IM 2 interrupt is chained from channel 2's timer via zc2->trg3).

Sur macOS, un fichier accentué du lecteur GEMDOS était introuvable

Un des deux items « faisables sans oracle » de l'inventaire des divergences, différé
depuis la 3ᵉ passe d'audit comme « spécifique plateforme ».

macOS rend les noms de fichiers en forme DÉCOMPOSÉE (NFD) : « café » y est stocké
« cafe » + U+0301, six caractères et non cinq. NeoST comparait ces octets tels quels au
nom demandé par le programme Atari — le fichier était donc introuvable depuis le TOS, et
le même dossier n'exposait pas les mêmes noms sur macOS et sur Linux.

Str_DecomposedToPrecomposedUtf8 (hatari/src/str.c:726) est porté en
neost::hostpath::precomposeUtf8, table des 53 couples (lettre, marque combinante) →
point de code précomposé reprise TELLE QUELLE — le sous-ensemble qui existe dans le jeu
Atari, pas au-delà. Branché sur les deux mêmes sites que Hatari : matchHostDirEntry
(≙ gemdos.c:1201/1214) et le listing Fsfirst (≙ gemdos.c:3182). determineMaxPartitions
n'en a pas besoin, Hatari n'y convertit pas non plus (seule la première lettre y est lue).

Le bug est MESURÉ, pas supposé : en retirant la recomposition, un fichier créé avec les
octets NFD est bel et bien introuvable sous sa forme précomposée — gemdos-selftest passe
de 14 OK à 13 OK / 1 FAIL. APFS préserve les octets tels qu'écrits, le cas se reproduit
donc sur la machine de développement.

Ce que le port apporte, exactement : ni NeoST ni Hatari ne convertissent le JEU DE
CARACTÈRES sur ce chemin (comparaison octet à octet, « conversion charset off » des deux
côtés). Le gain n'est donc PAS un affichage correct des accents côté TOS, mais la
COHÉRENCE macOS ↔ Linux — mêmes noms, même longueur, donc même troncature 8.3 et même
aller-retour listage → ouverture. C'est écrit ainsi plutôt que promis plus large.

Gardé à deux niveaux, délibérément :
- selftest_logic exerce la FONCTION PURE (13 cas : le « café » qui motive le port, une
  chaîne déjà précomposée qui doit rester STRICTEMENT inchangée, l'ASCII, les quatre
  familles d'accents, deux accents dans un nom, un accent en FIN de chaîne, une
  combinaison absente de la table, une marque combinante TRONQUÉE). Pure et sans #ifdef,
  donc exerçable depuis n'importe quelle machine — même discipline que `Style` pour les
  chemins Windows, et pour la même raison : un défaut spécifique à une plateforme n'est
  gardé que s'il est exerçable ailleurs.
- gemdos-selftest exerce le CÂBLAGE de bout en bout avec un vrai fichier écrit en NFD. Il
  ne peut pas être vert par accident : si le volume normalise de lui-même et rend déjà du
  NFC, la recomposition est un no-op et la recherche réussit pareil.

Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert (368 auto-tests logique, 25 étalons pixel,
MegaSTE 12/12, gemdos-selftest 14/0).

events.title: fix(tms9918a): sprite 0 priority and coincidence-flag detection
events.message:
fix(tms9918a): sprite 0 priority and coincidence-flag detection

renderSprites walked sprites 0->31 and overwrote unconditionally, so the
highest-numbered overlapping sprite won instead of sprite 0 (hardware:
lower sprite number has priority). The coincidence (C) status flag was
also never set — renderSprites had no collision detection at all, so
games relying on hardware sprite collision could never detect a hit.

Add a reusable per-scanline pixel buffer (mirroring the pattern already
used in v9938.ts): the first (lowest-numbered) sprite to draw a pixel
claims it, and any second opaque sprite pixel landing on an already-opaque
pixel sets ST_COINC. Transparent (colour 0) sprites still count toward
the 4-per-line/5th-sprite limit but draw nothing and never collide.

events.title: fix(tzx): correct CSW field layout and Jump/Call/Select relative offsets
events.message:
fix(tzx): correct CSW field layout and Jump/Call/Select relative offsets

Block 0x18 (CSW recording) read the sample rate as a 4-byte DWORD instead
of TZX 1.20's 3-byte field, throwing every other field after it off by one
byte and turning every embedded CSW recording into garbage.

0x23 Jump, 0x26 Call, and 0x28 Select computed their target as
index + 1 + offset; the spec's relative offset is against the block
itself (1 = next block, 0 = loop forever, -1 = previous), not the block
after it. 0x26 Call also only ever visited the first of its listed call
targets instead of the whole list, returning past the remaining ones.

events.title: Trois divergences ouvertes fermées — et deux l'ont été CONTRE le correctif qu'elles prescrivaient
events.message:
Trois divergences ouvertes fermées — et deux l'ont été CONTRE le correctif qu'elles prescrivaient

Les n°2, 3 et 4 de `TODO.md` § Divergences. Deux d'entre elles décrivaient un état
dépassé : leur entrée datait d'avant plusieurs correctifs intermédiaires, et personne
ne les avait re-confrontées à une image.

MFP (n°3) — le correctif prescrit est RÉFUTÉ, la vraie cause était ailleurs.
L'écart « pas de MFP_UpdateTimers avant lecture IPR/ISR en mode bloc » n'existait plus :
sur l'étalon mfp_poll, bâti exprès pour l'exhiber, IPRA est identique à Hatari sur les
100 lignes. Le port du runTo ciblé TIMER_* a été écrit pour le vérifier : il ne ferme
rien et dégrade l'étalon de 80 à 88 px (balayage de l'instant sur ±12 cyc, aucun offset
à 0 px) — retiré, et consigné pour qu'on ne le retente pas. Le résidu réel :
readTimerData lisait le compteur vivant sur l'échéance ARRONDIE au plafond entier du
Scheduler au lieu de l'échéance sous-cyclique déjà tenue (timerDueSub_), d'où un ceil un
cran trop haut sur 6 lignes / 100. Corrigé → 0 px contre l'oracle (100 octets IPRA ET
100 octets TADR) ; mfp_poll promu snapshot → oracle, le corpus oracle de la CI passe de
7 à 8. Garde vérifiée par mutation (retour au plafond entier = 80 px).

SON (n°2) — confronté, et l'oracle est le perdant.
L'exhibiteur manquait : make_dmasnd_poll_test.py → étalon dmasnd_poll (généré, ROM libre,
STE), 100 polls de $FF890B/0D pendant que le DMA joue. Il contraint ce qu'aucun test ne
touchait — le compteur ne doit avancer qu'au HBL — là où le WAV ne mesure que ce que le
DAC consomme. NeoST rend le découpage idéal impliqué par le débit (6,398 o/ligne ⇒ 19,9 %
de sauts de 8 ; mesuré 20,3 %) ; Hatari jitte sur 4/6/8/12, sa consommation DAC passant
par le rééchantillonnage vers le taux hôte. Débit moyen identique des deux côtés :
382 octets exactement sur la fenêtre. Hatari NE SE REPRODUIT PAS lui-même dessus (664 à
1432 px entre deux runs, --sound off comme --sound 50066 ; l'ancrage VBL de spec512_bands
n'y change rien) → ref_kind snapshot, premier étalon refusé à l'oracle pour
non-reproductibilité d'HATARI et non pour une raison de modèle.

FPU (n°4) — le double arrondi, corrigé par portage.
encodeFmt convertissait en `double` hôte AVANT toute conversion sortante : 64 bits de
mantisse contre 53, et deux arrondis ne valent pas un seul. L'étendu juste au-dessus de
0,5 rendait 0 au lieu de 1 en FMOVE.L. Réglés du même coup : INEX2 jamais levé, mode
d'arrondi du FPCR ignoré en sortie, UNFL absent, OVFL silencieux en D, NaN → 0 au lieu du
payload. floatx80_to_int32/16/8 et floatx80_to_float32/64 (+ roundAndPack*) portés depuis
extern/hatari/src/cpu/softfloat vers SoftFloatX80.hpp. Banc porté de 9 à 12 tests, les
trois nouveaux vérifiés par mutation. Restent ouverts : FSGLMUL/FSGLDIV, décimal
empaqueté, FMOVECR, FMOD.

Deux pièges d'outillage débusqués au passage :
- disks/etalons/fpu_testrom.img est COMMISE et n'est régénérée que si elle est ABSENTE :
  les tests ajoutés au générateur sont restés invisibles du palier fast jusqu'à la
  re-commettre. Un banc peut donc être vert en exerçant une version périmée de lui-même.
- une ROM `rom_generate` manquante était classée « TOS Atari absent → SKIP », un vert qui
  n'exécute rien, au lieu d'être régénérée (corrigé dans run_selftests.py, vérifié en
  effaçant l'image).

Réserve assumée : storeStoppedCounter a reçu le même changement que readTimerData par
cohérence (chez Hatari les deux chemins sont le seul MFP_ReadTimer_AB/CD), mais AUCUN test
ne le couvre — le muter seul laisse l'étalon vert. Port raisonné, pas correction mesurée.

Validation : `run_all.py --tier full` vert (25 étalons pixel, MegaSTE 12/12, cycle-bench,
séquenceur MIDI, auto-tests série dont fpu_cir).

events.title: fix(spectrum): select the 48K ROM when a 48K snapshot lands on a 128K-class machine
events.message:
fix(spectrum): select the 48K ROM when a 48K snapshot lands on a 128K-class machine

reset() leaves 128K ROM 0 (the editor/menu ROM) paged in and paging
unlocked; its 0x0038 interrupt vector jumps through a RAM stub the
snapshot never populated, so any 48K SNA/Z80/SZX/SP with IFF1 set crashed
on the first interrupt. Add SpectrumMemory.selectSnapshot48KRom() (7FFD=0x30
+ 1FFD bit 2 on 4-ROM machines) and call it from the snapshot service
whenever a 48K-format snapshot is applied to a 128K-class machine.

events.title: fix(tape): route the fast-ROM trap's success return through SA/LD-RET
events.message:
fix(tape): route the fast-ROM trap's success return through SA/LD-RET

The trap manually popped $053F off the stack and jumped straight to the
caller, skipping SA/LD-RET's border restore, BREAK check, and EI. Land PC on
the ROM's own bare RET at $05E2 instead (as FUSE does) so the CPU executes
through SA/LD-RET whenever $053F is on the stack, fixing a permanent hang
(interrupts left disabled) after LOAD "" of a non-autorun program.

events.title: zynaps: wave C landed — the resolve-stage twin, the callback door, the wait pacing
events.message:
zynaps: wave C landed — the resolve-stage twin, the callback door, the wait pacing

The corrected arithmetic IS the headline: the profiler row that scoped this
wave (211,784 cyc/frame of stage SELF) was ~95% busy-wait — the stage
contains the frame's two sync spins and Hatari charges a spin to the
enclosing function. The original's stage WORK is ~10-12.4K/frame; the twin
collected the real ~19.5K prize, not the imagined ~140K.

- Kit: the CALLBACK DOOR (oracle/shim.c + emu.py + asm_twin.py; off-target
  only) — a twin's trampoline site traps to the host and the door calls
  the verified C with marshalled registers (X in/out, leaked D0, Z for a
  following beq; takes_image=False for ikbd_send_cmd/hw_bset8), refusing
  loudly on an unregistered callee and POISONING the CCR on return. Kit
  suite 439 -> 463; buggyboy 292 unmoved.
- src/asm/frame.S: frame_resolve_hits_and_game_state transcribed —
  703/703 original instructions, five-exit return, 19 door stubs over 16
  game callees, body identical in door and target builds (jbsr door_* ->
  jsr the real core on target). Measured per band: 1.022-1.037x with
  per-band bars 7 cycles above the measurement; the prediction that
  base-relative addressing would beat 1.00x was WRONG (trampolines cost
  more than it saves) and the docs carry the measurement, not the argument.
- init.c: the original's `move.w #$64,d7 / dbf` pacing delay in the ATTRACT
  wait is now transcribed (the section-start fire wait gets NONE — the original runs it undelayed, and the reconstruction must not make the two waits the same shape) (it sits BETWEEN the send and the
  poll; the poll count per pass is unchanged, so the differential cannot
  see it) — this one omission explained BOTH call-count anomalies (~50x
  the IKBD interrogates and rand16 draws during waits).
- Review found a SHIPPING bug nothing here could see: `move.w %sr` is
  privileged on 68010+ and sat in the twin's on-target arm, reached on the
  first scoring kill — replaced with roxl.l #1 (unprivileged, 10 cycles
  cheaper). Mutations: collision walk / starfield / exit dispatch red; the
  X_OUT drop SURVIVES (the door's CCR poison returns X=1 deterministically)
  — recorded in STATUS with the cheapest closure.

Cadence: game 2.80 -> 2.67 vblanks/frame [2x199 4x100] = 18.7 fps
(original 2.211); ceiling 2.96 -> 2.82 (worst-of-eight + 36). Wave D
scoped in STATUS: the three remaining slice bodies, 699 instructions but
43 doors (~2.7x wave C's trampoline work) for ~44K — with the honest
caveat that "work" still includes the raster spin, so the true compute
excess is smaller than the 125K the number suggests.

Suites: zynaps make test 4368 (+146); kit 463; buggyboy 292; full matrix
green from clean builds, frame differential ZERO bytes.

events.title: Inline the strip wrap: WrapBufFwd is gone
events.message:
Inline the strip wrap: WrapBufFwd is gone

Two asserts, added to main.asm, carry the whole change:

  LO(BUF_BASE) == 0        BUF_BASE is &5800
  BUF_END      == &8000    so BUF_SIZE is &2800, LO() zero too

and three consequences follow:

  1. adding BUF_BASE cannot touch the low byte, so every
     `LDA lo : ADC #LO(BUF_BASE) : STA lo` in the port was a no-op;
  2. subtracting BUF_SIZE cannot touch it either, so the wrap is one
     high-byte SBC -- written `SBC #HI(BUF_SIZE)-1` with carry known
     clear, because SBC with C=0 subtracts the extra 1;
  3. "past the end" IS "bit 7 set", so WrapBufFwd's 16-bit CMP ladder
     becomes a single BPL, small enough to inline at all four of its
     call sites. The routine and its JSR/RTS are gone.

SetCRTCStart gets the same treatment sideways: with no low-byte add to
do, the value stays in A and shifts with ROR A instead of ROR sTmp.

  code image   &2FF1 -> &2FAE     67 B   (15 B free -> 82)
  bank 6       &BC63 -> &BC5D      6 B
  bank 4       &BFF2 -> &BFED      5 B

but the cycles matter more than the 78 bytes, and they are in the
hottest code in the port: SprNextUnit drops ~11 cycles a call (30 ->
19) and runs per 4-pixel column per sprite row; SprScanRow ~8; SetCell,
ra_row and ra_nohi similar. Static counts.

Verified exhaustively -- every changed routine over its FULL input
domain, old semantics against the exact 8-bit sequence assembled:

  SetCell                     1,146,880 cases   OK
  ra_row                        163,840 cases   OK
  SprNextUnit / ra_nohi          10,240 cases   OK
  SCANSTEP + SprScanRow          40,960 cases   OK
  SetCRTCStart                   10,240 cases   OK
  result always in [BASE,END)   327,680 cases   OK

One conditional subtract is enough because the pre-wrap offset is
always under 2*BUF_SIZE: worst case &4FF7 against &5000. That rests on
scrollS being 0..BUF_SIZE-1, and bufcore.asm's new header says so.

Runtime A/B in headless jsbeeb put it 191 buffer bytes from HEAD across
11 unit columns -- a door and two droids. For scale, the SAME binary
differs from itself by 2,129-2,224 bytes across 58 columns if boot
timing shifts the game-pass phase by 10ms, so cross-build comparison
here has a noise floor an order of magnitude above the result.

NOT included, raised with hexwab instead: a dead `STA bufp+1` before
the BPL in ra_row, and sTmp's low byte becoming dead now that
SetCRTCStart is its only user.

events.title: review: decoder addressing, char-safe names, kind-aware lookup, scrolling
events.message:
review: decoder addressing, char-safe names, kind-aware lookup, scrolling

Six review findings on the resource insight panes:

- The preview decoder derived its source layout from the clamped
  geometry, so clamping a hostile width, height, or plane count moved
  the plane and row offsets and scrambled what was shown. Source
  addressing now always follows the declared geometry -- clamps bound
  only the allocation and iteration -- so a clamped preview shows the
  top-left of the real layout.
- Resource names are guest bytes through from_utf8_lossy, and the
  byte-indexed String::truncate could panic inside a multibyte
  character when building the heat presets or the Resources rows; both
  now truncate by characters.
- Names are not unique (the registry replaces by address), so the
  palette.dump / copper.list lookup is now kind-aware: a bitmap
  registered under the same name no longer shadows the palette the
  client asked for, and a name that exists only with other kinds
  reports those kinds.
- The Resources table scrolls (cursor and page keys) so a registry
  larger than the ten visible rows stays fully reachable; the hint line
  counts entries above and below, and row clicks resolve through the
  same scroll window the rows were drawn with.
- Resource heat presets are capped at four so a large registry cannot
  push the machine windows -- notably the trailing 24-bit overview --
  off the single preset row; the Resources tab covers the rest.

Regression tests: declared-geometry addressing under plane and height
clamps, a multibyte name through both truncation sites, duplicate-name
kind preference, scroll reachability and clamping with offset-mapped
clicks, and the preset cap keeping 24-bit last.

events.title: debugger: guest uaelib resources in the insight panes, KPrintF in the console
events.message:
debugger: guest uaelib resources in the insight panes, KPrintF in the console

The resources a program registers through the uaelib trap
(debug_register_bitmap/_palette/_copperlist) now feed Copperline's own
panes. The Frame Analyzer grows a third tab listing the registry with a
decoded preview of the selection: bitmaps through a new pure planar
decoder (src/video/resource_preview.rs -- planar or interleaved layouts,
mask planes skipped, HAM shown indexed, hostile geometry clamped with a
note), drawn with the first registered palette resource or the live
Denise palette; palettes as swatch grids; copper lists disassembled at
their registered address. The Memory tab's window presets append one per
resource (guest-named, deduped like the machine banks) and the readout
under the map names the resource a hovered or pinned cell falls in.

The control protocol seeds from the same registry: palette.dump
{"resource"} reads a registered palette from guest memory (12-bit words
plus rgb24) and copper.list {"resource"} starts at a registered copper
list; an unknown name reports the names that do exist. The console gains
DBGRES (RESOURCES already lists Exec's OS resource nodes).

KPrintF text now reaches the debugger console pane: the trap keeps a
host-only bounded mirror of its stdout echo, fed inside the run-ahead
gate but not the stdout mute (a muted terminal must not blind the pane),
drained once per committed frame and pushed as DBG: lines while the pane
is open. Lines from while it was closed are not replayed: they already
reached stdout, and opening the console is a fresh view of the channel,
not a scrollback of the old one. The control protocol's single-consumer
debug event queue is untouched.

number and an existing name is skipped for the next one. A spawn that
never starts removes its empty log instead of leaving it in the temp dir.

events.title: review: restore GUI-removed session points, rebaseline watches after M
events.message:
review: restore GUI-removed session points, rebaseline watches after M

The break-state sync kept its ownership entry for a point the local GUI
had toggled off, so the insertion pass skipped it and GDB continued as
though an acknowledged breakpoint were armed when it was not. The
client's acknowledged break state is authoritative for its own points:
a desired point found missing from the machine drops its stale
ownership entry and is reinstalled by the same sync, for PC
breakpoints, word watches, register watches, and the loadseg catch
alike. GUI-owned points are untouched as before, and z-packet removals
still take points out for good.

An M packet refreshed only the core's private watch snapshots; the
machine-installed word watches kept their old baselines, so writing a
watched address through the stub reported a spurious hit on the next
step. Rebaseline them after memory-write packets, as CCP's memory.write
does.

Docs: the exclusion list gains --benchmark-until, and the stop wording
no longer claims a plain pause opens the debugger window.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: gdb: attach the stub to the interactive window with --gdb-gui
events.message:
gdb: attach the stub to the interactive window with --gdb-gui

--gdb serves a headless machine; a debugger session with the screen
visible previously had no RSP endpoint at all. --gdb-gui ADDR attaches
the GDB stub to the normal windowed session the way --control-gui
attaches the control server: an accept thread plus per-connection
reader/writer threads (gdbstub/windowed.rs) frame and checksum packets
off the socket, and the winit frame loop drains them at the top of
about_to_wait (video/window/gdb.rs), driving the same transport-free
GdbCore the headless driver runs.

What differs in a window, and why:

- The machine stays paced and visible, so continue defers its stop
  reply and lets the ordinary frame loop run; a stop that surfaces
  while the client's continue is outstanding answers the client instead
  of opening the local debugger panel. monitor warp on|off|status flips
  the App's warp hold (WarpSource::Gdb), released on disconnect.
- The core's session breakpoint list is polled per instruction by the
  headless continue loop and never seen by the CPU hot loop, so every
  core-held break translates into machine-installed debug state
  (GdbBreaks), with the control session's ownership rule: never touch a
  point the local GUI owns, remove exactly ours on detach. Watchpoints
  become per-word machine watches (capped at 8 words), the register
  watch monitors are intercepted onto the per-register toggle API (the
  core's own handlers write the whole bus list, which would clobber
  GUI-set watches), and the machine-level loadseg catch stands in for
  the headless driver's per-instruction tracker poll, narrowing to the
  --run target's name when that is the only consumer.
- k detaches instead of ending the session: the window belongs to the
  user, and VS Code sends k on Stop Debugging. Documented divergence
  from the headless driver.

--gdb-gui excludes --gdb, --control/--control-gui (both contend for the
pause state and the deferred-stop hook), and --benchmark-until; it keeps
live audio and the windowed path for captures, and suppresses the
launcher like the other serving flags. --run break-at-entry works as
with --gdb. docs/debugger/gdb.md gains the two-mode section.

Tests: reader framing/acks/NoAckMode/interrupt over a real socket, and
a socket-free drain suite (deferred continue completed by a breakpoint
with the panel left closed, synchronous step, interrupt, detach leaving
GUI-owned points alone, warp hold released on disconnect, k detaching,
qXfer library reads arming the machine loadseg catch).

events.message:
review: refuse a second profile.start, keep the pane armed on a failed stop

Starting over an active capture closed it with a null machine
descriptor and an empty resource list -- an invalid summary against the
documented contract -- and discarded any final write error. One capture
runs at a time now: profile.start while one is active is INVALID_STATE,
so the running capture always gets its real summary from an explicit
profile.stop.

The windowed dispatcher re-armed the frame analyzer for an open pane
only when profile.stop succeeded, but the capture disarms the analyzer
before its summary write can fail; re-arm on every outcome.

Also close the unterminated inline-code span in profiling.md that broke
the strict docs build, and document the one-capture rule.

events.title: review: forget a timed-out request so its late reply is dropped
events.message:
review: forget a timed-out request so its late reply is dropped

After a wait_ms expiry the bridge sent pause and waited 1 ms for the
pause's own reply; a reply arriving later stayed in the pending map
for good, so repeated timed resumes grew it without bound. The bridge
now has forget(id), which drops the pending entry so the reader
discards a late reply instead of parking it, and outstanding() to
count what is still open. resume_with_wait waits a short grace for
the pause reply (the server writes it right behind the stop), forgets
the id either way, and forgets the resume itself when it is still
unanswered after the pause grace; the timeout guarantee is unchanged.

The scripted server helpers move to a test_support module so the MCP
tests can use them: one test holds a pause reply back until the next
request and checks the map stays empty across three timed resumes,
another does the same for the bridge's forget on its own.

events.title: review: validate the JSON-RPC envelope and forward screenshot paths absolute
events.message:
review: validate the JSON-RPC envelope and forward screenshot paths absolute

handle_message dispatched envelopes that are not JSON-RPC 2.0: a
missing or wrong jsonrpc version and boolean, object or null ids were
accepted, and an object with neither method nor id was treated as a
notification. It now requires "jsonrpc": "2.0", accepts only string
and integer ids (a malformed id gets -32600 with a null id), rejects a
method that is not a string, and answers a message with no method and
no result or error with -32600; valid notifications with unknown
methods and stray responses are still ignored.

capture_screenshot forwarded a non-string path as if absent, taking a
temporary screenshot instead of surfacing the method's invalid-params
error; the value now goes through as it is. A relative path was
resolved by the emulator against its own working directory and read
back against ours, which differ for an attached session or a launch
with a cwd, so the image block quietly became a note while the tool
reported success: an explicit path is made absolute against
copperline-ctl's working directory before it is forwarded, and a PNG
that cannot be read back is an isError result. The control reference
documents both.

events.title: review: create the launched emulator's log owner-only
events.message:
review: create the launched emulator's log owner-only

The MCP bridge points a launched emulator's stdout and stderr at a log
file in the temp dir, and the emulator announces its control token on
stderr, so the log carried the token with the umask's permissions
(0644 as a rule) while the loopback endpoint was live. The log is now
created through the same owner-only options as the --control-info
file (0600 on unix, the platform default elsewhere), set as the file
is created rather than by a chmod after it, and with create_new so a
file or symlink planted under the predictable name is refused rather
than written through.

The launch test that runs a script in place of the emulator checks
the log's mode.

events.title: review: MEMW counts as a JIT-blocking hook, the 040 FPU shim does not, and the transparency test arms the diagnostic observers

review: MEMW counts as a JIT-blocking hook, the 040 FPU shim does not, and the transparency test arms the diagnostic observers

The JIT fallback warning now keys off a dedicated debug_hooks_armed
predicate. COPPERLINE_DBG_MEMW joins it: debug_check_memw runs only in the
precise loop, so a JIT machine with the watch armed silently stayed on the
batch path and never reported. The FPU-less 68040 leaves it: the host FPU
shim keeps that model on the precise loop whether or not anything is
armed, and the warning must not claim a debugger moved an undebugged run.

DiagnosticHooks / M68kMachine::arm_diagnostic_hooks switch on the
CPU-level observers the environment normally arms (MEMW, FC, SPREN, IRQ,
DIAG_IPL, DIAG_PCHIST, DIAG_CRASH) so tests/debugger_transparency.rs holds
them to the same per-frame comparison as the debugger struct; the
bus-level log-only knobs have no programmatic switch and stay covered by
the CLI probe on record. Two unit tests pin the predicate on a 68020 with
MEMW armed and on an FPU-less 68040.
