events.title: The animated tiles repaint in window B, not window A
events.message:
The animated tiles repaint in window B, not window A

The audit's corridor scenario showed ~29% of passes finishing the
tranche-A draw with the beam over the play area, and the recharge
pad's rotate pass was the recurring cost: AnimPaint in window A plus
its forcing of nearby sprites into tranche A.

The writers now carry a class: SprHitsDraw returns a byte (bit 0 the
window-A writers - band, columns, doors for now; bit 1 the animated
tiles) instead of a carry, and SprAssignTr forces a component to
tranche A on bit 0, to tranche B on bit 1, and refuses the split on
both - no tranche is safe under both windows' writers. On a split
pass AnimPaint bows out of window A (a gate at its head) and the
window-B block calls AnimPaintB between tranche B's restore and its
draw: the tiles land while every sprite that could be standing on
them is erased, and the draw's save picks them up. Whole passes keep
the old order.

AnimScanPass moves below the tranche-B block so window B paints the
list SprScanCls classified at the top of the pass, not a freshly
rebuilt one; its borrowed maprow is just as dead there, and a modal
arm skipping the rebuild costs nothing (the list is rebuilt from
scratch every normal pass). The main loop's two restore paths become
one - SprRestoreTr's argument is sprSplit minus one (0 = tranche A,
&FF = the whole pool) - which retires SprRestoreAll and pays for the
new call.

Verified in jsbeeb, player standing ON an animating recharge pad:
sprCls[0]=2 on rotate passes, the player forced into tranche B
(sprTr[0]=1) with the split kept, the pad animates under him with no
corruption - and the 128-pass histogram reads clean: every tranche-A
draw ends in state 0 (off-display), every tranche-B draw inside
window B, against 6/128 late with beam up to ~90 lines in before.

precedence, so a unix box that happens to export both keeps its

through XDG_CONFIG_HOME, which the chain no longer reads; they redirect
HOME and USERPROFILE now, so a local run can never sweep the invoking
user's real Documents/Copperline. The player exception gains the pure
resolver seam and test the comment wrongly claimed the player crate

events.title: A11 : l'oracle Hatari entre en CI — et sa première exécution trouve deux références non re-dérivables
events.message:
A11 : l'oracle Hatari entre en CI — et sa première exécution trouve deux références non re-dérivables

Dernière boucle de validation entièrement manuelle du projet. tests.yml compare
depuis août la capture NeoST aux références commises à chaque push : c'est une
non-régression, « NeoST rend encore ce qu'il rendait ». Il ne disait rien de la
question qui FONDE ces références — Hatari rend-il toujours la même chose ?

Le MODE manquait, pas seulement le job. `--oracle` ÉCRASE les références : il sert
à en poser une, jamais à en contrôler une, puisqu'il efface la preuve qu'il
devrait comparer. D'où `--oracle-check`, non destructif : il rejoue Hatari au pin,
retient via oracle_scan l'image identique à la capture NeoST du jour, puis la
CONFRONTE à la référence commise sans jamais écrire dans tests/reference/. Quand
il passe, trois choses sont vraies d'un coup :

    NeoST == référence commise == Hatari (aujourd'hui, au pin)

Garde vérifiée PAR MUTATION — 1 pixel modifié dans une référence commise suffit à
la faire échouer. C'est le contraire du garde-fou qui ne mord jamais (A38).

.github/workflows/oracle.yml : hebdomadaire + workflow_dispatch, jamais au push.
Le pin est LU dans setup_hatari.sh pour former la clé de cache plutôt que recopié
— une clé qui répète une constante finit par mentir sur ce qu'elle met en cache,
et un cache survivant à un changement de pin ferait tourner l'ANCIEN Hatari en
prétendant valider le nouveau. Mesuré au repos : 5 min 31 pour 8 étalons.

CE QUE LA PREMIÈRE EXÉCUTION A TROUVÉ, et qui n'était écrit nulle part : deux des
dix références oracle ne sont pas RE-DÉRIVABLES.

  · nocooper — son oracle exige une touche TENUE (espace, vbl ~900) que
    hatari_oracle.sh ne sait pas injecter (il faut --cmd-fifo). La référence avait
    été posée à la main. Second obstacle resté invisible : le run NeoST utilise
    --fastfdc alors qu'oracle_fastfdc est absent de l'entrée — les deux timelines
    ne sont même pas alignées.
  · spec512_bands — HATARI NE SE REPRODUIT PAS lui-même dessus : deux runs de la
    même ligne de commande, deux jeux de phases DISJOINTS (md5 des trames de la
    fenêtre : aucun commun). C'est la rançon exacte de ce que l'étalon mesure — un
    cycle CPU visible à l'œil — et le RNG de la position angulaire de la disquette
    décale le démarrage du programme. oracle_scan n'y peut rien : il corrige une
    renumérotation de TRAMES, le décalage est SOUS-TRAME. Les 4 phases d'une
    fenêtre de 181 trames diffèrent toutes de la référence, la moins pire à
    2 460 px, couleurs permutées sur 4 px au bord de chaque bande = 4 cycles.

Aucune des deux n'est un bug de NeoST, et aucune n'est une mauvaise référence :
celle de spec512_bands est un authentique oracle Hatari (elle porte sa LED
disquette) et prouve qu'un jour, sur un run donné, NeoST a rendu cette image AU
PIXEL comme Hatari. Une référence peut donc être VRAIE ET NON REPRODUCTIBLE — cas
que l'outillage ne prévoyait pas. Le manifeste le déclare (oracle_check: false +
oracle_check_note), la raison étant OBLIGATOIRE : sans elle le script refuse de
tourner plutôt que d'exclure en silence.

Périmètre réel en CI : 5 étalons (blitter_hog, cuddly_demos, scroll_8264,
scroll_8265, trace_odd) — les 3 spectrum512_diapo* dépendent d'une ROM Atari que
le dépôt ne porte plus. Décompte et noms imprimés à chaque exécution.

Paliers fast ET full verts, aucune étape sautée.

events.title: A41 : les 27 px de Closure sont à Hatari — il colore avec des écritures pas encore faites
events.message:
A41 : les 27 px de Closure sont à Hatari — il colore avec des écritures pas encore faites

Dernier écart oracle inexpliqué du dépôt. L'étalon `closure` tenait 27 px / 114816
contre l'oracle, TOUS sur la ligne 0 — la première ligne affichée (sl=34), celle
qu'ouvre le retrait de bordure haute — chaque pixel fautif d'une couleur voisine
d'un cran ($210 chez nous, $310 chez Hatari).

Verdict MESURÉ, pas déduit. Sonde temporaire dans `Spec512_StartFrame` (arbre
extern/hatari gitignoré ; sonde révoquée et binaire rebâti au pin f0736b2 juste
après — l'arbre est vérifié propre) :

  seed=000 100 200 210 310 310 320 420 430 531 442 541 552 652 652 763

Ces seize valeurs sont EXACTEMENT, registre par registre, le bloc que la démo
écrit aux cycles 438-508 de cette MÊME ligne 34 — relevé indépendamment côté
NeoST par NEOST_SPEC512_TRACE. Hatari colore donc les pixels des cycles 56-144
avec des écritures postérieures de 380 cycles. Aucun faisceau ne fait ça : la
palette causale de NeoST est la bonne.

Cause, chez Hatari : `nScanLine += OVERSCAN_TOP` sous V_OVERSCAN_NO_TOP
(spec512.c:233) saute les CyclePalettes des scanlines 0 à 28 — où vit justement
le bloc d'init de la démo — et l'amorce retombe sur pHBLPalettes[], que le
`pHBLPalettes -= OVERSCAN_TOP` de video.c:3429 (qu'Hatari commente lui-même
« FIXME useless ? ») a garni d'écritures postérieures. Relevé complet :
vover=3 nStartHBL=34 STScreenStartHorizLine=0 OVERSCAN_TOP=29 nScanLine=29 skip=5.

Aucune ligne de code d'émulation ne change — c'est le point. `closure` reste
ref_kind: snapshot DÉFINITIVEMENT, comme overscan_top : le passer en oracle
installerait l'anticipation d'Hatari comme référence, tandis que la self-capture
garde la non-régression AU PIXEL. Verdict écrit aux quatre endroits qui le
portent : ref_note de l'étalon, docs/CASE_STUDIES.md, docs/HATARI_DIVERGENCES.md
§ Cas où NeoST améliore Hatari, TODO (A41 soldé + décisions actées).

Le minimum a été CHERCHÉ avant de conclure, parce qu'un écart de 27 px sur une
démo qui anime sa palette ressemble d'abord à une capture mal alignée : 70 trames
NeoST voisines (10471-10540) contre l'oracle commis donnent 27 ou 43 px, jamais 0.

Deux pièges d'outillage consignés au CHANGELOG : la palette d'init change à
CHAQUE trame, donc une trace `--trace video_color` prise sur une autre trame que
la capture comparée mène à une fausse piste (vécu : un décalage de ligne
inexistant) ; et l'égalité de breakcond s'écrit `=`, pas `==`.

Plus aucun écart oracle inexpliqué n'est ouvert. Paliers `fast` ET `full` verts,
aucune étape sautée.

events.title: Le .app macOS est enfin SCELLÉ : signature ad-hoc (palier 0 de la signature)
events.message:
Le .app macOS est enfin SCELLÉ : signature ad-hoc (palier 0 de la signature)

Mesuré sur le .dmg 0.6 publié, pas supposé :

  codesign --verify NeoST.app  →  code object is not signed at all
  spctl -a -t exec NeoST.app   →  rejected (source=no usable signature)
  codesign -dvv NeoST.app      →  adhoc,linker-signed
                                  Info.plist=not bound · Sealed Resources=none

Le seul cachet était celui que le LINKER pose sur les Mach-O arm64 : le bundle
lui-même n'était pas scellé. C'est cette configuration exacte qui donne « NeoST
est endommagé, placez-le dans la corbeille » sur un fichier téléchargé — un
CUL-DE-SAC, l'utilisateur n'a aucun bouton pour passer outre.

`package_macos.sh` scelle désormais le bundle avant `hdiutil` : binaire SECONDAIRE
d'abord (neost-headless est du code, pas une ressource), bundle ENSUITE — il scelle
le reste et signe l'exécutable principal au passage. Deux gardes derrière :
`codesign --verify --deep --strict` et la présence de « Sealed Resources ». Résultat
sur le .dmg rebâti : Sealed Resources version=2, 27 fichiers, Identifier
net.gistlabs.neost, « valid on disk », « satisfies its Designated Requirement ».

Ce que ça ne fait PAS, et le README le dit : Gatekeeper refuse toujours (spctl :
rejected), parce qu'il n'y a pas de Developer ID et qu'aucune signature gratuite
n'en tient lieu. Mais le refus devient « développeur non identifié », qui a une
sortie : clic droit → Ouvrir. Le palier suivant est la notarisation (99 $/an) ; sa
recette complète est écrite dans docs/RELEASE.md.

AU PASSAGE, une panne que seul un empaquetage local pouvait révéler :
NEOST_WITH_SLIRP est désormais forcé à OFF. En AUTO, une machine de dev ayant la
libslirp de Homebrew — MONO-ARCH — ne peut pas lier la tranche x86_64 (« ld:
symbol(s) not found for architecture x86_64 » sur slirp_new & co, rencontré en
rebâtissant le .dmg 0.6). La CI n'installe pas libslirp, donc elle ne pouvait pas
le voir, et un paquet local aurait de toute façon différé de la release. Le paquet
doit être le même partout.

Vérifié : .app universel (les deux tranches), smoke du paquet 4/4 (version, boot
EmuTOS, disquette livrée, HD GEMDOS), palier `fast` vert.

events.message:
README réorganisé pour la 0.6, et Hatari y a enfin sa section

Le README affirmait deux choses FAUSSES depuis la purge du 2026-08-30 : que les
paquets bureau embarquent `tos102uk.img` et `tos162uk.img` (ils ne portent plus
qu'EmuTOS, `NEOST_PACKAGE_NO_ATARI_TOS=1` par défaut dans les 8 jobs de CI), et
que l'APK Android « n'a pas encore d'interface » (il a un menu tactile depuis le
2026-08-11 — ce qui manque, dit tel quel, c'est un essai sur un VRAI appareil).

Réorganisation : l'ordre va maintenant de l'envie à l'action — essai dans le
navigateur, ce que la machine sait faire, où la prendre, comment s'en servir.
Deux atouts de la 0.6 qui n'étaient nulle part : le **MIDI** (appareils réels des
deux côtés sur les trois plateformes, fusion de claviers, aiguillage par canal,
synthé GM, MT-32) et les **extensions** (UltraSatan, NetUSBee/EtherNEC et son
accès Internet réel, modem, clés). Ajouté aussi : la suite Q 12/12 du MegaSTE,
les trois démos livrées dans chaque paquet (on a quelque chose à regarder au
premier lancement), et l'avertissement de signature côté macOS — le `.dmg` non
notarisé se fait dire « endommagé » par Gatekeeper, la ligne `xattr` est donnée.

**Hatari a sa propre section**, avec le lien vers le site officiel
(www.hatari-emu.org) et vers les sources (framagit) : ce n'est pas une note de bas
de page mais la méthode du projet — sources lues comme documentation matérielle,
puis exécutées en ORACLE, et les écarts restants écrits noir sur blanc. Elle finit
en disant qui devrait utiliser Hatari plutôt que NeoST : c'est honnête, et ça évite
de vendre le mauvais outil.

`docs/RELEASE.md` gagne la règle posée par le mainteneur aujourd'hui : le message
de tag et les notes de la Release GitHub s'écrivent en ANGLAIS (c'est une
publication), le CHANGELOG reste en français (c'est de la documentation). Le tag
0.6 a été refait dans la foulée sous cette règle.

Ancres, chiffres et licences de la doc : verts. Palier `fast` vert.

events.title: paths: host data moves out of the hidden config tree and into Documents
events.message:
paths: host data moves out of the hidden config tree and into Documents

~/Documents/Copperline on macOS and Linux,
%USERPROFILE%\Documents\Copperline on Windows -- somewhere a person
browsing their own files can find their saves, screenshots, recordings
and configs, rather than a dot-directory built for tools. Capitalised,
because the folder sits beside other applications' folders in Documents
and reads as a product name there, not a unix binary. Whichever of
USERPROFILE and HOME the machine defines names the home; XDG_CONFIG_HOME
and APPDATA are no longer consulted for the emulator, the old locations
were simply where host data used to live, and portable.txt keeps meaning
what it meant.

Player builds deliberately stay where they were: a published game is an
appliance whose data nobody browses, and every bought game planting its
id at the top of Documents would strew it with loose folders -- so an
overridden identity keeps the hidden per-user tree, one ~/.config/<id>
(%APPDATA%\<id>) per game.

events.title: ecs: give new ink a FREE SLOT instead of the nearest wrong one
events.message:
ecs: give new ink a FREE SLOT instead of the nearest wrong one

Reported while verifying #166: on ECS an event's first text line renders bright
cyan and the following lines render dim grey, near-illegible against the box.

Measured on the HEIRS innkeeper event (amiberry, ECS/68000): line 1 ink
#00bbbb, lines 2 and 3 #888888 against a #555544 box. The split is not
temporal, it is SPATIAL and lands exactly on a copper band boundary — line 1
sits in band 13, lines 2-3 in bands 14-15.

Cause: the per-band cut is computed from the surface as it stood, and drawing
text never marks it dirty, so anything drawn afterwards resolves through
remap_rect's absent-colour bucket — the nearest slot the band happens to own.
Band 13 owns a cyan slot only because the event PICTURE is cyan there. Bands
14-15 sit below the picture, never saw a cyan pixel, and resolve the same
glyphs to grey.

The existing remedy was explicitly a placeholder: ecs_ink_hold skips ONE
present in case a palette install is following, and its own comment says that
failing that the ink "paints on the NEXT present via the bucket fallback
exactly as before". The bucket fallback is the grey glyph.

★ And the band had room the whole time. Instrumenting the text-box bands says
they use 7 to 11 of their 32 slots — 21+ empty — while the glyph is forced onto
a slot 3675 away. So nothing needs re-quantising and nothing needs sacrificing:
hand the colour an EMPTY slot, fix the remap, and patch that slot's copper
word.

Writing a FREE slot's COLOR word is safe in a way a palette install is not
(#165): free means no used index maps to it, so no pixel on screen wears that
slot and changing its RGB cannot recolour the outgoing frame. Under
FRUA_PLANAR the band's draw-time coverage is dropped and its rows re-announced,
because rows a writer already stamped used the old remap for that index.

Per-band, because a colour absent here may be present one band down; and only
when the bucket is genuinely bad (ECS_INK_NEAR), so a glyph whose colour the
band already holds costs one distance test.

Result on the same event: all three lines now measure #00bbbb. The drive
adopts 6, 21, 3, 1, 1 slots at its re-band points.

Runtime knob video.cfg inkadopt=off restores the old behaviour for A/B.

All four targets build; 483 tests pass. ECS-only code — Falcon, TT, ST/STE and
AGA are untouched.

Not yet confirmed on hardware.

events.title: Reshape 23 functions to compile byte-exact; fix the TILE member-offset bug
events.message:
Reshape 23 functions to compile byte-exact; fix the TILE member-offset bug

Function-by-function comparison against Disk_1/WERNER.PRG (relocations and
cross-function bsr displacements masked) showed 120 of the 238 reconstructed
functions compiled to different code. This batch closes 23 of them -- the
count goes from 118 to 141 byte-exact -- by restoring the original source
shapes the codegen reveals:

- The six *_load_assets: no WORD temps (ldimgf/decompi results assign
  straight into gfilesz/gimgdec), plain for-loop over gindex, the -1 check
  on the first file only, (BYTE)(n + '0') cast, no final return.
- ikbdup/sjoyon/ikbdjs: BYTE *cterm = CONTERM initialized at declaration.
- clrscr/sclrbot/sclrtop, srdinp, ikbdrd, blitspr, blitwh: register
  variables (register LONG counters/pointers, register WORD parameters),
  p = p + N (lea) rather than p += N (adda), chained zero assignments,
  a switch on grez, and dead locals that pad the frames to original size.
- ps7upd/pcpark: operand order (Alcyon evaluates the right operand of +
  first) and branch polarity (the compiler branches on the inverse of the
  written condition, so != vs == dictates block order).

The real bug: c068 keeps a single namespace for struct member names, last
declaration wins.  The TILE typedef in werner.h declared x/y at offsets
4/6 after XY declared them at 0/2, so every XY access in panik.c and
auto.c silently read and wrote one entry beyond the intended one --
self-consistent, so the game played, but pascrd writes ran 4 bytes past
the array into adjacent BSS.  TILE and PART now live in bau.c, and
werner.h documents why they must never return.

tools/cmpfn.py is the comparator (needs a symbolized relink: lo68 -r
without -s, then relmod to WSYM.PRG).

events.title: The rupture handover keeps a 312-line field
events.message:
The rupture handover keeps a 312-line field

KC caught it on b2 and photographed it (ref/beeb-paradroid-to-001-resync*
.png): the picture displaced downward mid-transition, which is a MISPLACED
field, not a wrong-length one -- exactly what a frame-length instrument
cannot see, and why jsbeeb read 39,93x throughout while b2 rolled.

The rupture's frame is three cycles with VSync 5 rows into the 13-row
tail, so a CRTC free-running in the tail's shape VSyncs every 104 lines.
Round two's aligned write started that cycle at line 64, so the next VSync
arrived at line 104 instead of 312. src/ruptalign.asm suppresses VSync
across the intermediate cycles and lets the first one the handler sees
arrive exactly one frame after the last:

    0     VSync of the last plain frame (row 31 of 39)
   64     that frame ends; a fresh one starts
  ~80     OSBYTE 19 + an 8-row spin land here; SetupRupture writes the tail
          shape and R7 = 255 goes straight over its R7
   64-168 cycle A    168-272 cycle B, R7 = TAIL_R7 written at ~240
  272-376 cycle C -- its row 5 is line 312. Three tail cycles ARE 312.

ROUND FOUR IS WHERE THAT LAST WRITE GOES. At ~180 it sat on cycle B's row
1, and whether that fires a VSync in B or only in C depends on the rule
this port measured -- R6/R7/R12/R13 take effect in the PREVIOUS cycle --
which the emulators disagree about. If it matches in B, VSync fires at
line 208 and again at 312: two bad fields where round two had one, which
is a picture displaced further, which is what KC saw. Past B's own row 5
at line 216 the two readings agree, so it goes in at ~240.

It lives in bank 5 because it wants ~50 bytes and no other bank has them;
ts_loads pages that bank in, the routine calls SetupRupture itself and
ends JMP PgData. Code image unchanged, PARBRF back to 18 bytes.

KC confirms it on b2. jsbeeb cannot see this class of fault at all.

The palette changes at fire 1, not wherever the main loop is

KC: "the top panel flickers (looks like a redraw)" going from the game
over static to Transmission Terminated. Nothing writes the panel's bytes
there -- GoWashStart put "Game over" up when the wash began, and IsStart
only parks the scroll, asks for the 16-row bottom edge and draws the page
in the strip. What changed was the ULA.

InfoCall's first act is SetTextPal, which ended in SetPalPlay: sixteen ULA
writes from main-loop code, wherever the raster happened to be. The panel
has its own palette, applied in exactly one place -- RuptVSync's
SetPalPanel, at VSync -- and it displays 64 to 96 scanlines later. A write
landing in that window left the panel in the DECK's palette for the rest
of the field: a one-frame flash across the top box that reads as a redraw.
About one transition in three, and worst at the game over, where the panel
is white and red and the wash is black and white.

So SetPalette builds palPlay and returns, and the next fire 1 makes it
live -- one field at the most, and at the one moment in the field that is
safe: fire 1 is at P+44, twelve scanlines after the panel's rows have
finished displaying. The IRQ's own write was never the problem.

Two screens have no rupture to apply it: SetupPlain's table already ends
with its own sixteen writes, and TiShow now calls SetPalPlay after
TiPaint. Everything else runs under the rupture.

Verified in jsbeeb, because a deferred palette could leave a screen in the
wrong colours: cold-boot title on its random deck palette, the 001 screen,
a deck, the wash's black and white, and the wash -> 999 transition stepped
a field at a time, panel intact in the field the palette changes in.

events.title: RuptAlign, second time: the rupture starts on a frame boundary
events.message:
RuptAlign, second time: the rupture starts on a frame boundary

Establishing the rupture costs three malformed fields, and they are a
phase problem: SetupRupture writes R4 = TAIL_R4 = 12 wherever the main
loop happens to be, and the plain frame is 39 rows, so the row counter is
usually PAST 12 and the 6845 runs on toward its wrap before the compare
matches. Frame lengths across the briefing exit, one field at a time:

  before   39,936  39,936 | 38,378  49,154  6,168 | 39,938  39,936
  after    39,936  39,936 | 39,939  39,936  39,936 | 39,936  39,936

RuptAlign waits for VSync with OSBYTE 19 and spins out the rest of the
frame -- 8 rows, 8,192 cycles, against a landing window of another 11
rows -- so the writes land in row 0 or 1 of a fresh frame where R4 = 12 is
ahead of the counter. ts_loads calls it immediately before SetupRupture.

THIS IS THE SECOND ATTEMPT. The first was reverted: KC judged it worse by
eye, but the blanks still leaked a row then, so a stripe of the play
buffer sat on screen through the whole seam and swamped it. With every
blank on R8 the alignment stands on its own.

Also measured on the way in and clean at 39,936: the 001 screen to deck
transition, where ReframeView swaps the bottom edge from 16 rows back to
15. What is visible there is the deck painting over the info screen for a
pass or two -- redraw cost, not sync.

It lives in PARBRF because it wants ~16 bytes of main RAM that need no
paging and the code image has seven; PARBRF is resident and valid on
every route into ts_loads, but NOT at HsEntry, which is why the call is

events.title: Every blank is R8, and the title is not watched being drawn
events.message:
Every blank is R8, and the title is not watched being drawn

R6 = 0 is not a blank: it leaks row 0, because the row counter is compared
at the END of a row. Measured twice today -- once in SetupMode, where the
leaked row was 512 bytes into the bank streams at DEPK_STREAM, and once in
SetupPlain, whose R12/R13 park on BUF_BASE and so put a stripe of the play
buffer on an otherwise black screen for the 3.7 s of the briefing exit and
the whole game-over seam. KC saw that as flicker at both.

So all four blanking points use R8_BLANK, the 6845's display-skew bits,
which gate the display enable itself: SetupMode, SetupPlain's table,
tiw_done and BrTimeout. The display comes back in exactly two places --
the rupture's IRQ, which writes R8 at fires 1-3 every field and covers
everything in the game, and the title, which has no rupture.

TiCRTC sets the title's shape but no longer unblanks. TiShow does, AFTER
TiPaint, so the RLE picture is painted into a dark screen and the logo
appears complete rather than a cell at a time (KC). Verified by breaking
inside TiPaint and screenshotting: black.

Costs nothing in the code image -- SetupMode's blank is the R1 write it
was already making, pointed at another register, and TiCRTC gave back the
ten bytes its R1 restore had cost PARTITL. code_end stays &2FF9. PARBRF
36 -> 18, PARTITL 37 -> 27, bank 4 unchanged.

Checked in jsbeeb over every path that could have come up black instead:
boot to title, the timeout into the briefing, the briefing exit into the
001 screen, a game, ESCAPE, the wash, the 999 page, and the high-score
entry -- the sharp one, because HsEntry displays on its own rupture
between two SetupPlains. Field lengths stay 39,93x throughout.

docs/raster-timing.md also records the teardown measurement (one 376-line
field), the three malformed fields at switch-on, and the RuptAlign
prototype that fixed those and was reverted as worse by eye.

The rupture is switched on next to the IRQ that drives it

ts_loads put SetupRupture right after the IS_BLANK and then ran FillPanel
and three table builds before InstallIrq, so the CRTC sat in the tail
cycle's shape with nobody servicing it for the whole of them: a picture
at roughly double rate with no stable 50 Hz sync, which is the flicker KC

Measured on the boot path, breakpoints on SetupRupture and IrqHandler:

  frames painted in that window        14 -> 1

The JSR moved down to sit immediately before the JMP InstallIrq. Nothing
in between needs the rupture -- FillPanel writes &4A00, the others write
tables at &5400 and up, and none of it is displayed while the frame is
blank -- so the title's ordinary 312-line 50 Hz frame stands until the
instruction that hands the display over. Zero bytes.

done: it saves one frame where the reorder saves thirteen, and polling
CA1 costs ~15 bytes of a code image with seven. docs/raster-timing.md

Reverse engineering of the Indy 3 (Atari ST) copy protection

The three Kixx floppies carry no media protection: all 480 formatted tracks

the transcribed key generator, a patch tool, the write-up and the printable
reconstructed card. No game data is included.

Console: the icons go back to even spacing, on a ladder of their own

KC: it is fine for the icons and the text to be offset. So the text
lines stay where they are and the icons return to 3/6/9/12 -- touching,
evenly spaced, the rows they had before the count lines.

They cannot share one ladder: an entry with two text lines needs a
four-row pitch, an icon is three rows, and four icons on a four-row
pitch from row 2 would put the last at 14 and write three rows past the
end of the buffer. Two ladders is legal because the two never collide --
icons in units 4-18, text from unit 24 -- and only the unit-type line
crosses the icon columns, which is why it keeps rows 0-1 and the first
icon starts at 3.

CON_ROW_ICON0..3 are new and the icon destinations derive from them;
consolesel.asm's CON_SEL* moved with them, and the ASSERTs that tie the
two together caught them, as they are meant to. There is an ASSERT on
the gaps being equal so this cannot drift back.

events.title: chipset: pace pre-display sprite DMA with the beam, and fix the IPL pipe
events.message:
chipset: pace pre-display sprite DMA with the beam, and fix the IPL pipe

Two independent timing faults, both of which corrupted the same thing: the
vertical-blank sprite control-word fetch. Ghostown's Spooky Town paints its
credit-scroll background by multiplexing sprites 4-7 five times per line
from the Copper, so losing one channel drops five 16-pixel columns out of
every line -- black stripes flashing over the background.

Sprite DMA runs from the top of the field, above the render window, so the
lines from the sprite-DMA start (PAL $19) to the display start were
reconstructed by a replay in frame_capture.rs. That replay ran as one batch
at the display start, but `fetch_sprite_words` reads chip RAM as it is
*now*: a fetch modelled at line $19 actually sampled memory as of line $2C.
Software routinely rewrites its sprite descriptors from the vertical-blank
interrupt in between -- Spooky Town restores the old header and writes a new
one, immediately after the fetch it expects to have happened -- so the
replay latched image data instead of the descriptor. `poke_ctl` then took
vstart's bit 8 from that garbage and the channel's comparators pointed at
lines the beam never reaches for the rest of the field.

The replay is now paced by the beam: a slot-granular cursor
(`SpriteDmaReplayCursor`) advances as the beam passes each of a line's
sixteen sprite slots, with the frame's DMACON, SPRxPT and SPRxPOS/CTL
writes applied in between, so each fetch reads chip RAM at its own beam
time. The provisional live pass for pre-display lines is dropped: the
replay already owned those lines, and running both fetched them twice. The
cursor is serialized, so a state saved inside the pre-display window
resumes where it stopped. Both that cursor and the per-source interrupt
deadlines below change the serialized layout -- STATE_VERSION 71.

That left about one bad frame per second, with a second cause. The demo's
descriptor update is scheduled relative to the fetch and should enter at a
steady raster line; it jittered across v=2..36, and the frames where it
straddled the Copper's line-24 SPRxPT write moved the buffer while the
pointer stayed stale. Both faults were in the IPL recognition pipe:

  - The pipe extended an idle STOP nap. `idle_fast_forward_chunk` bounds a
    halted CPU's nap by the next device event, but nothing accounted for an
    interrupt already latched in INTREQ and merely hidden by the pipe. A
    halted CPU has nothing else to wake it, so the nap ran on to some
    unrelated event and the handler was entered a whole nap late -- tens of
    raster lines, not the five colour clocks the pipe is worth.
  - A single countdown was restarted by every newly raised source, so a
    later source stretched an earlier one's delay. Each source has its own
    path through the level encoder and now has its own deadline.

Handler entry is back within the pipe's own length, and 1600 consecutive
frames of the scene are clean on both OCS and ECS.

The two E-clock-phase-sensitive golden probes (`bltprobe-pace`,
`timing-test`) shift by one count, as timing-test/README.md describes for a
boot-timing change; re-blessed. Delivering interrupts on time also costs
about 8% of headless throughput, because the guest was previously
under-executing the ISR work it now runs.

events.title: Merge branch 'claude/midi-windows-winmm' : le MIDI hôte de Windows atteint la parité macOS/Linux — backend winmm ajouté comme TROISIÈME branche #if dans les ponts existants (pas un fichier parallèle : appariement, décodeur, fusion, file horodatée et panique restent partagés), avec audio/MidiWinmm.hpp pour le spécifique. Windows gagne les destinations matérielles ET les sources ; sa page MIDI était vide de bout en bout, sa moitié « appareils » étant gardée à tort par portAvailable() (le port VIRTUEL) au lieu de la disponibilité des destinations. Deux surprises en chemin : Windows a bel et bien un identifiant unique — DRV_QUERYDEVICEINTERFACE rend le chemin d'interface, dont la partie médiane est le chemin PHYSIQUE (hub et prise), là où MIDIOUTCAPS ne donne rien (mid=65535 pid=65535 sur le Circuit Tracks) — ce qui met Windows au niveau de CoreMIDI et laisse ALSA seul sans identifiant stable ; et midiInOpen doit passer en CALLBACK_THREAD, winmm interdisant midiInAddBuffer depuis un callback alors qu'il faut ré-armer les tampons SysEx. timeBeginPeriod(1) tant qu'une sortie est ouverte : sigma 0,30 ms contre 5,34 ms sans, mesuré A/B sur matériel. La banque GM entre enfin dans les paquets — la case du chantier précédent était morte dans TOUS les binaires livrés. Seul manque, irréductible sans pilote tiers et dit dans l'interface : le port virtuel, que Windows ne sait pas créer (loopMIDI le fournit, et son port apparaît alors comme un appareil ordinaire). Vérifié sur matériel réel (Circuit Tracks USB) : 35 octets d'horloge dans l'ACIA en 1,3 s sans perte, GUI ouvrant les deux extrémités et apprenant l'identifiant, 0 octet en retard, gamme/SysEx/running status/panique éprouvés. Paliers fast ET full verts sous Windows — une première, qui a demandé quatre correctifs d'outillage sans rapport avec le MIDI (commit dédié).

events.title: La suite de tests tourne enfin sous Windows : quatre pannes d'outillage que personne ne pouvait voir
events.message:
La suite de tests tourne enfin sous Windows : quatre pannes d'outillage que personne ne pouvait voir

Aucune n'est liée au MIDI ; toutes empêchaient de valider quoi que ce soit sur la
plateforme, ce qui explique qu'elles aient survécu — la suite n'y avait jamais tourné, et
c'est invisible depuis un Mac ou une CI Linux.

· compare_screenshot.py : mkstemp rend un descripteur OUVERT, laissé tel quel avant de
  faire écrire ffmpeg dans le fichier. Sous POSIX, simple fuite de descripteur (une par
  comparaison) ; sous Windows le fichier est verrouillé, ffmpeg échoue — et l'unlink du
  finally échouait à son tour, MASQUANT le vrai message (« ffmpeg est requis »). Toute
  référence PNG (les captures d'oracle Hatari) était incomparable.
· check_doc_anchors.py : le motif [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* était passé à grep en argument.
  Sous git-bash/MSYS, grep.exe re-découpe la ligne de commande et prend ce motif pour un
  GLOB qu'il expanse. Résultat : « 197 ancres mortes » sur des symboles bien vivants
  (Machine::runFrame…). Le scan des lexèmes se fait désormais en Python — plus de
  dépendance à grep, et 0 ancre morte.
· Le suffixe .exe : les huit outils qui lancent un binaire le cherchaient sous son nom
  POSIX, donc la suite se déclarait « non bâtie » alors que tout était compilé. Le
  contournement évident — copier neost.exe en neost — est un PIÈGE : la copie ne suit pas
  les rebuilds, et on teste alors un binaire périmé sans que rien ne le dise.
· gui_available() sautait le boot GUI dès que DISPLAY/WAYLAND_DISPLAY manquaient, ce qui
  ne veut rien dire hors X11/Wayland. macOS était déjà excepté, Windows non : la cible
  neost n'était lancée par la suite sur AUCUNE des deux plateformes non-Linux.

Reste connu, non corrigé : les outils lisent leurs fichiers sans encoding="utf-8", or le
cp1252 de Windows échoue sur etalons.json — d'où le PYTHONUTF8=1 nécessaire devant
run_all.py sur cette plateforme.

Vérifié : paliers fast et full verts sous Windows 11 (llvm-mingw), les seuls SKIP étant
les données non redistribuables déjà recensées au TODO.

events.title: Le MIDI hôte de Windows rejoint macOS et Linux : backend winmm, appareils réels des deux côtés
events.message:
Le MIDI hôte de Windows rejoint macOS et Linux : backend winmm, appareils réels des deux côtés

Suite du chantier « le synthé GM cesse d'être un privilège macOS », sur la dernière
plateforme en retard. Sous Windows, MidiOutHost::destinations() et MidiInHost::sources()
rendaient des listes VIDES, et la page MIDI cachait sa moitié « appareils matériels » —
gardée, à tort, par portAvailable() (le port VIRTUEL) plutôt que par la disponibilité des
destinations. Un Windows avec un clavier maître branché voyait une page vide.

Backend winmm ajouté comme TROISIÈME branche #if dans les ponts existants (pas un fichier
parallèle : appariement, décodeur, fusion, file horodatée et panique restent partagés),
avec audio/MidiWinmm.hpp pour ce qui est propre à Windows.

· Sortie : midiOutOpen par appareil, midiOutShortMsg pour les messages courts,
  midiOutLongMsg + récolte différée des tampons pour le SysEx (un dump de 4 Ko met plus
  d'une seconde à sortir à 31250 bauds : ni attendre, ni libérer).
· Entrée : midiInOpen en CALLBACK_THREAD et non CALLBACK_FUNCTION — winmm interdit
  d'appeler autre chose qu'une courte liste blanche depuis un callback, et
  midiInAddBuffer, indispensable pour ré-armer les tampons SysEx, n'en fait pas partie.
  La file de messages rend l'opération légale et réutilise le thread déjà là pour ALSA.
· Identifiant unique, que Windows était censé ne pas avoir : MIDIOUTCAPS ne donne qu'un
  nom tronqué et, pour le Circuit Tracks testé, mid=65535 pid=65535 — rien.
  DRV_QUERYDEVICEINTERFACE rend le chemin d'interface, dont la partie médiane est le
  chemin PHYSIQUE (hub et prise) : deux appareils du même modèle sont discernables.
  Windows rejoint CoreMIDI ; ALSA reste seul sans identifiant stable.
· timeBeginPeriod(1) tant qu'une sortie est ouverte. Sans lui Windows réveille le thread
  de livraison par tranches de ~15,6 ms et tout l'horodatage serait arrondi à cette
  tranche. Mesuré A/B, 40 échéances de 50 ms vers le Circuit Tracks : sigma 0,30 ms
  (écart max 0,90) avec, contre sigma 5,34 ms (13,10) sans.
· shortMessageLength() : MM_MIM_DATA empaquette un message sans dire combien d'octets
  comptent ; pousser les trois aveuglément ajouterait une donnée fantôme après un Program
  Change, que le running status avale en silence. Fonction pure, 14 cas dans
  neost-selftest — donc éprouvée aussi sur macOS et Linux, sans clavier branché.
· La banque GM entre enfin dans les paquets : stage_free_data.sh n'embarquait pas
  roms/gm/, la case « Built-in General MIDI synth » était donc morte dans TOUS les
  binaires livrés, alors que THIRD-PARTY.txt annonçait le fichier.

Hors de portée, et dit dans l'interface : le port virtuel « NeoST MIDI OUT ». Windows n'a
aucune API pour créer un port que les autres applications voient (ni winmm, ni WinRT MIDI
1.0) ; loopMIDI le fournit, et son port apparaît alors comme un appareil ordinaire, en
destination ET en source. Windows MIDI Services le ferait nativement mais exigerait une
pile WinRT/COM que le zip autonome ne peut pas emporter.

Vérifié sur MATÉRIEL RÉEL (Windows 11, Novation Circuit Tracks en USB) : --midi-list
énumère l'appareil avec son identifiant ; --midi-in-device fait entrer 35 octets
d'horloge dans l'ACIA en 1,3 s, 0 perdu ; le GUI ouvre destination + source canalisée
d'un coup, apprend l'identifiant et livre 0 octet en retard ; gamme, SysEx, running
status et panique éprouvés sur l'appareil. Paliers fast ET full verts sous Windows.

events.title: ste: $FF820D is a HARDWARE difference, and the write is harmless — fix the comment
events.message:
ste: $FF820D is a HARDWARE difference, and the write is harmless — fix the comment

The comment above st_flip_super claimed only the hi/mid video-base bytes were
written, and that leaving $820D out 'keeps this correct on a plain ST too (no
$820D there)'. The code three lines below writes $820D. One of the two was
wrong; it was the comment.

Which one to fix needed measuring, on the configuration where it matters: a
plain ST with TOS 2.06 and an accelerator (Hatari --machine st --cpulevel 3
--cpuclock 32).

  - the write reaches the bus: 12 writes to ffff820d during boot, against 13
    each to ffff8201/ffff8203, so it is not dead code;
  - it raises no bus error. A full drive (boot, load, dungeon walk) took six
    bus errors, every one from the TOS ROM probing hardware it might not have
    (ffff8900 STE DMA sound, ffff8a00 blitter), and none from frua.

That is evidence rather than absence-of-evidence, because Hatari does model
this fault class on an ST — those ROM probes are exactly it, faulting and being
caught. The ST decodes the $FF82xx block coarsely and swallows the write. It
is harmless by construction too: pages are 256-byte aligned so the low byte is
0 on every flip, which is both its power-on value and the only value a plain
ST's fixed low byte can hold.

And it is a HARDWARE difference, not a TOS one (Compendium B.20: $FF820C
'Video Base Address Low' is STE-and-later silicon). Fitting TOS 2.06 to an ST
does not add the register; TOS 1.04 in an STE does not remove it.

events.title: review: the recovery path is real, and an automatic run keeps its manners
events.message:
review: the recovery path is real, and an automatic run keeps its manners

Copilot's three findings on #604, all correct.

The saved default was validated -- filesystem checks included -- before
the launcher branch was even consulted, so a default whose floppy image
had gone missing exited main before the screen that could fix it ever
opened, and the promised fall-back-to-the-launcher was never reached.
The bare start now decides on the raw file and validates nothing:
validation belongs to the Run button, where the error is a status line
over an open screen. That mends the same dead end for ordinary broken
defaults, auto-launching or not.

An automatic run also no longer overrides [emulation] power_on: pressing
Run is a statement, so the button still powers on regardless, but
nobody pressed it here -- the machine starts in the power state a
command-line start of the same file would give, warp-boot gate armed
for the power button rather than engaged.

And each of the two methods gets its own doc paragraph back.

events.title: docs: the 020 build downgrades to ST graphics — run it on an accelerated ST
events.message:
docs: the 020 build downgrades to ST graphics — run it on an accelerated ST

The runtime backend choice was documented in one direction only (the 68000
build running on a Falcon/TT and picking their higher-colour path). It works
the other way too: dsp_detect reads the _VDO cookie, so the 020 Falcon/TT
binary detects ST hardware and downgrades itself to the same 16-colour ST-low
banded backend. The graphics follow the machine; only the CPU decides which
binary you can run.

That makes the Falcon/TT zip the right binary for an accelerated ST, which was
documented nowhere. Measured in the guest's own clock (FRUA_STEPPROF), one
dungeon step's render: stock ST 8MHz with the 68000 build = 155 ticks; ST with
an 030 at 32MHz running the 020 build = 9-13. Small sample, so the section
quotes the magnitude rather than the ratio.

Also records that no Hatari patch is needed to try it (--machine st --cpulevel
3 --cpuclock 32, with Hatari's own TOS 2.06/EmuTOS and 32MHz-max caveats), and
corrects a stale claim in the ST/STE entry: 'no version check in the code, so
earlier TOS may well work - nobody has tried' was wrong twice over.
plat_stram_alloc DOES gate Mxalloc on Sversion() and fall back to Malloc, and
TOS 1.04 has now been tried - a stock non-e ST boots and plays.

Stock-ST colour, measured rather than assumed: the STE 4-bit palette encoding
carries its extra bit in bit 3, so a plain ST reads a correct 3-bit
approximation for free - an ST frame uses only the even gun indices, the STE
frame uses the odd ones too. Costs colour count (15 distinct vs 23 in a walk
frame), not band seams: the mod-8 band-boundary test scores ST 5/20 and STE
4/20 against a chance baseline of ~2.5. It cannot get worse either, because
the collapse is deterministic - the 3-bit path can only merge colours, never
split them, and merging cannot create a seam.

events.title: floppy: latch the motor on the /SEL edge, and index the sync-word scan
events.message:
floppy: latch the motor on the /SEL edge, and index the sync-word scan

Two fixes to the drive model, both found booting Ghostown's Spooky Town
under Kickstart 1.3.

The motor latch. Every Amiga drive, the internal DF0 included, feeds /MTR
into a latch clocked by its own /SEL falling edge: the motor state changes
only at the instant the drive becomes selected, and the level of the MTR
line while it stays selected is ignored. That is why trackdisk.device and
the trackloaders deselect, set MTR, then reselect. DF0 was modelled as
level-sensitive instead, so a loader that restores a stale PRB shadow with
MTR high while the drive remains selected stopped the motor it had just
started. Spooky Town's motor-on routine writes $F9 (deselect), $71 (select
DF0, MTR low -- the latching edge), then writes back its shadow $F1 (still
selected, MTR high) before polling CIA-A /RDY, and so dead-spun at $C704EC
on a white boot screen. Turn-on now takes MTR low on either side of the
select edge; turn-off needs it high on both, the rule WinUAE and vAmiga
derived from hardware. External units keep running their drive-ID shift
register off the same edges.

Also mirror the /TRK0 sensor onto DF0's /RDY while its motor is off: the
internal mechanism has no drive-ID circuit to answer with, which is what
the external units use those cycles for.

The sync-word scan. `TrackRev::bits_until_sync` walked up to a whole
revolution one cell at a time -- about 101k iterations for a standard
AmigaDOS track. `Emulator::idle_fast_forward_chunk` calls it through
`next_sync_irq_cck` on every idle slice while a trackloader sits in STOP
waiting on DSKSYNC, so the scan ran thousands of times per track and
dominated the profile during loading. Each revolution now builds a lazy
index of the offsets where a 16-bit window matches the sync word, and the
query is a binary search plus a wrap fold. The index is derived state:
rebuilt on demand after a save-state load, replaced when DSKSYNC changes.
Spooky Town's 5s..10s loading window drops from 11s of host time to 1s,
which is what its audio underruns were.

events.title: input: one stamp per key — the accelerator beep is a DOUBLE DELIVERY (#11)
events.message:
input: one stamp per key — the accelerator beep is a DOUBLE DELIVERY (#11)

Reported from the Mega STe: [P]lay / [L]oad / [B]egin each WORK but beep every
time, "don't recall it doing that before".

The chime is jt1080, fired by L2d3e Phase 5's `else` arm when no DLItem claims
the key. That arm is faithful — the Mac beeps at a key nothing wants. What is
not faithful is that the port hands Phase 5 the SAME keystroke twice: the first
read claims the accelerator and opens a modal, the second finds no item with
that letter in the modal that just opened, and chimes. The beep was the engine
telling the truth about a key the port delivered twice.

Traced end to end on a Mega STe, one physical press:

  plat_kb_poll  = 9836      one poll
  kb_to_event   = 9836      one event
  l6dd0 STAMP   = 9836      stamp #1 -> jt1133 reads 'l' -> CLAIMED, opens Load
  jt1125 STAMP  = 108       stamp #2, no new poll and no new event
                            -> jt1133 reads 'l' -> UNCLAIMED -> jt1080

That also settles the open question in plat_kb_poll's own #132 comment, which
set out the discriminator and left it unanswered: two polls for one press would
be IKBD repeat or the test injector, one poll and two engine reads is ours. It
is one poll and two reads. The repo has been blaming the harness injector.

Cause is the TaskList #84 stash. l725c pops an event, pushes a copy to
g_evfifo so jt1125's consumers still see what the pump ate, AND routes it to
l6dd0 — which for a key stamps the pending slot (-818/-820). jt1125 later pops
the stashed copy and its port bridge stamps the same key again.

On the Mac the two paths cannot collide: jt1125 reads a separate IRQ-filled
buffer while L725c reads the Toolbox queue, so exactly one stamp lands per key
and jt1125 does not stamp at all. The bridge is a port addition for the single
shared queue, where whichever path reaches the event first consumes it. It was
right to add; it just has to know when the other path already ran.

Fix: jt1125 stamps only for an event it fetched ITSELF, not one popped from the
stash. That restores the Mac's one-stamp-per-key invariant. The event is still
RETURNED either way, so l2d3e Phase 1's movement routing is untouched — that
path reads the returned event, not the pending slot, and a walk drive confirms
it (party 10,8 -> 12,8, innkeeper event fires, text renders).

Measured A/B, same fixture, keys P L B, Mega STe under Hatari:

  HEAD   1 beep — 'p' stamped by l6dd0 then again by jt1125, second read
         unclaimed. Which key doubles is a race and moves run to run ('l' in
         an earlier run), which is consistent with a machine whose timing
         favours it beeping every time.
  fixed  0 beeps, one stamp and one read per key, all three claimed.

Falcon: 0 beeps after, and it never showed the letter double before — only the
shared Return case — which is why this read as Mega-STe-specific.

An unclaimed Return in the Hall still chimes. That is the faithful arm, not
this bug: nothing there has a Return shortcut.

Adds FRUA_BEEPTRACE (every beep source plus each Phase-5 key with its claim
result) and harmonises the FRUA_KEYDIAG caps to 400 across boot.c, events.c and
input.c — they were 60, and this bug is only visible by correlating stamps
ACROSS those layers, which a per-layer cap mismatch silently breaks.

All four targets build; 483 tests pass.

Not yet confirmed on the reporting hardware.

launcher: a configuration can ask to run the moment it opens

[emulation] auto_launch, off by default and changing nothing while it
stays off. On, the launcher runs the configuration as soon as it opens
it -- a bare start with it saved as the default boots straight into the
machine with no configuration screen first, and Load... does the same
for the file it picks. A failed run leaves the launcher where it always
was, with the error on its status line.

The row is A/V & Emu -> Emulation -> Run on startup, directly under
Power on startup. Only the launcher reads the key: a machine given on
the command line was never going to see the screen this skips, so CLI
behaviour is untouched.

events.title: BUGS #12: the console opens mid-pass, and tranche B redraws over it
events.message:
BUGS #12: the console opens mid-pass, and tranche B redraws over it

Not the missing pool teardown the 2026-08-16 filing guessed. DoCharUnder
calls ConsoleEnter from below the main sprite draw and above the second
window's SprRestoreTr/SprDrawTr, so ConDraw paints the console and then
tranche B stamps the saved backgrounds and the droids back over it. The
modal arm that stops all sprite work is only reached next pass.

That also answers the open question in the entry: the bullets do not
keep updating behind the console. It is one pass's damage, left there.

ConMenuInit4 clears sprSplit -- three bytes, and the flag the tranche B
arm is gated on. SprSplitOK rewrites it on every pass that reaches the
draw, so nothing carries over.

Why the report named LASERS: the pool only splits when there is more
than one component of the overlap graph, and a droid standing next to
the player merges into the player's and goes to tranche A. A bullet
travels away from whatever fired it, so it is its own component and it
is what populates tranche B. Four scripted repro attempts with droids
beside the player all came out clean, which is consistent.

The visual repro was NOT reconstructed in the emulator and BUGS.md says
so plainly.

events.title: Console counts: the blank row, and the names' four-pixel left bearing
events.message:
Console counts: the blank row, and the names' four-pixel left bearing

The deck block moves down to row 10, which puts a blank row 9 between
the ship group and the deck group. I said that was impossible last
commit and it was not: only ICONS have to clear each other and only
TEXT LINES have to clear each other, so the alert icon at 13-15 sits
beside the deck's count at 12-13 quite happily. The ASSERTs are split
into an icon set and a text set so the rule is recorded rather than
re-derived wrongly.

The counts move one character right, to CON_COL_TEXT + 10. Measured in
the play buffer: at + 9 the digits and the names start on the same
character, but every capital in this font is inset four pixels -- an R
has no ink in the left unit of its first cell -- while a digit does
not, so the counts read four pixels left. Half a character would be
exact and pnCol cannot express it; a whole one is the nearest step and

events.title: Console counts: Alert to the top, aligned under the names, "1 droid"
events.message:
Console counts: Alert to the top, aligned under the names, "1 droid"

Four of KC's five follow-ups on the count lines.

The Alert LINE moves to the top beside entry 0's icon. Its own icon
could not come with it: the four icons are the menu's selection targets
and ConMenu4 walks conSel 0-3, so their rows have to ascend with conSel
or the marker jumps -- and conSel 0 is "leave", which the C64 puts
first. Three ASSERTs now hold that ordering. Entry 3 is the unlabelled
one now instead of entry 0.

The counts start at CON_COL_TEXT + 9, where the names begin: a label is
eight cells and ConTok's leading space is the ninth. That makes the
digits left-justified rather than blank-padded, so CnDigits4 drops the
leading zeros instead of blanking them.

The plural is a suffix CHARACTER in the shared block, 's' or a space,
not a flag: bank 6 prints it unconditionally because a branch is three
bytes it does not have. PnAscii maps a space to PN_SPACE and nothing
follows it on the line.

The fifth ask -- blank rows between the ship and deck groups -- is NOT
built and cannot be: entry 0's icon ends at row 4, the ship needs four
rows, so does the deck, and the alert icon then runs 13-15. Sixteen
exactly. DECISION 5 records the three ways to buy a gap and leaves the
choice to KC.

Bank 4 is down to 14 B and bank 6 to 7 B.

"1 droid" above "9 droids" with shipNumDroids poked to 1.

events.title: copperhf: M1 -- board, [copperhf] config, and synchronous register protocol
events.message:
copperhf: M1 -- board, [copperhf] config, and synchronous register protocol

First milestone of copperhf.device (COPPERHF-DEVICE-PLAN.md), Copperline's
emulator-only hardfile controller in the spirit of WinUAE's uaehf.device: a
Zorro II board whose doorbell takes a guest IOStdReq pointer and whose host
side executes the request directly against the shared HardDriveImage layer,
so RDB and RDB-less images behave identically to [ide]/[scsi]/[lide].

- [copperhf] unit0..unit6 config section reusing the shared drive-descriptor
  shape; CD image paths rejected (hard disks only)
- CopperhfBoard: doorbell/completion-queue protocol with idempotent
  COMPLETE_GET + explicit ACK (torn-read-safe on the 16-bit Z2 bus),
  INT2 gated on IRQ_ENABLE, sector-streamed CMD_READ/WRITE/UPDATE/CLEAR,
  TD_FORMAT/TD_MOTOR/TD_GETGEOMETRY; I/O is synchronous in M1 (async in M5)
- guest/copperhf/copperhf_board.h: shared register-map source of truth for
  the M2 boot ROM/device stub
- wired into build_machine behind cfg.copperhf.enabled(); save states ride
  the generic BoardDevice path

Redux (4): the high-score entry starts where you left off

GetInitial began every initial at 'A', so a third set of initials meant
walking the alphabet from A three more times. hsPrev remembers what was
typed and HsGet seeds from it.

It belongs in hstable.asm for that file's own reason -- PARTITL is
reloaded from disc every title, so hsSelFor is back to its assembled
value each time, while bank 7 is never reloaded after boot. Compression
does not enter into it: a bank is ordinary RAM once unpacked. The three
bytes ride plandata's ALIGN pad, so bank 7 still ends at &BFF9 and the
code image is untouched.

hsSelFor is remembered rather than the filed table entry, and before it
is filed, so the next entry starts from what was typed and not from
whichever end of the table it landed in.

screen, hsPrev read back 3/6/25, and the next game's HIGH-score screen
opened on D and seeded G -- through a reload of the overlay in between.

events.title: Redux (2): the deadlock does not reproduce, so it goes to the playtest log
events.message:
Redux (2): the deadlock does not reproduce, so it goes to the playtest log

A harness that stacks every droid on the player's own spawn, plus a
run-length counter on DrCollide's serviced pairs, over 60 s a deck.
The longest droid-droid contact was 35 passes on deck 0 and under 20
elsewhere; a stack of six disperses in seconds. Nothing saturated.

The mechanism is real all the same -- one pair a pass in a fixed order,
DrPause16 renewed on the higher slot, and drCollHit suppressing every
reversal until a pass finds no contact at all -- and the case the
harness cannot reach is the likely one: the player shepherding droids
into a dead end. So it is held open, not closed.

DECISION 3 records the mechanism, the harness recipe, the numbers and
the confound that made the first reading four times too high: a droid
leaning on the parked player wins the pair every pass. 12c now names
both this and DECISION 2 as things to watch for, with 1.4 s as the
baseline a jam has to beat to be news.

events.title: The briefing scroller parks the CRTC before it paints, so it stops hitching once a row
events.message:
The briefing scroller parks the CRTC before it paints, so it stops hitching once a row

KC saw it on real hardware and the rate was not the reason: sampled over
100 fields the scroll advances exactly 100 scanlines. What the display
gets is what the IRQ latches at fire 1, and across a row boundary that
read 7, 7, 1, 2 -- a field repeated and then two scanlines at once, six
times a second, with the average intact.

BrPaintRow is 35,850 cycles, measured against the User VIA's free-running
T1: ninety per cent of a field. br_scroll's SetCRTCStart came after it, so
on the one field in eight that paints a row the park missed the next
fire 1 entirely. Parking inside BrStep, as soon as line/scrollS/brTop are
complete and before the paint, puts it a few hundred cycles after fire 3
where it beats every latch; the paint still overruns into the next field
but invisibly, BrWaitField returning at once with fieldCount already
moved. No tearing: the row being painted is the staged brTop+15, below a
15-row window.

Verified at the same point in the travel -- iline now 3,4,5,6,7,0,1 with
pline tracking line on the wrap field where it used to lag -- and the
average re-checked over a second 100-field window.

The lesson is in the doc: position counters are not evidence about
smoothness, iline is.

events.title: CTRL+R on the briefing redefines the six controls, and the debug keys take CTRL
events.message:
CTRL+R on the briefing redefines the six controls, and the debug keys take CTRL

Z/X/K/M/L/SPACE become defaults in keyTab, and every one of the 36 places
that tested a control now goes through KeyDownIx and an index -- the same
two bytes the immediate was, which is what let the six sites in a code
image with six bytes left change at all. keyTab is those last six bytes:
no other main-RAM region is resident at all six moments a control is
tested, and PARTITL reads it directly because the font block that holds
KeyDownIx is not up at the first title of a cold boot.

The screen is bank 5, drawn through the briefing's own BrChar/BrCell, with
the panel left alone. ESCAPE abandons and restores; a key already taken
this run, or one the font cannot name, is refused; SHIFT and CTRL are
unreachable because the scan starts at &10, above the keyboard DIP links.
The chatter stops while it is up so the two beeps have voice 1 to
themselves -- the console menu step for a key taken, the collision bump
for one refused (the transfer's failure buzz was tried first: 2.5 s).

And with controls redefinable, R, C, W, [ and ] were a hazard -- bind LEFT
to R and every step repaints the viewport. All five want CTRL now, exiting
by the key-UP path so the press edge rearms. Moving the forced redraw's
test into bank 4 beside RedrawAll paid for it: the code image is back to
7 B free, bank 4 to 143.

Verified in jsbeeb, not by eye: the six rebound and read back, movement on
the new keys and nothing on Z, persistence across a game over and the
title, the high-score entry on PARTITL's direct path, chip writes counted
for the chatter and both beeps, and plain C against CTRL+C on the score.

events.title: engine: bound the event-tail hold by WORK, not wall-clock (#8)
events.message:
engine: bound the event-tail hold by WORK, not wall-clock (#8)

Reported from the Mega STe + ATW800/2: closing a picture event shows the pic
"unloading", draining out of the view square before the view redraws. The TODO
guessed this was a missing hold and proposed adding one. It is the opposite —
the hold has been there since #161 and has never once worked.

port_event_tail_expire bounded the hold at 30 ticks, reasoned as generous
against "a wipe and a repair inside one step render" and shipped with the note
that a slow machine exceeding it "simply gets the pre-#161 flash back".
Instrumenting the tail says every machine exceeds it, and not marginally:

  tail in        tick 14515
  tail out       tick 14549   jt23+jt935+jt937+jt938 = 34 ticks, 5 presents
  L63c0 release  tick 14569   90 presents swallowed

The honest window is 54-66 ticks over two events, nearly twice the bound, on a
Falcon030 in an emulator under fast-forward. So the expiry fired on every event
ever dispatched, and l63c0's release — the designed one, the one that discards
the intermediates and lands the tail as a single frame — never ran. On a fast
machine that costs a blink nobody noticed for a month. On a slow-present card
the expiry lands mid-tail and the rest of the teardown goes out one present at
a time, which is the reported drain.

Time cannot separate the two states this has to tell apart: "busy rebuilding
the frame" and "stuck, the engine has run on without me" both look like elapsed
ticks, and the legitimate case is already ~1s on the FASTEST target. That is
not a badly tuned constant, it is the wrong axis.

Presents swallowed is the right one, because it does not vary with machine
speed — the same code path issues the same presents at 7MHz and 50MHz, so one
cap holds on every target with no per-machine table. qd_hold_swallowed() counts
what the ref-counted hold ate (never the frame bracket, which has no engine
owner that can fail to release it); the honest window measures 71-92, so 512
clears the longest five-slot message several times over while a runaway, which
presents without bound because presenting is what it does, still trips it. The
wall-clock bound survives at 900 ticks as a last resort that is never expected
to fire.

Primary protection stays STRUCTURAL, which is what the two shipped freezes
taught: the walk-step gate in port_event_tail_hold, plus explicit drops
wherever the engine waits for the player. Added the one that defeated
enumeration twice — jt511's combat entry, the rider-and-ogres shape — so it is
caught there rather than hundreds of presents later by the net.

Measured A/B, same fixture, same key timing, HEIRS 13,8 tavern-brawl event:

  HEAD   444 bracket -> 9102 text -> 3895+3900 full -> 19759 step
         = 5 separate partial states presented
  fixed  3895+3900 = 2 presents, the two flip pages of ONE frame

At ~0.5s per present on the Nova card that is ~2.5s of visible teardown gone.

Also adds FRUA_SLOWPRESENT, the harness that made this reproducible at all.
Nothing we emulate is natively as slow as the ATW's VME writes, so bugs that
only appear at that cost cannot be found by running an emulator — the reason
this one needed a hardware report. -DFRUA_SLOWPRESENT=<ticks> burns that cost
per present and turns any machine into an ATW-class one for timing purposes;
at 30 it reproduces the drain on a Falcon. Diagnostic only, off by default.

Falcon/TT, ST/STE, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all build; 483 tests pass. Live
drive on the clean 020 build: the 13,8 picture event fires, pages, closes, and
the new view redraws with the command bar intact.

Not yet confirmed on the hardware that reported it — that is owed at the next
pass, along with the rest of 0.9.20.

events.title: La note de la page MIDI manquait : la police de TEXTE lui volait son codepoint
events.message:
La note de la page MIDI manquait : la police de TEXTE lui volait son codepoint

Rapport : « l'icône dans la fenêtre config du MIDI devrait être une note, elle
n'apparaît pas ». Elle était pourtant déclarée (ICON_FA_MUSIC, U+F001) ET
présente dans fonts/fa-solid-900.ttf — vérifié en lisant la table cmap.

CAUSE : collision de codepoints. fonts/DejaVuSans.ttf, notre police de TEXTE,
occupe une partie de la zone à usage privé — U+F000-F003 (ses ligatures
ff/fi/fl/ffi héritées) et U+F400+ — exactement là où vit Font Awesome. Or ImGui
parcourt ses sources DANS L'ORDRE et retient la PREMIÈRE qui sait fournir le
codepoint (ImFontBaked_BuildLoadGlyph, imgui_draw.cpp:4590-4610) : DejaVu,
chargée en premier, gagnait. La page MIDI rendait une ligature « fi » de 15 px
au lieu d'une note — indiscernable d'une icône absente.

Une SEULE des 35 macros est concernée (ICON_FA_MUSIC est la seule dont le
codepoint tombe dans le domaine PUA de DejaVu), ce qui explique que rien
d'autre ne manquait.

CORRECTIF : GlyphExcludeRanges = { 0xF000, 0xF8FF, 0 } sur la police de TEXTE.
Le champ existe pour exactement ce cas (« designed to exclude ranges from a
font source, when merging fonts with overlapping glyphs », imgui.h:3728) et
ImFontAtlasBuildAcceptCodepointForSource refuse alors ces codepoints à DejaVu,
si bien que la source Font Awesome est consultée. Sans effet collatéral :
aucune étiquette de l'interface n'utilise la PUA hors des macros d'icônes.

GARDE : tools/check_icon_glyphs.py (palier fast) ferme les DEUX façons de
perdre une icône en silence — codepoint absent de la police d'icônes, ou
revendiqué aussi par la police de texte sans GlyphExcludeRanges. Il lit les
tables cmap des deux .ttf et les macros de UiCommon.hpp. Vérifié qu'il ROUGIT :
exclusion retirée, il sort 1 en nommant ICON_FA_MUSIC (U+F001).

⚠ Non vérifié en image : la capture --shot du GUI ne contient que le
framebuffer ST, pas l'interface ImGui. Ce qui est prouvé tient au niveau des
polices et du chemin de sélection de glyphe d'ImGui, lu dans son code.

events.title: A42 : un CPU halté le DIT — et la réserve de No Cooper tombe à l'instruction près
events.message:
A42 : un CPU halté le DIT — et la réserve de No Cooper tombe à l'instruction près

Deux manques, et c'était le même : NeoST ne journalisait pas l'ADRESSE d'une
faute de bus. Faute de quoi (1) le GUI ne pouvait rien montrer d'un CPU halté,
et (2) la comparaison à l'oracle sur No Cooper s'arrêtait au « même mécanisme »,
sans pouvoir dire « même instruction ».

CŒUR — CpuState retient adresse, PC (getPC0), sens et validité de la dernière
faute de groupe 0 (équivalent des last_*_for_exception_3 d'Hatari,
newcpu.c:3086) ; Cpu68k::lastFault() les expose ; le message de halt les
affiche. Journal de la CHAÎNE complète en opt-in (NEOST_FAULT_TRACE, classé
« trace » dans tools/env_locks.json) : silencieux par défaut, parce que la
détection de machine du TOS fait fauter des dizaines d'accès par boot — Hatari
doit d'ailleurs les filtrer par liste blanche (M68000_IsVerboseBusError,
m68000.c:572-621), qu'on préfère ne pas maintenir.

LA RÉSERVE TOMBE. Sur No Cooper en Mega ST :
  NeoST  : reading at address $00FF820F, PC=$000056
  Hatari : Bus Error reading at address $ffff820f, PC=$58 op_e3=4228
Même adresse (NeoST masque en 24 bits, Hatari montre le miroir 32 bits), même
sens ; le PC ne diffère que par la convention de prefetch — la mémoire en $56
porte $4228 $FA0F = clr.b $FA0F(a0) (vérifié au --dump-at), donc NeoST nomme le
début de l'instruction et Hatari son mot d'extension, ce que son op_e3=4228 dit
lui-même.

ET LA CAUSE REMONTE AU CHIPSET : $FF820F est l'une des deux adresses que le
Ricoh du ST simple laisse « void » et que l'IMP du Mega ST fait FAUTER (Hatari
IoMem_FixVoidAccessForST/ForMegaST, ioMem.c:150-195 ; NeoST Bus.cpp:533-541,
déjà porté). Le verdict « FIDÈLE » n'est donc plus une observation, c'est une
chaîne complète.

INTERFACE (A42, soldé) — la fenêtre CPU affiche « CPU HALTED - double bus/
address error » avec l'adresse fautive et le vecteur, et un bandeau permanent
au-dessus de l'écran dit l'état, la faute et la seule sortie (reset). Affiché
aussi en borne : un visiteur devant un écran figé mérite de savoir que la
machine est morte, pas lente.

⚠ NON VÉRIFIÉ EN IMAGE : le bandeau lui-même. Le pousser jusqu'au halt demande
d'écrire dans le neost.cfg de l'utilisateur (le GUI lit sa config à côté de
l'exécutable, pas dans le cwd) — on ne touche pas à un fichier d'état vivant
pour faire une capture. Ce qui est prouvé : l'état halté est atteint et
correctement renseigné (headless), et les deux affichages sont gardés par ce
même cpu.halted(). Contrôlé au passage, le doute existant : le harnais
--run-frames du GUI ne réécrit PAS neost.cfg (md5 identique avant/après),
conformément à ce que promet A9a.

events.title: No Cooper « plante » en Mega ST : c'est un halt CPU, et Hatari halte pareil
events.message:
No Cooper « plante » en Mega ST : c'est un halt CPU, et Hatari halte pareil

Rapport GUI : « No Cooper plante après la page 1, puis la page 2 avec la
musique, puis Return Return ». La méthode a payé dans l'ordre où elle est
écrite — lire neost.cfg AVANT de soupçonner une régression : machine=megast.

Ce n'est pas une image fausse, c'est un HALT : dès que la démo prend la
touche qui fait avancer la partie, le 68000 part en double faute de bus
(exception vecteur 2) et la machine gèle, musique comprise. Le profil
machine seul est en cause, pas la ROM — matrice {megast, st} x {tos104fr,
etos192fr, tos102uk} : halt sur les trois megast, aucun sur les trois st,
où la démo déroule ses parties. Sans appui touche, megast tient 9 000
trames : c'est bien la transition déclenchée par la touche qui tue.

Oracle : Hatari en --machine megast, même ROM, même disquette, espace
injecté par --cmd-fifo, donne « Bus Error reading at address $ffff820f,
PC=$58 » puis « Detected double bus/address error => CPU halted! ». FIDÈLE
donc — No Cooper ne tourne pas sur un Mega ST, chez l'oracle comme chez
nous. Ce qui est apparié : le MÉCANISME et la dépendance à la
configuration, PAS l'instruction fautive (NeoST ne journalise pas l'adresse
et --until-pc 58 ne mord pas).

Le piège qui a failli produire un faux verdict est consigné : la démo
n'accepte l'espace qu'à partir de son écran « PRESS SPACE TO GO ON »
(~VBL 2800 sous tos104fr). La première injection, calée sur la trame 900 de
l'étalon, tombait pendant le chargement — Hatari restait sur son titre et
« ne plantait pas ». Conclure là aurait donné une divergence à l'envers.

Vérifié que le correctif A40 du même jour n'y est pour rien : le binaire
reconstruit depuis 4c38cc0 halte à l'identique, et le correctif n'écrit que
dans le tampon de pixels.

La note du 2026-08-01 de TEST_SOFTWARE.md (« No Cooper, Cuddly Demos,
Enchanted Land et Lethal Xcess "en panne" tournaient en machine=megast »)
passe de constat à mécanisme prouvé et confronté à l'oracle. Verdict dans
CASE_STUDIES.md avec la recette d'injection clavier.

A42 ouvre au TODO le manque d'ergonomie repéré au passage : le GUI ne dit
RIEN quand le CPU halte — le drapeau vit dans Cpu68k.cpp et aucun code de
src/gui/ ne le lit (grep = 0 occurrence). C'est ce qui transforme un
diagnostic d'une minute en rapport « ça plante ».

events.title: Pause is CTRL+P and mute is CTRL+Q, paid for out of four longhand pagings
events.message:
Pause is CTRL+P and mute is CTRL+Q, paid for out of four longhand pagings

KC asked for the modifier. It needs no machinery at all: keydown takes an
INKEY byte and EORs it into an internal key number, so CTRL is just
KEY_CTRL = &FE (INKEY -2, internal 1), and because keydown asks the
matrix about one key at a time a modifier is a second query with no
ghosting to design around.

CTRL gates the TRIGGERS ONLY. DoPause tests KEY_P four times -- the
trigger, two release waits and the held loop -- and only the trigger is
gated: you are already holding CTRL by the time you want out. KC: "unpause
with just P is fine." The mute has one site and it is a trigger, so
CTRL+Q throughout. At both sites CTRL-up branches to the SAME exit as
key-up, which is what keeps pausePrev and volQPrev honest -- a
half-pressed combo resets them exactly as letting go of the key does.

WHERE THE 14 BYTES CAME FROM, main RAM having had 6: none of
docs/ram-pass.md's reserves fit. sprsplit and SCANSTEP buy banks 5 and 6,
and door.asm is the only main-RAM one but is gated on freeing ~650 B of
bank 4 first. So it was paid for locally, from four sites writing
PAGEBANK out longhand where RAM pass 5 had already established the trade
of an 8-byte expansion for a 3-byte JSR: CbBulletFrame's two pagings
become JSR PgSpr / JSR PgData (-10 B), and sprite.asm's two effect-slot
pagings become a new PgSprSlot (-4 B) -- which needed a new helper
because those two set sprBank as well, which is exactly why neither
existing Pg* fitted and both had written the four stores out by hand.

Net zero: code_end was &2FFA before and is &2FFA after. Both are
transition or once-per-effect-slot code, so the 12 cycles a call cost
nothing.

Verified in jsbeeb by reading paused and sndVolume rather than by looking
at the screen: bare P held leaves paused 0, adding CTRL sets it, plain P
clears it; bare Q leaves sndVolume 15, adding CTRL drops it to 0, holding
the combo does not re-toggle, and CTRL+Q again restores 15.

docs/layer-11e-sound.md §12 carries it as DECISION 16 with the ledger,
§9 and §10 point at it, and the key lists in README and PLAN are updated.

events.title: A40 : le retrait gauche med recopiait le scroll d'Hatari sans son ancrage
events.message:
A40 : le retrait gauche med recopiait le scroll d'Hatari sans son ancrage

Closure sortait 4 px trop à gauche sur TOUTE l'image (oracle 64,08 %). Le
« couple de diagnostic » annoncé (Closure décalée / Cuddly bit-exacte) a
d'abord démoli sa propre prémisse : le masque PAR LIGNE des deux étalons,
relevé avec NEOST_RENDER_TRACE sur un --load-state d'UNE trame, dit que
cuddly_demos n'ouvre AUCUNE bordure sur l'image comparée (200 lignes
bm=000) — elle ne calibrait donc rien du chemin de retrait gauche. Le fait
décisif était le masque de Closure : LEFT_OFF_MED | RIGHT_OFF sur 274
lignes, le « remove left + med stab » qu'Hatari nomme d'après cette démo.

Cause établie par le calcul, puis mesurée. Hatari ne rend pas ces lignes au
faisceau : il RECOPIE la ligne dans un tampon de SCREENBYTES_LINE (208 o =
416 px) à partir de raster + 2 + VideoOffset (video.c:4014), PUIS décale
tout le tampon de STF_PixelScroll (video.c:4273). Son ancrage de recopie
est donc déjà 4 px à DROITE du faisceau. En repère buffer NeoST, les deux
rendus coïncident si et seulement si shEff = 4 + scrollFinal : le stab med
vaut -4, pas -8. Le -8 recopiait le scroll d'Hatari en oubliant l'ancrage.

Seconde maille : le décalage à gauche fait « entrer » par la droite des
pixels sans source, qu'Hatari laisse à l'index couleur 0 (video.c:4295).
En repère faisceau, ce sont les |scrollFinal| dernières COLONNES du buffer
— formulation qui vaut que les bordures soient rendues ou non.

Mesure, étalon closure contre l'oracle Hatari : 64,08 % -> 1,81 % (shEff)
-> 0,02 %, soit 27 px sur 114 816, TOUS sur la ligne 0, vérifié sur trois
trames voisines (27/43/27 px). Balayage de contrôle ±6 px x ±3 o autour de
l'optimum : aucun autre couple ne descend sous 53 %. Palier full vert,
aucun autre étalon ne bouge ; référence reposée et oracle Hatari commis à
côté (tests/reference/closure_oracle.png) pour re-mesurer sans relancer
Hatari.

Les 144 px d'overscan_top, eux, ne sont PAS un bug NeoST — dossier tranché
et fermé. Trace --trace video_border_h : Hatari détecte
« left+2 / right-2 60Hz 53<->373 », exactement le masque de NeoST. L'écart
est entièrement dans sa recopie, qui range les 2 octets « left+2 » dans les
2 derniers octets de la bordure gauche du tampon : or 2 octets en basse
résolution ne sont pas 4 pixels, c'est UN MOT DE PLAN sur 16 px. Prédiction
faite avant de regarder — tête = plans 0-2 à zéro + plan 3 à $FFFF = index
8, queue (memset right-2) = index 7 ; palette du run relevée à --dump-at
380 FF8240 32 : palette[8] = $333, palette[7] = $555, et l'oracle montre
bien 16 px de $333 en x=32..47 et 16 px de $555 en x=352..367. Le compte
tombe au pixel : 4 lignes bm=00a x 32 px + 1 ligne bm=002 x 16 px = 144.
NeoST rend le décalage physique de 4 px ; overscan_top reste donc
ref_kind: snapshot DÉFINITIVEMENT.

Non touché, faute d'exhibiteur mesuré : les cas de scroll « hardware »
13/9/5/1 et le -4 du left-off standard. La même algèbre les dit décalés de
4 px (resp. 8), mais le balayage des 10 500 trames de Closure montre que sh
n'y vaut jamais que 0 ou -4 et que LEFT_OFF n'y apparaît que combiné à
BLANK (lignes rendues à l'index 0). L'algèbre est écrite dans le code, pas
appliquée.

A40 sort du TODO ; A41 y entre pour les 27 px de la ligne 0 — couleur
voisine d'un cran, donc phase d'écriture palette en début de trame, pas de
la géométrie.

events.title: Show the roast, and stop hiding the graphics that have no colours of their own
events.message:
Show the roast, and stop hiding the graphics that have no colours of their own

Three colour fixes, all of them cases where a rule that was right for one kind
of thing was wrong for another.

$FF cells are drawn bright white on black rather than black. $FF means leave
this cell alone, so on a page with no room behind it there is no colour to
take; black made "not coloured here" look identical to "nothing there", and
lost four graphics outright -- the cave door frame, the wall shield and two
others whose every cell is $FF showed as empty rectangles. The partly
transparent ones read properly now too: the locked cave door has white
stonework, red bars and a yellow keyhole.

The health indicator is named and yellow. Following the life-force countdown's
"redraw the roast" to $8B8A leads to $C48D and $C543, which are graphics $B5
and $B4: the whole roast chicken and the carcass picked down to the bones, 48
by 30 each, counted down as the life force drains. Their attribute pointer is
the null table at $AEEA, and running the routine shows why -- it draws 78 bytes
of pixels and never touches the attribute file, because it draws into cells the
panel has already coloured. So their colour is in no table anywhere, and $46 is
set explicitly with a note saying it is what the game shows rather than
something derived.

And the food takes its commonest colour. Sprite colours came from INITIAL_STATE
only where every record for a code agreed, which is right for monsters -- placed
once each -- and wrong for the things there are many of. A food is red in one
room and yellow in another, so all eight fell through to white. Now the
commonest placement wins, ties to the lower attribute so the build stays
reproducible, and the page says that is what it is showing.

events.title: A40 : « permanent » était trop fort, et la nuance donne le levier
events.message:
A40 : « permanent » était trop fort, et la nuance donne le levier

Écrit ce matin sur la foi de Closure seule : « le décalage de la fenêtre gauche
est PERMANENT ». Vérifié depuis : 10 étalons sont à 0 px CONTRE L'ORACLE, dont
cuddly_demos et nocooper — deux démos qui ouvrent elles aussi les bordures, sur
la même machine ST et la même ROM. Le décalage de 4 px n'est donc pas universel,
et laisser « permanent » aurait fait croire que toute image NeoST est décalée.

La nuance n'affaiblit pas la trouvaille, elle l'outille : le décalage dépend de
ce que Closure fait et que Cuddly ne fait pas. Ce couple — même machine, même
ROM, l'un décalé de 4 px, l'autre bit-exact contre Hatari — est le levier de
diagnostic le plus serré qu'A40 ait eu. Le prochain pas devient « diffé ces deux
étalons » plutôt que « lire video.c à froid ».
