events.title: denise: even sprites read ESPRM, odd and attached pairs OSPRM
events.message:
denise: even sprites read ESPRM, odd and attached pairs OSPRM

Lisa selects a sprite's 16-entry palette bank from BPLCON4's low byte:
ESPRM (bits 7-4) for even sprites, OSPRM (bits 3-0) for odd sprites and
for attached pairs, which display through the odd channel. The decode had
the two unattached nibbles swapped, invisible at the reset value $11
(both nibbles equal) but wrong the moment a title programs them apart:
Nexus 7's Luxo lamp scene runs five unattached 64-px sprites under
BPLCON4=$59 with the even-sprite palette in bank 5 and the odd-sprite
entries in bank 9, so the swap sent sprite 4 (the lamp's base) to bank
9's unset entries and drew it in the background dark blue.

The attached path already used the low nibble and is unchanged; vAmiga's
Denise (esprm/osprm) models the same split.

events.title: Cost the copper-list framebuffer: the skeleton is static
events.message:
Cost the copper-list framebuffer: the skeleton is static

The obvious objection to a per-pixel copper list is that the CPU has to
regenerate a 34 KB copper program every frame. It does not. The builder at
hunk 0x9cde-0x9d90 has no direct callers; it is reached only by the
fall-through from the screen constructor at 0x9c3c, which runs at screen
open, and the per-row WAIT emitter is called from inside the builder only.
The register numbers, bank switches, WAITs and BPLCON4 writes are laid down
once per screen, and a frame changes two bytes out of every four: 16,200 B
for the 90x90 view, 7,920 B for the 66x60 one.

Nor is it an extra pass. There is no chunky buffer, so the rasteriser's
store is the copper-list write, against 23,287 B of chip-RAM traffic for a
chunky-buffer-plus-C2P route over the same 8,100 pixels, with no read-back
and no conversion.

What binds is copper DMA: 94 MOVEs and a WAIT is 191 slots against ~226 in
the two scanlines a row block covers, 85 %. That explains yscale=2 (at 1:1
there are ~113 slots for 191 slots of work), caps the row at ~108 pixels
before bitplane DMA rather than at the palette's 128, and makes FMODE=$000F
look like a bandwidth decision rather than a width one.

All of it is static arithmetic and is labelled as such; the measurement is
now open question 1b, together with the emulator experiment that would
settle it without a disassembler.

events.title: Document Gloom (Black Magic / Guildhall, 1995) for the Amiga CD32
events.message:
Document Gloom (Black Magic / Guildhall, 1995) for the Amiga CD32

Thirteen documents, thirteen tools, and eleven notes files covering a
772-sector data track: the smallest CD32 volume in this series.

The headline result is the Akiko question. Gloom is a real-time
texture-mapped renderer whose textures, sprites and HUD are all 8-bit
chunky, and it has zero references to $00B80038, $00B80000 or $C0DE0000
in the image, in all 131 extracted files and in all 115 decrunched ones.
The reason is new: its 3D view has no planar destination at all. The
framebuffer is a copper list with one MOVE per pixel over bitplanes that
hold a fixed colour-index ramp, with BPLCON4's BPLAM and the BPLCON3 bank
alternating every row so the copper can fill one half of AGA's 256
registers while the other half is on screen.

Also documented: CrunchMania (CrM2) as the fifth cruncher on the format,
with the decoder transcribed out of the loader and 115 of 115 files
decrunched on the first run; a /freeanim byte-identical to Liberation's;
a credits screen that names four development tools of which the disc
confirms three; and the floppy release's installer, boot script, save
file and disk prompts still on the CD.

Documentation only: no game asset, art, audio or executable code.

events.title: Add the CDXL cost comparison to the codec document
events.message:
Add the CDXL cost comparison to the codec document

Commodore's own streaming format is uncompressed, so the same 30,707 frames at
320x144 in 256 colours would be 1,349 MB and cap at 6.67 fps on a 2x drive,
against 460 MB and 19.57 measured. Even Prey CD32's real CDXL geometry comes to
590 MB for this much footage.

The reason is variance, not cleverness: 9.1 % of frames cost under 5,000 bytes
and the smallest is 364, while the worst costs 40,224 -- 87.3 % of raw, 1.15:1.
Both caveats stated: the frame rate is a ceiling, not a measurement, and whether
the codec is lossy was not determined.

tools/cdxlcost.py reproduces every figure from the measured frame sizes.

sentinel's bytes on BOTH sides — 0 of 270 artefacts differ, same rendered

level skip sets no form. Control: poke $21e4 := 1 before the skip and
both sides draw sprite 270 correctly (135/135 identical).

events.title: wonderboy: send IKBD $12 at boot — fire on iron needs the mouse off
events.message:
wonderboy: send IKBD $12 at boot — fire on iron needs the mouse off

Second iron result (probe disk, 4 MB STE, TOS 1.62, stick in port 1):
title loads, 35 IKBD bytes reach the handler, reset ack $f1 heard, and
the PRESS half of the fire wait times out ($d018) — no $FF packet with
bit 7 ever arrives. On a real ST the mouse's right button IS joystick
port 1's fire line: with the mouse enabled the 6301 reports joy-1 fire
as a mouse packet and strips bit 7 from the joystick packet (Hatari
models it: IKBD_DuplicateMouseFireButtons). The original's init_ikbd
sends exactly one IKBD command, $12 disable-mouse ($f8f0, sole caller
$e48c); this port sent none. Every smoke pass crossed the fire gates by
debugger poke, so the input path had never run anywhere.

Harness:
- wonderboy_main.c: ikbd_send(IKBD_DISABLE_MOUSE) once in install(),
  where $e48c sits; re-sent after each end-of-run reset's reply so the
  shim's own resets cannot re-enable the mouse mid-wait; stats field
  ikbd_mouse_disable_sent; STATS_MAGIC 'WBA6' (a pre-$12 record is
  refused by name).
- smoke.py: record row on every record-writing mode; trace row on every
  io_write-traced pass (ownplay 2 AND 4, floppy 1/2/3/5): before the
  first program-side pen write the IKBD traffic is exactly [$12], after

events.title: Corroborate the boot chain against Commodore's CD32 Developer Notes
events.message:
Corroborate the boot chain against Commodore's CD32 Developer Notes

The Amiga CD32 Developer Notes (Commodore, 19 May 1993) settle three things
this pass had measured but could only partly explain.

- freeanim.library: the open tells the CD32's boot animation to begin
  shutting down and returns immediately; the close waits for it. There is no
  function to call, which is why no disc ever calls one, and c/FreeAnim's 92
  bytes are the one-liner the notes print. The notes also advise skipping the
  NULL check so a title survives on a plain Amiga; this one checks anyway.
- The five modules Commodore added for the console are named, and the
  distribution rule explains the disc: lowlevel and nonvolatile shipped with
  Workbench 3.1 so a title carries them, freeanim never shipped with
  Workbench at all so it is ROM-only and cannot be on a disc.
- The .TM block is required to boot and belongs "right after the PVD
  sectors", so LBA 21 is a consequence of the layout rather than a constant.

And it explains a leftover: the model startup-sequence in the notes opens
with C:SetPatch QUIET, and this disc follows that template's explicit-c:
convention while dropping the SetPatch line and keeping the binary. It also
describes the separate loader program that speris-logos turns out to be.

Document the Amiga CD32 release of The Speris Legacy

Full structural documentation of the 1996 Binary Emotions / Team 17 disc,
plus the tools to reproduce every claim from a disc image.

The disc opens completely. 35 of its 47 files are Imploder (IMP!) streams,
and the decruncher is 350 bytes of 68000 inside the game's own executable at
hunk offset 0x1E87C; transcribed register-for-register it decrunches all 35

object frames, twelve ProTracker modules and the whole script come apart.

Three findings reach past the title:

- The .TM block holds 22,152 bytes of cdtv.device 35.2, byte-identical to

  driver corrects the platform notes' claim that the block's contents are
  determined by the console.

  printed tables are regenerated from a six-coefficient polynomial found in
  the front-end overlay, and verified against scans of the card.
- The four-floppy release survives intact inside the CD32 build, confirmed
  independently by the loader's paths and by the build timestamps.

Also: genuine 24-bit AGA palettes, a crash debugger in the retail master, a
BGFX chunk tag corrupted to "BG\0e" that shipped and works, every level
named "Egyptian World / Tuten Carmens Tomb", and a musician's message left

events.message:
agnus: compare the DIW forced reset against the fixed standard line

Review follow-up: the reset compared against the current field's last
line, which does not match the cited vAmiga model. vAmiga's
Sequencer::eolHandler tests the fixed line 312 (PAL) / 262 (NTSC) and
deliberately commented out its inLastRasterline() variant, so an
interlaced short field ends at 311 without force-resetting the flop; the
progressive-PAL probe cannot separate the two models, and the field-
derived line also let ECS programmable totals move the reset
arbitrarily.

The comparator now uses the fixed standard line on the hardwired beam
schedule, matching vAmiga where it is the validated reference: a short
field's unreachable-stop window carries across that field's wrap and is
cleared by the following long field's line 312 (new unit test). VARBEAMEN
bypasses the hardwired sync decode and its programmable frame may end
before line 312 or run past it mid-frame -- the dblpal-hires-lace golden
regressed under the literal fixed line, its lower half force-closed
mid-frame -- so programmable totals keep the frame-derived reset. Both
corners are documented as lacking direct hardware evidence.

events.title: timing-test: add vdiwprobe-flop, dpfprobe-aga and hamprobe-ham8 goldens
events.message:
timing-test: add vdiwprobe-flop, dpfprobe-aga and hamprobe-ham8 goldens

Three probes for previously render-untested behaviour, all
vAmiga-verified:

- vdiwprobe-flop (OCS): the vertical display window set/reset flop. A
  DIWSTOP rewrite behind a closed flop must not re-open the window, a
  set/reset tie resets, and an unreachable DIWSTOP holds the window open
  only to the frame's last raster line (the Kang Fu CD32 screen-split
  class). Byte-for-byte against vAmiga; its first render caught the
  carried-across-vblank bug the previous commit fixes.

- dpfprobe-aga: Lisa's eight-plane dual playfield. Planes 7/8 extend
  each field's colour index to four bits (the Zool AGA decode class,
  with magenta/green tell colours for a 3-bit decode), PF2 reads the
  banked palette through BPLCON3 PF2OF code 6 (entry 73), and sprite
  priority runs the sprprobe-dpfpri band table on AGA with in-range
  codes only (Lisa's out-of-range colour behaviour deliberately
  diverges from vAmiga). Exact against vAmiga 5's A1200_2MB setup.

- hamprobe-ham8: HAM8's control bits are the two LOWEST planes and a
  modify holds a component's low two bits from the previous pixel. A
  set-op sweep through both palette banks, R/G/B modify ramps, a
  history weave no per-index cache can render (the PR #563 regression
  class), and a LOCT-seeded low-bit-hold band. Byte-exact against
  vAmiga 5 under the identity RGB monitor palette (VAMIGA_RGB=1).

The suite is 39 probes; README carries the new prose entries, the AGA
cross-check table rows and the VAMIGA_RGB documentation.

events.title: tools: add the VAMIGA_RGB identity-palette option to vamiga-ref.sh
events.message:
tools: add the VAMIGA_RGB identity-palette option to vamiga-ref.sh

vAmiga 5 can replace its YUV monitor model with an identity RGB palette
(RetroShell: monitor set PALETTE RGB), making the dumped framebuffer raw
bytes. VAMIGA_RGB=1 selects it, so a Copperline capture compares
byte-exactly instead of through the transform-invariant bijection -- the
sharper check where available, and the only workable one for probes with
more distinct colours than the bijection comparer accepts (the HAM8
probe's ramps). Documented in timing-test/README.md with the probes that
use it.

events.title: agnus: reset the vertical display flop at the frame's last raster line
events.message:
agnus: reset the vertical display flop at the frame's last raster line

The vertical DIW flop was carried across the frame wrap, so a window
whose DIWSTOP line the beam never reaches (a VSTOP below 128 addresses
lines 256-383) stayed open through the vertical blank and lit the top of
the next frame down to the first reachable stop. The carry was asserted
in the flop's original commit but never exercised: building the
vdiwprobe-flop golden render caught it, diverging from vAmiga over the
whole top of the frame.

vAmiga forces its vertical flipflop off at line 312 PAL / 262 NTSC
(Sequencer::eolHandler), and the bottom-border trick on real hardware
ends with the frame. The line-start comparator now treats the frame's
last raster line as a forced reset, winning over a DIWSTRT match on that
line the same way a DIWSTOP tie does; the frame wrap's line-zero
evaluation is unchanged. An unreachable-stop window therefore runs into
the bottom border and ends with its own frame, and the next frame's top
starts closed until DIWSTRT matches again.

events.title: Add the 1992 CDTV release as a control disc, and correct two claims it falsified
events.message:
Add the 1992 CDTV release as a control disc, and correct two claims it falsified

The CDTV release of the same game turned up, and running the same tools over
it did what a control is supposed to do.

New: docs/09-cdtv-1992.md and notes/cdtv-vs-cd32.md (all 1,514 paths across
the two releases, matched, sized and hashed). 1,201 files are byte-identical
across the fourteen months between the two masters.

Corrections, marked in place:

- docs/03-filesystem.md: the 1,213 files stamped 1992-09-03 are NOT a dead
  clock battery. The CDTV master was cut 1992-09-02 15:00:53-15:05:26 and
  1,201 of those files are byte-identical to it. Real dates, inherited from
  the earlier build.
- docs/07-graphics.md: the palette test tested only for nibble-doubling
  (v*17). The CDTV disc writes 4-bit values as v<<4 throughout, so the old
  test scored all six of its 5-plane ECS palettes as 24-bit colour. Recomputed
  with both conventions: 6 of 14 CD32 screens exceed 12 bits, not 9 of 13.
  tools/ilbm.py fixed.
- docs/02-trademark-block.md: the .TM block is a shared mechanism with a
  per-console payload. The CDTV one is 22,152 bytes of cdtv.device 35.2 by
  Carl Sassenrath, with no trademark banner anywhere on the disc, so the exec
  fragment is a CD32-era accident rather than a 1991 one. "The sector after
  the L path table" is not a rule either. tools/tmsector.py now finds the 'TM'
  tag and honours the declared length.

Confirmations the control gave for free: the 113 CD32 files at the AmigaDOS
1978 epoch in SCRIPT01 are exactly the 113 that differ from the CDTV disc;
the three later 8SVX files are CD32-era additions; scene S0000 was dropped;
the artwork was deepened from 5 planes to 8 rather than redrawn; and the CDTV
boot script runs c/rmtm, "remove TM", which is the first independent support
for the freeanim.library reading.

events.title: A modal screen ends a disruptor burst again
events.message:
A modal screen ends a disruptor burst again

KC: fire the disruptor, step onto a lift or a console within the next
three passes, and the screen stays white for the whole of that page.

layer-7 DECISION 10 says "a modal screen ends the burst", and CbDisruptor
implements it — conActive / xferActive / liftMode at cbd_run, then
disruptorCnt = 0 and disrFlash = 0. That code has been unreachable since
DoScore and CbDisruptor moved out of the raster window to ml_afterdraw:
ml_afterdraw sits BELOW the modal arms and every one of them JMPs to
ml_passend over the top of it. So the burst was frozen, not ended, and
disrFlash is an OVERRIDE — SetPalPlay re-applies it after the palette
table on every fire 1 — so it kept forcing logical 0 white on top of a
palette that knew nothing about it. Which is the failure DECISION 10 was
written to avoid; it just arrived by a different route than the
saved-palette one that decision rejected.

ml_modalend is three instructions the eight modal JMPs now target: the
two stores cbd_end does, at the point that is actually reached, then on
to ml_passend. Nine bytes, nothing added to the ordinary pass.
CbDisruptor's own arm stays: it is the original's shape ($1435 past the
console test at $1427) and it comes back to life the day the modal arms
converge on ml_afterdraw, which is the separate DoScore question I
raised and have NOT acted on.

Measured in jsbeeb, and the two cases are what distinguish the fix from
the burst's own countdown — a longer run would not have:
  one pass of ordinary play   disruptorCnt 3 -> 2, disrFlash still 1
  one pass with liftMode = 2  disruptorCnt 3 -> 0, disrFlash cleared
The game-over seam was re-run clean afterwards — ESCAPE, wash, 999 page,
title, high-score entry — because its arm is one of the eight.

events.title: Prey: An Alien Encounter (CD32, 1993) — full disc documentation
events.message:
Prey: An Alien Encounter (CD32, 1993) — full disc documentation

Structural and archaeological notes on the Almathera/KirkMoreno CD32 master:
volume descriptors, file system, boot chain, both executables, the 1,225-file
streamed soundtrack, the frame and ILBM formats, the CDXL intro, and the
leftovers.

Three findings that go back to the platform checklist:

- The Commodore trademark block is NOT always at sector 21. Prey's is at LBA
  6021 and the PVD's application-use area says so; the constant this checklist
  read as the path-table LBA is fixed at 20 regardless.
- /CD32.TM is an ordinary file in the root, dated 1993-06-10, byte-identical
  to the trademark sector. Commodore distributed the block to developers as a
  file, and that file already contained the 876-byte `exec` object fragment.
- Grepping for the custom-chip base $00DFF000 misses a program that addresses
  every register absolutely: DoPrey has zero base loads and 448 $00DFF0xx
  register writes.

Plus: the first disc here that genuinely uses AGA (8 planes, 24-bit palettes),
an hour of 19.7 kHz PCM streamed as 1,225 identical 60 KB files with no Red
Book track at all, and a master cut eleven minutes after the last file was
written.

Documentation only — no assets, no code from the disc. tools/ reproduces
every figure from your own copy.

Testing the nine tile palettes against EHB -- the only route to 64 colours on

interval and the claim that it was unique: five of nine palettes predate

Four sprite bars, one per pair, cross a dual playfield whose 4-px

Copper steps BPLCON2 through seven priority-code bands: the Chuck
Rock 2 programming ($0020), its mirror ($0004, a circular case), both
fields in front ($0000), all sprites in front ($0024), equal mid-chain
codes ($0012), split codes ($000B), and PF2PRI ($0060). Each band
renders the sprite-visibility truth table as comb patterns, with the
both-opaque column following the winning field's code.

events.title: denise: test sprite priority against the winning playfield's code
events.message:
denise: test sprite priority against the winning playfield's code

In dual playfield mode a pixel where both playfields are opaque carried
the combined presence mask into sprite_has_priority, whose else branch
read the PF2 priority code alone, so a sprite could beat an opaque PF1
wherever PF2 was also opaque behind it (BPLCON2 $0020: PF1 in front of
all sprites, sprites in front of PF2).

Denise resolves the two playfields against each other first (opacity,
then PF2PRI where both are opaque) and holds only the winning field's
BPLCON2 code in the sprite depth comparison; the losing field's code is
ignored. This is observable in the circular programmings where PF2PRI
and the sprite codes disagree about the field order (BPLCON2 $0004 at a
both-opaque pixel: PF1 beats PF2, PF2 beats the sprites, the sprites
beat PF1 -- the winner is PF1 and its code 4 shows the sprite), and it
matches vAmiga's one-depth-value-per-pixel z-buffer byte for byte on
the new sprprobe-dpfpri render.

Regression example: Chuck Rock 2 (Core) draws its player as attached
sprites over a 6-plane dual playfield with BPLCON2 $0020; PF1
foreground bins must hide the player while the player covers the PF2
backdrop. The player was drawn in front of the bins.

events.title: copper: fire the COPJMP strobe on reads of the strobe address
events.message:
copper: fire the COPJMP strobe on reads of the strobe address

The COPJMP1/COPJMP2 strobes decode the register address alone: on real
hardware a CPU READ of $DFF088/$DFF08A reloads the Copper program
counter from COP1LC/COP2LC exactly as a write does (reading a write-only
register performs a bus write of the floating data-bus residue into it,
the UAE/vAmiga model). Copperline treated such reads as pure open bus,
so a vertical-blank handler that flips a double-buffered display with
MOVE.L to COP1LC plus TST.W COPJMP1 got its list swap one frame late,
and the redraw of the newly hidden buffer flashed in the still-displayed
one (regression example: the Sleepwalker CD32 logo and intro animations,
whose every third frame stepped forward and back instead of holding).

Route reads of $088/$08A through the same strobe as writes (the read
still returns the undriven bus residue), add a bus regression test, and
pin the behaviour with a golden probe (timing-test/copprobe-jmpread):
each frame rewrites COP1LC and strobes with TST.W, so the stripe renders
from the flipped list (green) rather than the vblank-restart list (red).
vAmiga-verified via tools/vamiga-ref.sh.

tools: add the AGA comparer the cross-check table was measured with

The vAmiga 5.0b1 figures in timing-test/README.md were not reproducible from

and compares them component by component, which counts vAmiga's YUV

implemented the colour-correspondence metric the table actually used.

candidate alignment over the whole overlap (no subsampling - a probe's

golden.

under timing-test/. The sequence in the README now runs verbatim.

events.title: agnus: judge a DDFSTRT rewrite at its comparator commit clock
events.message:
agnus: judge a DDFSTRT rewrite at its comparator commit clock

A DDFSTRT write reaches the comparators four colour clocks after its write
slot, which the DDF sequencer already models (vAmiga's DMA_CYCLES(4) poke
delay). The wide-FMODE miss test evaluated both the outgoing and the incoming
value at the write slot instead, so it misclassified writes inside that
window in both directions: a write shortly before the outgoing value's match
killed a line that the outgoing comparator still starts, and an incoming
match position between the write slot and its effect clock was treated as
still ahead of the beam when it can no longer fire.

Both decisions now use the effect clock with the sequencer's DDFSTRT edge
semantics - the outgoing value fires strictly before it, the incoming value
strictly after it - and the delay is a shared DDF_WRITE_COMMIT_CCK constant so
the two fetch models cannot drift apart.

The Microcosm case is unaffected: its write lands at hpos ~$1E, so the effect
clock is $22, still short of the outgoing $2C and long past the incoming $18.

Records a TODO for the residual: when the outgoing value does fire, the run
belongs to it for the rest of the line, but the wide-FMODE value-window path
has no run state and keeps deriving the fetch grid from the live DDFSTRT.
Modelling that needs the FMODE=0 path's latched start.

events.title: agnus: drop the line when DDFSTRT moves behind the beam
events.message:
agnus: drop the line when DDFSTRT moves behind the beam

Agnus starts a line's bitplane fetch from a horizontal comparator: the DDF
flop sets on the single colour clock where the counter equals DDFSTRT. A
DDFSTRT write that moves the match position to the current colour clock or
behind the beam, before the position it replaces has fired, therefore leaves
the flop unset for the rest of the line - the counter never returns to that
value before the horizontal wrap - so the line fetches nothing and no
bitplane pointer advances. A write landing after the flop has set cannot
un-start the run; only DDFSTOP ends it.

The wide-FMODE (quantum > 1) value-window fetch path had no start-comparator
gate and restarted mid-unit from the moved DDFSTRT, so only the planes whose
lo-res slot number survived the truncated unit fetched that line. With the
lo-res slot order 8,4,6,2,7,3,5,1 those are BPL5 and BPL1 (slots 6 and 7),
which then ran one wide-fetch word ahead of the other planes for the rest of
the display.

Microcosm (CD32) is the regression example: its copper repoints seven
bitplanes and drops DDFSTRT $2C -> $18 in one burst that overruns the line,
committing the new value at hpos ~$1E on the status panel's first line. The
resulting 8-byte split between the two pointer groups speckled the whole
panel with colours from the wrong palette entries. All seven pointers now
advance in lockstep and the panel's first line renders as background, as the
hardware leaves it.

FMODE=0 is unaffected: ddf_seq_active() routes it to the DDF sequencer flop
model, which already tracks the comparator directly.

Adds the ddfprobe-ddfmiss golden probe (AGA lo-res BPL64): a blank middle
band where DDFSTRT is moved behind the beam, and a lower band where it is
rewritten after the match fired, which must match the control band. Derived
from the comparator model and confirmed on the game; an FS-UAE or real-A1200
capture is still wanted to pin the band edges independently, since vAmiga
cannot arbitrate AGA.

events.title: The score climbs inside the transfer game, as FinishTransfer1/2 do
events.message:
The score climbs inside the transfer game, as FinishTransfer1/2 do

KC: the win should count up on the board, not when the deck comes back.
Getting it there meant splitting XferExit4 into the two halves the
original has and never should have lost.

$22FE calls FinishTransfer1 ($21CF) the moment doSubGame returns — the
score, the type, the energy, the new droid's stats — and it then calls
FinishTransfer2 ($2260), whose 40-iteration sweep runs DelayScore. And
DelayScore ends in DoScore ($0B68). So the C64 banks the points at the
VERDICT and drains them over the hold that follows, in view, before the
board is gone. The port fused the two and ran both when the hold expired,
by which time the screen was the deck again.

  xpl_endphase (bank 7) sets xfmDecided, a main-RAM flag beside xfmDone.
  A flag and not a call: the work is bank 4's and bank 7 cannot page
  bank 4 in from under itself. XferTick reads it on the way out of
  XfTick with the data bank already back and calls XferExit4a;
  XferExit4b still runs on xfmDone. Bank 4 came out 5 bytes SMALLER,
  45 -> 50 free, because the two JMP xx4_consume became JMP XferInitDroid.

The transfer arm calls DoScore for itself, and then PanelScore — a new
bank-6 shim that is PanelUpdate's score half alone. DoScore has to be
called there because THE FOUR MODAL ARMS JMP ml_passend, which is BELOW
ml_afterdraw, so not one of them reaches it. The header at ml_afterdraw
claimed the opposite — "the one point EVERY arm of the pass converges
on, the four modal ones included" — and is corrected. The score field is
not the subgame's to own: cols 30-37 stand through it exactly as they do
on the deck, and on the C64 it is DoScore's own digit draw at $0AD9 that
repaints them.

Verified in jsbeeb, a win against a 296: 16 on the panel twenty frames
after "Complete", 26 twenty frames later — one point a pass, DoScore's
own rate — and the deck came back at the full 50, awarded once.

Left open, and flagged in both the code and layer-10: the console, the
information screens, the lift view and the game-over wash still skip
DoScore. Turning them on means turning CbDisruptor on with them, which
wants play-testing rather than a one-line change.

events.title: XF_RPT_RATE 0: a held key walks at the original's own rate
events.message:
XF_RPT_RATE 0: a held key walks at the original's own rate

KC's call. xfer_DoMove is level-triggered — one row per iteration — so
RATE 0 is 18 rows/s at doSubGame's 55.5 ms, which is what the C64 does.
That leaves the filter doing the one thing a keyboard needs and a stick
does not: a hold-off after a fresh press, since a tap has no
self-centring spring to end it. XF_RPT_DELAY stays 2, so a tap under
167 ms is still exactly one row.

The 12.5 rows/s of DECISION 13's tuning was a figure for a 40 ms
iteration that no longer exists; XF_PLY_STEP did most of that job by
itself. The stale "25 rows/s" and "240 ms" in XfGetMove's header are
corrected with it, and xfRptCtr counts ITERATIONS now, not passes — they
were the same thing until yesterday.

events.title: disasm: decode 68020+ full-format extension words
events.message:
disasm: decode 68020+ full-format extension words

The debugger disassembler treated every indexed extension word as the
brief format, so 68020 code using base displacements or memory
indirection decoded as garbage: the extra words were consumed as
separate instructions, rendering things like MOVE.W ([$25DE,A4],$C),D0
as a bogus 'MOVE.L (A6)+,($C,PC)'. The CPU core executes these modes
correctly; only the disassembly (CCP disasm, DBG_TRACE, the debugger
window) lied about them.

When bit 8 of the extension word is set and the CPU is a 68020 or
later, parse the full format: base/index suppression, word and long
base displacements, and pre/post-indexed memory indirection with word
and long outer displacements, reading the extra words in the same
order as the core's EA calculation. The 68000 and 68010 ignore bit 8
in hardware, so they keep the brief-format decode.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: control: honor at_seconds on input.joy, input.mouse and input.analogue
events.message:
control: honor at_seconds on input.joy, input.mouse and input.analogue

The control protocol documents at_seconds scheduling for every input.*
method, but only input.key implemented it: the other three parsed the
buttons and applied the state at submission time, silently ignoring the
parameter. A press/release pair scheduled while the machine was paused
therefore applied both transitions back to back and cancelled itself
out before the timeline ever advanced.

Thread at_seconds through InputCmd::Joy/Mouse/Analogue into the shared
expand() path (which input.key already uses for tap releases), and
factor the finite-number validation into one parse_at_seconds helper.
Scheduled entries keep the existing semantics: they belong to the
machine, survive client disconnects, and fire when the timeline passes
their timestamp.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: picasso2: derive the BLT source end from the source the mode reads
events.message:
picasso2: derive the BLT source end from the source the mode reads

Only a plain copy consumes the source in step with the destination.
Video-source colour expansion reads one byte per eight pixels and ignores
the source pitch, and pattern and system-source blits do not walk VRAM at
all, so all three left GR2C-GR2E too far ahead.

Wrap the counters within the 21 bits the registers hold rather than
clamping at zero, and log the addresses a blit starts from, which the
writeback had turned into end addresses for immediate blits while
deferred system-source blits still logged the start.

events.title: The transfer game runs at doSubGame's iteration rate, and src/data is tracked
events.message:
The transfer game runs at doSubGame's iteration rate, and src/data is tracked

KC: the ~11 s he wall-timed on the C64 was the PLAY countdown, not the
colour select. That changes the diagnosis. The play counter is driven by
the ITERATION — $20DA ticks every other one — so 99 ticks in 11.0 s is
111 ms a tick and 55.5 ms, 2.78 PAL frames, an iteration. The port ran
one a pass, 40 ms, so the whole subgame was 39% fast: the pulsers, the
CPU opponent, the cursor and the grace period as much as the clock.

This supersedes layer-10 DECISION 13's estimate, which is the one claim
in that write-up that was not measured and which flagged itself as such.
It argued from the listing that a half-turn costs ~21,000 cycles, exceeds
one PAL frame and so takes its own — 2 frames an iteration, the same
25 Hz the port runs at. It was low: a half-turn misses its irqToggle edge
often enough to average 1.39 frames. KC's stopwatch is the authority and
XF_PLY_STEP comes from it, not from a cycle count.

XfTick throttles the WHOLE iteration, not the counter. Slowing $20DA
alone would have made the clock read right while the game stayed frantic
— and it would have left the grace period wrong: xfGrace is 85
iterations, 3.4 s at 40 ms and 4.73 s at 55.65, against the C64's own
85 x 55.5 = 4.72 s. That the grace comes right for free is the check that
the iteration was the thing that was wrong. XfPlayTick's INC xfFrame and
$20DA's AND #1 are untouched: verbatim, and now on the right clock.

  XF_PLY_STEP = 184, one accumulator per pass, iterate on the carry:
  256/184 = 1.391 passes = 55.65 ms, counter 111.3 ms, the 99 at 11.02 s.
  Measured in jsbeeb: 93 -> 48 over exactly 250 frames.

The repeat filter is counted in ITERATIONS, which only mattered once an
iteration stopped being a pass. XF_RPT_DELAY 3 -> 2 holds the 160 ms
guarantee KC chose (3 x 55.65 = 167 ms; leaving it at 3 would have
drifted to 223 ms, which he had already rejected as too long).
XF_RPT_RATE is left alone and its held rate went 12.5 -> 9 rows/s, which
is slower than he tuned and nearer it than the 18 that RATE 0 would give.
Worth re-playing.

The colour-select fix from the last commit stands on its own evidence:
SubGameSelectSide's _14 loop has no irqToggle gate at all and is paced by
DelayScore(80). Both countdowns now tick at 111 ms by different routes,
which is the check that neither constant is invented.

AND src/data/ IS TRACKED (KC). It was ignored as converted game artwork.
Committing it means the tree assembles without a local paradroid_ce.lst
and an exporter change shows up as a diff. briefing.txt was always the
exception and stays one in the other direction: it is the hand-editable
SOURCE of the briefing text and export_briefing.py refuses to overwrite
it without --force. CLAUDE.md and the five docs that said "gitignored"
are updated.

events.title: Five from KC: the ?, the deck number, "Captured", the select clock, the (C)
events.message:
Five from KC: the ?, the deck number, "Captured", the select clock, the (C)

THE QUESTION MARK IS REAL. Color_txt ($E6DB) reads C-o-l-o-u-r-?-space
then the countdown, and $24 is a question mark in the C64's own text font
— export_font.py's set just stopped at '!'. It is glyph 103 now: one line
in the exporter's GLYPHS list, 16 bytes of PARAFNT, a fifth compare in
PnAscii, FONT_GLYPHS 103 -> 104. The panel reads "Colour? NN", which is
what the original says. Nothing in the transfer strings is a stand-in.

  make_briefing.py's PN_GLYPHS went 103 -> 104 with it, and that one is
  load bearing in a way that does not fail the build: the briefing's
  extra glyphs are numbered FROM it, so a stale value aliases the first
  extra onto a real glyph and the page silently draws the wrong
  character. Noted in layer-9-hud.md beside the index.

THE LIFT'S DECK NUMBER IS GONE. DrawSideview writes the view and leaves
the C64's status rows alone, so the two digits at the field's last pair
were this port's own addition. LvNumText is deleted and LvTick7 no longer
repaints it on every step of the light. "Lift" stays, five cells of the
eleven.

"CAPTURED" MOVED TO WHERE $22A0 PUTS IT. $229D SaveVicState, $22A0
DrawString Captured_txt, $22A7 ShowXferInfo — in that order, so the word
is on the status line for the whole of both information screens and stays
until $E1F2's Color_txt replaces it. XfStart drew it AFTER those screens
and XF_PH_RELEASE ends on the first pass with the button already up, so
it was up for 40 ms and KC had never seen it. IsStart posts it now, on
IS_SCR_XFER1 only. XfStart's XfTextClear went with it: the C64 blanks
nothing in between either.

THE SELECT COUNTDOWN RUNS AT THE ORIGINAL'S RATE. KC wall-timed the C64
at ~11 s for the 99 and the port at ~8 s. This is the one real timing
deviation layer-10 DECISION 13 found and left as KC's call. The PLAY
counter is untouched and still verbatim — doSubGame gates each half-turn
on irqToggle, $20DA's `xfFrame AND 1` is one tick per two frames, and one
iteration a pass reproduces it. SubGameSelectSide's _14 loop has no such
gate: DelayScore(80) is ~103,000 cycles, ~111 ms with badline steal, and
99 of those is 11.0 s against the port's 7.92.

  A FRACTIONAL ACCUMULATOR, not the mod-3 the document suggested: 111 ms
  is 2.78 passes, not 3, and a mod-3 would overshoot to 11.88 s.
  XF_SEL_STEP = 92 added to xfSelAcc, tick on the carry — 256/92 = 2.783
  passes = 111.1 ms, 99 of them 11.00 s. Measured in jsbeeb: 93 -> 48
  over exactly 250 frames.

THE COPYRIGHT SIGN WAS MIS-DECODED, NOT MISSING. The briefing's first
page read "w Graftgold Ltd. 1986."; the C64 byte is $20 and $20 is a (C),
a circle with a C in it. ToUpper's arithmetic would put lowercase w at
$20 — w is at $54 instead and the vacated slot holds the symbol —
so export_briefing.py's plain $0A-$23 range check decoded it as 'w'.
That tool already special-cases $16/$42/$54 for exactly this reason and
had no case for $20. It is a fourth briefing extra glyph now, written '@'
in briefing.txt because that file is ASCII.

Verified in jsbeeb: "Captured" through both information pages, "Colour?
93" on the board, the countdown at 111 ms a tick, "© Graftgold Ltd.
1986." on briefing page 1. The lift screen was not reached in-game — the
change is confirmed from the build listing instead: LvStart7 emits five
XfGlyphAt calls ($16 $30 $47 $44 $52 = L-left L-right i f t) and RTSes.

events.title: picasso2: leave the BLT address registers where the transfer stopped
events.message:
picasso2: leave the BLT address registers where the transfer stopped

The CL-GD542x BLT source and destination addresses are counters, not
latches. PicassoII.card fills a run by writing one 8-pixel tile,
replicating it with a blit, then blitting the leftover pixels with only
the width and height reprogrammed, so the remainder has to land where the
replication ended. Reloading GR 0x28-0x2a from the register file dropped
it onto pixels already filled, leaving the tail of every run unpainted at
24 bits.

Fixes #569.

The play floppy booted a 4 MB STE (TOS 1.62) to the desktop: no title, no

events.title: datadisks: pre-reduce the art by default (PERBAND=auto)
events.message:
datadisks: pre-reduce the art by default (PERBAND=auto)

The user's call, from hardware: the ECS build looks worse than the ST's
despite better hardware, because ALL of the ECS's bigger colour budget is
spent by a runtime quantiser on a 7MHz 68000. Converting offline is what
fixes that, so it should be what happens by default rather than something
you have to know to ask for.

PERBAND now defaults to `auto`, which picks the budget from the target:
24 colours per band for `amiga` (ECS has 32 per copper band), 12 for
`atari`/`atari720`/`gotek` (ST/STE has 16). `PERBAND=off` restores SSI's
palettes untouched, `PERBAND=<n>` sets your own.

The trade is documented where it is made, because one disk set serves a
whole family (atari feeds the ST *and* the Falcon/TT; amiga feeds ECS
*and* AGA): converting is right for the bitplane member and slightly
flattens the 256-colour one, so `off` is the answer when the media is for
a Falcon/TT/A1200/graphics card only. Measured palette rms error 9.3 at
budget 24 and 14.5 at 12, against 26.3 for a global 32-colour cut and
34.6 for global 16 — even the ST budget lands far closer to SSI's
original than what the runtime quantiser produces on the machine it is
for.

Verified: `amiga` converts at 24 (4518 over-budget bands -> 0, rms 7.6),
`atari` at 12 (rms 13.2), `PERBAND=off` runs no conversion, and the
resulting images differ from the unconverted ones.

events.title: tools: perband reads DOS .TLB too, and mkdatadisks can apply it (PERBAND=)
events.message:
tools: perband reads DOS .TLB too, and mkdatadisks can apply it (PERBAND=)

Wires the per-band converter into the media the user actually installs
from, without adding a step or a prompt to any installer (the ADR-0019
lesson: installers stay pure-copy).

Two parts:

1. perband.py now converts SSI's DOS .TLB (HLIB) art, not just the Mac
   .ctl (GLIB) twin. That matters because the data disks ship .TLB by
   default and the engine derives the .ctl on first touch — convert only
   the .ctl and the reduced palettes never reach the machine. An HLIB
   palette entry carries the SAME RGB payload at the same +8 offset as its
   GLIB twin (only container endianness and header word order differ, and
   _convert_entry passes colour tables verbatim), so the tool converts to
   GLIB in memory, runs the analysis with the decoders already proven
   there, and writes the merged triples back into the ORIGINAL bytes by
   position. Verified on PICA.TLB: same length, magic preserved, all 8011
   changed bytes inside palette RGB blocks, and the result still converts
   to a valid GLIB.

2. mkdatadisks.sh takes PERBAND=<colours> and converts a COPY of the
   source tree before packing. Suggested budgets: 24 for Amiga ECS (32
   per copper band), 12 for ST/STE (16), leaving headroom for the chrome,
   roster and text box that share every band.

OPT-IN, deliberately. One set of data disks serves a whole family: the
atari disks feed the ST *and* the Falcon/TT, the amiga disks feed ECS
*and* AGA. Reducing the art helps the machine that must quantise and
slightly flattens the one that need not, so it is a choice made when
building media for a specific low-colour machine rather than something
done to everyone's art by default.

Verified end to end: PERBAND=24 over a real HEIRS tree converts 694
pictures (1 skipped, an art_convert layout it already could not read,
reported and left alone), worst band 197 -> 24 colours, 4518 over-budget
bands -> 0, rms 7.6 — and the built ADFs differ from the stock ones
(7053/29835/16215 bytes on disks 1-3), so the conversion demonstrably
reaches the media. 481 tests pass.

events.title: tools: perband.py — offline art reduction to the PER-BAND budget (ADR-0020 v2)
events.message:
tools: perband.py — offline art reduction to the PER-BAND budget (ADR-0020 v2)

The v1 global palette was the wrong target and the ECS proved it: reducing
a picture to one 32-colour palette throws away the copper's 25 per-band
palettes and looks flatter than what the runtime quantizer already
produces. The hardware's actual constraint is per BAND, so the target is:

    no 8-scanline strip may need more than "budget" distinct colours

A picture meeting that can still carry far more than 32 colours overall —
different strips spend their 32 on different colours — and every band then
quantizes EXACTLY: nothing merged at runtime, so no per-band seams and no
nearest-luma stray pixels.

Met by MERGING PALETTE ENTRIES ALONE, no pixel rewriting: a strip's cost is
its number of distinct RGB values, not indices, so giving two indices the
same RGB costs one colour wherever they co-occur. Pixels, offsets and
codecs are untouched (the by-construction-valid rewrite v1 proved). Each
merge picks the closest pair inside an over-budget strip, so fidelity is
spent only where the constraint binds. A picture lands at screen y=24, a
multiple of the 8-row band height, so its own strips align with the bands.

Decodes every colour codec the art uses: mode 2 + 0x40 (PackBits 8bpp),
mode 7 (transparency RLE), mode 9 (composite), and l2d4e's raw-8bpp
fall-through (modes 0 and 5 — mode 5 being the dungeon wall tiles). 1bpp
mono pieces draw in a single pen colour, so they constrain nothing and
must not disqualify their picture.

Whole HEIRS corpus at budget 24: 364 pictures, 0 skipped, worst band
197 -> 24 colours, 2323 over-budget bands -> 0, palette rms error 7.6 —
against 26.3 for v1's global 32 and 34.6 for global 16.

MEASURED ON ECS, artefact rows in the tavern picture:
  stock art, pre-#167    9 rows / severity 3.39
  stock art, post-#167   3 rows / 0.85
  per-band art           0 rows / 0.00   <- clean, modelling intact

7 new tests pin the budget guarantee and that ONLY palette RGB bytes
change; 481 pass.

events.title: ecs: load each band's palette in the PRECEDING hblank (#167)
events.message:
ecs: load each band's palette in the PRECEDING hblank (#167)

The A500 'the bigpics all had leftover pixels' report is a copper timing
bug, not leftover pixels. cop_build waited for the band's OWN first
scanline at hpos 0 and then issued 32 COLOR moves. A copper MOVE costs 2
copper cycles = 4 colour clocks, so 32 need 128 CCK, and the display
window opens at DIWSTRT hpos 0x81 = 129 CCK: one colour clock of margin,
before the four memory-refresh slots at the top of every scanline and any
blitter contention. The tail of the load lands inside the visible line
(or slips a line), so that scanline shows the PREVIOUS band's colours for
the registers not yet rewritten — a thin wrong-coloured line at every
band boundary, dashed because only slots that differ between the two
palettes look wrong.

Now waits on (line - 1, hpos 0x64 = CCK 200, past DIWSTOP's 193) so the
load owns the tail of the previous line plus the whole horizontal blank —
~156 CCK for the 128 it needs — and every register is in place before the
band's first pixel.

How it was pinned, since three plausible causes were wrong first:
  - draw-time planar layer: RULED OUT, PLANAR=0 is pixel-identical.
  - row-diff announcements: RULED OUT, a whole drive under
    FRUA_DIRTYCHECK logs 0 unannounced rows.
  - both palette caches: RULED OUT, palcache=off clutcache=off unchanged
    (and the log confirms 0 cache hits).
  - The Falcon renders the same picture from the same save perfectly:
    no copper, no band palettes.
  - Every artefact row sits at an exact multiple of ECS_RPB (game rows
    32/48/56/72/80/96, mod 8 == 0) and the SAME rows appear on two
    different pictures — positional, not content.

Measured on the HEIRS tavern-brawl picture, picture region only: 9
artefact rows / 3.37 severity -> 3 rows / 0.85, a 75% reduction. The
residual is most likely the genuine per-band palette seam rather than
timing; quantsim on the same frame says banding is otherwise worth
keeping (mean sq err 125.8 banded vs 249.6 global), so the answer there
is palette continuity or ADR-0020's offline pre-quant, not fewer bands.

AGA and ST/STE build; 474 tests pass.

events.title: wonderboy: the actor tier on a record view (x3.7 → x2.5), --gc-sections
events.message:
wonderboy: the actor tier on a record view (x3.7 → x2.5), --gc-sections

Reconstruction — the actor tier
- include/actor_view.h + src/actor_view.c: an ActorRecord VIEW of the
  actor's own record, proved ONCE per actor at the door instead of per
  field: inside the image it is a pointer (d16(An) fields, no mask, no
  guard); a record the image does not wholly hold runs against a 32-byte
  scratch pre-filled with the live prefix, writes masked by a per-byte
  `live` map (a dropped store must stay zero — six swoop cases say so),
  and given back whole at the close. Longword fields are whole-operand,
  as the shim's bus is. Every published routine keeps its (image, actor)
  signature as a door over a `_body`; 111 doors, all through one macro
  family; host-only REC_WITHIN_RECORD asserts on the accessors.
- src/behavior.c, map.c, player.c, actor.c: 591 + 131 + 59 field
  accesses moved onto the view; every actor.c helper that reached the
  caller's own record by address (actor_set_side_flag — the tier's last
  raw unguarded pointer — damage_template_hitpoints, defeat_and_score,
  start_motion_at_speed, …) has a record-taking body, so nothing writes
  the record behind an open door. The 61-row linear handler search is a
  switch (a compare tree under -fno-jump-tables). actor_fall_and_settle
  3,843 → 1,691 cycles a call, actor_behavior_pass 60.6 K → 42.3 K a
  frame walking vs the original's 17.1 K (x3.7 → x2.5); the frame is
  vblank-quantised, so walking reads 443 frames / 22.15 fps as before.
- Measured and rejected: a fast-arm mask branch (+8 KB for 0.3 K).

Build — --gc-sections adopted
- atari/build.sh: -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, --gc-sections;
  every symbol gate asks the OBJECTS (pre-collection) — the ELF-based
  clone gate had broken the six modes that draw no sprite; a mode-aware
  ELF check keeps the seam symbols that must be live. PRG text −15 KB,
  boot floppy 26,624 → 39,936 B free.
- atari/mkprg.py: fixups filtered to loaded sections, each read back
  from the flat binary and cross-checked against the ELF, the emitted
  GEMDOS table decoded and matched; every guard a real refusal (no
  assert); negative addends and a one-past-the-end pointer accepted.
- atari/tos.ld: `.bss SUBALIGN(2)` — byte-packed .bss put a longword at
  an odd address once collection reshuffled it (Address Error on
  target; Joust's copy carries the same latent fault — cross-noted in
  its STATUS); KEEP for the .s file's own .text.

Verification
- make test 6,457 green (new pin: slot 7's damage arm at a record
  straddling the image top — RED before the class was closed, GREEN
  after); make guarded clean (10,050 runs); full on-target ladder OK
  (m1 novbl m2 m5 m6 m3 boot ownplay floppy); mutations per change in
  STATUS.md.

Docs
- STATUS.md "Performance" (three actor phases, the view's semantics,
  holes registered honestly, gc-sections), atari/README.md, bus.h and
  backend seam census, docs/on-target-execution.md (the .bss/gc gotcha).

events.title: text: the typewriter presents its OWN ROWS, not the whole screen (#166)
events.message:
text: the typewriter presents its OWN ROWS, not the whole screen (#166)

The slow-text pacer (l435a) shows each glyph with a FULL present. On a
machine where that is expensive — a 7MHz ECS, or the ATW800/2 whose VME
full present measures ~0.5s — it costs far more than the glyph interval
the pacer was willing to give away, so the machine immediately falls
behind. The fell-behind arm returns before reaching the present at all,
so presents STOP and the remaining glyphs are drawn invisibly until
something else presents.

The player does not see a typewriter: they see a fragment, a pause, then
the rest at once — 'it will say The weary wande, pause for one or one
and a half seconds, then finish' (Mega STe + ATW hardware report). The
same thing reproduces headlessly on ECS: two consecutive frames read
THE WEARY WANDERER then THE WEARY WANDERER., the whole difference being
the final character.

Narrow the present to the rows the glyph actually announced, so the
per-glyph cost is one text line instead of 200 rows and the pacer stays
ahead. Falls back to a full present when the announcement says scan-all
or no span can be derived (identical to the old behaviour). Adds
qd_surface_width() so the row span can be presented full-width without
hardcoding a machine's geometry.

Verified on ECS at the same square that showed the split: the text now
arrives progressively — 15 consecutive distinct frames at 1s sampling
(THE COMMON ROOM IS FR ... FREE TO YOU RIFF-RAFF, BUT HAVE A CARE TO)
where before there were two. Falcon boots to menu unchanged; ST/STE and
020 builds link; 474 tests pass.

events.title: ecs: titles compose whole — defer the copper palette to the flip, drop the mid-body present (#165)
events.message:
ecs: titles compose whole — defer the copper palette to the flip, drop the mid-body present (#165)

Two independent causes behind the A500 field report ('half buffer, then
load more, and corruption', 'wrong colors for a brief moment'), both
reproduced in amiberry and fixed:

1. WRONG COLOURS. ecs_reband() installed the new per-band copper palette
   immediately, but when the caller is ecs_render() the planes that
   palette describes do not exist yet: the whole-screen remap + c2p take
   ~12 SECONDS on a 7MHz 68000 (measured via FRUA_ECSTRACE: render start
   rl 446597 -> end 637848). The copper spent all of it showing the
   OUTGOING screen under the INCOMING palette — old pixels, wrong
   colours, sliced horizontally because the bands ARE the copper's
   palette regions. Now staged and committed WITH the plane switch. The
   content-same (remap_same) arm still installs immediately and must:
   there the planes are already right and only the RGB moved (deferring
   that would re-create #140).

2. HALF-DRAWN SCREENS. l19d4's mid-body present deliberately shows the
   base image WITHOUT its overlay piece. Free on the Mac (the body ran
   between frames); here it is a real screen-building pass, so the
   half-composed title is what a slow machine shows for most of the
   title's life. HW-palette backends already skipped it; the same
   reasoning applies to any backend, and dropping it matches both the
   DOS release (titles arrive whole) and the Mac's net frame.

Also adds the tear-free threshold for the incremental full present
(video.cfg tearfree=<rows>, 0 = off): scene-sized row sets go through
the page flip instead of converting into the page the copper is showing.

Measured: 80 samples over 160s of the ECS title sequence now yield 3
distinct frames, each a complete correctly-coloured title (was a
succession of banded and half-drawn intermediates). Falcon boots titles
to menu unchanged; ST/STE and 020 builds link; 474 tests pass.

events.title: Capitals on the panel line: "Game over", the transfer game, "Game on!"
events.message:
Capitals on the panel line: "Game over", the transfer game, "Game on!"

Three things KC asked for, all the same defect underneath — every capital
in the original is sixteen pixels, two character cells, and XfGlyphAt
draws one cell a byte. PnWide does the wide ones and lives in bank 6,
unreachable from bank 7, so the panel-line words shipped in lower case.
No code was needed to fix it: the right half rides in the string as the
next byte, exactly as goTxtOver already did for its lowercase m.

  "Game over"  the wash's banner, capital G.
  the transfer game  Captured, Colour, Finish -, Complete, Burnt Out and
    Deadlock. $69F3's $48 is a CAPITAL O, which the lowercase version had
    lost. XF_COL_TIME 10 -> 11: with capitals the two timed strings are
    nine cells, which is $69BE's own count — Finish_txt is F i n i s h sp -
    then the digits at its indices 8 and 9 — so the countdown lands where
    the original puts it. The lift view's "Lift" went with them: same
    field, same engine.
  "Game on!"  the game-start 001 screen's panel line, which said nothing
    at all. layer-11d DECISION 4 puts that page up before the deck is
    drawn, so LoadDeck's PanelInit has run but PanelUpdate has not — the
    main loop short-circuits at infoActive — and both live fields sat
    blank for the whole 2.9 s hold. The C64 has no equivalent: $12C7
    reaches NewShipInfo through GotoHires and its status rows survive
    underneath. PnGameOn is PnBriefing's arrangement one screen earlier,
    and it spoils BOTH shadows: PanelInit has already run here, so the
    mode word would otherwise stay "Game on!" over the deck.

Two things that had to move. '!' was not in PnAscii and came out as a
space; it is four compares in, seven bytes. And GameStartInfo's tail is
GameStart2 in the code image — the low overlay is FULL, so JMP InfoCall
became JMP GameStart2, the same three bytes, and the panel call and the
LDX went where there was room.

One glyph is still missing: Color_txt's seventh cell is C64 code $24, a
question mark, and export_font.py's set stops at '!'. A space stands in.

Verified in jsbeeb: "Game on!" with the score at the 001 screen and
"Mobile" back on the deck after it; Colour 92, Finish -82 and Complete
through a transfer; "Game over" over the black-and-white wash. The lift
view was not reached this session — it is the same five glyph writes
through the same routine.

Bank 6 92 B free -> 46; code image ends &2EAA; bank 7's growth rode in
plandata's ALIGN pad as usual.

events.message:
M1 uzavren: fade palety 0x4a48 / 0x4a40 a driver 0x28b0

Posledni otevreny bod M1 se nemeril v emulatoru - rutina byla cela
citelna v disassembly.

- 0x4a48 NENI interpolator, ale bezstavovy skalovac: kazdy nibble RGB12
  * (256 - uroven) >> 8, tri nibbly pres rolw #8/#4/#4 (dohromady 16
  bitu, slovo vypadne zpet v poradi). 0x4a40 = notw -> 0x4a48 -> notw,
  tedy tataz rampa k bile
- uroven drzi fp@(11170) (cerna) a fp@(11166) (bila), obe 0-256, a
  krokuje je korutina 0x28b0 jednou za snimek: cerna +-16 dle znamenka
  fp@(142), bila znamenkovym krokem fp@(11168) (v kodu +16, -16, -4)
- fade plati jen pro registry 0x180-0x19F (cmpiw #384 / #416 na 0x5e4c
  a 0x5e52), cimz se nezavisle potvrdilo, ze barvy spritu od 0x1A0
  prochazeji nedotcene - a navic ze HUD (COLOR16 = 0x1A0) fade nepodleha
- API 0x2864 / 0x2868 blokuje: yielduje, dokud driver priznak nevynuluje.
  Obraz je hotovy po 16 snimcich, ale priznak spadne az 17. tikem,
  protoze subiw #16 na 0x28b8 do te doby nepodtece
- start hry se odcernuje (0x3092 a 0x330a volaji 0x2868)

OPRAVA docs/MAPS.md: tvrdilo, ze engine interpoluje barvy mezi
checkpointy pomoci 0x4a48. Neinterpoluje - kazdy paletovy prikaz mapy
je diskretni zapis a hladkost dela HUSTOTA prikazu v datech (RIVER: 19
zmen na 4127 px). 0x4a48 je samostatny globalni nasobic nad celou
paletou.

game.html: fade zapojen jako jediny prekryv nad bobovou vrstvou, ne
fade po paletach - hardware meni sdilene copper registry, takze zasahne
i bilou spawn siluetu, stiny a vybuchy, ktere pres paletu okna nejdou.
HW sprity granatu a HUD se kresli az za prekryvem.

check.py: novy radek meri osm konstant fadu primo v obrazu.
uitest.py: regrese hlida schodiste 256->0 po 16, pad priznaku az 17.
tikem, cernou plochu na startu i svitici HUD behem fadu.

events.title: The game over's static is the C64's four characters, in black and white
events.message:
The game over's static is the C64's four characters, in black and white

$379F picks (rnd AND 3) + $7A out of the deck charset and $7A-$7D are not
in the ported set, so the wash has been standing on four invented
densities of black since 11b-2. They cannot go through the shared charset
— export_bbc.py ships only the codes a TILE references, and &0400-&0C90 is
exactly 137 * 16 bytes with lowbss immediately above it — so they ride in
goWashPat as finished MODE 1 cells instead, in the same 64 bytes the
densities cost. CHARCOLOR is $00 for all four: bit 3 clear, so they are
hires C64 characters, 8 px wide, and a MODE 1 cell is 8 px wide too.
left = row >> 4, right = row AND &0F, and nothing is chosen.

And the colours are the original's. $378B writes Irq1bgColor = $F1 —
white, reaching $D021 at $6F59 — and $37A6 writes colour RAM $F0, black,
for every cell: the wash is monochrome and the deck's scheme is gone.
GoWashStart writes the eight palPlay entries for logicals 0 and 1 and
leaves 2 and 3 alone, because goWashPat never draws in them. Nothing
restores it; the 999 page follows and SetTextPal rebuilds palPlay.

Verified in jsbeeb: boot, play, ESCAPE, overPhase 2, palPlay+0..7 =
00 10 27 37 40 50 67 77, and the play area is black-and-white static in
the C64's own broken bands. 21 bytes in bank 7, absorbed by plandata's
ALIGN pad — PARXFER is still 16377 of 16384.

Closes the "open and cosmetic: the wash renders blue" note in
layer-11-sound-title.md and the TODO beside DECISION 7.

events.title: The player flashes on ship entry, at the C64's rate
events.message:
The player flashes on ship entry, at the C64's rate

KC: "the player sprite should flash black and white on entry to the
ship when the siren sounds."

THE FLASH IS NOT AN ENTRY EFFECT. _entership ($1289) sets droidEnergy
to SEVEN ($12A5), posts the siren as fx 7 ($1332), runs the game for 32
iterations ($1336-$1343), then puts energy AND maxEnergy to $40
($1345/$134A). The flashing is the ordinary low-energy warning --
AnimateDroids' tail cycles LowNrgColor_t (light grey, grey, dark grey,
BLACK, back up, ending WHITE) into the player's sprite colour whenever
energy < 8. Entry triggers it by holding him under the threshold for 32
iterations and by no other means; the alarm comes from the same
condition, so siren, beeping and flash are one window. Both routes go
through it: a new game after fx 6, a cleared ship after fx $B.

The port had the flash (layer-9 DECISION 5), the alarm and fx 7, but no
window -- so nothing was ever below 8 to see. EntryHold now owns it and
both routes arm entryHold with 32: it applies the 7 on its first pass
and $40 to energy and maxEnergy when the count expires. Arming rather
than writing energy directly is what lets lowcode2 use it, that being
the low overlay where drEnergy's bank may not be paged.

It runs in the play path beside SndAmbient, which is the design and not
convenience: the port replaced the C64's 32-frame animation with the
IS_SCR_001 screen, which is modal and ends the pass earlier, so the
window starts once the screen is dismissed and the deck is up.

AND IT FOUND A LIVE BUG. The next-ship route set the 7 at InfoHigh and
NOTHING ANYWHERE set it back -- the port had no equivalent of $1345 at
all, so boarding ship 2 would have left the player on seven energy
permanently, flashing and alarming until he found a recharge pad. Fixed
by the same routine.

THE RATE WAS WRONG TOO (KC: "the flash is quite fast compared with the
C64 version"). sprite.asm counted fieldCount, one per FIELD: half-period
4 fields = 0.08 s, a 6.25 Hz strobe. The C64 counts frameCount, which
increments once per GameLoop ITERATION -- two to three frames -- so its
half-period is ~10 frames, about 2.5 Hz. The old comment carried the
error in plain sight: "fieldCount is the IRQ's own count at fire 3, one
per field, so it is frameCount." It is not; main.asm's gameTick is the
port's frameCount and says so. On gameTick the half-period is 4 passes
= 0.16 s, 3.1 Hz.

fieldCount and gameTick are not interchangeable: anywhere the C64
counts frameCount the port must count gameTick. That is now stated in
docs/layer-9-hud.md, and it is the second rate this session that came
out wrong from picking the faster counter.

Verified in jsbeeb: mid-window entryHold 7, drEnergy 7, the player
solid white in one frame and solid black four fields later; after
expiry entryHold 0, drEnergy &40, maxEnergy &40.

  cont-only action file — `:trace` prints no VBL line, and any debugger

Reconstruction (the walking frame)

  low half first then swap as the original stores, dbf counts held by a
  COUNT_BARRIER — fill_column 87.7 K → 67.9 K a call (x1.42 → x1.10).

events.title: The lift tile gets its detail back on decks 0, 5 and 9
events.message:
The lift tile gets its detail back on decks 0, 5 and 9

KC: "decks 0, 5 and 9 have no details in the lift tile - it's just
empty." Exactly the three decks whose logical 0 and logical 3 are both
physical white, which is layer-14 DECISION 2's deliberate collision. It
was not a coincidence and it was not the collision either.

THE LIFT IS TILE 3. Not tiles 23-27, which docs/graphics.md's tile
table calls "lift shaft" elements -- deck 0's map contains none of
them. The lift is placed from liftTileCol/liftTileRow and the tile at
that position is 3, on deck 0 and deck 1 alike. graphics.md now carries
a warning at that table, because its naming cost half an hour.

Tile 3 has three colour groups. On these decks 10 of 16 cells land on
the floor's own physical colour, against ZERO on every other deck:

   6 structure  dk grey -> blue (0/9) or black (5)   fine
   6 highlight  white -> white                       DECISION 2, correct
   4 detail     grey (0/9) / yellow (5) -> white     THE DEFECT

The 6 highlights are DECISION 2 working as intended -- solid white on a
50% floor, and KC confirms they read right. The 4 detail cells are the
bug: C64 grey and C64 yellow merge onto logical 0, which IS the floor,
so they are not low-contrast, they are literally the floor colour.

Fix, three bytes of deck_palettes.json: decks 0 and 9 send C64 grey to
logical 1 (black, since the structure is already blue); deck 5 sends
C64 yellow to logical 2 (red, since its structure is already black).
Blast radius measured before applying: 4 cells, all in tile 3, on those
three decks only. Nothing else in the 32-tile set uses those colours on
those schemes; the floor is C64 light grey (15) and is untouched, as is
white.

A REJECTED FIX IS RECORDED WITH IT because it looked obvious and was
wrong twice over. The first attempt re-pointed C64 WHITE off logical 3
on those decks: it repainted 200 cells -- all the white linework, since
white is the main linework colour there -- and fixed only 6 of the 10
dead cells, the other 4 coming through grey/yellow. KC: "the white
highlights were correct before, now they are red on deck 5 and the lift
details are still not visible." Measure which colours the failing cells

events.title: Flush the MOS's buffers before handing the IRQ back: it was playing the charset
events.message:
Flush the MOS's buffers before handing the IRQ back: it was playing the charset

KC heard a quiet sequence of rising notes after every game over, which
Q could not mute, pausing during the high-score entry and stopping only
when a real effect played.

&0400-&0C90 is the MODE 1 charset in reclaimed OS workspace. Inside it,
&0800-&08FF is the MOS's: &800-&83F sound workspace, &840-&87F the four
channel queues, &8C0-&8FF the envelope definitions. While we own IRQ1V
nothing reads any of it and the overlap is free -- which is why this has
never mattered. GoTitle calls UninstallIrq, the MOS's 100 Hz sound
driver wakes up, finds its queue pointers and buffers full of character
bitmaps, and plays them. The pitch sweeps because it is chewing through
glyph data; it is quiet because the attenuations it finds are 13-14.

Q could not touch it because Q sets sndVolume, and sndVolume only gates
OUR driver's writes. Any sound the mute cannot silence is not ours --
that mismatch is what identifies it.

Measured: after a muted game over, SndSilence had left all four
channels at attenuation 15, yet the chip read 14/13/-/14 with the tone
periods falling steadily (CH1 401 -> 146 -> 95, pitch rising). Zeroing
&0800-&087F stopped it instantly and restored all four to 15, which
pinned the cause. Sound suppression (OSBYTE &D2, the flag at &0262) did
NOT stop it: suppression gates new SOUND commands, not a queue already
draining.

Fix: OSBYTE &0F, X=0 -- flush every buffer -- BEFORE JSR UninstallIrq.
The ordering is the fix being airtight rather than nearly: our IRQ is
still installed there, so the MOS's sound IRQ is definitively not
running and cannot be halfway through draining a note while we reset
the pointers under it. After the uninstall there is a window between
its CLI and the flush where one garbage note can start. It costs a few
charset bytes, which do not matter -- BuildCharset repaints the set at
the next deck load and nothing between reads it.

Not caused by this day's work, though the Q mute is what exposed it.
Nothing in the volume, pause, transfer-button or keydown changes goes
near &0800, the charset's address, this seam or the MOS sound path. Not
bisected against an older build, so that is reasoning, not measurement.

Verified: silent through the death, game over and high-score entry, and
the briefing beyond plays its chatter normally.

The standing lesson is now in CLAUDE.md's memory map: the overlap is
safe only while we own the IRQ, so any future path that hands the
machine back must flush first. There is exactly one such seam today.

events.title: keydown reads the matrix directly: 243 cycles becomes 69
events.message:
keydown reads the matrix directly: 243 cycles becomes 69

Ported from thrust's test_inkey (BEEB/Repos/thrust/thrust.6502), which
is the canonical form of this. Port A is the slow bus, port B's low
nibble is an addressable latch choosing who listens ((value << 3) |
line), and line 3 is the keyboard's write-enable: drop it and the
hardware's free-running column scan stops, so the matrix can be driven
by hand. DDRA = &7F puts the internal key number out on PA0-PA6 and
leaves PA7 an input carrying the answer. One write, one read -- this
tests a key we NAME, so there is no iteration.

&FE4F and not &FE41: the no-handshake register. &FE41 strobes CA2.

Measured both ways, JSR to RTS inclusive: OSBYTE &81 = 243 cycles,
direct = 69. The OSBYTE figure was taken twice by independent routes
(the title loop's turn rate, and a DEBUG_TIME bracket round ReadKeys)
and they agree to a cycle. At ~12.5 key tests a pass that is ~2,175
cycles a pass, 2.7% of the budget -- four of those tests arrived this
afternoon, which is what made it worth doing.

THE RASTER WAS THE RISK, NOT THE SAVING. The sequence runs under
PHP/SEI/PLP so neither the MOS nor the sound driver (same port A, from
the IRQ) can interleave it: 26 masked cycles, twelve times a pass,
against a rupture whose T1 stages are deadline-driven. It costs them
nothing -- 25.0 Hz exactly before and after, rupture holding, boundary
clean while scrolling. NOT claimed: what the MOS masks for inside
OSBYTE &81, which was never measured.

The emulator showed the mechanism outright. Testing Z (IKN &61): key up
reads back &61, key down reads back &E1 -- the same seven bits we
wrote, with PA7 as the answer.

KNOCK-ON: TiWait's body WAS one OSBYTE, so the title loop is now 3.15x
faster (11,508 turns/s against 3,654). The volume gate goes back to
1-in-1024 (was rejected there at 3.6 Hz on the old build; it is 11.2 Hz
now, where the other two call sites sit), and the timeout into the
briefing falls 17.9 s -> 5.7 s. That is not a regression: the C64's is
256 frames, 5.1 s, and TiWait's header always claimed the wrap was "the
same order as the original's". KC to say if 18 s was preferred.

AND A TRAP IN DEBUG_TIME, now in its header: the bracket first reported
ReadKeys costing 2,903 cycles AFTER the conversion against 1,009
before. T1 free-runs from its latch, so the subtraction is modular
arithmetic only while the counter does not pass zero between the two
reads; when it does that pass contributes ~65,536 spurious ticks. The
excess was 1.96 x 65,536 exactly -- two wraps -- and the baseline had
none. The reload point drifts through the pass, so bad readings come in
consecutive runs, not at random. jsbeeb breakpoints DO fire now, so a
breakpoint pair and an elapsed_cycles difference is the honest tool for
anything short.

Verified through every path: title volume/mute and fire (MOS IRQ live
there, which is the harder case), movement and scrolling, P both ways,
SPACE transfer, [ deck hop.

events.title: SPACE as a second transfer button, and the redraw moves to R
events.message:
SPACE as a second transfer button, and the redraw moves to R

DECISION 12 in docs/layer-7-combat.md. An addition the C64 has no
equivalent of, and the reason is the keyboard: DoMoveMode ($31B9) has
one button to divide three ways, so it disambiguates by direction and
by time -- fire WITH a direction draws the weapon, fire with NONE
settles for eight passes and then enters transfer mode. On a joystick
that reads as intent. On a keyboard you must come to a stop, hold L and
wait a third of a second before touching a droid means anything, by
which time the droid has moved.

A dedicated button has nothing to disambiguate, so the settle is
SKIPPED rather than reproduced: SPACE puts moveMode at Transfer on the
next pass and holds it while the key is down, direction or no
direction. The fire route is untouched -- a second door into the same
room, not a change to the first. KC picked the semantics.

It forces the state AND the button, and both halves are needed:
mm_transfer holds moveMode at 0 only while fireDown is set and drops to
Mobile the moment it is not, so the mode alone would last one pass.
Setting fireDown is safe -- DoMoveMode is its only reader, and with the
mode already 0 the arm it lands in never calls DoFire, so holding SPACE
cannot shoot. Checked, not assumed.

Placement is forced three ways: below the L block (which writes
fireDown from scratch every pass), above DoMoveMode (which consumes
it), inside the overPhase guard (a corpse does not transfer). The
movement is untouched -- ReadKeys/CalcSpeed/ApplyMove have already run
by there, so ignoring the direction costs nothing and he enters
transfer mode mid-stride.

The forced RedrawAll moves SPACE -> R. It is the buffer-diff oracle
that CLAUDE.md's verification recipe and layer-3-scroll.md are written
around, so it could not just be dropped; R has been free since
DEBUG_RESTART went. The live instructions now say R; the historical
session records that mention SPACE are left as they were.

Verified in jsbeeb: SPACE from Mobile -> 0 in one pass, panel reads
"Transfer"; released -> &80; SPACE while walking -> 0 with
sprActive[7] still 0; the fire route unchanged (L with no direction
&80 -> 2, mmDelay 8 -> 6 over three passes -> 0, release -> &80); R
breaks on RedrawAll and SPACE runs ten passes without it.

Also recorded, because it cost half an hour: moveMode freezes wherever
it stood whenever a modal screen owns the machine, since all five modal
arms end the pass above the fire block. It looks exactly like a stuck
key. An unnoticed opening 001 info screen was the culprit.

events.title: v0.5.1: career depth (training, diary, records, youth) + AI shooting fidelity
events.message:
v0.5.1: career depth (training, diary, records, youth) + AI shooting fidelity

CAREER — the manager finally has levers, and the club has a memory.

* WEEKLY TRAINING (new). Pick a drill, an intensity and up to six players; the
  session is graded and slowly loads their skills. Modelled on FIFA 18's
  weekly graded session and CM 01/02's intensity dial, mapped onto SWOS's seven
  0..7 skills. Deterministic (CareerRng only) and completely skippable.
  Design + sources: docs/decisions/04-training-and-development.md
* YOUTH INTAKE DAY (plan #6). The academy's new players once a summer, each
  with a scouted RANGE rather than a number.
* CLUB DIARY (plan #7). One line per event across the whole career: signings,
  milestones, thrashings, runs, intakes, the board's verdict, the season's
  finish. Read-only by design — no unread counter, nothing to clear.
* APPEARANCES + GOALS and a CLUB RECORDS board (plan #8). New APP/GLS columns
  in the squad screen and an all-time appearance list that a sold player keeps
  his place in.

Three long-standing defects these screens exposed:

* every regular in every career was pinned at 100 fatigue — i.e. playing at
  FatigueModel.SkillPenalty's -2 tier for whole careers. Recovery between
  matches was FLAT and could never catch a big enough per-match gain; a flat
  rate cannot have an equilibrium below the cap. It now also sheds 35 % of the
  carried fatigue over a week's rest, and a pre-season divides it by five.
* the youth academy fell permanently silent after ~3 seasons: a club at the
  squad cap was given no intake at all.
* FormModel.FormSkillDelta had no caller outside a test. Form was computed,
  stored, displayed — and ignored by the match. It and the new sharpness now
  apply in CareerMatchTeam.ToPlayerRecord, capped at one SWOS level either way.

GAMEPLAY — closer to the original, and the CPU shoots straight.

* The AI no longer curves the ball away from goal. A port-only chase heuristic
  with no counterpart in the reference fired 25 410 of 30 000 ticks and
  overwrote the team-wide currentAllowedDirection from an arbitrary off-ball
  sprite. That value is also the AI's after-touch input, so it was bending
  every AI shot at random. Measured over five fixtures, shot-flight rotation
  against the rotation needed to steer toward goal: 53/39 toward/away with the
  heuristic on, 78/12 with it off. Ten fixtures scored 16 vs 13 goals, so the
  fidelity fix costs nothing.
* Spin direction now matches the asm. In the original D2 is ONE register, so
  the 769/129 write also seeds the low byte the spin sign test reads later.
  The port kept a separate d2Byte at 0, which made both teams always spin
  left; the real defaults are opposite spins per team.
* --swos-smoke prints shot-count, distance and curve telemetry so this class
  of question can be argued with numbers instead of impressions.

Also: version stamp (V0.5.1) in the bottom-left of every menu screen, read
from application/config/version so there is one place to bump it.

The browser career client is kept out of this repository. Main.cs reaches it
only through `partial void` hooks, so the tree compiles and runs without it.

events.title: Pause on P, in the shape DoPause is written in
events.message:
Pause on P, in the shape DoPause is written in

DoPause ($3B7C) ported. Called from ml_passend beside the volume keys,
which is where the C64 calls it from too -- GameLoop $13E6, ABOVE the
consoleState test, so the console, the transfer game and the lift are
all pausable.

DECISION 17: a blocking loop, not a flag the pass tests. The flag looks
tempting (the pass keeps drawing, so the picture stays alive for free)
but the pass has five modal arms that each end it at their own point,
so the flag would need honouring in six places and the console would
still answer its keys while "paused". A loop freezes all six by
standing in front of them, which is why the original is written this
way.

P both ways, KC's request. Resuming on fire -- which the manual offers
-- was dropped: it would fire the weapon on the way out, which is what
the C64's wait-for-release dance at $3BEB exists to prevent. clr-home's
quit has no port either; ESCAPE is always available and does it
properly.

The message costs almost nothing because the panel was already built
for it: PanelUpdate picks a mode word by index and repaints when a
shadow byte says the index moved, so "Pause" is a fifth pnTxtTab entry
and both the paint and the repaint fall out of the existing compare.
Five trailing spaces because Pause_txt has five. sndState 0 in and $12
out, as $3B8F/$3C0F. gameTick needs no save/restore -- it counts passes
and the pause happens inside one, so the C64's pair is a no-op here
rather than an omission.

DECISION 18: the picture freezes solid and the C64's does not -- its
loop keeps AnimateDroids and the font animation running, so the rotor
spins and the tiles cycle behind a frozen game. That needs the sprite
pool's window and tranche handling reproduced outside the main loop.
Recorded as wanted, not built.

AND A BUG THE FIRST BUILD HAD, worth the paragraph: WaitNextPass waits
for passF0 + FRAME_LOCK, stamped at the top of the pass we freeze in.
WaitUntilField's distance is signed and good for 127 fields either way;
its header said "2.5 seconds, and nothing here waits that long", true
until this routine existed. Measured: after a seven-second pause the
game came back and then did not move for two seconds. Two instructions
re-date passF0 on the way out, and the invariant is now stated at
WaitUntilField where the next person to block the pass will read it.

overPhase gates the whole routine: no pause under the death wash, where
the exit's sndState $12 would restart the sound mid-death.

Verified in jsbeeb: "Pause" in the mode field where "Mobile" was;
gameTick frozen across a seven-second hold; sndState 0 and all four
channels silent; the volume keys still stepping while frozen; P
restores the word, the sound and 25.0 Hz within 0.2 s; P held two
seconds during a death does not pause, and the death, game over and
high-score entry run through untouched. NOT exercised: pause with the
console, transfer or lift view up.

Cost: 93 B code image, 22 B bank 6, two state bytes.
