events.title: platform: reuse a palette already cut for this CLUT (ST/STE, #139)
events.message:
platform: reuse a palette already cut for this CLUT (ST/STE, #139)

"Pin the palette" turns out to mean CACHE it, because the walk is not one scene
whose palette drifts -- it is a handful of scenes alternating.

A 300-key HEIRS drive: 14,336 presents, 85 re-bands, of which the new-ink
overflow path accounts for 11. The other 74 are qd_set_palette. The #142 comment
in this file asserted the opposite ("s_dirty is never set that way during it"),
which is why the task had been aimed at INK_MAX; that comment is corrected here
rather than left to mislead the next reader. Across the 76 play-phase re-bands
there are 18 distinct CLUTs and 58 land on one already cut. The backend does
remember a CLUT -- s_clut_banded -- but it remembers exactly ONE, and one is the
wrong number for an alternation. Measured LRU hit rate by size:

    1: 0%   2: 2%   3: 2%   4: 53%   6: 65%   8: 73%   13: 76%

Nothing until four, because the cycle is walk -> cleared viewport -> walk ->
event picture. ST_PCACHE is 8: two thirds of the ceiling for ~20 KB.

Fidelity, priced offline over the 58 repeats (tools/quant/qpin): viewport +7.9%,
everything outside it -3.7% -- a fresh cut on a frame whose viewport just filled
with a portrait re-partitions the roster panel too, and a cached cut does not.
On screen, an A/B on one binary differs in game rows 24..111 and NOWHERE else:
0 of 7,680 pixels above the viewport band, 0 of 28,160 below, all of it speckle
across textured granite. The roster text's histogram is identical across arms.

Time, one binary, video.cfg palcache=off selecting the arm, RNG pinned, 150 keys:

    in-present   56,893 -> 63,033 t200      band branch  16,455 -> 20,636
    the cut alone 3,156 -> 6,768 (-54%)     slot align      328 -> 329 (control)

  ! QUOTE -6.6%, NOT -11.1%. The band branch is the only part the cache touches
    and it is 4,181 of the 6,140 saved; the rest is run-to-run variation (54 vs
    57 re-bands, 2176 vs 2144 presents -- key injection against emulator
    wall-clock is not deterministic even with the seed pinned).

  ! AND THE FORCE-FULL SURVIVES. The hope was that a restored palette would be
    likelier to clear st_align_group with no USED index moving slot, skipping the
    whole-frame rebuild. It is not: FORCE-FULL moved -5.2% and no-skew fired 0
    times against 1. Coming back to CLUT A after a re-band on CLUT B, the
    alignment permutes A's palette to match B's numbering, so A's used indices
    land where they were only by luck. At 14,480 t200 the rebuild is still ~23%
    of in-present on the walk, and nothing here touches it.

Also recorded: 40% of the walk's re-bands quantise a BLACK viewport (the engine
clears, presents, then draws; reband-on-stale is 0, so this is not the
lazy-chunky hazard), and keying the cache on the used subset of the CLUT instead
of all 768 bytes buys nothing -- 18 classes either way, so #139's q12/q13
anecdote does not generalise.

All five configs build; 471 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: tools/quant: price a pinned palette, and drive a walk long enough to price it
events.message:
tools/quant: price a pinned palette, and drive a walk long enough to price it

#139's next step was blocked on data: only 2 of the 14 QDUMP captures were
dungeon walks, and they were near-identical, so "one fixed palette across many
walk screens" could not be measured at all. #147's headless route makes a wider
drive cheap, so this adds one.

st_walkcap.sh is st_profile.sh's drive minus the profiler: boot, beginplay, the
HEIRS entry-event chain, then arrows until the capture budget is spent. During
the walk the re-band trigger is the new-ink overflow path, so every re-band a
walk causes is by construction a frame the current palette does not cover --
which is exactly the frame a pinned palette would have to survive. Walk far
enough and the per-re-band dump IS the dataset. ST_MACHINE lets the same drive
ask a chunky backend the same question as a planar one.

qpin scores each captured frame three ways: re-cut fresh (what ships), the
palette cut on the first frame carrying this CLUT (what a cache serves), and one
cut over every frame carrying it (the best fixed palette that colour space
admits).

  ! IT COMPARES ONLY WITHIN ONE CLUT, AND THE FIRST CUT OF THIS TOOL DID NOT.
    Pinning every frame to frame 0's palette reported a 25x error, which is not
    a fidelity result -- the walk's CLUT moves, so that is one colour space
    scored against another's palette. A pin can only mean "reuse the palette we
    already cut FOR THIS CLUT".

It also reports the LRU hit rate by cache size over the re-band order, which is
what sizes a fix; the distinct-CLUT count does not, because what matters is how
far apart a CLUT's uses are.

events.title: docs: what SSI shipped on the Amiga, and how not to measure it
events.message:
docs: what SSI shipped on the Amiga, and how not to measure it

Curse of the Azure Bonds (Amiga, 1991) on a plain A500, against our ECS build
on the same corridor.

NO COPPER SPLIT: COLOR00 is one value — black — down the entire frame, title
screen and corridor alike. Same instrument that caught our own 25-band border
striping. SSI used a single palette.

THEY DID ENRICH THE AMIGA OVER THE ST, about 1.5x: same corridor, 10 colours
whole-screen / 8 in the viewport on the ST against 15 / 11 on the Amiga, and
the extra entries are shading rather than new hues — two dark blues where the
ST had one, three teals where it had one, two browns where it had one.

AGAINST OURS the budget is a tie and the spending is opposite: 15 genuine
colours for them, 16 for us, but theirs goes on chroma (teal chrome, cyan text,
green, brown door) and ours on a nine-step grey ramp, because our corridor is
quantised photographic stone and our chrome is a granite texture. Different art
pipelines, not better or worse.

★ AND A MEASUREMENT TRAP WORTH MORE THAN THE FINDINGS: amiberry's default
capture BLENDS (gfx_linemode=double2 plus a lores->hires upsample). A panel
that is flat by construction — our own ECS HUD — read as 30 distinct colours in
a 40x40 crop, and a whole frame as 4086. Any colour count off a default capture
measures the scaler. The fix is exact-pixel config keys (kept in a SEPARATE
openua-ecs-exact.uae, because the run-amiga-port skill's click coordinates
assume the 720x568 window) plus a filter to genuine palette entries: 4 bits per
gun means every channel of a real colour is a multiple of 17, and a population
floor clears the residue.

The first version of that filter kept pixels in a flat run of >= 3 instead,
which is biased against a TEXTURED image and in favour of a flat one — exactly
backwards for this comparison. It scored us 14 and them 10; the population
floor scores us 16 and them 15.

Also records a question about our own build: 16 colours frame-wide against 11
per scanline, with 25 independent band palettes available, suggests the ECS
split is buying little on a tonally uniform screen. Hypothesis, not finding —
the population floor could be hiding band-local colours.

events.title: ecs: the copper's 25 palettes striped the border, and had all along
events.message:
ecs: the copper's 25 palettes striped the border, and had all along

COLOR00 is the Amiga's border as well as playfield colour 0. DIW is exactly
320x200, so every scanline of the overscan shows it — and the copper rewrites
all 32 registers, COLOR00 included, at each of the 25 band boundaries. Twenty-
five independent cuts put twenty-five different colours there.

Measured down one column of the left overscan on a boot frame: 21 distinct
colours in 28 runs, changing every 8 scanlines, one of them pure white. After
the fix: 3 and 4 for the whole column, and across the display rows themselves
1 and 1 — a single colour, on the title sequence and on the main menu.

This shipped with the per-band copper palette and nothing caught it, for the
same reason the ST version went unnoticed for a day: every check looked at the
320x200 image, where there is nothing wrong. The ST hit the identical bug when
its raster split landed (f93795be) and its three bands flattered it — this is
the same shape with twenty-five.

ecs_unify_border() mirrors st_unify_border: pick the slot nearest band 0's slot
0, permute it into position 0 (palette and remap together, so no pixel changes
meaning), set its RGB to band 0's exactly. Matching band 0 rather than forcing
black is deliberate — uniform is the requirement, and band 0's colour is what
the border had before the split existed. ecs_repalette gets the no-permute half:
its premise is that slot numbering does not move, so it forces the copper WORD

events.title: ste: the viewport palette split is on by default (#139)
events.message:
ste: the viewport palette split is on by default (#139)

It shipped opt-in for a day while the screen sweep ran. That sweep is done and
every screen class is accounted for:

  boot / title / main menu   one group, AE=0 against the pre-split build
  dungeon walk               three groups, 21 colours in the game area
  town / BIGPIC events (x3)  three groups, correct, roster text keeps red/cyan
  treasure / XP              three groups, correct
  combat                     one group — exactly 16 colours, measured after #147
                             made a combat screen reachable headlessly

Borders uniform throughout since f93795be. Marginal cost over the dungeon phase
is +2.3% now Timer B fires on group boundaries rather than band boundaries
(8406a028), and screens without a viewport were already the s_ngrp == 1 path so
the flip cannot touch them.

Both directions verified on the fixture walk with ONE binary: no video.cfg gives
21 distinct colours in the game area and AE=0 against the opt-in vpbands=on
render; vpbands=off gives 15 and AE=0 against the pre-split render. The parser
takes both keys now, so a config written against either default keeps meaning
what it says.

It stays a RUNTIME knob rather than a compile-time one even with the default
flipped — one binary has to hold both arms or an A/B is comparing two builds,
which has misled this port before. And vpbands=off is the first thing to reach
for if a real ST ever disagrees with Hatari about the one-line-early fire and
the spin: that is the one part of this an emulator cannot settle, and it now
restores a byte-identical pre-split frame rather than a rebuild.

captive: transcribe GM.EXE cell translator; document GM.EXE as the level generator (v1.1.147)

Resolve the long-open question of what generates Captive DOS's 64x32 dungeon map:
it is a separate child program, GM.EXE, that CAPPO.EXE launches via INT 21h AH=4Bh
(EXEC) from its level-setup path (0xC9D9 -> 0x0DBC, name at DGROUP:0x08 = "GM.EXE").

GM.EXE never ran and every state-1->3 transition bounced back to the menu.

game files: it reads mission params from 0000:04F4, generates a 64x32 base via a
placement state machine (0x1F00) + a 2048-cell generate/translate loop (0xEE), and
writes the map to 0x2CF:0x5A68 — producing distinct real base layouts per mission.

Transcribe GM.EXE's per-cell code translator (0x129) byte-for-byte into
captive_gm_translate.c, verified in test_captive_gm_translate.c against the full
256-entry ground-truth table captured from the real GM.EXE plus the door/aux/marker
special cases. Document the full chain in docs/CAPTIVE_DOS_DUNGEON_RE.md and correct

Four features and two defects, 2026-08-19/20.

MEMORY

  claims &0C90-&10FF -- reclaimed DFS and OS workspace -- as a staged
  low overlay, leaving the NMI workspace and the ROM private-workspace

events.title: Reverse-engineer, replay and convert the Nitro Amiga TW music
events.message:
Reverse-engineer, replay and convert the Nitro Amiga TW music

Second driver in the repo: Tony Williams' "TW" format, from tw.Nitro
(Psygnosis, 1990). Unlike the JPO module this is a raw position-independent
68k blob with no container at all -- code, tables, sequence data and 90 KB
of 8-bit PCM in one file, entered by calling offset 0 once per vertical
blank.

- docs/TW_FORMAT.md: the reverse-engineered spec, from the disassembly in
  docs/nitro_dis.txt. Six subsongs, a 50 Hz sequencer with a tempo divider,
  13 sampled instruments, per-frame ADSR / vibrato / portamento / arpeggio,
  a priority-based SFX channel, and the ProTracker period table.
- tools/tw.py: routine-for-routine replayer sharing the Paula emulation in
  tools/jpo.py, including the driver's off-by-one volume table read.
- tools/twrender.py, tools/twdump.py.
- tools/twtomod.py: ProTracker conversion. One driver row is exactly one MOD
  row with zero drift, notes are bit-exact and samples are byte-exact;
  modulation is mapped onto the effect column. Verified against the Amiga
  render at 0.92 envelope correlation with onsets matching to -5 ms.
- tools/twtovgm.py: SN76489 / BBC Micro conversion. Instruments are sorted
  into pitched and percussive by autocorrelation and their cycle lengths
  measured, since the driver itself does not know them. Verified by
  measuring the rendered VGM: 100 of 103 pitch probes correct.

events.title: GUARD the code image, and move the debug readouts into bank 6
events.message:
GUARD the code image, and move the debug readouts into bank 6

KC: DEBUG_VSYNC corrupts the player sprite and the frame digit is
illegible. It was not the debug code -- it was that the flag adds 143
bytes to a code image with eleven spare, and NOTHING SAID SO. `CLEAR
FONT_ADDR, ...` releases beebasm's overwrite check over exactly the
range an over-long image spills into, so `PARA` shipped with its tail
sitting on the front of the text font; `*RUN PARA` scribbled on PARAFNT
and the PARAFNT load scribbled back over the code. The only bound in the
file was `code_end <= SPR_SAVE`, right when the font lived at &3C00 and
3,584 bytes too slack since.

So, KC's suggestion: GUARD FONT_ADDR, which fires during assembly at the
instruction that crosses the line and names the routine rather than a
total at the end, plus the ASSERT to match.

DbgFrameCount, DbgPosOut, DbgEnergyOut, the shared 4x5 digit font and
DbgHexDigit/DbgHexByte move to src/dbgpanel.asm, in bank 6 beside the
panel code they draw over -- the right home, not merely a free one.
Their shims are in lowcode2. DbgEnergyOut's droid type and energy are in
bank 4 and cannot be read with bank 6 paged, so its shim mirrors them
first. DbgSetBg and DbgDeckBg stay resident and must: the blitter calls
them with a sprite bank in.

VSYNC, POS and ENERGY now each build and run -- verified in jsbeeb, the
panel reads FF 11 FF 88 FF, the digit 2, two fields a pass, sprites
intact.

RASTER (59 over), DRAW (83), TIME (154), MAPGUARD (1 K of bank 4) and
POS+ENERGY still do not fit. All of them were silently corrupting the
build before today and all of them now fail it instead. They are the RAM
situation rather than the debug code, and RASTER's and DRAW's
instrumentation cannot move to a bank at all -- the interrupt and the
blitter call it. main.asm's debug header now carries the table of which
flags build, and BUGS.md #17 the whole story.

events.title: Handle WebGL context loss/restore in the Emscripten CRT shader path
events.message:
Handle WebGL context loss/restore in the Emscripten CRT shader path

Mobile Chrome (Pixel 8a observed) drops the WebGL context under GPU
memory pressure more readily than desktop. With no handler, the
default webglcontextlost behaviour never restores the context, so the
canvas goes black forever while audio and game logic keep running on
unrelated threads. Install lost/restored listeners (preventDefault on
loss to allow restore) and recreate the program/vbo/texture -- which
don't survive a context loss even though the context handle does -- on
restore.

events.title: Fix Pixel 8a canvas blackout: gate glitch hash/sin() chain on u_glitch
events.message:
Fix Pixel 8a canvas blackout: gate glitch hash/sin() chain on u_glitch

A live u_glitch uniform (vs. compile-time const 0.0) stops the compiler
folding away chq_hash()'s sin() call, so it runs every frame even with
glitch disabled. mediump sin() on this GPU can return NaN, and NaN
survives "* u_glitch" regardless of value. On the tile-based renderer
this corrupted the whole canvas to the clear colour, matching every
symptom seen (no GL error, no context loss). Root cause isolated by
on-device bisection of each uniform between const and real.

Fix: skip the hash/sin() chain entirely unless u_glitch > 0.0 (a
uniform, not varying, branch -- no divergence cost). Applied to all
three shader variants (GLES, MSL, SPIR-V) to keep their math in sync.
Zero effect under default params (glitch = 0.0 in both presets).

events.title: ste: the raster split banded the BORDER, and cropping hid it (#139)
events.message:
ste: the raster split banded the BORDER, and cropping hid it (#139)

Colour register 0 is what the ST shows in the border, and with a raster split
every group gets a turn at it. Three independent cuts put three different
colours there, so the border grew a horizontal band exactly as tall as the
viewport: measured on the left border strip, #555544 above and below against
#555555 inside.

Every check so far had cropped to the 320x200 image, where there is nothing
wrong — the AE comparisons, the montages, the colour counts. It was found by
looking at a full screenshot while checking the combat and town screens.

st_unify_border(): in each later group, find the slot nearest group 0's slot 0,
permute it into position 0 (palette and remap together, so no pixel changes
meaning), then set its RGB to group 0's exactly. The permutation is free; the
assignment costs a little fidelity for whatever indices live in that slot, and
buys a border that is one colour. Re-measured after the fix: #555544 at all
three sample heights, on three consecutive walk frames.

st_repalette passes may_permute = 0. That path's premise is that slot numbering
does not move, so the planes already on screen stay valid and no force-full is
needed; permuting there would renumber slots behind those planes, which is the
"brown chrome" failure. It still needs the RGB assignment, because the slot
reps are per group and each group would otherwise re-derive its own slot 0 and
band the border again on the fast path.

Also drops the `g == 0` gate on the alignment's position-0 claim, which was
written when only band 0's palette reached the border.

SCREENS CHECKED with vpbands=on, 33 re-bands over two drives: three groups only
ever on screens that commit a viewport. Boot, title and the main menu stay at
one group and are unchanged. The dungeon walk (24-27 colours), three different
town/BIGPIC event screens and the treasure/XP screen all render correctly with
a uniform border.

COMBAT IS NOT VERIFIED. It could not be reached headlessly: the CBTSND/CBTAUTO/
CBTPLAY harness (#74) bus-errors during boot on the ST build — with vpbands OFF
as well, so it is not this change — CBTSND alone boots but its `k` hotkey does
nothing from the walk (the letter-key hit-test eats bare letters there), and the
HEIRS slot-A chain resolves its combat faster than a 2 s sampling interval
catches. By construction it should stay at one group, since st_group_layout
requires s_vp_active and combat does not render the viewport, but that is
reasoning rather than measurement and is recorded as such.

AE=0 with vpbands off against the build before this change.

Measurement, not reconstruction (0 C changes, +4 cases, suite 5,855):
- THE ROW DID NOT FLIP, and the blocker is measured on the original's own
  code: $a4a (walk) and $a4e (weapon) are ADJACENT bsr's, so the frame
  alone must supply player_weapon_fire's entry X — two seeds differing in
  two record bytes leave BYTE-IDENTICAL memory at $a4e and then diverge at
  exactly one address ($b449, the shot count, $03 vs $04; the diff set is
  now ASSERTED, not prose, and the assertion is the one form that catches a
  seeded second divergence — equality, not membership). Identical memory
  in, one byte out: the difference travels in a CPU flag the oracle does
  not report. The overlap_mask_exit_extend treatment claimed for $1260 is
  refuted. PHASE E = threading the walk's exit X (probes $10a2/$1170 +
  $ec8), then the flip.
- Phase C's cost list was short, not wrong: it enumerated the batteries the
  flip would move, never the routine the flip would write. Annotated.
- $a38 body read off raw bytes (# ctx off): nine bsr's, tst.w d7/bmi.w,
  guards tst.w $6ef0.l (abs.LONG) and tst.w $a32.w (abs.WORD) — both
  fixed globals, not the record.
- cmt 0x6ef0 was wrong in both directions: EIGHT operand sites and FOUR
  readers, not three and one; the frame's own fall guard was among the
  missed. THE REAL AXIS IS ROUTINE COVERAGE, not encoding — the old plate
  enumerated one site per routine it had read and stated the total as
  image-wide (the encoding story was refuted three ways from the bytes;
  a lesson's mechanism must be what actually happened, second false
  mechanism caught this phase).
- A NINTH sweep-lie mode, found live: an anchor spanning a line break

events.title: ste: Timer B fires on group boundaries, not band boundaries (#139)
events.message:
ste: Timer B fires on group boundaries, not band boundaries (#139)

The raster-split viewport palette cost +18.5% on the dungeon phase, and almost
all of it was Timer B firing 25 times a frame when only TWO of those boundaries
are a real palette change. A fast exit for the unchanged ones was tried first
and measured 807 cycles/fire against 771 for the full handler — entry and exit
are the whole bill at that cadence — so it was reverted (3929e850) and the timer
is reprogrammed per fire instead.

    presents   off      25 fires   2 fires
        16    13814      13814     13649
        32    19980      19949     19851
        48    23580      24216     23535

Marginal over the dungeon phase (32 -> 48): +18.5% becomes +2.3%. The rendered
frame is AE=0 against the 25-fire version — the split lands on exactly the same
scanlines — and AE=0 with vpbands off against the build before this change.

MFP68901 event-count mode: a write to TBDR while the timer RUNS sets the data
register only, so a written interval takes effect one fire later. Each descriptor
carries both halves — `expect`, the counter's reload while this fire runs (the
spin waits for the counter to drop below it, and that used to be the constant
ST_RPB), and `next`, the interval to program now for the fire after the next one.
The last live fire programs 255, which cannot underflow inside 200 display lines,
so the frame ends quiet and the VBL re-phases from scratch. Trailing sentinels
make a request latched while masked and serviced late (#91) install the last
group's colours again rather than walk off the table.

The variable compare needed a scratch register, so the palette loads into d0-d6
and a1 rather than d0-d7 — still eight registers and 32 bytes, and moveml's
register order is fixed, so the load and the store agree.

st_prof_tbcost is disarmed and says why: it armed Timer B by force, which worked
when the cadence was fixed regardless of content, but forcing it on a uniform
screen now arms a timer with nothing scheduled and would report the cost of an
idle timer as the cost of the split. The wall-clock fixture A/B above replaces
it — one binary, vpbands on vs off.

Still default-off, but no longer for cost: it has only been exercised on the
dungeon walk (the only screen that commits a viewport, so the only screen where
s_ngrp is ever 3), and the one-line-early fire plus the spin is timing-sensitive
in a way Hatari may not reproduce exactly. The gate is a real-hardware check.

events.title: ste: the viewport gets its own palette, on the raster split (#139)
events.message:
ste: the viewport gets its own palette, on the raster split (#139)

ADR-0016 B1 collapsed the ST's per-band palettes into ONE cut replicated to
every band, because per-band palettes produced the #40 seams — a flat panel
spanning a boundary in stripes. That holds for boundaries chosen by arithmetic.
It does not hold for a boundary placed exactly where the content changes, and
the dungeon screen has two: the top and bottom edges of the viewport. Split
there and the 3D view stops sharing its sixteen slots with the roster text and
the granite chrome.

Measured with tools/quant/qvp on the captured walk frames, against the true CLUT
colour of every pixel:

                        viewport   whole screen
    one group             392.5        155.0
    three groups          232.5        107.2      -41% / -31%

and the second walk capture agrees (395.7 -> 245.3, 161.0 -> 106.9). BOTH halves
improve: the chrome is not paying for the split, because it was the chrome's own
colours crowding the viewport out. On screen the night sky goes from near-black
to blue and the frame carries 24 distinct colours instead of 16.

Cost, matched present counts, same binary, only the runtime knob differing:

    presents   wall ticks off   on
        16         13814      13814
        32         19980      19949
        48         23580      24216

Identical through the boot (no viewport yet, so both run one group), +2.7% by
48. The MARGINAL cost over the dungeon phase alone is +18.5%, which is the
honest number — the split only exists on dungeon screens.

So it ships DEFAULT OFF, behind `vpbands=on` in video.cfg. Runtime, not
compile-time: one binary has to hold both arms or an A/B is comparing two
builds, which has misled this port before.

The band count is the RASTER RESOLUTION, not the palette count. ST_NBANDS goes
10 -> 25 because the viewport is at y=24 and 88 tall, so 24/112/200 are all
multiples of 8 and 20-row bands cannot express those edges. Groups (s_ngrp,
s_grp_b0) are runs of bands sharing one cut, and every band inside a group holds
an identical copy — so a tile straddling a band boundary within a group still
bakes the right slots, and `band = y * nbands / h` is untouched in the c2p and
in every draw-time writer in the engine. s_ngrp == 1 is byte-identical to the
old path: the same scripted walk gives AE=0 against the pre-change build.

Almost all of the 18.5% is Timer B: the handler now fires 25 times a frame where
only two boundaries are a real change. A fast exit for unchanged bands was
written and MEASURED — 807 cycles a fire against 771 for the full handler, i.e.
no change, because entry and exit are the whole bill at this cadence. It was
reverted rather than shipped: complexity in an IPL-6 handler for a measured
zero. The lever is fewer fires (a variable TBDR, twice a frame), and that lives
in the spin test, which is the one place in this file with a documented deadlock
(#91). Recorded in docs/planar-plan.md as the open item.

Also fixes a guard that could not fire: the no-force-full test read
s_have_prev_pal, which st_reband sets to 1 a few lines above it, so the
no-predecessor arm was dead and the first re-band compared against an all-zero
previous remap. It forced a rebuild anyway — index 0 is almost never slot 0 in a
fresh cut — but by luck, not by construction. It tests `first` now.

events.title: quant: the remap was the CUT'S BOXES, not the nearest colour (#139)
events.message:
quant: the remap was the CUT'S BOXES, not the nearest colour (#139)

quant_banded built a good palette and then labelled the pixels with the
median-cut BOX each colour fell in. A box is not the entry nearest to its
contents: the split that separated two colours happened before either box had
its final representative, so a colour could sit closer to a neighbouring box's
entry than to its own. Measured on the QDUMP captures, same palette both ways,
against the true CLUT colour of every pixel:

    frame                 box      nearest
    SSI logo             889.1      324.3    -64%
    Forgotten Realms     589.0      378.2    -36%
    UNLIMITED ADVENTURES 1481.3     401.1    -73%
    dungeon walk          198.3     155.0    -22%
    dungeon walk (2)      252.8     161.0    -36%

and inside the 3D viewport alone, 692.6 -> 392.5 on the walk frame.

Visible, not just numeric: the SSI logo's red gradient had a PURPLE wash across
its top-left corner and the UNLIMITED ADVENTURES title had black blotches down
its edges. Both are gone. Rendered through the shipping header by the new
tools/quant/qrender, and confirmed on a live STE walk.

The search runs only over the colours the band actually contains (m of them,
ntot entries each), because those are the ones on screen; absent colours keep
the 4x8x4 bucket table. That is why this costs m*ntot and not 256*ntot, and it
is what makes it affordable: measured on the STE at matched checkpoints of the
same scripted walk — identical reband counts, so the comparison is honest —

    presents  rebands   band t200 old   new
        16       10         3675       3795
        32       15         4582       4713
        48       17         5250       5400

+2.9% on the re-band, about 44 ms of an 8MHz walk, for the fidelity above.
Exact-preservation is untouched: the reserved slots are applied AFTER the
search, so a kept colour still lands on its own slot.

tools: qvp prices a dedicated viewport palette against the shipping whole-frame
cut (this is where the 8-colour question from Curse of the Azure Bonds gets
answered), and qrender prints the picture rather than the number — build it
against two revisions of quantize.h and you have a before/after with no
emulator. quantize.h is now a Makefile dependency; without it an edit left
every tool reporting the OLD numbers.

Also untracks four .ppm renders that dd228b1d committed by mistake. They are
320x200 frame buffers of FRUA title art — exactly what this task's own note
says never to commit — and *.ppm is now ignored.

events.title: wonderboy: batch 41 phase C — $b1a, the unportable verdict dissolves
events.message:
wonderboy: batch 41 phase C — $b1a, the unportable verdict dissolves

Reconstruction:
- $b1a player_pending_event_gate (526 B, $b1a..$d27) RECONSTRUCTED WHOLE —
  the routine batch 40 recorded as impossible to port. The verdict dissolved
  rather than the bytes changing: every callee ($1f54, $19ac, $fe8c, $539e)
  was ported by phases A/B, and the three stack unwinds are exit reports at
  stop_pc checkpoints (six codes over five endings; code 2 deliberately
  absent — the bra.w $1622 arm reports the SAME triple-pop code as $151a).
- The first arm is the game's GAME OVER sequence, read here for the first
  time: the corpse rises a pixel a frame swaying along the type-30 drift
  table through a SECOND cursor at $4f58, then message $17/$40 per
  WB_LIVES, then a two-latch fire prompt (restart vs data-disk screen).
- Two data words live INSIDE the routine's code (WB_LIVES $be2, $c26) —
  the reason the linear listing desyncs here; every instruction decoded
  from raw image bytes; the 526-byte entry pin matched first assembly.
- $a38 NOT taken, measured: flipping the last row removes the
  UNPORTED_TYPE eight boundary cases stand on — a phase, not a tail.
  Remaining unported in the band: exactly $a38's 62 B + $1f34's dead pair.
- 301 fns / 40,000 B / 90.4%, suite 5,796 → 5,851.

Review gate (5 angles + 4 verifiers, 19 confirmed + 2 plausible, 0 refuted):
- THE C BODY CAME BACK CLEAN — first phase with no correctness defect in
  the port. All 21 findings were plates, headers, docs, test structure.
- Byte-verified plate fixes: the reset lea at $fed2 not $fed4; $c6a's
  longword disarm victims are $b0e/$b10 (never $b12, which has its own
  named clr.w at $c6e); the armour write sits three instructions above
  the pop; one branch reaches $d22, the other arrival falls through.
- names.txt lagged its own satellites (WB_LIVES five sites; the $e5ba
  exit-code split); PORTABILITY's $b1a row annotated (440 was the
  desync-truncated scan figure).
- The retraction rule violated a third batch running — the retired verdict
  quoted in four new sites, one inside its own grep-to-zero certification;
  all reworded to describe, certification now names the historical hits.
- Sweep-lies mode 8's mechanism was FALSE PYTHON as documented
  (str.replace('', old) inserts, never no-ops); the true mechanism
  recovered: the runner's count guard refused correctly, the shell loop
  status-checked the APPLY and not the REVERT.
- Test dedup: _record_copy_writes (4 spellings), actor_drift_x_step hoisted
  (gate + type30 share one body, encodings noted per site),
  premise+claim folded into one runner so a copy cannot drop the premise.
- Sweeps: 21 written, 2 equivalent, 19 kept — round 1 caught 15/16, the
  survivor's repair exposed a second site of the same class; final 19/19;
  +8/8 re-spelt over the restructured helpers. hw_portability 56 green.

Deferred (queued): $a38 frame top (62 B) — the 62/62 phase, with the
UNPORTED_TYPE retirement it forces; $e032; the odd drift cursor;
spine/on-target/playable .PRG after the row flips.

events.title: Découple les étalons des ROM Atari, licences dans les paquets, Cuddly ré-activé
events.message:
Découple les étalons des ROM Atari, licences dans les paquets, Cuddly ré-activé

Trois chantiers d'un même fil : rendre la suite d'étalons indépendante du
contenu sous copyright, et réparer l'usage qu'on faisait de l'oracle.

DÉCOUPLAGE (le verrou du 🚨 TODO : 79 Mo de contenu sous copyright suivi par un
dépôt public, dont le retrait « cassait mécaniquement la CI »)

- 4 étalons à disque GÉNÉRÉ migrés sur EmuTOS (overscan_top, trace_odd,
  scroll_8264/65). Neutre et VÉRIFIÉ : leur secteur de boot est autonome, la
  capture EmuTOS vs TOS propriétaire = 0 px / 114816, les références sont
  INCHANGÉES, et l'oracle Hatari est lui-même identique entre les deux ROM.
- ROM absente : deux cas au lieu d'un (rom_is_free). Une etos* manquante reste
  un ÉCHEC (dépôt cassé), une tos* manquante SAUTE l'étalon et le RECENSE.
  Vérifié en retirant les deux ROM : suite verte, 6 étalons déclarés non
  exécutés, au lieu de 8 échecs.

L'ORACLE N'EST PAS DÉTERMINISTE (et ça invalidait un verdict)

- cuddly_demos était désactivé depuis le 2026-08-01 pour « phase d'animation
  différente » (16023 px au mieux). RÉFUTÉ : NeoST rend cette démo
  BYTE-IDENTIQUEMENT à Hatari — 0 px / 114766 sur 220 trames CONSÉCUTIVES.
  Ce qui manquait était la bonne trame oracle : Hatari fait
  Hatari_srand(time(NULL)) (sdl/main_sdl.c) et tire la position angulaire
  initiale de la disquette (fdc.c), donc la durée du boot et la numérotation
  des trames changent d'un run à l'autre (mesuré : n+61 ici, n−2 là).
- D'où oracle_scan : hatari_oracle.sh accepte HATARI_ORACLE_SCAN (fenêtre au
  lieu d'une image) et --oracle retient la trame IDENTIQUE à la capture NeoST,
  jamais la moins pire — sinon échec bruyant, et c'est une vraie divergence.
  Les 7 étalons qui bootent un disque en sont équipés. cuddly_demos repasse
  actif, ref_kind: oracle, max_diff_px: 0. Plus aucun étalon désactivé.
- scroll_8264/65 promus ref_kind: oracle (0 px vs Hatari) ; .ppm supprimés.
- Résidus oracle MESURÉS et consignés, pas maquillés : overscan_top 194 px,
  trace_odd 22 px, tous deux sur les premières lignes de trame et indépendants
  de la ROM (11ᵉ passe de HATARI_DIVERGENCES.md).

LICENCES ET PAQUETS

- Les paquets partaient sans AUCUN texte de licence alors qu'ils embarquent
  EmuTOS (GPLv2) et NeoST (GPLv3). stage_free_data.sh copie
  licenses/{GPL-3.0,GPL-2.0,THIRD-PARTY}.txt (offre de source incluse), l'APK
  aussi, et les 8 vérifications de paquet de la CI échouent si une manque.
- NEOST_PACKAGE_NO_ATARI_TOS=1 construit un paquet 100 % libre, gardes CI
  comprises. Le défaut est INCHANGÉ (décision du mainteneur) — mais le TODO
  disait « les paquets bureau étaient déjà propres », ce qui était faux.
- Préréglages du GUI : repli EmuTOS si le TOS d'origine est absent. « Mega STE »
  pointait sur tos206fr, qui n'a jamais été empaquetée.

Aussi : extern/hatari est gitignoré, n'est pas un sous-module et rien ne le
rapatrie — il était ABSENT ici alors que CLAUDE.md le disait « bâti dans le
dépôt ». Recette de clone + build documentée, options macOS comprises.

Paliers fast et full verts avant comme après.

events.title: tools: qstable — price the stable-palette designs, and the guard that looked exact
events.message:
tools: qstable — price the stable-palette designs, and the guard that looked exact

Next step on #139 was "build the stable palette". Measuring first changed what it
should be, and then caught the obvious cheap version being WRONG.

★ A STABLE PALETTE IS NOT FREE. qstable quantises through the engine's own
quant_banded and scores every pixel against its true CLUT colour, over five
captured frames that share one CLUT:

    ST  16 col   A per-frame 750.0   B CLUT-only 1575.1 (+110%)   C union 1076.5 (+44%)
    ECS 32 col   A per-frame 200.7   B CLUT-only  966.7 (+382%)   C union  331.9 (+65%)

B derives the palette from the 256 CLUT entries alone; C from the union of a
scene's content weighted by summed populations, which models an ART-derived
palette. Even C costs 44% more error. That is the argument #139 says has to be
made before an engine change, and it says: not like this.

★ AND THE CAPTURES SHOWED SOMETHING BETTER. The walk's CLUT changes at nearly
every re-band, so there is little reuse to exploit — but of 13 re-bands, TWO
changed no colour that was on screen at all. One moved 225 of 256 entries and not
one of them was drawn. Each of those cost the full ~364 t200 re-band (quant + used
scan + whole-frame FORCE-FULL), about 1.8 s of ST time, to produce an identical
frame. The shipping guard cannot see it: it is an exact memcmp over all 768 bytes.

★ THE FIX THAT LOOKED EXACT IS UNSOUND, AND THE SCREENSHOT CAUGHT IT. Comparing
only s_used_idx entries, snapped to the hardware's bits, seemed pixel-identical by
construction — and skips jumped 2 -> 7. The frame came back with a BROWN sky
instead of blue. s_used_idx is filled by the used-index scan INSIDE st_reband, so
at guard time it describes the LAST re-band's frame, not this one: anything drawn
since whose colour moved is invisible to the test and renders through the old
mapping. Reverted; the engine is untouched by this commit.

For a future attempt the guard needs a used set that is current at DECISION time.
Candidates: pair it with s_dt_new_ink == 0 (nothing unseen drawn since the last
scan) — plausible but it fired 7 times here and still went wrong, so verify before
trusting; or maintain s_used_idx incrementally as rows are built rather than
rebuilding it per re-band, which also attacks the 82 t200 scan (b59a2781).

qstable is committed with the tools; the engine change is not.

make test 471 passed.

Refs #139, #142, #141.

events.title: Port the collision matrix, friendly fire, and the disruptor
events.message:
Port the collision matrix, friendly fire, and the disruptor

CollisionType ($6D6D) and DoCollision2 ($1B51) replace the two
hard-coded arms the port has carried since Layer 6 -- reverse the first
droid, pause the second. That was the table's $08 entry and nothing
else, which is why droid-versus-droid worked and everything else in the
matrix was missing. The table ships whole, all thirty-two bytes: a
transcription is faithful by construction and a trimmed one is faithful
until the first thing it gets wrong. The player's own collisions are
still separate, because $1A43 branches to _ply_droid before
DoCollision2 is ever reached; his bullet is too, because ours is slot 7
with no droid-table entry and DrBulletHit already handles it.

What the table turns on: EnemyFireEnemy ($1BF6), so a droid's shot and
a droid's EXPLOSION both hurt whatever else they touch, for
2 * (40 - type) of the target's own weakness -- and FreeSpriteTmp2, so
the shot is spent when it lands.

The disruptor is weapon 3, and it is an area effect rather than a
bullet: everything the player can see takes that same damage at once,
and the firer takes energy + type - shipLevel - $20 unless its type is
on DisruptorImmune. Only the 711 and the 742 carry one and both are
immune, which is what makes them worth taking. It runs for four
iterations; the sweep is the first and the flash is the rest.

[DECISION, agreed with KC] THE SCREEN SHAKE IS NOT PORTED. $23A3 jitters
the VIC's fine-scroll registers for three frames; our play strip is
exactly sixteen rows inside one hardware wrap, so a vertical jitter
fetches rows that were never drawn and a horizontal one shows a column
the incremental draw has not written.

The flash is an OVERRIDE, not a saved-and-restored palette. Writing
palPlay looked right until the console opened mid-burst: the transfer
game and the lift view both save palPlay and install their own, so a
flash caught by one of them would be restored later as the deck's
colour. SetPalPlay forces logical 0's four entries white after the
table instead, stores nothing, and a modal screen ends the burst.

Space: main RAM had 90 free bytes and the disruptor wanted 245, so this
also claims &0D60-&0DEF -- Econet and mouse workspace and the extended
vector table -- as the low overlay's second chunk, one file and two
copies, with the NMI workspace and the ROM private-workspace bytes left
alone. LUTs moved to &54C0 and three droid arrays to &0C90 to buy bank 4
back the room its half of the matrix needed.

Verified in jsbeeb: a disruptor kills a visible 123 for 72, costs the
player 64 -> 31 by the original's own arithmetic, pays the score, flashes
for three passes and puts the deck's colour back; an explosion parked on
a droid kills it through the matrix; the pass is still exactly two
fields.

events.title: Reclaim &0E00 for code, and animate the recharger and the alert lamp
events.message:
Reclaim &0E00 for code, and animate the recharger and the alert lamp

Main RAM was down to 48 free bytes and bank 4 to 10, and the two banks
that have room are both paged out during play. &0E00-&10FF is DFS's
shared workspace, live only while the filing system is, and dead from
the last *LOAD on -- the same argument the charset at &0400 already
rests on, one page up. So PARALOW is a sixth disc file, staged clear of
the font and copied down after every other load, and lowbss.asm puts its
mutable state in the 112 bytes at &0C90. Page &0D is deliberately left
alone: the NMI handler, the extended vector table and the sideways ROMs'
private-workspace bytes all live there.

THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE TRICK. PageLowIn writes the workspace DFS is
using, so it has to come after the last filing-system call, and PARAFNT
owns the staging address -- so PARALOW loads last and stages on the
panel. Done the other way round the next *LOAD hangs in the 8271 poll.

DrawDoorTile's body moved there as DrawTileCells, parameterised by a
definition and a list of cells, because the two new features want
exactly what a door wanted: repaint a tile that changed while the view
stood still. That is 200 bytes back out of the code image as well.

The recharger is AnimAllInsideFont ($38C4): rotate characters 76-79
inside the charset every other iteration. Ours needs a repaint after it,
because the charset is not the screen's source here -- AnimScan walks
the eleven visible tile columns for tile 20 and AnimPaint redraws the
eight cells that hold those characters. Rotating the CHARSET rather than
the map's codes is what keeps every draw path agreeing, RedrawAll
included. ChrAnimData1's other group, characters 122-125, is not ported:
no tile references it, so it is not in the 137-character export.

The alert lamp is BUGS.md #13, and MODE 1 has no fourth colour to give
it -- see the [DECISION] in lowcode.asm. Character $16 gets its own
logical instead: black, the deck's highlight, white, and white blinking.

Verified in jsbeeb: the four characters rotate one step every second
pass; a pad poked into the map paints, animates, and agrees with
RedrawAll; the lamp rebuilds and repaints at each threshold.

Cut PLAN.md to what a session actually needs: 535 lines to 156

the decisions of record, and a one-line-per-layer table. The burn-down

events.title: Add a JPO vs ProTracker technical comparison
events.message:
Add a JPO vs ProTracker technical comparison

docs/COMPARISON.md weighs the two formats against each other: sequence
density (676 bytes vs 11392 for the same 153.6 s), where modulation lives
and why that forced 16 of 18 samples in the converted MOD to be

events.title: tools: graduate the quantiser analysis tools, with a way to feed them
events.message:
tools: graduate the quantiser analysis tools, with a way to feed them

#139 cites qfid/qpre/qdither as available tooling. They were in a scratchpad, and
two things were wrong with that.

★ THEY DID NOT BUILD AGAINST main. All three passed a tenth argument to
quant_banded — a band_used out-param that does not exist in platform/include/
quantize.h. It was declared, passed and never read in any of them, so dropping it
is lossless, but a future session would have hit the error and had to work out why.

★ AND THEY HAD NO INPUTS. The frames were captured ad-hoc in an earlier session
and nothing in the tree produces them, which is the difference between a tool
existing and a tool being usable. So -DFRUA_QDUMP now writes the quantiser's own
inputs at each re-band: the 320x200 index surface and the 768-byte CLUT exactly as
quant_banded is about to see them, viewport overlay included (qsrc is s_shadow
when a viewport is committed). Verified end to end — captured a real walk frame
and ran all three on it.

The point of these tools is that they #include the ENGINE'S quantize.h rather than
re-implementing it, so a number is comparable to what the machine renders.
tools/quantsim.py median-cuts an RGB image directly and models an IDEALISED
per-pixel dither; it measures a different pipeline and overstates what is
shippable. The README says so, along with two traps: MSE RISES with any dither
(judge by eye), and the ST runs nbands = 1 today, so multi-band numbers describe a
configuration that is not shipping.

★ AND RUNNING THEM CONTRADICTS #139's OWN CLAIM. The task states that weighting
the cut by AREA (box choice, split point, representative) "is now in". It is not:
quantize.h builds its cut list from PRESENCE — `if (cnt[i] && !kept[i])`, each
colour once, no population — and uses cnt[] only for the exact-slot reservation.
qpre on a captured walk frame: A shipping 252.8, B population-weighted 230.9,
C B+diffusion 594.3. So that 8.7% is an AVAILABLE win, not a banked one.

Both discrepancies point the same way: the earlier work lived in a variant of
quantize.h that never landed, and the task was written up from its results. #139
corrected accordingly.

Captures are frame buffers of copyrighted art — the README says never commit one;
they land in the git-ignored gamedata dir. Shipping binary carries 0 QDUMP strings.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST QDUMP, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #139, #138.

events.title: The wrap fallback drew its digits white, because it never sees colPix
events.message:
The wrap fallback drew its digits white, because it never sees colPix

KC spotted it straight away: black rotor, white number, intermittently.

SprDrawSlot has two paths. A sprite that clears the up-front wrap test
runs the compiled program and takes its pixels from colPix. A sprite
that does not — about one in five — runs the per-row fallback, and in
that loop the digit block never opens: all eight rows go through
SprFetchRow and are blitted interpreted from drSprData, which is stored
at logical 3. Nothing recoloured them. The rotor stayed black because
its rows are still compiled unless they individually straddle, and
usually none do — which is exactly why the number was the visible half.

SprFetchRow's mask loop already holds the byte in X, so the recolour is
three instructions in the same loop, on a path whose own comment says
correctness matters and speed does not.

Reproduced on demand rather than waited for: patching LDA sprNoWrap to
LDA #0 at the fast-path test forces every sprite down the fallback.
Same deck, same droid, same frame — before, a black rotor around a
white 329; after, all black, with the player still white as a control.

Effect sprites are untouched: SprEfDraw builds and blits its own rows
and never calls SprFetchRow.

events.title: diag: the slot churn is mostly the CUT, not the labelling — #146 retargets to #139
events.message:
diag: the slot churn is mostly the CUT, not the labelling — #146 retargets to #139

#146 was opened on a measurement (57.2% of used indices change slot per re-band)
and an assumption (B3.2's stable-slot alignment is weak). The assumption is mostly
wrong, and the counter that settles it is small enough to keep.

A permutation can only RELABEL — it cannot preserve a colour the new median cut no
longer produces. So split every move: does the index's NEW slot hold the same
colour its OLD slot did (labelling could have kept it) or a different one (the cut
moved, and no labelling could)? Over six re-bands of a fixture walk, 124 moves:

    moved, IDENTICAL colour available    22   18%   avoidable by better labelling
    moved to a NEAR colour (<=1 gun)     52   42%   cut shifted slightly
    moved, CUT changed the colour        50   40%   unfixable by permutation

So 40% are beyond any alignment, and the existing greedy is nearer its ceiling
than "57% churn" suggested. It is not naive: it builds a tab[new][old]
correspondence over USED indices, reserves slot 0 for the border by colour, takes
the strongest correspondences greedily, then falls back to nearest colour. An
exact 16x16 assignment would recover the 18% — worth having, but see below.

★ AND THE PAYOFF I OPENED #146 FOR DOES NOT ARRIVE THAT WAY. The force-full skip
(3f39203f) fires only when ZERO used indices move. Going from 55 moves to 45 does
not reach that threshold; only a STABLE CUT does. Better alignment buys fewer
stale planes and fewer #141 freckle opportunities — real, but not the 297 t200
rebuild I was chasing.

So #146 retargets to #139 (offline pre-quantise): fix the palette at build time and
re-bands stop renumbering at all, which collapses the force-full, the freckles and
B5's staleness fallbacks together.

Counter is FRUA_STPROF-only; a shipping build carries none of it.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST STPROF, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #146, #142, #141, #139.

events.title: The player flashes below energy 8, which is the only energy cue there is
events.message:
The player flashes below energy 8, which is the only energy cue there is

$3DEE tests the player's energy against 8 and, under it, indexes
LowNrgColor_t with frameCount AND 7 — or LowNrgXferCol_t in transfer
mode. Both are eight entries and both are a symmetric pulse out of the
base colour and back, ending on white: greys down to black in normal
mode, yellow-orange-red in transfer.

This matters more here than it does on the C64. Layer 9 decision 4
dropped the port's own energy bar because the original has none, which
left the flash as the whole of the readout — and layer-9-hud.md
decision 5 then said the flash could not be built, because a compiled
blitter bakes its colours in. That is no longer true, and this is the
first thing the colour indirection buys back.

[DECISION, KC 2026-08-19] Take the RATE, not the ramp. Eight inks
collapse onto three and two already mean "enemy" and "player", so the
tables cannot survive: rank-quantising them leaves the transfer cycle
barely flashing, every colour in it being mid luminance. So it is the
base colour for four fields and black for four — bit 2 of the same
8-field cycle the C64 counts — which reads at speed as the flash it is
meant to be. Rejected alternatives are recorded with their numbers.

Worth knowing before it looks like a bug: a 001 you fall back to after
dying gets energy 7 from BlowInto001 ($1591), under the threshold, so
it flashes continuously until it finds a recharge pad. A fresh game
starts at $40 and does not. Both are the original's.

Verified in jsbeeb by poking drEnergy: at 5 the player alternates FF
and 0F on a four-field duty, and at 64, with maxEnergy raised to match,
it holds FF across the boundary.

events.title: The player is white, and something else in transfer mode
events.message:
The player is white, and something else in transfer mode

$3DE5 runs at the tail of the C64's rotor-animation pass and writes
sprite 7's colour register every frame. Two arms: moveMode not 0 gets
$F1, white ($3E06), and moveMode 0 gets clr6_xfer ($3E21). MM_TRANSFER
is 0 here too, so the test ports across unchanged, and the port's
SprAnimateAll is the same place in the same order — the last thing
before the draw.

clr6_xfer is SLOT 6 of the deck's 12-byte colour record, the record
Layer 1 already took deckBg from as slot 0. It is never written by any
routine, which is what gives it away. Ripped across the seven schemes
it is orange, yellow, dark grey, red, blue, light blue and cyan — a
different colour on every deck, like the floor.

We cannot have that colour, and cannot even approximate it by the
usual route. Pushing clr6_xfer through each deck's own colourMap sends
it to logical 0 on decks 13 and 14 — the background, an invisible
player — and to logical 1, the enemy droids' black, on six more. So
transfer mode takes logical 2, the deck's highlight: the only ink left
that can be confused with neither, and per-deck like the original's.
The alternative and its numbers are in docs/layer-7-combat.md.

Verified in jsbeeb: L to Transfer puts moveMode 0 and sprColour+0 = F0,
the panel reads Transfer and the droid draws in the deck's highlight;
back to Mobile and it is FF and white again.

events.title: Enemy droids are black, which is what the C64 has always drawn
events.message:
Enemy droids are black, which is what the C64 has always drawn

dMd0_droid's _new arm ($18FA) writes $F0 into SpriteColor — C64 colour
0 — the moment a droid is given a hardware sprite, with SpriteMC clear,
and nothing changes it while that droid lives. Only the player is ever
another colour. The port drew every sprite in logical 3, white, because
that is what the compiled artwork happened to be stored as.

So drs_place, our dMd0 slot arm, sets sprColour to SPR_COL_BLACK. It is
set every pass rather than once at allocation: a slot that has been
round the pool as a bullet or an explosion comes back with the right
colour without anyone having to remember to put it back. The player
cannot reach this code — DroidsUpdate's loop starts at entry 1.

Verified in jsbeeb on deck with a 5xx in view: sprColour reads FF FF FF
FF FF FF 0F FF, and breaking on SprSetColour with that droid in hand
gives colPix = 01 02 03 04 06 07 08 09 0C 0E 0F — the white set with
the high nibble gone, which is logical 1. On screen the droid is black
against the deck and the player is still white.

events.title: Give the compiled sprite a colour it can be told at run time
events.message:
Give the compiled sprite a colour it can be told at run time

The C64 puts every sprite's colour in a register of its own. We draw
from generated code, and a generated immediate is the same colour every
time it runs — which is why the low-energy flash was written off in
layer-9-hud.md as something a compiled blitter cannot do.

It can. export_droids.py writes the artwork at DROID_COLOUR = 3, so an
opaque pixel sets bit 7-n AND bit 3-n and every pixel byte the compiler
emits is P | P<<4 for a 4-bit opacity pattern P. Choosing a colour is
choosing a nibble: &0F leaves logical 1, &F0 logical 2, &FF logical 3.
Across 24 types, 8 phases and 4 shifts only ELEVEN patterns occur, so
the code reaches its pixels through eleven zero page bytes and
SprSetColour rewrites them when the colour changes.

ORA zp is 3 cycles against ORA #'s 2 and the same two bytes, so the
1,038 converted sites cost one cycle each and not one byte of bank —
banks 5 and 6 end exactly where they did. Around 75 opaque bytes go
into a sprite, so ~600 cycles on a full eight-slot pass, plus ~200 per
colour change; sprColCur keeps that to twice a pass once the sources
are wired up. Main RAM pays 61 bytes, 148 free down to 87.

Behaviour is unchanged, and by construction: every slot starts at
SPR_COL_WHITE, and colPix is then sprColPat masked with &FF, which is
sprColPat itself — the same eleven bytes the immediates used to hold.
Confirmed in jsbeeb rather than argued: breaking on SprSetColour with
the player in hand and reading &05-&0F gives 11 22 33 44 66 77 88 99 CC
EE FF, exactly the immediates the previous build baked in. The opcode
stream differs only where it should — 750 ORA # to ORA zp, 288 LDA # to
LDA zp, and 18 new instructions for SprSetColour and its two callers.

A cross-build play-buffer diff is NOT available as a check here: the
title's dwell seeds drSeed, and a build of a different size reaches the
title at a different cycle, so the two pick different decks and there
is nothing to compare. Pin the seed first if that check is ever wanted.

events.title: build the needle geometrically, center the ring, and hide it when stopped
events.message:
build the needle geometrically, center the ring, and hide it when stopped

Three faults Duane spotted, all in the same small piece of art.

**The ring was not centered.** Its pattern was eight wide but the shape sits in
columns 0-6 with the last blank, which is how the sprite byte holds it -- so the
ring drew half a pixel left of its node's center while the needle sat exactly on
it, and the two were never concentric. Most visible due north and due south, as
reported. Trimmed to seven, so both patterns are 7x7 about their own middles.

**The diagonals were wrong**, because the needle was a hand-drawn plus with a
tail bolted on, and a plus does not rotate. It is now constructed: the stem runs
inward from the rim toward the middle, and a short bar crosses it perpendicular
at the outer end. One construction, eight directions, and the diagonals fall out
of it correctly rather than needing their own drawings.

**And it stayed up after the expedition stopped.** The original simply leaves
sprite 0's bitmap empty when not moving. A step here is instantaneous, so the
needle is shown on each step and taken away again shortly after the last one.

events.title: one marker for both modes, a cross for the bearing, and a much denser sea
events.message:
one marker for both modes, a cross for the bearing, and a much denser sea

Three corrections, all from Duane playing the original and from reading the
sprites while the party was ashore.

**There is no landing party sprite, and there never was.** Ashore, sprite 1 has
the same pointer ($2D) and the same seven bytes as at sea: the expedition is one
ring either way, and only the bearing beside it changes. So the invented party
figure is gone -- it was solving a problem that did not exist -- and the two
modes now share a marker. That also explains why no party sprite ever turned up
in $5529 or anywhere else: there is nothing to find.

**The ring is chunkier than it was drawn.** Both sprites are hardware-expanded in
x and y ($D01D = $D017 = 03), so an 8x7 shape with two-pixel-thick edges draws at
16x14 -- about one map tile across. The previous version was 11x11 with
single-pixel edges and read thin and spindly. The shape here follows that
measured geometry rather than being copied byte for byte, which for a hollow
diamond outline amounts to the same drawing.

**The bearing is a cross, not a square.** Sprite 0's shapes are three or four
bytes forming a small cross, drawn in $D027 = $2 red against the ring's $D028 =
$1 white, and it sits on the rim toward the heading rather than out past it.

**And the sea was six times too empty.** Measured on a live frame: 12 specks
among 70 water glyphs, about 0.17 a glyph. A tile is four glyphs, so roughly 0.7
specks per tile -- most tiles carry one. The previous version stippled one tile in
eight. Each of 48 appearances now draws up to one speck per quadrant at the
measured rate, and which appearance a tile uses is still a pure function of its
map position, so the stipple stays fixed to the world.

96 tests pass.

Three things the captures described and the viewer was not yet doing.

static ring -- a diamond OUTLINE with a hole in it -- and a bearing that is a pip
rather than an arrow, three or four bytes rewritten in place at whichever point
of the rose is being steered toward, and left empty while stopped. The viewer had

on it in the direction of the last step, and hides the pip until the expedition

with a red pip riding on it, which is the difference Duane spotted.

**The sea is stippled, and it moves.** There is no wave art to load: the tile
buffers the $5529 table points at hold a uniform $55, every bit-pair 01, which is
solid $D022. A wave is one pixel-pair zeroed inside an otherwise-uniform water
byte so it draws in $D021 -- measured $54, $51 and $45 against $55, and $D021 in
the map region is yellow, 176 pixels of it against 8,800 of water on a captured
frame. On that frame 17 of 144 glyphs carried exactly one speck and 127 were
bare, and diffing both charset buffers across a voyage showed those bytes moving.

So water now gets eight variants, each an animated SKTileDefinition whose cycle
is bare except for a single frame, with the speck in a different place and the
cycle at a different phase per variant. That keeps the sea mostly empty and
twinkling rather than blinking in unison, and SpriteKit runs the animation so
nothing is redrawn per frame. Which variant a tile uses is a pure function of its
position, so the pattern does not shuffle when the view is rebuilt.

**The party is a figure now** rather than a colored block -- still invented, and
still flagged as such. $5529 has no entry for a landing party and the sprite was
never captured: the quest that would have shown it ran out of food first.

All of these are drawn from patterns in source rather than extracted, because the

events.title: Reorder the level-draw zero page so eleven bytes come free
events.message:
Reorder the level-draw zero page so eleven bytes come free

The sprite colour work needs eleven zero page bytes and &00-&8F has no
gaps. It does not need them to be globally dead, though: the colour
table only has to survive inside SprDrawAll, so anything the blitter
and the IRQ do not touch will do.

&00-&0F splits cleanly on that test. bandDo, colFirst, colCount and
sDelta cross a sprite draw — SprSplitOK reads bandDo and colCount, and
ReframeView clears the pair after SprDrawAll has run. The other eleven
are consumed no later than the end of DoRedraws, which the main loop
runs before SprDrawAll. So the five move to &00-&04 and the eleven to
&05-&0F, where the table can alias them as one contiguous run.

Nothing but the addresses changes. Reducing both listings to a stream
of opcode bytes gives 20,238 instructions, identical; the 164 lines
that differ at all are zero page operands inside &00-&0F.

events.title: write down what the position hunt found, and what it ruled out
events.message:
write down what the position hunt found, and what it ruled out

Two sessions of memory archaeology have narrowed where the expedition's position
lives without closing it, and the negative results are worth as much as the
positive ones because they stop the next attempt repeating them.

Ruled out: the position is not a coordinate that counts. The whole 64 KB was
diffed across twenty confirmed single-tile westward moves and then ten
northward, and no byte and no 16-bit pair moves by the step count or by any
consistent multiple on both axes. $0032 survives one axis and dies on the other
-- +10 on twenty west, still going north -- but 135->145 cannot be a column in a
128-byte row. The four bytes at $E22E-$E234 move in lockstep, so they are one
quantity mirrored rather than coordinates.

The likely reason: the map is streamed in pages. $8C = 145 and $256C = 96 held
constant across moves, so what they describe is quantized to a page rather than
to a step, which is consistent with the game reading map regions off the disk as
it scrolls, and explains the complete absence of anything per-step.

What does work is matching terrain, and it is the technique to build on. The
buffer at $B600 holds one tile per byte -- not nibble-packed the way the disk
is -- and a 40-tile run of it is unique enough to find in the decoded 256x400
world by plain string search. That fixed a position at (134,145) with no memory
archaeology at all.

But $B600 is not the display buffer, and this is the correction that matters:
the visible 6x6 window, classified off the composed charset, matches nowhere in
that page, and the page's row breaks only fit a 48-tile stride relative to one
anchor rather than absolutely. So every origin calculation made against it was
against the wrong region. $B600 is probably what is streamed ahead of the ship.
Finding the buffer the view is actually composed from is the next step, and
$3107/$58B8 are where to read for it.

Also recorded because it cost real time: joystick input does not reach the game
through vice-mcp, tapped or held, on either port.

events.title: record what the running game showed: waves, sprites, and a position that hides
events.message:
record what the running game showed: waves, sprites, and a position that hides

Duane got a real quest running on the historical map, which made three of the
open questions answerable and one of them harder.

**The waves are solved as a mechanism, and need no more capture.** The sea is
flat: the buffers the $5529 table points at ($94B0 deep/shallow, $94D8 medium)
hold a uniform $55 -- every bit-pair 01, solid light blue -- and $94D8is often
all zeros. There is no wave art anywhere to extract, confirmed twice: both
buffers are all zeros in the decrypted program image, and $94B0 read as uniform
$55 on a live frame. A wave is instead one pixel-pair zeroed inside an otherwise
uniform water byte, stamped into the *composed charset*: $54, $51 and $45
against a $55 background, pair index 3, 2 and 1 set to 00. On one frame 17 of
the 144 terrain glyphs carried exactly one speck and the other 127 were pure
$55. And they animate -- diffing both charset buffers across twenty moves shows
those same bytes toggling all over the surface. What is left is the placement
rule, which is a reading job in the composition step rather than a capture job.

**The marker question is closed** and already fixed in the viewer: two overlaid
hardware sprites at sea carrying a compass rose, and the $3 ship tile is a map
tile -- which is what the historical disk's fourteen cells of terrain $3 are.
Whether the sprite pointers cycle with heading is still open; they hold steady
while stationary, and Duane reports the heading only shows under way.

**The start position got harder, and that is the useful part.** The expedition's
map position is not a plain coordinate anywhere in $0000-$BFFF. Diffed all 48 KB
across twenty confirmed westward moves: not one byte changed by 20, by 10, or by
any consistent amount, and no 16-bit pair moved by a plausible step. $86/$87,
which $58B8 reads map bytes through, held at $B600 throughout. Two candidates
from a narrower 4 KB diff were disproved by the wider one. The suspicion worth
chasing is that the position is held as a disk track/sector plus offset rather
than as x/y, since the game streams map regions off the map disk as it scrolls.

Also recorded, because it cost a lot of time: joystick input does not reach the
game through vice-mcp, tapped or held, on either port. Movement has to be driven
by hand, which is exactly what boot_demo.py built the demo path to avoid.

events.title: perf: skip the force-full when a re-band moved no USED index
events.message:
perf: skip the force-full when a re-band moved no USED index

#142, after the profile put st_present at 51% re-band during the walk and the
re-band's own split at FORCE-FULL 297 t200 / quant 93 / used_idx 82.

★ FIRST, WHAT THE FILE ALREADY SAID. The obvious fix — rebuild only the rows
holding a value whose slot moved — was TRIED AND REMOVED (2026-07-26, during #61).
Its dirty map is computed once per re-band against the remap ONE page was last
drawn with, and the pages alternate, so the map is wrong for the other page: the
"brown chrome". Reading that comment before proposing it saved re-inventing a
known-bad design.

★ AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS IT COULD NOT PAY ANYWAY. The b4audit counters over 19
re-bands of a fixture walk: 57.2% of USED indices change slot per re-band (range
0-86%). At that churn effectively every row holds a moved index, so a dirty-row
map skips nothing. The force-full is genuinely necessary — usually.

Usually, not always: one re-band moved 0 of 59 used indices, B3.2's stable-slot
alignment succeeding completely. There every plane on screen still encodes the
right colour and the 297 t200 rebuild is pure waste. So skip it in that case —
all-or-nothing and page-independent, which is why it does not inherit the removed
smart-skip's bug. s_remap_gen is left alone too, so B5's copy path (2b1acdd7)
survives a change that changed nothing rather than dropping to the conversion.

Unused indices may still have moved: harmless, since no pixel carries one and
anything drawn afterwards is stamped through the new remap.

MEASURED: fires on 1 of 14 re-bands; AE = 0 against the arm that matches the
256-colour Falcon. Small and exact — roughly one re-band in fifteen, ~2-3% of
in-present on this sample. Booked as that, not as more.

★ THE REAL LEVER IS THE 57.2% ITSELF. B3.2 exists to keep colours on their slots
and is achieving ~43%. Every point gained there shrinks the force-full AND the
#141 freckle class together, because both come from the remap moving under
already-stamped planes. That is a quantiser problem, not a present-path one.

★ AND A HARNESS DISCIPLINE, WRONG THREE TIMES TODAY IN THREE DIFFERENT WAYS: an
AE comparison is only meaningful when both frames are in the SAME game state. The
pre-command-bar reference (#141), a twelve-step drift, and here a twenty-step
drift each produced an authoritative-looking number that meant nothing. Screenshot
for AE at the settle, THEN drive for counters.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST STPROF, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #142, #141.

land the expedition, walk it around, and let it row back to the ship

Chunk four: the coast stops being a wall. The rules are in SevenCitiesCore as
`Expedition`, not in the scene, because landing and walking are game rules and
this project's whole method is to make rules testable rather than clickable.
WorldScene now draws whatever `Expedition` says and contributes none of its own.

The two rules that are not simply "stay on your own terrain" are the ones that
make the harness work, and both are deliberate:

  - Aboard, stepping at land is not refused -- it IS the landing. The ship moors
    on the water it is already floating on and the party walks ashore. There is
    no separate "land" command, exactly as there is none in the original.
  - Ashore, stepping at the ship's own tile re-boards it. Every other water tile
    is refused, so the ship is the only way back off the continent.

Rivers are land here, via `Terrain.isLand`, which is what the manual means by
calling them the fast route inland.

screen and the rule belongs to the core. The message line now carries the

where the original effectively keeps it too.

Two causes behind the jerkiness and ghosting while moving, both fixed here.

The camera and the ship disagreed. The ship's position was set outright while
the camera was handed an 0.08s move(to:), so for an eighth of a second the ship
slid across the world instead of the world sliding under the ship. That is the
ghosting, and it is worst exactly where the tiles are biggest -- the classic
aperture -- because the same tween has to cover more pixels. Both now move in
one step. Snapping is also what the original does: it scrolls the map by whole
tiles and never between them.

The fog repainted all 102,400 cells on every step, which cost more than the move
that triggered it. But a step can only change the alpha of cells that fell in or
out of the sight radius -- a block around where the eye was and one around where
it now is -- and everything else is already painted correctly. Only those two
windows are touched now. `full` still forces the whole map, which is needed the
first time and after the fog has been hidden, since while hidden the state keeps
advancing and the two windows would no longer describe everything that changed.

TODO gains three things, all of which want the game running under VICE and
nothing else, so they belong in one sitting:

    as `animated: true` with a single flat fill. The viewer therefore draws the
    sea as a solid blue field where the original has white specks across it.

    the most conspicuous thing still wrong with the exploration view. The
    bitmaps are sitting in RAM; reading those two buffers off a running game is

events.title: remember where the expedition has been, and offer the original's window instead
events.message:
remember where the expedition has been, and offer the original's window instead

Two apertures, and the explored mask that one of them needs. Game > Aperture
switches between them; Classic is the default because it is the faithful one.

Classic is the original's window: six map tiles square, no fog, and no black.
That distinction took a wrong turn to find and is worth recording. The first
version of this shipped a "Fog of War" toggle described as the purist's setting,
which was backwards -- switching the fog off left the wide window showing
everything in it, which reveals far MORE than the C64 ever did. The original's
constraint was never darkness. It is the size of the hole: every one of its
thirty-six tiles is drawn, nothing is remembered on screen, and what you cannot
see is simply outside the frame. So the toggle now switches the aperture rather
than the drawing, and because the classic grid is fixed the integer scale is
free to rise -- the whole screen is drawn about half again as large as the wide
one manages, which is the point of having it rather than it being a smaller
version of the other.

FogOfWar is game state, not a rendering trick, and the discovery screen is what
proves it: LAND, RIVERS, NATIVES, MINES and SPECIAL are reported there as
percentages *found*, and none of those is computable without a per-cell record
of where you have been. So it carries exploredCount and exploredFraction beside
the three visibility states. Chebyshev rather than Euclidean, because the
original's aperture is a square window and not a circle of sight: radius 3 is
its 6x6 window recentered on the expedition, so nothing is ever revealed that
the C64 would not have revealed. Nothing occludes anything in open ocean, so
there is no shadowcasting and none is wanted.

The drawing is one 256x400 texture, a pixel per cell, stretched over the world
and linearly filtered. That filtering is the whole mechanism: dimming has to
feather ACROSS cell edges rather than step at them, or the explored frontier
reads as a staircase of hard squares. A per-cell overlay of flat quads cannot be
interpolated -- each quad is its own texture and filteringMode samples within a
texture, not between them -- which is the same reason buildOverviewMap draws the
world as one small image rather than as tiles.

Four faults found by running it, all worth keeping:

  - The fog drew mirrored, so the lit circle sat two hundred rows from the
    expedition and everything you could see was black. buildOverviewMap flips
    vertically because it DRAWS THROUGH a CGContext, whose coordinates are
    bottom-up. This writes bytes into the backing buffer, and a bitmap buffer's
    first row is the image's top row. Flipping as well was one flip too many.

  - Explorer's default zoom was 3.0, at which the window shows about five and a
    half tiles -- entirely inside the seven-tile lit block. Every visible cell
    was genuinely `.visible`, so nothing was ever dimmed and the fog looked
    broken while working perfectly. An aperture tighter than its own sight
    radius cannot show fog by construction. Now 1.0.

  - Releasing the classic lock left the classic zoom behind, so switching back
    to the wide aperture inherited a 2x zoom and looked unfogged for the reason
    above. The zoom is restored on the lock-to-unlock transition only, so a
    window resize does not fight the user's own zooming.

  - updateFog held exclusive access to fogPixels while building the texture from
    it, which traps at runtime ("Fatal access conflict detected"). The image is
    now made inside the closure and everything else outside it.

The status under the viewport is two short lines now, because the classic
aperture is a NARROWER screen than the wide one and the old forty-character line
ran off both edges of it. Zoom came out of it: it means nothing while the
aperture is pinned, and the two lines the original has there are better spent on
the world than on the renderer.

Seven tests, including the one the plan called for: sail a straight line and
every column well clear of the ends is explored for exactly rows -3 to +3 and no
more. 87 tests pass in all.

events.title: perf: st_present is RE-BAND bound — and the used_idx scan is store-bound (negative result)
events.message:
perf: st_present is RE-BAND bound — and the used_idx scan is store-bound (negative result)

#142's next item after the tile hit path and the clock. Profiled with the
backend's own FRUA_STPROF breakdown, walk phase separated from boot by diffing
consecutive dumps (the counters are cumulative, and mixing the phases is what
made #125's divide conclusion wrong).

WALK PHASE, per present:  in-present 69.4 t200, of which
    band (re-quantise)  35.3   51%
    pass1                9.4   14%
    vpcomp               1.6
    copy                 0.4
and per re-band (~2 per 16 presents):
    FORCE-FULL rebuild  297 t200
    quant_banded         93
    used_idx scan        82

So st_present is dominated by RE-BANDING, not by conversion or by the composite.
`rows converted` is ~0 during the walk, which means the obvious target from the
cycle profile — planar_c2p_span_stlow at 132.8M — is the wrong half.

★ NEGATIVE RESULT, RECORDED IN THE CODE. The used_idx scan carries a #63 note
calling it "a SECOND full-frame pass ... priced before it is removed", and it ran
a byte at a time through a LONG index. Reading it long-wise — one fetch feeding
four table stores, the same substitution that took the row compare from 93
cycles/byte to ~30 — changed the marginal cost per re-band by NOTHING: 82.0 t200
before, 82.0 after, over 9 re-bands each way. Reverted.

The reasoning did not transfer because #63's win was on a COMPARE (loads only)
while this is a SCATTER-STORE: 64,000 byte writes into a 256-entry table, one bus
cycle apiece. The loads were never the cost. A future attempt has to remove
STORES, and the two candidates are now written where it will be found — including
that the "obvious" halving (scan only the rows quant_banded samples) is a
SEMANTIC change rather than an optimisation, since scanning every row makes
s_used_idx a superset of what the quant actually saw.

★ AND AN EARLIER READING OF MY OWN WAS WRONG: I first scored this as -16% by
comparing cumulative averages across runs with different re-band counts. The
marginal figure is what is comparable, and it is flat.

The real target is FORCE-FULL at 297 t200 — the whole-frame rebuild a remap
change forces, which is the same fact behind the B5 regression fixed in 2b1acdd7
— and behind that, why a steady walk re-bands at all. Both are structural and
shared with #141/#139.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #142, #141.
