events.title: Layer 9a/9b: the text font, the panel engine and the live HUD
events.message:
Layer 9a/9b: the text font, the panel engine and the live HUD

The panel stops being Layer 3's placeholder box and becomes the status
display: droid number, energy, the ageing ceiling, the move mode, the
score, the deck, the alert level and how many droids are left.

THE FONT IS 8 x 16 AND CAPITALS ARE 16 PX WIDE. The $7000 charset stores
a glyph's top half at code c and its bottom half at c + $80, so a MODE 1
glyph is two stacked 16-byte cells, 32 bytes. And DrawChar ($0C5F), after
writing both rows, tests

    AND #$7F : CMP #$3A : BCC _1 : CMP #$5A : BCS _1   ; "see if it was wide"
    LDY #1 : ADC #$20 : STA (cpyDest),Y ... : INC prntX

so a capital's right half is at code + $20 and it occupies two cells.
The export splits each capital into two glyphs and PnStr draws the second
whenever the first is in the capital range -- the same test in the same
place. The map was confirmed against Mobile_txt ($698A), which reads
$46 $18 $0B $12 $15 $0E = M o b i l e, and against Weapon and Transfer.

Consequence, and it is geometry not effort: a glyph is two character rows
tall, so the 5-row panel holds exactly TWO lines of 40 characters where
the C64's eight status rows hold four.

Where things live, and why:
 - the font ships in bank 6 (2,944 B; the only bank with room) and is
   copied to &3C00 in main RAM at boot by PageFontIn, because the panel
   engine is in bank 4 and only one bank is visible at a time. Main RAM
   is reachable from both, and from Layer 10 later;
 - the engine and the HUD are in bank 4, next to drType/drEnergy/drCount;
 - (pnSrc),Y and (pnDst),Y borrow swSrc/swDst, the startup bank-copy
   pointers, dead from LoadDeck on. There was no third pair to borrow for
   the string, so PnStr patches an absolute instead;
 - drNum, the tens and units of the droid number as packed BCD, is added
   to bank 4 by export_droids.py. The blitter's drDigit0/1/2 hold the
   same digits but live in the sprite bank, which the panel cannot page.

Two flag bugs found and fixed in the mode field, both of which read as
"the field never changes" while the shadow byte tracked correctly:
CMP leaves N from the subtraction rather than the value, so the dispatch
needs a reload; and LDY sets N too, so the string pointer cannot be
loaded before the branch. Both are written up where they happened.

DEBUG_MAPGUARD off (its 1K no longer fits below the panel now the font
has &3C00 -- droid.asm says what to move to get it back), DEBUG_VSYNC off
(it wrote its digit over the HUD's droid number), DEBUG_ENERGY off (it
owns the same panel row; turning it on suppresses the HUD rather than
colliding with it).

Verified in jsbeeb: the HUD renders, the energy bar falls as the player
is hurt, the ceiling ages 064 -> 062, and holding fire with a direction
switches Mobile to Weapon.

events.title: Plan Layer 9: what the C64 status area and console actually are
events.message:
Plan Layer 9: what the C64 status area and console actually are

Reading the listing first changed the shape of the layer, so the plan is
written down before any of it is built.

The one-line plan in PLAN.md ran two separate things together. The C64's
in-game status area is eight character rows at the top of the screen --
DrawScreen writes the deck to $4940, 320 bytes into the $4800 screen --
and almost nothing is written there: DoScore puts the score at row 2
column 30 when it changes, and DoMoveMode puts Mobile/Weapon/Transfer at
row 2 column 2 on the transition. There is NO energy bar; energy is the
player's own sprite flashing through LowNrgColor_t once droidEnergy < 8
(AnimateDroids, $3DE5). The console is a separate full-screen mode
entered from character 66, not part of the status area at all.

The constraint that shapes everything: the text font at $7000 is 8 x 16,
not 8 x 8 -- the glyph's top half is at code c and its bottom half at
c + $80. Mobile_txt reads $46 $18 $0B $12 $15 $0E = M o b i l e, which
confirms the map. A MODE 1 cell is 16 bytes, so a glyph is 32 bytes in
two stacked cells, and our 5-row panel holds exactly two lines of 40
characters where the C64's eight rows hold four.

Seven decisions are marked in the doc for KC to revisit, the load-bearing
ones being: the font copied to &3C00 in main RAM rather than read from a
bank; the console taking over the play area rather than the whole screen,
because suspending the three-cycle rupture is a bigger change than this
layer should carry; and an energy bar shown at all, which the original
does not have.

events.title: Plan Layer 12: balance, fidelity and feel
events.message:
Plan Layer 12: balance, fidelity and feel

Not a feature layer. Everything is built by then; this is the pass that
decides whether it plays like Paradroid. Four strands, and the order
matters -- verify before tuning, or a fidelity bug gets balanced around
instead of fixed.

12a, the fidelity audit: every gameplay routine walked against the
listing, each one confirmed identical or its departure written down with
the reason. Output is a table -- C64 address, our label, identical /
deviates / not ported. Seeded with the six deviations already known, so
the audit starts from them rather than rediscovering them. The case for
doing this at all is that 7f and 7g both shipped a constant read out of
the listing without following where its input came from: AddBullet's
"distance" that was a normalised direction, and a debounce applied to
three arms where the original applies it to one. Playtesting does not
find those.

12b, the Redux fix list. Redux is a different codebase -- docs/
decisions.md has the evidence at 1-3% match -- so its fixes cannot be
lifted as code. What it gives is a list of what Braybrook thought was
wrong, and each entry becomes a question about our own port: does the
defect exist here, and do we want it fixed or preserved? Two of the
original's own bugs are already ported deliberately and set the
precedent.

12c, playtesting and balance. The dials are already isolated and listed.
Feedback goes into a session log with the deck and the situation.

12d, performance and graceful degradation. Two questions: is the feel
consistent, given FRAME_LOCK is a floor and a busy deck therefore runs
at a different rate from an empty one; and does an overrun degrade
gracefully. The honest answer to the second today is no -- the tranche
split is the only relief valve and it only fires when the level draw has
nothing to do. Options to cost are listed.

Entry condition is Layers 9-11 done, so it measures the finished game.

events.title: The player explodes where he falls before respawning
events.message:
The player explodes where he falls before respawning

The last thing deferred from Layer 7f. CbCheckDeath is now a state
machine: on the pass energy hits zero the speeds are zeroed, any bullet
in flight is cleared and slot 0 becomes an effect at EF_EXPLODE; one
frame a pass after that; and on the last frame the slot goes back to
being a droid and the existing reset and respawn run.

$15B0 is a MODAL LOOP -- BlowInto001 calls RunGame and RunDroids itself,
eleven times, stepping the explosion image between iterations. We cannot
nest the main loop, since the rupture, the two-window sprite split and
the field waits all live in it, so the same eleven iterations are
counted one per pass and CbCheckDeath returns each time.

SLOT 0 BECOMES THE EFFECT, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE. The C64
draws both: $1577 reads sprite 7's state (the player's), $157C retargets
SpriteNum to 0 -- the bullet sprite -- and $158A writes the player's
position back out as sprite 0 with the explosion image in it. Sprite 7
is never disabled and $15A9 rebuilds it as a 001, so there the explosion
burns on top of the droid. Built that way first and KC spotted it at
once: our player slot is drawn as a 001 whatever he is riding, because
nothing writes sprType+PLY_SLOT until Layer 10, so a rotor spins through
every transparent pixel of the explosion and the two sprites fight.
Taking slot 0 instead also needs no position tracking, because the slot
being animated is the one DeadZone and PLY_Y already place.

THE ORDER IS OURS TOO. The C64 resets the type, the energy and the
weapon before its loop and never moves the player at all, so it can
afford to. We respawn on waypoint 0, and exploding after that teleport
would light him up somewhere he never died -- so only the speeds are
zeroed up front and the rest is held back to the last frame.

DoFire checks plyDying: a burning droid does not shoot.

Verified in jsbeeb over two death cycles: the burst plays with no droid
under it, plyDying clears, drEnergy comes back at 7, the sprite is a 001
at the waypoint and the slot is released with nothing left on screen.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Enemy lasers: the speed is a direction, and a bullet hit is not debounced
events.message:
Enemy lasers: the speed is a direction, and a bullet hit is not debounced

BUGS.md #11, both halves reported by KC from play: "the lasers are
sometimes very slow moving", and "the lasers don't always hit the player
if they are moving slowly, I can move through them".

AddBullet ($34B5) shifts deltaX/deltaY down five, and those are not the
raw droid-to-player offset. LineOfVisibility ($24AE) differences the two
CHARACTER positions, then runs them through CalcDeltaAdd ($25AF), which
doubles both and then adds the originals until the longer of the two
sits in [128, 255] -- a normalised direction vector in 8-bit fixed
point. DoEnemyFire runs immediately after, in the same dMd0_droid arm,
so AddBullet inherits the SCALED pair and >> 5 gives 4-7 pixels an
iteration on the dominant axis at any range.

We had read the listing without following where deltaX comes from and
used the raw pixel offset, so speed was proportional to distance -- and
a droid fires at point-blank range, where that gives 0 or 1. Hence the
crawl, and hence walking through them: a bullet with both speeds 0 never
arrives anywhere.

Two more details of AddBullet were missing and both matter: the shift is
LOGICAL (LSR A / ROR, $34BE) rather than arithmetic, and both speeds are
NEGATED at $3560, which is what turns droid-minus-player into a velocity
towards the player.

CalcDeltaAdd is factored out of DrLineOfSight as DrScaleDelta and shared.
The C64 gets that sharing free by leaving the vector in deltaX/deltaY;
ours tests one sight line a pass rather than all six, so the pair in hand
belongs to another droid and has to be recomputed.

The second half is the collision debounce. DoCollision tests byte_0_6C
in _ply_droid ($1A77) and NOWHERE ELSE -- _ply_bullet ($1AF1) and
_ply_xplosion ($1B1A) test nothing, because a bullet frees its own
sprite the instant it lands and so can only count once, and standing in
an explosion is meant to hurt every pass. Ours had it in front of all
three arms. Worse, drCollHit was set on any colliding pair, and a bullet
crawling at zero speed sits inside the droid that fired it, so the flag
was held down permanently and the player's own bounce went with it. The
C64 writes byte_0_6C in ReverseDroidDir ($1C67), i.e. on a BUMP, so that
is where ours sets it now.

Also corrected: the sprite choice. The subtract chain at $353E is not
the symmetric rule it looks like -- vertical whenever |dy| > |dx|,
horizontal only at |dx| >= 2|dy|, diagonal in between.

Verified in jsbeeb, deck 1 with shipLevel poked to 31: a spawned bullet
has drSpdX +2 / drSpdY -7, and drEnergy[0] set to 64 is down to 15 after
75 passes -- six hits of 8 against ~0-1 from aging.

events.title: Load the disc before the rupture takes VSync away
events.message:
Load the disc before the rupture takes VSync away

The game could not be booted in jsbeeb at all: the second *LOAD hung
forever in DFS's 8271 status poll at &ACAE (BIT &FE80 / BMI, command
busy set, nothing ever completing).

Not the disc image. The identical *LOAD PARASPR typed at the BASIC
prompt succeeds. Bisecting SetupScreen one CRTC write at a time, with
the three loads patched to return afterwards, pins it on R7:

  through R6 (R1, R8, R4, R5, R6 set)   all three loads complete
  R7 as well                            the SECOND load hangs

TAIL_R7 is deliberately behind the row it should fire on, so VSync never
happens and the CRTC free-runs -- which is what makes the rupture lock on
the first field. The MOS's disc code needs VSync. The first load survives
because the drive is already selected; the second needs a seek, and that
is what never finishes.

So SetupScreen splits in two. SetupMode does VDU 22/23, OSBYTE 4, the
C0/C1 latch and R1/R8, all of which leave an ordinary MODE 1 frame
running; SetupRupture does R4-R7, SetCRTCStart, R12/R13 and RuptInit.
The three *LOADs sit between them.

This is the same rule as InstallIrq's, one step earlier: no filing-system
call once the CRTC is in rupture shape. Both are now stated in
bufcore.asm's header.

events.title: Fix the level corruption on death: a teleport must re-frame the view
events.message:
Fix the level corruption on death: a teleport must re-frame the view

BUGS.md #10. The tile map was never the thing being written; the guard
was right and its hypothesis was wrong.

CbCheckDeath respawns the player through SetPosFromWaypoint, which ends
in SetMapFromPos and ASSIGNS mapHX. scrollS does not follow, because the
incremental scroll only keeps the two in step by adding the same delta to
both and a teleport has no delta. That breaks the one condition COPYCHAR
depends on --

    scrollS/8 == mapHX  (mod 2)

-- and the band draw then writes a character's second half 8 bytes past
&8000, into whichever sideways bank is paged. During the level draw that
is SWRAM_DATA, whose first bytes are chardata, then colours, then
tiledefs: the tile characters and the tile layout, which is exactly what
was reported, and which survives a deck change because BuildCharset and
BuildLevel re-read the corrupted source.

COPYCHAR's own header names this failure mode. Nothing had ever violated
it before Layer 7f gave the player a way to be teleported mid-deck.

LoadDeck's re-framing block becomes ReframeView -- scrollS parity from
mapHX, line/iline, bandDo/colCount, every sprSaved dropped, SetCRTCStart,
RedrawAll -- and CbCheckDeath tail-calls it. Any teleport must go through
it. That also fixes the stuck laser sprite and the wrong-looking level,
which were the same omission: the buffer still held the old view and
every slot's saved background belonged to it.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 40 phase C — the honest stop at 61
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 40 phase C — the honest stop at 61

player_stage_transition ($1f54, 656 B) and scene_clear_marker_pair
($1b46, 34 B — renamed from speech_script_step; its callers are BOTH
in the scene-spawn tree, and $151a never calls it): verified 292 /
37,016 B (83.6%); suite 5,438 -> 5,525. The transition's finds: the
swing's first frame is indexed by the SFX ID, its cursor ships zero
with exactly two operand sites — so three of eight authored attack
frames never reach the screen, reproduced and now pinned by a census
CASE, not prose; the $21e4 word is the player's FORM, with SIX writers
— the sixth hiding in the one absolute-LONG encoding among five short
ones, inside the unportable gate, on a stack-unwinding exit: LOSING A
LIFE COSTS THE ARMOUR. The census case immediately caught two-byte
address errors in the plate it pins.

THE ROW DID NOT FLIP, and refusing to flip it is the point: $151a
carries a busy-wait an interrupt clears (non-terminating under the
oracle) and a triple-pop unwind; $b1a is unportable on THREE
stack-unwinding exits (phase C found the third — through another
routine's stack pop); the $19ac tree measured at ~1,220 B against a
592 B partition price, reaching a fourth dispatch table. Inventing a
boundary to make the count go up is the false green PORTABILITY
exists to price. PORTED_SLOT_COUNT stays 61.

The sweep minted two lessons for the canon: A SURVIVOR'S FIRST
EXPLANATION CAN BE TRUE AND STILL NOT BE THE CAUSE (the posture
selector needed two stacked repairs), and pytest's rewrite cache keys
on mtime+size — a same-size restore within a second re-runs the
mutant's module. The overlay hazard's canonical docstring now carries
its two spellings and true count (five firings). The circular
tripwire (measuring a band with the constant it guards) became two
independent statements, all three trims proven red.

What remains of the table: $151a (busy-wait — needs an oracle-side
convention), $b1a's composition, the re-priced $19ac tree, and the
frame top. The endgame's horizon after the flip: the spine, on-target
backends, the playable .PRG.

events.title: DEBUG_MAPGUARD: catch whatever is scribbling on the tile map
events.message:
DEBUG_MAPGUARD: catch whatever is scribbling on the tile map

KC reports the map itself going bad in play -- collision data included,
so this is &3800-&3BFF being written, not stray pixels in the play
buffer. Deck 8, on meeting a droid that fires, surviving until the deck
is reloaded. BUGS.md #10.

NOT REPRODUCED on demand. Two runs on deck 8 with droids firing and the
player taking damage: the buffer oracle came back 0 of 10240 and the
tile map 0 of 1024 changed. Inspection has not found it either, so this
is an instrument rather than another guess.

THE LEADING SUSPICION IS ADJACENCY. The sprite save areas were seven
pages, &3000-&36FF, with &3700 free below the map at &3800. Layer 7c's
eighth slot took that page, so they now end at &37FF and the map begins
at the very next byte -- any save-area overrun that used to land in
dead space now lands on the map, which is exactly the symptom. The
ASSERT still passes but is now exact rather than slack, and main.asm's
comment claiming "&3700-&47FF is clear" was stale and is corrected.

Ruled out so far: not the tranche split (sprSplit was 1 through a clean
run), and not BUGS.md #9's level-draw defect, which does not touch the
map.

The guard snapshots the map to &3C00 at the END of LoadDeck and compares
a quarter of it each pass, ~4,000 cycles, so a corruption is caught
within four passes. The FIRST hit is kept and checking stops, so the
readout shows where it began. Five bytes on the DEBUG_ENERGY line:

  hit  quarter  offset  got  want

Verified by poking one map byte: reported quarter 1, offset 44, got FF,
want 00 -- exactly the byte poked -- and no false positive over a clean
boot.

The snapshot must be the LAST thing LoadDeck does. The first version sat
in unreachable code after a JMP and never ran; moved to just before
ld_spawn it captured boot staging garbage and fired at once.

events.title: wonderboy: plain .st black-screens on real ST; flux-splice disinfection works
events.message:
wonderboy: plain .st black-screens on real ST; flux-splice disinfection works

Correcting the earlier optimism: a plain disinfected .st (no protection
band) black-screens on a real Atari ST — the Copylock IS enforced on
hardware; Hatari's .st emulation was just lenient. A disinfected playable
disk must keep the cyl 0-4 band, so disinfection happens at the flux
level. Built wb_disk1_disinfected.scp: in-place IBM-MFM splice of only
track 0's boot-sector data field (swap sector 1's 512 bytes + recompute
CRC, re-emit track 0 flux; every other track incl. the fuzzy band on
cyls 1-4 copied bit-for-bit). Verified independently: atarist.400/440
decodes identical to original except the boot sector, cyls 0/4 keep
their 12-sector protection layout, boot checksum 0x1892 (!=1234), virus
gone. Write via the proven flux route.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 40 phase B — the walk and the weapon
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 40 phase B — the walk and the weapon

player_step_and_arm ($ec8, 436 B) and player_weapon_fire ($1208,
300 B), both CLEAN: verified 290 / 36,326 B (82.1%); suite 5,353 ->
5,438. Six of the player frame's nine calls now run. The walk is five
sections falling into each other — knock-back, fire edge, the flicker
whose last frame ends invulnerability, the hurt drift that landing
cancels, and the accelerator — with two real asymmetries: turning
right sheds speed twice as fast as turning left, and the run ceiling
is a WORD add compared as a SIGNED BYTE, so a state word of $00fc
clamps the walk to a standstill while leaving the jump at 4. The
weapon is the special attack: DOWN held + FIRE edge spends one BCD
unit off the newest inventory record and spawns the player's shots
into slots 48-50 — a full pool costs nothing, now witnessed at the
allocator's own refusing instruction, not inferred from silence.

The $1f54/$1fa2 extent conflict was resolved by MEASUREMENT: exactly
one instruction names $1fa2 (a beq inside $1f54) — it is a
continuation arm, not a routine, and its fn directive is deleted
before the next reapply could re-create the Ghidra truncation. The
weapon's fireball arm produces its borrow inside the run, making
$1260 the project's first threaded sbcd site a differential can
drive; the other three arms carry the walk's exit X as a parameter,
with the X-preservation census now complete enough to close from the
plate alone.

The gate's round: entry-extend was driven on one arm of three (now
parametrized, arm-local mutant red); the refusal cases had no witness
of WHICH gate refused — and the fix taught a distinction now in the
helper's docstring: the PC bitset marks the ORACLE's execution, so
the witness is a premise guard on the seed, proven by a seed mutant,
not a port pin. A retraction had inherited its target's error (the
wrong flag-raiser, with the correct census three lines away); a
phantom rename existed only in the sentence announcing it; and the
SIDE_BIT plate's "only reader" was 139 operand sites.

Phase C: $b1a's composition (the gate itself is unportable — two
stack-popping jmp exits), the $19ac tree + shared speech_script_step,
$151a, $1f54, then the frame top and the row flip.

events.title: Layer 7f: the droids shoot back, and can kill you
events.message:
Layer 7f: the droids shoot back, and can kill you

An enemy bullet is a DROID-TABLE ENTRY in mode 1, type $25, sharing the
same pool of six sprites -- so a deck full of bullets is a deck with
fewer droids drawn, exactly as on the C64, and the per-pass sprite cost
does not grow.

  DrEnemyFire   gated on the sprite being LIT, which is the C64's own
                gate: DoEnemyFire sits inside dMd0's SpriteEna arm, so
                a droid that cannot see the player does not shoot at
                him. The random draw against shipLevel is the
                difficulty curve -- ship 1 fires on one draw in 32.
  DrAddBullet   speed is the distance to the player shifted down five,
                so a shot from across the deck travels faster and the
                flight time comes out roughly constant. The original's.
  DrBullet      the type counts $25 down to $20 and the bullet is
                INVISIBLE while it does -- four passes inside the droid
                that fired it. At $20 it arms, and on a wall it becomes
                an explosion in place, which is why DrExplodeSprite
                takes it with no special case.
  DrHurtPlayer  the three arms that cost energy: a droid (the stronger
                hurts the weaker, his halved and theirs doubled), an
                enemy bullet, and standing in an explosion. Episode
                edge only -- the C64 debounces damage with the same
                test as the bounce, or a droid you lean on drains you.
  CbCheckDeath  BlowInto001 minus its modal loop: back to a 001 with
                energy 7, maxEnergy FLOORED at 7 rather than restored,
                and waypoint 0. No game over -- Layer 11 owns that.

A BANK-4 ROUTINE CANNOT PAGE ITSELF OUT, and this is where that bit.
DrAddBullet needs efBullet, which is in bank 5 with the artwork, and a
PAGEBANK SWRAM_SPR there swaps bank 5 in at &8000 while the 6502 is
executing from &8000 -- the next instruction fetch comes out of the
blitter. It crashed instantly, PC = &B3C9 with a ROM paged in. The fix
is CbBulletFrame, a four-line lookup in MAIN RAM, which may page freely
and which bank code may call. bufcore.asm's one-way rule covers exactly
this; it is just easy to walk into when all you want is one byte.

Measured on deck 2, one droid armed by hand (type 14, weapon 1) with
shipLevel raised so the gate passes often:

  fire     a new entry at type $25, energy $25
  arming   seen at $20, counted down and visible
  damage   player $3F -> $27: 24 lost, exactly three hits of 8
  volume   three bullets in flight, two armed and one in the muzzle
  death    energy 0 -> energy 7 and plyX 1038 -> 805, waypoint 0

Deferred and written down: the disruptor, EnemyFireEnemy's friendly
fire, the bullet's colour flicker (needs efAlt from bank 5 and a second
per-entry field), and the player's own explosion before he respawns --
the droids' deaths animate, so it is the sequencing that is missing.
CollisionType is still not needed: every pair that can meet is handled
directly.

Main RAM &1100-&2EC5, 315 B free -- the binding constraint now.
Bank 4 ends &BA92, 1390 B free.

events.title: Layer 7e: shoot a droid and it explodes
events.message:
Layer 7e: shoot a droid and it explodes

The half of 7e that needed the effect sprites: a player bullet kills a
droid, which explodes and scores. The arms that damage the PLAYER --
the bump, the enemy bullet, walking into an explosion -- and the death
that follows go to 7f, because nothing can hurt him until enemy fire
exists and they are all the same DoCollision arm. CollisionType,
BumpScore and EnemyFireEnemy go with them.

All of it is in droid.asm, BANK 4, not combat.asm: every byte it
touches is a droid-table byte and DrCollided was already there. It
calls out to main RAM for AddScore and alertLvl, which is the direction
the bank rule allows. Main RAM did not move -- still 403 B free.

  DrBulletHit       tested BEFORE the pair loop, not inside it.
                    DrCollide acts on one pair a pass, as the original
                    does, and a bullet that lost the draw would pass
                    straight through a droid. One bullet against six
                    droids is six box tests, so the question goes away.
  DrPlyFireEnemy    the original's arithmetic including its carry: the
                    ADC #8 picks up the carry out of the second ASL. A
                    droid too strong for the weapon takes NOTHING,
                    which is the whole reason to transfer upward.
  DrKillDroid       Alert += type, saturating; score by CLASS.
  DrExplodeSprite   the droid does not die and get replaced -- its own
                    table entry BECOMES the explosion, keeping its slot.
  DrExplode         mode 2: eleven frames, one a pass, drifting on the
                    dead droid's last speed halved each pass.

Two slot-reuse guards came with it, both the kind that would surface as
garbage much later. sprType means a droid TYPE to a droid slot and a
FRAME to an effect slot, so allocating a slot to a droid now clears
sprKind. And an explosion still owns a slot and still has a table
entry, so it turns up in DrCollide's pair loop and must not be shoved
about like a droid.

No CollisionType matrix yet: it earns its keep once bullets, explosions
and enemy fire can all hit each other. With only player-fire-hits-droid
a direct test is smaller and says what it means.

Measured, driving it deterministically by placing a bullet exactly on
droid 1 (type 4, energy $40) rather than trying to aim:

  damage      (0+2)*4+8-4 = 12, *4+16 = 64 -- exactly its energy
  alert       0 -> 4, the droid's own type
  score       scoreAdd 0 -> 50 = drShootScore[drCent[4]]
  explosion   drType -> $40, slot 6 -> sprKind 1, frame 0
  frame rate  frame 1 -> 6 over 5 passes: exactly one a pass
  end         slot freed after 11 frames
  compaction  the entry vanished, the droid behind it moved down

Bank 4 ends &B7C8, 2104 B free.

Rendering CRTC unit 0 against RedrawAll pins it down. Every feature in

line was 4 at the time. CLAUDE.md's standing warning is that every
scrolling bug so far has hidden in non-zero line, odd/even mapHX, or a
diagonal -- so DrawColumn's starting map row is where to look.

area, so it is close to invisible on screen. That is why it went

events.title: Layer 7d: L fires, and the bullet flies in world space
events.message:
Layer 7d: L fires, and the bullet flies in world space

DoMoveMode ($31B9) is the four-state machine the fire button drives --
Mobile, Weapon, a settling state, Transfer -- and it is more than
plumbing for the trigger: DoCollision's _ply_droid arm takes the
transfer branch only when moveMode is 0, so Layer 10 inherits it.

fireDown is TRUE-MEANS-PRESSED, the inverse of the C64's joyFire. The
key read normalises it once so every test here reads the opposite way
round to the original. Worth the inversion: getting that polarity
backwards is what made the plan claim lifts were automatic.

THE BULLET'S POSITION IS WORLD, NOT SCREEN. The C64 keeps it in the VIC
sprite registers and compensates for the scroll by adding the player's
own speed at $32EA; in world space there is nothing to compensate, so
that fudge does not port at all. CbFirePlace converts to slot
coordinates exactly as DrScreen does for a droid, and kills the bullet
when it leaves the view -- the blitter would cull it, but a culled
bullet is still flying and the slot would never come free.

The two animation frames are held rather than looked up: DoFire reads
efBullet and then efAlt once, MovePlyFire swaps the pair. Frames that do
not animate point efAlt at themselves, so the swap is a no-op needing no
test -- which is why the weapon-0 bullets sit still.

L is read once at the top of the pass and the whole block moved up from
below the level draw, because DoFire activates slot 7 and SprSplitOK's
tranche assignment has to see it. The lift gets first refusal on the
press edge and the weapon takes it if LiftEnter declines. Nothing in
LiftEnter/LiftExit draws, so moving it is safe.

Measured: Mobile -> Weapon on a press with a direction; Z gave
plyFireDX = -12 and X gave +12, both with frame 11 = efBullet[3], the
horizontal bullet; plyFireX 616 -> 628 over exactly one pass, the
original's own BulletDisplacement_t; firing into a wall spawned nothing
but still charged the delay, as $341C does.

Main RAM &1100-&2E6D, 403 B free. Tight, with 7e and 7f to come.

BUGS.md #9 opened on the way: after horizontal scrolling the buffer
differs from RedrawAll by ~62 bytes WITH EVERY SPRITE DISABLED AND THE
DROIDS REMOVED -- two scanlines of one 4-pixel column, repeated down 13
of the 16 strip rows. Sprites, the effect blitter, the eighth slot and
the bullet are all ruled out by that control; it is in the incremental
column draw. Also recorded there: zeroing sprActive does NOT quiesce the
pool for an oracle run, because DrScreen re-activates droid slots from
drSlotOwner every pass.

events.title: Layer 7c: the interpreted blitter, and an eighth sprite slot
events.message:
Layer 7c: the interpreted blitter, and an eighth sprite slot

Effect sprites become a second sprite class sharing every part of the
slot machinery -- the same pool, the same page-per-slot save areas, the
same restore-before-draw ordering, the same tranche assignment -- and
differing only in how the pixels get there.

  SprEfSetup    SprSetSlot's tail for an effect: no digit block, no
                rotor sequence, and bank 5 FORCED
  SprEfBox      frame -> box and row pointer
  SprEfSkip     down efRow0 scanlines; both passes take the same walk
  SprEfFetch    one row, shifted, plus masks
  SprEfDraw     save the background and blit the box
  SprEfRestore  the mirror, from the frame the DRAW used

FORCING BANK 5 IS LOAD-BEARING. PAGESPRBANK picks bank 5 or 6 from the
shift because the compiled shifts are split across them. The effect
artwork is only in bank 5, so an effect at shift 2 or 3 would otherwise
read its rows out of bank 6.

efSrc borrows psrc: it must be in zero page for (efSrc),Y, zero page has
been full since Layer 5, and psrc's only user is SprFetchRow -- which an
effect slot never calls.

sprKindS and sprEfFrmS join sprShiftS/sprNoWrapS/sprSeqBaseS for the
reason those exist: the restore runs a frame later, by which time the
slot may have animated, moved, or been freed to a droid.

One wrap decision per sprite rather than per row. The droid path tests
every row because a compiled row cannot express a walk; the walked path
here is correct either way, so one test up front is enough.

SPR_SLOTS 7 -> 8, slot 7 = the player's bullet at save page &3700, which
fills the gap up to the tile map at &3800 exactly -- the assert now says
that rather than the looser <= PANEL_ADDR.

AND IT INTRODUCED A BUG, CAUGHT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. DrFindSlot started at
SPR_SLOTS-1 and would have handed slot 7 to a droid; FindFreeSprite
($32A8) searches 6 down to 1 for exactly this reason. SPR_SLOTS-1 and
the last pool slot were the same number until now and silently stopped
being one. DroidsUpdate's line-of-sight round robin had it too. Both now
use a named SPR_POOL_LAST = 6.

Measured:
  draw     explosion frame 5 at shift 3 -- 224 opaque pixels in 21 rows,
           an exact pixel-for-pixel match against the frame computed
           independently from the C64 bytes
  restore  0 of 10240 bytes different from the pre-draw buffer
  oracle   0 of 10240 against a forced RedrawAll, after ~75 passes
           scrolling with an effect live throughout
  space    main RAM &1100-&2BBC, 1092 B free

save_memory pauses wherever the cycle count lands, which is often
mid-blit: three snapshots a few thousand cycles apart showed 12 rows, 9
rows and then all 21. The first two look exactly like a blitter dropping
rows and cost a detour chasing a bug that was not there. Sample until
two readings agree. Same class of trap as the &F4 bank check in 7a.

events.title: Layer 7c: the effect artwork, and it goes in bank 5 rather than bank 4
events.message:
Layer 7c: the effect artwork, and it goes in bank 5 rather than bank 4

31 frames -- 11 explosion and 20 bullet -- exported by
tools/export_effects.py as per-frame BOUNDING BOXES: first row, height,
first byte column, width, and only the bytes inside. Unclipped they
would be 4557 bytes and would not fit anywhere; boxed they are 2748,
because most frames are a streak across a mostly empty 24x21 sprite.

  explosion, multicolour, $39-$43   11 frames    945 B
  bullets, hires                    20 frames   1803 B
  tables                                         198 B
                                               -------
                                                2946 B

THE EXPLOSION WAS NEVER THE EXPENSIVE HALF. The bullets are, at nearly
twice the size: BulletSprite_t has 12 entries but every image >= $56
animates as a pair, so 20 frames ship for 12 table slots. The
frame-thinning decision would have cut the wrong thing.

2946 does not fit bank 4's 2565 free. It fits bank 5's 4010 with 1064
to spare, and bank 5 is the better home anyway:

  PAGING   drSprData is in bank 4 because SprFetchRow reads it on about
           one row in fifty and can page around itself. An effect
           sprite is drawn ENTIRELY by the interpreted path, so its
           rows are read every row of every frame -- paging per row
           would cost more than the blit. An effect never uses a
           compiled shift, so it does not care which sprite bank is up.
  SCARCITY bank 4 became the tighter of the two when the level draw and
           the droid AI moved into it. export_droids.py calling the
           sprite bank "the scarce one" was true when written, not now.

So no frames are cut and the twelve-iteration indirection table is not
needed. The decision stays on the record in case bank 5 tightens.

Every opaque pixel becomes logical colour 1, which on the explosion
loses two of its three C64 colours. The deck palettes force it: logical
1 is white on all 16 decks, logical 2 is black on fourteen, and logical
3 is BLACK ON DECKS 4 AND 11. $D025/$D026 could not settle it anyway --
the game never writes them and the listing's dump has text data over
$D022 upwards.

Hires bullets, multicolour explosions, per dMd1_bullet ($187F) writing
SpriteMC = 0 and ExplodeSprite ($1BE8) writing $FF -- which
export_droids.py's header had already worked out and written down.

Verified by round-trip: every frame rebuilt from its stored box and
compared against an opacity grid computed independently from the C64
bytes -- 31 frames, 0 mismatches. efAlt self-inverse over all 31, every
efBullet entry points at a bullet frame, every box inside 21 x 6.

Bank 5 ends &BBF7, 1033 B free; PARASPR 49 -> 60 pages. Boots and runs:
boot staging now reaches ~&6C00 rather than &68B5, further into the play
buffer, safe for the same reason as before.

The interpreted blitter path and SPR_SLOTS -> 8 are still to come.

events.title: wonderboy: disk 2 checked — clean; virus write-protect logic explains it
events.message:
wonderboy: disk 2 checked — clean; virus write-protect logic explains it

Disk 2's boot sector is blank (checksum 0x496b != 0x1234, 430 code
bytes zero, no $140 body anywhere) — only disk 1 is infected. Not
luck: the infector aborts on a Flopwr error ($296 bmi), so a
write-protected disk can't be infected; disk 1 (boot/key disk,
write-enabled) caught it, disk 2 (data disk, kept write-protected)
did not. Also noted: a flux write-back reproduces disk 1's infected
boot sector, so written copies carry the virus; the game boots from
AUTO/SWB.PRG and the Copylock is on the data band, so a boot-sector-
zeroed disinfected image would play identically and spread nothing.

events.title: Layer 7b: the recharge pads, and energy costs score
events.message:
Layer 7b: the recharge pads, and energy costs score

DoCharUnder ($2E7B) is a dispatch on the CHARACTER under the player,
not the tile. Only the recharger arm is built here:

  char 20     RECHARGER. One energy point every 4th iteration while
              below maxEnergy, and 5 off the score for each
  chars 43-46 lift. NOT ported -- the C64 gates it on moveMode, which
              is to say on the fire button, and lift.asm already
              enters a lift on fire. KC's call: L keeps doing both
  char 66     console. Layer 9, with the consoleState countdown that
              both of those arms need and this one does not

SubScore ($3EC4) came with it: AddScore's mirror, its own scoreSub
accumulator, saturating at zero where AddScore saturates at 99999999.
The score is a resource in this game and not just a tally, and the pad
is the one thing that spends it.

Character 20 is uniquely the recharger, checked offline: &14 occurs
exactly once in all 32 tile definitions, as the 2x2 CENTRE of tile 20.
Being the centre of a 4x4-character tile is what stops the countdown
firing as you clip a corner -- you have to stand on the pad. The worry
was that docs/graphics.md lists TILE 20 as the console/recharge station
while the C64 tests CHARACTER 20; they are different numbering spaces
that genuinely agree here.

DoCharUnder calls MapChar, which is in bank 4. Main RAM may call in
only with SWRAM_DATA paged -- true from the main loop, and door.asm's
DoorScan already calls MapChar exactly this way.

Measured in jsbeeb, by poking the tile under the player to 20 so the
identical path runs:

  rate       energy 48->58 in exactly 40 iterations, scoreSub 0->50
  ceiling    drained to 0, filled, stopped exactly at maxEnergy (61)
  BCD        305 debits off a poked 1000 -> 745, one wrap of 255, and
             scoreSub = 305-256+1 = 50. Both exact
  saturate   score BCD 10 with 250 banked -> floored at 0, not 99999999
  control    tile restored: 50 iterations, energy and scoreSub unmoved
  real pads  deck 2's live tile map holds tile 20 at (30,4), (32,4),
             (30,6), (32,6); deck 1 has none, matching level_stats.txt

Main RAM &1100-&2993, 1645 B free.

events.title: Layer 7a: the player gets energy, and the droid he rides wears out
events.message:
Layer 7a: the player gets energy, and the droid he rides wears out

Entry 0 of the droid table is the PLAYER, not a sentinel. droid.asm's
header has said otherwise since Layer 5, and it was true of everything
Layers 5 and 6 do -- every loop there stops above index 0. But the C64
reads droidType, droidEnergy and droidFireDelay UNINDEXED all through
the combat code, and unindexed is index 0. BlowInto001 ($1573) writes
exactly those three.

src/combat.asm is main RAM rather than bank 4 beside the droid table,
because both sides of the bank split reach it: droid.asm pays the
deck-cleared bonus through AddScore and the fire code to come is in
main RAM. Bank code may call main RAM freely; the reverse holds only
with SWRAM_DATA paged.

  CombatInit  seeds the player from StartGame ($1345) -- droid 001,
              energy and ceiling both $40, weapon from drWeapon[0]
  AddScore    4-byte BCD, a direct port; SED/CLD behave identically
  DoAging     DoAlertAndAging ($3E32): alert decay and its payout on
              1 iteration in 16, and maxEnergy ageing on
              drAgingMask[drCent[type]] with energy following it down

DroidsInit no longer clears entry 0. It did, under a comment reading
"the sentinel is always empty" -- harmless through Layer 6 and a reset
of the player's droid and energy on every deck change and lift ride
from here on. Only drSprNum[0] is still cleared.

gameTick is a new main-RAM counter, once per iteration and never reset
-- the C64's frameCount. drTick was the obvious candidate and is wrong:
DroidsInit zeroes it per deck load, restarting the ageing phase every
time you change deck.

export_droids.py emits drCent, drWeapon, drAgingMask and drAlertScore,
56 bytes, checked against the listing byte for byte.

Measured in jsbeeb: maxEnergy $3F->$3B over ~530 iterations, 4 points
against 530/128 = 4.1 for class 0's $7F mask, with energy tracking it
down; drType[0] and drEnergy[0] survive a hop to deck 2, which is the
regression the DroidsInit change exists to prevent; frame lock still 2.
Main RAM &1100-&2922, 1758 B free; bank 4 ends &B5FB, 2565 B free.

DEBUG_ENERGY defaults on and puts the state on panel row 1 as hex. The
panel is Layer 9's, so nothing in the rest of this layer is verifiable
by eye without it. ~800 cycles, 1% of a pass, after the drawing where
it touches no buffer.

events.title: Add porting sections, starting with U1.INTRO; fix %def collection
events.message:
Add porting sections, starting with U1.INTRO; fix %def collection

Every implementation chapter will end with a porting section on its own
page: a complete specification of one original file, written so a reader
who never opens the assembly can reimplement it. The named targets are a
plain Python program and a Godot project, and the second is why no
pseudocode may assume a blocking frame loop.

New chapter "The porting path" closes Part I with the contract, the
pseudocode conventions, the asset tree, and the order to build a port in.
Part I keeps the cross-cutting design; porting pages own module-local
behaviour and link back rather than restate.

The pilot is the title sequence: six figures, four tables, the actor
frame loop and every actor as pseudocode, timing in milliseconds, the
host interface, and what to drop. Artwork is extracted to assets/intro
and assets/titles by export_assets.py, registered in targets.json
site_pregen; weave_html.py copies the tree to the site as game-assets/.

A throwaway Python program written from the rendered page and the assets
alone reproduces one attract pass. It found three gaps, all fixed here:
no screen coordinates for the pennant, star and glint bytes; no exported
full-screen images; and a "title image" that is really the publisher's
logo. The evidence also corrected five claims: the five STEP_IMG_PTRS
frames are caption panels and panel 3 is never shown; SCORE_BEAT's
pennant flutter is driven by bit 2, not bit 0; the star twinkles only
after the castle sweep; STRIP_CASCADE is never called; and INTRO_FLAG is
a pass counter with a sixteen-pass cycle, not a mailbox shared with
MI.U1.

weave.py collected only the first @ %def line of a run, because each
further line opens a doc chunk of its own and the old loop looked one
chunk back. It now walks the run forward from the code chunk, which
makes 355 previously dropped identifiers linkable. Honouring every line
collides ten soft-switch and ROM identifiers that each target
legitimately redeclares, so defining chunks are recorded in source order
and only a repeat within one chunk name is an error. weave_html.py
resolves a symbol to the definition on the current page when there is
one.

16/16 targets byte-perfect, chunk placement clean, site builds with 29
pages and no broken links.

events.title: Merge layer7-raster-tranches: the sprite pool splits across the two windows
events.message:
Merge layer7-raster-tranches: the sprite pool splits across the two windows

A pass is two fields and each opens a 24,576-cycle window with the play
area blanked. Restoring and drawing the whole pool costs 36,274, so it
cannot fit in one — and a sprite erased in one window and redrawn in the
next is displayed missing in between, which is the flicker.

The pool now splits into two tranches, each restored AND drawn inside its
own window. Tranches are unions of connected components of the overlap
graph, not slot ranges, so the player and a droid walking beside him
share a window instead of refusing the split. It never refuses on
balance: an unbalanced split still gives one tranche a clean window, and
if everything overlaps it all lands in tranche A and the pass behaves as
it did before.

The loop counts windows in the IRQ rather than consuming a flag, because
a boolean coalesces and turns a small overrun into a whole extra field.
A pass is now dated from the window it starts in: not shorter than
FRAME_LOCK fields, and allowed to be longer.

Still drawn whole on any pass where something else writes the buffer — a
band, a column, or a door mid-move — because tranche B is on screen while
the level draw runs. That is what step 3 in docs/raster-timing.md is for.
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Never refuse the split on balance
events.message:
Never refuse the split on balance

SprAssignTr gave up and drew the pool whole when a tranche came out
bigger than the four sprites a window holds. That is the wrong trade: an
oversized tranche is doing exactly what the whole pool does today, and
the other tranche still gets a clean window, so an unbalanced split is
strictly better than none.

The degenerate case now falls out of the same rule rather than needing
its own: if everything overlaps everything it is one component, it all
goes to tranche A with the player, tranche B is empty, and the pass
behaves as it did before any of this. SPR_TR_MAX goes with the branch.

Verified that it still builds, runs and splits. I did not manage to
stage a five-sprite cluster live to exercise what the cap used to
refuse: poking droids into a heap does not survive a pass of their own
AI, which walks them apart again. The change only deletes a rejection
branch, so the assignment it falls through to is the one already
verified byte-exact against RedrawAll.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Tranches are overlap components, not slot ranges
events.message:
Tranches are overlap components, not slot ranges

Splitting the pool by slot index put the player in tranche A and a droid
walking beside him in B, so the commonest thing on screen tripped the
overlap guard and the split almost never fired — which is why the
flicker was unchanged in play.

Overlapping sprites have to share a tranche, so the tranches are unions
of connected components of the overlap graph. SprAssignTr labels each
active slot with its own index, merges labels across every overlapping
pair, and hands whole components to whichever tranche is emptier. Slot 0
is looked at first and ties go to A, so the player is always in the
window drawn first. Seven slots makes the naive algorithm free.

It gives up and draws the pool whole when a component comes out larger
than SPR_TR_MAX = 4, which is what a window holds, and on the one pass a
droid leaves the window: a slot that is no longer drawable but still
holds a saved background must be restored at the position it was DRAWN
at, and the assignment does not know that position.

The restore and draw now walk the whole pool and skip slots not in the
tranche, so within a tranche two overlapping sprites are still put back
in the reverse of the order they were drawn.

Verified on deck 1, where the fixed split was refused continuously:
sprSplit is 1 at the spawn, the player and a droid land in A and B when
apart, and the oracle on a split pass with all three draw sites disabled
is 0 of 10240.

The prose carried artifacts of the investigation that produced it. A

Removed:

    and the bullet already states the dimensions.
  - "rounds" as a unit of RE effort, in four places ("verify in the
    castle round", "the TWN and CAS rounds cover the other half",
    "noted to verify in the later overlay rounds", "confirmed in the
    TWN and CAS rounds"). These now name the chapter or section.
  - staleness markers: "settles that chapter's last open question",

events.title: Count windows in the IRQ instead of consuming a flag
events.message:
Count windows in the IRQ instead of consuming a flag

drawFlag was a boolean and boolean state coalesces: work that runs past
two of the IRQ's window openings sets it twice, the loop can only see
one, so it consumes a stale release and then blocks for the next —
turning a 2.3-field overrun into a 3-field pass. With two waits per pass
that is easy to hit.

fieldCount is bumped at fire 3 and WaitUntilField spins until the
counter reaches a target, returning at once if it is already past it.
The comparison is a signed subtract, so it is right across the 8-bit
wrap for anything within 127 fields.

It also makes the pass's contract explicit and puts it in one place: a
pass is dated from the window it starts in, waits for start+1 to open
the second window and start+FRAME_LOCK to begin the next. Not shorter
than FRAME_LOCK fields, and allowed to be longer — an overrun carries on
from wherever it landed rather than being rounded up to the next
boundary, so a heavy pass costs what it costs and the rate recovers on
the next one. That is a trade against the movement model, which wants a
fixed-length pass: a brief overrun now reads as a brief speed-up instead
of a step down to 16.7 Hz for as long as the load lasts.

The DEBUG_VSYNC digit still reads 2 stationary and scrolling on the
diagonal with droids on screen, and the picture is unchanged. The buffer
writes and their order are untouched by this, so the oracle has nothing
new to catch.

events.title: Step 2: the pool splits across the two off-display windows
events.message:
Step 2: the pool splits across the two off-display windows

Each tranche is restored AND drawn inside one window, so no field ever
displays a sprite that has been erased and not yet put back — which is
the flicker. Per sprite the pair costs 5,814 and a window is 24,576, so
four fit one and eight fit the two.

Two guards, both in SprSplitOK, and a pass that fails either draws the
pool whole as before:

  - nothing else may write the buffer, because tranche B is still on
    screen while the level draw runs and a band, column or door tile
    over it corrupts its save permanently. A door being HELD OPEN is
    static and does not count: bit 6 is set by the probes in CheckWalls,
    which now run before the decision, and DoorsUpdate neither
    decrements nor dirties it. Testing numDoors instead cost the split
    almost everywhere on deck 1, where four doors are usually open.
  - no sprite may straddle the tranches, since restore-all-then-draw-all
    only holds within one.

The movement moved above the erase so the first guard is answerable — it
is what decides how much work DoRedraws has. Nothing is lost by it: the
restore replays the addresses the draw recorded.

Verified: renders correctly, sprSplit goes to 1 when both guards pass,
and on a split pass with all three draw sites disabled the buffer is
0 of 10240 against a forced RedrawAll.

Honest limitation, written up in docs/raster-timing.md: the fixed 0-2 /
3-6 split means a droid walking beside the player is in the opposite
tranche, so the commonest thing on screen refuses the split. Assigning
tranches by overlap component rather than slot index is the next move.

events.title: Step 1: the droid AI runs after the drawing, not before it
events.message:
Step 1: the droid AI runs after the drawing, not before it

DroidsUpdate writes nothing into the play buffer, and at ~17,000 cycles
it was the single largest thing standing between the off-display window
opening and the level draw. Measured, the work ahead of DoRedraws came to
30,780 cycles against a 22,016-cycle deadline — the CRTC latches the new
scroll at fire 1 — so the newly exposed column was being written while
the beam displayed it. That is the edge tearing.

Moving it below SprDrawAll puts it in the play area's own display period,
where a routine that touches no buffer costs nothing visible. The player's
movement stays above the level draw because the scroll depends on it.

128 passes scrolling on the diagonal, entering with the play area on
screen:

  DoRedraws     116 of 128  ->  0 of 128
  SprDrawAll    120 of 128  ->  0 of 128
  leaving SprDrawAll   75   ->  35 of 128

So the level draw is wholly inside the window now, and the sprite draw
starts inside it and finishes there on 93 passes of 128 — and on those 93
the restore and the draw share a window, which is the condition for a
sprite never to be displayed erased. Step 2 closes the other 35.

Cost is one pass of latency on droid positions, invisible at 25 Hz. The
three properties that make it safe after the draw are written out at the
call site. Frame lock untouched: 128 passes in 10,223,616 cycles exactly,
and the buffer oracle is 0 of 10240 after a diagonal scroll.

events.title: droid.asm moves into bank 4
events.message:
droid.asm moves into bank 4

It reads waypoints, droid speeds and the per-deck tables, and it calls
MapChar on every wall probe — all of which are already in bank 4 — so it
belongs beside them rather than in the main RAM it was crowding out.
Main RAM goes &1100-&2F99 -> &1100-&2600, 2,560 bytes free against 116;
bank 4 ends &B5C3 with 2,621 free.

The rule in bufcore.asm's header is what makes it safe, and all four
entry points satisfy it: NewShipDroids at startup, DroidsInit and
DrSpawnPoint from LoadDeck, DroidsUpdate from the main loop — every one
of them with SWRAM_DATA paged, which is the resting state. The other
direction was already free: bank code calls main RAM whenever it likes,
which is how DrCheckAdvance reaches DoorProbe and how DrScreen writes
sprite.asm's slot arrays.

Verified: 0 of 10240 against a forced RedrawAll after a diagonal scroll,
drCount 12 on deck 1 and 7 on deck 8, and the droids still patrol.

events.title: Where the main loop sits against the raster, and a correction
events.message:
Where the main loop sits against the raster, and a correction

docs/raster-timing.md: the frame in scanlines and cycles, which phases
write the play buffer, where each one actually lands against the beam,
and a staged plan for the flicker and the edge tearing KC reported after
Layer 6 went in.

It corrects layer-5-blitter.md, which had the off-display window at 184
scanlines and 11,776 cycles and concluded no rescheduling could fit. Both
numbers were wrong — a scanline is 128 CPU cycles at 2MHz, not 64, and
the window is 192 scanlines. It is 24,576 cycles and there are TWO per
pass: 49,152 against 36,274 of sprite work. The work fits. It is in the
wrong places.

Measured with the ruptState histogram, 128 passes scrolling diagonally:
DoRedraws runs with the play area on screen on 116-124 passes of 128 and
SprDrawAll on 120, finishing during the display more often than not. Only
the restore is inside the window.

Both symptoms fall out of that. The edge tears because the level draw
writes the newly exposed column after fire 1 has already latched the new
scroll. Sprites blink at 25 Hz because the gap between the erase and the
redraw is ~40,000 cycles — longer than a field — so a display period
always falls inside it.

Layer 6 is what pushed it there, and the arithmetic is direct: the work
ahead of DoRedraws went from ~13,800 to 30,780 against a 22,016-cycle
latch deadline, almost all of it DroidsUpdate.

events.message:
Empty the table entry when a deck's roster has no droid there

DroidsInit skipped an index whose roster slot was empty, leaving the LAST
deck's droid in it — type, energy and position. drCount is then set to the
whole table on the assumption that a hole has zero energy so the
compaction drops it, and a hole did not have zero energy. Every deck after
the first inherited the previous deck's droids, standing at the previous
deck's coordinates inside the new deck's walls.

KC found it in play and the decisive detail was "two 247s": a duplicate
droid number is a ghost, not a pathfinding failure. Four of the stuck
droids on deck 8 stood on rows 6, 18 and 26 — deck 8 has no waypoints
there and deck 1 has them exactly.

Deck 8 from a cold boot, same route: drCount 14 -> 7 (it holds 6 droids),
droids on a solid cell 4 -> 0, stuck 8 of 13 -> 2 of 6 with both of those
explained. Deck 2 now gives exactly its 2 droids. Buffer oracle still
0 of 10240.

The table starts zeroed, so the first deck entered is always clean and
only the second shows it — which is why every unattended check in Layers
5 and 6 missed it. They all ran on deck 1 from cold.

events.title: wonderboy: boot sector is a resident virus, not the Copylock
events.message:
wonderboy: boot sector is a resident virus, not the Copylock

Disassembled disk 1's factory boot sector (freshly dumped, checksum
0x1234, the sector the TOSEC preservation copy lost). Premise refuted
on every axis, independently re-verified: no SR write, no trace/illegal
vectors, no $ff86/88/fa hardware access, body entropy 5.68 bits/byte
(plaintext) — none of the Rob Northen trace-vector-decoder markers. It
is a self-replicating boot-sector virus: 430 bytes resident at $140,
hooks hdv_bpb, rewrites every floppy's boot sector, mouse-reverse
payload every 5th infection. Returns to TOS — the game boots normally
from AUTO/SWB.PRG, which is why it went unnoticed.

The Copylock lives in SWB.PRG's encrypted body, consistent with the
existing note on disk_check_signature ($5e3e): boot+2 must be $face,
reached only from the encrypted body, and no surviving boot sector
satisfies it. The black-screen hang is that Copylock issuing raw READ
TRACK against an hxcfe STX with no track image — not the boot sector.

Corollary: SAGROTAN did not overwrite the TOSEC boot sector at random —
it disinfected an infected disk. Both surviving disk-1 boot sectors are
post-infection; the genuine $face master is preserved nowhere here.
Acceptance test for any future dump: word at boot+2 == $face.

Note: projects/wonderboy/notes/bootsector.md (full annotated disasm,
READ-TRACK-by-elimination, no game-side key handoff).

events.title: stop the World Maker hanging on the seeds that never finish
events.message:
stop the World Maker hanging on the seeds that never finish

The World Maker does not always produce a world. Swept over its whole input
space -- every seed from 1 to 65,535 in all three configurations, 196,605
worlds -- 37,000 of them produce no map: 28,508 that never terminate and 8,492
that hit $2473's restart, which the port throws rather than loops. That is
18.8%, not a corner case. The viewer draws a fresh seed on every "Generate
World", so roughly one click in five would have hung the app forever.

TODO.md called this insurance against something that "terminates on every seed
and configuration measured". Nine seed and configuration pairs had been
measured. Nine is not a sample.

What is here:

WorldMakerRNG counts draws and carries a ceiling. Every unbounded rejection
sampler in the pipeline gives up when the count passes it -- $0FF8 redrawing
until its throw lands on land, $22B4 until the byte falls in range, $4373 until
an even row falls inside a band, $4A37 until a village fits. None of those can
spin without drawing, so one counter on the generator sees all of them,
including any nobody has enumerated. WorldMaker.world(config:seed:) throws
WorldMakerRNG.Stuck; there is no partial result worth keeping, because the
loops give up where they stand and everything after them is drawn from a
generator that is out of step.

Counting draws was not enough, and that is the finding worth keeping. A whole
second class of loop spins without ever touching the generator, so no counter
on it can see them: $194E and $1961 (the flood fill's row scans), $17F2 and
$1816 (the isthmus), $3268 (the treeline), $369F (the river carry) and $4021
(the land runs) all step a wrapping column with no stop of their own, and
$16D1's unwind can walk the undo ring forever. Each of those now bounds itself
at the point where it would be repeating work it has already done -- one lap of
a wrapping column, one pass of the ring -- and reports through declareStuck().

$16EC is a real hole in the original rather than a transcription slip. Its
ring-full guard compares the slot counter $46 against the slot the search
started from, which $2507 computes as $46 + 1 as a byte. The ring holds 201
entries, so $46 runs 0 to 200; a search beginning on the last slot looks for
slot 201, a value the counter never takes, and the unwind circles the ring
without ever recognizing that it has come all the way round.

The ceiling cannot decide what a seed generates, and that is measured rather
than argued. The whole space was swept twice, at twenty million draws and at
the fifty million shipped here, and the two runs agree exactly: the same 37,000
failures split the same six ways, and the same worst finishing world at
13,175,820 draws (seed $5D28, configuration 1). A third run with the ceiling at
two billion -- off, for all purposes -- agrees as well. Not one world anywhere
was rescued or cut off by where the ceiling sits. What extra room does cost is
time, since a run going nowhere spends its whole budget before anything
notices: two billion took eight times as long to give up for identical answers.
Fifty million is margin against the long tail without the wait.

The viewer now tries eight seeds a click instead of beeping on the first
failure, which at 18.8% puts an empty click at about one in two million.

All 80 tests pass, and pass unchanged, which is the check that matters: the
watchdog altered no map.

The method is in NOTES.md and is the reusable part. Three of these sites were
found by running the sweep, waiting for it to stall, and sampling the stalled
process -- the call graph names the routine outright, in minutes each, where
reading would have taken hours. The third was invisible from the caller,
because the loop that never returned sat one frame below the guard meant to
stop it. Reasoning about which loops could spin produced a list that was right
about the samplers and missed the wrapping scans entirely; a fix that does not
make the sweep get further is not a fix.

events.title: Correct the prose claims the evidence contradicts
events.message:
Correct the prose claims the evidence contradicts

An audit against the assembly, the reference binaries and the figures
turned up a handful of statements the document could not support.

The engine's extent was the substantive one. MI.U1 is 6589 bytes, so it
spans $7000-$89BC and reaches 103 bytes past $8956 -- the disk-layout
chapter claimed it "ends exactly where the overlay region begins", and
the memory map repeated the wrong end address. That tail is not slack:
it is OVERLAY_ENTRY's one-shot startup code, which hooks Reset, BLOADs
STUPH, and is overwritten by the first overlay the engine loads. Three
other chapters already had $89BC right. The same map understated the
overlay region as ending at $ABFF when DNG reaches $B098, and omitted
MAKE.INDATA entirely; CLAUDE.md carried the engine error too.

Smaller corrections: TCMAPS is a 20-byte pointer directory plus ten
764-byte records (10 x 764 left 20 bytes unexplained); the packed world
map arrives at MAP_BASE and is stashed up to MAP_PACKED by OUT, which
is inside the overlay window, not above it; the two references to a
"data appendix" now cite the game-data chapter (via a new sec:tcmaps
anchor) and the TWN chapter's own data section; chapter 15 no longer
describes itself as a work in progress. Prose naming symbols that do
not exist is fixed at the source -- HIT_ENEMY -> EXPLODE, CMD_MOVE_N ->
TM_MOVE_N, DRAW_BOX..DRAW_LADDER_DN -> the real span DRAW_COFFIN..

events.title: Measure the flicker instead of inferring it
events.message:
Measure the flicker instead of inferring it

The raster-ordered updating item had never been instrumented. ruptState
says where the beam is — state 2 means the play area is on screen — so
four histograms bumped either side of the two pool calls answer it for
about 20 bytes and no cycles worth counting.

Over 128 passes: the restore runs inside the off-display window every
single time, and the draw is still running with the beam over it on 120
of them. That is the flicker, and it is not a race that sometimes goes
wrong — it is the normal case.

It also rules out the cheap fix. The window is 184 scanlines, 11,776
cycles, and the draw half alone is about 24,000, so no scheduling of the
existing work fits inside it. What remains is ordering the pool against
the beam, which means restoring and drawing a sprite as one unit, which
breaks the restore-all-then-draw-all invariant for the same reason
round-robin did. The overlap problem has to be solved first.

The instrumentation is not kept: main RAM has 116 bytes left. The method
is written down in docs/layer-5-blitter.md and takes ten minutes to redo.

tenth of the whole pass, on a question whose answer only changes when a
droid walks through a doorway. The slots take turns instead, and a droid
that has just come into view is tested at once rather than waiting for
its turn — so the only visible cost is that a droid stepping behind a
wall can stay drawn for five more passes, a fifth of a second.

  DroidsUpdate, 11 droids, before round-robin   20,238
  after                                         16,967
  six droids poked around the player            14,146

against 15,576 for Layer 5's movement alone, so line of sight and
collision together now cost about 1,400 cycles a pass. The loop still
holds its two-field lock in every case: 128 passes in exactly
10,223,616 cycles.

with the draw disabled, at line = 1 after a full-speed diagonal scroll.

events.title: Layer 6: mode dispatch, line of sight, and collision
events.message:
Layer 6: mode dispatch, line of sight, and collision

DroidRun now dispatches on the mode in the top bits of the type, as
DroidModeJump does; bullets and explosions arrive in Layer 7 and until
then a type claiming to be one is simply not run.

DrLineOfSight is LineOfVisibility ($24AE) with CalcDeltaAdd's scaling
trick intact — double the delta pair while both fit in a byte, then add
the originals — so the long axis steps about one character and there is
no division. The original walks a pointer into a 16K character map and
compares pointers to know when it has arrived; we have no such map, so
the coordinates are held apart and the walk ends when the dominant axis
reaches its target, which is the same test written differently. A droid
behind a wall keeps its sprite slot and is not drawn, which is what the
C64 does with SpriteEna. That needed slot OWNERSHIP separated from
sprActive: drSlotOwner is what DrFindSlot now scans.

DrCollide replaces the one thing with no faithful port available. The
C64 reads $D01E, the VIC's pixel-exact sprite collision latch; a
software blitter knows what it wrote, not what it overlapped, so this is
a box test — and deliberately a box smaller than the sprite, because
most of a droid's corners are the rotor's transparent gaps. One pair a
pass, as DoCollision does. Droid v droid reverses the first and pauses
the second; player v droid pauses and reverses the droid and bounces the
player, with the bounce clamped to CAM_TOPSPD because our band redraw
brings in one character row a pass and the C64's doubling would skip one.

DrLineOfSight does NOT preserve X — the scaling loop uses it, the way
CalcDeltaAdd does. Missing that made the caller write sprActive through
an index read out of the wrong array: slots nobody owned were switched
on with no position in them, and the player vanished behind three slots
of rubbish.

Verified: 0 of 10240 against a forced RedrawAll with the draw disabled,
and a droid walking into the player is paused for 16 iterations while the
player is nudged clear.

events.title: The droid's cell was right only for the first 512 pixels of a deck
events.message:
The droid's cell was right only for the first 512 pixels of a deck

DrCharPos shifted the high byte of the position once and rotated the low
byte the rest of the way, which computes the cell modulo 512. A deck is
2,048 pixels across, so every droid past x=512 looked up someone else's
map cell: FindWaypoint missed, CheckDroidAdvance saw walls that were not
there, and the whole deck froze except the one droid near the origin.

The C64 holds the high byte in A across all three LSR/ROR pairs at
GetDroidCharPos ($299A) for exactly this reason. Ours does now too.

Eleven of eleven droids patrol deck 1 after 20 seconds, none standing in
a wall, and the restore is still byte-exact: 0 of 10240 against a forced
RedrawAll with the draw disabled.

events.title: Top speed 8, so the camera's 4 px step divides it
events.message:
Top speed 8, so the camera's 4 px step divides it

At a top speed of 7 the world must average 7 px a pass, and the CRTC
scrolls in 4 px units once per 2 fields — so the camera can only ever
move 0, 4 or 8, and it settles into 8, 8, 8, 4. That periodic 4 px
hiccup is the jerk. The average is forced by arithmetic, so no deadzone
or camera policy can remove it; only a top speed the 4 px step divides.

CAM_TOPSPD (main.asm) is that number, and 8 makes the step uniform.
It is the one movement constant in the port not taken from the C64 —
14 % fast, bought deliberately for a scroll that does not stutter, and
it lands exactly on the one-row-per-pass ceiling the ASSERT guards.
Verified in jsbeeb: xSpd clamps at &0800, ySpd at &F800, picture clean
at full speed on both axes.

Four settings were built and played; the table is in the layer doc.
Two are worth knowing about:

  CAM_TOPSPD = 4     lands within 15 % of the 1985 release's 117 px/s,
                     but PLY_ACCEL is not scaled with it, so the ramp
                     is 0.20 s against the original's 0.52 s. Right
                     terminal velocity, wrong ramp.
  PLY_ITER_FRAMES=3  the only setting that reproduces 1985 properly,
                     speed AND ramp, because it scales velocity by 2/3
                     and acceleration by 4/9 together. Lost on feel:
                     4.67 does not divide 4 either.

Also records two camera schemes that were costed and rejected, both of
which look right on paper:

  A fixed-rate lazy camera cannot keep up — 3 px/pass deficit against a
  140 px margin, and the decks are far too long to hide it. The longest
  horizontal open run is 1088 px (decks 3, 10, 11), measured by decoding
  levels.asm + tiledefs.asm; the table is in the doc.

  Splitting the CRTC step across the pass's two fields corrupts the
  picture. 15 rows of 80 units are 9600 contiguous bytes of a 10240-byte
  ring, so rows are ADJACENT: moving the displayed start back one unit
  splices rather than translates, taking each row's left column from the
  row above's right column — the leading edge just redrawn. It was built,
  and a still screenshot looked clean; exaggerating the lag to 20 units
  in jsbeeb showed the re-frame. Same wrap geometry as 39315d0.

Corrects the layer doc's speed table, which still carried the
FRAME_LOCK = 1 era's 52/44/3.5 per-frame figures, and the matching
stale comment in ApplyMove.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 38 — the pickup tier, and what the items are called
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 38 — the pickup tier, and what the items are called

Slot 38 ($5408, 236 B), text_post_bonus_points_a4be ($6938, 82 B — the
plate said hud_write_bcd_long; the bytes patch five BCD digits into the
shipped "Bonus Points." string), and all FOURTEEN pickup_effect_*
handlers ($105e4..$10799, 438 B): 52 of 62 rows live, ten remain;
verified 274 / 33,910 B (76.6%); suite 4,992 -> 5,140. The handlers
are named from the messages they post — Wing Boots, Helmet, Gauntlet,
Revival Medicine, the four spell appends (which push the same words as
effect_push_record_*, making effect_record_list an inventory), two
meter grants, attack-level, vanish — two identifying HUD slots nothing
else had named, and one resolving the $b444 tension (the signed bump
turns the reset's $ff into $00ff, un-emptying the list). Slot 38's
payout dispatch is the tier's second UNBOUNDED table: 56 of 65,536
indices dispatch, the refusal is a fourth out-of-band code proven
against the image, and the sign-extension mutant fell only to a true
differential — an entry address seeded below the table that the
ORIGINAL jsr's to. One duplicate cmt discharged; batch 28's census
correction corrected (operand vs instruction addresses).

THE GATE'S ROUND: the semantics all held — the findings were claims
outrunning coverage. The loudest claim (three id-0 handlers CANCEL the
bonus box) was stated on four surfaces and executed on none: every
dispatch row seeded score 0, so no run had both posts live, and
reordering the effect before the bonus survived green — now pinned,
reorder mutant red. The waiting arms had silently lost their
out-of-contact premise to an unconditional seed overlay; the
digit-runaway guard walked rows its own site excludes while missing
the 106 it admits (failure mode: a counterless-loop HANG). Row 0's
"zero" score is $20; the seven leading spaces are six; "instruction
for instruction" fell again. And the grep-to-zero discipline caught
its own round's defect: an unbounded str.replace had inserted the
findings block into five earlier batch sections — the sweep returned
6 where it should return 1. Full mutation sweep re-run after all
edits: 35/35.

events.title: Fix the sprite smear at the strip wrap: the interpreted row fell into the wrong tail
events.message:
Fix the sprite smear at the strip wrap: the interpreted row fell into the wrong tail

sd_slow ends by putting bufp back to the row's first column, so it has
NOT advanced a scanline - and it ran straight into sd_nextnw, the tail
for rows that walked themselves. Every row after the first wrapping one
was drawn on top of it. sr_slow had the same fall-through. The fix is one
JMP sd_next and one JMP sr_next.

The two tails arrived when the compiled rows took over their own walking,
and the comment above them says in as many words that "blank rows and the
interpreted paths do not" advance - which is precisely the case then left
falling into the wrong one.

This is BUGS.md #5, open since 2026-08-14 and misdiagnosed twice. A row
only takes the interpreted path when its seven columns straddle the end
of the circular strip, which depends on scrollS - so it fires at
particular scroll offsets, which for a given route are the same map
positions every time. That is why it looked like a doorway bug: doors are
where you stop and look.

WHY NO TEST CAUGHT IT: the restore mirrored the fault exactly, collapsing
the same rows onto the same scanlines it had drawn them at, so the
background came back correctly and the buffer diff against RedrawAll -
which runs with the DRAW DISABLED - reported 0 differences. The fault was
only ever in the drawn sprite. Every oracle we had was blind to it.

Reproduced deterministically: player at unit 37, line 0, scrollS = &17B0
puts seven of the sprite's 21 rows across the wrap. Before, the droid is
a one-row streak; after, at the identical position, it draws in full.

KC found the thread: pixels erasable at both &5800 and just below &8000
means rows landing across the wrap, which is the interpreted path.

events.title: quantize: reserve exact palette slots for each band's flat AREA colours
events.message:
quantize: reserve exact palette slots for each band's flat AREA colours

The median cut in quant_banded is PRESENCE-weighted — a colour counts once
however many pixels it covers, because the population isn't known at
set_palette time. So a flat panel filling half a band was averaged into a box
with its neighbours and came back a different colour. Two consequences, and
the second is why per-band palettes are currently switched off:

  - Fidelity. Measured on captured HEIRS frames at the ST's 16-colour budget
    (tools/quantsim.py), mean squared RGB error: 3D walk view 446 -> 207,
    BigPic event 828 -> 429, the UNLIMITED ADVENTURES title 1713 -> 466.
  - SEAMS. A flat colour spanning bands was averaged against DIFFERENT
    neighbours in each one, so it came back as different shades either side of
    a boundary — the striping (#40) that drove ADR-0016 B1 to abandon per-band
    palettes for a single global one. On the same frames a plain per-band cut
    costs 685 seam pixels; with this it costs 100.

So before cutting, each band now reserves up to QUANT_KEEP (6) slots for the
colours covering at least QUANT_KEEP_PCT (3%) of it and reproduces them
EXACTLY. A colour that big is a flat area — chrome, a panel, a backdrop — and
exactness is both what it wants and what makes it identical across bands.
Two CLUT indices that snap to the same hardware colour share one slot.

Restructured the presence histogram into a per-band population histogram taken
band by band, which touches the same pixels, drops the 10 KB `used` static, and
costs 512 bytes of counters. Slot selection is at most QUANT_KEEP max-scans
over 256 rather than a sort.

tests/test_quantize.py grows flat_area_test, which reproduces the #40 seam: a
panel colour with neighbours spread far ABOVE it in one band and far BELOW in
the other, four slots available. MUTATION-CHECKED — with QUANT_KEEP forced to 0
it fails with "the flat panel is 200,120,72 in band 0 but 184,88,40 in band 1",
so it is pinning the behaviour and not recomputing it.

Backends still pass nbands=1, so this lands the fidelity win with NO change to
the band machinery; flipping st_reband/ecs_reband to real per-band palettes is
the next step and is what the seam guarantee above unblocks.

469 passed, 6 skipped; 020 / 68000 / amiga-AGA / amiga-ECS all build.
