events.title: Split PLAN.md into docs/, rewrite GRAPHICS.md, delete the dead source files
events.message:
Split PLAN.md into docs/, rewrite GRAPHICS.md, delete the dead source files

PLAN.md had grown to 2,125 lines, most of it implementation detail from
layers that are finished. It is now 240: state of the port, memory map,
open items, and one paragraph per layer saying what landed and where the
detail lives. The detail moved to docs/, one file per layer, plus
decisions.md (including the evidence for which Paradroid the listing is)
and master-extensions.md.

Nothing was lost - every original line is either in a docs/ file or was
rewritten into the new PLAN.md. Headings were promoted so each file reads
standalone, and the cross-references that said "at the end of this
document" became links.

Three things were promoted rather than just moved, because they were
load-bearing and only findable by reading 600 lines:

  - abs,X and zp,X are both 4 cycles, so indexed tables gain nothing from
    zero page. Caps any future zero-page work.
  - The listing-diff verification technique, beside the buffer-diff oracle.
  - A pointer that the blitter document records REJECTED options too, so
    round-robin updating does not get revived without reading why.

GRAPHICS.md was badly stale and is rewritten as docs/graphics.md. It
targeted BBC Master MODE 2 throughout: every byte count and every "BBC
port considerations" block assumed 8 colours at 4bpp. The port is MODE 1
on a Model B - a character is 16 bytes not 32, the charset is built at
deck load rather than shipped, and sprite masks are derived rather than
stored. Worst of it was a proposed fixed C64->BBC colour table, which is
not merely inaccurate: a fixed table collapses two logical colours onto
one physical and silently erased detail on 12 of the 16 decks. That
section now documents the per-deck greedy assignment that actually works.

The C64-side analysis - charset addresses, sprite regions, tile
catalogue, level RLE, side view, title screen, transfer board - is
accurate and kept. Each section now ends with a Status note saying what
has been ported and what has not, so the two cannot drift apart again.

Deleted src/zeropage.asm, hardware.asm, macros.asm, hal_video.asm and
hal_irq.asm - five inherited files targeting a Master 128 in MODE 2 with
shadow RAM and a HAL this project rejected. None were included by
main.asm; the build output is byte-identical and the game still boots and
plays. hal_video.asm in particular carried unverified CRTC arithmetic
with "TODO: verify in emulator" still in it, and sat there for months
looking like working code.

The only thing in them with a future was hardware.asm's SN76489 encoding,
now recorded under Layer 11 in PLAN.md - with the caveat that it was
never verified either.

Also fixes a reference to tools/export_player.py, which export_droids.py
superseded.

Move the remaining per-pass working variables into zero page

The last of the free zero page - &10-&3F, &60-&63 and &65, 53 bytes -

events.title: record the landmass tables, and the mirror fixup they need
events.message:
record the landmass tables, and the mirror fixup they need

$2E32 draws its mountain ranges from the landmass position tables at $0300
and $033C — three-byte (row, column, radius) entries that $1B5F files as each
landmass is placed. LandMassStage now records them, including the case that
makes the tables awkward: a continent tall enough to reach into both bands is
filed twice, once in each, which is how a phase working on one band can see a
landmass whose centre is in the other.

They are filed before the mirror, and $1D42 fixes them up when it fires. Two
of its routines are read and verified against captured tables: $1C2A turns a
column into ($80 - x) + $80, which is 256 - x — one more than the 255 - x the
bit reversal gives, and enough on its own to put a landmass a cell off. $1C3D
turns a row into ($C8 - row) + 7, which is 207 - row, because the tables hold
rows relative to a band, so flipping the map flips an entry between the two
tables and mirrors it within 208 rows rather than 400. Checked: (166,94)
northern comes back as (90,113) southern, and (89,55) southern as (167,152)
northern.

What is not read is the rest of $1D42 — it stages entries through a scratch
buffer at $9100, re-sorts them between the tables, and rewrites $63/$64 from
byte offsets into entry counts. Without that, two of five entries come out
right. So the recorded tables are pre-mirror and say so, and $2E32 cannot use
them yet. Better an honest gap than a fixup that is right twice out of five.

events.title: record what $4CF2 and $2E32 are
events.message:
record what $4CF2 and $2E32 are

$4CF2 does not touch the map. It walks eight three-byte entries at $E2F1 —
the table the pipeline clears on the way in — and calls $4C87 for each
non-empty one, 18 times over the two bands, but the band digest before and
after is identical. Eight entries in a game called Seven Cities of Gold is
suggestive and nothing more; it needs no port for the map.

$2E32 is read as far as $2EBC and not ported. It is a series of full band
sweeps: every plain cell through $2C3A, every cell holding 4 or 5 through
$2CDB, then plain to forest on a draw against a threshold — $96 for band 0
and $36 for band 1. Each sweep starts at row 0 for band 0 and row $10 or $0E
for band 1, which is the sixteen-row overlap being skipped rather than done
twice. More sweeps follow. At 1,750 addresses it is the biggest phase in the
pipeline and the next real piece of work.

events.title: port $2D23, and mirror the satellite positions
events.message:
port $2D23, and mirror the satellite positions

$2D23 marks the deep water in a radius-10 box around each satellite — the
lake-makers — as $0F, and the second call turns $0F back into water. One
routine run twice with three bytes rewritten between: $2D70 is the operand of
the CMP that says what to look for, $2D74 the operand of the LDA that says
what to write, and $2DA6 an LDX that becomes an RTS. It marks the sea around
the lakes so that whatever runs in between can tell that water apart. The
terrain generator and the rivers both run inside the marks; which of them
cares is still open.

It needed something the port had quietly wrong. $1BF9 files a satellite's
position as it is placed — before the mirror at $1C89 moves the map — and
$1D42 rewrites the tables when the mirror fires. Without that fixup a
satellite marks a box of open sea: 441 cells, the whole box, against the 26
the original marks. The second wave's islands never showed the fault because
they are filed after the mirror, which is why the island phase was exact
while this was not.

LandMassStage.Run now carries the satellites alongside the islands, filed the
way $1BF9 files them and split at row 215 — four rows off the 219 the second
wave uses, for no reason yet apparent.

With this the band after the pipeline's first two phases matches the
original's, nibble for nibble and byte for byte.

The band it leaves hashes to what the original handed the next phase. $2AE9
is three things, and the middle one hides: $28F1 goes over each island, then
a coin flip at $2AEC throws one more feature at a *random* position rather
than an island's, and only then does $2B42 mark. That stray accounts for 107
of band 0's 856 shading writes, all of them nowhere near any island, which is
precisely what an island-driven port cannot explain.

$2977 is the coastal shading, and two readings of it were wrong until the
writes were diffed one by one.

$295B's edge test and $2972's coin flip both jump to $296F JMP $29D0 — the
middle of $2977, not past it. So what they skip is the feature placement, not
the shading, and the shading runs for every island. Guarding the whole
routine on them leaves a coast with a fifth of the water it should have: 131
cells of medium against 644.

$2A78 is one routine with a hole in it. $2A96 is a branch whose opcode is
rewritten — $F0 for BEQ, $D0 for BNE — and the four bytes at $2A98 are its
body, copied in from $2ADB. $2ABC makes it count non-water neighbours; $2AD5
makes it write water into them. Same nine cells, opposite jobs. $2A02 then
patches the coin flip at $2A9E into a BNE for the second pass, so shallow
water shades its own neighbours flatly to medium, which is what gives a coast
two rings rather than one.

$22F7 is reused here against nibbles rather than the bit mask — the same code
at the same address, with $141C and $1B4E patched into JMP $0FAE and
JMP $0FC3 and $13D3 rewritten to F0 0F. The port writes it twice rather than
patching anything, which is the honest trade.

The diff that found all of it needed one fix of its own: $15 is set once, to
the centre row less one, and the row pointer advances without it, so an
instrumented comparison has to report that rather than the true row.

events.title: note that game rules need an oracle built first
events.message:
note that game rules need an oracle built first

Measured, the two halves are closer in size than the file sizes suggest:
game3 is 18,432 bytes with 265 JSR targets and 8,125 bytes reachable as code,
while the decrypted game is 36,096 bytes with 388 targets and 11,451 bytes of
code — twice the file, 1.4x the code, the rest tables and text.

Volume is not what decides it. The World Maker is a pure function with a
perfect diff, and that is why it moved fast: every structural correction to
the coastline walker came from diffing traces and not one from reading the
disassembly. Game rules are the other shape — more legible code, since
movement cost and trade price are human concepts, but no oracle, because
state evolves from player input.

So the first move there is to build one: run `game` under sim6502 with
vdrive.py serving a generated map disk, stub the joystick and keyboard to a
scripted input sequence, and diff state after n frames. Same trick that
unblocked terrain today.

events.title: port the terrain scatter, and settle what nibble 3 means
events.message:
port the terrain scatter, and settle what nibble 3 means

$2BEA is small and it answers a question that has been open since the map
disks were first decoded. A draw of four picks $0C forest, $0D mountain or
$0E swamp — and the fourth outcome, which arithmetic would make $0B plain, is
rewritten to $03 instead. That is the same nibble $2B67's island marking
writes. So $03 is *plain, provisionally*: it marks ground the phase has been
over so later phases can tell it apart, and something downstream turns it
back, which is why a finished map has none of it and the historical disk has
fourteen stray cells in one corner.

$1021 gates the swamp outcome and turns out to be a latitude test. Band 0
allows swamp from row 110 down, band 1 up to row 108 — map rows 110 to 299.
The World Maker puts swamp in the tropics and nowhere else. A forbidden draw
is redrawn rather than replaced, so the gate costs randomness as well as
outcomes.

Both are ported, along with $28F1's scatter over the island boxes: every land
cell gets a coin flip and half go through $2BEA, which is why by the time
$2B67 marks, the original finds 165 plain cells in band 0 where the raw band
would give 308.

Neither test passes yet and the gap is exact. The scatter alone gets 42 cells
of $3 against 51, 55 of forest against 61, 46 of mountain against 51 — close
— but the original's band also holds 644 cells of medium water and 212 of
shallow, which nothing in the scatter writes. $2977 makes those. It is the
coastal shading, it consumes randomness, and that is what moves the rest of
the counts. Both tests are disabled with that written out rather than
deleted.

The fixture now records the generator state at each phase boundary, because
it carries through from the land-mass phase and the band writer and a port
cannot derive it yet — a phase can only be graded from the state it actually
started with.

events.title: start on the terrain phases: the band, the box, and what $2AE9 really is
events.message:
start on the terrain phases: the band, the box, and what $2AE9 really is

TerrainPhases.box is $2A45, graded against every distinct box a whole run
computes — 200 of them. The clamps are asymmetric and that asymmetry is the
whole routine: x saturates at 0 and $FF, the width of the map, but y
saturates at $CF, the last row of the *band*. That is how every phase
downstream stays inside its 208 rows without any of them knowing bands
exist.

markIslands is $2B67-$2BA9, which walks the island tables the second wave
filled and turns every plain cell in a radius-10 square into nibble 3. The
captured boxes confirm the tables directly: the first two are (118,16) and
(39,111), which are the port's own first two islands, and $67/$68 come out
5 and 2 against the port's five northern and two southern.

It cannot be graded yet, and finding out why is the useful part. $2AE9 is
three things, not one. $28F1 goes over the same island boxes *first* and
rewrites land through $2BEA on a coin flip per cell; a coin flip at $2AEC can
send it through a placement search at $2977; and only then does $2B67 mark.
So the marking's input is whatever $28F1 left, not the raw band — measured,
the original marks 165 cells in band 0 where the raw band gives 308. The test
is disabled with that diagnosis rather than deleted, and the digests it will
need are already in the fixture.

tools/terrain_reference.py records the pipeline phase by phase per band, plus
the bounding boxes and the marked-cell digests.

events.title: unpack the band the terrain phases start from
events.message:
unpack the band the terrain phases start from

The land-mass phase ends with a 1-bit mask at $5700; everything after works
on 4 bits a cell, 128 bytes a row, in the same memory. TerrainBand is that
view, and it is built straight out of the mask the port already reproduces:
one bit becomes one nibble, water $0 and land $B.

Band 0 of seed $1234 config 0 hashes to the same digest the original had at
$2AE9's entry, so the join between the two halves of the World Maker holds
and the terrain phases can now be graded against captured digests without
porting the band writer first.

The band structure is settled while I was here. 208 rows — which is what
$2C14 bounds its row counter at and what $2A45 clamps its bounding boxes to —
and two bands cover 400 rows: 0 to 207 and 192 to 399, overlapping by
sixteen. Only the first can be built from the mask alone; by the time the
second is loaded those sixteen rows already carry terrain the first band
generated.

The two addressings share their machinery, which is worth knowing before
porting anything downstream. $2AF1 patches $141C and $1B4E — the 1-bit row
pointer and cell test — into JMP $0FAE and JMP $0FC3, and $2B02 rewrites the
bit-mask table at $13D3 from 80 40 20 10 ... to F0 0F. Everything built on
them, $22F7's clearance test included, then works on nibbles without knowing.

tools/terrain_reference.py captures the pipeline phase by phase per band.

events.title: $2AE9 is what reads the island tables
events.message:
$2AE9 is what reads the island tables

$2B4E and $2B60 patch the operand of $2B6B to $038C or $03B4 — the two
position tables the second wave fills — choosing between them on the sign of
$10, with $67 and $68 as the counts. It walks the chosen table two bytes at a
time into $22/$23 and, where the nibble already there is $0B, writes $03.

That answers a question that has been open since the second wave was read.
What it does not answer is what $03 means, because it does not survive: the
band still holds 213 cells of it as late as $2C14 and the finished map has
none at all. Something between takes it away, most likely the second $2D23,
which is parameterized to undo what the first laid down. So $03 is
scaffolding the terrain generator stands on rather than terrain — which would
also explain the fourteen stray cells of it in the top-right corner of the
historical map disk.

events.title: map the terrain pipeline
events.message:
map the terrain pipeline

The map is built a band at a time — 208 rows, 26,624 bytes of nibbles at
$5700, which is why $2C14 bounds its row counter there and how 51,200 bytes
of map fit on a machine with nothing like room for it. $0E20 is the pipeline
and runs once per band.

Reading the nibble histogram at each phase entry says what the phase before
it did, and that is enough to name most of them:

    $2AE9   1, 2 and 3 appear off the coast       water depth
    $2D23   F appears, about 26 of them           a spread pass
    $2E32   B 15,422 -> 10,194, C -> 3,989        the terrain generator
    $3961   small movement in 4-A                 river seeds?
    $3EAD   5 79 -> 233, 8 50 -> 245, E -> 443    rivers, and swamp
    $2D23   every F gone                          the same pass, undoing
    $47DF   F 0 -> 127                            villages
    $4CF2   nothing in the histogram              unknown
    $2C14   —                                     writes the band out

$2D23 is the interesting one. It runs twice, and $0E32-$0E4A and $0E58-$0E66
patch three bytes inside it before each call: $2D70, $2D74 and $2DA6 go from
$00/$0F/$A2 to $0F/$00/$60. One routine, parameterized to lay a marker down
and then take it away, with $A2/$60 almost certainly LDX # against RTS. The
pipeline also patches the bit-mask table at $13D3 to $80/$40 on the way in,
so the phases reuse the mask machinery two bits at a time rather than one.

events.title: the whole World Maker now runs: seed to finished map disk in 320s
events.message:
the whole World Maker now runs: seed to finished map disk in 320s

The drive had a hole. Under TALK it served the error status whatever channel
was asked for, so every U1 read came back as 256 bytes of "00, OK,00,00".
A drive that only ever gets asked for status looks exactly like that, and it
passed every earlier test because the land-mass phase only ever writes.
Serving the channel's buffer instead — from wherever B-P left the pointer —
was the whole fix.

Telling a loop from slow progress is what found it. Running in
50-million-instruction chunks and watching the set of distinct program
counters: 2,598 in the first chunk and not one new address in the next two,
with $0B16 called 22,500 times per chunk. After the fix the set kept growing
— 2,600, 3,682, 4,460, 4,720 — which is what progress through new code looks
like.

$0E1C is JMP $0E1C. The World Maker prints its last message, closes the drive
and spins there, so wm_disk.py now runs to that address rather than to a step
budget, and says which of the two it stopped on.

What comes out is a real map disk with the full terrain set on it — deep,
medium and shallow water, all seven river tiles, plain, forest, mountain,
swamp and village — which map_preview renders without complaint. 414 sector
writes, 320 seconds.

Every phase after the land mass is now traceable the same way the land-mass
phase was: capture from the interpreter, port, diff. That was the point of
building the drive.

wonderboy/atari: batch 34 — the collectable band closes whole

Slots 32-37 ($5046..$5407, 694 B, all CLEAN): the hopping gold
collectable with three globals of its own, the clock pickup, the shop's
item cursor (not a creature), the event animation pair sharing one
global cursor — slot 36 RETYPES itself to row 0 and keeps its slot,
pinned against the image's table like slot 60's — and the riser. The
band $4e38..$5407 now runs end to end bar one 30-byte non-dispatch
helper. 32 of 62 rows live; verified 237 / 27,206 B (61.5%); suite
4466 -> 4558. Slot 35's scouted 134 bytes were 38 — the rest was its
frame data, a record template, and an already-named routine.

The independent gate's theme was CLAIMS WEAKER THAN STATED, three ways:
the $5160 table census said two readers and the bytes say THREE (a
lea $5160.w at $58f8 inside unported slot 46 — the exact one-encoding
operand-scan trap this batch added to docs/methodology.md, sprung on
its own correction; the wrap pin is honestly a two-of-three until
slot 46 ports); the sweep survivor's equivalence clause was false
against the bus predicate (a record at $ffff7 satisfies the gate while
its counter drops — the survivor holds because the CONSUMING store
drops with the re-read source, the argument now actually written); and
the entry-X audit's "proved" over-read two sites whose X is produced
inside snd_trigger_effect, data-dependently — downgraded to what the
rows establish. The same re-sweep found a second reader of the
type-30 drift table at $b84 (batch 33 called its cursor word a pad)
and a second reference to $1044c — both registered.

Fixed with the gate: the second-record cases now genuinely thread the
first run's ledger into the second run's seed; the sweep recipe
snapshots only after the green check and refuses to overwrite (the
step that destroyed this batch's reconstruction once — the process
failure is recorded in STATUS); $1fa2/$2394 (a third animation
stepper) got their own directives and a queue entry.

Remaining: slots 9-27 (the monster-prologue nineteen), 38 (pickup),
39-46, 57, and the player. Queued: scene_copy_record_fields ($539e),
the $b84 drift reader, slot 46's table reader, abcd_byte -> kit.

&00-&3F turned out to be entirely unused — 64 bytes of language
workspace nothing had ever claimed, on top of the &40-&8F already in
use. Everything the draw loops read went into it.

The ones that pay: colSubX, colHalf and colTileRow are read once per
row of every column drawn; dbTile and dbSub once per tile of every
band; subRowOfs once per tile. An absolute read is 4 cycles against 3.
bandDo/bandRow/bandRc, colFirst/colCount, dbOdd and sDelta came along
because they cost nothing to bring.

  one band pass 12,244 -> 12,138

The build also came out 79 BYTES SMALLER, because a zero page operand
is a byte shorter than an absolute one. Faster and smaller for an
address change.

Scoped to screen.asm and scroll.asm, which the RedrawAll oracle
verifies byte for byte. sprite.asm has its own absolute scalars and is
40K of the pass, but there is no equivalent oracle for it — the buffer
diff is taken with the sprite draw NOPed out — so that wants a
different verification approach rather than being swept along here.

events.title: L10n: Extremely early RTL support and HE script/localization
events.message:
L10n: Extremely early RTL support and HE script/localization

The Elite //e clone used SI 960 which is another 7-bit encoding that
replaces the English lowercase letters in code points 0x60-0x7A with
Hebrew letters. So... it is plausible to support.

There's a lot involved in BiDi support for RTL languages, and this
change does... almost none of that.

This change updates the import pipeline which starts from the
localization spreadsheet, and uses helper scripts to convert RTL
strings from logical to visual ordering (etc), which are then
transcoded to the relevant 7-bit encoding and output as resource
strings. Escape sequences (like \x1F for Open Apple, or %0d for
replacements) make it through in the correct order for use by the
code. The font definitions include code points for U+05D0 through
U+05EA. But I don't know the script well so I may be missing nuances.

This change does *not* tackle changing any UI layout, though. So any
place where the display is produced with multiple strings, for example
a label on the left and a value on the right, will be in the wrong
order. Therefore, this change doesn't introduce HE builds, because
they're not going to be of acceptable quality.

All that said, early versions of Mac OS (e.g. 7.1) appear to make a
pretty weak effort here. Menu items, radio buttons, and checkboxes are
flipped, and text is generally aligned to the right by default within
alerts, text boxes, and list boxes. But the menu bar, window headers,
and general dialog layouts are not mirrored, as is done in modern RTL
UI. So "perfect" doesn't need to be the enemy of "good", but this
change doesn't get us close enough to "good" to be considered usable.

events.title: Inline ColCharPtr, unroll the column copy, table the address maths
events.message:
Inline ColCharPtr, unroll the column copy, table the address maths

Three things in DrawColumn, all of which KC spotted:

ColCharPtr had one caller and ran 16 times a column, so it is inlined
and its tile-row miss put out of line — once every four rows, and it is
what keeps the loop branch in reach. The 8-byte copy uses COPYCELL
instead of its own DEY/BPL loop: 13 cycles a byte against 16.

The bit shifting is now two tables. tdp = tiledefs + tile*16 was PHA,
AND, four ASLs, PLA, four LSRs, ADC — 35 cycles to multiply by 16 over
32 possible tiles. maprow = tilemap + tileRow*64 was 30 cycles over 16.
Both are pure functions of labels fixed at assembly time, so unlike
CHAR_PTR they need no builder and no RAM: 96 bytes of the code image
that beebasm fills in.

colRight went with them. It is constant down a whole column, so the row
loop was testing it 16 times to add 8; ColSetup now stores 0 or 8 in
colHalf and the loop adds it unconditionally to the CHAR_PTR read. That
is both faster and 10 bytes shorter, which is what brought the loop
branch back into range after inlining.

  one column  4,663 -> 3,811
  horizontal  8,067 -> 6,594

-852 a column, -18%, against ~736 predicted.

The same tdp table now serves the band's tile walk and BandSetRow uses
the mapRow one, but the band measured 12,244 against 12,245 — no change
where ~200 a band pass was expected. Unexplained; the column result on
the same build is clearly right, so the harness is working. Noted for a
controlled check rather than claimed as a saving.

MapChar and HalfPtrLeft deliberately left alone: RedrawAll is the
oracle these changes are verified against, and changing both together
would let a shared mistake hide.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out: 0
differences in 10240 at odd mapHX 137 / scrollS 5928 and even mapHX 220
/ scrollS 960, both with rows that wrap mid-row.

events.title: give the interpreter a 1541; the World Maker now writes a map disk
events.message:
give the interpreter a 1541; the World Maker now writes a map disk

vdrive.py replaces the IEC layer rather than simulating it. $1243, $12E6,
$126C, $12F4, $1329, $1305 and $1314 all become RTS, along with the line
pokes underneath them, and Python does the work — no serial timing anywhere.
The only subtlety is $13BC, the line reader, which has to come back
non-negative for the one wait that survives at $10E6.

Finding the receive routine took a wrong guess first. $126C looks like it and
is not: it sends a secondary address that $C4 already holds. The real
receiver is $1329, which shifts $DD00 into $C9 and returns it.

The drive itself is deliberately not a DOS. It understands B-P, U1 and U2,
keeps a 256-byte buffer per channel, and answers "00, OK,00,00" on the error
channel. Anything else is accepted, ignored and recorded in `unhandled` so a
command that turns out to matter cannot slip past unnoticed. Parsing the
arguments needs care: pulling digits out of the whole command string picks up
the 2 in U2 and shifts every argument by one, which quietly writes the band
to track 0.

With it attached, wm_disk.py runs the World Maker through the land-mass phase
and on into writing the map: 200 sectors, tracks 22 to 34, 51,200 bytes.
Decoded with map_preview's deblocker — a sector is a 32x16 tile block, and
only in write order, not by track and sector index — it is identical to the
Swift port's mask, zero cells differing. The original 6502 and the port now
agree on a real map disk.

The nibbles on it are only 0 and $B, deep water and plain, so the band writer
runs before terrain and the terrain phases rewrite what it laid down. What is
not yet established is how long those take: 900 million interpreted
instructions (820s) leave the generator still inside $0B16. Either they need
several times that or a stub has it looping, and that is a question about the
harness rather than the port.

The disk this produces is a generated map and is written wherever --out
points. Nothing goes in the repo.

events.title: Walk the tile row instead of cellX
events.message:
Walk the tile row instead of cellX

BandCharPtr spent most of its 74 cycles rediscovering where it already
was: derive the tile column from cellX, compare against a cache, then
rebuild (cellX AND 3) + subRowOfs as an index. But a tile is 4
characters wide and those 4 codes are 4 consecutive bytes of tiledefs.

The row is now walked as tiles of four, with the tile's row folded into
tdp when it is built — (tile AND 15)*16 is at most 240 and subRowOfs at
most 12, so the add cannot carry — leaving the four characters at
Y = 0..3. cellX is not maintained across the row at all; the trailing
half of an odd mapHX recomputes it, and forces tileCol to miss rather
than trusting a column dbTile has moved past.

A 40-character row starting anywhere covers eleven tiles with a partial
one at each end, so each tile draws min(4 - sub, remaining) and every
tile after the first starts at 0. That composes with the odd-mapHX
halves without a second special case.

dbN and dbCount went into the zero page slots halfSel and dirty had
been holding since both were retired.

  band pass      13,398 -> 12,245
  vertical, 7px  11,803 -> 10,787
  full diagonal  20,065 -> 19,172

-1,153 a band pass for +111 bytes. THE ESTIMATE WAS 2,240 AND THIS CAME
IN AT HALF: the per-tile block is 111 cycles rather than the ~61 first
counted, because the walk's state does not all fit in zero page and
LDY abs / INC abs cost a cycle or two more than their zero page forms,
and the min() is 46 of the 111. The zero page move recovered 162.
Count the addressing modes, not just the instructions.

The level draw is now 62% cheaper vertically and 50% on a diagonal than
this morning, and 8,320 of a band pass's 12,245 cycles is the
irreducible byte movement — 13 cycles a byte for (zp),Y on both sides,
640 bytes. Two thirds of what is left is the copy itself, so the next
real gains are elsewhere.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out: 0
differences in 10240 at odd mapHX 137 / scrollS 5928 and even mapHX 220
/ scrollS 960, both with rows that wrap mid-row, and again on the
shipping build after the zero page move.

events.title: find out what it takes to run the phases after the land mass
events.message:
find out what it takes to run the phases after the land mass

The land-mass phase ends JMP $0C89, and $0C89 opens by printing "INSERT A
'BLANK' DISK IN DRIVE #1". From there the map goes to disk a band at a time:
$0C9B unpacks the 1-bit mask into 4-bit nibbles — ASL on its own operand
bytes, using the instruction stream as scratch — and writes the result out.
Every phase after the land mass is interleaved with that, at band
granularity, so the interpreter stops two calls past PHASE_DONE, debouncing
$DD00. Measured: 60 million steps, 17 million reads of that one address.

The useful part is what the protocol turns out to be. Stubbing the IEC layer
— $1241 LISTEN, $123E TALK, $12E6 secondary address, $12F4 send, $1314
UNLISTEN, all hand-rolled reimplementations of the Kernal routines — and
watching what would have gone down the wire shows the World Maker using
nothing but direct block access:

    B-P: 5 0            buffer pointer, channel 5, offset 0
    <256 bytes>         the band, on channel $65
    U2: 5 0 22 17       write buffer 5 to track 22, sector 17
    TALK                read the error channel

No files, no directory, no BAM allocation. So a virtual 1541 good enough to
run the rest of the World Maker needs three DOS commands, a 256-byte buffer
per channel, a d64 behind it and "00, OK,00,00" on the error channel — and
none of the serial timing, because the stubs sit above it.

That is the difference between the remaining phases costing what this one
cost and costing several times more, so it goes in before terrain.

events.title: Inline CellXInc, and walk Y in the copy instead of reloading it
events.message:
Inline CellXInc, and walk Y in the copy instead of reloading it

CellXInc is 8 cycles of work behind 12 of JSR and RTS. Inlining it in
the band loop would have pushed the branch at the bottom past its
128-byte reach, so the copy macros changed from LDY #n per byte to one
LDY #0 and INY between. Identical at 13 cycles a byte — LDY #n and INY
are both 2 — but 5 bytes a copy against 6, which paid for the inlining
twice over: the build came out 19 bytes SMALLER.

  band pass      13,878 -> 13,398
  vertical, 7px  12,225 -> 11,803
  full diagonal  20,482 -> 20,065

-480 a band pass, exactly as predicted. The level draw is now 59%
cheaper vertically and 48% on a diagonal than it was this morning, and
a character's 318 cycles are more than half pixel copy.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out, both
parities, both at positions where rows wrap mid-row: 0 differences in
10240 at odd mapHX 137 / scrollS 5928 and even mapHX 220 / scrollS 960.

Noted while measuring, not done: BandCharPtr spends most of its 74
cycles rediscovering where it is, when a tile is 4 characters wide and
those 4 codes are 4 consecutive bytes of tiledefs. Walking the tile row
instead of cellX is worth ~2,240 a band pass — five times anything else
left — but a 40-character row starting at an arbitrary cellX covers 11
tiles with a partial one at each end, which has to compose with the
existing odd-mapHX half at each end. That wants its own pass and the
full diff matrix, not a tack-on. Written up in PLAN.md.

events.title: port the paired continent; the land-mass phase is complete
events.message:
port the paired continent; the land-mass phase is complete

All three configurations now go from a seed to the original's finished mask,
checked at both of the phase's checkpoints against landmass_reference.json —
the digests captured from the original under VICE — for all nine seed and
configuration pairs.

Configuration 1's command places one continent and gets two, and the second
is not placed at all: it is grown by the walk. $2519 watches the second
quadrant, and when dx comes back down *below* $4E — BCS skips the jump, so it
is the small side that fires — $24FD stops proposing and goes to $17C8.

$17C8 files the walk's geometry into $47-$4D and draws an isthmus: a one-cell
column extended row by row down the coast, each row stepping left until both
the cell and its left neighbour are water, random(radius/8) + 5 rows and then
onward until ten clear cells stand to the left of the last. Where that ends
becomes the partner's centre, a radius further down, and the walk restarts
there with $50 set. Those writes go straight to the mask at $17FF rather than
through $1728, so they appear in no trace — the same blind spot as the flood
fill, and it made the two write streams look 11 cells apart when they were
identical.

$15ED watches for the way back: once the partner's walk is in its last
quadrant and has climbed above $B5/$B6, the isthmus row plus thirty, $186C
restores the first continent's centre, works out where the walk stands
relative to it, takes the quadrant from the two signs and trims the seam.
$1537 refuses anything left of $B4 meanwhile, so the two cannot grow into
each other. $2629 then runs $2655 twice, so each continent of the pair gets a
lake.

Two things this turned up that were wrong before:

  - $1A48 is a recovery, not an ending. Both of $16D1's PLA/PLA exits land
    there, and what happens is that the walk erases where it stands, casts
    about three cells across and a row down for the nearest land, works out
    the quadrant and carries on with a fresh ring. Treating it as the end of
    the walk stopped a paired continent several hundred cells early. It fires
    once in a whole continent and never in configurations 0 or 2, which is
    why it stayed hidden.

  - $1880 STX $2B marks the ring unwrapped on the way back. Without it the
    unwind runs past where the original stopped and off into records left
    from before the isthmus.

$24FD's modulate moved out of proposeStep and into the proposal loop, because
$17C8's trigger reads a working radius that JSR $178A has just recomputed —
and every way back into $24FD, including the stall, goes through both.

events.title: Copy a character's two halves as one 16-byte run
events.message:
Copy a character's two halves as one 16-byte run

The halves are 16 consecutive bytes in the charset and the two units
they go to are 16 consecutive bytes in the strip, so one Y running
0-15 addresses both. The chp+8 and the BufNextUnit that sat between
them are gone: 46 cycles a character for nothing.

The obstacle looked like the buffer wrap. It lands on a UNIT boundary,
so it could fall between a character's halves, and the second half
would then be written 8 bytes past &8000 — into sideways RAM, not a
wrong pixel. The plan was to find the straddling character in the
prologue and split the loop around it. It cannot happen:

  W = 1280 - off/8 units from the row start to the wrap, where
  off = (scrollS + rCount*640) MOD 10240. rCount*640 is 80 units, so
  W == scrollS/8 (mod 2). Characters begin at even units when mapHX
  is even and odd units when it is odd, so the wrap lands on a
  character boundary exactly when scrollS/8 == mapHX (mod 2).

That is invariant: both move by dUnits horizontally; a vertical step
moves scrollS/8 by 80 and mapHX not at all; scrollS wraps at 1280
units; 80, 1280 and 0 are all even. A clamp is safe too, because
sDelta is computed FROM the mapHX difference rather than alongside it.

LoadDeck now sets scrollS to 0 or 8 to match mapHX's parity instead of
always 0. As things stand that is a no-op, since CentreOnDeck produces
charX*2 — but the consequence of the invariant being false is a write
outside the buffer, and that should not rest on another routine's
arithmetic staying as it is.

The per-character wrap test stays; only the mid-character case had to
be excluded. Its fixup moved out of line, which keeps the loop branch
in range and makes the common path a not-taken BCS at 2 cycles rather
than a taken BCC at 3.

  band pass      16,237 -> 13,878
  vertical, 7px  14,304 -> 12,225
  full diagonal  22,810 -> 20,482

-2,359 a band pass for +23 bytes, against -2,320 predicted. The level
draw is now 57% cheaper vertically and 47% on a diagonal than it was
this morning, and more than half a character's 330 cycles is the pixel
copy itself, against a third when the day started.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out, both
parities, both with rows that wrap mid-row, positions confirmed
identical across each pair: 0 differences in 10240 at odd mapHX 137 /
scrollS 5928 and at even mapHX 200 / scrollS 800.

events.title: State bitmap array sizes as their dimensions
events.message:
State bitmap array sizes as their dimensions

A bare byte count says nothing about the shape of the sprite it holds.
Write each pixel_t array's size as width * mask * height * entries, the
form already used in CommonData.h, so the declaration itself says how the
bytes are laid out.

Every array here is unmasked -- the title glyphs are OR-blitted verbatim
and both bank-7 blitters memcpy their source -- so the mask factor is 1
throughout. Widths and heights are taken from the data as written, and
the byte totals agree with them.

The end-shot blobs do not fit the four-factor form: each is 64 rows of
13 bitmap bytes followed by 8 attribute rows of 13, consumed as one
contiguous blob by draw_endshot, so the attribute tail stays a separate
term.

While here, correct the title-glyph comments. They described the arrays
in row-pairs, which is the blitter's loop count rather than the number of
rows present, and gave glyphs 24-27 and 103-114 a width of 6 or 7 bytes.
That figure is the width-class selector the blit dispatch switches on --
blit_width6 and blit_width7 draw 2 and 1 bytes respectively, as the
comment there already records -- not the width of the data.

events.title: Precompute the charset address of every character code
events.message:
Precompute the charset address of every character code

charRemap packs the used-character index into a byte, and all three
lookup paths unpacked it into a 16-bit pointer at the point of use:
PHA, AND, four ASLs, PLA, four LSRs, ADC. Forty-one cycles of address
arithmetic per character drawn — more than the tile-map lookup it
follows, which is cached three calls in four and costs ~11 amortised.
The expensive part of decoding a tile was not the decoding.

BuildCharPtrs folds it into CHAR_PTR_LO/HI at startup, so a lookup is
TAX and two indexed loads: 16 cycles. Both tables are page aligned so
the abs,X never crosses a page. It is a pure function of charRemap and
the charset base, both fixed for the whole run — BuildCharset rewrites
the charset's contents per deck, never its address — so once is enough.

  band pass      17,290 -> 16,237
  one column      5,005 ->  4,663
  vertical, 7px  15,280 -> 14,304
  horizontal      8,759 ->  8,067
  full diagonal  24,249 -> 22,810

-1,053 a band pass and -342 a column against -1,000 and -400 predicted.
Unlike the previous two changes this one helps every path that draws a
character. Costs 512 bytes at &5500-&56FF, of the scratch between the
panel and the strip that nothing else wanted; the code came out 3 bytes
smaller, three unpack blocks against one builder.

charRemap is now read only at startup. tiledefs is what still pins the
data bank in during play.

The level draw is now half what it cost this morning: vertical 28,527
-> 14,304, diagonal 38,472 -> 22,810.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out, both
branches of the odd/even split, positions confirmed identical across
each pair of dumps: 0 differences in 10240 at odd mapHX 137/line 1 and
at even mapHX 180/line 1 on deck 2.

events.title: Unroll the band's cell copy, now that its run length is constant
events.message:
Unroll the band's cell copy, now that its run length is constant

CopyRun took bandScan and bandRun as variables and cost 18 cycles a
byte to do it. Since the band went to whole rows, DrawBandRows has one
caller and it always passes 0 and 8 — so that generality was being
paid 640 times a band pass to support a case that no longer occurs.

Unrolled into a COPYCELL macro with an immediate Y: 13 cycles a byte,
the floor for (zp),Y on both sides. Inlined at the two sites inside the
loop; the two edge halves of an odd mapHX call CopyCell instead, since
they run once a pass against the loop's 40 and 12 cycles of call is not
worth 48 bytes each. bandScan and bandRun are deleted.

  band pass      22,311 -> 17,290
  vertical, 7px  19,655 -> 15,280
  full diagonal  28,143 -> 24,249

-5,021 a band pass for +114 bytes, against -4,560 predicted. Columns
measure 5,260, unchanged, confirming the saving is where it was meant
to be. Cumulatively the level draw is 46% cheaper vertically and 37% on
a diagonal than before today's work.

A character's 414 cycles are now 43% pixel copy, 24% BandCharPtr, 16%
the two BufNextUnit calls. Copy loop overhead went from 146 to 32.

Verified against RedrawAll with the sprite draw NOPed out, covering
both branches of the odd/even split: 0 differences in 10240 at odd
mapHX 137/line 1 (leading and trailing halves + 39 characters) and at
even mapHX 180/line 1 on deck 2 (the plain 40-character loop).

events.title: the "satellite" is a lake generator
events.message:
the "satellite" is a lake generator

Rendering the finished mask settles what $2629 is for, and it is not what the
name suggests. The radius-3 landmass it places sits inside the continent's
outline, in water the flood fill has not reached. When the fill runs from the
continent's centre it spreads through everything it can reach — everything
except what that ring encloses. The ring is land surrounded by land and
disappears. What survives is its interior: a small inland lake, 20 to 43
cells, one per continent.

Measured across six generated worlds: two continents give two lakes, one
continent gives one, no exceptions, and each lake sits where the satellite
was placed once the mirror has moved it. The port's masks match the
original's digests bit for bit, so the original does the same thing.

The code still calls it a satellite, since that is what $2794 literally
walks, but the doc comment and NOTES now say what it produces. Worth knowing
before terrain is ported on top of it.

Also adds an env-gated diagnostic that writes finished masks out as raw
bitmaps, which is how this was found.

events.title: Draw whole character rows, not the scanlines a move exposed
events.message:
Draw whole character rows, not the scanlines a move exposed

A band's cost is almost entirely its 40-character lookup walk — 10,954
cycles against 1,371 for a scanline of copying across the width — and
drawing only what a move exposed paid that walk on every pass that
moved at all, twice whenever the exposed scanlines straddled a
character boundary. That is 7 passes in 8 at top speed: 2.03 walks per
map row against a floor of 1, measured.

The strip now holds whole map rows, and the only thing that exposes new
vertical content is mapYr changing. The row to draw is the one the move
vacated, and it is vacated exactly when its replacement's first
scanline becomes visible, so the handover needs no extra row and the
visible window stays 15 rows.

Copy volume is identical at every speed, so the whole saving is the
eliminated duplicate walk — ~10,000 cycles a pass at any non-zero
vertical speed, including 1 px/pass where the old scheme paid a full
walk to move one scanline.

  vertical, 7 px    28,527 -> 19,655   -31%
  full diagonal     38,472 -> 28,143   -27%
  worst single pass 31,505 -> 22,311

It also retires the split row: no display row aliases two map rows now,
so DrawColumn's repair, RedrawAll's repair and DrawHalfScan/
DrawHalfPart all go — 230 bytes — and RedrawAll becomes a valid oracle
at any value of `line`, which it was not. BUGS #1 is probably moot.

Verified by diffing the play buffer against RedrawAll with the sprite
draw NOPed out: 0 differences in 10240 at odd mapHX/line=1 (down-right),
odd mapHX/line=4 (up-left then down) and even mapHX/line=3 after an 11M
cycle diagonal through the vertical clamp.

The scheme needs a pass to cross at most one row boundary, so
PLY_MAXSPD <= 8 px is now an ASSERT rather than an accident.

Also: DEBUG_TIME, the T1 cycle-timing harness, as a build option rather
than something rebuilt by hand each time; and DEBUG_DRAW gains a third
band so the level draw is separable from the sprites.

events.title: port the second wave; the land-mass phase runs end to end
events.message:
port the second wave; the land-mass phase runs end to end

LandMassStage now goes from a seed to the original's finished mask for
configurations 0 and 2, checked at both of the phase's checkpoints —
tableStage and phaseEnd — against landmass_reference.json, whose digests were
captured from the original under VICE. Nine seed and configuration pairs, two
independent captures, one port.

The second wave at $280A is two to seven more radius-3 islands, eight to
twelve in configuration 2, scattered anywhere clear rather than placed
against anything. Each is drawn as a radius-10 candidate, retested at radius
5 and only then built at radius 3 — three radii for one island, which is what
keeps them well apart. Rows 195 to 218 are refused outright.

$281F patches $222F, the BCS at the end of the placement loop's clearance
test, to RTS. That turns JSR $21B8 into "compute the bounds, draw a position,
test it, return the carry" instead of a loop that places by itself, and the
window it computes is the ordinary one for a radius-10 landmass — so the port
reuses LandMassPhase.bounds unchanged.

This also settles what the two position tables are. Below row 219 an island
goes into $038C as (row, column); at or above, into $03B4 as (row - 192,
column), which keeps the row in a byte. $03DC holds the last column filed
either way, and $2894 halves $67 and $68 to turn each byte offset into a
count. Rows 195 to 218 cannot appear in either table, which is why the split
boundary and the refusal band do not have to agree. What reads them is still
unknown.

The islands walk through $2794, the same path a continent's satellite takes,
so they draw from the second generator and from the same seed pool — pristine
by now, $167B having restored it after the last continent, and not rebuilt
between islands the way $1666 rebuilds it between continents. That made
SeedPool need an explicit pristine case rather than always spending entries
0, 1 and 20.

Left in the phase: configuration 1's paired continent, built by the walk's
$50 mode at $1860/$186C. LandMassStage refuses that configuration rather than
approximating it.

events.title: finish $44EF; the command-table stage now runs from a seed
events.message:
finish $44EF; the command-table stage now runs from a seed

LandMassStage runs end to end for configurations 0 and 2 — seed in, the
original's land mask out. The check closes a loop worth stating: the port is
graded against interior_reference.json, captured in the interpreter, and that
fixture's final mask digests agree with landmass_reference.json's, captured
earlier from the real thing under VICE, on all nine seed and configuration
pairs. Two independent captures, one port.

What was missing was the second of $44EF's two searches for the second site.
$4676 samples; $46BC walks. It starts at the far end of whichever half of the
band is longer, rounded up to an even row, and steps two rows at a time back
toward the first site until it finds a row whose first land run is at least
30 wide. Then it draws columns there until one is far enough away, and then
keeps walking, two rows at a time, for as long as that column stays far
enough. The two ends of that walk bracket a range, a final row is drawn from
it, and a column that turns out to be water in that row falls back to where
the walk began.

It does this by patching $4373 in two places at different times: $4414
becomes RTS so $43E7 can be called for the row scan alone, and later $43E7
becomes RTS so what is left of $4373 is the row draw alone. $2139 and $2143
put both back at the start of every phase. Transcribing that meant splitting
$4373 into the two halves the original reaches by patching.

$47B2 then files a byte at $EBCE from $0B16 — twelve draws summed, centred on
1536, halved as a signed value, scaled by a spread and clipped at zero. A
rough normal, and the only non-flat generator found anywhere in the World
Maker so far. Which distribution depends on whether a second site was found:
centred on 1 with spread 1 if so, on 2 with spread 6 if not — and in that
second case a result of 2 or more overwrites the *first* site's kind with 9,
so the fixture reads the sites at $44EF's exits rather than as they are
chosen.

SiteSelection.Result drops secondaryUnported, which no longer has anything to
describe, and carries the $EBCE parameter instead.

Left in the land-mass phase: configuration 1's paired continent, built by the
walk's $50 mode at $1860/$186C, and the second wave at $280A-$2894.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 33 closes — the BCD extend chain carries
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 33 closes — the BCD extend chain carries

The four packed-BCD accumulators take the extend bit as an argument and
return their carry-out; nothing in the original clears X on entry, so
the caller's X is an input the old interface could not carry. Both
recorded chains proven live before fixing: the case written first went
RED against the unfixed C, off by one in exactly the predicted byte
(slot 28's counter at $9996 carrying into the score; the payout draw
carrying into the counter at award $0096). The kit cannot set an entry
CCR, so the chains are pinned at caller level — the carry produced
inside the run, folded by the oracle, matched by the port.

The independent gate then caught the fix's own blind spot: $6c26 was
mis-filed as an entry-CCR case, but the `lsl.w #2,d2` that leaves
spawn-type bit 14 in X runs INSIDE actor_defeat_and_score — the oracle
produces the carry itself, and the hard-coded clear diverged (proven
red at $4000/$ffff seeds; the old seed-refusal had excluded exactly the
exposing type on a premise the template table cannot support — it has
no shipped bytes). The bit now threads, the refusal is gone, and the
sbcd "equivalent" survivors turned out to be coverage holes: borrow-in
and borrow-out are pinned model-side (leaf.run_candidate_only), sweep
16/16 with no survivors.

Every call site carries its reading: three proved clear from the bytes,
three threaded, and the shop's sub-counter ASSUMED clear under its own
constant — quantified by reading the caller chain: the assumption fails
exactly one frame in 65,536 (frame_tick_b39a's $ffff->$0000 roll, one
extra gold that frame), an open row pending kit entry-CCR support.
Remaining unpinnable, named at the sites: a run ENTERED with X set
($e064, unported) and that one frame.

Verified unchanged at 231 / 26,512 B (59.9%); suite 4451 -> 4466.
Batch 34 = slots 32-37.

events.title: Factor out constants duplicated across the facade and its hosts
events.message:
Factor out constants duplicated across the facade and its hosts

Three values were defined independently in several places, each pair or
group of which has to agree:

- MAXSTAMPS (4), the depth of the stamp()/sleep() nesting, was defined
  four times: in the ZX facade, in the SDL host, as MAX_STAMPS in the
  RISC OS host and as FAKE_MAXSTAMPS in the unit tests. The facade's
  stack and each host's stack are pushed and popped in lockstep and both
  assert rather than grow, so a divergence would show up as a crash in
  one build only. It now lives in Spectrum.h with that contract
  documented.

- The 48K and 128K CPU clock rates were CHQ_CLOCK_48K/CHQ_CLOCK_128K in
  the RISC OS host, bare 3546900.0/3.5e6 literals in two SDL host
  ternaries, and CPU_HZ in a test. They are Spectrum facts, not host
  choices, so they become CPU_CLOCK_48K/CPU_CLOCK_128K in Spectrum.h.

- GAMEWIDTH/GAMEHEIGHT (256/192) in the SDL host duplicated
  SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT from the Spectrum.h it already includes.
  The RISC OS host already used the header's names; the SDL host now
  does too.

No behavioural change. AY_CLOCK_FREQ is deliberately left as its own
literal: 1773400 is not CPU_CLOCK_128K / 2 (1773450), and folding it in
would have shifted the AY's tone pitch.

events.title: Drop round-robin sprite updating, on measurement
events.message:
Drop round-robin sprite updating, on measurement

Every note in this plan treated round-robin as the next step and the
biggest remaining lever, on the basis that seven sprites cost 68K of an
80K pass and left nothing. After the blitter work they cost 40.7K, and
the loop spends 39,212 of its 79,872 cycles idle - 49% of the pass, with
all seven sprites live, measured with T1 around WaitVSync over 127
passes. There is nothing left to buy.

It was also never costed. It breaks the restore-all-then-draw-all
invariant that keeps overlapping sprites from stamping each other into
the buffer permanently; it leaves stale sprites for DoRedraws to repaint
over, which invalidates their saved background; and it drops droids to
~14 Hz against the player's 25.

Recorded rather than deleted, with the numbers and the two hazards, so
the decision is reversible if a later layer eats the headroom. If one
does, the cheap half-step is not round-robin but skipping a sprite that
provably cannot have changed - correct with no visual cost, though it
only pays when droids are stationary or low-energy.

Raster-ordered updating is now the only sprite-pool work outstanding.

events.title: port the site selection at $4500 and map the rest of $44EF
events.message:
port the site selection at $4500 and map the rest of $44EF

$2277 JSR $44EF turned out to be a whole phase of its own — 573 distinct
addresses across $41E6-$47DE, sharing the land-mass generator, sitting in
the middle of the command loop. This ports the part of it that was tractable
and writes down the rest, so the seam is a known quantity rather than a wall.

What it does: after the mirror, it picks two sites and files five zero-page
bytes for each ($77-$7B and $7C-$80) — column, row, a flag set for rows at
or past $D0, and a kind that is either 9 or 7, the second always taking the
other via $46B5 EOR #$0E. What reads them is not established. Two positions
far apart, one of each of two kinds, on land at least 30 cells wide; the
shape fits the game's two advanced civilizations and that is a guess, so the
port names nothing it cannot show.

$4503 measures the mask first: one scan down from row 110 for the first row
with land and then the first without, another up from row 300 doing the
same, both clamped into rows 125 to 280 but only where they already straddle
those bounds. $5D records whether the bands are disjoint. $45F3 picks the
band to draw from — the first, unless it is under 40 rows and the second is
both usable and no worse.

$4373 is the interesting routine. Its row comes from two draws in the
*opposite* order to $247B: the first supplies the high byte through its
sign, the second the low byte, and the second is redrawn until it comes up
even. A row outside the band, or one whose first land run is under 30 cells
wide, discards everything and starts over from the row, which is why a
single call can burn dozens of draws. The column then comes from $22B4 over
left+9 ..< right-9 — the +9 is a +8 plus the carry the width test left set.

$4479 decides whether two sites are far enough apart: squared distance
against 11,968, each difference reduced to a byte before squaring with the
sign taken from the full 16-bit subtraction, so a pair 260 rows apart
measures as 4.

Ported and verified against the original for all nine seed and configuration
pairs: everything above plus the second-site search at $4676-$46B9.

Not ported, and now described rather than merely absent:

  - $46BC, where the original goes whenever that search does not apply — a
    systematic walk outward from the first site's row through the single
    band there is, reusing $43E7 with $4414 patched to RTS and leaning on
    $44B5, $44C3 and $44D9. One measured run drew 3,187 bounded values.

  - $47B2, whose $47BC JSR $0B16 sums twelve draws. An averaging generator
    rather than a flat one, and the first of those to turn up.

SiteSelection.Result carries secondaryUnported so a missing second site
cannot be mistaken for a site the original did not place, and the fixture
records what the original chose either way, keeping the gap visible.

LandMassStage still stops after the first command, but it now covers all of
it: the continents, the satellites, the fills, the mirror and the sites.

events.title: drive the land-mass stage from a seed instead of a fixture
events.message:
drive the land-mass stage from a seed instead of a fixture

LandMassStage is the loop itself — $2158's command table, the placement at
$21B0-$227F, the walk, the satellite, the flood fill and the mirror — and it
runs from a seed and a configuration alone. Graded on all nine seed and
configuration pairs the other fixtures use, matching the original's step
order and its mask exactly.

The satellite is the part worth describing. $2655 scans the column through
the continent's centre for the coast above and below, pulls that window in
by two, then draws a row inside it and a column inside the water span of
that row ($28AB). Rows 185 to 214 are excluded outright. What it draws has
to be at least sixteen cells from the continent's centre on one axis or the
other, and then pass $22F7 three times, at radii 16, 7 and 12 — not the
redundancy it looks like, since $22F7 samples a cross rather than an area
and a smaller radius can fail where a larger one passed. Its walk is seeded
from a pool of 21 constants at $229B that $1666 copies to $0200 with three
entries pre-spent, and runs on the second generator with $1666 patched to
RTS so it neither recurses nor floods.

It stops after the first command, deliberately. $2277 JSR $44EF does more
than mirror: past $4500 it scans the mask's land extents and places
something with them, about 300 instructions over $41E6-$47C5 with a tail
through $1C2A-$1E98, and it makes seven draws on the shared generator whose
bounds come from what it finds. Those cannot be faked, so the port stops and
says why. Configuration 1 is refused outright — its continent is paired, and
the partner is built by a $50 mode of the walk that saves state at $186C and
re-enters $15AD, so one $23D3 yields two continents and one pass of $2629
places two satellites.

Widening the seed coverage turned up two more places where near-identical
routines differ in one detail:

  - Only the horizontal stepper redraws on $FF. $1564 loops while the value
    comes up $FF; $1592 takes what it gets. This stays invisible until a
    turn clears the biases and opens the path at all.

  - The closure plots the candidate without adopting it. $16AF passes
    $16/$17 to $1728 in the registers and leaves $14/$15 alone, so the span
    fill that follows starts from where the walk stands rather than from the
    cell just drawn. Adopting it added one cell to the seam.

Each showed up as a single wrong cell about 700 writes into a continent, in
a seed and configuration different from the one being tested at the time.

The satellite seed table is 21 constants lifted from $229B. It is RNG seeds
rather than content, and the port cannot reproduce original worlds without
it; same category as the direction table at $13DA and the bit masks at
$13D3, both already inline.

events.title: finish the coastline walker and port the interior fill
events.message:
finish the coastline walker and port the interior fill

The land-mass stage now replays from an empty mask and matches the original
bit for bit: eleven steps, 31,307 land cells, every write sequence and every
mask digest exact.

Three fixes finished the outline trace, all found by diffing traces rather
than by reading the disassembly:

  - `$25F8 STY $30` pre-marks slot 4 of the tried-direction set, so "no
    movement" can never be drawn at `$2619`. Leaving it free let the port
    pick a direction the original would have redrawn for, desynchronizing
    the generator without moving anything.

  - `$2613 JSR $16D1` returns to `$260B`, not `$2603` — so every unwind is
    followed by another `INC $1E` and another bounds check, and a restored
    position that had already tried all nine directions unwinds again
    immediately. `$1E`'s invariant is that it equals the number of marked
    slots, which is what lets `$16F6` resume a half-finished search by
    recounting the restored record. Missing the extra pass is what left the
    island stopping one unwind short.

  - `$1622` draws a byte and compares it with `CMP #$00`, which can only set
    the carry, so `LDX #$FF` is unreachable and both direction biases are
    cleared on every turn. The draw still has to happen. The port had
    guessed a threshold there; it survives the satellite and the island,
    which never turn with a radius over `$46`, and shows up 522 writes into
    a continent.

`$16D1`'s two non-local exits are now implemented as well: the ring-full
guard at `$16EC CPX $4F`, and the one that actually fires at `$16D3`, where
`$2B` set with `$46` at zero means every step has been undone and the
original either re-proposes from the origin or abandons the landmass.

InteriorFill is `$194A`, a scanline flood fill with an explicit stack in the
`$9100` region the undo ring has just finished with. Its writes never go
through `$1728`, which is why the walker fixture showed no trace of the
interior at all.

Two things about the surrounding order turned out to be unguessable. Walks
and fills are not paired: a continent's walk arranges the paired satellite's
walk, and only that walk reaches the flood fill, which then fills both. And
`$4500 JSR $1C89` mirrors the entire mask partway through the stage, on two
independent coin flips — reversing all 256 bits of every row, and swapping
row r with row 399 - r. Nothing about it goes through the mask's write path,
so a replay built from traced writes alone cannot see it; what found it was
hooking memory writes instead of the program counter and noticing `$1CC6`
writing all 12,800 bytes. `LandMask` gained both mirrors.

Fixtures: `walker_reference.json` gains a SHA-256 over each fill's whole
write sequence, so the continent is held to all 871 writes rather than the
150-event prefix it commits. `interior_reference.json` is new and records
the stage as an ordered list of outlines, fills and mirrors with a mask
digest before each step. Digests throughout — a continent is ~14,000
interior writes and committing those would be committing generated maps.

Still unported: `$1666` and `$2629`, which decide that order, so the replay
is fixture-driven for now.

events.title: The glyphs save what they draw, so the digit block loses its save pass
events.message:
The glyphs save what they draw, so the digit block loses its save pass

The block saved all seven columns of all eight rows before the glyphs
drew, because under a 2 px shift a glyph was expected to spill into the
next position's first byte - and then neither position could own saving
the shared column.

It never spills. Every glyph's rightmost two pixels are blank, so the
generated code uses relative columns 0 and 1 and never 2: 120 and 143
uses of drYcol0/drYcol1 against ZERO of drYcol2. The three positions are
disjoint - columns 0-1, 2-3, 4-5 - and column 6 is never written at all.

So the save folds into the draw, where the byte is being loaded anyway:
one extra STA (rowq),Y per position. All sixteen of a glyph's positions
are saved, transparent ones included, so SprBlkRest stays generic - over
six columns now rather than seven.

SprBlkSave is gone, and with it a whole extra walk of the eight
scanlines. SprBuildRowPtrs fills both pointer sets in one pass and
leaves bufp/svp on row 14, which is where the save pass used to leave
them, so nothing else changes.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 4,283 -> 3,844, SprRestoreAll 2,095 -> 1,970; 6,378 -> 5,814.

Cumulative over the whole run: 9,616 -> 5,814, a 39.5% cut. Seven
sprites cost 40.7K of the 79,872-cycle pass - just over half of it -
against 67.3K at the start.

Cost: 16 bytes of zero page for rowq, and the glyph code grows from 2.7K
to 3.7K. Sprite bank 56 pages, 2,242 bytes spare.

The blitter now depends on a property of the ARTWORK rather than of the
geometry, so the exporter asserts it: a glyph that ever emitted a lit
pixel in column 2 would corrupt its neighbour's saved background
silently, and would do it only under a shift.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites, static and scrolling.

events.title: Roll up the restore's repeated calls, and tail-call the last row
events.message:
Roll up the restore's repeated calls, and tail-call the last row

Two things visible in the generated programs rather than in the model.

A JSR immediately before the program's closing RTS is a tail call
written the long way. JMP instead: 9 cycles and a byte cheaper, on both
sides.

And the restore's ten calls are FIVE IDENTICAL PAIRS - 00,00 02,02 03 |
03 02,02 01,01. A restore routine is keyed on the column set, only four
sets exist, and which one a row uses depends on nothing but shift and
phase>>2. So the ten collapse to two calls into a routine per half with
all five rows inlined: eight routines cover all sixteen sequences and 8
of the 10 JSR/RTS pairs go. The bottom half also omits its final walk,
because nothing reads the pointers after the last row - which collects
the 42 cycles the unroll was knowingly wasting.

The draw gets only the tail call. Its ten rows are ten DIFFERENT
routines, and merging them would need a copy per phase of the rows that
are currently shared - which is the thing that made the draw expensive
to unroll in the first place.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 4,300 -> 4,283, SprRestoreAll 2,243 -> 2,095; 6,543 -> 6,378.

Cumulative over the whole run: 9,616 -> 6,378, a 33.7% cut. Seven
sprites cost 44.6K of the 79,872-cycle pass, against 67.3K at the start.

Sprite bank 52 pages, 3,289 bytes spare.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites, static and scrolling.

events.title: island outline: 79 of 93 plots, with the unwind matching exactly
events.message:
island outline: 79 of 93 plots, with the unwind matching exactly

Three bugs fixed, each found by where the divergence sat rather than by reading.

A proposal that moves nothing must re-propose, not commit. $25E6 compares the
direction index against 4 -- the centre of the 3x3, meaning neither axis advanced
-- and JMP $24FD runs the generator again without plotting. My loop treated it as
a normal iteration and duplicated the cell. The original stands still at (8,7)
for two iterations before moving to (9,7), and that is exactly where the island
diverged. Fixing it took the match from plot 9 to plot 79.

The acceptance test has four refusals, not two. Beyond the neighbour count and
the $FF offsets, $152D refuses a resolved column of 0 or $FF and $1547 refuses a
row of 0 or one that has reached $018F -- row 399, the last on the map. Omitting
those is not cosmetic: a wrongly accepted candidate changes how many directions
the search tries, which changes how many numbers it draws.

The unwind erases before it restores. $16F0 precedes $16F3, so the cell cleared is
the one the walk is standing on, not the one being returned to, and the counter
is decremented only after the record is read. It also revalidates through $1A00
and unwinds again on refusal.

With those, the deep unwind at plot 79 now reproduces event for event: eleven
erases in identical order, (189,4) back to (195,13). What still differs is where
it stops -- the original resumes at (196,12) and the port at (195,12), one step
short -- so the ring content is right and the revalidation is accepting one
unwind too early.

Also adds an erase callback to traceOutline. Comparing plots alone could not show
that the unwind itself was correct.

the satellite outline now matches the original exactly

All 23 plots, in order, from the same starting state. The first rung of the
ladder is done: the walk loop, the direction search, the quadrant turns, the
closure and the span fill are all correct for a fill that never backtracks.

Two things were missing when the trace first ran and matched 21 of 23.

The span fill at $1648 closes the outline with a vertical run at dx = 0, stepping
dy from wherever the walk finished toward the radius. Without it a coastline is
left open at the seam where the quadrants meet. The original picks the direction
by patching its own loop -- $1654 writes $E6 (INC) or $C6 (DEC) into $1657 -- which
is transcribed as a signed step, since the effect is a direction and nothing else
reads those bytes. It plots with dx taken from the accumulator rather than $14,
the same distinction that mislabelled four events when the reference fixture was
first captured.

The closure at $1690 fires when the heading is 3 and dx is **below 2**, not when
dx reaches zero. So the final quadrant ends as soon as the walk comes near the
vertical axis rather than landing on it, and my loop ran past the point the
original stopped. It tries directions 3, 6 and 0 with bases (1, 0), and plots
whatever candidate is left even when all three refuse -- the third is evaluated
for its side effect.

The divergence report is what made this findable: matching 21 of 23 and failing
at the plot where dx first resolved to 0 said the walk was right and the ending
was not.

events.title: Fix sampled sound playing ~12x slow in the web build
events.message:
Fix sampled sound playing ~12x slow in the web build

The game thread's catch-up cap was expressed as a multiple of the sleep
the caller had just asked for:

    if (next_deadline < nowSecs - duration * maxLagFrames)
      next_deadline = nowSecs - duration * maxLagFrames;

That reads sensibly for the 20ms frame sleeps it was written against --
four frames, 80ms of catch-up -- but 'duration' is whatever the caller
passed. play_speech_128k asks for SPEECH_NIBBLE_TSTATES between nibbles,
447 T-states or 126us, which collapses the budget to 504us. Any stall
longer than that moved the deadline forward and discarded the debt, so
the game clock lost time it could never claw back.

Under emscripten the host clock's own granularity exceeds 504us, so
every tick bled time: measured with per-second counters, the game thread
emitted ~660 speech nibbles a second against the 7936 the nibble rate
implies, and the samples played back at about a twelfth of their pitch.

Cap the lag as an absolute span instead (CHQ_MAX_LAG_SECS, 0.08 --
the same 80ms the frame path always had, now independent of request
size), and skip waits too short for the host to time rather than
attempting them, leaving the debt on the deadline for the next call.

Also revert the sample-frames hint from 0b7cd90. Its premise was that
the ScriptProcessorNode was underrunning; the counters disproved that
(zero drops, zero dry samples, callbacks pulling the full device rate),
and it cost ~85ms of latency for nothing.

events.title: port the candidate generator and direction mapping
events.message:
port the candidate generator and direction mapping

$24FD chooses which axis moves and how far, and $25B9 turns the result back into
one of nine direction indices.

Both axes move every iteration and the order carries meaning. The smaller
coordinate goes first, ties broken by a coin flip at $252D, with a threshold
scaled from its own value -- so an axis that has run ahead becomes reluctant to
move again. The other follows with a threshold derived from the radius error,
which is what pulls the walk back onto the circle. Together those two are the
arc.

The threshold is inverted for two of the four quadrants ($2578 and $2592), which
is easy to miss because the branch tests the heading against different constants
on each side.

$25B9 maps the stepper's movement to a direction index arithmetically rather than
by lookup: index 4 means no movement, the x delta shifts by one and the y delta
by three, each sign-flipped when its base is zero. An index of 4 sends control
back to $24FD to try again rather than committing a step that went nowhere.

Also documents what the undo ring actually holds, now that $25EF makes it clear:
$2C-$34 are nine tried-direction flags, one per direction, and they are in the
record so that an unwind resumes the direction search rather than restarting it.
That is why the record is twelve bytes and why the flags come first.

events.title: correct: backtracking does not rewind the random state
events.message:
correct: backtracking does not rewind the random state

An earlier commit claimed that an unwind restores the generator along with the
position, reasoning that $1F/$20 sit inside the block $1B55 copies. Measured
across every backtrack in a continent fill, that is false -- the position changes
and neither generator moves.

The undo record written at $15CA is $2C-$34 followed by $14, $15 and $1A: nine
bytes of working state plus position and heading. $16D1 restores exactly those
twelve bytes. So an unwind rewinds where the walk is, not what it will draw next,
and a retried step gets fresh numbers.

$1B55, which copies $47-$4D into $1F-$25, is a different mechanism whose callers
are $1879 and $1AED, neither on the backtrack path. I conflated the two because
both are save-and-restore of a zero-page run, and the conflation was load-bearing
for a conclusion I stated confidently.

The two-generator finding itself stands: $0A9D is real, $27D4 does swap the
vectors, and satellites do draw from $1F/$20. Only the consequence was wrong. A
port needs both generators; it does not need to snapshot them per step, which
makes the walker simpler rather than harder.

Worth noting $1F/$20 read 0,0 throughout a continent fill -- the second generator
is genuinely untouched there, which is consistent with the vector swap being
per-landmass rather than per-step.

events.title: port the step evaluator and its neighbourhood scan
events.message:
port the step evaluator and its neighbourhood scan

$1476 is the test that actually shapes a coastline, as distinct from $1A00, which
only validates positions restored during an unwind. For each of nine directions it
proposes an offset and counts land in a 3x3 block around it. Candidate proposals,
scan origin and neighbour counts all now match the original across 154 recorded
evaluations.

The direction table at $13DA is indexed twice with different bases -- at
2 * (direction mod 3) + $1B for x and 2 * (direction div 3) + $1C for y -- so the
nine directions enumerate a 3x3 neighbourhood rotated into the current quadrant.
An error in either index rotates the whole neighbourhood rather than moving one
candidate, which is the kind of fault that produces plausible coastlines in the
wrong places.

Three capture bugs, each found because the failure had a shape.

The scan row was read at $150C, after the loop. The outer loop calls $289D once
per iteration, so the pointer sits three rows below where the scan began; every
row was wrong by exactly 3, while columns were right because the loop advances
$02 rather than $0C.

The captured cells were centred on the origin. The original decrements both $0C
and the row pointer before building its pointer, so the block runs from the
origin down and right -- origin..origin+2 on each axis, not origin-1..origin+1.
That left counts short by exactly one wherever land sat on the far edge.

Splitting scanOrigin from neighbourCount is what made those separable. With the
origin derived inside the counting routine, both faults presented identically as
a wrong count; taking the origin as a parameter meant the origin test failed on
its own and said the row was off by 3.

events.title: port the walker's candidate validation
events.message:
port the walker's candidate validation

$1A00 decides whether a restored position is usable: the offset must sit on the
coastline circle within a tolerance of three, and the row must be clear for about
ten cells either side. All three parts now match the original -- the circle test,
the radius modulation it performs on the way through, and the clearance scan.

$1A00 turns out to be the backtrack validator, not the main candidate test. Its
only caller is $16D1, which is why the satellite -- the one fill that never
unwinds -- makes zero calls to it, where the continent makes hundreds. The main
candidate test is the tail of $1476.

The distance metric at $19CC is (dx*dx + dy*dy) / workingRadius, and $0A6E builds
its quotient in $03 as well as returning it in A, which is how $255D can read $03
immediately afterwards as the metric.

The clearance scans are asymmetric. Left runs from max(column - 10, 1) up to but
not including the column, and is skipped entirely when the column is 1. Right
runs from column + 1 through column + 10. The left clamp is to 1, not 0.

Capturing this needed two corrections. $1A00 has two reject exits and I hooked
only one: $1A24 is the clearance scan finding land, but $1A05 returns straight
after the circle test refuses, and that is where most traffic goes -- hooking one
captured 7 calls out of 421. And the clearance scan reads the mask, so the
fixture now records the cells around the resolved column; without them only the
circle test is checkable, which is 69 of 73 cases but not the interesting four.
