events.title: Unroll the rotor: the walk moves into the rows, the rows into a program
events.message:
Unroll the rotor: the walk moves into the rows, the rows into a program

Two changes that only make sense together, and only fit now the blitter
has a bank of its own.

C - every compiled rotor routine ends by walking a scanline. The walk
was the one thing that had to happen between rows, so putting it inside
each row leaves nothing between them at all.

B - a straight-line program per (shift, phase). Sixteen for the draw and
sixteen for the restore, each ten JSRs with the digit block and the two
blank rows in the middle. Entering one is a table read, a poke and a
JMP: the program ends in RTS, so the tail call returns straight to
SprDrawSlot's caller. No index, no counter, no end test, no dispatch
per row - a rotor row costs a JSR and an RTS.

The interpreted fallback keeps the sequence lists and the per-row test,
because only that can decide which rows drop to the slow path. But the
compiled rows it calls now walk on their own account, so it needs a tail
that does not walk again: sd_nextnw and sr_nextnw, taken only from the
self-modified call site. Blank rows and the slow path still use the
walking tail.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 4,566 -> 4,300, SprRestoreAll 2,454 -> 2,243; 7,020 -> 6,543.

Cumulative over the whole run: 9,616 -> 6,543, a 32.0% cut. Seven
sprites cost 45.8K of the 79,872-cycle pass, against 67.3K at the start.

Cost: the sprite bank goes from 33 pages to 48, leaving 4.2K spare. Main
RAM shrinks by 179 bytes - the two dispatch loops are gone.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites, static and scrolling.

Left on the table: the program's last row walks and nothing reads the
result, because the routine it calls is shared with rows that do need
it. 42 cycles, and it wants a no-walk variant of the four end-kind
routines to collect.

events.title: port the walker's shape parameters
events.message:
port the walker's shape parameters

$1731 computes six values and they do not all come from the same radius. $0F and
$13 use the command's nominal radius while $12, $25 and $11 use the working
radius that $178A modulates, so mixing them changes a coastline's character
without changing anything obviously. Verified against the parameters the original
held at each of the three fills.

$178A and $17A6 are continents only, returning immediately when the nominal
radius is below $46. That matches the traces exactly: $21 sits constant at 3 and
10 for satellites and islands while a continent's climbs 70, 71, 72, 73, 74.

$11 divides by target minus working radius, which is zero for a radius-3
satellite. The original's divide answers $FF rather than faulting and the port
inherits that through Arithmetic, where the same wart was already preserved
deliberately.

events.title: port the walk's steppers, matching coordinates and generator state
events.message:
port the walk's steppers, matching coordinates and generator state

$1555 and $1583 are the walk's only consumers of randomness, so they set the
whole sequence. Both now match the original across 160 recorded steps, on the
coordinate reached and on the generator state afterwards.

The generator state is the half that would have gone unnoticed. These routines
consume a variable number of draws, because $1564 redraws while a value comes up
$FF -- measured over one continent, one draw 1,106 times, two 299 times, three
once. A stepper landing on the right coordinate having burned a different number
of draws desynchronizes everything after it, and the finished mask is the only
place that surfaces.

Two bugs found by the fixture rather than by reading.

The steppers index different tables. $1555 reads $13DA (01 FF) and $1583 reads
$13DE (FF 01) -- the same pair reversed, four bytes further along. Using one for
both mirrors every vertical step, and I had written exactly that.

The fixture initially recorded $CD/$CF as the generator for every case, which is
wrong for satellites: $0B11 is patched between $0AE2 and $0A9D, and the
satellite's state lives in $1F/$20. Recording the wrong pair made $CD/$CF appear
frozen across all 40 satellite steps -- the fixture said "expected $C923" every
time, unchanged, which is what identified it. The active vector is now read
rather than assumed, and both pairs are recorded.

Adds WalkerState, which groups $1F-$25 as a single Saved value. That grouping is
not cosmetic: it is the block $1B55 copies, and it contains the generator, so an
unwind restores the randomness along with the position. Keeping them together
makes it structurally hard to restore one and forget the other.

events.title: Move the whole sprite blitter into its own sideways bank
events.message:
Move the whole sprite blitter into its own sideways bank

The blitter outgrew what was left of one bank once every rotor row and
every glyph became compiled code, so the sprite half moves out on its
own: artwork, the compiled rows, the glyphs and the sequence lists to
SWRAM_SPR, and tiles, levels, palettes and the droid game data staying
in SWRAM_DATA. The export splits at the same seam - droids.asm is the
sprite bank, droidgame.asm the speeds, waypoints and per-deck type base.

Only one bank is visible at a time, which is workable because the two
halves are never wanted at once: DoRedraws reads tiles and charRemap,
the blitter reads none of that, and they run at different points in the
pass. SprRestoreAll and SprDrawAll page SWRAM_SPR in and SWRAM_DATA back
out around themselves, so the data bank is the resting state and no
caller has to know. Two swaps a pass, 8 cycles each.

The IRQ is what would break this, and does not: RuptVSync and RuptTimer
touch the CRTC, the VIA and their own variables and read nothing out of
either bank. Checked rather than assumed - an interrupt that read tile
data would corrupt at random with the sprite bank in.

Two beebasm mechanics worth writing down:

  CLEAR is what lets the same &8000-&BFFF be assembled twice. beebasm
  tracks which bytes have been written and refuses to overwrite them,
  which is the guard you want everywhere except here.

  SAVE writes out whatever the image holds AT THE TIME IT RUNS, so each
  bank must be saved where it is assembled. Both SAVEs left at the
  bottom of the file silently wrote the sprite bank into PARADAT - the
  deck rendered as garbage and the droid types came out as 164-169.

Data bank 27 pages, sprite bank 33; 7.8K spare in the sprite bank, which
is what the full unroll is going to spend.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites, static and scrolling.

The save AREAS differ, in bytes nothing reads. A slot's 256-byte page is
only partly covered - blank rows save nothing and a compiled row saves
only the columns it draws - so the rest keeps whatever the PARADAT or
now PARASPR staging copy left at &3000. The buffer being identical is
the proof that none of it matters: the save area exists only to be read
back into the buffer, so a differing byte that was ever read would show
up there, and over 40 passes every slot restores 40 times.

events.title: Dispatch the rotor by sequence, and write out the shape of a sprite
events.message:
Dispatch the rotor by sequence, and write out the shape of a sprite

The ten rotor rows a sprite draws are fixed once its shift and phase are
known, so the sequence is a property of (shift, phase) - sixteen of them
- and not of the sprite. drSeqLo/Hi list the ten addresses in drawing
order, so dispatch becomes an indexed read and a poke with no row->slot
lookup, no add and no row counter.

And a sprite that cleared the wrap test up front has no row that CAN
wrap, so its shape is a constant: five rotor rows, a blank, the digit
block, a blank, five more. Writing that out removes the row counter, the
blank-row table lookup and the end test from every iteration - all the
work the loop did to discover what it already knew. Four sprites in five
come through it.

The interpreted loop stays for the fifth, because only a per-row test
can decide which rows fall back - but it now runs ONLY with sprNoWrap
clear, so it drops that test from every row and its digit-block arm goes
entirely: the block never opens there.

The list is indexed by X, not Y: the compiled rows use A and Y and would
eat an index kept in Y. X they never touch.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 5,093 -> 4,566, SprRestoreAll 2,913 -> 2,454; 8,006 -> 7,020.

Cumulative over the six steps: 9,616 -> 7,020, a 27.0% cut. Seven
sprites cost 49.1K of the 79,872-cycle pass, against 67.3K at the start.

Cost: 192 bytes of bank - 640 of sequence lists against 448 of dispatch
tables deleted - leaving 1,369 spare.

---

THE TILE MAP NOW HAS A FIXED HOME, at &3800. It used to sit at the next
page boundary after code_end, which was fine while the code was small
and silently walked into the sprite save areas at &3000 when it was not.
This commit is what made it not: the first build put the map at
&2D00-&3100, straight over slot 0's saved background, with no assert to
catch it. There are asserts now, on both ends and on code_end.

&3700-&47FF is clear - the save areas end at &36FF, SPR_MASKTAB is at
&5700 and the panel starts at &4800 - and the move gives the code the
whole of &1100-&3000. Headroom goes from 143 bytes to 1,005, which is
the constraint that would otherwise have blocked the next layer as much
as this change.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites - play buffer and all seven save areas, static and scrolling.

events.title: two generators, and backtracking rewinds the random state
events.message:
two generators, and backtracking rewinds the random state

$0A9D is a second LFSR -- byte for byte the same algorithm as $0AE2, four ROLs,
the same taps, the same all-zero escape, but on $1F/$20 instead of $CD/$CF. $0A87
mirrors $0ACB as its modulo wrapper. $27D4 and $27DE swap the vectors at
$0B11/$0B14, so the same walker code draws from whichever generator is installed:
continents and islands use $CD/$CF, satellites use $1F/$20.

Found by counting entries to $0AE2 during each fill. The satellite made zero,
while $1555 unconditionally calls $0B10 -- so the routine had not stopped drawing,
it was drawing somewhere else. I first reported that as "the satellite makes no
random draws", which was the measurement read at face value.

The consequence matters more than the mechanism. $1F/$20 live inside the walker's
saved state block: $1B55 copies $47-$4D into $1F-$25 and $17C8 copies back, and
that block is the second LFSR's state, the working radius, the centre and a shape
parameter. So when the walker backtracks it restores the random state along with
the position, and the retried step re-draws the same numbers rather than fresh
ones. An unwind is a true undo, not a retry with new luck.

A port keeping one global generator, or treating the RNG as outside the walker's
state, diverges the first time a landmass backtracks -- 155 times in a single
continent. Nothing in the routine listing suggests any of it.

Also settles the retry loop at $1564 as live rather than dead: over one continent,
stepper calls consumed one draw 1,106 times, two draws 299 times, three draws
once.

events.title: the walk loop spans two regions, and $18 is computed per step
events.message:
the walk loop spans two regions, and $18 is computed per step

$15AD is half the loop. $16B8 does JMP $24FD, and that region generates the next
candidate before control returns to $15AD to commit it -- recompute the shape
through $178A, choose an axis, compute the step threshold, advance one
coordinate, then validate.

The walk always advances its smaller coordinate, breaking ties with a coin flip
at $252D. That is what carries it around the arc: dx rises while dy falls, and
whichever is behind moves next.

Corrects a reading from earlier today. I searched for writers of $18, found them
all outside $14xx-$1Bxx, and concluded the step thresholds were inherited from
another phase. They are not: $2542 writes $18 on every step, and it is in the
walk path -- just not in the address range the walker appeared to occupy. $18 is
the chosen coordinate scaled by $10, which is itself $80 / $0F, so the further
along an axis the walk has gone the larger $18 becomes and the less likely
$1555/$1583 are to step again. That is the mechanism that bends a straight walk
into an arc, and I had it as a constant.

Neither region is comprehensible alone and nothing in the call graph marks them
as one routine, which is the same trap as $194A: reading by address range finds
parts, not algorithms.

events.title: port the walker's offset resolution, verified cell by cell
events.message:
port the walker's offset resolution, verified cell by cell

$13E0 turns an offset and a heading into an absolute cell, and everything the
walker draws goes through it. CoastlineWalker.cell transcribes it, checked
against every cell the original itself wrote across all three fills -- plots,
erases and span fill.

The quadrant table is asymmetric and not what you would guess: dx negates for
headings 0 and 1, dy for 0 and 3. The arithmetic is modular on purpose, x wrapping
as a byte and y as sixteen bits, which a landmass near an edge relies on.

Getting this verified took two corrections to the fixture, both found by small
clusters of disagreement rather than wholesale failure, which is what made them
diagnosable.

First, $13E0 reads its arguments from A and Y, not from $14/$15. The walk passes
$16/$17 through $16AF, but the span fill at $1648 does LDA #$00 / JSR $1728 and
plots a whole column at dx = 0 while $14 still holds the walk's last value.
Recording $14/$15 mislabelled exactly the span-fill plots -- four events, all at
the tail of each fill.

Second, capturing A and Y at $1728 and $1B3B is right for one and wrong for the
other. $1728 is entered with its arguments already loaded by its caller, but
$1B3B loads $14/$15 into A and Y as its own first two instructions, so at its
entry the registers still hold the caller's leftovers. That mislabelled the
erases instead. Hooking $13E0 itself is correct for every caller, since the
arguments are by definition right at the point that reads them.

Both readings were the obvious ones and both were right for the great majority of
events. Without a fixture recording the cell the original resolved -- read out of
its registers rather than computed by me -- neither would have surfaced, and the
port would have drawn correct coastlines with wrong span fills. walkDx and walkDy
are kept alongside the real arguments because the divergence between them is
itself informative.

events.title: Fix web build audio: main-thread starvation and needless resampling
events.message:
Fix web build audio: main-thread starvation and needless resampling

The Emscripten build played sound samples as a low chugging buzz, worse in
Chrome than Firefox. Four compounding causes, all downstream of one wrong
assumption: that SDL3's Emscripten audio backend runs the callback on its
own thread.

It does not. SDL_emscriptenaudio.c sets ProvidesOwnCallbackThread and drives
playback from a ScriptProcessorNode, so chq_audio_callback runs on the main
browser thread, interleaved with emscripten_set_main_loop's game and render
frame. Every long frame underruns the node.

- The SDL_HINT_AUDIO_DEVICE_SAMPLE_FRAMES "256" hint was asking for a
  smaller buffer to help a producer/consumer race that does not exist. The
  backend doubles the hint, so it gave a 512-frame node -- 10.7ms at 48kHz,
  on the thread that also renders. Ask for 2048 (4096 frames) instead;
  latency is the only cost.

- chq_apply_due_audio_events locked queue_mutex once per sample, i.e. 44kHz
  of lock traffic on the main browser thread, which cannot Atomics.wait and
  so spin-waits when the game Worker contends -- and it contends heavily
  during speech, at three AY writes per nibble. Hoist the lock to one
  acquisition per callback chunk.

- The backend forces the device to audioContext.sampleRate (48kHz on most
  Windows machines), so every callback resampled 44100 to 48000 on that same
  main thread. Query the opened device's rate, set the stream's source rate
  to match, and emulate the AY at that rate. The replay cursor counts sample
  periods in it too, otherwise it would advance at 44100 while the callback
  produced 48000 samples a second and slide events progressively late.

- AY_REPLAY_CUSHION_NS had been raised to 120ms to paper over the above. The
  cushion is also how long the chip holds its last state after the queue
  runs dry, so that turned each starve into a long low chug rather than a
  short click -- the buzz itself. Back down to 50ms.

Native behaviour is unchanged where the device already opens at 44100.

events.title: DEBUG_VSYNC: fields per iteration, as a digit in the panel corner
events.message:
DEBUG_VSYNC: fields per iteration, as a digit in the panel corner

A single 4x5 digit in the top-left of the panel, showing how many TV
fields the last main-loop iteration consumed. FRAME_LOCK is the nominal
reading, so a 2 means the iteration fitted and a 3 or more means it
overran and the rate degraded to 16.7 Hz, 12.5 Hz and so on.

It goes in the PANEL, not the play area: the panel does not scroll, so
the digit stays where it is put and never has to be saved or restored
under a sprite.

ONE BYTE PER SCANLINE IS THE WHOLE TRICK. A MODE 1 byte is four pixels
and consecutive bytes within a character cell are consecutive
scanlines, so a 4x5 digit is five bytes at five consecutive addresses -
five loads and five stores, no masking, no row stride. The whole
routine is ~80 cycles against the 80,000 in a pass, which is what makes
it safe to leave running while measuring something else. A font that
needed masking, or that spanned more than one byte per row, would start
measuring itself.

The font is stored as 4-bit row patterns multiplied by 17: logical
colour 3 wants both of a pixel's bits set and they sit four apart in a
MODE 1 byte, so the pattern goes in both nibbles.

vsyncCount was already being bumped once per field by IrqHandler's CA1
arm, so the reading is one subtraction. Called immediately after
WaitVSync returns, where the boundary has just happened, so the digit
describes the iteration that has just finished.

Verified in jsbeeb: reads 2 as it stands, 3 with ~26,000 cycles of
delay patched into the loop, and 4 with ~64,000.

Off by default. Enabling it costs 117 bytes and leaves 26 before the
tile map at &2C00, so it and anything else do not both fit.

events.title: Give the digit block eight row pointers so the glyphs stop walking
events.message:
Give the digit block eight row pointers so the glyphs stop walking

The block is eight known scanlines. SprBuildRowPtrs works out all eight
addresses once into zero page and each compiled glyph row addresses its
own as (rowp+2r),Y, so the three glyph passes no longer advance a
pointer at all. That deletes 21 scanline advances a sprite - the largest
single item left after the walk itself was made cheap - and pays for one
build of eight pointers instead.

THE POSITION MOVES FROM THE POINTER INTO Y. The three digit positions
used to be reached by offsetting bufp by 0, 16 and 32, which with eight
pointers would have meant offsetting all eight per position. Instead the
glyph holds the position in X for its whole body and loads
`LDY drYcol0,X`, giving Y = pos*16 + col*8. That is two cycles a column
against ~100 a position, it tops out at Y=40 so the save area still fits
one page, and it is what lets the three positions share one set of
pointers. The shifted glyphs' spill into a shared column still lands on
the right byte: position p column 2 and position p+1 column 0 both come
out at Y = (p+1)*16.

With bufp untouched by the glyphs, the block needs no mark and no
rewind: SprBlkSave is the only pass that walks, so it is also what
leaves bufp and svp on row 14 for the caller. SprBlkMark, SprBlkReset,
sprMulStep, blkPtr, blkEnd, blkEndSvp and SprNextScanB all go.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 5,587 -> 5,093. SprRestoreAll 2,879 -> 2,913, which is the
+/-50 code-layout noise floor - the restore never enters a glyph.

Cumulative over the five steps: 9,616 -> 8,006, a 16.7% cut. Seven
sprites cost 56.0K of the 80,000-cycle pass, against 67.3K at the start.
Code is 51 bytes smaller and the bank 157 bytes smaller.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites - play buffer and all seven save areas, static and scrolling.

Harness note: anchoring the rotor phase has to happen at a LOGICAL
point, not at a fixed cycle count. Zeroing sprFrame mid-pass lands
either side of SprAnimateAll depending on where that build happens to
be, and the two runs then differ by one phase - same signature as
before, every rotor row differing while the digit rows match. Park the
game first, zero while parked, then resume: write JMP <the routine's own
resume path> over the self-park, run ~2000 cycles to let the CPU out,
and put the self-park back.

  (sans EtherNEC), serialize() écrivait un vecteur vide et l'invariant
  « mem_ taille inattendue » rejetait TOUT .state au chargement — F7/« load

events.title: Stop the sprite row loops after the last row that draws anything
events.message:
Stop the sprite row loops after the last row that draws anything

Row 20 is blank for every droid, so its iteration tested a table, wrote
nothing, and then advanced both pointers to a scanline no one reads. The
row 19 -> 20 advance was dead for the same reason.

Both loops now stop at SPR_LASTROW, and the walk moves to AFTER the end
test rather than before it, so the last row drawn does not step off the
end. Nothing else changes: rows 5 and 14 are still ordinary blank-row
iterations, because the generic loop cannot know statically that they
follow rows 4 and 13.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 5,773 -> 5,587, SprRestoreAll 2,939 -> 2,879; 8,712 -> 8,466.

Cumulative over the four steps: 9,616 -> 8,466, a 12.0% cut. Seven
sprites cost 59.3K of the 80,000-cycle pass, against 67.3K at the start.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites - play buffer and all seven save areas, static and scrolling.

Harness note: anchor the ROTOR PHASE before the counted passes. The
oracle parks the game after N passes by patching the JMP at the bottom
of the main loop, but that patch is installed at a fixed cycle count,
and once the code speed changes the two builds are not in the same pass
when it lands - here they parked three passes apart. Every rotor row of
every sprite then differs while the digit rows match exactly, because
the rotor depends on phase and the digits on type. Zero sprFrame and
sprDelay after settling and before installing the park. It is safe to
do mid-run: the restore replays sprTabBaseS, which records the phase the
draw actually used.

events.title: Inline the scanline walk at the four sites that can take it
events.message:
Inline the scanline walk at the four sites that can take it

SprNextScan was a subroutine called 42 times a sprite, and 12 of its 33
cycles were the JSR/RTS pair. Only four places walk with svp in hand -
sd_next, sr_next, SprBlkSave and SprBlkRest - so it becomes a macro,
SCANSTEP, expanded four times at 17 bytes each. The step drops from 33
cycles to 21.

The compiled glyphs keep calling SprNextScanB: 140 call sites in the
bank, and inlining there would cost 2.7K against 1,404 bytes spare.

The row crossing stays out of line as SprScanRow. It is taken on one
step in six and it is 23 bytes, so putting it behind a JSR is what keeps
the macro small enough to expand. WrapBufFwd's RTS returns straight to
the macro site, as it did to the caller before.

The macro is SCANSTEP, not NEXTSCAN, because NEXT is a BeebASM keyword:
a macro whose name starts with it assembles fine and then fails at every
invocation with "Bad expression" pointing at the use rather than the
definition. P%+4 and P%+5 skip the following instruction because a macro
body cannot declare a label - the second expansion would redefine it.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 6,038 -> 5,773, SprRestoreAll 3,177 -> 2,939; 9,215 -> 8,712.

Cumulative over the three steps: 9,616 -> 8,712, a 9.4% cut. Seven
sprites now cost 61.0K of the 80,000-cycle pass, against 67.3K before.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites - play buffer and all seven save areas, static and scrolling.

Harness note: the measurement and input stubs live between code_end and
the tile map, and this commit pushed code_end from &2B7B to &2BA4. A
stub left at &2BA0 lands on vsyncCount and oldIrq1V, and the corruption
reads exactly like a sprite bug that only appears when scrolling. Check
code_end against the stub address after every build.

events.title: Read the sprite scanline out of bufp instead of counting it
events.message:
Read the sprite scanline out of bufp instead of counting it

Every term of bufp is a multiple of 8 - BUF_BASE is &5800, a display
row is 640 bytes, a column is 8, and the hardware wrap subtracts
10240 - every term except the scanline itself. So `bufp AND 7` IS the
scanline, and SprNextScan was keeping a counter in step with something
it could have read. Advance the pointer first and ask afterwards:
landing on a multiple of 8 means the character row just ended.

The walk drops from 31 cycles to 27 in the common case and pays 8 more
at a row crossing, which it takes 2-3 times in 21 rows, so it comes out
ahead by 4 cycles on 5 steps in 6. sprScan survives only as the sprite's
STARTING scanline - SprCalcAddr sets it, SprSetSave seeds svp from it,
and it is stashed per slot for the restore to replay. Nothing updates it
during a walk any more.

That also empties the digit block's mark and rewind: the scanline rides
in bufp's low bits, so restoring the pointer restores the walk position
with it. blkScan and blkEndScan are gone.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 128 passes:
SprDrawAll 6,226 -> 6,038, SprRestoreAll 3,226 -> 3,177; 9,452 -> 9,215.
Code is 34 bytes smaller.

Byte-identical to the pre-optimisation build over 40 passes with seven
sprites - play buffer and all seven save areas, static and scrolling.

Note when comparing builds: measure over ~128 passes, not 16. The rotor
phase cycles every 8 and the per-phase spread is a few hundred cycles,
so a 16- or 17-sample average is biased by which phases it happened to
catch. There is also a noise floor of roughly +/-50 cycles between
builds from abs,X lookups landing on different sides of a page boundary
once the code shifts.

events.title: Drop the dead svp maintenance from the glyph passes
events.message:
Drop the dead svp maintenance from the glyph passes

The compiled glyphs address every byte as (bufp),Y and never touch svp:
the digit block hoists the save into SprBlkSave and the restore into
SprBlkRest, so a glyph has no background of its own to put anywhere.
Advancing svp in step through the 21 glyph walks therefore produced a
value nothing read - SprDigitBlock overwrites svp from blkEndSvp the
moment the block finishes.

SprNextScanB is SprNextScan without the svp half. The glyphs call it;
everything else still calls SprNextScan. The two must keep the same
row-crossing pattern, since the glyph passes have to land on the same
scanlines SprBlkSave did.

With svp out of the glyph passes, SprBlkMark/SprBlkReset no longer need
to mark it and SprBlkGlyph's position offset applies to bufp alone.

Measured, one sprite, static view, averaged over 16 passes:
SprDrawAll 6,368 -> 6,213 (-155). SprRestoreAll unchanged at ~3,420, as
expected - the restore never enters a glyph.

Verified byte-identical to the previous build over 40 passes with seven
sprites, both the 10K play buffer and all seven save areas, static and
scrolling. (Drive the scroll by patching ReadKeys, not by holding a key:
a keypress at a fixed cycle count lands a pass earlier or later once the
code speed changes, and the runs then diverge for reasons that have
nothing to do with the change under test.)

events.title: net: arrêt du lecteur TCP par shutdown→join→close (course de réattribution du fd)
events.message:
net: arrêt du lecteur TCP par shutdown→join→close (course de réattribution du fd)

close() avant le join libérait le NUMÉRO de descripteur pendant que le thread
lecteur détenait encore sa copie : l'OS pouvait réattribuer le même numéro à
la connexion d'un autre canal (worker HTTP) et le lecteur périmé consommait
jusqu'à 200 ms de SES octets. sockShutdown() (nouveau, neonet) coupe les deux
sens sans libérer le fd — recv retourne, le thread sort, closeLocked ferme
après le join.

events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 33 phase A — the collectable band and the gold chain

Six routines, 506 bytes, all CLEAN: slots 28/30/31 ($4e38/$4eca/$4f9c)
and the helper cluster $517a..$5207. 26 of 62 dispatch rows live.
Verified 231 / 26,512 B (59.9 %); suite 4359 -> 4451 (test_behavior
846).

The band is the walking collectables and their payout. Slot 28 walks by
the byte the damage arm stamps and tests its step with the tier's only
`tst.w` (the probes leave a map column in the high byte — a word
helper, pinned against the byte form). Slot 30 hovers on a 32-word
signed drift triangle behind a GLOBAL cursor at $4f5a — two live
records share one phase, pinned as such — and carries a shipped meter
bug reproduced as-is. Slot 31 is 78 bytes, not the scouted 146: $4fea
is actor_select_sprite_by_flag, ported since batch 29.

Two # ctx names fell to the bytes. $517a is
hud_award_gold_from_descriptor — three witnesses tie bcd_counter_bd6e
to the gold ("gold get.", the digits $51d8 patches into that string,
the shop price compare). $51d8 is text_write_gold_digits_a2ac: TWO
characters at $a2ac..$a2ad, tens blanked to a space — not "four ASCII
digits". And $51ac is bcd_add_random_1_to_4: the scout's `and.b` was
`abcd d1,d0` mis-decoded (see the prg_dis commit) — it ADDS a
packed-BCD 1..4 into the award, seeded from the two video-counter
bytes the kit modeled last commit; its differentials declare them per
case, and an undeclared read refuses.

The independent gate closed three coverage holes proven by mutant:
slot 30's signed meter compare (casts dropped survived 4447 green; the
$7ffe wrap row reds it), slot 31's flicker equality (was pinned only
through slot 30's site), and the sweep's two battery holes. bcd/meter
models promoted to leaf.py; the ported-row count is pinned by test
after drifting twice; WB_ACTOR_TYPE30_DRIFT_STRIDE split from the
frame-stride constant it coincided with.

Known divergence, recorded not hidden: hud.c models BCD entry X = 0;
this band is the first ported code chaining accumulators back to back.
Exposing seeds are in STATUS; fixing it moves hud.h and three
batteries — queued as the rest of batch 33. Batch 34 = slots 32-37.

wonderboy/atari: batch 33 opens — the rng false green retired

The kit's new video-counter slots land on this game's registered
T3-DATA false green and close it: rng_next's entropy term ($ff8209) was
served a fabricated 0 on both sides of every differential since the
generator was ported. It now reads hw_read8 under a per-case
declaration — 22 cases across four batteries refused the moment the
byte became modeled, every path through the generator declares it, and
the XOR is pinned AS AN OPERATOR for the first time (five declared
bytes against one seeded state; 0x5a^0xff separates from addition).
Two consumer cases drive the respawn kind-draw at non-zero counters, so
the entropy's spenders are pinned by variation too. The retirement is
qualified honestly: audio capture still serves the counter a fabricated
0 by design (the profile's known-mask excludes it), and artifacts made
before this commit embed the zero-entropy generator.

leaf.py now owns the modeled-hardware address home (VIDEO_COUNTER_MID/
LOW beside MFP_GPIP/SHIFTER_SYNC, full-table equality pin restored from
the [:2] prefix that assumed slots only append) and hw_declared() — the
batteries stop importing a kit fact from a sibling battery. The old
false-green prose is retired from every surface that carried it
(test_rng's docstring — rewritten as history, not deleted — rng.h,
behavior.h, wonderboy.h, names.txt cmt 0x51ac, both READMEs,
PORTABILITY §3/§0i with the dated §0g/§0j scans marked in place).

events.title: capture one fill per rung as a unit test for the walker
events.message:
capture one fill per rung as a unit test for the walker

Records the machine state at $23D3 entry and every mask write that follows, for a
single landmass. That turns "port the walker" into a closed problem: given this
starting state, produce this sequence of cells. Three cases, easiest first --
satellite at radius 3 with 23 plots and no backtracking, island at radius 10 with
93 plots and 13 backtracks, continent at radius 70. If the satellite passes and
the island fails, the bug is in backtracking; if the satellite fails, it is in the
core walk.

Digests would not do here. For the mask a SHA-256 gives a bit-exact test in 16
characters, but for a port under development it says only that the walk went
wrong, not where. Per-event resolution is the entire reason the interpreter
exists, so the fixture carries events.

Records writes as offsets from the landmass centre rather than absolute cells.
The centre lives in $22/$23:$24 and never moves during a fill while $14/$15 are
what the walk advances, so absolute coordinates would bake in my own reading of
$13E0 -- and the fixture would then agree with a port that got $13E0 wrong in the
same way.

Captures all 256 bytes of zero page rather than a chosen subset. The walker reads
at least $0F-$13, $18, $19, $1A, $21, $25, $2B, $46, $50 and $B0-$B3, and I have
been wrong three times today about what this code depends on. Choosing fields in
advance risks discovering a dependency only after the port disagrees, at which
point it is unclear whether the fault is in the logic or the setup.

The continent case is truncated to 150 of its 1,026 events, which drops the
fixture from 153 KB to 43 KB while still covering 30 backtracks. A port diverges
at its first wrong cell, so the tail costs bytes without adding diagnostic power.
The fixture records eventsTotal alongside eventsRecorded and a truncated flag, so
it cannot be mistaken for a complete trace.

events.title: input: stretch the TOS key-repeat delay, and add FRUA_KEYDIAG (#132)
events.message:
input: stretch the TOS key-repeat delay, and add FRUA_KEYDIAG (#132)

MEASURED baseline, which is the finding: TOS hands us Kbrate = 0x0F02 — a key
starts repeating after 15 ticks (0.3s) and then repeats every 2 ticks (25/sec).
That is desktop tuning. On an 8MHz machine where one FRUA repaint can take most
of a second, an ordinary keystroke can outlast 0.3s and emit a second character —
rare, unpredictable, and impossible to see under the test harness, where injected
keys press and release in ~0.1s. That last point is why this has historically
been blamed on the injector.

plat_input_init now asks for a 90-tick (~1.8s) delay and leaves the rate alone,
so a deliberate hold still repeats but a normal press cannot. The old value is
restored at shutdown (Kbrate returns delay in the high byte, rate in the low).
Atari-only: the Amiga has its own input layer.

FRUA_KEYDIAG (opt-in) traces a key through every layer it crosses —
plat_kb_poll (the lowest point a key enters the port), kb_to_event, the jt1125
and l6dd0 stamps, and the jt1133 read — so COUNTS separate "the key arrived
twice from below" from "we processed one key twice".

What it has already shown, in the char-gen name field:
- 15 consecutive keys: 15 polls / 15 events / 15 stamps / 15 reads. Clean.
- ONE anomalous run: 3 polls but 4 READS — an extra read with no key behind it,
  i.e. the engine delivered a stale -818 twice. Real, and NOT injector doubling
  (the poll count was correct).
Ruled out for that extra read: the l6dd0 path (it always sets -818 AND -820
together — line 25656 — and never fired here at all) and event-queue
duplication (queue_push is only used for mouse edges and PostEvent, never
keyDown).

So #132 is NOT closed: the Kbrate change addresses a real hardware-only
doubling mechanism, but the engine-side extra read is reproduced-once and
unexplained. Note when reading the trace that dbglog DEFERS lines written from
interrupt context, so the sequence can be reordered — trust the counts, not the
order.

469 passed, 6 skipped; 68000 / amiga-ECS both build.

events.title: the outline is walked one quadrant at a time
events.message:
the outline is walked one quadrant at a time

$15AD's loop, now read end to end: bump $46 and wrap the ring at 201, write the
12-byte undo record, adopt the candidate ($16,$17) as the current ($14,$15), plot
it, then test whether the walk has reached an axis. $160F picks $14 or $15 by
heading parity, and when that coordinate reaches zero the walker turns with
INC $1A and adjusts $B3 through $17A6. Four turns close the circle, and $1642
catches $1A == 4 and falls into the span fill.

That explains the traced offsets. dx climbing monotonically while dy drifts is
quadrant 0; the other three are the same walk rotated by $13E0, which is why the
trace of a single fill looked like a quarter arc rather than a circle.

So a landmass is three steps, not one: trace a perturbed circle with backtracking,
span fill at $1648 with the self-modified INC/DEC at $1657, then flood fill the
interior with $194A. A port that implements only the trace produces coastlines
with nothing inside them.

events.title: engine: delete by erasing the cell, not by drawing a space (jt1078)
events.message:
engine: delete by erasing the cell, not by drawing a space (jt1078)

#131. Maintainer's read of the symptom was the key: "maybe it's only doing a
move left and not move-left-and-delete". That is precisely what the code could
do, because the erase was a PRINTED SPACE and the tail cleanup was the repaint's
single trailing space ("%s ") — both of which only erase if a space glyph paints
its BACKGROUND opaquely. Where it does not, the letter stays on screen, the next
keystroke lands on top of it, and the field reads as corrupted.

Deletion no longer rests on that assumption: the vacated cell (plus the old
cursor cell after it) is cleared with jt1161, a filled rect in the field's bg —
the same primitive this loop's own cursor block uses, so it cannot depend on
glyph rendering at all.

Both display modes in the report are the SAME Mega STe (Control at boot skips
AUTO for ST-Low; letting AUTO load the xVDI drivers gives the card), so a
backend-specific cause was never likely — a rendering assumption shared by both
fits far better.

Verified in Hatari (FRUA_CHARGEN drops straight into char-gen), and the rect is
checked not to over-erase: HELLO -> BS -> BS = "HEL" (prompt and remaining
letters intact), + P = "HELP" (typing after a delete is clean), then backspaced
to empty with one extra press at empty — field blank, "CHARACTER NAME:" prompt
undamaged.

Together with 3a36487a (the Atari DELETE key was a no-op) this should close #131
on hardware. 469 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: $194A is the interior fill, and $9100 is a shared region
events.message:
$194A is the interior fill, and $9100 is a shared region

The walker traces an outline; it never fills it. $194A does that, by scanline
flood fill: walk left while the cell is land to find an edge, walk right to the
span start, fill leftwards with ORA $13D3,X / STA ($29),Y until a set bit stops
it, seed the rows above and below, and pop the next span until $46 wraps to $FF.

So each landmass is two stages: trace a perturbed circle, then flood its
interior. That was not visible from the routines alone -- $194A only appeared in
the coverage list, and reading it was deferred as one of the "still unread"
items.

The region at $9100 is shared and the record size depends on the caller. $16BF
computes $9100 + $46 * Y, with $16BB passing 12 for the walker's undo records and
$19B0 passing 3 for the flood fill's span stack of (x, pointer low, pointer
high). An earlier note called it a ring of 201 twelve-byte records without
qualification; that describes only the walker's use of it.

This also explains the $1900 call pattern. The flood fill steps the row pointer
by whole rows, so it is the routine most likely to leave the buffer, which is why
$1900 is called 68 times for an island and 530 for a satellite and not at all
during a continent's outline trace.

events.title: trace the small fills: an incremental order for porting the walker
events.message:
trace the small fills: an incremental order for porting the walker

Each continent is followed by an unregistered radius-3 fill. For seed $1234
configuration 0 the sequence is (166,94)r70, (201,93)r3, (89,247)r70,
(106,267)r3, (187,14)r10, (190,348)r10 -- six fills for four registrations. The
satellites sit 20-35 cells from their continent, inside its footprint, and
islands get none, which fits the $B0 >= $46 size test that gates $178A and $17A6
elsewhere.

They add land rather than carving it: 23 plots, zero erases, zero backtracks. So
they are satellite blobs, not lakes, which is worth knowing before assuming a
fill can only ever grow a landmass.

That gives an order for porting the walker, easiest first: the radius-3 satellite
at 21 walk iterations and no backtracking at all, then the radius-10 island at 91
iterations and 13 backtracks, then the radius-70 continent at 701 and 155. The
satellite isolates the walk, the plot path and the candidate tests before the undo
ring matters.

Corrects a claim in the previous commit. I wrote that the $1900 guard never fired
during the continent fill; the counter counts entries, and the routine was never
called at all. It is called heavily for smaller features -- 68 times for an
island, 530 for a satellite -- and passes every time. The restart path remains
unobserved, which is consistent with it being rare but is not the same evidence
as a guard being exercised and holding.

events.title: trace the walker: the $21 drift was a measurement artifact
events.message:
trace the walker: the $21 drift was a measurement artifact

$21 equals $B0 at every registration across seeds $1234, $BEEF and $0001. There
is no drift. The 71 that appeared in placement_reference.json came from an
emulator capture that overshot $1B5F -- VICE's checkpoints halt late -- into code
that had already modified $21. The program was never doing what the fixture said.

That cost three rounds of checkpoint archaeology, a bricked emulator and a
falsified hypothesis, and the interpreter answered it in one run. Consequences:
the radius field in placement_reference.json is unreliable and b0 should be used
instead, which the Swift tests already do; and any measurement reading memory at
a mid-phase address is suspect the same way, while stage boundaries are safe
because writing has stopped there.

Tracing one fill also corrects the shape of the walker itself.

The position never moves. $22/$23:$24 hold the landmass center for the whole
fill, fixed at the coordinate placement chose. $14/$15 are offsets from it, and
those are what the walk advances, with $13E0 resolving offset-plus-center at each
plot. A port that walks an absolute position would be structurally wrong however
faithfully its routines were transcribed -- which is what I had been about to
write.

The walk traces a circle and modulates its radius. From (dx, dy) = (0, radius),
dx climbs steadily while dy drifts noisily down -- (1,71) (2,70) (3,69) (4,68)
... (22,66), staying within a cell or two of radius 70 -- while $21 climbs 70, 71,
72, 73, 74 as $178A recomputes it from the current dy. So $21 differing from $B0
inside the walker is not corruption, it is the shape mechanism: a circle whose
radius is perturbed as it is traced, rather than a blob roughened afterwards.
Treating that signal as noise is what made the false registration reading
plausible for so long.

Backtracking is the main loop, not an error path: 701 walk iterations, 716 plots,
155 erases and 155 backtracks in one radius-70 fill, so 21.6% of plotted cells
are erased again. The $1900 guard fired zero times, so the restart path is as
rare as assumed.

One loose end: the trace shows fills at radius 3 with no matching registration,
within the command-table stage rather than the second wave -- at (201,93) after
the continent at (166,94), and at (106,267) after (89,247). Not yet identified.

events.title: engine: the Atari DELETE key erases in text fields (jt1078)
events.message:
engine: the Atari DELETE key erases in text fields (jt1078)

#131, partial. The line editor's erase arm handled 8 and 262 only, so the Atari
DELETE key (0x7F) fell through to the printable-insert arm, where `key > 126`
just beeps. Measured in Hatari on the char-gen name prompt (FRUA_CHARGEN):
pressing Delete left the frame BYTE-IDENTICAL. After the fix "XY" + Delete -> "X".

Why the gap existed: on the Mac the key labelled "Del" IS backspace and arrives
as 8, so one case covered that keyboard. An Atari has two distinct keys —
Backspace 8, Delete 0x7F — and only the first was wired.

Noted in a comment while here: 262 is NOT a delete code in this port. jt1125
maps scancode 0x4b (LEFT ARROW) to 262, so Left is destructive in a text field.
Left, so as this editor has no cursor movement for it to do instead, but it is a
port artifact rather than the Mac's meaning.

NOT the whole of #131. The reported "backspace overwrites the letter and
corrupts the text" does NOT reproduce here: on ST-Low, Backspace deletes
correctly ("AABC" -> "AAB") and typing after it appends cleanly ("AABD"). The
erase depends on the repaint's trailing space painting an opaque background, and
that works on this backend; the machine/keypress for the corrupting case still
needs pinning down.

Also observed while testing, as evidence for #132: typing A, B, C produced
"AABC" — the first keystroke doubled, in the emulator, on the FIRST field entry.

events.title: add a 6502 interpreter and reproduce the land-mass phase in-process
events.message:
add a 6502 interpreter and reproduce the land-mass phase in-process

The coastline walker is a backtracking search with three self-modifications and a
stack-discarding non-local exit. Transcribing it and comparing the finished
12,800-byte mask gives exactly one bit of feedback -- "the walk went somewhere
else" -- with no way to localize a fault. sim6502.py makes every intermediate
state observable instead, so a port can be diffed against the original step by
step, and every later phase gets the same.

It reproduces all 18 mask digests: 9 seed and configuration pairs, both stages,
bit-exact, across about 84 million simulated instructions.

That also corroborates the mask fixtures independently. They were captured from
VICE; these come from different starting states through an entirely different
execution engine and agree byte for byte, which settles an earlier worry that
imprecise checkpoint halts might have corrupted them.

Scope is official NMOS opcodes, binary arithmetic, no interrupts. Unknown opcodes
raise rather than being skipped, because a silently ignored instruction produces
plausible wrong output, which is the failure this tool exists to prevent.
Decimal mode raises too. The self-test replays the LFSR at $0AE2 and the multiply
and divide at $0A51/$0A6E against fixtures captured from the real 6502 -- 5
sequences and 3,840 arithmetic cases -- so agreement is evidence about the
interpreter rather than about the routines.

Three things had to be worked out to get a usable starting state.

The interpreter cannot boot the World Maker. Initialization talks to the 1541
over the serial bus: $13BC reads $DD00 twice to debounce and shifts the DATA line
into carry, and $1287/$128C spin on the result. With no drive that never
completes, measured at 855,591 reads of $DD00 and no progress. So wm_snapshot.py
lets the emulator boot and dumps RAM early in the phase, and the interpreter
resumes from there. $D012 must also read $FE or the raster sync at $0A49 spins,
since nothing advances it without interrupts.

VICE's checkpoints halt reliably but late. The machine really is paused and stays
paused -- verified stable across repeated samples -- yet it stops somewhere after
the target by a variable amount: a checkpoint on $212A landed at $143A, $0AF6 and
$230E, and disabling warp did not help. Three attempts went into trying to
control that before it became clear it does not need controlling. Resuming needs
a consistent state, not a particular one, so the snapshot records wherever the
machine actually stopped along with the full register set including flags, which
matter because this code branches on carry across call boundaries.

A checkpoint halt does not survive a long read sequence. Dumping 64 KB let the
machine resume partway through, producing torn snapshots whose PCs came back as
$1B51, $1B54, $1438 and $2373 rather than the target -- and which looked entirely
successful otherwise. The capture now pauses explicitly and compares PC and SP
before and after the dump, rejecting anything that moved.

Also hardened boot(): game3 runs with ROM banked out ($01 = $35), so if a run
ends with the CPU halted inside it the next reset has no ROM to reset into --
$FFFC reads RAM and VICE answers "Machine power cycled" while the PC never moves,
sometimes reporting a PC of 0x10002. That wedged the emulator twice today, once
needing a manual restart. boot() now pauses, restores $01 to $37 and resets
before doing anything else, every time rather than only in recovery.

Snapshots are 64 KB of the game's own code, so they are game data and live in
local/, which is gitignored.

the walker erases as it backtracks

$1B3B clears a mask bit. LandMask asserted the original had no way to do that,
which was wrong -- the routine simply had not been read yet. Land is not
write-once: a backtracking search has to undo what it drew, so the port needs
clearLand alongside setLand.

Also read this round:

$19CC computes ($14^2 + $15^2) / $21, a distance metric over the current radius.
$19EE wraps it -- recompute the radius through $178A, take the absolute
difference against it, and return carry set at 3 or more -- so it answers whether
a point sits on the coastline circle within a tolerance of 3.

$1A00 is the full candidate test: $19EE must accept, and then the mask is scanned
horizontally from $0C - $0A to $0C and from $0C + 1 to $0C + 1 + $0A, rejecting
if anything is already set. A candidate needs the right radius and roughly ten
clear cells either side.

$1A48 erases the current cell, and in one branch patches $1B38 to $60, an RTS,
calls $1A69, then patches it back to $4C, a JMP -- disabling a routine for the
duration of a single call. That is the third self-modification in this phase
after $22B4's bounds and $1657's INC/DEC, and like them it has to survive into
the port rather than being tidied into a flag.

$1A69 steps left and up to find the edge of existing land and rewrites the
heading $1A from comparisons against $22 and $23/$24 -- the wall-following half
of the walk.

events.title: the coastline walker is a backtracking search, not a turtle
events.message:
the coastline walker is a backtracking search, not a turtle

The ring of 201 twelve-byte records at $9100 is an undo stack, not a trail.
$16D1 reads records back out of it: decrement $46, wrapping $FF to $C8, restore
$2C-$34, $14, $15 and $1A from the record, retry through $1A00, and loop back to
$16D1 if that fails as well. It discards its own return address with PLA / PLA
and leaves by JMP, unwinding the caller with it.

This changes how the port has to be approached. A turtle can be transcribed one
routine at a time with each piece testable on its own. A backtracking search
cannot be checked until enough of it exists to run, because a bug anywhere
presents identically as "the walk went somewhere else". The undo record is the
part to get exactly right: nine bytes of $2C-$34, then $14, $15 and $1A.

The steps are a biased random walk. $1555 and $1583 each maybe-step one axis by
one: draw, compare against $18, then $19, then $B1 for x or $B2 for y, and take a
signed delta from $13DA or $13DE indexed by $1A & 1. EOR #$FE flips the sign,
turning $01 into $FF and back, which is how a single table serves both
directions.

$178A rewrites $21 as the absolute value of $B3 + $15 / 2 and re-runs $1731 to
recompute the shape parameters from it, so the radius really does change during a
walk -- 2,158 times in one measured phase. That is not an explanation for the $21
drift seen at registration, since the walker only runs after $226A and $217B
resets $21 at the top of each iteration, but it does account for $21 and $B0
disagreeing everywhere inside the walker.

Mapped so far: $15AD, $1476 with its 3x3 neighbor count, $1555, $1583, $1648,
$1728, $13E0, $16BB, $16D1, $178A, $17A6. Still unread: $1A00, $19CC, $19EE,
$1B3B, $194A, $1A48, $1C2A-$1C89, and the rest of $15AD's state machine.

events.title: port the placement loop, verified on first placements
events.message:
port the placement loop, verified on first placements

runCommandStage transcribes $2173 through $227F. It reproduces the original's
first chosen position -- x, y and radius -- exactly for all nine seed and
configuration pairs in the fixture.

That is a stronger result than it looks. The first placement only lands in the
right spot if the LFSR is in step through the entire setup: the pairOffset draw
via $0ACB and its redraw-while-1 loop, the coin flip whose result is thrown away,
the bounds for the command including configuration 2's latitude clamp and the
paired case's two shifted edges, the byte draw for x, and the word draw for y at
two advances per candidate. One draw out of place and all nine land elsewhere.

Two draws in that setup look skippable and are not. pairOffset is drawn at $2186
before the code knows whether the command is paired, then overwritten with $FF at
$21B4 when it is not; the $B1/$B2 coin flip at $2193 is likewise overwritten for
islands at $21A8. Both still advance the generator.

Added nextModulo for $0ACB, which is a different sampler from $22B4 and differs
in a way that only shows up in the sequence: one draw reduced by repeated
subtraction, against rejection and redraw. A limit below 2 returns 0 without
drawing at all, so it does not advance the register.

Only the first placement of each run can be checked until the coastline walker
exists. With no walker the mask stays empty, isClear accepts every candidate
immediately, and later placements diverge because the original was rejecting
collisions with land already drawn -- nothing to do with this loop. The test says
so rather than quietly comparing one element. The placement count is separately
checkable and matches the command table for every run, including configuration 1
yielding three where the fixture has four, which is the walker registering the
pair's partner.

This also bears on the parked $21 question. Using $B0 reproduces the original, so
the drift did not affect placement here -- but not conclusively: the first
placement runs against an empty mask, so the radius only enters through the
bounds, and a value of 71 would shift those by one at each edge, changing the
outcome only when a draw lands exactly on an extreme.

NOTES records the search for what writes $21 so it is not repeated. Twelve direct
writers found and none in the span; that scan is incomplete by construction
because indexed stores are invisible to it, their operand byte being the base
rather than the target; and the obvious hypothesis, that the drifting entries
were walker registrations via $1866, is falsified -- $1866 fires zero times in
configuration 0 for all three seeds, two of which drift.

whose low 7 bits are the final letter. Marking each string's byte

of DEFB or misdisassembled instructions, covering the police-radio

and confirms the credits screen's programmer tags, JOBBEEE and BILL,
byte-for-byte against retail bank 0. Also adds small B filler
sub-blocks around the credits/menu text so the code disassembler
stops trying to decode the leftover control bytes before each string

events.title: capture the placement positions and fix the bounds
events.message:
capture the placement positions and fix the bounds

$1B5F is called once per accepted landmass, and at that moment zero page holds
the chosen position and everything that fed it. Breaking there gives an oracle
for the placement loop that needs no coastline walker -- 45 placements across
9 seed/config pairs, coordinates and radii only.

It is a demanding oracle. A position only comes out right if the retry loop
discarded the same rejected candidates, the paired retest at $2231 agreed, and
every draw consumed the same number of LFSR steps.

Capturing it immediately falsified three things in the previous commit.

The pair's horizontal offset is drawn, not fixed. $4E comes from $2186 as
$0ACB($0F) + 1, redrawn while it lands on 1, where $0F is radius * 5 / 7;
measured values include 48 and 6 for radius 70. Only the vertical offset,
2 * radius + radius / 8, is constant. $0ACB is also not $22B4: it takes one draw
and reduces it modulo the limit by repeated subtraction, self-modifying the
operand of its own CMP and SBC at $0AD9, where $22B4 rejects and redraws. Both
are used in the same loop.

The paired case moves two bounds that xRange and yRange modelled as fixed:
xLower becomes $4E + radius and yUpper becomes $0185 - (3 * radius + radius / 8),
reserving room to the left and below for the partner. Replaced both accessors
with bounds(), and added partner() for the offset itself. The old tests only
covered configuration 0 and the configuration 2 clamp, which is why they passed.

$1BD9's copy loop runs once, not twice. LDX #$01 followed by DEX / BNE exits
immediately, so it stores $22 and never $21.

Two further findings the fixture made visible. $B0 is the radius and $21 is
scratch: across all 45 registrations $B0 is always exactly $46 or $0A, while $21
drifts to 71, 82, 75 and 62. And $1B5F has two call sites -- $226A in the
placement loop and $1866 inside the walker -- splitting 4/0 for configuration 0
and 3/1 for configuration 1, so a paired command registers once from the loop and
its partner is registered later by the walker.

Also recorded, for anyone porting the loop: the draws at $2186 and $2193 happen
whether or not their results are used. $4E is overwritten with $FF for unpaired
commands and the $B1/$B2 coin flip is overwritten for islands, but both still
advance the LFSR, so skipping them desynchronizes every later draw.

Still open: why $21 already reads 71 at the first registration for some seeds.
Nothing between $217B and $226A appears to write it. This matters rather than
being a curiosity, because $22F7 reads $21 and not $B0, so the placement test
runs at the drifted radius and one unit shifts every bound it computes.

events.title: platform: put the desktop's palette back on exit (ST/STE, ST-High, Nova)
events.message:
platform: put the desktop's palette back on exit (ST/STE, ST-High, Nova)

Reported on hardware: quitting from the ST-Low build AND the xVDI 640x400x256
build drops to a desktop with black icons and black window contents. The Falcon
backend has restored its palette for a while; the others never did.

Each backend saved the resolution and the screen bases and restored those, but
not the COLOURS — while owning the colour hardware outright for the whole run:
- display_ste.c: the per-band raster split rewrites all 16 registers at 0xFF8240
  several times a frame, so the desktop's palette is long gone by exit.
- display_sthigh.c: same omission (mono only lights 0 and 15, but this backend
  also runs on a colour monitor booted into ST High).
- display_nova.c: worse since we started writing the card's hardware LUT
  directly and re-stamping it every present — closing the VDI workstation does
  not undo that, so TOS inherits the game's 256 colours.

Fix, same shape everywhere: snapshot at init (Setcolor/COL_INQUIRE on the ST
side, a straight 256-entry read of the LUT on the card, taken BEFORE the first
write) and restore at shutdown. Palette goes back AFTER the mode change /
workstation close, matching the Falcon's default exit order — Setscreen can
reinitialise the VDI and its colour table, so the restore must have the last
word.

A/B'd in Hatari (--machine ste) rather than assumed, because "the desktop looked
fine afterwards" is not evidence on its own — a trap this repo already paid for.
With the restore disabled the reported bug reproduces exactly (near-black
desktop, black icons, unreadable window contents); with it in place the desktop
returns normal. The Nova arm is the same mechanism but is NOT emulator-testable,
so it stays unverified until the card says otherwise.

68000 / 020 / amiga-ECS all build.

events.title: engine: restore the main-menu Quit confirm; strip the freeze instrumentation
events.message:
engine: restore the main-menu Quit confirm; strip the freeze instrumentation

#130 — QUIT FROM GAME dropped straight to the desktop, so a mis-click or a stray
'Q' lost the session with no warning. The Mac does confirm; the port had dropped
the arm. Faithful lift of CODE 22 + 0x5292:

  jsr JT[76]                   ; jt76()
  movel %a5@(-14292),%sp@-     ; the prompt string POINTER
  jsr JT[159]                  ; jt159(prompt, 0)
  tstb %d0 / beqs L52aa        ; NO  -> back to the menu loop
  moveq #0,%d0                 ; YES -> return 0 = quit

-14292 is read by exactly one instruction in the whole game and written by none,
i.e. a DATA-seeded pointer. It arrives seeded: measured live, it holds the Mac's
own wording "Quit Game? ", so no invented text is needed and the maintainer's
"Quit to TOS?" only exists as a fallback for an empty slot (PORT_QUIT_PROMPT,
Workbench on the Amiga) — the DOS release's "Quit to DOS?" would be a lie on a
machine that has neither.

Verified headlessly on the STE, both arms: the dialog paints "QUIT GAME? YES NO",
NO restores the full main menu and keeps running, YES still tears down
(ExitToShell). 68000 / 020 / amiga-ECS all build; 469 passed, 6 skipped.

Also strips the diagnostics that did their job:
- FRUA_FREEZELOG entirely (ua_main, l07dc, l120c, l23b4, nova appl_init/exit).
- The FRUA_NOVA_PALTRACE block in load_menu_ui.
- The "slot15 CLOBBERED" log: the VDI overwriting that slot is the EXPECTED
  steady state now, so it was noise every boot, not a signal. The unconditional
  re-stamp remains — that is the fix.
- nova_white_pen / the novawhite key, a knob born of a theory the LUT read-back
  disproved. Slot 15 is now never sent to vs_color at all (pen 1 addresses slot
  255, so the write both missed AND clobbered a live art colour).

events.title: nova: assert the hardware LUT last, and once per present
events.message:
nova: assert the hardware LUT last, and once per present

Field result on the card: with the direct LUT write the hotkey letters now come
up WHITE (so index 15 does reach the card) but go black a moment later. Two
corrections to the earlier reading, both from the maintainer:
  - the char-gen page turns the letters CYAN, not white, so it never "unlocked"
    anything — that page just draws them in the pressed style (clut 11);
  - the letters change back on their own, i.e. something re-emits over us.

Not `dim`: a dimmed item draws BODY=0 too (the whole label would go black), and
the label body stays grey. So the letter really is index 15 and slot 15 is being
lost after we set it.

Two changes:
1. Assert the LUT AFTER the batch's vs_color calls, not inline. Writing LUT[15]
   at i=15 and then calling vs_color for 16..32 let the VDI re-emit its table
   (where slot 15 is black) microseconds later — self-inflicted, in the same
   loop. nova_lut_assert() also re-stamps EVERY slot ever set, so a re-emit
   triggered by an unrelated range cannot leave an older slot wrong.
2. Assert once per full present, so any VDI re-emit between palette installs is
   corrected within a frame rather than persisting.

Also added a bounded (8-line) check kept in the SHIPPING build: if slot 15 is
found holding anything but the white we last wrote, log it. That distinguishes
the two mechanisms that look identical on screen — a CLUT clobber (log fires,
and these changes fix it) versus an engine-side repaint with a different index
(log silent, palette innocent, look at the draw path instead).

Nova-only; ST/STE boot re-verified. Filed the missing main-menu Quit confirm
("Quit to DOS YES|NO?", maintainer suggests "Quit to TOS?" on Atari) as a task.

events.title: Identify demo engine routines that differ from retail only by address literal
events.message:
Identify demo engine routines that differ from retail only by address literal

47 of the remaining "not yet identified" $8000+ engine gaps turned out
to be the same routine as retail, byte-identical except for one
embedded 16-bit address operand (a data table living at a different
offset in this build's memory layout) - which is why the earlier
straight byte-diff missed them.

Found via masked comparison: disassemble the gap, wildcard the 16-bit
operand bytes of any instruction whose disassembly contains an
address, then search retail memory for a match on the unmasked bytes.
Any hit is safe by construction - the search can only succeed if every
non-operand byte already matches, so a match can't be a coincidence on
short/generic sequences.

events.title: $280A ends the command table, not the land-mass phase
events.message:
$280A ends the command table, not the land-mass phase

The $FE sentinel jumps to $280A, and I read that as the end of the phase without
reading what $280A does. It starts a second wave:

    $280A  count = random(2..8), or random(8..13) for configuration 2
    $2824  place at radius 3, via $21B8 and $22F7
    $2837  reject y in $C3..$DB (195..218), a latitude exclusion band
    $285E  file into $038C,($67) or $03B4,($68) by whether the row is below 219
    $2894  end of phase

So the phase adds a further 2-7 small islands after the command table finishes
and records their positions into two separate tables. Measured at seed $1234,
blob counts roughly double between the two points: 4 -> 11, 4 -> 9, 8 -> 16.

This does not disturb the command-table reading. Those counts were measured
exactly at $280A, which is precisely where the table finishes, so 2+2, 1+2 and
1+6 remain right for the thing they were testing. What was wrong is the naming:
LANDMASS_DONE claimed a meaning the address does not have, and the fixture was a
valid mid-phase checkpoint labeled as phase output. The constants are now
TABLE_STAGE_DONE and PHASE_DONE, and the fixture captures both in a single run --
the table stage stays useful as an incremental milestone for the port, and
phaseEnd becomes the real oracle.

The 64-of-207 coverage figure has the same defect: it was measured to $280A and
excludes the second wave. wm_coverage.py now runs to PHASE_DONE; NOTES carries
the caveat until it is re-measured.

Also found: generation has two independent give-up-and-restart paths. $2473 is
reached from $1900's bounds guard and from the raster IRQ, which compares the
frame counter's high byte to 8 and regenerates the whole world if a single fill
runs past roughly 2,048 frames. One spatial watchdog, one temporal. That is
likely a large part of why generation takes about 18 minutes, and it means a port
assuming the phase runs exactly once reproduces the original's usual behavior
rather than its behavior.

Finally, determinism is now verified instead of assumed. An early capture of seed
$0001 configuration 0 produced a mask differing from every run since by a single
isolated cell. Three candidate causes were tested and ruled out: the disk is not
an input (three different images give identical masks), a hard reset does
reinitialize RAM (so leftover drivers at $C000 cannot carry over), and the frame
counter reaches only the watchdog, which can restart everything but cannot change
one cell. The cause is still unknown, so capture_fixtures now runs every case
twice and fails loudly if the two disagree. All nine cases pass that check.

The common thread in this and the $1900 correction is finding a jump and naming
its meaning without reading the destination. A byte scan during this
investigation reported a DEC $BD at $111B that is really the operand of CMP $C6
followed by the opcode of LDA $11DD,X -- the same mistake one level down.

events.title: nova: own the hardware LUT (RGB565) — fixes the black hotkey letters
events.message:
nova: own the hardware LUT (RGB565) — fixes the black hotkey letters

MEASURED on the card (read-back of the ATW800/2 FPGA LUT, per the Programmer's
Manual the maintainer pointed at):

  Logbase()       = 0xFEA00000   card video base (ADDR jumper at 0x(FE)A00000)
  LUT             = base+0x1FF000 = 0xFEBFF000   reads fine
  base+0x3FF000   = 0xFEDFF000                  BUS ERROR on a 2MB card

  slot   7 = 0xAD55 -> (172,170,172)   the alternating-bit 565 grey
  slot 254 = 0xFFE0 -> (255,255,0)     yellow
  slot  15 = 0xF81F -> (255,0,255)     magenta  <- never got the UI white
  slot 255 = 0xFFFF -> (255,255,255)   WHITE    <- where the UI white went

Root cause: nova_hw_inverse is the 16-COLOUR VDI pen->register table, in which
register 15 is reached by pen 1. On a 256-colour device pen 1 is black = index
ncolors-1 = 255, so every UI-white write (14 per session, always 0xFFFFFF) landed
on slot 255 — leaving the accelerator letter on UNPRESSED buttons wrong (the
reporter's "black hotkey") AND clobbering a live art colour. Slot 11 -> pen 14
works, which is why PRESSED buttons showed their cyan correctly; that asymmetry
in the field report is what localized it. Engine side was blameless: values and
ordering verified correct on the ST backend (the UI palette installs LAST, after
both clut-129 installs, with the right cyan/white).

Fix: bind the card's hardware LUT and write it directly — index == slot, so all
256 entries are reachable and the pen table's unreachable slots are gone. Entry
format RGB565 big-endian, decoded from the read-back against known colours (not
assumed from the manual's 15bpp PIXEL layout). vs_color is still called for
idx != 15 so VDI's own CLUT shadow stays in step for any VDI/AES redraw; slot 15
no longer writes pen 1 at all, ending the slot-255 corruption.

Safety: the offset is DERIVED from Logbase() and verified by write/read-back/
restore, never probed speculatively — the diagnostic build's blind 4MB candidate
read bombed a 2MB card (2 bombs, crash to desktop; my error). video.cfg keys:
novalut=off (back to vs_color only), novalut=4mb (4MB cards). Falls back silently
if the read-back fails. Nova-only; ST/STE boot re-verified unchanged.

This is a plain shipping build — no diagnostic flags needed.

events.title: diag+nova: measure where the UI white lands — read the ATW800/2 hardware LUT
events.message:
diag+nova: measure where the UI white lands — read the ATW800/2 hardware LUT

The card log settled the black-hotkey symptom to ONE slot. Slot 15 (the UI white
= the accelerator letter on an UNPRESSED button) is written 14x per session,
always 0xFFFFFF, always through vs_color PEN 1 — and never shows. Slot 11 (pen
14) works, which is why PRESSED buttons show their cyan accelerator. Values and
ordering are correct (verified engine-side on the ST backend), so only this pen
fails.

Why: nova_hw_inverse is the standard 16-COLOUR VDI pen->register table, where
register 15 is reached by pen 1. But pen 1 is VDI's BLACK, and on a 256-COLOUR
device black is index ncolors-1 = 255. So the white most likely lands on slot 255
and slot 15 keeps whatever the art palette left there. PALTEST derived the table
from pens 2/3/6 (-> slots 1/2/3) and never exercised pen 1.

Rather than guess a replacement pen (a wrong one silently corrupts another UI
colour — pen 15 drives slot 13), measure. Per the ATW800/2 Programmer's Manual
(maintainer's pointer) the FPGA LUT is memory-mapped READ/WRITE at
screen_adr + 0xFF000 (+1MB for a 2MB card, +3MB for 4MB; the manual's absolute
Mega ST/STE/TT addresses are the 2MB case), 0x200 bytes = 256 16-bit entries.

Added: a Supexec LUT read-back dumping slots 0/1/7/11/13/15/254/255 for both the
2MB and 4MB candidate bases, fired right after the 1st and one later slot-15
write. That answers both open questions at once — WHERE the white landed (15 vs
255) and the ENTRY FORMAT (slot 11 is a known-RGB sample, so the raw word decodes
the encoding; the manual documents only the 15bpp PIXEL layout and assuming the
LUT matches would be a guess).

Also: novawhite=<pen> in video.cfg overrides the slot-15 pen, so alternatives can
be A/B'd on hardware without a rebuild. Read-only probe; no write path changed.

events.title: port the land mask and the placement test
events.message:
port the land mask and the placement test

LandMask is the generator's 1-bit land/water bitmap: 32 bytes per row at $5700,
bit $80 >> (x & 7) of byte y * 32 + x / 8. Not to be confused with the map
proper, which game3 addresses through $0FAE at 128 bytes per row and four bits
per cell. Both live at the same base, and mixing them up yields output that
looks structured and is wrong.

The buffer covers $5700..$9100 rather than just the map's 400 rows, because the
original's own guard at $1900 is looser than the map: it only restarts
generation when the row pointer's high byte leaves $50..$91. No spill past row
400 was actually observed across four seed/config combinations, but sizing to
the guard costs 2 KB and avoids a bad failure mode -- an array sized exactly to
the map would trap on a write the original absorbed silently.

LandMassPhase.isClear transcribes $22F7, verified against the original across 18
positions. Despite sitting where an area test would, it is not one: it samples a
cross through the bounding box, three rows and three columns, and rejects if any
sampled cell is already land. Two landmasses can overlap substantially without
either noticing. That is a property of the original's output, not a bug, and a
port that did a real area test would build visibly different worlds.

Three details bite when transcribing it. Both scans are do-while, so the body
always runs once and neither samples its far edge -- written as pre-test loops
with <=, which is what I had first, it is wrong twice over. The bounds clamp
asymmetrically: the right edge becomes $FE only if x + radius carries out of a
byte, and the bottom clamps to $8E only once y + radius crosses 256. And $62,
the shift count that turns a row into an address, is set by the phase at $2130
and not by $22F7, so a harness calling the routine directly must set it too.

That last one wasted a fixture. The first attempt used a uniformly random
12.5%-density mask and returned 32 cases, every one blocked, which is what a
cross sampling ~840 cells will always do at any plausible density -- and which a
port that simply returned false would have passed. The fixture now builds land
from a few rectangles instead, giving 13 clear and 5 blocked, and a test asserts
both outcomes are present so that failure cannot recur silently.

The command table is expressed as named values rather than a byte blob, which
also keeps it plainly a reimplementation rather than copied data.

events.title: port the World Maker's bounded draws
events.message:
port the World Maker's bounded draws

$22B4 (8-bit) and $247B (16-bit) become nextByte(from:below:) and
nextWord(from:below:) on WorldMakerRNG, with randrange_reference.py capturing
what the original returns across 4 seeds: 40 byte cases and 24 word cases.

Three things had to be right.

They are rejection samplers, and the waste matters. Each rejected candidate
still advances the LFSR, so a port that reduced one draw by modulo would produce
entirely plausible values and desynchronize every later draw in the world. The
byte fixture is therefore a sequence captured from a single seeding rather than
independent cases, so it tests that the port throws away the same candidates.

$247B consumes two advances per candidate, not one. The first supplies the low
byte; the second is drawn only for its sign, and the high byte is 1 when that
draw is below $80, else 0 (LDA $CF / BMI / INX at $24E1). Results therefore cap
at 511, which is exactly enough for the map's 400 rows and looks deliberate.

The bounds are two parameters rather than a Range. Swift's Range traps at
construction when inverted, so it cannot represent lo > hi -- which $22BA
explicitly handles by returning lo without advancing the register. Modelling
these bounds as a Range would impose an invariant the 6502 does not have and
convert a reachable path into a crash. Two of the three tests failed that way
before the signature changed; the type system was reporting a real mismatch.
