events.title: tools: verify every JT-call lead by hand — one real bug, five tool defects
events.message:
tools: verify every JT-call lead by hand — one real bug, five tool defects

Worked through all the outstanding leads against the disassembly. The result is
worth stating plainly: the tool was wrong far more often than the engine was.

Every one of the 16 surviving shape-matched leads is now read and cleared —
idiom substitution (max/min, memset, vsprintf, _NewPtr/_FreeMem), an omitted
error-alert path, or a deviation the code already documented (l5c1e pumps l725c
via jt1134; l01be uses design_save_path because GEMDOS has no HFS ':'; l1276
paints its own name; l0004's desk-accessory arms are the HAL-moot class). l78fa
turned out to be an inline expansion: jt118 IS jt108(1) + jt1001(...), which it
calls. Full table in docs/jt-call-audit.md.

So the whole exercise yielded exactly ONE genuine drop — l309c's pending-text
flush, fixed in 5e8218a7 — out of roughly thirty raised. A hit from this tool
is weak evidence; the doc now says so.

Three more defects found in the tool while verifying, on top of the two already
fixed:

- Callbacks installed by ADDRESS were invisible. `l63c0(..., (long)&jt237,
  (long)&jt236)` never matches a `name(` pattern, so every callback
  installation in the engine was reported as a drop: jt241, jt240, jt169,
  l1bfe, jt511, l2558, jt239, jt127, l100c. Now matches bare identifiers — with
  comments and string literals stripped first, because PROBE("jtNNN") and the
  doc comments would otherwise satisfy every check and the tool would find
  nothing at all. Stripping also exposed drops those comment mentions had been
  hiding, so this cut both ways.
- Extracted helpers, in three flavours, all of which hid the call: a
  `<name>_suffix` sibling (l0980_slots holds l0980's JT[661]/JT[670]), a
  suffixed lift of the entry itself (jt1154_pg IS JT[1154], so jt52 and jt965
  were reported for a call they make), and a helper named after an asm label
  INSIDE the parent's span (l45f0_menu holds jt955's four jt155 calls and its
  jt182 "Blocked:" prompt). All three are credited now, the last one bounded to
  labels within the function's own address range so it cannot launder an
  unrelated function's calls.

Net across the sweep: 174 -> 75 drops, 32 -> 16 shape matches, and the
calibration held through every change (pre-fix l09dc reports JT[124], HEAD is
clean). Two new tests pin the pointer and comment/string behaviour.

469 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: engine: l309c flushes pending text before blitting, as the Mac does
events.message:
engine: l309c flushes pending text before blitting, as the Mac does

The one finding from the JT-call sweep that survived verification. CODE 5
@0x30d6 calls JT[1124] with no arguments, right after the l2856 lookup's
null check and before the bearing adjustment; our l309c did not.

JT[1124] is CODE 4+0x4d88 = l4d88, which we had already lifted faithfully and
in full: it takes the deferred character count (-936), derives the bounding
rect ((mode ? 8 : 12) * count wide), fills it, InvalRects it, then clears the
count and resets the buffer pointer to &-1041. The Mac empties the pending
glyph buffer before drawing art over that area. Skipping it leaves buffered
text to be painted over, with the stale invalidation resolved later.

Call-site census says this was an isolated miss rather than a pattern: the Mac
has 16 (13 pc-relative within CODE 4, 3 through the jump table), our C had 14.

Falcon regression frame is md5-identical, so nothing visible changed on the
char-gen screen — the buffer is empty there at that point. To be clear about
what this is: a faithfulness fix with NO user-visible symptom attributed to it.
It is not a claimed fix for any of the outstanding text bugs.

Two traps recorded in docs/jt-call-audit.md while settling this. L2856 sits
immediately beside the dropped call and reads like the same routine, but
CODE 4+0x4d88 and CODE 5+0x2856 are different code — l2856 is NOT an alias for
JT[1124]. And CODE 5's L25f4, another JT[1124] caller, is not this repo's
l25f4, which is CODE 13+0x25f4 (the same-offset-different-segment trap);
CODE 5's is simply unlifted, so the audit never covered it.

Also documented, as understood rather than outstanding: l309c's other drop,
JT[1200] at 0x3172, where the Mac shifts bpp_w left by 3 only when
jt1200() == 0. Our l2d4e is re-parameterised and applies the *8 internally and
unconditionally, which agrees exactly in the jt1200() == 0 case our 8-bit
targets are in. It would diverge only on a colour screen that is not 8-bit
deep, which the port does not produce.

467 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: tools: jt_call_audit — fix two false-positive sources, document the top three drops
events.message:
tools: jt_call_audit — fix two false-positive sources, document the top three drops

Following the sweep to its conclusion. Both of the tool's own defects were
found by reading the asm instead of trusting its output, and both inflated the
findings:

- Multi-line forward declarations parsed as definitions. The decl-vs-def test
  only looked for a trailing ';' on the FIRST line, so a two-line declaration
  fell through and brace-matching ran on into the next function. This made the
  tool report l33ac as dropping JT[1200] and JT[394] — a confident, wrong, and
  very plausible-looking finding, since l33ac is the GLIB loader and those two
  calls are exactly what a loader would use. Its real body (49k lines further
  down, un-annotated) makes both calls. Now decided by whichever of ';' or '{'
  comes first.
- Wrapper/implementation splits reported the whole body as dropped. The port
  often lifts one Mac function as a thin wrapper plus the real body (jt110 is
  an 8-line forwarder to l33ac; both are CODE 6+0x33ac), so the full asm was
  being compared against the wrapper: 13 phantom drops. One level of delegation
  is now followed, for a small body with a single callee. jt110: 13 -> 1.

120 drops -> 112; 32 shape matches -> 29. Calibration unchanged in both
directions (pre-fix l09dc reports JT[124], HEAD is clean).

What the three most-dropped targets actually are, now written down so nobody
re-investigates them: JT[1200] is the display-mode query, JT[399] is memset,
JT[394] is sprintf. Their frequency is idiom substitution, not near-misses —
jt21 and jt910, for instance, zero their buffers with plain C loops.

The useful find: JT[1200] picks the file EXTENSION. In l33ac the display mode
chooses "%s.ctl" vs "%s.tlb" (and "%s%d%03d.ctl" vs ".tlb" for the numbered
form) — mode 3 asks for .TLB. Our l33ac does this faithfully. The distinction
is live in the DOS-converted set: all 23 .CTL/.TLB pairs are the same SIZE but
different BYTES, so they are genuinely different art. The matching sizes read
like a collapsed conversion at first glance and are not one.

And the 1.0-vs-1.2 question: none of this is version skew. The audit compares
against the 1.0 disassembly, which is the lift target, so every drop is
1.0-internal by construction — and the jump table is permuted between the forks
(1208 vs 1207 entries), so JT numbers are not comparable across them anyway. Of
the three, only JT[399] appears in the 1.2 worklist (hunk 8, fill 0 -> 1 in
l36e0_c10), already ported. Both 1.2 passes are complete, so the DOS data
switch remains the thing that changed under this code.

467 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: tools: jt_call_audit — find lifted bodies that drop a JT call the Mac makes
events.message:
tools: jt_call_audit — find lifted bodies that drop a JT call the Mac makes

#137 took seven weeks because nothing could see it. The char-gen icon grid had
65 hand-written lines where CODE 17 has one `jsr JT[124]`; it compiled, ran,
and carried a comment explaining why the JT call was skipped. The workaround
was correct when written and silently wrong nine commits later, when the
loader it assumed (jt468) changed underneath it.

This is the structural check for that class. For each of the 1422 functions in
boot.c annotated `(CODE NN + 0xXXXX)`, extract the matching asm body, collect
the JT[n] targets it calls, and report the ones the C never calls. An lXXXX
alias for the same address counts as the call (docs/lxxxx-jt-aliases.md).

Calibrated against the bug itself, in both directions: run it on
12917a32^:src/engine/boot.c and it reports `l09dc NOT in C: JT[124]`; run it on
HEAD and l09dc is clean. tests/ pins the behaviour on synthetic fixtures, since
the real disassembly is git-ignored and CI has nothing to point it at.

The first run was useless and that is worth recording: 174 hits, 100+ of them
CODE 1's low jump-table entries. Those are THINK C runtime, not engine calls —
JT[1]/JT[2]/JT[3] are the sparse/sparse-long/range switch dispatchers, and
JT[4]..JT[8] are 32-bit mul/udiv/umod/sdiv/smod. A faithful lift writes
`switch` and `*` and `/`, so none of them can ever appear. Verified by
disassembling CODE 1 0x130..0x20c and against boot.c's own jt4..jt8, which are
literally `return a * b;`. Excluding them: 120 real drops, 32 matching the
#137 shape (big C body, one or two drops, no admitted TODO).

One finding verified by hand so far: l309c (CODE 5+0x309c) omits a zero-arg
JT[1124] at 0x30d6. The near-miss there is instructive — the asm calls L2856
at 0x30c4 and our C does too, so it looks like the same routine appears twice,
but CODE 4+0x4d88 and CODE 5+0x2856 are different code. l2856 is NOT an alias
for JT[1124].

The other 31 are leads, not findings, and docs/jt-call-audit.md says so — this
is an instrument that needed its own exclusion list fixed before its output
meant anything, and it still cannot tell a declared deferral from a hidden one.

467 passed, 6 skipped.

events.title: engine: the char-gen icon grid commits its palette with jt124, as the Mac does
events.message:
engine: the char-gen icon grid commits its palette with jt124, as the Mac does

The 7x7 body-icon grid rendered every sprite black on ALL FIVE backends
(verified Falcon/VIDEL and ST-Low here, reported on NovaGPU) because this
site did not do what CODE 17 does.

The Mac is three instructions:

  0a4c: pea 0x47b0            ; "DUNGCOM1"
  0a52: jsr %a5@(914)         ; JT[110]  bind
  0a5e: jsr %a5@(1026)        ; JT[124]  commit the palette
  0a68: jsr %a5@(954)         ; JT[115]  free the slot

We had 65 hand-written lines in place of the jt124: navigate outer item 1 ->
its item 0, parse the colour-table header, clamp it away from 0..31, and
install via port_clut_install. That was written in June (e05e625b) for a real
reason -- back then jt468("DUNGCOM1") returned the OUTER DUNGCOM.CTL, so
jt124 -> l3eea -> jt993 read a nested GLIB's stub header as a colour table
and splattered 0..255, wrecking the stone frame.

The GLIB pool flip (2026-07-13, cw_setglib_load) removed that premise:
"jt468(group) IS the extracted sub-GLIB, so the old l37aa(base, set) index
step disappears". The wall-set code was updated for it. This site was not,
so its extra l37aa(...,1) then walked one level too deep, landed on a TILE
instead of the set, and l37aa(tile,0) returned 0 -- no palette installed at
all. The sprite pixels (indices 87/72/79) were left resolving against clut
129, where all three are RGB(0,0,0). Hence black, on every backend, which is
what proved it was not a display bug.

The faithful call reaches the right table unaided: jt1017 reports index-type
0 (hdr[11] of the set GLIB), so jt993 fetches sub-item 0, whose header
already declares start=32/count=224. The 0..31 UI range is protected by the
DATA, not by a clamp we invented -- which is why the stone frame survives
without the hand-rolled guard.

Verified on Falcon (14MB, VIDEL) and Mega STe (4MB, ST-Low): 49 coloured
sprites on silver cell grounds, frame chrome intact. 461 passed, 6 skipped.

Two theories this kills: the 4MB memory ceiling (the Falcon shows it at
14MB) and any Nova palette involvement (three unrelated backends, one fault).

tools: icongrid_repro.sh — a bisectable pass/fail probe for the black sprites

The char-gen body-icon grid renders its sprites COLOURLESS (black, with one
mask-only silhouette) on the live route; it was fixed once and has regressed.
Now that the failure reproduces headlessly, the fastest route to the culprit is
git bisect, and this is the probe: exit 0 = grid is COLOURED (good), 1 = not
(bad), 125 = build failed (skip).

It drives the LIVE route (p Return c d d <name> Return) at --memsize 4 against
a copy of the shipping card data, because the bug does not appear through the
FRUA_BODY harness. Verdict is the count of DISTINCT colours in the grid region
rather than a screenshot diff, so it is robust to cursor position and the name
typed: coloured measures well above the threshold, black collapses to a handful
of greys. Calibrated on HEAD (known bad) = 5 colours.

PACING IS LOAD-BEARING. driver.sh start returns on "menu: modal up" but input
is not accepted for a couple more seconds, and each screen needs time to
compose. Without the sleeps every key is swallowed, the run sits on the main
menu, and the probe reports a FALSE PASS — an instrument that never ran. That
bit once here and is the reason the delays are explicit.

events.title: scripts: qclip / qpaste mac ↔ guest clipboard bridge
events.message:
scripts: qclip / qpaste mac ↔ guest clipboard bridge

Ship two shell wrappers over the amiga_mcp devbench REST endpoints
`/api/tools/clipboard/get` and `/api/tools/clipboard/set` — which
call the bridge's CLIPGET/CLIPSET, which wrap the text in an IFF
FORM/FTXT/CHRS envelope on clipboard.device unit 0. No new guest
binary needed — the plumbing was already there, this just makes
it usable from a mac shell prompt.

  qclip [text | pbpaste | stdin]   — push into guest clipboard
  qpaste [--copy]                  — read guest clipboard,
                                     print to stdout (+optional pbcopy)

Primary use case is dropping a URL into TrapezePDF's
File → Open URL from Clipboard: `echo https://... | qclip` then
R-Amiga + U inside TrapezePDF fetches and renders it.

Newline handling: the bridge protocol is line-based (`CLIPSET|<text>\n`)
and sanitize_text() folds newlines to spaces on the guest side anyway,
so qclip pre-folds `\n` → ' ' when the input is multi-line and
prints a warning explaining why. Single-line URLs / snippets go
through untouched.

events.message:
Trace MONA's W (write to tape) command end to end

Four inputs, not the two the manual describes: filename, First:, Last:
and Start:. The last supplies the entry address written into the file
header. The file is opened before the addresses are asked, which is why
all four abort branches converge on CLOSE_AND_EXIT instead of returning.

Running it and capturing the firmware call shows what is actually
passed: CAS OUT DIRECT receives HL = First, DE = Last - First, BC = the
Start address, A = 2 for a binary file.

That length is one short. For First=&5000 Last=&500F it passes 15, so
the byte at Last is never saved, and First = Last writes nothing at all.
The sibling commands do add the one - CMD_COPY does INC BC, CMD_FILL
does INC HL - and both were verified inclusive by running them. So W is
inconsistent with I and P, and with the manual, which calls the range
inclusive for all three.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: sarnau

events.title: Trace MONA's P (fill) command end to end
events.message:
Trace MONA's P (fill) command end to end

Twenty-five bytes, with two details worth recording.

The abort test is out of order on purpose. CP &FC at &0F9E sets Z, then
LD A,L, EX DE,HL and POP BC all leave the flags untouched, so the RET Z
three instructions later still acts on that compare - the check is made
before the registers are rearranged for the loop, and acted on after.

The loop is three instructions because CPI is used purely for its side
effects: it increments HL, decrements BC and sets P/V from BC, while the
comparison it performs is thrown away. RET PO leaves when the count hits
zero. Two bytes where INC HL, DEC BC and a test would need four.

Verified by running it rather than by reading: &5000..&500F fills
exactly, both endpoints included and the following byte untouched, and a
single-byte range writes one byte - confirming the INC HL that turns
Last-First into the count.

A range with Last < First never reaches this code; INPUT_FIRST_LAST
abandons the command first, which is the abort the manual documents for
P as well as for I, T and W.

events.title: Trace MONA's I (intelligent copy) command end to end
events.message:
Trace MONA's I (intelligent copy) command end to end

The whole command is 36 bytes and contains exactly one decision, which
is the "intelligent" part the manual names: compare First against To.
If First >= To the destination lies below the source and a forward LDIR
is safe; if First < To the destination overlaps above, so both pointers
are advanced to the far end and LDDR runs backwards. BC arrives from
INPUT_FIRST_LAST as Last-First and is incremented to the count.

Verified by running it rather than by reading: copying &5000..&500F to
&5004 reproduces the block intact instead of smearing the leading bytes
through it, and the reverse overlap picks LDIR.

The abort turns out not to live in this command at all. INPUT_FIRST_LAST
checks Last >= First and, when it is not, resets SP to MONA's stack and
redisplays rather than returning - so the documented "aborted if the
start address is greater than the end address" is inherited by every
command that asks for a range: I, P, T and W.

events.title: diag: fix the paltrace encoding, log the icon-grid CLUT guards
events.message:
diag: fix the paltrace encoding, log the icon-grid CLUT guards

Encoding bug in the Nova paltrace (mine): r/g/b are 0..255 but were packed into
decimal 1e4/1e2 fields, so r>=100 spilled into the index field — the card log
duly showed index 8 twice and indices 16/17 from a probe that only records
below 16. Bit-pack instead (idx<<24 | r<<16 | g<<8 | b). The call SEQUENCE from
that run is still sound and useful: seven full 0..255 installs plus small ranges
at 208/176/184, i.e. the UI range is rewritten wholesale several times.

icontrace now logs the four guards of the icon-grid palette install (bind
handle, outer set, item-0 colour table, ph[7]&15), because a real-hardware run
proved the install NEVER RUNS on the live path — 49 cells blit with a valid art
handle and no CLUTstart line is emitted.

Also kept: the l09dc clamp now DROPS palette entries below index 32 instead of
sliding the table up to meet 32 (sliding installs every colour one index above
the pixels using it). Verified non-regressive on the working case, but it is
defensive — NOT the cause here, since the block is never reached.

Three theories eliminated by evidence this round, recorded so they are not
re-tried: (1) art failing to load — the handle is valid and no cell is refused;
(2) HEIRS shipping its own DUNGCOM — HEIRS.DSN contains no DUNGCOM art, both
paths bind the same root DUNGCOM.TLB; (3) sprite pixels resolving to black —
the histogram was sampling an EMPTY grid, not coloured sprites.

What the hardware photo actually shows: one cell renders, as a mask-only
SILHOUETTE, and the other 48 draw nothing. Silhouette = the mode-1 two-plane
composite (l2d4e, commit 5574a36b) not running — the same failure that commit
originally fixed.

Local repro secured: -DFRUA_CHARGEN boots jt574, the REAL "Create Character"
entry, straight to the PICK screens. The FRUA_BODY harness that has been
passing all along calls jt573 (the review screen) directly and never walks this
path, which is why it could not see the bug.

events.title: Run MONA's own disassembler over every opcode
events.message:
Run MONA's own disassembler over every opcode

optable.py decodes MONA's tables statically. This does the opposite:
tools/disasm_run.py executes the real decoder in the emulator and reads
the rendered text out of the line buffer, so the output is what MONA
actually prints - including the prefix handling and operand emitters,
none of which are stored as data.

Against the static decode the live run agrees on 250/252 base entries,
the two exceptions being JR and DJNZ, where the live decoder resolves
the relative displacement to an absolute address.

It also corrects two claims I had inferred from the tables rather than
observed:

- The undocumented SLL does not print with a blank mnemonic. CB 30..37
  are routed to the invalid-opcode path and come out as NOP flagged with
  an asterisk.
- DDCB does not "print only the documented form". When the register
  field is not 6 the prefix is dropped altogether, so DD CB 05 00 prints
  as RLC B rather than anything involving IX.

Cross-checked against tools/z80dis.py: 247/256 base, 248/256 CB, 56/56
ED, 197/256 DD agree, with the remainder being MONA's own limits - 8 SLL
slots and 72 unused ED opcodes flagged invalid, IXh/IXl shown as H/L,
and the DDCB copy forms.

would be wrong on the first paint too — so log every palette write (first,

which the boot log shows happening twice; ST survives it because hw_palette = 0
forces a re-quantise that re-derives valid slots, while Nova (hw_palette = 1)

events.title: Crack TAB_MNEMONICS by running GENA's own matcher
events.message:
Crack TAB_MNEMONICS by running GENA's own matcher

Decoding the table by hand kept failing because it is a program, not a
table. So this runs it instead: tools/z80emu.py is a small Z80 emulator
and tools/mnemonics.py drives the real matcher at &1466, exploring the
language it accepts by feeding characters and backtracking on rejection.

The result validates against the manual: all 77 reserved words in
Appendix 2 are accepted, none missing. Of the 55 further strings
accepted, 53 are proper prefixes of documented words - the matcher works
one character at a time - leaving exactly two complete mnemonics the
manual does not list: BRK and RCAL. MONA's independent mnemonic table
carries the same two plus SYS, so they are real, not an artefact.

The second table at &1CCB turns out to be the register and condition
vocabulary in the same format - A B C D E H L I R, AF BC DE HL IX IY SP,
and Z NZ C NC P M PE PO - which is what &1562 loads when parsing an
operand. Renamed TAB_REGISTERS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Identify TAB_MNEMONICS as an interpreted match program
events.message:
Identify TAB_MNEMONICS as an interpreted match program

It is not a table of records, which is why looking for one kept failing.
The region is a program executed by the matcher at &1481, one item at a
time against the source line. Common prefixes are shared between
alternatives, so names appear in fragments - "CAL" and "CALL" both
occur because one is a prefix of a longer path.

At the dispatch point an item byte, masked to 7 bits, means:

    < &20      character class: indexes TAB_GROUP_A, whose pointer picks
               a byte list in TAB_CPIR_BYTES, searched with CPIR
    &20..&6F   literal character, compared against the input
    >= &70     register or condition test, folded with XOR B

Bit 7 marks an alternative boundary, and after a failure the scan
resynchronises on the low 3 bits of a following byte. This also explains
TAB_GROUP_A and TAB_CPIR_BYTES, which have sat unexplained since the
first pass over the data region.

Entry boundaries are still not established, so the region stays raw
bytes. Recording the negative result too: classifying every byte does
not decode the table - only 77 of the 204 bytes below &20 are valid
TAB_GROUP_A offsets, because the interpreter reads bytes only at
specific points and the rest are operands to earlier items.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: sarnau

events.title: Trace GENA's A (assemble) command end to end
events.message:
Trace GENA's A (assemble) command end to end

Documents the whole path: frame-pointer setup, the Table size and
Options prompts, the absent-symbol pass, and the closing report.

Three findings worth the trace:

- The default symbol table size is computed, not fixed. An empty reply
  to "Table size:" gives (text length / 8) + 100 bytes, then the result
  is checked against HIMEM - 256 and refused with "No Room!". That is
  the manual's "a size that it thinks is suitable for the size of the
  text", made concrete.

- RUN_VECTOR at &202F explains three things at once that I had found
  separately. It is a three-byte slot in the dead relocation table.
  Assembly initialises it to RET; an ENT directive overwrites it with
  JP <address>; the closing report tests the byte for &C3 to decide
  whether to print "Executes: nnnnn"; and CMD_RUN is literally
  JP RUN_VECTOR. Before any assembly the slot still holds relocation
  data, which is exactly why the manual warns against using R until an
  Executes message has appeared.

- "Pass 1" and " errors: " are separate strings, the second being the
  tail of "Pass 2 errors: " entered six bytes in - the same storage
  trick as MONA's "No Printer?" / "Printer?".

The absent-symbol pass also shows the symbol table layout: names stored
bit-7-terminated, with bit 0 of byte +4 marking a symbol as defined.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: sarnau

events.title: Format TAB_OPERATORS as character classes
events.message:
Format TAB_OPERATORS as character classes

The table at &1AC1 is not a flat list. Its consumer at &17C3 reads a
class byte, then walks the characters belonging to it; a byte with bit 7
set starts the next class, and &FF ends the table. A new GRPTAB
directive renders one group per line.

The six groups it resolves into match the syntax the manual documents:
field terminators, the operand separator, comment and end of statement,
the operators of section 2.5 (& AND, @ OR, ! XOR, ? MOD), the location
counter '$', and the % # " number prefixes. '-' is absent from the
operator group, so subtraction is recognised elsewhere.

TAB_MNEMONICS is left as raw bytes. Its names are plainly visible in
ASCII, interleaved with encodings, but tracing the consumer did not
establish the record structure, and guessing a shape for it would be
worse than leaving it flat.

events.title: ste: take the palette blanket-mark fix too — in-present -56% on idle presents
events.message:
ste: take the palette blanket-mark fix too — in-present -56% on idle presents

The ECS fix (3cb6c121) applies verbatim here, and the chain was verified before
touching it: st_set_palette's `count >= 32` sets s_dirty; st_present turns that
into st_repalette() or st_reband(), whose tail sets s_force_full and rebuilds
BOTH pages — a branch that bypasses pass 1 entirely. A smaller write sets
nothing at all, and pass 1 compares chunky against its shadow, which no palette
write touches. So the shim's blanket row mark could only ever make pass 1
re-read 200 unchanged rows.

hw_palette stays 0 (4 planes hold a quantised 16-slot value, not the index, so a
CLUT move really can invalidate pixels); this is the other flag,
palette_self_invalidates. g_qd_touched is still set, which matters MORE here
than on ECS: pages == 1, so the ST/STe is the backend the #152 clean-present
skip actually applies to, and suppressing it would skip frames outright.

MEASURED on Mega STe (Hatari, HEIRS slot I, A/B via FRUA_STE_PALBLANKET),
steady-state per-window deltas, per present:

  rows scanned   200 -> 62    (-69%)
  pass1 t200    20.1 -> 8.1   (-60%)
  in-present    20.6 -> 9.1   (-56%)
  rows converted 976 -> 976   (the semantic invariant, every window)

Correctness: the autoload-slot-I resume frame is md5-IDENTICAL to the baseline
(2a45561d, whole PNG), and a live AREA-map toggle renders correctly with the
right colours — the scene-change/reband check that a broken palette path would
fail. Shipping CPU68K=68000 build clean, 0 020-insns in code; Atari 020, Amiga
ECS and AGA all still build; 461 host tests pass.

events.title: Format the opcode tables, and correct TAB_OPCODES
events.message:
Format the opcode tables, and correct TAB_OPCODES

TAB_OPCODES_MAIN now renders one record per opcode, labelled with the
opcode it serves and the packed word it holds, instead of anonymous rows
of eight bytes:

    DEFB  &84,&00     ; 07A2: &00 = &8400
    DEFB  &01,&D2     ; 07A4: &01 = &01D2

RECTAB grows options for this: first= sets the index origin, hex shows
it as an opcode, be also prints the trailing two bytes as the
big-endian word. The ED table uses be as well.

Tracing the consumer also corrected a mistake. TAB_OPCODES and what I
had called TAB_RST_OPCODES are not two tables: the single-stepper at
&0FEC scans them flat with LD B,&31, one 49-byte list running from
&1392 to exactly where MSG_BANNER begins. The layout is positional, so
the four-per-condition shape is preserved even for PO/PE/P/M, which
have no JR form and carry &00 padding. TAB_COND_OPCODES now names that
middle section.

events.title: Document TAB_OPERAND_ALT and the operand emitters
events.message:
Document TAB_OPERAND_ALT and the operand emitters

TAB_OPERAND_ALT has exactly one consumer, PUT_ALT_FIELD at &02BA,
reached only when operand 1 is absent and operand 2 is not. All 13
entries are used, covering 14 instructions - entry 1 does double duty
for RST 0 and IM 0. Nothing in the table is dead.

    1 "0"      RST 0, IM 0       8 "AF,AF'"  EX
    2 "8"      RST 8             9 "(n),A"   OUT
    3 "#10"    RST 10           10 "A,(n)"   IN
    4 "#18"    RST 18           11 "#28"     RST 28
    5 "#20"    RST 20           12 "#30"     RST 30
    6 "1"      IM 1             13 "#38"     RST 38
    7 "2"      IM 2

Names the surrounding path: UNPACK_OPERANDS splits the packed word into
the two 5-bit codes, then either PUT_ALT_FIELD or PUT_OPERAND_PAIR runs,
both converging on AFTER_OPERANDS which clears the index-register flag.
PUT_TABLE_ENTRY is the shared emitter - PUT_OPERAND is just the wrapper
that preloads TAB_OPERAND_NAMES.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: sarnau

events.title: Document the cursor-key path from TAB_CURSORKEYS
events.message:
Document the cursor-key path from TAB_CURSORKEYS

Formats the table as the 4 two-byte records it is, and documents every
piece of code that touches it. TAB_CURSORKEYS has exactly one consumer:
KEY_DISPATCH. FIND_PAIR looked like it had two callers, but the second
reference is its own loop-back.

The encoding is a bias: each record holds a firmware key code and a
delta plus 16, so one unsigned byte can carry a negative step. The
consumer cancels the bias with ADD HL,&FFF0 before ADD HL,DE.

    &F3 right -> &11 = +1     &F2 left -> &0F = -1
    &F1 down  -> &18 = +8     &F0 up   -> &08 = -8

which is the manual's one byte horizontally, one display row of eight
vertically.

Names the rest of the path: MOVE_MEM_PTR applies the step, FOLD_CASE
uppercases only 'g'..'z' because the commands below 'G' are control
codes, and STORE_MEM_PTR is the shared tail every repositioning command
ends at.

events.title: Format the ED instruction table as 3-byte records
events.message:
Format the ED instruction table as 3-byte records

TAB_OPCODES_ED was rendering as DEFM strings, because the bytes of a
packed instruction word happen to be printable, which hid the record
structure completely.

Adds a RECTAB directive - RECTAB <start> <end> <size> - that emits one
fixed-size record per line with its index. Applied to the ED table, the
56 records now read as (opcode, word-hi, word-lo) and end exactly where
the CB mnemonic list begins.

The word is big-endian, so it stays raw bytes rather than DEFW;
extracted/MONA31-opcodes.txt carries the decoded mnemonics.

events.title: Recover code from relocated operands
events.message:
Recover code from relocated operands

VEC_READ_KEY rendered as DEFB &C3 + DEFW because nothing calls it, so
neither flow analysis nor pointer-seeding reached it. The evidence that
it is code was in the relocation table all along: the relocator only
patches instruction operands, so an entry at &005B implies an
instruction at &005A.

analyse.py now seeds from that. For each relocation offset below the
code boundary it tries the two addresses that could own it - one back
for unprefixed forms, two for ED/DD/FD - and accepts when the length
works out and the usual plausibility checks pass.

An audit for the general case leaves one relocated offset in MONA not
owned by an instruction, at &0524. That one is genuinely a standalone
pointer in a fragment nothing references or branches into; the JP that
follows it at &0529 is real code by the same test. Both are dead.

The clearest of these confirms documented behaviour: BAD_OPCODE writes
'*' into the line buffer, blanks the rest of the line and re-enters the
decoder with A=0, so an unrecognised byte prints as NOP flagged with an
asterisk, exactly as the manual says. FLAG_INVALID is its second entry
point, reached from the decoder without the stack pop.

MARK_IF_CURRENT compares an address against the memory pointer and
prints the character only on a match - that is how the front panel marks
the current location.

events.title: Port CRT shader to Linux via SPIR-V, fix F4 backend-swap freeze
events.message:
Port CRT shader to Linux via SPIR-V, fix F4 backend-swap freeze

Compiles apps/sdl3/shaders/crt.{vert,frag} to SPIR-V with glslangValidator
at build time (cmake/EmbedSPIRV.cmake embeds the bytecode), mirroring the
existing MSL path for macOS. CRTShader.c picks the shader format/entrypoint
per platform; CMake wires up the Linux build step and enables
CHQ_CRT_SHADER=1 there.

Toggling the CRT backend back on after switching away (F4) froze the
window on Linux: re-claiming a GPU swapchain on a window that already had
a swapchain of any kind torn down on it presents without error but the
compositor never shows the new frames. Recreating the SDL_Window before
re-claiming gives it a fresh surface, which fixes it. In the process, found
and fixed a latent use-after-free on quit: cleanup destroyed the original
local `window` pointer instead of the possibly-recreated `state.video.window`.

events.title: fix: .po parser out-of-bounds write; bind original Liberation font data
events.message:
fix: .po parser out-of-bounds write; bind original Liberation font data

Memory safety:
- parse_po_line's unrecognized-escape branch emits two bytes behind a
  guard that reserved one and could never fire (the loop condition
  already caps i at out_size - 2). A catalog string filling the buffer
  to its last free slot wrote the pair into that slot and pushed the
  terminator one byte past the end of load_po's stack buffer. Reachable
  from any shipped translation catalog. The new regression test was
  confirmed to fail against the unfixed parser before the fix went back.

Original font data (the seven invented 5x7 glyph tables cannot render
lowercase, so non-English translations lose most of their text):
- Added verified SHA-256 entries for 0Liberation.FNT / 1Liberation.FNT,
  extracted from the CD32 disc with the project's own iso_list --hash.
- Proved end to end that both load through liberation_data_read and
  decode: 114 proportional glyphs, two bitplanes, all 95 printable ASCII
  characters resolve.
- Split resources into required and optional. Every verification loop
  demanded the full manifest, so appending the fonts would have broken
  Amiga floppy loading outright, as no Amiga font hash is known.
  Re-verified against real data afterwards: verify_liberation still
  reports the CD32 source as verified.

Stopped short of the glyph blitter on purpose: the two bitplanes give a
2-bit value per pixel and the font file does not say which palette
entries those four values select. Guessing it would be inventing colour
data. Logged in TODO with the exact blocker.

Also checked the earlier claim that map_gen.c overwrites the verified CA
output. It does not: carve() only sets CELL_FLOOR, so rooms are added on
top. Left unchanged, and recorded in DONE.

All 61 tests pass.

events.title: fix: hash-verify CD audio, remove synthesized sprites, 6 gameplay bugs
events.message:
fix: hash-verify CD audio, remove synthesized sprites, 6 gameplay bugs

Data integrity (hash verification is a hard project rule):
- CD32 audio tracks were loaded by hardcoded filename, bypassing the VFS
  and any verification. Now located by SHA-256 through vfs_find_sha256,
  with the ten track hashes computed from the original disc image.
- The texture atlas omitted the six ALIEN sheets from its all-or-nothing
  loaded gate, so a missing sheet passed as a complete atlas and reached a
  procedural fallback drawing invented creature rectangles. Gate fixed and
  the fallback removed, along with the invented ceiling/floor gradient.
- Game-over and endgame screens now use the original CAPPO.EXE strings,
  which were transcribed but unused. The invented wording and the
  rank ladder Captive never had are gone.

Gameplay:
- Liberation quicksave inside a building interior silently discarded the
  interior's progress: the key reached the Captive save path, which
  rejects a Liberation session.
- Entering a building interior did not reset the puzzle list, leaving
  stale puzzles at coordinates from the previous map.
- Purchases that did not fit the city inventory were destroyed after the
  gold was already debited; they now stay pending.
- Shop buy/repair and grenade throw acted on key auto-repeat.
- Clicking out of settings left an invisible active text field.

Tests: replaced three assertions that could not fail, and a silent skip
that reported PASS while verifying nothing.

Also documented two synthetic-data fallbacks (shop backdrop, Liberation
3D palette) that the test suite actively asserts, so they need a decision
rather than a silent change.

events.title: ecs: the palette blanket row-mark was 81% of an idle full present
events.message:
ecs: the palette blanket row-mark was 81% of an idle full present

The ECS narrowing landed correct but inert: qd_set_palette blanket-marked every
row ~1x per present, so all 200 rows were rescanned regardless (measured, 49ee295a).

The fix is NOT hw_palette — display.h is explicit that ECS fails that test, its 5
planes holding a quantised slot rather than the index, so a CLUT move really can
invalidate converted pixels. What is wrong is the TOOL: qd_touch_all answers two
questions at once (#152's "must a present happen" and #63's "which rows changed"),
and a palette write is exactly the case where the first is true and the second is
EMPTY — the CLUT moved, the chunky surface did not. A row-diffing present compares
chunky against its shadow, so the blanket can only ever make it re-read 200
unchanged rows. What actually re-renders after a CLUT move is the backend's own
flag: ECS's s_dirty -> ecs_reband/ecs_render, a branch that bypasses the row scan
entirely. Both ECS palette paths therefore ignore the row set already — a
substantial write rebands, and a small write changes nothing the scan could find.

So: split the two jobs (qd_touch_present_only keeps g_qd_touched, leaves the row
set alone — suppressing BOTH is the trap that once made qd_present skip a frame
with pending work) and add dsp_backend_t.palette_self_invalidates for backends
that own their invalidation. Last field, so every positional initialiser that
stops earlier keeps the historical blanket; only ECS opts in. The ST/STe is
eligible on the same argument (its reband sets s_force_full, which also bypasses
pass 1) but is shipping and measured, so it is deliberately left alone.

MEASURED on real ECS (amiberry, HEIRS slot I walk, A/B via FRUA_ECS_PALBLANKET,
both arms WITHOUT the police — the DIRTYCHECK build re-scans every skipped row
and hides the whole win):

  idle full present   1323 -> 248 rl   (-81%)
  rows scanned/present 200 -> 23
  display share       346 -> 134 /1000 (-61%)
  conv rows            782 -> 782      (the semantic invariant, every window)

Correctness: FRUA_DIRTYCHECK read ZERO unannounced rows over 771 full presents
(154,200 police checks). Walk frame and a live AREA-map toggle both render
correctly with the right colours, which is the scene-change/reband check.

Shipping builds unaffected (Amiga ECS+AGA, Atari 020 + CPU68K=68000); TT/Nova
initialisers untouched; 461 host tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: amiga: AGA census + ECS scan narrowing — and the blanket marker, named
events.message:
amiga: AGA census + ECS scan narrowing — and the blanket marker, named

Two things, both asked for by the ECS profiler's first census.

1. AGA census (FRUA_AMIGAPROF, `apaga:` lines): the same rect/full present +
   rasterline accounting as the ECS one, over aga_present/aga_present_rect, with
   the draw-time-planar row path counted separately from the c2p_amiga transpose
   (dt frames). AGA is 8 planes on an 020, so that split is its version of the
   question the ST composite work answered.

2. ECS full-present scan narrowing, ported from the ST: only rows a writer
   ANNOUNCED (planar_touch_rows — the shared machine-neutral set the ST already
   drives) can have moved, so scan those and skip the rest unread. ONE pending
   set, not the ST's per-page pair: ECS's incremental path always writes
   s_planes[s_front] and never flips, and the only flip (ecs_render) rebuilds the
   whole page and re-syncs the shadow, so the page it flips in is current by
   construction. Conservative by default (uninitialised, or "scan everything"
   from the shared set, means every row is pending), and FRUA_DIRTYCHECK ports
   the ST's police: re-run the OLD unconditional diff on every skipped row and
   report any that changed unannounced.

VERIFIED SAFE, then MEASURED USELESS — and the second half is the finding.
The police read ZERO unannounced rows over 644 full presents x 200 rows =
128,800 checks. But `rows SCANNED` is 128,800 too: exactly 200 per full present,
so nothing is being narrowed. g_qdt_hits (the TT's site labels, gate extended to
FRUA_AMIGAPROF and dumped in the census) names the culprit without guesswork —
across that walk qdt3 palette went 29 -> 665, i.e. 636 blanket qd_touch_all()s
in 644 presents, while grab/fill/glyph did not move at all. Only 782 of the
128,800 scanned rows had actually changed (0.6%).

So ECS is hitting the TT's #99 trap exactly: qd_set_palette's unconditional
qd_touch_all() forces a whole-frame rescan ~1x per present, which is what the
dsp_backend_t.hw_palette flag exists to suppress. ECS cannot simply set that flag
(its planes hold a quantised 5-bit SLOT, not the index), so the fix needs its own
decision and is left for one — the narrowing is in place and correct, and pays
the moment the blanket mark goes.

Shipping builds byte-neutral (0 profiler refs in both no-flag Amiga objects);
Atari unaffected; 461 host tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: amiga: FRUA_AMIGAPROF — the ECS play-loop profiler (b63play analog)
events.message:
amiga: FRUA_AMIGAPROF — the ECS play-loop profiler (b63play analog)

The Amiga had NO play-loop instrument (the phase counters are FRUA_STPROF,
Atari-only), so the ECS/AGA walk cost could never be quantified the way the ST
composite work was. This builds the missing one.

amiga_prof.h: a fine raster-line timer (~64us) — the VBL frame counter
(g_amiga_vbl_ticks) combined with the beam line (VPOSR/VHPOSR), monotonic,
double-read across the frame boundary. Far finer than the 50/60Hz VBL alone,
which cannot resolve a single viewport present.

display_ecs.c: a b63play-style census (FRUA_AMIGAPROF) over ecs_present /
ecs_present_rect — rect/full present counts + rasterline times, the conversion
(remap + c2p_amiga_n_rect) as a subset, converted-row count, wall clock, and a
display-per-1000 share. Dumps to DBG.LOG every 8 rect presents.

First census on a real ECS walk (amiberry, HEIRS slot I, 24+ turns):
  - display is 34-63% of wall — substantial, the same order as the ST
  - a viewport rect present is ~5000 rl (~330ms) on the 7MHz 68000 — the
    per-step c2p, and what the just-landed two-redraw fix halves the count of
  - FULL presents outnumber rect presents (16-102 vs 8/window) yet convert only
    ~0-100 rows each: idle re-presents whose cost is the whole-frame row-diff
    SCAN finding nothing changed — the exact pattern the Atari pass-1 work
    attacked, now measurable on the Amiga for the first time.

Shipping builds byte-neutral (0 amiga_prof refs in the no-AMIGAPROF ECS object);
AGA build unaffected (does not include the header yet).

events.title: nova: remap the low-16 palette through the VDI pen->hardware table
events.message:
nova: remap the low-16 palette through the VDI pen->hardware table

The card renders indices 16..255 identity (the PALTEST hue wheel is a smooth,
correctly-ordered spectrum), but the low 16 UI colours landed on the wrong
slots — VDI reserves pens 0..15 and maps pen p to a permuted hardware CLUT slot
for p < 16, while a framebuffer byte selects the hardware slot directly. So a
vs_color(i, C) for i < 16 set the colour of the wrong slot, and the engine's low
UI indices (e.g. the cyan title) showed another slot's colour (gold).

Confirmed on the real ATW800/2: the PALTEST corners write framebuffer bytes
0/1/2/3 with vs_color(0..3)=R/G/B/W, and the photo shows corner 1 = pen 2's
blue, corner 2 = pen 3's white, corner 3 = pen 6's orange — i.e. pen->hw
{2->1, 3->2, 6->3}, exactly the standard Atari VDI 16-pen table. Route each
low framebuffer index i through hw_inverse[i] so vs_color lands on hardware
slot i. Pens >= 16 (the art/3D indices) are untouched.

events.title: Bank3.c: Fix high-score row draw missing $C350-$C352 leading erase
events.message:
Bank3.c: Fix high-score row draw missing $C350-$C352 leading erase

draw_table_field_scrolling drew each glyph's 7 rows starting at the
scroll-triggered address with no erase step, so successive frames'
unclamped blits left every prior frame's rows in place -- smearing
each character downward as its row scrolled through the visible band.

The real rsn_char_loop ($C304-$C378) writes a single zero byte at the
character's own (D, E) first, then draws the glyph one scanline below
it (rsn_draw_row's INC D runs before each row's write, not after). The
erase-ahead is what stops each frame's blit from streaking: it wipes
the last row the previous frame's glyph occupied a moment before the
new glyph is redrawn one line further on.

Also fixes blink_hiscore_row's erase phase, previously a no-op: it
substituted an all-spaces string into the same draw path, but spaces
are always skipped (both real draw and erase loops treat them as
no-ops), so nothing was ever written. rsn_char_loop2 ($C37B-$C3AC) is
a separate 8-row, no-offset, write-then-advance loop; draw_table_field_scrolling
now takes an erase flag and runs that path with the row's real text.

events.title: ste: #90 align the viewport composite — kill the scalar edge columns
events.message:
ste: #90 align the viewport composite — kill the scalar edge columns

The dungeon-walk composite ran 3 scalar 8px edge columns per row because the
88px viewport sits at an unaligned x=24. Those columns measured ~43% of the
composite and were overhead-bound (528 calls/present + strided single-byte
video stores), not compute-bound — so c2p4st_8 barely moved them.

Composite a 16-ALIGNED span instead (x=16..112 = three fast c2p4st_32 blocks
per row, no edges). The alignment adds up to 15px of frame border on each side;
seed those into the scratch from s_chunky (the live surface, static chrome) so
the composited border is byte-identical to what is already on screen, while the
viewport interior still comes from the scratch. A trailing-16px fallback keeps
an exotic non-32-multiple width correct via the slow edge path (the live 96px
viewport never reaches it).

Measured on a real Mega STe (HEIRS slot I walk): viewport composite 249 -> 195
t200, -22%. Resume frame md5-IDENTICAL to the pre-alignment build (whole PNG,
status bar included; game-area AE 0 px) — provably lossless. 461 host tests
pass; shipping CPU68K=68000 build clean, 0 020-insns.

events.title: c2p4st: add c2p4st_8, the half-group (8px) nibble c2p
events.message:
c2p4st: add c2p4st_8, the half-group (8px) nibble c2p

An ST viewport that does not start on a 16-pixel boundary presents 8-pixel
edge columns; converting them with a scalar per-bit scatter was measurable on
the FRUA dungeon walk. c2p4st_8 is the same word-parallel butterfly as
c2p4st_32 restricted to the 8 pixels that occupy each lane's top byte: load
the 8 remapped nibbles into the <<24 slot (lower bytes zero, so the 4-shift
merge stays within each byte), run the identical merge + delta-swap network,
and read the top byte of the four plane lanes. Fills out[0..3] = plane 0..3,
bit 7 = leftmost pixel.

Byte-identical to the naive scatter over 4000 random pixel/LUT trials
(tests/test_c2p4st.py).

events.message:
ste: route the viewport edge columns through c2p4st_8

half-group c2p instead. Byte-identical output (host-tested in the c2p-68k
subtree), and it drops the walk composite ~4% on a real Mega STe.

The edge columns turned out to be ~43% of the composite but overhead-bound
(528 calls/composite + strided video byte-stores), not compute-bound — so the
faster arithmetic is a small, honest win, not the big one. The remaining edge
cost is the per-column call/store overhead (align-the-composite territory),
and the ~57% block half is c2p4st_32 compute (Stage C draw-time planar). Video
stores measured ~free, so Stage C is not store-capped. See docs/planar-plan.md.

perf: #90 the viewport composite is 45% scalar edge-columns, not fills

Census the fast-composite spans (FRUA_STPROF): flat 32-blocks (the fills
Stage A would convert), textured 32-blocks (walls + tiled floor/starfield
ceiling), and the scalar 8px edge columns. Measured on a real Mega STe walk
(HEIRS slot I corridor):

  32-block split: ~8% flat / ~92% textured
  A/B (stub st_c2p8): edge columns = ~45% of the composite, blocks ~55%

doing: the floor/ceiling composite as texture, not flat runs, so only ~8% of
blocks are flat and the flat-detect already makes those ~free — ~1% of cost
for real risk. The win is elsewhere: the scalar st_c2p8 edge columns (a fast
table/SWAR c2p4st_8 replaces them, ~low risk) and the textured walls (Stage C
draw-time planar, the hard part). See docs/planar-plan.md #90.

tools: standalone Nova/xVDI palette-mapping diagnostic (novapaltest)

FRUAPAL.PRG is the full engine binary — it boots the engine and needs the
copyrighted FRUA data to reach the palette test, so it can't be handed to
testers. novapaltest.c is a self-contained TOS program (build -m68000, no
engine, no game data, freely distributable): it opens the current VDI screen,
and if it's an 8bpp graphics-card mode (planes==8) paints a diagnostic into the
card framebuffer, waits for a key, and exits; on any other screen it prints one
line and exits without touching video.

The diagnostic pins the framebuffer-value -> colour mapping: a top strip of 16
distinctly-coloured index bars (value 0..15 against a fixed known key) over a
hue wheel (values 16..255). The first real card run (FRUAPAL) showed the hue
wheel SMOOTH and correct (identity — no channel swap or gross permutation) but
the low-index corner blocks wrong, i.e. the first few VDI pens are reserved/
offset — which is why FRUA UI colours (the cyan title -> gold) shifted while the
art looked fine. The 16-bar strip reads that offset directly.

events.title: ste: stop the double viewport composite per walk step (#90 double-redraw)
events.message:
ste: stop the double viewport composite per walk step (#90 double-redraw)

The #90 walk measurement flagged "two redraws per action, halving is worth as
much as any present optimisation." Found it: it's a redundant SECOND viewport
composite each step, from stale page bookkeeping.

st_vp_composite() writes the viewport into BOTH pages in one call — the fast
path c2p's per page (the pg loop), the slow path c2p's once and blits both (the
B4 "drop into BOTH pages" comment). But the dispatcher still cleared only the
SHOWN page's s_vp_owe, a leftover from #61 when the composite touched one page.
So after a walk step commits (owe[0]=owe[1]=1), the first present composites
both pages and clears one owe; the SECOND present of the step (l63c0 issues
jt312's qd_present_rect then a qd_present) sees the other page still owing and
re-runs the whole both-page composite — pure redundant work, ~a full viewport
c2p per step.

Fix: clear BOTH owes after the composite, since it already did both pages. Both
pages stay current, so #61's "a flip never shows a stale viewport" guarantee is
preserved (verified: corridor + a turn both render correctly on the shipping
STE build). Measured A/B on the same drive: composites per viewport-commit drop
1.43 -> 1.11 (approaching the theoretical 1.0; a clean event-free corridor,
where every step double-presents, gets the full 2->1). Each composite is ~one
present's cost, so this is real time off the walk's 43%-present redraw.

Also adds a vpcomp COUNT line to the FRUA_STPROF dump (diagnostic build only).

events.title: Decode the CB and DD/FD instruction paths
events.message:
Decode the CB and DD/FD instruction paths

Neither uses a table of packed words. CB derives its mnemonic
arithmetically from the opcode - op>>3 below &40, else (op>>6)+7 - into
an 11-entry name list at &0A86, with the register operand taken as
(op & 7) + 1 in the operand table. DD/FD set flags and re-use the base
or CB table, substituting only the three HL-bearing operand codes.

That substitution rule explains three limits of MONA's disassembler,
all confirmed against tools/z80dis.py:

- entry 7 of the CB name list is empty, so the undocumented SLL prints
  with no mnemonic;
- H and L are never substituted, so IXh/IXl cannot be expressed and
  appear as plain H/L;
- DDCB prints only the documented form, without the register-copy
  suffix.

Also reformats the bit-7-terminated name tables. A new STRTAB directive
renders one entry per line with its index, so the 31-entry operand table
now reads as the 5-bit field it indexes instead of a wall of hex.

events.title: Decode MONA's instruction database
events.message:
Decode MONA's instruction database

Each instruction is a 16-bit big-endian word: 6 bits mnemonic index,
5 bits operand 1, 5 bits operand 2, with index >= 60 marking an invalid
opcode. Operand fields index a 31-entry name table whose strings embed
control codes for the immediates and the IX/IY displacement. When
operand 1 is absent and operand 2 is not, operand 2 instead indexes a
13-entry table holding the whole operand field, which is how the RST
targets, AF,AF' and the IN/OUT forms are expressed.

The base table is 256 dense 2-byte entries indexed by opcode; ED
instructions are a 56-entry sparse 3-byte table searched linearly.

tools/optable.py decodes the database and verifies it against the
independent disassembler in tools/z80dis.py: 252/252 base entries and
56/56 ED entries agree. The decoded dump is checked in.

The base table is stored big-endian, so it stays rendered as DEFB in the
listing; DEFW is little-endian and would misstate the values.

events.title: Trace MONA's T (disassemble) command end to end
events.message:
Trace MONA's T (disassemble) command end to end

Names the disassembler pipeline and its workspace: the prompt sequence,
the per-line loop, opcode lookup, operand rendering, symbol lookup and
line output, plus the packed opcode and operand tables it drives.

Findings:

- T runs the whole disassembly twice when a symbol table is requested.
  VAR_FLAGS bit 4 marks pass 1, which only collects label addresses; it
  is then cleared and the address and data-area pointers rewound for the
  output pass. This is the "short delay while the symbol table is
  constructed" the manual mentions.
- Each output line is built in a buffer that sits at &16D7 - the
  relocation table itself, dead once relocation has run.
- The documented loss of breakpoints is explicit: T resets the
  breakpoint pointer and count before doing anything else.
- The overwrite abort compares the text pointer against a relocated
  reference to MONA's own code.
- &12F8 "Printer?" is the tail of "No Printer?" stored at &12F5. Nothing
  references &12F5, so the "No " prefix is dead in this build; the name
  at &12F8 is corrected to MSG_PRINTER.

events.title: Name more routines; stop labelling unrelocated immediates

Name more routines; stop labelling unrelocated immediates

Adds 24 names to GENA and 16 to MONA: string and number output, hex
input, the tape open/close wrappers, and MONA's textfile emitters.
MONA's number routines take their destination in BC (zero = screen,
non-zero = the generated textfile), which the names now reflect.

Also fixes a mislabelling the new names exposed. A 16-bit immediate is
only an address if the relocator patches it; LD BC,&0000 selects an
output stream and was being rendered as LD BC,ENTRY_RELOC because
&0000 happened to be a branch target elsewhere. Branch operands are
still labelled unconditionally.

events.title: Extract and disassemble HiSoft DEVPAC for the Amstrad CPC
events.message:
Extract and disassemble HiSoft DEVPAC for the Amstrad CPC

Recovers GENA3.1 and MONA3.1 from hidevpac.dsk and disassembles both.

Both binaries are assembled at ORG 0 and self-relocate via a table of
16-bit offsets, so the AMSDOS load address is not where the code runs.
That table also serves as a correctness oracle: every genuine in-image
address is relocated, so an unrelocated absolute JP/CALL cannot be code.

Includes the extraction toolchain, the detokenised BASIC loaders, and
per-binary annotation sidecars carrying symbol names and region
directives. Each disassembly run asserts that the listing reproduces
the input byte for byte and that every referenced label is defined.

platform: fill in the Nova card backend from the real ATW800/2 NOVA.LOG

The card's graf_handle live query confirmed: 640x400x256, planes=8, lut=1 (8bpp
chunky), framebuffer aperture at Logbase()=$FEA00000, EdDI + xVDI cookies. Both
VDI paths agreed on the card, so the "640x400x2" was only the engine's own
dsp_detect (Getrez()==2), which the FRUA_NOVA hook already sidesteps.

display_nova.c now renders for real: base = Logbase(), card 640x400, the engine's
320x240 chunky surface centred into it with a black surround (clears the whole
framebuffer once at init). This is a first render to validate base/pitch/format/
palette on hardware before the 2x-scale-to-fullscreen pass (640x400 = 2x
320x200). Pitch is the card width (640) for a linear chunky mode; the present
loops per row so a padded pitch is a one-constant fix. Palette via vs_color;
hw_palette=1.

Safe by construction: dsp_backend_nova() detects planes!=8 and hands back to the
ST/STe backend (verified on an emulated STe — boots to the menu normally). Empty
object without -DFRUA_NOVA, so the default build is unchanged. Test binary is
FRUACARD.PRG on the card; docs/nova-card.md has the confirmed values and how to
read the first render.

events.title: platform: query the LIVE screen (graf_handle), not Getrez(), for the card depth
events.message:
platform: query the LIVE screen (graf_handle), not Getrez(), for the card depth

Real ATW800/2 + xVDI finding: at the card's lowest mode (640x400x256) Getrez()
returns 2 (ST-High). That poisoned every device-id path — the engine's
dsp_detect did Getrez()==2 -> ST-High mono backend, and the probe's
v_opnvwk(Getrez()+2) opened the 640x400x2 ST-COMPAT workstation — which is the
"detected 640x400x2" symptom the user saw, not the card's real 256-colour mode.

Fix: ask the VDI for the actual depth via vq_extnd() on the AES physical handle
from graf_handle() (the live desktop workstation = the card), never trust
Getrez(). nova_probe.c now dumps the "LIVE SCREEN via vq_extnd(graf_handle)"
block (colours[13], planes[4]) alongside the device-id path so the divergence is
on record; display_nova.c's dsp_backend_nova() reads planes from the physical
handle too, and its dsp_detect hook already runs before the Getrez()==2->sthigh
branch.

Also: xVDI sets none of NOVA/EdDI/NVDI/fVDI, so the probe's early cookie gate
wrongly skipped the query. Gate removed — it now queries whenever the AES is up
(appl_init succeeds), which is safe (the v_opnvwk hang was the old physical-open
path, already replaced by the AES/v_opnvwk sequence). Verified on an emulated
STe: graf_handle=1, 320x200x16 planes 4, no hang, boots to menu.

Note 640x400 = exactly 2x 320x200, so the backend integer-doubles the surface.
docs/nova-card.md records the finding. Default build unaffected (both files are
empty objects without -DFRUA_NOVA / -DFRUA_NOVAPROBE).

events.title: engine: snap the camera to the party on l63c0 deep re-entry (end-of-event teleport)
events.message:
engine: snap the camera to the party on l63c0 deep re-entry (end-of-event teleport)

Hardware-confirmed on the Mega STe: after a CHAINED event chain ends (roadwarden
message -> ogre combat -> treasure -> return to the walk), the first-person view
renders ONE frame "from another area", then snaps back to the corridor. The
ogre-fight dead-bar fix (29376921) did NOT cure this — it is a separate bug.

Root cause (mapped, not the GEO): combat never swaps the dungeon map or level;
the map buffer g_a5_long(-12300) and g_a5_18878 stay resident. The stale state
is the VIEW CELL g_a5_-12288/-12287/-12286 (the camera). l63c0 is re-entered
through jt948->jt240 after the chained combat, and its a_deep ENTRY force-full
(jt312) renders with whatever the view cell holds — left at combat's arena /
the pre-move entry cell, because jt297's per-step forward-snap does not run on
this entry path and g_event_modal_shown is cleared at the top of the branch. So
the entry frame draws the wrong cell until the next step snaps it forward.

Fix mirrors l143e (the save-load restore, which renders correctly precisely
because it writes the camera BEFORE rendering): snap the view cell from the
authoritative party mirror rec[46..51] right before the entry jt312. Deep play
only; idempotent on every ordinary command re-entry (verified: slot H still
lands at (5,17) with the corridor correct on the Mega STe); per-command entry
path, not the hot per-frame path.

Cure to be confirmed on hardware: slot H -> fight -> treasure -> hallway, watch
for the wrong-area flash. FRUA.PRG on the test card is this build.

tools: batch 26b — the classifier re-priced against Phase 7

The registered follow-up, run per the §0g/§0h discipline (byte-for-byte
reproduction first — and the Phase 6 pin-break did NOT recur, for the
structural reason that Phase 7 added rather than moved).

The rule: T2 PSG_SEEDED_READ → T2 SEEDED_READ, folding byte reads of
$fffa01/$ff820a — fold not new-tier, argued from the lattice's
ordering principle (identical verification strength: declared input,
ordered ledger, loud refusal). Wide/straddling/unsized over modeled
bytes stay T5; writes stay dropped T3; outside the set stays T4. The
write-then-read stale refusal is a run property a static classifier
cannot see — reported per-site instead, now including unattributed
code.

Re-pricing (runnable UNCHANGED function-for-function): false-green
28 fns / 3,348 B → 20 / 2,224 — the first movement of that figure
since the original measurement. All 8 leavers named; none joined; the
sound subsystem's false-green row is zero. New positive control
$ff8609 (the FDC counter Phase 7 rules out structurally, so it cannot
quietly become modeled). Cross-check: the new default equals the old
rule with --model mfp:read shifter:read — §6's second-biggest lever
measured as delivered.

Review gate (3 finders; code path verified sound): docs/on-target-
execution.md's tier table updated (it still taught PSG_SEEDED_READ and
'every hw read returns 0'); the unsized-below-boundary edge STATED at
both models (Access.span owns the assumption; two lattice rows pin
today's answer; the PSG half was pre-existing and unstated); capability
pins compare function SETS not totals; the stale-write sweep walks
unattributed code with a synthetic case proving it isn't silent by
accident; --model help records what is BUILT; closed_scan()/
at_seeded_surface dedups; report self-consistent under write-model
flags. Tests 37 → 56, sweep 12/12 (one bad-mutation methodology note
recorded beside §0g's __pycache__ caveat).

events.title: platform: Nova/NVDI graphics-card probe + backend scaffold (ATW800/2)
events.message:
platform: Nova/NVDI graphics-card probe + backend scaffold (ATW800/2)

A graphics card is the cleanest non-Falcon Atari target: an 8bpp chunky
screen with the palette in hardware — the TT/AGA identity — so there is
no c2p/bitplane work at all. But it's hardware-only (no emulator models a
Nova/VME card), so the first artifact is a probe that dumps what a backend
author needs, then the backend gets coded from real numbers.

nova_probe.c (-DFRUA_NOVAPROBE): runs once before dsp_detect, writes
NOVA.LOG — the cookie jar (NOVA/EdDI/NVDI/fVDI prove the card+driver; _VDO
stays STE so detection can't use it), the framebuffer base (Physbase/
Logbase/_v_bas_ad), and the VDI screen caps via the documented AES path
(graf_handle -> v_opnvwk -> vq_extnd): work_out[13]=#colours,
vq_extnd(1)[4]=planes. Flushes after each phase, so a blocking VDI call
still leaves the essential data + a breadcrumb on disk; skips the VDI open
on a plain machine with no card cookie (which would block). Proven on an
emulated STe: handle 2, 320x200, 16 colours, planes 4 — the code is right;
the card reports planes 8 / 256 colours.

display_nova.c (-DFRUA_NOVA): provisional backend scaffold — detection in
dsp_backend_nova() so dsp_detect falls through to the ST/STe backend on a
non-8bpp screen; hw_palette=1; render-local-then-push-to-VRAM (display_rtg
model); vs_color palette. Four TODO(NOVA.LOG) spots (aperture, pitch, mode,
CLUT) get filled from a hardware dump. Empty object in shipping builds.

Both gated so the default CPU68K=68000 build is byte-identical to the
shipped ST/STe binary (verified). docs/nova-card.md has the workflow.
461 passed, 6 skipped.

The read: BOTH detect bits are ACTIVE LOW (GPIP bit 7 SET = colour,
sync bit 1 SET = 50 Hz) — a port from the register names gets both

events.title: engine: rebuild the walk bar after a NON-movement event return (ogre-fight fix)
events.message:
engine: rebuild the walk bar after a NON-movement event return (ogre-fight fix)

play_screen_relayout() — the only thing that rebuilds the walk command bar /
DLItem pool after an event resets it — had one call site, inside the a_deep
(movement) branch of l63c0's re-render. So the bar was rebuilt only after an
ARROW key. An event that returns to the loop on a NON-movement iteration left
the relayout undone. On real Mega STe hardware (slot H, a few steps before the
HEIRS ogre fight) that is: after the fight, (A)rea and (E)ncamp do nothing, but
Escape opens camp, and the view "draws a weird place (~0,17) then snaps back,
can't move past the bodies."

One cause, both symptoms: the DLItem pool still holds the event's own bar, so a
bare accelerator matches nothing in Phase 5 (dead A/E) while Escape works
because it is the DIRECT key arm (kc==27), not a DLItem; and the view cell
(-12288..) is stale until a movement step snaps it — the teleport.

Fix: the non-movement `else` branch (previously just jt280) now runs the SAME
repair the a_deep branch does — snap the view cell to the party mirror,
play_screen_relayout, force a full recompose — but ONLY when g_event_modal_shown
is pending. Provably non-regressive: without the flag the branch is
byte-identical to before, and the flag is set only by events/modals, for which
a relayout is always the correct response.

Why only combat and not, say, the tavern: a DIRECT cell event fires inside the
entering step, so the a_deep branch consumes the flag that same iteration —
verified, KOBOLD.DSN's (3,4) combat relayouts fine, and the tavern text event
tested clean all session. Only a DEFERRED path — combat reached through a
CHAINED message (roadwarden text -> chain -> fight), or a modal that exits and
re-enters l63c0 — returns on a non-movement iteration and strands the flag.
tools/mk_chaincbt_design.py (added) authors that chained structure for a fast
repro.

VERIFIED: builds on all three targets; non-regression confirmed on the
deterministic path — slot-B fixture walk, single 'a' still claims AREA (ph5
113) and movement still renders. The direct-combat path (KOBOLD) is unaffected
by construction (its flag is consumed in a_deep).

NOT yet verified live: the chained-combat cure itself, because the headless
repro would not stabilise this session (the authored module's entry pool-install
timing + a col/row hook-axis mismatch; the real ogre fight is long and
FRUA_CBTPLAY stalls once the roadwarden NPC joins). The definitive check is a
2-minute hardware test the user already has the save for: slot H -> fight the
ogre -> try A/E. If they work, done; if not, the flag also needs setting at the
chained combat's return point (the fix location is right either way).

events.title: diag: FRUA_CBT_CURGEO — fire a combat event in the loaded geo (post-combat repro)
events.message:
diag: FRUA_CBT_CURGEO — fire a combat event in the loaded geo (post-combat repro)

Adds a compile-time branch so the FRUA_CBTSND fire path can run l709e(EV) in
the ALREADY-LOADED area instead of jt198(7)+l709e (which reloads GEO007 for
the old combat-sound harness). Lets a combat be fired in the fixture's own
area for the post-combat walk-return test.

Investigation result (the ogre-fight dead bar + teleport, reported on real
Mega STe hardware): CAUSE CONFIRMED BY INSPECTION. play_screen_relayout() —
the only function that rebuilds the walk command bar / DLItem pool after an
event resets it — has exactly ONE call site (boot.c:18320), and it is inside
the `if ((unsigned char)a_deep)` movement block (opened 18272). So after
combat returns to the walk loop, g_event_modal_shown is set but the relayout
that consumes it runs ONLY on the next ARROW key:
  - a bare A/E accelerator matches Phase-5 DLItems against the stale pool and
    claims nothing -> "dead";
  - Escape works because kc==27 is the direct key arm, not a DLItem;
  - the view cell (-12288..) is stale until the a_deep block snaps it to
    rec[46..], so the first render shows the wrong cell (~0,17) then snaps
    back -> the teleport. One bug, two symptoms.

Why headless accelerator tests all passed and the tavern event did not show
it: text/tavern events fire ON the entering step, so the relayout runs in that
step's a_deep block. Combat EXITS and re-enters the walk loop (jt948->jt240->

next pass uses a lighter in-place combat via this flag.

events.title: diag: FRUA_ACCTRACE — trace a key from jt1125 stamp to Phase-5 consumption
events.message:
diag: FRUA_ACCTRACE — trace a key from jt1125 stamp to Phase-5 consumption

Four guarded trace points for the walk-screen accelerator lag found on the
real Mega STe ("(A)rea didn't work, (E)ncamp didn't, Escape opened the encamp
screen"): the jt1125 pending stamp, the masked-return branch, l2d3e's Phase-5
gate/consumption, and a rate-limited walk-loop spin counter.

What is established so far, all on the SHIPPED build in the emulator:
  - single 'a' in the walk: nothing happens; a later key flushes it and the
    AREA overlay appears — the accelerators run ONE EVENT BEHIND;
  - the user's Esc-opens-encamp is the pending 'e' being flushed by Esc;
  - de8931b6's "AREA toggle still fires" verification was a multi-key
    scripted drive, where the next key always flushes the previous one —
    structurally blind to the lag; single keypresses (a human) expose it.

Code-reading says Phase 5 (l31ea -> jt1118 reads -820; jt1133 consumes) should
fire on the SAME l2d3e poll that stamped the letter, which contradicts the
observed lag — hence tracing over more theory. The instrumented runs have not
yet caught the lag in the act: the HEIRS drive keeps dying at the treasure
screen, and the slot-A save fixture turns out to have been taken BEFORE the
entry events completed, so loading it replays the caravan chain and the keys
land in the event loop (g_walk_input still 0 — the trace's silence was
correct). Next: complete the chain once, save INSIDE the live walk to make an
instant fixture, then read the trace.

Also corrected today (user, verified on the real Mac): Mac FRUA — 1.0
included — HAS letter accelerators on the walk command bar. The earlier
"the Mac doesn't" conclusion came from failed xdotool injection into the Mac
emulator being read as a missing feature. A negative from an injection
harness needs a positive control before it is a fact.

diag: FRUA_BOOTTRACE breadcrumbs + FRUA_NOBOOST gate — field-proven

Eight dbg_file_str markers from main() entry through st_init, written to
DBG.LOG regardless of the console/file sink switch, plus a compile-time gate
that disables the Mega STe 16 MHz boost. Built for the real-hardware
black-screen hunt, and they earned their keep on the first outing: the diag
build moved the first file write BEFORE the display takeover, which turned an
invisible TOS timeout alert into a visible one and named the real culprit —
the SD card's writes time out on the UltraSatan (TOS "output device is not
receiving data"), leaving torn FAT updates (a directory loop on C:). Nothing
in the engine was hanging at all.

Boost A/B on emulated Mega STe at real speed, same binary otherwise:
boot-to-menu 50 s boosted vs 73 s not (-31%). Hatari 2.6.1 models the
$FFFF8E21 switch and the 16 KB cache (its status bar shows "16MHz(CE)").
On real hardware the walk loop feels similar either way, and that is
expected: the present-dominated phases are memory-bound against a bus that
still paces at 8 MHz, so the 16 MHz core + cache mostly accelerates the
compute between bus accesses — near-2x at boot, ~1.2-1.4x in blit-heavy play.

Verified on the real Mega STe today: boots, plays HEIRS through the caravan
event (the composite fix shows the merchant portrait on real silicon),
combat runs, event bigpics work.

events.title: ST: FIX the wrong event picture — the composite repainted a stale 3D scratch
events.message:
ST: FIX the wrong event picture — the composite repainted a stale 3D scratch

The "wrong picture" during the caravan event was never a wrong picture being
DRAWN: it was the last-rendered 3D corridor, repainted over the freshly-blitted
event bigpic by the viewport composite, and re-coloured through the event's
palette. The user called both halves of this from two phone screenshots
("scrambled the palette first, then never loaded the bigpic") after the
measurements had been read as "a different image". Settled with a palette-
independent edge-map test against frames from ONE run: the wrong frame shares
71.1% of its edge structure with the corridor and 42.9% with the merchant
portrait — the different-image floor is 43.6%, the same-image ceiling 100%.
A per-band colour test agrees (70.2% banded consistency vs a 36.3% control;
global mapping is the wrong test on a per-band quantiser).

Mechanism, in order:
  1. walk step: 3D view -> st_vp_scratch, commit sets s_vp_have and both
     pages' owes; the composite paints it and clears the owes — but
     s_vp_have stays set forever;
  2. event: the bigpic lands in chunky (and s_dt) via l2d4e/l309c;
  3. the event's palette install triggers a reband -> force-full, which
     rebuilds both pages from s_dt (the merchant IS there) — and then
     re-arms both owes because s_vp_have is still set (#61's fix: a page
     rebuilt from s_dt has a hole where composite content was, because the
     composite writes the PAGE, never s_dt);
  4. next present: the composite paints the STALE corridor scratch back
     over the merchant, through the new palette's remap. Deterministic, so
     byte-identical for eight days and untouched by every bridge flag —
     the composite is not a bridge.

The #61 re-arm is correct while the 3D view is the newest viewport content
and exactly wrong after a blit REPLACES that content. Fix: a superseding
screen blit now invalidates the committed scratch —
planar_viewport_overwrite(rect) in planar.c (no-op where no composite is
registered; only display_ste.c registers one), called from BOTH art writers:
l309c (the l2d4e path — where event bigpics actually land; a CopyBits-only
first attempt changed nothing, which is how that was learned) and the
CopyBits screen path. ANY overlap invalidates: compositing the whole scratch
would clobber the blit wherever they intersect, over-invalidation self-heals
on the next walk step's commit, and under-invalidation is this bug. Both
calls sit OUTSIDE the FRUA_DIAG_NO*BRIDGE guards — invalidation is about
what chunky holds, not about plane stamping, and the diag flags must not
resurrect the bug they exist to bisect.

Correction to 94f8e96b's claim: chunky never held a wrong picture. The
bridge eliminations only proved the bridges innocent; the composite writes
the PAGE directly, which is why every chunky-side probe looked clean.

Verified on the shipped ST planar config, same drive as every earlier arm:
the event viewport is now pixel-identical to the PLANAR=0 reference
(AE=0 vs the portrait, 28800 vs the old bad frame), the second text beat
keeps the portrait (matches the DOS oracle), the treasure screen's own
bigpic still shows, and the "thank you" epilogue returns to the portrait.
020 and Amiga builds clean (ECS/AGA register no composite and are
unaffected); 461 tests pass.

Known residual: fill/wipe writers (qd_pixmap_fill) do not yet invalidate.
A wipe that covers the viewport followed by NO re-render would composite
stale content back — no reachable screen does this today (the #140 wipes
are followed by a full recompose that re-commits), so it is left for the
day a screen proves otherwise.
