events.title: diag: FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE — the other half of the art-bridge bisect
events.message:
diag: FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE — the other half of the art-bridge bisect

FRUA_DIAG_NOBRIDGE drops l309c's art-leaf plane stamp. That is NOT the path an
event picture takes: CopyBits carries "art/event pics" and stamps through
dc_plane_bridge_span, which NOBRIDGE leaves running. Testing the wrong-event-
picture bug with NOBRIDGE alone therefore proves nothing, and I read one result
that way before noticing. This flag drops just the CopyBits stamp so the two
can be used separately or together.

What the pair has established for the ST/STe planar wrong-picture bug:

  PLANAR=0                          -> correct portrait
  PLANAR=1 (shipped)                -> wrong picture
  + FRUA_PERPIXELBRIDGE             -> wrong, byte-identical
  + FRUA_DIAG_NOBRIDGE              -> wrong, byte-identical
  + FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE          -> wrong, byte-identical
  + BOTH diag flags                 -> wrong, byte-identical

So the span encoder (#126b) and both art bridges are exonerated. With no art
plane-stamping at all those rows are rebuilt from chunky by st_dt_build_row, so
the CHUNKY SURFACE already holds the wrong picture — this is not a plane
conversion fault.

Also settled: it is not a palette permutation. Over the picture interior the
planar->chunky colour mapping scores 28.5-37.8% against a 28.6-31.7% noise
floor (chunky vs a 7px-shifted copy of itself); a slot permutation would sit
near 100%. The earlier greyscale-equalised comparison was suggestive but
assumed a monotonic colour error, which a permutation is not — the joint
histogram with a shifted-self control is the test that actually decides it.

That leaves an odd shape: nothing under FRUA_PLANAR in the engine or the shim
changes WHAT is written to chunky (every block is a parallel plane store), yet
chunky differs. The remaining hypothesis is layout sensitivity — the flag also
allocates ~160 KB of ST-RAM for s_dt/s_dt_cov/s_dt_idx/s_dt_rowcov and moves
every later allocation. docs say to settle that class with a RUNTIME switch in
ONE binary (see the #91 write-up: four compile-time probes changed the
incidence and some masked it entirely), which is the next step.

events.title: uainst: build frua.rsc from CKIT.EXE on the machine itself
events.message:
uainst: build frua.rsc from CKIT.EXE on the machine itself

frua.rsc was the one file you still needed a PC to produce. uainst now builds
it natively on the Atari and the Amiga, so a set of DOS floppies and the retro
machine are enough on their own — an ST reads DOS 720K/1.44M disks natively and
CrossDOS is standard on Workbench 2.1+, so the originals mount without help.

Drag CKIT.EXE onto UAINST.TTP, or `uainst CKIT.EXE .`. Dispatch is on the .EXE
extension so the existing ZIP flow, the GEM selector and the ASL requesters all
keep working untouched, and nothing in the fan corpus is a .EXE.

VERIFIED BYTE-IDENTICAL TO THE PC TOOL, THREE WAYS. The host build of the C and
tools/rsrc_from_dos.py agree over the real executable; then the SAME archive
came out of an emulated 8 MHz ST running UAINST.TTP (identical MD5, all three);
then the engine booted from that ST-built archive and drew correct menu text —
which is the functional check that matters, because STRS *is* the string pool,
so a wrong offset table would show up as garbage on screen rather than as a
load failure.

Memory was designed for the small machines: it never loads the 574 KB
executable. SHA-256 streams it in 4 KB chunks and the 2108 extractions are
seek+read, so peak use is the 29 KB pool — it runs on a 512 KB ST.

It refuses a build the map was not derived against, checking BOTH size and
SHA-256. A size-only gate would pass a same-length repack and emit a plausible
archive full of wrong strings; the test exercises both a truncated file and a
one-byte-flipped one and asserts no output file is created either time.

The 37 port-authored Mac-only strings are IMPORTED from tools/rsrc_from_dos.py
by the generator, never retyped — two hand-maintained copies would drift and
the drift would only surface as a wrong filename much later. The positions
table is generated into installer/strs_map_dos12.h at build time from the
committed JSON, the same way src/engine/a4_map.c is; positions only, no
extracted text, so the build stays redistributable.

events.title: platform: ask a Mega STe for 16 MHz and its cache
events.message:
platform: ask a Mega STe for 16 MHz and its cache

A Mega STe boots at 8 MHz with its 16-byte cache OFF and stays there unless a
control panel or an AUTO-folder CPX says otherwise. Nothing in this engine had
ever looked — grep for _MCH / 8e21 / "mega" across src, compat and platform
returned nothing. The 68000 targets are exactly the ones that notice: the
ST/STe play loop is ~1.1 s per action at 8 MHz.

plat_cpu_boost() writes 0xFF (16 MHz + cache) to the byte at 0xFFFF8E21 and
plat_cpu_boost_restore() puts the user's value back at shutdown. The speed is
their setting, not ours.

Two details that decide whether this pokes the right machine at all:

  The register is at 8E21, not the 8E20 the Compendium's memory map prints.
  That table lists the region base with size "OB" (one byte), and ST-era
  byte-wide I/O lives at the ODD address of the word — the same convention as
  the rest of the 0xFF8xxx map.

  The gate is the WHOLE _MCH cookie == 0x00010010, not its high word. The
  Compendium's cookie table is ST 0/0, STe 1/0, ST Book 1/8, Mega STe 1/16,
  TT030 2/0 — so an "is the major 1?" test would write a nonexistent register
  on an ST Book. A plain ST has no cookie jar at all (TOS 1.04); that reads 0
  and is correctly not a Mega STe.

Verified in Hatari on all three machines, which is the specificity control that
matters for a flag like this: --machine megaste logs "Mega STe -> 16 MHz +
cache" and reaches the menu with blitter = 1; --machine ste and --machine st do
NOT log it and still reach the menu. The message lands on the CONSOLE, not
DBG.LOG — it fires before the backend takes the screen.

020 and Amiga builds unaffected (the Amiga backend does not define these and
the calls are #ifndef FRUA_AMIGA). 456 tests pass.

events.title: fix(crt): choisir la version GLSL à l'exécution (150→140→130) — débloque le Pi
events.message:
fix(crt): choisir la version GLSL à l'exécution (150→140→130) — débloque le Pi

Le préambule « #version 150 » était codé en dur : sur le V3D des Raspberry Pi
(Mesa), qui plafonne à GLSL 1.40, activer les effets CRT échouait avec
« GLSL 1.50 is not supported ». Le corps des shaders n'utilise pourtant que des
constructions GLSL 1.30 (in/out, texture(), fwidth()).

Le dialecte est désormais déduit de GL_SHADING_LANGUAGE_VERSION puis essayé en
cascade 150 → 140 → 130 (300 es sur contexte GLES natif) : un pilote peut
annoncer une version et la refuser dans ce contexte, seule la compilation réelle
tranche. Les tentatives de repli sont silencieuses et errorOut est vidé en cas
de succès, sinon l'UI afficherait « shader indisponible » alors que tout marche.
Ajoute une ligne de diagnostic « [CRT] GLSL 140 (pilote : 1.40) ».

Validé sous Mesa llvmpipe à version forcée : 4.60→150, 1.40→140 (cas Pi),
1.30→130, pile prête et image rendue dans les trois cas. Pas encore rejoué sur

events.title: tools: a bisect harness for the ST/STe planar path
events.message:
tools: a bisect harness for the ST/STe planar path

Builds any SHA as the SHIPPED ST/STe planar build, drives it to the Skull Crag
caravan event, saves the frame and scores its viewport against two exact
references. Written to bisect the wrong-event-picture bug; kept because the
ST planar path has no other end-to-end regression handle.

Three traps are baked in, each of which cost a run to find:

  -DFRUA_PLANAR is passed EXPLICITLY. It only became the CPU68K=68000 default
  on 0be209c9 (26 Jul), but release-ste passed it by hand before that, so a
  bare `make CPU68K=68000` silently builds the CHUNKY path on the older half
  of the window — two different programs under one name. That produced one
  wrong conclusion before it was caught.

  It does NOT use driver.sh beginplay. That sequence assumes the Hall's letter
  accelerators ACTIVATE an item; on builds before ~27 Jul they only HIGHLIGHT
  it, so the party is never seated and the run ends in the Hall scoring as
  neither good nor bad. The extra Return here is harmless on newer builds.

  `shots` is called with gap=5, not the 0.4 s default. This screen loads a
  picture as it opens and one quiet interval mid-load reads as settled (#106) —
  that is what produced a black viewport once already.

Scoring is exact-match against both references rather than a threshold, and it
prints both distances so the caller can see "matched neither", which is what a
run that fell short of the event looks like. Do not read equal-ish distances as
a verdict; open the PNG.

events.title: fix(asm): eight encoder defects found by diffing third-party sources (#38)
events.message:
fix(asm): eight encoder defects found by diffing third-party sources (#38)

Assembling four unmodified Amiga source repositories against
vasmm68k_mot found eight defects that every existing test passed.
Each is pinned in the new tests/reference_bytes.rs as a measured byte
string rather than a roundtrip: a roundtrip only proves the encoder
and decoder agree with each other, and all eight survive one.

Rejected outright, though ordinary in real sources:

- ADD/SUB/CMP with An as destination. The ADDA/SUBA/CMPA encoders
  existed but were reachable only through the explicit mnemonic; the
  dispatcher excluded AddrReg saying it was "handled by enc_add
  itself", which enc_add did not do.
- A MOVEM range crossing the bank boundary (`d0-a6`). The numbering is
  flat over D0..D7,A0..A7, so requiring both ends in one bank was wrong.
- A one-register MOVEM (`movem.l a1,-(sp)`). With no `/` or `-`, `a1`
  is recognised as an ordinary register operand and never reaches the
  list parser; it is still a register list of length one.
- A column-1 label before an instruction without a colon
  (`.loop  move.l ...`), the ordinary Amiga loop idiom — 14 files.
- `NAME = expr`, the assignment spelling of EQU.
- The condition aliases HS/LO (= CC/CS), missing from Bcc/DBcc/Scc/
  TRAPcc and from is_branch_mnemonic, so they were not even relaxed.

Silently mis-assembled, which is worse:

- `beq end` ended the assembly. split_line read "label beq, directive
  end", because directive names are also label names. No error, just a
  truncated program. Fixed via the new tokens::is_mnemonic, driven by
  opcode_patterns() plus expanded condition codes — that table spells
  the conditional families as placeholders, so `bne` appears in it
  nowhere literally.
- A PC-relative MOVE destination encoded quietly. enc_move passed ALL
  for its destination instead of DATA_ALT | AREG. PC-relative modes are
  not alterable on any 68k, not just pre-68020, so there is nothing to
  write back to; CLR and ADD were already strict, only MOVE was not.

ALIGN implemented CNOP's semantics under ALIGN's name. Its argument is
a bit count, so `ALIGN 4` reaches a 16-byte boundary rather than a
4-byte one, and padding is zero bytes — $4E71 belongs to CNOP. The
second operand is accepted and ignored: it is not a fill value, which
is why `align 0,4` is the no-op the Shrinkler headers rely on. Verified
across every bit count and starting offset (77 cases).

Assembler::assemble_bytes disagreed with the CLI on any source with
byte data: it concatenated whole words and ignored byte_len, inserting
a pad after every odd-length item. It now goes through the same
output::generate_binary_to path the CLI uses.

Four whole-program tests come with this, each byte-identical to the
reference so the addresses in their header comments are measured:
recursion with a link/unlk frame, a word-offset table beside a branch
table, inline arguments after a jsr, and self-modifying code. Three
record correct behaviour. The fourth records a limit honestly — inline
arguments are read as code, and without modelling a callee that
advances its own return address those bytes are indistinguishable from
instructions. A stricter data heuristic is not the fix.

Byte parity against the reference: amiga_examples 5 -> 24/147,
assembly-m68k 12 -> 20/34, and no mismatches anywhere in the corpus.
743 tests pass.

fix(cpu): dispatcher les événements échus AU point d'IACK (≙ CycInt_Process)

Dernière trouvaille ouverte du bug hunt 10ᵉ passe. En mode bloc, les SYNC de
l'entrée d'exception ne dispatchent rien : un timer dont l'échéance tombait
dans la fenêtre « frontière d'instruction → IACK » (~10-26 cyc) n'avait pas
posé son bit IPR quand Mfp::iack élisait le vecteur — l'élection ne regarde
que les IPR déjà posés. Hatari appelle CycInt_Process() + MFP_UpdateIRQ_All
juste avant la séquence d'IACK, dans les DEUX branches (newcpu.c:2938-2946
MFP, :2998-3003 vidéo).

MESURÉ (NEOST_IACK_DISP=1, banc SHO in-game) : un événement est réellement
échu à 5,7-7 % des IACK — deux ordres de grandeur au-dessus de l'estimation
« ~26/40106 » du rapport de chasse (qui ne comptait que le Timer C).

⚠ PIÈGE attrapé par le banc avant commit : le syncTo doit être précédé du
REBASE DU QUANTUM (Cpu68k::rebaseQuantumAndSync), exactement comme le saut
d'attente STOP — sinon le temps couru depuis le début du quantum est facturé
une DEUXIÈME fois par le runTo(now+ran) de Machine et tout le raster glisse
de ~16 cyc (mesuré sans rebase : écritures palette {104..128} → {120..156},
réveil STOP {68,72,76} → {80..96}). Troisième incident de cette classe :
tout dispatch déclenché depuis un hook Moira doit rebaser.

Gate NEOST_IACK_SYNC (défaut ON) + diag NEOST_IACK_DISP.

Validation : banc SHO inchangé vs oracle (±0,1 pt, réveil STOP 40/40/20),
A/B du gate = comportement bien modifié (un handler démarre une ligne plus
tôt), run_all --tier full VERT, --save-state-test déterministe.

events.title: tools: an `st` capture target, and the TOS matrix it uncovered
events.message:
tools: an `st` capture target, and the TOS matrix it uncovered

capture_demo.sh had targets for falcon/tt/ste/aga/ecs but none for a plain ST,
so --machine st (TOS 1.04) had no caller anywhere in the project and the ST
arm of the ST/STe build had never actually been booted. Add the target, plus
an EXTRA_HATARI hook so it can name its own ROM.

It pins TOS 2.06 rather than the 1.04 the harness would pick, and the comment
says why at length: 2.06 is a real and widely fitted ST upgrade, but it is
also the ROM that dodges the Mxalloc bug fixed in the previous commit, and a
clean `st` capture must not be misread as evidence that a stock ST is fine.

docs/tos-compatibility.md records the GEMDOS-version table the bug turned on,
the five verified machine/ROM boots, the two ROM traps that each cost a run
(TOS 1.62 is STE-only and Hatari silently switches machines for it; TOS 1.04
does support GEMDOS HD emulation), the plain-ST DMA-sound gap, and the fact
that FRUA_MEM defaults to 14 MB — a size no real ST or STe can have.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: platform: Mxalloc is TOS 2.01+, and its absence bus-errors the ST
events.message:
platform: Mxalloc is TOS 2.01+, and its absence bus-errors the ST

The Atari backends allocated every screen, shadow and DMA-sound buffer with
Mxalloc(size, 0). Mxalloc is GEMDOS 0x44, "available from GEMDOS version 0.19"
— and the Compendium's Sversion table pins 0.19 at TOS 2.01. So the call is
MISSING on every plain-ST ROM (1.00/1.02/1.04, GEMDOS 0.13/0.15) and on TOS
1.62 (0.17), the ROM most STes actually shipped with.

Missing is not safe. An unimplemented GEMDOS opcode returns EINVFN (-32), not
NULL, so the `== NULL` guard at each call site waved it through and st_init
then memset through 0xFFFFFFE0. Observed: frua on an emulated ST with TOS 1.04
takes a double bus error immediately after the backend logs its name, at 4 MB
and 14 MB alike.

Ruled the harness out before blaming the engine. The same TOS 1.04, same
emulated ST, same GEMDOS mount, no frua.prg: boots to the GEM desktop with a
HARD DISK icon and zero bus errors — so 1.04 does support GEMDOS emulation.
The same ST hardware with TOS 2.06 reaches the main menu. The ROM was the only
variable, which is why our whole ST/STe matrix never saw this: it has always
run TOS 2.06 (ste) and would have run 1.04 only through a target that had no
caller.

Route every site through a new plat_stram_alloc(), which picks Malloc below
GEMDOS 0.19 and collapses GEMDOS error codes to NULL so the existing NULL
checks become correct. Falling back loses nothing, provably rather than
hopefully: alternative RAM is reached through Maddalt, which is ALSO 0.19-only,
so a system without Mxalloc has no non-ST RAM for Mxalloc(size, 0) to have been
avoiding. TT and Falcon are 0.19 and 0.30 and keep the Mxalloc path.

Verified after: plain ST + TOS 1.04 reaches "menu: modal up" with
"ste: blitter = 0"; STe + TOS 1.62 reaches it with "blitter = 1"; the 020
Falcon build still smoke-boots to the menu. Sound still reports "init failed
(continuing silent)" on a plain ST — that is the absent DMA sound hardware,
tracked separately, not this.

events.title: docs: #90 closed — the ST/STe and Amiga ECS play loops are measured, and equal
events.message:
docs: #90 closed — the ST/STe and Amiga ECS play loops are measured, and equal

Twelve walk actions on WALKTEST.DSN, 24 redraw samples per target, same
jt312 RECT path, party seated, 60 Hz ticks on both.

  Atari STE 8 MHz (4 planes, 16 col): render 17 + present 18 = 35 ticks
  Amiga ECS 7 MHz (5 planes, 32 col): render 11 + present 22 = 34 ticks

~1.17 s and ~1.13 s per walk action. They are the same speed, which is not what
I expected — a slower CPU pushing more bitplanes should have been worse. The
split is what differs: ECS renders faster and presents slower.

Present is 51% (STE) / 65% (ECS) of a redraw, and both issue TWO redraws per
action, so that is where the next work belongs rather than in the renderer.

Records the two traps that cost time: the play screen animates, so a
settle-detector never fires and reports its poll limit as the step time; and
fast-forward is valid for tick measurements but not wall-clock ones.

events.title: Droid sprites are hires, not multicolour
events.message:
Droid sprites are hires, not multicolour

KC spotted it playing the real game in VICE: every droid is a single
colour plus transparency. The code agrees and is unambiguous:

  $190C  dMd0_droid, allocating a slot   LDA #0   / STA SpriteMC
  $187F  dMd1_bullet                     LDA #0   / STA SpriteMC
  $1BE8  ExplodeSprite                   LDA #$FF / STA SpriteMC

so only explosions are multicolour, and $190E-$1912 clear SpriteXExp and
SpriteYExp too, so there is no doubling in either direction.

A hires sprite is 3 bytes of 8 single-bit pixels - 24 pixels at the C64's
full 320-wide resolution. MODE 1 is also 320 wide, so it is a straight
1:1: 24 source pixels to 24 destination pixels, 4 per MODE 1 byte.

Worth recording WHY this survived a build, a run and a screenshot. Read
as multicolour, the same three bytes give 12 double-width pixels doubled
to 24 - the same WIDTH and the same BYTE COUNT. Nothing downstream could
catch it: the data fitted identically, every assert passed, the shifted
copy and the derived mask both still worked, and the result looked like a
droid. Only comparing against the actual game could find it.

The mask derivation is unaffected - a pixel is still transparent exactly
when both of its bits are clear - so no blitter change is needed and
drSprData stays 1743 bytes.

Colour is now DROID_COLOUR, one constant. It is logical 1: the C64 gives
enemy droids colour 0, black, but MODE 1's four logical colours belong to
the deck, and logical 1 is white on all sixteen decks whereas logical 2 is
black on fourteen and green on the other two. Per-type colour from
DColorTheme_t is a question for the combat layer.

events.title: perf: the step profiler was timing its own logger
events.message:
perf: the step profiler was timing its own logger

First measurement of the ST/STe PLAY LOOP (docs/TODO.md #4, open since the
"~47% of rows convert" figure was shown to be a BOOT number). It needed the
instrument fixed first.

`pdpf l67ca tk` sampled TickCount() at LOG time — after three dbg_log_num
calls, each an Fopen + Fseek + 3x Fwrite + Fclose through GEMDOS. It was
timing the logger. The giveaway was the value itself: 222 ticks on 40 of 43
samples (223 on the other three), because three open/write/close cycles are far
more deterministic than the work they stood in for. It also put one bracket at
3.7 s inside a step the wall clock timed at 2.4 s, which is what exposed it.
Now differenced from a stamp taken before the block, like every other bracket.

The deeper flaw was structural: J76_T/L67_T log INLINE, so any outer bracket
spanning them measures their logging too. The per-piece breakdown is now opt-in
behind -DFRUA_STEPPROF_DEEP; plain -DFRUA_STEPPROF gives clean outer totals.

With that, 24 clean samples from a 12-action walk on an 8 MHz STE (cycle-exact
Hatari, WALKTEST.DSN, ticks are 60 Hz: _hz_200 * 3/10):

    setup 0 | render 17 | present 18  = 35 ticks = 583 ms per redraw
    2 redraws per action              = ~1.2 s per walk action

Present is ~51% of a step even after the #63 work. The heavier full-recompose
path (entered via camp/menus) measured ~2.4 s per action by wall clock.

Two traps for whoever measures next: the play screen ANIMATES (torch/fire), so
"wait for two identical frames" never settles and silently reports the poll
limit as the step time; and fast-forward is safe for tick measurements (the
emulated 200 Hz timer tracks emulated time) but not for wall-clock ones.

events.title: Layer 5: two blitter optimisations, measured at 11%
events.message:
Layer 5: two blitter optimisations, measured at 11%

Skip the always-transparent rows, and hoist the strip-wrap test out
of the row loop.

Rows 5, 14 and 20 are transparent for EVERY droid - the C64's
BuildDroidSprite and AnimateDroids simply never write them, so the
exporter points all three at the one blank row. A row that writes
nothing needs no background saved and none restored, so both passes
skip it: 14% of the rows for the price of one table lookup on the
other 18.

The wrap test was a JSR and ~27 cycles, 42 times a sprite, to answer a
question that depends only on where the sprite starts. The walk
advances at most 3 row-crossings, so if bufp + 3*ROW_BYTES + SPR_SPAN
clears SPR_WRAPLIM no row can straddle the end of the strip and every
row takes the fast path blind. True about 80% of the time; the rest
fall back to the per-row test.

Measured by A/B over 25 frames of full-speed diagonal with 7 sprites,
which is the worst case:

    before   22 px / 25 frames   3.98 frames/loop   ~19,850 cyc/sprite
    after    24 px / 25 frames   3.65 frames/loop   ~17,640 cyc/sprite

That is ~2,200 cycles a sprite, against ~1,900-2,400 predicted by the
cost model, so the model can be trusted for what is left.

Note this also corrects the figure in the previous session's notes.
14,500 came from a 10-frame sample whose +-1 px resolution is +-9%;
the 25-frame samples put the real baseline at ~19,850.

events.title: amiga: centre the AGA display window on PAL
events.message:
amiga: centre the AGA display window on PAL

First real-hardware report from the Amiga side (A1200 + Icedrake, AGA backend
on SAGA): "it also shifted the screen to the top of the monitor (might be the
fault of my monitor though)". It is not the monitor. DIWSTRT 0x2C81 /
DIWSTOP 0xF4C1 are the NTSC numbers — 200 lines from V=44 fills a 262-line
NTSC frame, but PAL has 312, so the picture sits against the top with a fat
border underneath. This file's own header already admitted it as a bring-up
simplification ("on PAL the 200 lines sit in a 256-line frame's top").

A PAL display is 256 lines from V=0x2C, so centre 200 inside it: +28 lines.
DIWSTOP's VSTOP is 8 bits with V8 implied as the complement of bit 7, so
244+28 = 272 encodes as 0x10. Safe to move — the palette is set in the copper
prologue and the list carries no line-locked WAITs, so nothing is pinned to a
scanline.

Detected at runtime from GfxBase->DisplayFlags, and logged, so a DBG.LOG says
which branch ran. Verified in amiberry (PAL by default): the log line appears
and the borders go from ~50 above / ~143 below to 102 / 91.

events.title: Layer 5 step 3a: generalise the blitter from one sprite to a pool
events.message:
Layer 5 step 3a: generalise the blitter from one sprite to a pool

sprite.asm now draws any of SPR_SLOTS sprites rather than just the
player. Slot 0 is the player; 1-6 are the droid pool, which is the
C64's arrangement too - one hardware sprite for the player and a pool
of six for everything else - so the same "no free slot" cases arise.

Per-slot state becomes arrays and the background save areas are a page
apart rather than packed into 147 bytes. A slot's save base then
differs only in its high byte, so retargeting the blit's seven
absolute addresses is seven pokes; packed bases would need a 16-bit
multiply per slot and a slower inner loop. That costs 763 bytes out of
the 5.8K step 1 released.

Restore walks the slots backwards and draw walks forwards, so where
two sprites overlap the one drawn last is restored first and the
background comes back in the order it was covered. All slots restore
before any slot draws, for the same reason.

CULLED, NOT CLIPPED for now: a sprite whose columns or scanlines do
not all fall inside the play area is skipped, so droids will pop in
and out a sprite's width from the edge. Clipping needs the slow path
taught a column and row range; deliberate for this step so the fast
path stays exactly as fast while the per-sprite cost is measured.

The cull limit also earns its keep elsewhere: with sprY <= 99 and
line <= 7 the last scanline is at most 126, one short of the strip, so
a sprite can never wrap the row 15/0 boundary and collide with the
scroll redraws.

The 2 px shifted artwork is no longer built into the gap below the
play buffer - at 1743 bytes for 24 types it does not fit. It is built
at startup directly into spare sideways RAM instead. Shipping it
pre-shifted was tried and reverted: PARADAT is staged in main RAM at
&3000 before being copied into the bank, and the extra 1743 bytes
pushed that staging area into the play buffer at &5800.

export_player.py is superseded by export_droids.py and is deleted, as
is its generated src/data/player.asm. Type 0's rows were verified
byte-identical to the old ones before removing them.

Verified in jsbeeb: the player renders and animates as before, moves
and scrolls without corruption on the shifted path, and the
runtime-built shift table at &A800 matches the Python reference byte
for byte (row 2: 00 03 F3 FF 0C 00 00 -> 00 00 3C FF CF 00 00).

events.title: Layer 5 step 2: export droid sprites, waypoints and type tables
events.message:
Layer 5 step 2: export droid sprites, waypoints and type tables

New tools/export_droids.py emits src/data/droids.asm. It supersedes
export_player.py: the player is droid type 0, so one table serves every
droid including him. Verified rather than assumed - type 0's rotor rows,
digit rows and blank row come out byte-identical to the existing
player.asm. The old files stay until sprite.asm is generalised in step 3.

Sprites: the rotor is identical for every droid and only the number
differs, so rows are shared - 5 rotor rows x 8 phases, 2 alternating end
rows x 8 phases, 8 digit rows x 24 types, one blank = 249 rows of 7
bytes. That needs two lookups, not one: a single table indexed by both
type and phase would be 24 x 8 x 21 entries. drOfs[] covers the rows
that depend on the phase, drDigit[type] the rows that depend on the type.

Waypoints: 239 records over 16 decks, 3 bytes each - char X, char Y and
a bitmask of permitted exits. Two asserts earn their place: every deck
has at least one waypoint, and each deck's records are sorted by Y,
which FindWaypoint relies on to bail out early.

Speeds are exported as both the raw C64 per-iteration value and an 8.8
per-frame conversion. Enemy droids use DSpeed_t directly - 1/2/4/8 px
per iteration, so 0.5/1/2/4 per frame - and only the player chains it
through PlayerSpeed_t.

Waypoint 0 is reserved for the player's per-deck spawn: InitDeckDroids
starts placing droids at waypoint 1 and never touches 0. Confirmed that
all 14 of deck 1's waypoints resolve through MapChar to floor, so
waypoint coordinates really are in our tile map's char space - worth
checking, since deckX/deckY in levels.asm are side-view positions
rather than map extents.

FillPanel moves out of SetupScreen to after PageDataIn: the staging area
for PARADAT now reaches past &4800 and would wipe the panel. Nothing is
displaying that early, since the IRQ is installed later.

Verified in jsbeeb: wpCount at &9FA6 and deck 0's records at &9FD6 match
the C64 byte for byte, and the deck still renders with its panel intact.

events.title: Layer 5 step 1: move PARADAT into sideways RAM
events.message:
Layer 5 step 1: move PARADAT into sideways RAM

Frees &3000-&4707 (5.8K), which Layer 5 needs for droid state and
per-slot background save buffers. Only 243 bytes were free below the
tile map.

PARADAT is assembled at &8000 so its labels resolve to their addresses
in the bank, but carries a catalogue load address of &3000 and is
copied up by PageDataIn. It cannot be *LOADed into the bank directly:
while the filing system is working the MOS has DFS paged in at &8000,
so the bytes would land in the ROM socket and be discarded.

The bank stays selected for the whole run, because MapChar reads
tiledefs and DrawHalf reads charRemap every frame. That displaces
BASIC, which we never return to, not DFS, which is in its own socket
and which the MOS pages in and back out around each of its own calls.

Banks 4 and 5 rather than 0 and 1: a Master 128's sideways RAM is
banks 4-7, so the same numbers work on both machines. A Model B SWRAM
board is jumpered to whatever you like, so nothing is lost. Probing at
boot is the eventual answer and is noted in the source.

ROMSEL and ROMSHAD are both written everywhere. The MOS restores
ROMSEL from its copy at &F4 after a service call, so writing one
without the other leaves them disagreeing and the next OS call pages
something unexpected back in.

Verified in jsbeeb rather than assumed: banks 0-7 are RAM in
B-DFS1.2; at runtime &F4 reads 4; tiledefs at &8800 is byte-identical
to the source; and changing deck still works, which exercises
BuildCharset, SetPalette and BuildLevel all reading from the bank.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 21b — the PSG chain runs, and the RNG meets the bus
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 21b — the PSG chain runs, and the RNG meets the bus

Reconstruction:
- src/sound.c: snd_psg_silence ($17f30, the seeded-read model's first
  consumer: select 7 -> READ -> ori #$3f preserving bits 6-7 -> write,
  volumes zeroed — a candidate ignoring the read-back is the kit's own
  mutant class, caught by the event ledger), snd_stop, snd_stop_all_sfx
  (plates corrected: the shadow block, not the mix; tail jumps, not
  falls; SR save/restore window reproduced).
- src/actor.c: actor_defeat_and_score ($6bb8 — 164 real bytes, the F
  record folded its own score table; TWENTY-NINE control-flow sites,
  24 of them the defeated-bit test after every damage path, so the
  $6cdc respawn continuation is HOT, not residue). First game-logic
  differential running the sound module's PSG writes on both sides.
- src/rng.c (NEW): rng_next (counters CLEARED AT EQUALITY, not modulo
  — plate corrected; the degenerate-entropy false green stated and
  measured: ^ vs + irreducible at entropy 0) + stage_random_kind8
  (BCD tens-carry ladder, WORD-half row, the $e382 kind table).
- THE REVIEW'S MEASURED FIND: the table index guard missed the 68000's
  24-BIT BUS WRAP — d2 bits >= 2^24 alias back into the image on the
  oracle side while the unmasked C served 0 (probed RED). Fixed with
  WB_BUS_ADDR_MASK (scraped, so the differential case that crosses the
  bus pins shim.c's own copy) — and the FIX's first form was itself
  under-pinned: a 23-bit mask survived until a width-discriminating
  case at $00800000 landed. blit.c's off-image idiom queued for the
  same audit.
- Verified 155 -> 161 fns / 18,102 B (70.2 %); suite 3052 (the audio
  battery's 13 now inside the count — accounting corrected). Sweep 51
  mutants, 50 caught, 1 irreducible; + 4 review re-verifications.
  THIRD SWEEP LIE recorded in the README recipe: a suite that fails to
  COLLECT reports every mutant caught — re-green before sweeping.

Review gate (3 consolidated angles, 10 findings, fixed): the a32
word-read and BCD-signedness mutation survivors pinned (byte/unsigned
mutants now redden single named cases); RUNNER_SENTINEL_INSN and
PSG_SELECT/PSG_DATA hoisted (the stale concurrent-session deferral
retired by git evidence); the X-flag refusal enforced at the seeding
site; DEFEAT_INSN_CAP's derivation corrected (+28 stub's four); the
eleven-vs-fourteen tail contradiction and the transcribed transfer
offset replaced by the search-the-bytes pattern; rng_counter_mod*
renamed (the disproved reading was one line below its own correction);
$e1c8's # ctx retired with a full plate; psg_port_write registered as
the first reconstruction that cannot link on-target yet.

Kit friction filed from Phase 6's first consumer: leaf.run psg_seed
threading (done here), the runner sentinel, the entry latch.

GEMDOS — hdEmuDir restait LEXICAL (makeAbsoluteName seul) alors que tout `host`
produit par clampToSandbox est physicalCanon() (realpath, liens résolus). Sur un
montage dont le chemin traverse un lien symbolique (macOS /tmp→/private/tmp, ~ ou
/var symlinkés sous Linux), les deux vivaient dans des espaces de noms distincts :
- gemChDir comparait host canonique vs hdEmuDir brut → Dsetpath échouait TOUJOURS
  en EPTHNF (« Impossible de définir le dossier par défaut »), un installeur qui
  chdir avant d'écrire déversait ses fichiers à la racine ;
- gemSFirst("C:\") calculait rootLen sur la longueur brute → split au mauvais
  séparateur → scan du dossier PARENT du bac à sable (franchissement de frontière).
Fix racine : canonicaliser physiquement hdEmuDir une fois au montage (initDrives,
dossier confirmé existant) → gemChDir/gemSFirst/gemDgetpath/createHostFileName
partagent l'espace de noms canonique. Idempotent, montage normal inchangé.

Save-state — 3 champs chargés sans borne (trous résiduels de la campagne de
durcissement, .state forgé à CRC valide) :
- Shifter::glueLineStart_ : restauré sans check de taille, indexé sans garde de
  lecture dans advanceGlueLive (glueLineStart_[wl], Shifter.cpp:454/461/493) →
  lecture hors-tas d'un int64_t. Garde d'invariant == glueLines_.size() ajoutée.
- Machine::curLineLen_ : longueur de ligne en cycles, consommée par advanceLine
  (lineCarry_ += cpl_ - curLineLen_) → forgée absurde, désancre lineCarry_ APRÈS
  son propre check → planification HBL aberrante. Bornée ]0,4096] comme cpl_/lpf_.
- Cpu68k::g_cpuMul : sélecteur 8/16 MHz multipliant l'horloge Moira
  (addBusWaitCycles : n * g_cpuMul) → forgé énorme = bond d'horloge. Validé ∈ {1,2}.

Vérifiés FIDÈLES sans régression (2 faux positifs écartés) : Bus/MMIO whitelist,
Blitter, FPU, ACIA/SCC série.

events.title: feat(disasm): name AmigaOS library calls (#34)
events.message:
feat(disasm): name AmigaOS library calls (#34)

* fix(hunk): accept executables whose BSS is larger than the file

The parser bounded the total declared hunk size by the file size, to
stop a crafted header from driving a huge allocation. But a BSS hunk
declares its size in the header and contributes *no* bytes to the file
— that is its entire purpose — so real executables are routinely larger
in memory than on disk, and those were rejected outright.

Two of four real Amiga executables on hand could not be read at all:

  bm68k_test   declares 4340 bytes across three hunks in a 3804-byte file
  a-bootes     declares 49848 bytes in a 15692-byte file

Both now load. Bound by a generous multiple of the file size instead,
which still refuses the crafted headers the check exists for — the
existing rejects_hunk_size_exceeding_file_length test still passes
unchanged.

This affects every tool in the repo that reads Hunk files, not just the
disassembler.

Found while testing an abstract-execution tracer against real
executables; the tracer itself is a separate question and is not in
this commit.

713 tests pass (was 712); clippy, fmt and MSRV 1.88 clean.

* feat(disasm): name AmigaOS library calls

`jsr -$1e(a6)` is the AmigaOS calling convention: a negative offset
against a library base selects an entry in the jump table below it. The
offsets are a documented ABI, so they can be named.

This is the gap worth closing. Counting computed jumps across four real
hunk executables, `jsr -$xx(a6)` outnumbers `jsr (an)` roughly ten to
one (44/7/48/56 against 3/3/3/8). Those targets live inside the
library, outside the image, so nothing — not tracing, not emulation —
recovers code for them. Naming them recovers the meaning, which is what
a reader is after, and costs a table.

Adds `m68k-core::amiga_lvo` with exec/dos/graphics/intuition, and
annotates matching calls as a trailing comment. The comment is a
separate field on `DisassembledLine`, not appended to `text`, so the
instruction text stays exactly what the assembler accepts.

**The offset alone is ambiguous** — `-$1e` is exec/Supervisor but
dos/Input — so a blanket setting mislabels calls. My first attempt did
exactly that: `--lvo dos` called `jsr -$126(a6)` "FGetC" where the
preceding `movea.l $4.w,a6` makes it exec/FindTask. Confident wrong
names are worse than none.

So the library is tracked where the code says it outright: `movea.l
$4.w,a6` is ExecBase by definition and without exception. Any other
load into a6 clears it rather than guessing, and the tracked value is
reset at each label, since a jump into an address arrives with whatever
the caller had. `--lvo LIBRARY` supplies an answer for the stretches
this cannot determine, and the tracked base wins over it where both
apply.

Automatically named, with no flag at all:

  test_hello    4 of 44    bm68k_test   1 of 7
  a-bootes      7 of 48    ira_68k     10 of 56

  00000018:  movea.l $00000004.w, a6
  00000022:  jsr     -$126(a6)      ; FindTask
  0000002e:  jsr     -$228(a6)      ; OpenLibrary

`--lvo dos` takes test_hello from 4 to 29, for a reader who knows what
the program keeps in a6.

722 tests pass (was 712), 10 new; clippy, fmt and MSRV 1.88 clean.

events.message:
fix(shifter/dmasound): save-state OOB scroll STE + 3 écarts son/vidéo vs Hatari

Suite du bug hunt (agents « CPU/MFP/reset » et « Ikbd/DmaSound/YM/Shifter »).
Les axes MFP_Reset_All, instruction RESET, STOP/liveNow et double-faute de bus
ont été vérifiés fidèles sans régression ; Ikbd et YM2149 sont des ports 1:1.
Quatre écarts nets corrigés :

- Shifter save-state : hwScrollCount / newHwScrollCount_ étaient les deux seuls
  champs oubliés par la campagne de durcissement. Le scroll fin STE est un
  compteur 4 bits (chemin MMIO masqué & 0x0F) qui sert d'OFFSET de lecture
  idx[c + hwScrollCount] dans renderLine (tampon de pile de 660 o). Un .state
  forgé à CRC valide posant hwScrollCount=255 → lecture hors pile de ~234 o
  (fuite d'info / crash). Gardes ar.check(< 16) et (>= -1 && < 16) ajoutées.
  MOYENNE (primitive de lecture).

- DmaSound liveCounter ($FF8909/0B/0D) : appelait fifoRefill() APRÈS updateDac,
  alors que DmaSnd_GetFrameCount (dmaSnd.c:748) n'appelle QUE Sound_Update. Le
  refill se fait au HBL (onHbl) ou à vide (fifoPull). Ce refill de trop re-topait
  curAddr_ à chaque lecture → un poll serré du compteur voyait l'adresse de fetch
  avancer en continu au lieu de sauter par paquets au HBL comme le vrai STE.

- DmaSound startNewFrame : remettait phase_/haveCur_ (rééchantillonnage du chemin
  mono mix()) à CHAQUE relatch repeat. DmaSnd_StartNewFrame ne touche pas cet état
  (≙ DmaInitSample), remis au SEUL front PLAY 0→1. Déplacé dans write8 case 0x01,
  à côté de dacRem_=0 — supprime un click/dérive d'un octet par boucle de sample.

- Shifter videoCounter : l'extrapolation par-ligne créditait extra (line-offset STE
  + prefetch scroll) à TOUTES les lignes, y compris NO_DE, alors que le commit
  endVideoLine le conditionne à bpl>0 (≙ video.c:4213). Divergence des deux chemins
  → le compteur reculait entre deux lectures $FF8205/07/09 encadrant un HBL.
  Extrapolation alignée sur le commit.

events.title: fix(bus/scheduler): audit du commit perf — OOB ROM en read16 + 3 pièges d'invariants
events.message:
fix(bus/scheduler): audit du commit perf — OOB ROM en read16 + 3 pièges d'invariants

Chasse aux bugs façon ingénieur émulation, ciblée sur le commit de
performance 5c2088e (chemins chauds inlinés + caches). Quatre correctifs,
tous à sortie émulée inchangée (selftests 100 %, boots ST/STE/MegaSTE
pixel-identiques, save-state déterministe OK).

- read16 chemin rapide ROM : `off + 1 < rom.size()` débordait à
  `addr == romBase-1` (off = 0xFFFFFFFF → off+1 = 0), rendant
  `0 < rom.size()` vrai et lisant rom[0xFFFFFFFF] — lecture hôte hors
  bornes ~4 Go au-delà du tampon. Atteignable par un programme invité :
  GemdosHd::trap lit read16 à une adresse prise dans la USP (A7 posée à
  $DFFFFF sous un TOS 256 Ko, puis trap #1). read8 était immunisé (une
  seule comparaison) ; c'est bien l'addition qui wrappait. Garde
  `off < rom.size()` ajoutée avant l'addition. read32/write* passent par
  read16/write8 déjà sûrs.

- Cache de décodage MMU : la revalidation ne comparait que (config, taille
  RAM), alors que rebuildMmuCache dépend AUSSI de `machine` (règle banque 1
  ST/Mega ST vs STE, Bus.cpp:245). Une bascule ST↔STE à chaud
  (Machine::reconfigure) sans changement de conf/RAM laissait le cache
  rance. Latent (les limites ST/STE coïncident sur les tailles standard),
  mais on ne laisse pas le piège armé : `machine` ajouté à la clé.

- Scheduler::schedule(s, kInactive) corrompait nextDue_ : `atCycle < nextDue_`
  était vrai (-1 < tout) et posait nextDue_ = kInactive alors que d'autres
  sources restaient armées → assert de nextDue() en debug, dispatch gelé en
  mode sync. Traité comme un cancel, et la préemption de timeslice ne se
  déclenche plus sur -1. Aucun appelant actuel ne le fait, mais le nouveau
  code tient ce cache EXACT et en dépend.

- Scheduler::serialize : nextDue_ est purement dérivé de due_ ; on le
  recalcule au chargement (comme armed_) au lieu de faire confiance à la
  valeur sérialisée — un état sauvé par un build antérieur (cache minorant)
  ou forgé faisait avorter nextDue() en debug.

events.title: test: whole-program corpus, and the two disassembler defects it found (#31)
events.message:
test: whole-program corpus, and the two disassembler defects it found (#31)

* test: add a whole-program corpus, and two findings from it

The existing suites check instruction *forms* — assemble one
instruction, decode it, reassemble it. A single instruction has no
surroundings, so nothing there can tell whether the disassembler
separates a jump table from arithmetic, or a copyright string from
code. That is where every real defect in this area has been.

Adds five small programs under tests/programs/ whose source we control,
so the truth of every byte is known: which addresses are instructions,
which are data, what each pointer points at. ROM measurements can never
establish that — on a ROM nobody knows which answer is right.

  jump_table.s            indexed dispatch, a compiled `switch`
  strings_between_code.s  NUL-terminated text between routines
  pc_relative_data.s      lea table(pc),a0 — a target that names data
  nested_loops.s          pure code, no data: the control case
  mixed_data_code.s       byte/word/long data interleaved with code

Two defects fell out immediately, both invisible in ROM work:

**A 3-entry jump table is not recognized.** MIN_POINTER_TABLE requires
four consecutive in-image pointers; three is an entirely ordinary
`switch` size. jump_table.s renders its table as `ori.b #$0e,d0`.
Lowering the threshold to 3 moves Kickstart 1.3 from 10 tables / 87
targets to 24 / 129 — whether those extra ones are real cannot be
decided on a ROM, but can be decided here.

**Text detection can swallow real code.** In pc_relative_data.s the
bytes `4e75 4440 4e75` are `rts; neg.w d0; rts` — all printable
("NuD@Nu") — and the dc.w after them supplies the NUL terminator the
heuristic requires. Two real instructions are lost. The cause is
reachability rather than the heuristic: `negate` is reached only
through the pointer table, so the walk never claims those bytes, and
unclaimed bytes are what the text test may judge. Recognizing the table
fixes this one too.

Both are recorded as tests asserting today's behaviour, so they are
reproduction cases rather than silent knowledge; each says in its
failure message to invert it once fixed. Fixes are deliberately not in
this commit — the corpus and the findings stand on their own, and
changing the thresholds needs its own measurement.

Also asserted for all five: byte-completeness, every byte in exactly
one line. That is the invariant that must hold regardless of how the
classification decisions land.

717 tests pass (was 712); clippy, fmt clean.

* fix(disasm): recognize jump tables off the longword grid, and at 3 entries

Both defects the whole-program corpus turned up, with the more serious
one being the second.

**MIN_POINTER_TABLE was 4.** A 3-way `switch` is an entirely ordinary
thing to write. Now 3.

**The scan walked a longword grid.** It read candidate pointers at
offsets 0, 4, 8, ... from the origin, so it could only ever see tables
whose distance from the origin is a multiple of four. Nothing makes
that true — a table follows whatever code happens to precede it.
tests/programs/jump_table.s puts one at origin+$1a, which was invisible
at *any* threshold. The scan now walks a word grid, stepping runs by
two slots since a pointer spans two of them.

Fixing only the threshold would have left that file still broken. It is
the kind of half-fix a ROM measurement cannot expose, because on a ROM
nobody knows which tables were missed.

Also fixes the reachable half of finding 2: clamp_to_traced cuts a
string run where proven code resumes, which can leave two bytes, and
those were emitted as `dc.b "Nu"` — swallowing the `rts` tail of a
routine. The minimum length is now re-checked after clamping.

The other half of finding 2 stands and is now asserted as such: with
only the program's own entry point, nothing proves `negate` is code,
and `4e75 4440 4e75` is a genuine NUL-terminated printable run over the
threshold. The remedy there is better reachability, not a stricter
string test, which would start losing real strings instead.

  jump_table.s   before  0000101a: ori.b #$0e, d0
                 after   0000101a: dc.l  label0     (+ labelled targets)

Kickstart 1.3 roundtrip unchanged (OK 80.7%, MISMATCH 424); byte parity
unchanged (10/10); --scan-tables recovers 348 more lines of code there.

718 tests pass (was 717); clippy, fmt clean.

events.title: Identify the source release: original/CE, not Redux
events.message:
Identify the source release: original/CE, not Redux

The listing this port is built from was documented as a disassembly of
Paradroid Redux. That was never verified, and it is wrong.

Unpacked all four C64 releases by running them under VICE and dumping RAM
at a checkpoint, then diffed them against the listing. It matches the 1985
original / 1986 Competition Edition lineage: 82.4% on the code image and
99.8% on core code at $1000-$3FFF, with "VERSION 1.0" present at $6E90.
Heavy Metal and Redux relocate everything and match at 1.2% and 2.9%.

So nothing extracted so far needs redoing, and the port is already faithful
to the original rather than to a community fork.

Original vs Competition Edition turns out to be very nearly a non-choice:
their staged code+data block differs by 8 bytes, core code is identical, and
PlayerSpeed_t/DSpeed_t are byte-for-byte the same. CE is faster because it
completes more GameLoop iterations per second, not because it moves droids
further per iteration - so on this port that dial is PLY_ITER_FRAMES.

Redux's bug list is adopted as a specification rather than as code; several
of its fixes are C64 platform bugs that cannot occur on the Beeb. Heavy Metal
is parked as a possible later tile set.

Adds tools/unpack_prg.ps1 so the unpacking is reproducible, documenting the
three runtime states a dump can land in and which regions are stable in each -
getting that wrong makes two near-identical releases look 99% different.

events.title: docs: settle the two open P3 questions (#30)
events.message:
docs: settle the two open P3 questions (#30)

Both had been carried since the July audit as "deliberately undecided".
Re-measured against vasmm68k_mot rather than trusting the old notes,
and they turn out to be different kinds of item.

**ORI.B #x,An is gone, not undecided.** The divergence disappeared with
the address-register byte rule in ea_encode.rs (PR #28): an address
register has no byte-sized access on any 68k, and the immediate family
uses DATA_ALT, which excludes AREG at every size. Re-checked
ORI/ANDI/EORI/ADDI/SUBI/CMPI against .b/.w/.l — both assemblers reject
all 18 combinations. Noted on the existing regression test.

**Zero-distance branch: keep our behaviour, deliberately.** The
fileloader.asm evidence did not reproduce — that file uses AmigaOS
symbols with no includes and fails in *both* assemblers, the reference
already at `moveq #ERROR_HANDLE_FILE_OPEN,d0`. The underlying question
is real though:

  bra.s to next insn   ref: warns, substitutes lea (a6),a6 (2 bytes)
                       us:  6000 0000 word form (4 bytes)
  bsr.s to next insn   ref: error 2029, rejected
                       us:  accepted
  dbra                 identical

The byte form is impossible here — disp==0 is the word-form marker
byte. Our word form branches to pc_after_opword+0, i.e. the following
instruction, which is correct (verified by roundtrip). Keeping it emits
the instruction the source asked for instead of substituting a
different one, at a cost of two bytes. For BSR ours is the better
answer outright: a zero-distance BSR is not a no-op, it pushes the
return address, which can be intentional.

Documented at enc_bcc/enc_bsr and pinned by two new tests so neither
can drift back silently.

712 tests pass (was 710). Byte parity unchanged (10/10 and 12/16 with
the same 4 REF_FAIL); ROM roundtrip unchanged at MISMATCH 169 for
limit=8000 — no encoder regression, as the working rules require.

events.title: recreate_kit: Phase 6 — the seeded PSG read model
events.message:
recreate_kit: Phase 6 — the seeded PSG read model

The wall the Wonder Boy campaign's remaining work stands behind, built
on the registered finding: a write-ledger replay recreates the exact
false-green class it exists to fix (the RMW sites preserve bits the
game never writes), so THE CHIP'S CONTENTS ON ENTRY ARE AN INPUT —
supplied identically to both sides via psg_seed, or the run refuses.

The model: one 16-byte register file + known bitmask fed by the direct
path; select latched at $ff8800 (latch-known: a read before any
select REFUSES — the latch is an instruction, not a seed); data writes
store + append to an ordered EVENT ledger that now records READS too
(a candidate reading the wrong register is caught by the stream, not
trusted to the file); reads served only from seed or same-run writes;
unseeded reads refuse naming the remedy; final file + known part of
the differential surface. Always on; only the seed is opt-in —
nothing about the model is a claim about the game, so there is no
waiver to enforce. High-nibble selects refused (the real chip demands
a zero high nibble). Per-run reseed lives in enter_from_reset (the
CCR lesson, applied before the bench path could drift). Candidate API
include/psg.h + src/psg.c (psg_port_read/write), auto-linked.

Audio-capture mode re-based onto the shared file as a documented
relaxation; arm-from-off and audio_reset clear file AND latch (the
cross-worker leak, empirically reproduced then pinned); emu.run
refuses under an armed capture outside audio_capturing(); the
extraction re-run BYTE-IDENTICAL to the committed 43 assets.
Two-doors guard: psg_seed vs psg_regs() mis-aims refuse loudly.

Verification: kit 187 -> 247 (incl. a harness-level differential
smoke over a miniature candidate — the plumbing is exercised, not
claimed); 11/11 review mutants + 7/7 build mutants reddened;
buggyboy 292, joust 4369, wonderboy 2925 all green from clean
rebuilds; the kit's own make test now builds the oracle first (a
swept tree was silently skipping the smoke).

Docs, same commit: TRAP_MODEL Phase 6 (model/refusal tables, the
honest unpinned list); Joust STATUS's 0x152dc row (the PSG wall is
LIFTED — psg_seed={14:...}; Super is the sole remaining blocker);
BuggyBoy README's g_REFRESH latent-trap note; capture contract
docstrings aligned; the register file answers to ONE name.

events.title: feat(disasm): tell code from data instead of decoding everything (#29)
events.message:
feat(disasm): tell code from data instead of decoding everything (#29)

* feat(disasm): use hunk relocations to tell code from data

The hunk parser read both HUNK_RELOC32 and HUNK_RELOC32SHORT, applied
every relocation, and then dropped the offsets — so nothing downstream
could tell which longwords hold pointers. A DATA hunk's bytes were fed
to the decoder like any other, producing invented instructions and
desynchronizing the stream until it happened to realign.

Retain the reloc offsets as absolute addresses on Section::relocs and
hand them, plus non-code hunk spans and the entry point, to the
disassembler. This is the linker's own account of the layout, not a
guess from the bytes: callers with only a raw blob supply nothing and
get the previous behavior unchanged.

Pointers are emitted as a single dc.l and their targets get labels, so
the listing reassembles to the same pointer rather than hardcoding a
load address. Other data runs are emitted word-wise. Both passes share
the same data check, so they agree on where lines begin — otherwise
labels would attach to addresses pass 2 never emits.

On a two-hunk executable, the DATA hunk went from
  0000400c: de ad be ef   add.l   -$4111(a5), d7
to
  0000400c: de ad be ef   dc.l    $deadbeef

add_entry_points is recorded but unused: the linear scan ignores it,
and it is the attachment point for target-following, which is what
the remaining ROM gap needs.

682 tests pass (was 673); clippy and fmt clean.

* feat(disasm): follow control flow, with text and jump-table detection

A linear scan cannot know which bytes are code, so a ROM's copyright
strings and tables decode into invented instructions. Add tracing from
caller-supplied entry points, plus the two things that make it usable
on real images.

Tracing alone is not enough, and measuring said so: on Kickstart 1.3,
following control flow from the reset vector reaches 212 of 80619
instructions. Almost all of a ROM is entered through vector tables and
`jmp (a6)`/`jsr (a5)` — 2974 computed jumps in that image, 1091 of them
`jsr (a5)` — whose targets are not in the opword. Treating unreached
bytes as data would therefore have hidden 99.7% of the code. So
unreached bytes are still decoded linearly; what tracing adds is the
authority to *override* that where the bytes positively look like data,
and to stop a linear decode from swallowing a proven instruction start.

Text detection requires a NUL terminator and at least 4 printable
bytes. Requiring the terminator is what separates strings from
printable code (`nop` is "Nq", `rts` is "Nu"); without it the run also
tends to start a byte early. Runs are padded to even length: an
odd-length data line would leave every following line decoding at an
odd address and desynchronize the whole listing.

Jump-table seeding (`--scan-tables`) takes runs of >=4 consecutive
in-image longwords as entry points, recovering code reachable only
through tables. This is explicitly a heuristic and opt-in, unlike hunk
relocations. Note a Kickstart ROM has no vector table of its own to
read — it starts with a reset `jmp` and a version string, and its
exception vectors are written to RAM at run time.

Kickstart 1.3, 68000, from the reset vector at $fc00d2:

  linear                    80619 instr,  2827 dc.*,    0 strings
  trace only                  212 instr, 130684 dc.*
  trace + text               74277 instr,  5023 dc.*, 2336 strings
  trace + text + tables      74482 instr,  4982 dc.*, 2267 strings

Recovered strings are the real ones: "exec.library", "Software
Failure. ", "Guru Meditation #%08lx.%08lx".

Supplying no entry points keeps the previous linear behavior exactly,
verified for raw blobs; text detection is gated off in that case
because `nop; rts` is four printable bytes.

Known imprecision, documented at string_run_len: a printable
instruction tail immediately before a string is absorbed into it
("Nuciab.resource"). It costs one word, shifts nothing, and fixing it
needs the trace to have claimed the preceding instruction.

702 tests pass (was 692); clippy and fmt clean.

* fix(disasm): keep control characters out of quoted dc.b output

Tab, newline and carriage return count as string content when detecting
a run — Amiga message strings embed them routinely — but emitting them
literally split the dc.b across several output lines, so the listing
could not be reassembled. Kickstart's version banner produced a line
ending mid-string at "exec 34.2 (28 Oct 1987)<CR><LF>".

Restrict the quoted span to printable bytes and emit the rest as hex:
  dc.b     "exec 34.2 (28 Oct 1987)",$0d,$0a,$00

Measured on Kickstart 1.3 (68020, base $fc0000, 20000 instructions,
.local-tools/romcheck.py):

  linear baseline          OK 79.3%   MISMATCH 430
  trace, before this fix   OK 80.4%   MISMATCH 495
  trace, after             OK 80.7%   MISMATCH 424

The multi-line output was the whole of the earlier MISMATCH regression.

romfull.py, the whole-range byte comparison, over the first 4000
instructions:

  linear baseline    903/12724 bytes identical   ( 7.10%)
  trace              5155/13736 bytes identical  (37.53%)

* feat(disasm): support PC trace tables, and read jump tables from them

Static analysis cannot follow `jmp (a6)`/`jsr (a5)`, and Kickstart 1.3
has 2974 such computed jumps. A PC trace — the program counter values
recorded while the image actually ran — settles them without having to
reason about them at all, which is why Oxore/m68k-disasm makes trace
tables its primary mechanism rather than a heuristic. Adopt the same
file format (one value per line) so traces can be shared between the
two tools; `$hex`/`0x` and `#`/`;` comments are also accepted.

Each recorded PC is taken as a proven instruction start *and* as a walk
entry point, so straight-line code between two samples is recovered
without needing a sample per instruction. Odd and out-of-image values
are dropped: the 68000 fetches instructions word-aligned, so those
indicate a trace from a different image, which the CLI reports rather
than silently ignoring.

A trace is also negative evidence, and that is what makes it pay off
twice: a longword pointing at a proven instruction start, sitting where
no proven instruction is, is a jump-table entry. Recognizing those
turns the table a computed jump dispatches through into `dc.l label0`
instead of invented arithmetic. This needs no run of several entries,
unlike --scan-tables, because the evidence per entry is far stronger —
the target is known-executed code, not a plausible-looking address.

On a purpose-built jump-table binary, where ground truth is known:

  before   00001010: ori.b   #$08, d0     <- table read as code
  after    00001010: dc.l    label0       <- and handler labelled

707 tests pass (was 702); clippy and fmt clean.

Not measured against a real ROM trace: no 68k emulator is available
here, and a trace derived from our own output would be circular. The
m68000 crate (docs.rs/m68000) is an instruction-level interpreter that
could generate one honestly.

* fix(disasm): emit the trailing byte of an odd-length image

Both passes need a full word to attempt a decode, so their
`remaining() >= 2` loops left a final odd byte unconsumed and it never
reached the output. A 5-byte input disassembled to 4 bytes, and a
1-byte input produced no output at all — the listing could not
reassemble to the original.

Emit that byte as `dc.b $xx` after each loop, and record it as a line
start in pass 1 so a branch to it still gets a label instead of being
rejected as landing mid-instruction.

Predates the tracing work: reproducible with no entry points and no
trace, on plain linear output. Found while roundtripping a purpose-
built test binary that happened to be odd-sized.

  before  5-byte input -> 4 bytes reassembled
  after   5-byte input -> byte-identical

Images of even length are unaffected: Kickstart 1.3 and the raw-blob
corpus produce identical output.

710 tests pass (was 707); clippy and fmt clean.

---------

events.title: Fix host pacing loop compounding usleep() overshoot into frame rate
events.message:
Fix host pacing loop compounding usleep() overshoot into frame rate

chq_sleep_handler re-anchored its "consumed" measurement from a fresh
stamp() every frame, so usleep()'s per-call overshoot (~4ms on this
host) never got clawed back and compounded frame after frame, giving a
steady ~42fps at speed=100% instead of 50fps. Switch to an absolute
wall-clock deadline that advances by the nominal duration each call, so
overshoot on one frame shortens the next frame's sleep instead of
repeating forever. A max-lag cap prevents a fast-forward burst after a
genuine stall (pause, breakpoint).

Park the Master shadow-RAM route to 2 px horizontal scrolling

Both buffers live at the same address, &5800-&7FFF, one in main RAM
and one in shadow: same 10K wrap, same R12/R13, same scroll
arithmetic, and the only difference between displaying one and the
other is ACCCON's D bit. So none of the addressing problems that
rule it out on a Model B apply - we are not fitting two circular
strips into one wrap region, we are using the same region twice.

Confirmed by KC rather than assumed: the Master's screen wrap is
driven the same way as the Model B's, via the System VIA addressable
latch, and writing ACCCON D takes effect instantly, even
mid-scanline.

Parked on cost, not feasibility. Either buffer might be displayed
next field so both must stay current, which doubles all drawing -
about +60-80% once B's edges are produced by shifting bytes out of A
instead of redrawing from the tile map, since the lookups are the
expensive half of a band. Roughly +12-16K cycles against ~5K spare.

Also corrects the Layer 3 note, which gave the Model B obstacle as
"no room for the second buffer". It is not room; it is that a
circular strip's period must equal the hardware wrap span and there
is only one such region - which is exactly why sharing one address
range across main and shadow works.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Layer 4a: dead-zone camera and 2 px sprite positioning
events.message:
Layer 4a: dead-zone camera and 2 px sprite positioning

The CRTC's horizontal granularity is 1/80 of the display width in
every mode - it addresses in 8-byte units and a row is 80 of them -
so a scroll step is always ~4 MODE 1 pixels and at low speed the
whole world lurches. Two 10K circular strips would fix it and cannot
work on a Model B: a strip's period must equal the hardware wrap
span and there is exactly one wrap region, 10K at &5800.

So the camera moved instead. plyX is the player's own world
position at 1 px; posX only follows once the player leaves a +/-8 px
window, and then in whole 4 px units. Walking slowly the world holds
still and only the droid moves; at speed the window saturates and it
scrolls as before. Vertically nothing changed - the scroll is
already 1 scanline, so the player stays pinned.

The sprite is positioned every 2 px, which spills 24 px into seven
bytes, so rows are stored seven wide and there are two copies:
unshifted on disc, shifted built at startup into the spare space
above the panel. 2 px is not only thrift - a C64 multicolour pixel
is exactly two MODE 1 pixels, so the artwork holds no finer detail.

Masks are no longer stored. Every opaque pixel maps to logical 1, 2
or 3 and never 0, so a pixel is transparent exactly when both its
bits are clear and a 256-byte table recovers the mask. The sprite
data got smaller despite doubling.

Moving the collision reference from the view to the player changed
its offset from 159 to 11, and the C64's round-up snap then tips the
cell over - the one-pixel wall jitter, back by a different route.
Both snaps now stay inside the current cell.

Verified: 3.5 px/frame still holds on a full diagonal, and the play
buffer diffs byte-clean against RedrawAll at odd mapHX and non-zero
line with the sprite at a 2 px shift - 0 differences in 10240.

events.title: tools: the $bca2 diagnosis — Ghidra's 68000 sleigh is one deref too deep
events.message:
tools: the $bca2 diagnosis — Ghidra's 68000 sleigh is one deref too deep

HwPortabilityScan dropped TEN resolved `jsr (d16,An)` call edges image-
wide, $bca2 among them: 68000.sinc exports the (d16,An) operand as a
MEMORY varnode and spells the call `call [operand]`, so constant
propagation 'resolves' the site to the opcode STORED AT the target —
in no function — and the edge loop dropped it silently, while the
non-empty flow list kept it out of the I ledger. In neither ledger,
exactly as the batch-3 register entry recorded.

Fix: when a computed transfer's pcode reaches its target through a
LOAD, take the propagator's READ reference (the true EA) as the edge;
emit I whenever a computed transfer produced no row. Invariant kept:
every call/jump in exactly one ledger. 68000-specific by design.

Measured cost (Wonder Boy): +10 E rows, none removed, ten I rows
byte-identical; edges 233 -> 240. $bbca honestly -> $17b14 ->
snd_trigger_effect and STAYS runnable; the real casualty is
game_routine_6bb8, T3 -> T4 behind snd_psg_silence's PSG read —
runnable 223/21,624 B -> 222/21,334 B (82.7 %). Unreachable 116 -> 112
(+376 B of T0 sound entries). predictions 14/14 green; scan idempotent.

Docs: on-target-execution.md rule 4 carries the mechanism (was
'undiagnosed'); PORTABILITY.md gains §0d + headline annotations;
STATUS.md's batch-3 register entry closed, re-scan bullets annotated.
The fall-through blind spot is a DIFFERENT mechanism and stays open.

events.message:
docs: the objdump codegen check needs -m m68k:68020 on Amiga hunks

An Amiga hunk binary carries no CPU tag, so objdump falls back to 68000 and
silently misdecodes 020 instructions. The AGA build shows 433 mulsl / 233
bfextu with -m m68k:68020 and zero without it, so the bare recipe reports a
good 020 build as broken — which is exactly the wrong direction for a check
whose whole job is catching a flag that did not take.

events.title: tools: a drawer icon needs DrawerData, and the engine had no icon at all
events.message:
tools: a drawer icon needs DrawerData, and the engine had no icon at all

Two gaps found while staging an Amiga hard-drive install.

make_amiga_icon.py hardcoded do_DrawerData to NULL, so `--type drawer` emitted
a BROKEN drawer icon — Workbench has nowhere to keep the drawer window's
geometry. That matters more than it sounds: a folder with no valid .info does
not appear in Workbench at all, only via the Shell. Decoded WB3.2's own
Storage.info / Devs.info as the oracle (628-byte drawer icons: do_Type 2,
do_DrawerData non-zero, then a 56-byte block right after the 78-byte
DiskObject) and construct an equivalent here rather than lifting Commodore's
bytes, same rule the glyph already follows. Tools and projects still get NULL,
which is correct for them.

And there was no frua.info, so the engine could not be launched from Workbench
even though uainst could. Adds one, with a UA glyph (tools/ua_icon.glyph) and
the same STACK=200000 tooltype, and ships it in the Amiga zips.

Verified on a real Workbench 3.2 under amiberry, not just structurally: the
drawer icon renders, the drawer OPENS on a double-click (which is what the
DrawerData fix buys), and the frua icon inside it draws "UA".

Also worth recording: objdump on an Amiga hunk binary defaults to 68000 and
silently misdecodes 020 instructions, so CLAUDE.md's `grep muls.l` check
reports a false negative there. `-m m68k:68020` shows the AGA build's 433
mulsl / 233 bfextu; without it, zero.

events.title: tools: hdr[2] is the pool's used-region length, and writing 0 was a real bug
events.message:
tools: hdr[2] is the pool's used-region length, and writing 0 was a real bug

Grounds the STRG fix in the engine instead of in statistics, and corrects the
TODO entry that sent it to the wrong layer.

l4e8a (add a string) and l501e (delete) both use header word 2 as the extent of
their jt406 move — `hdr[2] - slot` and `hdr[2] - (off+size)` — and adjust it by
+/- size. With the 0 we used to write, both go NEGATIVE for any slot past the
first, so adding or deleting a string in the in-game editor on a generated
module would move the wrong span over the packed data. That reclassifies this
from "fidelity gap, not a functional break" to a corruption bug on every module
mk_*_design.py has ever produced.

The same function settles the terminator without appeal to sampling: it takes
`len = jt423(text) + 1` and allocates `size = (len * 3 + 3) / 4`, which is
ceil(3*(strlen+1)/4) — our packing of strlen+1 codes exactly.

Adds two DATA-FREE tests for both rules, because the guards that drive the
encoder needed real areas and therefore skipped in CI: a dropped terminator was
invisible to CI even after the previous commit.

Verified end to end: a regenerated KOBOLD.DSN (hdr[2] = 163 where the old
encoder wrote 0) boots in Hatari and the engine renders its text at (3,3).

events.title: tools: geo.py STRG was not byte-faithful — the header word and the terminator
events.message:
tools: geo.py STRG was not byte-faithful — the header word and the terminator

Re-encoding a decoded SSI area rewrote 6628 of 7168 bytes. docs/TODO.md blamed
the 6-bit alphabet ("every character code comes out exactly ONE LESS than
SSI's"). That was wrong: re-packing all 1270 used strings in HEIRS reproduces
SSI's bytes EXACTLY. The alphabet and the 4-codes-per-3-bytes packing were
already right, and the accusation aimed the work at the wrong layer.

Two real defects, both outside the codec:

- STRG header word 2 is the USED BODY LENGTH (sum of the index). We wrote 0.
  Every one of the 26 HEIRS areas disagreed on exactly this field.
- SSI packs each string PLUS a NUL terminator, so the allocation is
  f(len+1), not f(len). 1218 of 1270 real strings carry it.

And one thing no encoder can derive, which is why the TODO's proposed oracle
("re-encode every SSI area and require byte equality") was unsatisfiable as
posed: SSI's allocation is EDITING HISTORY, not a function of the string.
GEO005 slot 4 and slot 67 are both 38 characters and carry different
allocations, 29 and 30 bytes, in the same file. The body tail is likewise full
of deleted-string residue (1740 nonzero bytes in GEO001).

So fidelity now comes from preserving provenance instead of deriving it:
strg_read() records each slot's index byte and raw bytes plus the tail, and
strg_write() reuses them for any string it did not change. Editing one string
perturbs that string and the offsets after it — not all 400 slots. Pass
preserve=False to force a fresh encode.

Oracle: 635 of 635 real SSI-authored areas now re-encode byte-for-byte (the
only 6 files that change are our own generated fixtures, which the old encoder
wrote with the zero header). tests/test_geo.py gains six checks over real areas
that skip when data/ is not unpacked; the pre-fix encoder fails five of them.
