events.title: fix: fourteen encoder/decoder defects found against the reference (#28)
events.message:
fix: fourteen encoder/decoder defects found against the reference (#28)

* fix: three bugs found by ROM roundtrip analysis

Found by disassembling a real Kickstart 1.3 ROM, reassembling each
instruction, and classifying every failure by cause rather than reporting
one aggregate rate. That classification is the point: the previous "73%"
hid three distinct defects, two of which silently produce a different
instruction.

**MOVEC put the register number in the wrong field.** The extension word
is bit 15 = A/D, bits 14-12 = register, bits 11-0 = control code. The
register was shifted left by 4 instead of 12, so it landed inside the
control-register field: `movec d1,vbr` encoded as `4e7b 0811` where both
the reference and the ROM itself have `4e7b 1801` — a different control
register, no diagnostic. Address-register operands were rejected outright,
though `movec a0,vbr` and `movec a7,usp` are valid and appear in real
code. The decoder was already correct, which is why the roundtrip suite
never caught it: a wrong encoder feeding a right decoder still comes back
as *an* instruction.

**`.w` on an absolute address only worked upper-case.** The suffix check
tested for ".W" and ".L" literally, so `lea $400.w,a6` silently emitted
the 6-byte long form while `lea $400.W,a6` emitted the 4-byte short one.
Lower case is the common spelling, and the README documents the suffix as
forcing the short form.

**The disassembler dropped two things needed to round-trip.** Absolute
short operands printed as `$00000400`, indistinguishable from an absolute
long, so reassembling grew the instruction by two bytes; they now print
with a `.w` suffix, which both this assembler and the reference accept on
a bare address and on a label. And `CMP` printed without its size, so
`cmp.l (a0),d0` (b090) came back as `cmp.w` (b050) — again a real
instruction, silently the wrong one.

Effect on the measurement (KS1.3, 6000 instructions, classified):

    before   OK 73.0%   MISMATCH 258
    after    OK 75.0%   MISMATCH 142

The remaining mismatches are concentrated in the ROM header, where the
embedded copyright text is read as code by a linear disassembler.

Verified: 660 tests green (+10, including 8 new coverage cases), byte
parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13, clippy and fmt clean.

* fix: DBcc condition codes and six swapped FPU opcodes

Found by sweeping the instruction set family by family against the
reference — 880 forms across the 68000 base, the 68020 extensions, the
FPU, the MMU and every addressing mode — and diffing the bytes.

**DBcc used DBF's encoding as its base.** `0x51C8` is the encoding of
`DBF`/`DBRA` specifically, whose condition code is 1; using it as the base
ORs that 1 into every condition, so all eight *even* codes came out as the
odd one above them. `DBT` assembled as `DBF`, `DBHI` as `DBLS`, `DBNE` as
`DBEQ`, and so on — a loop that never terminates where the source asked
for one that terminates immediately, and the reverse. The base is
`0x50C8`.

This survived because the only test covered `DBF`, the single condition
where both forms agree. An existing test asserted `DBNE` = `0x57C9`
(which is `DBEQ`) and has been corrected; there is now a test over all
sixteen conditions.

**Six FPU opcodes were shuffled among themselves.** `FTAN` sat at 0x0B,
which is unassigned, while 0x0F held `FTENTOX`; the exponential and
logarithm group was rotated by one. Every affected instruction assembled
to a *different but perfectly valid* FPU operation:

    fetox  -> ftwotox      flogn  -> flog10
    ftan   -> (0x0B)       flog2  -> (0x14 = flogn)

Nothing failed anywhere, because the assembler and the disassembler each
kept their own copy of the table and both copies had drifted identically.
They agreed with each other; neither agreed with the hardware. The table
now lives once, in `m68k-core`, with both sides reading from it — the
duplication was the actual defect, the wrong entries only its symptom.

Sweep results after the fixes: 312/312 on the 68000 base instruction set
across all sizes and EA modes, 322/322 on the remaining 68000 families,
63/63 on the 68020 extensions, 136/136 on the FPU, 18/18 on the MMU,
23/23 on the addressing modes. No mismatches anywhere.

661 tests green, byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13, clippy and fmt
clean.

* fix: reject MOVEQ and shift-count operands that do not fit

Two more silent-wrong-value cases from the same sweep, both found by
checking where we accept what the reference rejects.

**MOVEQ wrapped its operand.** The caller cast with `as i8`, so
`MOVEQ #256,D0` assembled as `MOVEQ #0` and `MOVEQ #-129,D0` as
`MOVEQ #127`. The program simply got a different value than the source
asked for, with no diagnostic.

The check has to accept three spellings of the same encoding, since the
reference takes all of them and the disassembler prints the last:
`#-1`, `#$FF`, and `#$FFFFFFFF` are one instruction. Only values that
genuinely do not fit are refused. Caught while writing this: an initial
version rejected `#$FFFFFFFF` and broke the golden-vector roundtrip.

**Immediate shift counts wrapped too.** The field is 3 bits with 8
encoded as 0, so `count & 0x7` turned `asl.b #9,d0` into a shift by 1 and
`#0` into a shift by 8. Now 1..=8 only; larger or variable counts need
the register form, which the error message points at.

664 tests green, byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13.

* fix: reject the address-register forms the reference rejects

Closes the last gap between this assembler and the reference: three cases
where we accepted an instruction that does not exist, emitting bytes the
CPU would decode as something else.

**Byte-sized access to an address register.** An address register is
always written in full, so there is no byte form in the encoding. Most
instructions already excluded it through their EA category, but MOVE
(which allows every mode) and the immediate family did not, so
`move.b a0,d0` and `move.b d0,a0` assembled. Enforced in `encode_ea`
rather than per encoder, since the rule holds for all of them — and
indirection through an address register stays valid, as it is the
register that has no byte form, not the memory behind it.

**The immediate family had no business accepting An at all.** `ADDI.W
#1,A0` is not an instruction; `ADDA.W #1,A0` is. Six encoders (ORI, ANDI,
EORI, ADDI, SUBI, CMPI) passed the `ALL` category, which includes address
registers, so all of them emitted bytes at every size. They now use
`DATA_ALT`, which is what the PRM specifies.

Measured against the reference after the change:

    68000 base, all sizes x EA modes    312/312
    remaining 68000 families            322/322
    68020 extensions                     63/63
    FPU                                 136/136
    MMU                                  18/18
    addressing modes                     23/23
    immediate family x 6 destinations   108/108
    strictness cases (reference rejects)  17/17

No mismatches, nothing wrongly rejected, and the strictness now matches
exactly — every form the reference refuses, we refuse too.

664 tests green, byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13.

* fix: include guards, the CCR/SR/USP sentinel collision, and \@ prefixes

Four defects found by assembling a real Amiga source tree that uses the
system headers. Each one alone stopped the file dead or, worse, changed
its meaning.

**`MOVE.W #-1,D0` assembled as `MOVE CCR,D0`.** CCR, SR and USP were
represented as marker immediates (-1, -2, 0x800), which collide with those
values written literally. `#-1` produced 42C0 and `#-2` produced 40C0 —
different instructions, no diagnostic — and `MOVE.L #-2,A0` was rejected
outright. They are `Operand::Special` now, the variant that already
existed for exactly this purpose.

**Include guards were skipped in pass 2.** `IFND SYM` asks whether a
symbol is defined *yet*, but by pass 2 the symbol table holds everything,
so the answer flips. The idiom every Amiga system header opens with —
`IFND EXEC_TYPES_I` / `EXEC_TYPES_I SET 1` / body / `ENDC` — took the
branch in pass 1 and skipped the entire body in pass 2, so the header
contributed nothing. Pass 1's verdict is now recorded per line and reused;
only IFD/IFND need this, since every other conditional evaluates an
expression that does not move between passes.

**`\@` could not be used as a label prefix.** It expanded to `0001`, so
`\@BITDEF SET 1<<\3` in exec/types.i became `0001BITDEF` — not a legal
identifier, reported as an unknown mnemonic. It now expands to `_000001`,
with the leading underscore that makes the fragment valid in prefix
position; the reference substitutes the same shape.

**A byte immediate filled its whole extension word.** `move.b #-1,d0`
emitted 103C FFFF where the reference has 103C 00FF; the high byte must
be zero.

Also: an operand that fails to parse in pass 2 now reports *why*. By then
every symbol is known, so a failure is a real error — but the encoder only
saw a missing operand and reported the instruction's shape, so
`move.l #MEMF_CHIP,d1` came out as "MOVE requires source and destination"
instead of naming the undefined symbol.

Sweeps unchanged at 312/322/63/136/18/23, byte parity unchanged at 11/11
and 13/13, 670 tests green.

On the ROM roundtrip this moves 18 cases from MISMATCH to REASM: they are
invalid instructions the disassembler produced from data regions, which we
now refuse to assemble rather than encoding wrongly.

* fix(disasm): validate addressing modes against the opcode patterns

The patterns have always carried `src_ea`/`dst_ea`, and nothing ever read
them. The disassembler therefore rendered encodings that do not exist:
`000A 0050` came out as `ori.b #$50,a2`, a byte-sized write to an address
register, which is not an addressing mode. Bytes like these come from data
regions a linear disassembler walks into, and printing them as
instructions is worse than printing `dc.w` — reassembling the output then
fails or, before the assembler was tightened, silently produced different
bytes.

`decode_next` now checks the opword's EA field against the matched
pattern's category and moves on to the next candidate if it does not fit,
falling through to `dc.w` as it already does for an unknown opcode.

Two things made this less mechanical than it looks:

`src_ea`/`dst_ea` follow *operand order*, not bit position. For
`MOVEM D0-D7,-(SP)` the opword's EA field is the destination while
`src_ea` describes the register list, so a check against the wrong field
rejects an ordinary instruction. Each parser now declares which of the two
its standard EA field corresponds to, and parsers that put the EA
somewhere else (MOVEP, the register-pair forms, the coprocessor
extensions) are left alone.

Several categories were themselves wrong, which only became visible once
something read them:

  NBCD, CLR, Scc, TAS, NEG, NEGX, NOT, MOVE from SR  ALTERABLE_MEMORY
                                                     -> DATA_ALT
  ADDA, SUBA, CMPA                                   DATA -> ALL
  ORI/ANDI/EORI (EA destination)                     0 -> DATA_ALT
  ADDI and friends                                   ALL -> DATA_ALT

All verified individually against the reference: `nbcd d0`, `scc d0`,
`adda.l a0,a1` are valid and must keep decoding; `addi.w #1,a0` is not.

Also adds the missing `MOVE CCR,<ea>` pattern (68010+). The assembler
emits `42C0` for it, but no decoder pattern existed, so it read back as a
data word — the roundtrip was broken in one direction the whole time.

Verified: all 907 instruction forms in the sweep corpora still decode (0
lost), sweeps unchanged at 312/322/63/136/18/23, byte parity unchanged at
11/11 and 13/13, 673 tests green.

On the ROM roundtrip, REASM drops from 124 to 94 and DATA rises
correspondingly: invalid encodings are now recognised as the data they
are, instead of being rendered as instructions that then fail to
reassemble.

* fix: emit label definitions, plus four operand-form gaps

Found by reassembling the disassembler's own output as a whole file rather
than line by line. That is the test that matters — a linewise check cannot
see branches at all, since `bcs.s label13` in isolation has no label to
resolve.

**The output defined no labels.** 7271 references, zero definitions:
pass 1 discovered branch targets and pass 2 substituted the names into
operands, but nothing ever emitted `labelN:` on its own line. The
disassembly could not be fed back into the assembler at all. Now 9733
references and 9733 definitions.

**MOVEP lost the top half of its displacement.** It is a full 16-bit
field, decoded with `sign_extend_8`, so `0d0a 1234` read back as
`movep.w $34(a2),d6` — a different address. The operand was also rendered
through `AddrDisp`, which shortens a zero displacement to `(a2)`; MOVEP
has no such addressing mode, so that form did not reassemble. Negative
displacements now print in decimal, since the reference rejects
`$fffe(a2)` but accepts `-2(a2)` for the same bytes.

**`(bd,Xn.size*scale)` did not parse.** A 68020 full-format EA with the
base register suppressed — the encoder has always been able to emit one
(`base_reg` is an `Option` precisely for it), but no parser produced it.
Encoding it also needed I/IS = 0 rather than the indirect range, hence the
new `is_indirect` flag: `($1000,d0.w*8)` came out as `07a1` where the
reference has `07a0`.

**`($1234)` did not parse.** A parenthesised absolute address; every
register-bearing form is tried first, so what remains is just an address
with redundant parentheses, which the reference accepts.

Also corrects six more pattern categories that only became visible once
the decoder started reading them: BCHG/BCLR/BSET write, so they take
DATA_ALT rather than ALL — only BTST may be PC-relative — and CMPI has no
address-register form. Nine further parsers whose categories were already
correct are now covered by the check.

Verified: 907 instruction forms still roundtrip with none lost, 673 tests
green, byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13, clippy and fmt clean.

events.title: engine: a text event chaining into COMBAT froze the screen too — bound the hold
events.message:
engine: a text event chaining into COMBAT froze the screen too — bound the hold

Third shape of the #161 hold, reported from real hardware: the rider-and-ogres
encounter on the southern edge of HEIRS. The dialogs run, combat starts — turn
sounds and all — and the display keeps the rider's bigpic. Everything after the
event is drawn into a frame nobody is allowed to show.

The step-context gate (6106cf5d) was right as far as it went, and the backstops
in l4d26 and l1806 covered a chained TEXT event and the Return prompt. A
step-triggered text event that CHAINS INTO COMBAT goes through neither: jt511's
loop runs to completion while the hold from l4d26's tail is still outstanding,
and only the walk loop's step render drops it — which cannot run until combat
returns.

Reproduced with a fixture instead of by navigating to that HEIRS cell: a message
event whose `chain` points at a combat event on the same square. Five Returns,
identical frame hashes throughout. The -DFRUA_NOEVHOLD control on the same drive
reaches the combat field, and this build now produces that field BYTE-IDENTICAL
(AE = 0) to the control.

The fix deliberately changes the KIND of guarantee. Twice I believed I had
enumerated the exits and was wrong, which is evidence that enumeration is the
wrong shape for this. The hold now records the tick it was taken on, and
port_event_tail_expire() — called from jt1134 (the tick) and l604e (the event
pump), between them reached by every interactive loop in the engine — drops any
hold older than 30 ticks (0.5s) and shows the frame. The exact releases stay,
because they keep the common case flicker-free; what the bound adds is that
missing one costs a BLINK rather than a frozen game. The worst outcome now
available is the pre-#161 flash, which is where this started.

Also recorded in the wall doc: if a fourth shape appears, delete the hold. The
per-glyph typewriter present (6543b358) is independent and is what actually
fixed the reported text problem; the hold only removes the end-of-event flash,
and that is not worth a third regression.

Verified: chained combat renders (AE=0 vs control); the #161 text-square
coalescing is intact (typing -> settled, no blank-box intermediate, known-good
settled hash); the merchant chain still reaches the treasure screen. 446 host
tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

events.title: Layer 4: the player droid - sprite, controls, wall collision
events.message:
Layer 4: the player droid - sprite, controls, wall collision

The player is pinned at the centre of the play area and the deck
scrolls underneath it, driven by the C64's own acceleration model.

The sprite does not exist in the C64 data: the dynamic sprite area
ships zeroed and BuildDroidSprite / AnimateDroids construct every
droid at runtime. tools/export_player.py replays both offline for
droid 001 and emits MODE 1 data - 8 rotor phases, 768 bytes.
PlayerSprite_dat puts the player at x=148, a multiple of 4, so it
lands on a CRTC unit boundary and needs no pre-shifted variants.

Scrolling is now a 16.8 pixel position rather than a fixed step, so
ScrollUp/Down/Left/Right and DrawScanline are gone, replaced by
ApplyMove and DrawBand. The addressing invariant that makes this
work is documented in scroll.asm.

The C64 speed constants are per GameLoop iteration and an iteration
is 2-3 frames, not 1 - DrawScreen alone is ~17,250 cycles against
~18,300 usable in a PAL frame. Converted to per-frame, top speed is
3.5 px rather than 7. That also halved the redraw work, so the frame
budget closes: 35 px per 10 frames on both axes of a full-speed
diagonal, frame-locked.

Collision is the 12-probe diamond from CheckPlyAdvance. The
reference cell must use the C64's ceiling-rounded origin, or the
snap moves the cell and the player jitters against walls.

Charset moved to &0400 - Layer 4 filled the space below &3000.

Verified: play buffer diffed byte-for-byte against RedrawAll at odd
mapHX and non-zero line after diagonal scrolling, 0 differences in
10240.

docs: an empty SAVE folder making Load a no-op is FAITHFUL, not a bug

Two independent confirmations. The Mac's jt582 enumerates the design's SAVE
folder, compacts the present slots, and returns silently when none are found
("if (idx[0]==0xFF) return") — no alert, no message. DOS 1.2 does the same,

screenshot byte-identical to the one before the keypress.

Recorded because the obvious "fix" is a divergence. SSI plainly knew how to post
that notice — the CHARACTER roster builder jt589 calls jt42 with "No characters
to load." when ITS list is empty — and chose not to for the save picker.

Also recorded: designs do NOT ship a save game. Nothing on the DOS install disks
and nothing in an installed HEIRS.DSN, so a fresh install of any design sits in
this state until the player saves once. The SAVGAMA.CSV/VAULTA.DAT in our staged
gamedata are our own July DOS-session artefacts.

events.title: docs: a pgrep -f poll loop matches its own shell and never exits
events.message:
docs: a pgrep -f poll loop matches its own shell and never exits

Four background waiters were found still alive after 9, 6, 3 and 3 days, each
respawning a `sleep` forever and burning a few seconds of CPU per day. Three of
them were the same mistake:

    until ! pgrep -f "make release-all" >/dev/null; do sleep 10; done

That can never exit. The shell evaluating the pgrep has "make release-all" in
its OWN command line, so the pattern always matches something — itself — and the
loop polls until killed. The fourth waited for a marker string in a task output
file whose task had already died, which is the same shape of never.

This repo already warns "never pkill -f hatari — -f matches your own shell", in
CLAUDE.md and in the run-falcon-port skill. The warning was right and I wrote
the polling version of it anyway, three times. Generalised in the skill's
gotchas, with the fixes: wait on a marker the work itself writes, bracket the
pattern (`[m]ake release-all`), or run it in the foreground with a timeout.

Same family as de4455fc — a harness command that can wait forever eventually
does, and the cost is litter that outlives the session that made it.

events.title: harness: hatari_ui.sh could hang forever on the command FIFO
events.message:
harness: hatari_ui.sh could hang forever on the command FIFO

Two shells were found still alive after 7 days and 4 days respectively, each
holding Hatari's --cmd-fifo open and doing nothing — one blocked in `dbg`, one
in `quit` — long after the sessions that started them had ended. Zero CPU, no
output, no notification: exactly the kind of leftover nobody notices.

A write to a FIFO blocks until something opens it for reading. With Hatari dead
(or never started) `echo > "$STATE/cmd.fifo"` waits forever, and the
`2>/dev/null || true` on two of those call sites does not help at all, because
the block is in open(2) — there is no error and no exit status to ignore.

All six writers now go through fifo_send(), which refuses when hatari is not
running and bounds the write with `timeout` regardless, returning non-zero
instead of hanging. Callers decide whether that is fatal: `dbg` and `dump` die,
`quit` and the two start-time options carry on.

Also: `start` now checks DISPLAY itself. This script does NOT bootstrap an Xvfb
— driver.sh does — so calling it directly under `env -u DISPLAY` reached SDL and
produced "could not initialize the SDL library: x11 not available", which reads
like a broken X install on a machine where X is the only thing available. It
means DISPLAY is unset. That message is what the 7-day-old shell had logged
before it wedged, and it sent the diagnosis in the wrong direction.

Verified: `dbg` with nothing running exits 1 in under a second where it used to
hang; `quit` with nothing running exits 0; `start` with no DISPLAY names the
real cause. The live paths are unchanged — boot + stable screenshot + graceful
quit with --confirm-quit off completes in ~1s, which is the path that finalizes
an --avirecord AVI and the only reason `quit` exists.

events.title: feat(floppy): add AmigaDOS filesystem write support (#27)
events.message:
feat(floppy): add AmigaDOS filesystem write support (#27)

* feat(floppy): add AmigaDOS filesystem write support

Closes the last open item in plan.md P3. `amigados.rs` could read OFS/FFS
volumes; `adf_writer.rs` could create empty images and repair bootblocks.
Nothing could put a file on a disk.

New `amigados_write.rs` covers the full set: a block allocator over real
bitmap blocks, write_file/delete_file, create_dir/delete_dir, rename
(which doubles as move), and set_comment/set_protection/set_volume_name.
OFS and FFS, with extension blocks once a file outgrows the 72-slot table
in its header.

Found along the way: format_empty_ofs_disk/format_empty_ffs_disk produced
volumes with *no bitmap blocks at all* — just bm_flag=-1 and an empty page
list. AmigaOS mounts such a disk but cannot create anything on it, because
there is nothing to allocate from. The formatter now writes real bitmap
blocks, marks its own structures used, and clears the bits past the end of
the volume.

Every layout detail was read off a real AmigaDOS disk rather than derived
from documentation:

  - the bitmap starts at block 2 and a *set* bit means free
  - a bitmap block's checksum makes its longwords sum to zero
  - a file header's block table is filled from the end backwards, so the
    last slot holds the first data block
  - OFS data blocks carry a 24-byte header, leaving 488 payload bytes

Verification, in increasing order of strength:

  - 31 unit tests, including 100 KB files spanning three extension blocks,
    200 files colliding across 72 hash buckets, and deletion from the
    middle of a chain
  - every test reads its result back through the *reader*, which is a
    separate implementation — the two agreeing is the actual check
  - field-by-field comparison of a file we wrote against a real one on a
    real disk: every comparable field identical, checksums valid on both
  - writing into a real third-party disk whose bitmap and hash chains we
    did not create: the new file lands correctly and every pre-existing
    file still extracts byte-identically
  - a new fuzz target driving the write path over deliberately corrupted
    volumes, 125k runs with no findings

The CLI gains --format, --add-file, --delete-file, --make-dir,
--delete-dir, --rename, --set-comment and --set-protection. These operate
on the raw image rather than through the backend abstraction, because IPF
is a flux-level format that cannot be written back and UAE images have
variable-length tracks; a sector-addressable image is the only kind a
filesystem writer applies to.

643 tests green, clippy and fmt clean, byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and
13/13.

* fix: five bugs found by an August 2026 sweep against the reference

All five were found by assembling the same source with this assembler and
with the reference and diffing the bytes — not by reading code. Two of
them produce wrong output with no diagnostic at all.

**`SECTION name,TYPE` did not assemble.** The second argument was only
ever parsed as an origin expression, so `SECTION code,CODE` failed with
"undefined symbol: CODE" — the spelling essentially every real Amiga
source uses. The type keyword (CODE/DATA/BSS, with the optional _C/_F/_P
memory suffixes) is now recognised, and the numeric form stays as a local
extension.

**A declared type was ignored in favour of the section name.** `SECTION
mydata,DATA` became a Named section, and the hunk writer mapped every
Named section to HUNK_CODE — declared data shipped as executable code.
Sections keep their name as identity (the reference emits one hunk per
name, verified), with the declared type recorded alongside.

**A BSS section holding only `DS` vanished from the output.** Output
writers filtered on `instructions.is_empty()`, and `DS` emits no
instruction, so `SECTION vars,BSS / buf: DS.B 1024` produced no hunk at
all. Any code referencing `buf` pointed at nothing. Sections now report
reserved size as well as emitted size.

**Hunk order was alphabetical, not declaration order.** Writers sorted by
base address then name; with every section based at 0 that reduced to
sorting by name, so `SECTION zdata,DATA` before `SECTION acode,CODE` put
a data hunk at index 0 — which is where LoadSeg() enters. Sections now
carry a declaration index, since the backing map is unordered.

**`CHK.L` assembled as `CHK.W`.** The size sits in bits 8-7 (3 = word,
2 = long); the encoder hardcoded the word form. No error, just the wrong
operand size at run time. The decoder had no pattern for the long form
either, so it did not round-trip.

**`CALLM` put its argument count in the reserved half of the extension
word.** `callm #4,(a0)` encoded as `06d0 0400` instead of `06d0 0004` —
the value 1024 rather than 4. The decoder read the same wrong bits, which
is exactly why the roundtrip test passed: it proves the two sides agree
with each other, not with the hardware. An existing unit test asserted
the wrong bytes and has been corrected.

**Octal literals were missing entirely.** `@17` failed to parse in all
three number parsers, in instructions, DC and expressions alike.

Verified: 651 tests green (+8), byte parity unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13,
hunk structure now byte-comparable to the reference for type, size and
order, fuzzing clean.

* feat(asm): support nine directives the reference accepts and we rejected

Each of these made an otherwise valid Amiga source fail to assemble at
all. All nine now produce byte-identical output to the reference.

**EQUR / REG** — register aliases (`CNT EQUR D3`) and named register lists
(`SAVE REG D0-D3/A0-A2`). Both are textual substitutions applied to
operands in both passes, so the aliased source encodes exactly like the
spelled-out one. Aliases deliberately do not enter the symbol table: they
name a register, not an address, and listing them in `--sym` output
pointing at the current PC would be misleading.

**MACHINE / CPU / FPU** — let a source declare its own target, so a file
saying `machine 68020` assembles without `-c 68020` on the command line.
`FPU <n>` raises the floor to a model that has one.

**INCDIR** — adds an INCLUDE search path from within the source. It has
to be handled during include expansion rather than in pass 1: includes are
resolved in a separate sweep, so by the time pass 1 sees the `incdir` line
the `include` below it has already been resolved, and failed.

**NEAR / FAR / AUTO / INLINE / EINLINE** — optimisation and placement
hints this assembler has nothing to act on, but rejecting them stops an
entire source dead.

One subtlety worth recording. `tokens::split_line` keeps its own directive
list, used to decide whether `NAME DIR args` is a label plus a directive.
Adding every new name there broke `BEQ far`: `far` was claimed in the
operand position too, so the line parsed as a label `BEQ` followed by a
directive `far`. The reference accepts `far`, `near`, `auto`, `reg` and
`cpu` as ordinary labels, so only genuinely label-taking directives belong
in that list — and `REG`, which needs a label but is also a plausible
symbol name, is recognised only when a register list follows.

Verified: 658 tests green (+7), all nine features byte-identical to the
reference, the five colliding names still usable as labels, byte parity
unchanged at 11/11 and 13/13, clippy and fmt clean, fuzzing clean.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: gameplay batch 13 — the spawn pass; vector-page claim pinned and corrected
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: gameplay batch 13 — the spawn pass; vector-page claim pinned and corrected

actor_spawn_pass ($ff42) + actor_template_set_hitpoints ($1006a), the
$2b5a/$2b82/$2b8e side-flag family (shared 8-byte tail proven from the
image's own displacements), hud_draw_lives ($e80c — both screen buffers
at absolute addresses), and the reset pair $fe4a/$fe8c — ONE Ghidra
function that is really TWO (one entrant each; lives=3 set before the
fall-through; the $ffff empty-word is the head's alone).

The vector-page pin landed and CORRECTED the registered claim: with
both pools seeded full, the spawn stamps EIGHTEEN bytes over $0..$1f
(ten fields: both reset vectors, bus-error high, address-error low,
all of illegal-instruction, TRAPV low), not 32. Writing better code —
testing the allocator before the spawn — reddens the cases.

The four-word spawn header below the table pointer is named from its
other users (the death decrement at $6c3e makes -6 the live count);
the hitpoint seeder is a difficulty ramp (half the kills + per-type
base, fields named from $6b46/$6bfa). Fifth 68000 doc lesson: the
lea at $ff8c carries extension word $0000 — the long index the lsl
built is discarded, sign-extended low word taken (41f0 0000 vs the
.l-form 2372 0800 in the callee); prg_dis's idx(An) rendering hides
exactly this and is now on the doc's known-gaps ledger.

Test: 559 new cases in scope (suite 2146; committed tree 2159 with
the audio battery). Mutations 41: 40 killed, 1 order-equivalence.
First sweep found a do/while hole (closed by an empty-table case) and
the gate's fix round added a capacity-crossing/pool-exhausting sweep
case that one mutation is killed ONLY by. Four encoders hoisted per

events.title: recreate_kit: opt-in audio-capture mode — the oracle can drive a PSG replayer
events.message:
recreate_kit: opt-in audio-capture mode — the oracle can drive a PSG replayer

The differential deliberately refuses PSG reads and answers hardware reads
as 0; an asset extractor needs the opposite. emu.audio_capture(True) serves
three reads: the $ff8800 register-file read-back (a 16-byte YM2149 model fed

profile bytes are refused, not fabricated; the PSG ledger now counts dropped
writes and run() sinks a truncated capture; harness.differential() vets the
mode off — a leaked capture can no longer false-green a differential.

latch persistence, $ff8802/data-port + odd-alias + word-wide refusals, and
the differential vet; 1 joust case pins the mixed-path guard on the served
read. Mutation sweep: data-port serve, fused clear-on-arm, per-run latch
reset all die. Suites: wonderboy 1600, joust 4369, kit 131, buggyboy 292.

leaf.py gains the two byte-op emitters; names.txt the tick-drop var.

events.title: engine: the #161 hold froze the Merchant chain — arm it only for a walk step
events.message:
engine: the #161 hold froze the Merchant chain — arm it only for a walk step

Shipped in v0.9.4-beta, reported from real hardware the same day: "the second
screen from the Merchant, when you hit enter, it seems the game freezes (I
think that is when it normally tries to load the treasure screen)."

It does, and it is the event-tail present hold from af8149bf. The repair half
of that hold lives in l63c0's per-step re-render, so it is only safe where that
re-render is guaranteed to follow. The area-ENTRY chain (jt948/jt953 -> l709e)
is not such a place: the HEIRS caravan pages run and hand off to the
give-treasure modal without ever reaching the step render, so a hold taken in
l4d26's tail was released by nobody, every later present was swallowed, and the
display stopped while the engine ran on behind it.

Reproduced in one drive (autoload.dat onto a HEIRS save): the caravan hand-over
page takes the Return — the button visibly highlights — and nothing advances;
ten seconds later the frame is byte-identical. The A/B settles the attribution
outright: the same drive on a -DFRUA_NOEVHOLD build goes straight to "EACH
CHARACTER RECEIVES 100 EXPERIENCE POINTS", and the fixed build now produces
that frame BYTE-IDENTICAL to that control.

Three changes:

  - g_event_step_ctx: the hold arms ONLY inside the walk step's event dispatch,
    the one context that provably reaches the release.
  - l4d26 drops any outstanding hold on entry, so a chained event cannot draw
    under the previous one's.
  - l1806 drops it too — that is the "Press RETURN to continue" wait, and the
    rule it encodes is the general one: NEVER WAIT FOR THE PLAYER BEHIND A HELD
    FRAME. That is exactly what "the game freezes" looks like from the chair.

Both behaviours verified on the Falcon. The Merchant chain now runs through to
the treasure pile with VIEW|TAKE|POOL|SHARE|EXIT; and the #161 case this hold
exists for is still fixed — a burst capture of a step onto an unprompted text
square goes typing -> settled with no blank-box, no-command-bar intermediate,
and the settled frame matches the known-good hash.

A hold whose release lives in a different function than its acquire is only as
safe as the narrowest path between them, and the cost of getting that wrong is
not a flicker — it is a frozen game.

446 host tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

events.title: Fix diagonal scrolling corrupting the split row
events.message:
Fix diagonal scrolling corrupting the split row

DrawColumn writes all 8 scanlines of every row it touches, including
display row 0 - which is the split row, where scanlines 0..line-1
belong to map row mapYr+16 rather than mapYr. A column redraw
overwrote them. Those scanlines are invisible at the time, so the
damage only surfaced once `line` wrapped and that row rotated round
to the bottom of the window, which is why it read as mess being left
behind rather than a column drawn wrong.

DrawColumn now repairs its display-row-0 cell from mapYr+16 after
the main loop, via DrawHalfPart.

RedrawAll had the same blind spot, and that mattered beyond the bug:
it is the diff oracle, so every byte-clean result so far had been
blind to exactly the region where this class of bug lives. It now
applies the same repair across all 80 units, making a full redraw a
true repair at any scroll position and the oracle valid at any value
of line.

Verified at line = 3, where the split row is live: diagonal
right+down and diagonal left+up both 0 of 10240 bytes differing.

Note recorded in PLAN.md: the oracle must be allowed ~1,500,000
cycles to settle after releasing SPACE. RedrawAll plus its split
pass runs longer than that, and sampling it mid-redraw shows display
row 0 rewritten by the main loop but not yet repaired - which looks
exactly like the fix having failed.

Reverse engineered from the Atari ST game. The title track is not YM2149

channel 8-bit sample mixer at 19200 Hz that uses the YM's three volume

its data is packed into MIDIMAZE.CMP.

Contents:

events.title: Layer 3d: smooth vertical scrolling at 1-scanline granularity
events.message:
Layer 3d: smooth vertical scrolling at 1-scanline granularity

Vertical steps drop from 8 scanlines to 1, using R5 (vertical total
adjust) to give the playfield cycle `line` extra scanlines and take
them back from the cycle above it, so the frame total stays at 312.
Three CRTC cycles now, not two: with only two, the variable adjust
falls between VSync and the panel and the panel slides while
scrolling. A third tail cycle carries VSync so both adjusts sit
after the panel, where they cancel.

Buffer row 0 is a split row holding two map rows at once, in
disjoint scanline ranges, so a step costs one 80-byte scanline strip
rather than a 640-byte row. DrawRow is deleted along with the defect
it produced three times.

Hard-won details, all recorded in PLAN.md:

- R4/R5 belong to the cycle that samples them; R6, R7 and R12/R13
  must be written during the PREVIOUS cycle. Writing R7 at the row
  it should fire on means VSync never happens and the chip
  free-runs.
- Never write R5 near a cycle boundary. The vertical adjust compares
  a rising count against R5, so changing it after the count has
  passed runs the adjust on to its 5-bit wrap.
- The display window must fit inside ONE hardware wrap: the address
  translator subtracts once when MA12 goes high and does not
  iterate. 16 displayed rows is therefore the ceiling with the 10K
  wrap, so the play area is 15 visible rows - 320x120, not 320x128.
- Blank/unblank via CRTC R8 skew bits must land in horizontal
  blanking or it cuts a scanline part-way across. T1_PROBE measures
  the phase by cutting the solid panel box.

Verified by diffing the buffer against RedrawAll: 0 of 10240 bytes
differing across up, down, and mixed runs at odd mapHX with scrollS
wrapped mid-row. Frame confirmed at exactly 312 scanlines by
counting 1000 VSyncs in 39,936,000 cycles.

events.title: Widen the scroll redraw window and fix diagonal CRTC ordering
events.message:
Widen the scroll redraw window and fix diagonal CRTC ordering

Release the main loop when the play area stops displaying rather than
at VSync. The play area is frame rows 8-23 and the panel draws from
&4800, so writing the play buffer while the panel shows is safe. That
makes the usable window rows 24 to 8 of the next frame - 24 rows,
against about 23 for a worst-case redraw. Releasing at VSync (row 34)
gave only 13 and was overrunning every step.

T1s three fires have to land in different windows and one period cannot
do it: cycle 1 setup needs rows 0-7, cycle 2 setup rows 8-15, and the
redraw release rows 24-26. The latch is therefore rewritten during fire
1; T1 reloads its counter at underflow, so the write takes effect one
reload later, keeping fire 2 at 8 rows while moving fire 3 out to 13.

SetCRTCStart is now called once, after all key handling and before any
drawing. Previously each Scroll routine parked the address itself, so
on a diagonal move the second ones park landed after the first ones
redraw - past frame row 3, where the IRQ latches R12/R13. The CRTC then
used an address missing one axis while the buffer held the combined
position, giving one frame of wrong graphics on the trailing edge. The
scroll routines now only set flags and DoRedraws does the drawing.

Redraws run in raster order: row 0 first since it displays at frame row
8, then the columns spanning rows 8-23, then row 15 which is not shown
until row 23. A diagonal does two redraws in one window, so the tightest
has to go first.

Adds a DEBUG_DRAW build flag that tints the background for the duration
of the redraw, making the scanlines it occupies visible. That is what
measured the window; the redraw is ~23 rows, not the ~14 previously
estimated. Off by default.

Corrects the record on the DrawRow defect. It was characterised as unit
39 onward after an odd offset; both halves are wrong. A diagonal diff
found it corrupting units 2-78 with mapHX even. Every column and every
other row matched a full redraw exactly, so DrawRow alone is at fault.
Diagonal movement calls it every step, so the artifact is now permanent
rather than occasional. PLAN.md recommends reverting DrawRow to the
pre-optimisation version, which diffed byte-clean twice.

events.title: Layer 3c: vertical rupture - static panel above scrolled play area
events.message:
Layer 3c: vertical rupture - static panel above scrolled play area

Two CRTC cycles per TV frame. Reprogramming R4 mid-frame ends a cycle
early and the next reloads VMA from R12/R13, so each cycle has its own
screen start:

  cycle 1  static panel  R4=7   8 rows   R6=5   R7=255  &4800/8
  cycle 2  scrolled play R4=30  31 rows  R6=16  R7=26   (&5800+scrollS)/8
                                -------
                                39 rows = 312 scanlines

Cycle 1 shows 5 rows of panel then 3 blank - the title-plus-gap the C64
has above its play area. VSync lands at frame row 8+26 = 34, which is
MODE 1's default R7, so the TV sees an identically phased frame.

Three things were needed to make the split hold steady, and the first
two were wrong before KC spotted them:

Interlace off (R8=0). The OS leaves MODE 1 at R8=1, interlace sync,
which offsets VSync by half a scanline on alternate fields. Fixed
intervals measured from VSync then land the split in a different place
every other field.

System VIA T1 in continuous mode, not T2. T2 is one-shot only, so the
interval starts when the handler writes T2C-H and every interrupt's
service latency feeds into the next interval - jitter accumulates. T1
continuous auto-reloads from its latch at underflow, so the period is
exact however late we are serviced. VSync restarts it to keep the
stages phase locked.

IRQ1V taken over outright, nothing chained, so the MOS handler never
runs ahead of ours adding latency. Costs the MOS 100 Hz tick and with
it MOS sound. Keyboard is unaffected (OSBYTE &81 scans the matrix
directly) and the filing system is only needed before takeover, so
*LOAD now runs before InstallIrq. Both VIAs have every interrupt source
disabled except System VIA CA1 and T1; anything unserviced would hold
the IRQ line asserted. The MOS saves the interrupted A in &FC but not
X or Y, so the handler saves those itself.

Both stage interrupts deliberately land 3 rows inside their cycle
rather than on the boundary, leaving ~4 rows clear of the deadline
(C4 reaching the old R4).

SetCRTCStart no longer writes R12/R13 - the IRQ owns them - so it
computes the address and parks it, with SEI around the store.

Adds a DEBUG_RASTER build flag that tints the background at entry to
each interrupt, making the scanline each one lands on visible. That is
what diagnosed the margin problem; reasoning from the timing numbers
had led the wrong way. Off by default.

events.title: Optimise vertical scrolling; fix two DrawHalf/DrawRow bugs
events.message:
Optimise vertical scrolling; fix two DrawHalf/DrawRow bugs

Vertical scrolling is now frame-locked, matching horizontal: 10 steps
in 10 frames, up from 4.

Two changes. Replacing the SetCell add-640 loop with lookup tables
moved vertical 4 -> 5, so that loop was not the dominant cost - that
diagnosis was wrong. The win came from rewriting DrawRow to hoist what
is constant across a row: cellY does not change, so the tile-map row
base and sub-row offset are computed once rather than 80 times, the
tile pointer only moves every 4 characters, and the character code is
fetched once per PAIR of units because a character is two 4-pixel
halves. DrawRow no longer calls DrawHalf/MapChar and reuses their zero
page.

Fixed: DrawHalf computed halfX >> 1 by shifting halfX+1 in place and
restoring it with ASL, which only works when the low bit was 0. Only
RedrawAll walks halfX incrementally, so the damage was written at deck
load and then persisted, because incremental scrolling only redraws
edges and never repairs the interior. Triggers when mapHX+79 crosses
256 - decks 2 and 14.

Fixed: on a row starting at an odd unit, DrawRow's right-half path read
chp before it had ever been set, drawing a stale character in the
leftmost column. chp is now primed by FetchChar before the loop.

KNOWN DEFECT, accepted for now: after scrolling to an odd unit then
scrolling vertically, the last row DrawRow drew is wrong from unit 39
onward - where its 6th tile begins. 41 cells, confirmed against both
RedrawAll and the tile map directly, so DrawRow is at fault. Root cause
not isolated. See PLAN.md for the revert option.

Adds a debug key (SPACE) that forces RedrawAll, so the incremental
buffer can be diffed against a full redraw at the same position. That
is what isolated both bugs. Note that two earlier runs of that harness
reported zero differences and were worthless: both used an even number
of horizontal steps, so the odd-column path never executed.

events.title: Go direct to hardware for palette and vsync
events.message:
Go direct to hardware for palette and vsync

Removes both OS calls from the main loop.

Palette: SetPalette writes the video ULA palette register &FE21
instead of going through VDU 19. The register takes
(logical << 4) | (physical EOR 7), and the logical field is a
content-addressable match - in a 4-colour mode only bits 7 and 5 are
compared, so bits 6 and 4 must be written in every combination or the
colour comes out split. All 16 entries are written, each mapped back
with logical = ((n AND 8) >> 2) OR ((n AND 2) >> 1), giving four
entries per logical colour and covering 0-15 exactly.

VSYNC: IrqHandler sits at the head of IRQ1V, counts fields and chains
on to the OS so its timers and keyboard scan keep working. Polling the
System VIA IFR bit 1 directly would race the MOS, whose own handler
services vsync and clears that flag before a poll is likely to see it.

Verified: palette output identical to the VDU 19 version, and
horizontal scrolling still measures exactly 10 steps in 10 frames.

keydown still uses OSBYTE &81. Replacing it means driving the keyboard
matrix directly, which contends with the MOS scan in its IRQ handler,
so it belongs with a full IRQ takeover rather than done piecemeal.

events.title: Layer 3b: CRTC hardware scrolling with edge redraw
events.message:
Layer 3b: CRTC hardware scrolling with edge redraw

Play area verified against the C64: DrawScreen writes to $4940, which
is $140 past the $4800 screen base, so character row 8, and draws 17
rows by 39 columns. That includes the fine-scroll margin, so the
visible area is 38x16 chars = 304x128 px = 9.5x4 tiles.

Rounded up to 10x4 tiles = 320x128. 10240 bytes is exactly 16 rows of
640, and the BBC supports a 10K wrap natively - System VIA addressable
latch lines 4 and 5 both high select subtract $2800, restart $5800 - so
both axes wrap cleanly. Rounding up rather than down also avoids
narrowing the play area.

The buffer is a circular strip, not a flat grid: display cell (row,
unit) lives at BUF_BASE + ((scrollS + row*640 + unit*8) MOD 10240). The
CRTC gives a one-dimensional scroll through linear memory, so a
character leaving the left reappears one row up on the right. Drawn as
a flat grid that is corruption, and it scales with the offset - at 80px
the right quarter shows the wrong rows. Treated as a circular strip it
is just where the next column lives, and a step costs 16 cells
horizontally or 80 vertically instead of a ~640 character full redraw.

A MODE 1 CRTC unit is one byte per scanline = 4 pixels, and characters
are already stored as two 8-byte halves, so a 4-pixel column is exactly
one stored half-character. Sub-character horizontal scrolling needs no
pre-shifted data.

WaitVSync (OSBYTE 19) puts both R12/R13 writes and the edge redraw in
the blanking window. The two writes form a 14-bit value; a CRTC sample
landing between them would show a frame at a half-updated address.

Measured over 10 frames with the key held: horizontal 10 steps,
vertical 5. Replacing the SetCell add-640 loop with lookup tables took
vertical from 4 to 5, so that loop was not the dominant cost - that
diagnosis was wrong. OSBYTE 19 quantises to whole frames, so vertical
is sitting just above the one-frame boundary and crossing it jumps
straight to 10. MapChar is the likely remaining cost: it rebuilds the
tile-map row base per cell, which for DrawRow is constant across all 80.

Source split into screen.asm (buffer addressing, DrawHalf, MapChar,
RedrawAll), scroll.asm (scroll directions, SetCell, offset tables) and
level.asm (deck decode, charset build, palette, framing). Data moved to
&3000: the OS believes the screen is &3000-&7FFF but only &5800-&7FFF
is now fetched for display.

events.title: Fix $D023, and confirm multicolour ALERT lettering is faithful
events.message:
Fix $D023, and confirm multicolour ALERT lettering is faithful

$D023 was set to 6 (blue) on a guess when I could not find where the
play area sets it. Tracing every write: the only character-mode writes
to $D022/$D023 are in DrawSideview ($308A/$308F), setting $F1/$F0, and
those persist into gameplay. The other hits in that area are +3/+4/+$C,
which are the sprite multicolour registers, not the character ones. So
$D023 is 0 (black). Having it wrong corrupted every multicolour cell on
every deck.

$D021 remains an assumption. It comes from bgColor, which
SetIntroColors loads from slot 3 of the deck record, but slot 3 does not
match the lavender floor in the reference screenshot - so gameplay sets
it somewhere not yet found. 14 is taken from the screenshot and is
marked [assumed] in export_bbc.py.

The joined ALERT letters are faithful, not a port bug. Row 0 of tile 22
is the lettering and sits on palette slot 7, which is multicolour under
8 of the 16 deck schemes - 4 pixels wide, so single-pixel letter gaps
cannot exist. The C64 renders it the same way. Keeping fidelity for now
rather than forcing those characters to hires.

New tools/compare_tile.py renders a tile side by side, C64 against port,
which is what settled this. analyse_alert.py was checking row 1 rather
than row 0, so it reported every deck as fine while eight of them drew
the letters in multicolour; it now checks the lettering itself and
distinguishes faithful joining from an actual port bug.

events.title: Correct the tile format: hires and multicolour cells are mixed
events.message:
Correct the tile format: hires and multicolour cells are mixed

The tiles are neither 1bpp hires (first assumption) nor wholly
multicolour (second). $D016 bit 4 enables multicolour text mode
globally, but within that mode the choice is made PER CELL by bit 3 of
the colour RAM nibble: 0-7 renders hires, 8-15 renders multicolour. For
deck 1 the split is 930 hires cells to 190 multicolour.

That is why the ALERT lettering keeps single-pixel letter spacing while
the floor still carries four colours - a 4-pixel-wide multicolour
character could not produce the former. Much of the apparent richness is
per-cell colour rather than multicolour: adjacent hires cells with
different foregrounds read as a multi-coloured tile.

The mode is driven per character code by CharColor ($0800), whose upper
nibble is a palette slot. NewCharColors ($3577) rewrites the lower
nibble per deck from a 12-slot record at $6A44 selected by
deckColorScheme ($F160), and BuildLevel writes that byte to colour RAM.
Only slot 5 is multicolour in every scheme and only slot 11 is hires in
every scheme, so a character's mode genuinely changes between decks.
charset.asm is therefore built for deck 1 only; PLAN.md records
generating it at deck-load time as the way to cover all sixteen, which
needs less data than one converted charset.

export_bbc.py now selects the mode per character and assigns MODE 1
logical colours from measured usage across the tile set rather than by
assumption - for deck 1: 0 floor, 1 white highlight, 2 red shadow,
3 yellow grid. verify_bbc.py decodes back mode-aware, skipping
characters whose colours collide and so cannot be distinguished.

New tools: analyse_charmode.py dumps the slot/mode analysis,
rip_deck_mixed.py renders a deck as the C64 actually displays it, and
rip_tiles_mc.py renders the tile set as pure multicolour. Note the
colour records at $6A44 number 8, not 16 - entries past that hold values
above $0F and so are not colour data.

Palette is now blue floor, white highlight, black shadow, magenta grid.
ref/ is gitignored alongside the other original-game material.

events.title: Layer 3a: map browser - scroll by character, switch decks
events.message:
Layer 3a: map browser - scroll by character, switch decks

Z/X/K/M scroll the viewport one character at a time; UP/DOWN switch
deck. Full-screen redraw per step, no hardware scroll yet. This proves
DrawScreen renders correctly from an arbitrary map origin, which is the
prerequisite for the CRTC scroll in 3b.

DrawScreen generalised to a (charX, charY) origin over the 256x64
character map. The row base is cheap because tilemap is page aligned
and 1K: lo = (tileRow AND 3) << 6, hi = HI(tilemap) + (tileRow >> 2).

Deck keys are edge triggered. A blocking wait-for-release deadlocks:
hold UP before releasing DOWN and it spins forever, swallowing the
press.

CentreOnDeck frames a deck on load, since decks sit at varying offsets
in the grid and a (0,0) origin lands in empty padding. Uses the
centroid of non-empty tiles rather than the bounding box - several
decks are two clusters far apart, and the midpoint of the extremes
falls in the gap between them. Division is by repeated subtraction; the
quotient cannot exceed 63 and this runs once per deck change.

Code moved to &1100 rather than DFS PAGE of &1900: &1100-&18FF is
random-access file buffer space that simple *LOAD never touches. 2K
reclaimed.

Measured: a full-screen redraw is ~466,000 cycles, about 11 frames, so
roughly 4 scroll steps per second. plot_char dominates at ~256 cycles
for its 16-byte copy. That is the number 3b has to beat by beating
redrawing only the leading column - 25 characters instead of 1000.

Confirmed INKEY codes: Z -98, X -67, K -71, M -102, UP -58, DOWN -42,
with *FX 4,1 to stop the cursor keys doing cursor editing.

events.title: Layer 2: static deck render
events.message:
Layer 2: static deck render

BuildLevel RLE-decodes a deck into a tile map; DrawScreen renders the
viewport from it.

Divergence from the C64: the original expands every tile into a 256x64
character map at $8000 (16K). We keep only the 64x16 tile map (1K) and
expand tiles to characters at draw time - two extra lookups per
character against a ~100 cycle 16-byte copy, for a 15K saving. Scrolling
redraws only the leading edge, so that overhead lands on a column of 25
characters rather than the whole screen.

Code and data now build as two disc files. VDU 22 makes the OS clear
what it still believes is its screen, &3000-&7FFF, so data loaded above
&3000 was wiped before BuildLevel could read it. PARADAT is *LOADed
after the mode change instead. The eventual fix is to program the video
ULA and CRTC directly rather than going through VDU 22.

verify_bbc.py --tilemap diffs a tile map dumped from the emulator
against a fresh Python RLE decode. Decks 1 and 3 both match all 1024
bytes, with non-empty counts agreeing with level_stats.txt. Deck 3 was
picked deliberately: its RLE lives above &3000 and so exercises the
clear-on-mode-change bug, where deck 1 sits below &3000 and rendered
identically either way.

events.title: Layer 1: graphics data pipeline
events.message:
Layer 1: graphics data pipeline

tools/export_bbc.py converts the C64 data to BeebASM sources in
src/data/: the $7800 charset to MODE 1, plus tile definitions, deck
maps and metadata carried over byte-identical.

The 1bpp -> MODE 1 conversion turns out to be a nibble split. MODE 1
holds pixel n low colour bit in bit 3-n, so storing the foreground as
logical colour 1 makes the left four pixels of a scanline (b >> 4) and
the right four (b & 0x0F). Two things fall out of that: per-deck
recolouring is a palette change rather than baked into the tiles,
mirroring the C64 CharColor table; and a character is 16 contiguous
bytes, so plotting one is a flat 16-byte copy with no shift or mask.

src/main.asm now renders all 32 tile definitions as an 8x4 sheet,
matching tools/output/tiles.png. tools/verify_bbc.py independently
round-trips the generated data back to C64 form and diffs it against
the listing - 5/5 checks pass.

src/data/ is gitignored: it is converted game artwork and level data,
so the same copyright position as tools/output/. Regenerate it with

events.title: engine: saved characters become <design>.DSN\SAVE\<NAME>.CCH
events.message:
engine: saved characters become <design>.DSN\SAVE\<NAME>.CCH

The last save-interop gap, and it was ours. Both original releases keep saved
characters as <NAME>.CCH in the design's SAVE folder — DOS demonstrably, and
the Mac through jt584, which builds design + "SAVE" + name + "cch" via jt431
and has been lifted in this tree the whole time. The slot-numbered
CHAR0000.CHR in the flat gamedata folder was this port's 8.3 workaround from
before that path existed, not a 1.0-vs-1.2 or Mac-vs-DOS difference.

The name goes through the faithful jt130 — strip the 17 filename-hostile
characters at A5 -31268, truncate to 8, uppercase — which is exactly DOS's 8.3
rule: LADY ILLIS -> LADYILLI.CCH, STRANILLA -> STRANILL.CCH. The list still
shows the full name; that comes from rec[96] inside the file.

The two formats turned out to be identical. A DOS BARBARUS.CCH and our
CHAR0000.CHR are both 506 bytes with the name at offset 96, so nothing had to
be converted — only named and filed correctly.

Verified in BOTH directions on the Falcon. A DOS-authored BARBARUS.CCH dropped
into HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\ appears in ADD A CHARACTER and joins the party at the
AC -3 / HP 62 the DOS release itself shows for it; and after our engine had
rewritten that file, DOS FRUA still lists it in its own Add screen.

Existing installs migrate on first boot: when the SAVE folder holds no .CCH the
loader falls back to the flat CHAR*.CHR and immediately writes the roster out
under the new names (all six HEIRS characters, verified). The old files are
left in place — a failed migration that also deleted the source would be
unrecoverable.

★ THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO SWEEP OF THE SAVE FOLDER. The old save_roster
deleted every CHAR*.CHR it had not just written, which was safe because it
owned that namespace. It does not own this one: DOS- and Mac-authored
characters live in the same folder, and "delete what we did not write" would
destroy them. Each pool slot now remembers the file it owns and drops only that
file when the character is renamed or deleted.

Two things this turned up on the way:

  - the Add-a-Character list is fed by l01be enumerating FILES, not by the
    in-memory pool. So a migrated roster looked EMPTY until something wrote the
    new files — the pool was full and the folder was not. Hence the immediate
    save after a migration read.
  - my own truncation bug cost a boot: l01be built its open path with a 19-char
    cap sized for a bare 8.3 name, so "HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\BARBARUS.CCH" was cut to
    "HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\BARB", FSOpen failed, and the list rendered as a blank box
    — indistinguishable from "no such file" until the pattern and the read were
    traced separately.

Also fixes cg_roster_merge_files, which required a 512-byte read of a file that
is ~506 bytes: the test could never pass, so that merge has been silently dead.
It now scans the SAVE folder and requires only enough bytes to hold the record.

446 host tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: vault: the format was never unknown — and we were writing it to the wrong place
events.message:
vault: the format was never unknown — and we were writing it to the wrong place

Asked to "figure out the VAULT<c>.DAT files". They are already figured out:
`jt74` (read) and `jt75` (write) are full lifts, and the port has been writing
the file since long before anyone looked — into the FLAT gamedata folder, which
is exactly why nobody noticed. `VaultA.DAT`, `VaultB.DAT` and friends have been
piling up at the root next to frua.rsc while their saves lived in the design
folder. They now follow the slot into <design>.DSN\SAVE\, through the same
design_save_path() the slot files use (jt583 load, jt586 save).

Layout, now written down in docs/vault-format.md: 12 bytes of little-endian
money, a 4-byte header (0xFFFF sentinel + item count), then one 18-byte record
per item, then padding from the item-template table. Item kind 73 is a bundle
whose members follow inline, so the header counts top-level items only.

The Mac pads to 200 records and DOS to 50 — verified both ways (`cmpiw #200` at
CODE 6 + 0x63f0 in the disassembly; a DOS-written VAULTF.DAT is 916 = 12 + 4 +
50*18). It makes no difference to reading: jt74 takes the count from the header
and never touches the pad.

Which is the real result here: DOS SAVES LOAD AS THEY ARE. A DOS-written
SAVGAMA.CSV (10 285 bytes) + VAULTA.DAT (916) dropped into HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\
loaded through PLAY -> LOAD SAVED GAME -> A with all six characters and their
AC/HP (BARBARUS, LADY ILLIS, MALTIER, NIVLOC, CLARANA, STRANILLA); saving to
slot B then wrote SAVGAMB.CSV + VaultB.DAT beside them. The one-byte length
difference does not obstruct it — the deserializer is field-driven.

Also settles a question that was asked as "1.0 vs 1.2, or Mac vs DOS?": the
character-file naming is NEITHER. Both releases use <NAME>.CCH in the design's
SAVE folder, and the Mac's jt584 — already lifted — builds design + "SAVE" +
name + "cch" through jt431. `CHAR0000.CHR` in the flat folder is the PORT's own
8.3 workaround, and it is now the only real save-interop gap left.

446 host tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

events.message:
engine: put saves where SSI puts them — <design>.DSN\SAVE\SAVGAM<c>.CSV

The port wrote "<design>.DSN\SavGam<c>.csv": right folder, missing the SAVE
level, and mixed case. DOS FRUA 1.2 writes into the design's SAVE subfolder in
upper case, which is now what we do.

Not inferred — driven. `tools/dosdrive.sh` took the DOS release headlessly
through PLAY -> Add BARBARUS -> SAVE CURRENT GAME -> slot F, and it produced:

    HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\SAVGAMF.CSV   10 285 bytes
    HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\VAULTF.DAT       916 bytes

★ That drive is the whole commit, because the file system LIED. A pair of
DOS-written SAVGAMA.CSV / VAULTA.DAT sits at a design ROOT in the staged
gamedata, which made the flat layout look confirmed; they had been moved there
by hand at some point. Watching the program write a file beats reading where a
file happens to be.

The SAVE folder is created on demand: GEMDOS Fcreate will not make it and
neither will AmigaDOS Open(), so a first save into a design that had never been
saved would just fail, and l00e0 reports that as "couldn't write" with no clue
why. DirCreate treats an existing directory as success on both backends, so
savgam_dir_ensure() is idempotent. The design-name cap drops 31 -> 26 chars to
keep the longer path inside the smallest caller buffer (fn[44]).

Upper case because that is what DOS writes: TOS and FAT do not care, but the
Amiga and any host-side staging do, and a name differing only in case works
everywhere except the machine that matters.

Verified live on the Falcon: Hall -> SAVE -> slot F wrote

events.title: falcon: the quit teardown DOES run — and make the desktop restore selectable
events.message:
falcon: the quit teardown DOES run — and make the desktop restore selectable

The dark-blue-desktop-on-exit report is still live on hardware with both
previous fixes in. This round did not fix it; it made it diagnosable, and
settled three things that were quietly wrong.

**The teardown runs.** The user's DBG.LOG simply stopped at "menu: modal up"
after a clean quit, which reads like no shutdown at all. Reproduced headlessly,
then traced: the main menu's QUIT reaches jt415 -> ExitToShell, so `ua_main`
never returns and none of main()'s markers ("main: ua_main rc =", "main:
shutdown ok") are ever written. ExitToShell now logs both sides of its teardown,
so a log can say which door was used.

**The number I asked the user to send could not have existed.** `videl_init:
old mode = NNN` is logged BEFORE dbg_log_screen_owned(), i.e. to the console —
which the screen takeover then paints over. Asking for it out of DBG.LOG was
asking for a line the file never contains. It is now repeated into the file
after the switch, with the new mode beside it. Measured here: old mode = 162
(STMODES|PAL|BPS4), new mode = 36 (PAL|BPS16).

**An emulator cannot answer this.** Hatari never draws a desktop before an
auto-started program, so the desktop it shows afterwards is not evidence about
our restore — already paid for once, when a pale-green shifted desktop was
reported as a reproduction and turned out to be Hatari's own `--auto` path.

That leaves a real hypothesis and no way to test it here. VsetScreen
reinitialises the VDI but NOT the AES (Compendium p.290), so restoring the
saved palette after it can leave the desktop drawing the VDI's fresh notion of
an index against a palette we forced back to something else — which is exactly
the reported symptom: right layout, wrong colours. Whether the palette should
go before, after, or not at all is genuinely not obvious.

So `video.cfg` takes a second token, `exit=full|vdi|palfirst|mode`, and
DBG.LOG records which ran and the mode word being restored. That turns an
untestable guess into four one-line experiments on the machine that has the
problem. Default is `full` — today's behaviour, so nothing changes for anyone
who does not opt in. A file containing only `exit=` leaves the mode automatic.

Also fixes the COL_INQUIRE redefinition warning (mint/falcon.h defines it too).

events.title: engine: the event text really was drawn twice — hold the frame across the tail
events.message:
engine: the event text really was drawn twice — hold the frame across the tail

Reported from real hardware, twice: an unprompted square-text event (the "THE
WEARY WANDERER" kind, no [RETURN] prompt) "starts to print it out, stops, then
prints the whole thing along with a frame redraw", plus "a few extra, quick
redraws around encounters".

The 5 Hz-present fix (6543b358) was right about the typewriter and did not
touch this. There IS a second draw, and diffing the QuickDraw surface stage by
stage across one event on the Falcon says exactly where:

  l4d26 types the text        rows 136..166 arrive glyph by glyph (a burst
                              capture shows T, TH, THE W, THE WEA ... so the
                              per-glyph present is working)
  l4d26's tail runs jt23()    the play screen is recomposed: the text box goes,
                              and so does the command bar
  play_sticky_text_replay()   redraws every line AT ONCE — its before/after
                              diff is byte-identical to the whole-message diff
                              (136:148 137:102 138:86 ...), i.e. the box really
                              had gone blank again
  the step's relayout+jt312   repaints rows 187..197, ~300 of 320 pixels per
                              row: the command bar

Eight full presents fall between the last glyph and the settled frame (present
census), so all of that is on screen. Held side by side, the A/B is plain: the
control run goes typing -> BLANK BOX WITH NO COMMAND BAR -> settled, and the
fixed run goes typing -> settled, with the same final pixels (AE = 0).

The engine's own frame bracket cannot coalesce this, because the wipe happens
inside l4d26 and the repair one call frame up in the walk loop's re-render. So
the hold spans exactly that: l4d26 takes it before the jt23 refresh, l63c0
drops it once the bar is back, and releases on every other way out of an
iteration so it can never outlive the step. Release discards the held
intermediate, so the step then owes a port_present_full() — a single present
would seed one flip page and leave the other showing the pre-event frame.

Also: the typewriter's own present was capped at one per TWO ticks. One per
tick is the real ceiling (nothing faster is visible), and the fell-behind
return above it already governs the fast case by measurement rather than by a
constant. Slow machines are untouched — they take that early return.

Two things worth recording, both of which cost a build:

  - THE FIRST FIX I MEASURED MY WAY INTO WAS WRONG. The pool is bit-for-bit
    identical across an unprompted text event (13 items in, 13 out), so gating
    the relayout on "did the event disturb the DLItem pool" looked exactly
    right — and shipped a dungeon with no command bar. The relayout is not
    repairing the pool there, it is repairing the BAR.
  - the instrument that found it also nearly hid it: it bucketed every changed
    row from 136 down as "text box", so a command-bar repaint reported as a
    text repaint. Rows 136..186 are the box and 187..197 the bar; the probe
    now says which.

tools/mk_texttest_design.py is the fixture — confirm_mask=0 is what selects
the sticky arm, so the existing kobold message (confirm after every line) does
NOT reproduce this. Build with -DFRUA_EVFRAME for the per-row diffs and
-DFRUA_NOEVHOLD for the control arm.

Verified on the Falcon: unprompted text (sticky, bar intact), prompted text
(clears on Return, bar back), and a step onto a combat square through to the
treasure screen and back to a live command bar. 446 host tests pass; ST/68000,
Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all still link.

events.title: fix(test): make m68k-floppy's TempDir names collision-free (#26)
events.message:
fix(test): make m68k-floppy's TempDir names collision-free (#26)

* ci(release): drop the source archive and per-file checksums

#24 landed with 11 assets per release. Two of those categories are
redundant.

The source archive: the source is identical for every platform — the
target is a compile-time switch, not a separate codebase — so shipping it
per release adds nothing, and GitHub already attaches "Source code (zip)"
and "Source code (tar.gz)" to every release automatically. Ours only
added two more entries that look like they mean something different from
the two already there.

The per-file .sha256: exactly the same bytes as the corresponding line in
SHA256SUMS. One combined file is enough — `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`
checks whatever the user downloaded in a single pass.

That leaves the four files a release actually needs: three platform
archives and one checksum file. The checksum step now also excludes
SHA256SUMS by name rather than by pattern, so a re-run cannot end up
checksumming its own output.

Also drops the checkout from the publish job, which was only there to
give `git archive` a work tree.

Verified locally against the published v2.1.0 archives: SHA256SUMS
verifies, and verifies again after regenerating it a second time.

* fix(test): make m68k-floppy's TempDir names collision-free

The macOS CI job has been failing on every run since the platform matrix
landed, while Linux and Windows stay green. Two tests in adf.rs fail with
"No such file or directory" and a missing error string — but the code
under test is fine; the test helper is not.

Four modules (adf, uae, ipf, factory) each carry a copy of the same
TempDir helper, all producing names of the form

    m68k_floppy_test_<pid>_<nanos>

Rust runs these tests as threads in a single binary, so the pid is
identical across all of them and uniqueness rests entirely on the
timestamp. Where SystemTime resolves finer than a nanosecond that holds;
where it does not — macOS runners, in practice — two concurrent
TempDir::new() calls can produce the *same* path. Whichever finishes
first then drops, and its Drop deletes the directory the other test is
still using. The failure surfaces in whichever test lost the race, which
is why it looked like an adf.rs bug.

Measured, not assumed: replaying the old scheme with the timestamp
rounded to microseconds produces 983 duplicate names out of 1600 across 8
threads; at nanosecond resolution it produces none, which is exactly why
this never reproduced on Linux.

Uniqueness now comes from a per-module atomic counter instead of the
clock, and each module gets a distinct prefix so the four helpers cannot
collide with each other either. Same replay with the counter: 0
duplicates.

Verified: 30 consecutive runs of `cargo test -p m68k-floppy --lib
--test-threads=16` with no failures, plus the full 612-test suite green.

---------

events.title: ci(release): produce the complete asset set in one run (#24)
events.message:
ci(release): produce the complete asset set in one run (#24)

The release workflow built three platform archives and uploaded each from
its own matrix job. Everything else a release needs — checksums, source
archives, stripping — was left to be done by hand afterwards, and a
mid-matrix failure could leave a half-populated release with no single
place to notice it.

Now one tag push yields the finished release:

- Source archives (.tar.gz and .zip) via `git archive` on the tag, so they
  are reproducible and honour .gitattributes, unlike GitHub's generated
  tarballs.
- A .sha256 next to every asset plus a combined SHA256SUMS, verified with
  `sha256sum -c` in the same job that wrote them — a bad upload candidate
  fails there rather than at whoever downloads it.
- Binaries stripped on Linux and macOS (~0.5 MB off the Linux archive).
  Windows MSVC keeps debug info in a separate .pdb that is not shipped, so
  there is nothing to strip.
- README and LICENSE inside each archive; an archive of bare executables
  says nothing about its own terms.
- Version in the archive names (m68k-v2.1.0-<target>) so downloaded files
  stay identifiable.

Publishing moves into a single `publish` job that collects the matrix
output as artifacts, so the release either gets the complete set or fails
visibly. `fail-fast: false` on the build matrix keeps a break on one
platform from hiding the state of the others.

Each build job also smoke-tests its binaries before packaging: assemble a
two-instruction source, check the exact bytes, pipe it back through the
disassembler. That catches an archive of binaries that cannot run at all,
which a successful `cargo build` does not.

Verified by running the packaging, source-archive and checksum steps
locally against the v2.1.0 tag: checksums verify, and the stripped
binaries still assemble and disassemble correctly after unpacking.

events.title: docs: correction — DOS FRUA IS fully keyboard-drivable; and its save is 10,285 B
events.message:
docs: correction — DOS FRUA IS fully keyboard-drivable; and its save is 10,285 B

Retracting a claim I made one commit ago (edcb2587). I wrote that "FRUA's DOS
menus are MOUSE-ONLY" and put it in the driver's header and the DOS-reference
note. That is wrong, and the user said so.

Verified with no mouse at all: `p c d <name> d y a Down a e b` goes from the
main menu into the dungeon, and `e s <slot> n l` drives camp — the same
accelerators as the port.

What fooled me: pressing `l` at the Hall did nothing, so I concluded the key
was dead and switched to clicking. The picker was simply EMPTY. With no save on
disk it returns without painting anything, exactly as the port's jt582 does
(`if (g_a5_24126[0] == 0xFF) return;`). With a save present, `l` opens it. My
own transcript already contradicted the claim — `p` had driven PLAY THE GAME
two steps earlier — and I did not look. A silent control is not a dead control:
check its preconditions before blaming the input path.

The mouse helpers stay in the driver for controls with no accelerator, but the
header now says to reach for `key` first.

New finding from the same session, and the more useful one: **the DOS save is
10,285 bytes; the port writes 10,284.** The 10 284 figure quoted throughout
these notes came from the Mac side. Dropping a port-written SAVGAMB.CSV into
DOS's SAVE folder and opening the camp picker lists only the DOS-made slot A —
DOS will not enumerate ours. Supplying a VAULTB.DAT alongside does not change
it, so the per-slot vault file is not the gate; the save itself is. 1360 bytes
differ overall, mostly party content, but the LENGTH is the cheap suspect and
the first thing to check if cross-loading is ever wanted.

Nothing about the camp SAVE/LOAD conclusion changes: DOS still lands in the
Training Hall after a camp LOAD, which is what the port does.

events.title: tools: dosdrive.sh — drive DOS FRUA headless; camp LOAD settled against it
events.message:
tools: dosdrive.sh — drive DOS FRUA headless; camp LOAD settled against it

The question was whether camp LOAD should resume the dungeon or land in the
Training Hall. Reading the Mac said Hall; the report from real hardware said it
felt wrong. SSI's own DOS 1.2 build is the arbiter, so it got driven end to
end: roll a fighter, Begin Adventuring, ENCAMP -> SAVE -> slot A ->
"EXIT PLAY?" -> NO, then ENCAMP -> LOAD -> slot A.

DOS LANDS IN THE TRAINING HALL with the loaded party — exactly what the port
does. Nothing to change on that leg; the SAVE leg fixed in 632bfd92 was the
whole of the reported bug.

Three things had to be learned to drive it at all, and they are in the script's
header so the next session does not re-learn them:

  - FRUA's DOS menus are MOUSE-ONLY. The letter accelerators that drive the
    Mac/port builds do nothing here — pressing `l` at the Hall did nothing,
    clicking the same control opened it.
  - the captured mouse is delta-driven AND ACCELERATED: the host->screen ratio
    measured 0.92/0.78 on one move and 0.99/0.88 on the very next, so a
    computed jump does not land. Every click closes the loop instead.
  - the cursor is found by its YELLOW (255,255,85), largest blob. Bright cyan
    is useless as a signature — the title screen paints 6685 pixels of it.

Two format findings from the same run, recorded in docs/save-load-wall.md and
worth acting on separately:

  - DOS keeps saves in `<design>.DSN\SAVE\` — SAVGAMA.CSV and the character
    .CCH files all land there. The port flattens them into the design folder,
    so saves do NOT interchange between DOS FRUA and the port in either
    direction. The Mac built the same `<design>:SAVE:` path.
  - DOS writes a per-slot `VAULTA.DAT` beside SAVGAMA.CSV that the port never
    writes at all. Relevant to the vault event (l3a32).

Also a parity signal in the port's favour: the "Game not saved, load anyway?"
confirm did NOT appear on that camp LOAD because the save had just happened,
which is exactly the port's -27946 gate.
