events.title: chore: declare MSRV, widen CI, and close out the P2 quality items (#22)
events.message:
chore: declare MSRV, widen CI, and close out the P2 quality items (#22)

Works through plan.md P2 (P2.1 through P2.6) plus P1.5.

MSRV (P2.3): declared as 1.88 in [workspace.package], inherited by all
five crates. Determined empirically rather than guessed — 1.87 fails with
E0658 on the let-chains in m68k-core, 1.88 stabilized them. The upper edge
was checked too: the full test/clippy/fmt chain is green on 1.97.1, the
current stable. cargo now reports "requires rustc 1.88" instead of a
cryptic compiler error. No rust-toolchain.toml: it would pin every
contributor to one version and override the MSRV job in CI, making it
useless.

CI (P2.4): `build` becomes a matrix over ubuntu/windows/macos with
fail-fast disabled, so a platform-specific break stays distinguishable
from a real regression. Build and test run everywhere; fmt, clippy and the
release artifacts only on ubuntu, since they are platform-independent.
Two new jobs: `msrv` (cargo check on 1.88.0) and `audit`, the latter
continue-on-error because the advisory database changes independently of
this repo and a new entry must not turn unrelated PRs red.

Silent unwrap_or(0) (P2.2): all 14 sites assessed individually. One real
bug: `REPT $ZZ` with a malformed hex count became `REPT 0` and dropped the
block body without a word, while the reference assembler rejects it
outright (verified empirically: we emitted 2 instructions instead of 3,
silently losing the NOP). Passing the line through was not enough --
`rept` is a known name in is_directive_name and lands in a no-op arm,
which would have assembled the body once, unguarded. It now reports a
real diagnostic. The other 13 are legitimate and are now documented as
such, including a debug_assert on the S-Record checksum helper whose
input is hex by construction.

CNOP (P2.6): argument evaluation, validation and the padding formula move
into `Assembler::cnop_padding`, called by both passes instead of being
written out twice. Validation deliberately re-runs per pass, because a SET
symbol as the alignment can change value between them. Adds the regression
test for that case, which plan.md described as tested but which did not
exist.

Golden vectors (P2.5): decided to keep them frozen. The snapshot's value
is that it does not move — it predates several audits and so catches
regressions that the encoder and a freshly regenerated expectation would
agree on. Documented in golden_assembler.rs, instruction_coverage.rs
(named as the authoritative suite) and AGENTS.md.

P1.5 turned out to be moot: m68k-floppy no longer has a --cpu flag at all.

Verified: 612 tests green, clippy and fmt clean, byte parity unchanged at
11/11 and 13/13 against the reference assembler, fuzzing clean on
assembler_pipeline and disassemble.

events.message:
docs: sync documentation with the actual tool and endpoint surface

The docs had drifted from the code in ways that break for users:

- 15 MCP tool names in the README were missing their runtime_ prefix
  (send_key, mute, ping, toggle_fullscreen, …), so callers would use
  names the server rejects. Tool coverage is now 133/133, and the
  duplicated list_configs row is now runtime_list_configs.
- Three curl examples pointed at routes that do not exist:
  /runtime/toggle-rtg, /runtime/toggle-status-line and
  /runtime/toggle-mouse-grab are /runtime/rtg, /runtime/status-line
  and /runtime/mouse-grab.
- /roms/identify was documented as POST with a JSON body in all three
  docs; it is GET with a rom_path query parameter.
- Clone URLs and [project.urls] pointed at github.com/midwan/
  amiberry-mcp-server, which does not exist. Repointed to BlitterStudio.
- 23 HTTP endpoints were undocumented in the README (the /process/*
  group, /health, /logs/tail, /runtime/memory/*, /runtime/active-instance,

events.title: feat(cli): implement stdin/stdout support promised by the README (#21)
events.message:
feat(cli): implement stdin/stdout support promised by the README (#21)

README.md documented `-` as standard input for both `m68k-disasm` and
`m68k-asm`, but neither tool implemented it — both aborted with
`cannot read '-': No such file or directory` (plan.md P1.3).

- `m68k-disasm <input>`: `-` now reads the image from stdin as raw bytes.
  Hunk executables are not valid UTF-8, so this deliberately does not go
  through a text read.
- `m68k-asm <input>`: `-` reads the source from stdin. There is no
  filename to derive an output path from in that case, so `-o` becomes
  required rather than silently writing to a file named after `-`.
- `m68k-asm -o -`: writes to stdout for *every* format. Only the binary
  format handled this before; srecord/intel-hex/elf/ieee695/hunk-exe
  called `fs::write` unconditionally and created a file literally
  named `-`.

Diagnostics now say `<stdin>`/`<stdout>` instead of `-`.

Also corrects the `m68k-disasm` options block in the README, which
listed five flags that do not exist (`--org`, `-x/--hex`, `-u/--upper`,
`-s/--symbols`, `-out/--output`), gave the wrong short form for
`--address`/`--raw`, and named the wrong `--cpu` default (68000, not
68060) for both tools.

New `crates/m68k-cli/tests/stdin_stdout.rs` (7 tests) drives the real
binaries via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_*` — the CLI wrappers had no test coverage
at all until now. One test asserts the stdin path produces byte-identical
output to the file path.

Verified: byte parity unchanged (11/11 and 13/13 against
vasmm68k_mot -no-opt), fuzzing clean on assembler_pipeline and

events.title: fuzz: cover AmigaDOS filesystem, fix OOM and two unbounded pointer chains (#20)
events.message:
fuzz: cover AmigaDOS filesystem, fix OOM and two unbounded pointer chains (#20)

amigados.rs and adf_writer.rs had no fuzz coverage at all — notable,
since both of the July 2026 filesystem bugs lived there. Adding a target
found three robustness defects, all reachable from a corrupt disk image.

The target builds a structurally valid disk (correct size, DOS bootblock,
root block of the right type) and lets the fuzzer corrupt everything
inside it. A purely random byte array is rejected by mount's signature
check and never reaches the traversal code; a first attempt that only
XOR'd over the block area plateaued at 311 edges because random pointers
fail the sec_type check and every chain ends after one hop. Planting a
handful of valid headers and wiring them into the root's hash buckets
raised it to 535 edges with the corpus still growing.

Fixed:

* read_file sized its output buffer straight from the header's byte_size
  field. A header claiming 0xFF000000 made it request 4 GB from a 901 KB
  image. Now bounded by the disk's own capacity.

* The file extension-block chain was followed without a bound. A block
  whose extension pointer refers back to itself loops forever — not a
  panic, so no fuzzer timeout would have caught it as a crash either.

* The directory hash chain had the same problem, in both list_dir and
  find_entry.

All three bounds derive from the disk's block count: no legitimate file
is larger than its disk, and no chain can be longer than the number of
blocks, since each link occupies a distinct one.

Verified: the OOM reproducer now completes in 6 ms, 181k further fuzz
iterations clean, all 981 files across the eight Workbench 1.3/3.1 disks
still list correctly, Workbench integration tests green, byte parity
unchanged (12/12 and 13/13), 603 tests passing (was 600).

The new target runs in CI alongside the other six.

events.title: fix: PFLUSH and PLPAR/PLPAW roundtrip, add MMU coverage (#19)
events.message:
fix: PFLUSH and PLPAR/PLPAW roundtrip, add MMU coverage (#19)

The instruction_coverage suite had a group named "68030+/MMU/cache" that
contained no MMU instruction at all — PMOVE, PFLUSH and PTEST had zero
roundtrip coverage. Adding it surfaced two bugs immediately.

* The disassembler had no case for the EA-less `PFLUSH #fc,#mask` form
  (extension word mode 100). It fell into the three-operand branch, which
  read an EA field the opword does not have, and rendered
  `PFLUSH #0,#0` (F000 3010) as `pflush #0,#0,d0` — an invented operand
  that then failed to reassemble.

* PLPAR/PLPAW were encodable but not decodable: the CACHE pattern's
  0xFC00/0xF400 mask covers their opcodes and precedes them, so
  `plpar (a0)` (F5C8) came back as `cinvl bc,(a0)`. Added dedicated
  patterns ahead of CACHE plus a Plpa parser. Their opcode bases, marked
  "unverified" in the encoder, are now confirmed against a reference
  assembler: PLPAR F5C8, PLPAW F588, register in bits 2-0.

* `PFLUSH (An)` — the 68040 single-operand form — was rejected by the
  operand-count check. Reference encoding F508; the encoder already had
  enc_mmu_single_reg, it just wasn't reachable.

Coverage: 19 MMU forms (PMOVE both directions for TC/SRP/CRP/TT0/TT1/
MMUSR, all three PFLUSH spellings, PTESTR/PTESTW with and without An),
plus PLPAR/PLPAW and the 68040 PFLUSH forms, all as byte-for-byte
roundtrips.

Verified: all 19 MMU forms byte-identical to a reference assembler, cache
instructions unaffected (14-form roundtrip identical), byte parity
unchanged (12/12 and 13/13), 600 tests passing, 165k fuzz iterations on
the disassembler clean.

events.title: engine: camp SAVE -> "Exit Play? YES" dropped back into the dungeon
events.message:
engine: camp SAVE -> "Exit Play? YES" dropped back into the dungeon

Reported from real hardware, against DOS: "(E)ncamp, (S)ave, pick a slot,
Exit Play? YES, this takes you to the main menu". On the port it went back to
the dungeon, and the only way out was (E)ncamp -> (L)oad, which exits as a side
effect of the load path.

The Mac's post-camp decision (CODE 20 L4cda) is:

    tstb -27982 ; beqw L4be8    -- clear: keep playing (inner loop)
    tstb -27982 ; beqw L4a1a    -- clear: reload the level
    clrb -27982 ; <walk party list> ; if (L4738) JT[582] ; rts

The lift turned that second test — redundant, of the shape THINK C emits —
into `if (l4738() == 0) continue`, which is a different predicate entirely.
Camp case 6 sets -27982 but NOT -4944, so l4738() read 0 and the loop went
round again. Camp case 5 (Load) additionally calls jt942(1), which is the ONLY
reason exiting via Load appeared to work.

With the flag as the predicate, as the asm has it, both camp exits leave jt948
and l4738() decides only whether the slot picker opens on the way out.

Verified live: ENCAMP -> SAVE -> slot J -> "Exit Play? YES" now lands on the
main menu and writes HEIRS.DSN/SavGamJ.csv (10284 bytes). The LOAD leg still
leaves play with the A/B/J picker up, unchanged.

Normal camp EXIT cannot be affected: in a dungeon camp the menu is rows 0-6
plus 8 (row 7 is filtered out when -18485 is clear), EXIT is row 8, and row 8
never sets -27982 — so the ENCAMP arm `continue`s and never reaches the changed
code. The one behaviour that does change is a res==6 stairs swap arriving with
the flag clear: it now continues to the outer level reload (the Mac's L4a1a)
instead of falling through and ending play. Not driven live.

Also narrows the ST-palette restore added last commit to ST-COMPATIBLE modes.
Those registers are "simulated for compatibility on newer model machines"
(Compendium p.740), so writing them on a Falcon reaches VIDEL colour registers
0..15 — the range a desktop lives in. In a native Falcon mode VsetRGB has
already restored all 256 with more precision and the 4-bit ST words would only
degrade them. Hatari's TOS 4 desktop is mode 434 (BPS|VGA|PAL|STMODES|VERTFLAG),
so the ST path is still the one exercised there; the clean-exit check is
unchanged at 268 differing pixels of 390,096, all in the free-space text.

events.title: engine: the typewriter presented at 5 Hz, so text arrived in jumps
events.message:
engine: the typewriter presented at 5 Hz, so text arrived in jumps

Reported from real hardware: "it starts to print out 'The wandering traveller'
... it gets to about 'the wandering trav' then it redraws and finishes."

There is no redraw. Nothing presents during a typewriter run: the glyphs go
into the QuickDraw buffer and the only thing putting them on screen is the
idle-visibility concession inside jt1134, rate-limited to one present every 12
ticks. So the text does not type — it arrives in chunks at 5 Hz, and the last
chunk completes the word. The faster the machine, the more characters per
chunk, which is why an accelerated Falcon shows it plainly.

The present is added in l435a, the slow-text pacer, and specifically AFTER the
"have we fallen behind" test. That placement is the whole design: the branch is
only reached when t <= target, i.e. when the pacer is about to burn the rest of
the glyph's interval in its busy-wait, so the present spends time the engine
was already giving away. A machine that has fallen behind returns earlier and
never reaches it, so the slow case is exactly what it was — which matters,
because the 12-tick limit was measured into existence for the 8 MHz ST, where
a present costs more than a tick and presenting per glyph starved the engine.

Measured over 60 glyphs of the same message on both ends:

              glyphs  behind  slack  presents added
  Falcon 030      60      32     27      27
  STE 8 MHz       60      58      1       1

The machine the limit protects gets ONE extra present; the fast machine gets 27
where it had none.

Two things this cost, both worth recording:

  - the first instrument LIED. Logging tick stamps per glyph with dbg_file_num
    is an Fopen/Fwrite/Fclose each, which made the pacer fall behind on every
    glyph and produced a tidy "5 glyphs per 12-tick present" that was mostly my
    own logging. In-memory counters dumped once give the numbers above.
  - the present needs l4d88() first. The glyph is drawn before l435a is called,
    but its rows are not ANNOUNCED until the pending InvalRect is flushed —
    which is the first thing jt1134 does. Without the flush, qd_dirty_any()
    reads false here every time: measured 0 presents at the new site, jumps
    completely unchanged, looking exactly like the fix not working.

events.title: platform: let the player pick the Falcon video mode (video.cfg)
events.message:
platform: let the player pick the Falcon video mode (video.cfg)

Requested from real hardware: "it still doesn't really do a resolution
check/change", and on being asked, specifically the ability to choose rather
than have the engine decide from the monitor type alone.

One token in `video.cfg` beside the binary:

  auto (or absent)  from the monitor type, as before
  rgb200            RGB/TV timing — 320x200, NO letterbox, on ANY monitor
  vga240            VGA + double-line: 320x240, 20-line bands
  vga480            VGA, no double-line: 320x480, 140-line bands
  0x<hex>           a raw VsetMode word

rgb200 is the point of the exercise: `auto` will never choose an RGB timing on
a VGA monitor, so there was no way to ask for the unletterboxed frame even on a
monitor or scaler that would sync it. Measured on both monitor types:

  auto   vga -> 320x240 letterbox 20      auto   rgb -> 320x200 letterbox 0
  rgb200 vga -> 320x200 letterbox 0       rgb200 rgb -> 320x200 letterbox 0
  vga240 vga -> 320x240 letterbox 20      vga480 vga -> 320x480 letterbox 140

★ THE TOKENS NAME A MODE WORD, NOT A GEOMETRY. The first cut of this offered
"320x200" and "320x240" as if they were monitor-independent; measured, they
produced 320x480 on VGA and 320x400 on RGB, because VERTFLAG means opposite
things on the two — it halves the vertical resolution on VGA (480->240) and
doubles it on RGB/TV (200->400). There is no 320x200 VGA mode, which is exactly
why a VGA Falcon letterboxes at all. Renaming them after what they select is
the honest fix.

A forced mode still has to give a 320-wide frame with at least the engine's 200
lines — a shorter one would drive g_top_border negative — and falls back to the
automatic choice with the width and height logged if it does not. So a wrong
line in video.cfg cannot leave an unusable display, and a 0x<hex> experiment on
a real monitor documents itself in DBG.LOG.

events.title: platform: restore the video mode through VsetScreen, and the ST-compat palette
events.message:
platform: restore the video mode through VsetScreen, and the ST-compat palette

Two gaps in the Falcon exit path, both against the documented contract. Found
chasing "it doesn't drop out cleanly to TOS (turned my screen to a dark blue)"
from real hardware. NEITHER IS REPRODUCED — see the caveat below.

1. The VDI was never reinitialised for the restored mode. "VsetMode() does not
   reset the video base address, reserve memory, or reinitialize the VDI. To do
   this, use VsetScreen()" (Compendium p.289) — and the VsetScreen that
   followed passed SCR_NOCHANGE for both mode and modecode, so it only moved
   the bases. Replaced the pair with one VsetScreen(log, phys, SCR_MODECODE,
   saved), the form that does reinitialise the VDI and the VT52 emulator
   (p.290).

2. The ST-compatible 16-colour palette was never saved or restored. In an
   ST-compat mode — which a TOS 4 desktop usually is — the colours come from
   the ST/e palette registers at 0xFF8240, not the 256-entry VIDEL palette that
   VgetRGB/VsetRGB reach. Snapshot with Setcolor(i, COL_INQUIRE), which reads a
   register without changing it (p.274), and restore with Setpalette().

★ CAVEAT, because I got this wrong once already this session: I could NOT
reproduce the user's symptom. What I first took for it — a desktop coming back
pale green and shifted up with its menu bar cut off, on --monitor vga — turned
out to be Hatari's own `--auto` desktop: pointing --auto at a NONEXISTENT
program, with frua never running at all, produces the identical green and the
identical offset. So these two changes are grounded in the documentation, not
in a reproduction, and the real machine is what can confirm them.

What is verified is no regression: the case that already exited cleanly (RGB
monitor, plain boot) comes back byte-identical bar the free-space counter —
248 differing pixels of 390,096, all in the "bytes used" text and the cursor.

events.title: engine: the AREA map transposed every wall — l54f2 passed its coords in reverse
events.message:
engine: the AREA map transposed every wall — l54f2 passed its coords in reverse

Reported from real hardware: on the automap "there appears to be walls where
there are none, and [I] was prevented from moving forward where it looked like
a hallway, but was in fact a wall, which I could see when in 3d view."

The 3D view and the movement code were right; the automap was wrong. All four
Mac call sites in L54f2 push `dir`, then fp@(8), then fp@(10) — and 68k C
pushes RIGHT TO LEFT, so the LAST push is the FIRST argument. L5484 therefore
receives (fp@10, fp@8, dir), the reverse of the order L54f2 got them in. The
lift passed them straight through, which transposed the whole map.

Two independent facts pin which coordinate is which, so this is not a guess —
and this is the file where guessing has shipped a regression before
(v0.5.12-beta, see the map-axis-pairing note):

  - L50fe clamps the OUTER (screen-Y) loop count with lvl[2] = WIDTH and the
    INNER (screen-X) count with lvl[3] = HEIGHT. Those only pair correctly if
    screen-Y walks COLUMNS and screen-X walks ROWS. Under the old reading the
    clamps were crossed; under this one they are exactly right.
  - the scroll origins agree independently: -12278 is clamped against lvl[2]
    in l5368 and used as the COL in `ds[3]*(-12278) + (-12276)` (~18330),
    while -12276 is the row. L50fe adds -12278 to the outer index.

So the automap really does run columns down the screen, and the port's only
job was to stop transposing it. Fixed by renaming l54f2's parameters to what
they actually are, which makes the existing l5484(maprow, mapcol, dir) calls
correct; no call-site order changed.

Verified live on HEIRS from the same save both ways. Before: a dense lattice
with a wall bar immediately east of the party, where the 3D view shows open
corridor. After: coherent corridors, and stepping east moves one cell and then
stops at 10,9 with a wall drawn immediately east of the marker — matching the
3D view, which shows a stone face dead ahead.

events.title: media: Gotek/FlashFloppy images — the ST engine raw, and ALL data on one disk
events.message:
media: Gotek/FlashFloppy images — the ST engine raw, and ALL data on one disk

A Gotek running FlashFloppy is not bound by the floppy capacities this
pipeline was designed around, and the assumption that it was is now wrong in
two places (mkhwdist.sh's header, HARDWARE.md's "why the Mega ST disk is
compressed").

The trick is not a faster disk. A stock ST's WD1772 is locked to 250 kbit/s
and nothing changes that. FlashFloppy slows the emulated ROTATION instead, so
more sectors pass the head per revolution at the same bit rate, and it serves
up to 255 cylinders rather than 80. Geometry and rpm figures are from
phjanderson/flashfloppy-atari-disks.

Two new artefacts:

  openua-st-gotek-<v>.st       80 x 2 x 18, 150 rpm, 1.44 MB
      The 68000 engine RAW — no PC-side unzip. The 720K zipped disk stays for
      anyone with a real drive, since this one is Gotek-only.

  mkdatadisks.sh gotek         255 x 2 x 36, 75 rpm, 9.4 MB
      The ENTIRE data set on ONE image instead of six. Measured: ART=tlb is
      97 files / 4.37 MB with 4.6 MB spare; even ART=both fits at 120 files /
      7.73 MB with 1.19 MB spare.

Capacity numbers are MEASURED from the BPB mformat emits, per this pipeline's
existing rule: 512-byte sectors, 4096-byte clusters, 512 root entries, 18360
total sectors, 2289 clusters — under FAT12's 4085-cluster ceiling, so TOS
still sees FAT12.

mkhwdist.sh now also writes IMG.CFG next to the images. Without it FlashFloppy
recognises standard floppy sizes only and neither image mounts.

Verification is uneven and HARDWARE.md says so: the 1.44 MB Gotek ST image was
BOOTED on an emulated stock ST (`--machine st`, TOS 2.06 — the 68000 engine
autostarts from it), but the 255-cylinder image cannot be tested in Hatari at
all. Hatari decodes standard floppy geometries only; a 2.35 MB 255-cylinder
image mounts and then autostarts nothing, while a standard 1.44 MB one on the
same command line boots fine. So the big one is verified as a filesystem, not
by booting it.

events.title: docs: the Falcon conout log ends at videl_init BY DESIGN — not a hang
events.message:
docs: the Falcon conout log ends at videl_init BY DESIGN — not a hang

Chasing a reported "the engine stalls when you boot it off the floppy image"
turned up no stall. The engine initialises completely from the disk:

  videl_init: buffers 3 / vbl flip 1 / lutblit asm ok / done (16bpp LUT)
  main: display up / sound chip locked / shim up
  main: frua.rsc loaded, bytes = 67213
  data_pool: runtime replay bytes = 31336, relocs = 1026

...and then stops, because the 1.44 MB delivery disk has no game data and the
minimum install is ~7.4 MB. It is the same black screen you get running from a
hard disk with the data missing — confirmed with that control.

What made it look like a hang is that `dbg_log` has TWO sinks and swaps
between them: Cconws until the display takes the screen, then DBG.LOG.
`dbg_log_screen_owned()` does the swap immediately after the `words/row` line,
so on EVERY healthy Falcon boot the conout log ends exactly there and the rest
of the trail is in $GEMDOS_DIR/DBG.LOG. Booted off a floppy there is no
DBG.LOG either — Fcreate("DBG.LOG") fails on that path — so the run leaves no
trail at all and reads as a stall.

Recorded in the run-falcon-port skill (including how to get the full trail on
the console: comment out dbg_log_screen_owned and build with the RELEASE flags,
since a dev frua.prg is 4.6 MB and will not fit on a 1.44 MB disk) and in

events.title: engine: boot auto-load as an opt-in port option (autoload.dat)
events.message:
engine: boot auto-load as an opt-in port option (autoload.dat)

"Boot auto-load" had sat in save-load-wall.md as the last open save/load item.
It is not a faithfulness gap — the Mac has no such thing, checked three ways:

  * the whole binary holds exactly three "SavGam" string references, and all
    three are in CODE 15's INTERACTIVE save/load (jt582's picker, jt585's
    save). No boot path names a slot.
  * the port's own boot auto-load, port_load_savgame, was retired ON PURPOSE
    in 2026-07 under direction (B) of docs/play-entry-wall.md.
  * start.dat's second field, which jt128's comment calls "the resume flag",
    is really -18476: the packed area (mode, kind) nibble pair that jt275
    writes and l4810 reads. The comment guessed.

So what ships is a convenience, opt-in and off by default: one byte — the slot
letter A..J — in "autoload.dat" beside the game data. It resolves against the
current design (so it follows start.dat), fires at most once per run, and the
load itself is not a new path: it is exactly what jt582 does after the player
picks a slot (l143e + the position-restore tail), with only the picker skipped.
That reuse is why it resumes at the SAVED cell rather than the design entry.

It runs at play-entry, in l07dc, not at the boot seed — running l143e at the
seed was tried in 2026-06 and reverted, because -28006 is not live until
ua_main's l4cc0 has run. ua_main additionally skips the main menu for the first
pass, but ONLY when the slot actually opens, so a dud configuration leaves the
faithful boot alone instead of stranding the player in a menu-less Hall.

Two things this walked into, both now in the docs:

  * skipping jt315 also skips load_menu_ui, and then every scrap of HUD text
    is invisible — roster, coords, clock, labels — because port_hud_text_clut
    bails on g_menu_state != 1 and the dungeon's clut 129 leaves the text
    indices grey-on-grey. Chrome and the 3D view render perfectly, so it reads
    as a font bug. frua_areatest_entry already had the call for the same reason.
  * with the option armed, the harness marker "menu: modal up" never fires.
    Wait for "autoload: resumed" instead.

Verified zero-key into the dungeon on the Falcon and on Amiga AGA, with the
party restored and the HUD fully painted. tests/test_autoload_boot.py covers
armed / dead-slot / unarmed; both assertions mutation-checked (dropping
load_menu_ui gives 140 cyan pixels vs 1032; dropping the slot probe loses the
menu fallback).

events.title: harness: fix Amiga input — windowactivate needs a WM the Xvfb doesn't have
events.message:
harness: fix Amiga input — windowactivate needs a WM the Xvfb doesn't have

The Amiga port looked like it couldn't take input: clicks positioned the
pointer on a button and nothing happened, keys did nothing, and the save/load
round-trip stalled at 3 of 5 ports with AGA and ECS unverified.

It was the driver. `xdotool windowactivate` drives EWMH _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW,
which a bare Xvfb (no window manager) does not support. The driver chained it
into a single invocation — `windowactivate --sync $w key p` — so the failure
aborted the whole chain and the keystroke was never sent, silently. The same
chain wrapped `start`'s mouse-capture click, so the emulated mouse was never
grabbed either; the "pointer moved but the click didn't commit" symptom was
the driver's own position bookkeeping, not the emulated pointer.

`windowfocus` sets the X input focus directly and needs no WM. With that,
keys and clicks both commit, and AGA + ECS complete the save/load round-trip
exactly like Falcon/TT/ST — party restored from slot B, then into the
authored dungeon. ECS also wrote a save from camp (SavGamC.csv, 10284 bytes,
46 bytes different from the fixture).

Second harness bug, found on the way: flatpak's x11 socket sharing rewrites
DISPLAY inside the sandbox, so `--env=DISPLAY=:99` was ignored and the window
kept opening on the user's desktop. Only the launching shell's DISPLAY counts.

Also recorded in SKILL.md: the drive is keyboard-only and therefore portable
(p / l / slot letter / b), and a committed click on the 7 MHz ECS build can
take ~30 s to paint — which reads exactly like a dropped click.

events.title: perf(core): ~2,4x plus rapide a sortie octet-identique (callgrind + PGO/LTO)
events.message:
perf(core): ~2,4x plus rapide a sortie octet-identique (callgrind + PGO/LTO)

Campagne d'optimisation menee au callgrind sur un profil de boot TOS et un
profil en jeu. Mesure a recette IDENTIQUE (meme script build_native_pi.sh,
meme machine, code d'origine reconstruit dans un worktree propre) :

  boot TOS 1.62, 500 trames : 0,80 s -> 0,31 s   (x2,6)
  Enchanted Land, 900 trames: 1,63 s -> 0,67 s   (x2,4)

Soit -37 % venant du code et -34 % de la recette de compilation, qui se
multiplient. Mesures faites sur x86 : la transposition au Cortex-A72 du Pi
400 est une EXTRAPOLATION, pas une mesure (aucun Pi n'a ete utilise ici).

Aucune valeur emulee ne change : 15 etalons pixel-exacts a 0 pixel d'ecart
apres chaque etape, auto-tests verts, et les variantes de compilation
verifiees octet-identiques sur des captures de 6801 et 29500 trames.

Cote code
- Bus : le decodage MMU ($FF8001) etait refait a CHAQUE octet (12,8 M
  d'appels pour 300 trames). Memorise et revalide par comparaison de ses
  deux seules entrees (octet de config, taille de ram[]) plutot que par une
  invalidation posee aux sites d'ecriture. read8/read16/write8 passent dans
  l'en-tete. La 1re version ne couvrait que la RAM et ne rendait que -4 % :
  le code du TOS s'execute depuis la ROM, ajoutee au chemin rapide -> -20 %.
- Scheduler : le balayage chaud etait nextDue() dans la boucle de trame, pas
  celui qu'on croyait. Supprime plutot qu'accelere (minimum calcule pendant
  la passe de dispatch, cache nextDue_ rendu EXACT -> O(1)). Une variante
  sans branche a ete essayee puis retiree : +1,4 % d'instructions.
- Shifter : de-entrelacement des bitplanes par table (8 px par operation 64
  bits, independant du boutisme) ; palette convertie 16 fois par ligne au
  lieu d'une fois par pixel.
- busFaultN et busDiag : deux appels gratuits retires du chemin chaud.

Cote build (packaging/raspberry)
- build_native_pi.sh --pgo, pgo_train.sh et pi-borne.yml compilent en deux
  passes guidees par profil puis avec LTO. PGO seul -20 %, +LTO -34 %.
- Piege documente et verrouille : GCC nomme les .gcda d'apres le chemin de
  l'objet, donc deux repertoires de build differents ne trouvent AUCUN
  profil, et -Wno-missing-profile rend l'echec muet. Une premiere mesure
  annoncait ainsi -4 %, qui n'etait que du bruit. Les scripts echouent
  desormais si aucun profil n'est collecte pour Cpu68k/Bus/Shifter/Moira.

Methode, mesures ligne a ligne et fausses pistes : docs/PERFORMANCE.md

events.title: fix(borne): garantir que NeoST attende PipeWire, et lire l'utilisateur au lieu de le deviner [skip ci]
events.message:
fix(borne): garantir que NeoST attende PipeWire, et lire l'utilisateur au lieu de le deviner [skip ci]

Deux défauts trouvés en relisant le mode Bluetooth avant de graver la carte :

1. ORDRE DE DÉMARRAGE. Si le service kiosk démarre avant que pipewire-pulse de
   l'utilisateur ait ouvert sa socket, miniaudio échoue sur le backend
   PulseAudio et RETOMBE SUR ALSA — il essaie les backends dans l'ordre. NeoST
   serait alors cloué sur l'HDMI pour toute la session et l'enceinte Bluetooth
   ne recevrait jamais rien : tout le mode BT serait vain, sans message
   d'erreur. Drop-in systemd (mode BT uniquement) qui fige XDG_RUNTIME_DIR et
   attend la socket au plus 20 s, sans jamais échouer — une borne doit démarrer
   même sans son. Repasser en HDMI supprime le drop-in, sinon chaque démarrage
   traînerait 20 s pour rien.

2. neost-bt.sh devinait l'utilisateur de la borne (défaut « neost ») alors qu'il
   doit parler au pipewire-pulse de CET utilisateur via sudo -u +
   XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. install_kiosk.sh écrit maintenant NEOST_KIOSK_USER dans
   /etc/neost-kiosk.conf, y compris quand le fichier existait déjà.

+ README : section « sortie son » (HDMI par ELD vs A2DP), et mode binaires
pré-compilés récupérés depuis la CI plutôt que 20-40 min de compilation sur le Pi.

events.title: feat(borne): Raspberry Pi qui démarre directement sur NeoST + latence audio réglable
events.message:
feat(borne): Raspberry Pi qui démarre directement sur NeoST + latence audio réglable

Le Pi 400 de la borne saute le son par à-coups. Deux causes possibles, que NeoST
distingue DÉJÀ dans sa sortie d'erreur (`[Audio] underrun anneau … XX trames/s
réelles`) : boucle d'émulation trop lente (CPU), ou gigue d'ordonnancement.
Cette série s'attaque aux deux.

--audio-latency MS (persisté `audio_latency_ms=`) : le coussin d'amorçage de
l'anneau audio était figé à 85 ms dans Audio::start. Réglable, borné [20,250]
par Audio::setLatencyMs — au-delà on s'approcherait de la capacité de
SampleRing{32768} (341 ms à 48 kHz stéréo) et le producteur jetterait des
échantillons à chaque trame. Vérifié bout en bout (CLI et neost.cfg).

packaging/raspberry/ : la borne proprement dite. X NU sur le VT 1 par systemd
(ni gestionnaire de fenêtres ni compositeur — une recopie plein écran par trame
en moins), gouverneur `performance` (Pi OS met `ondemand`, d'où le hachage
périodique), IRQ épinglées sur le cœur 0, swap et services inutiles coupés.
install_kiosk.sh est idempotent et réversible (--uninstall, sauvegardes
.neost-orig des fichiers de démarrage).

Audio : le Pi 400 n'a PAS de jack, c'est HDMI ou Bluetooth.
 · par défaut, aucun serveur de son (ALSA en direct) et détection de la sortie
   HDMI réellement branchée via l'ELD — le Pi 400 a deux ports ;
 · --bluetooth-audio installe PipeWire, seul chemin vers l'A2DP : miniaudio ne
   sait pas parler Bluetooth. Ce qui rend le mode possible SANS toucher au code,
   c'est que miniaudio classe PulseAudio AVANT ALSA (ma_backend est ordonné par
   priorité) : NeoST se branche sur pipewire-pulse, qui déplace le flux vers
   l'enceinte quand elle se connecte, même en pleine partie. 48 kHz verrouillé
   (NeoST sort déjà en 48 kHz → aucun rééchantillonnage), profils HSP/HFP coupés
   (une enceinte qui bascule en HSP passe en 8 kHz mono).
   neost-bt.sh + timer de reconnexion : l'enceinte allumée APRÈS la borne est
   rattrapée toute seule, cas normal en exposition.

Deux pièges refermés dans les scripts plutôt que dans un ticket : miniaudio
demande SCHED_FIFO pour son thread ALSA et ÉCHOUE SILENCIEUSEMENT sans
LimitRTPRIO= (le thread audio reste préemptible → underruns) ; le libglfw3 de
bookworm est X11 uniquement, ce qui exclut un kiosk Wayland (cage) sans
recompiler GLFW. Et un garde-fou refuse de couper le Wi-Fi quand c'est le seul
lien réseau — se priver de SSH sur une borne sans écran de service.

CI : workflow pi-borne.yml (workflow_dispatch) qui compile dans un conteneur
debian:bookworm sur runner ARM64 natif avec -mcpu=cortex-a72, vérifie le
plancher glibc <= 2.36 et publie un tar.gz de binaires. Compiler sur le Pi
prend 20-40 min ; provision.sh préfère ce paquet s'il est présent.

⚠ Aucun de ces scripts n'a encore tourné sur un Pi réel.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: stub the Copylock — and pin the CPU it depends on
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: stub the Copylock — and pin the CPU it depends on

load_resource_by_index calls the protection on the first resource load, so every
run crossing the boot path or the resource loader hits `jsr copylock_entry`.
The blob is a Rob Northen trace-decryptor: 1,970 of its bytes never exist as
plaintext, so there is no source text to port and running it is not an option
either. This gets an oracle run past it — and proves afterwards that it got past.

Two mechanisms, both applied by default, because choosing between them is a
judgement about the run's entry point a caller can get wrong SILENTLY:
- DISARM pokes copylock_arm_flag := 0. Patches no code; it is the game's own
  steady state, since the guard does `clr.w` after the first call. Valid only
  below an arming site — crossing $e51e or $e6dc re-arms it.
- ENTRY_RTS pokes `rts` over copylock_entry. Valid anywhere, because an arming
  site cannot undo a patch to code it does not write. An instruction-shaped
  sweep found EXACTLY ONE entry into the blob (the `jsr` at $e7bc), so nothing
  in the program can get past that `rts`.
ENTRY_RTS is also immune to harness._attribution_check's poison pass, which
inverts every oracle-written byte: under DISARM alone the game's own `clr.w`
puts the flag in that set, so the poisoned re-run would start RE-ARMED.

THE WITNESS IS A MEMORY DIFFERENCE, NOT A WRITE SET, and that is load-bearing:
at load_base 0x3f8 the relocator's copy to $400 is an IDENTITY copy that writes
every byte of the image — all 2,220 of the protection's — so a write-set witness
reports "the protection ran" for a `move.l (a0)+,(a1)+` loop. Measured both
ways: relocator 2,220 writes / 0 differing bytes; blob fires.

WHAT THE INDEPENDENT REVIEW BROKE, and how it is closed. The witness had two
demonstrated false negatives, both reproduced before being fixed:
- a SIX-checkpoint blind window at the blob's entrance ($ecca $eccc $ecd2 $ed46
  $ed48 $ed4c). The blob's first image write is the `movem` at $ed4c, so a run
  stopping before it returned green with the `jsr` demonstrably executed;
- twelve bytes of caller poke blinded it completely. The blob's entire durable
  delta is 12 bytes, and `pokes` was never vetted against the witness window, so
  feeding them back put them on BOTH sides of the comparison.
Both are now loud errors: a poke overlapping the witness range is refused, and a
stop_pc inside [copylock_entry, code_end) is refused.

The over-claim is corrected too. The witness fires on any run that COMPLETES the
movem at $ed4c, and is input-independent BY ENFORCEMENT rather than by nature.
And its soundness rests on the blob being unable to complete: a trace decryptor
re-encrypts and restores its vectors by design, so a completed Copylock would
leave only the save area as evidence. That contingency is now stated.

THE CPU CONFIGURATION IS NOW PINNED. The oracle could not run the blob because
M68K_EMULATE_TRACE is OFF, so the single-step exception the decryptor needs never
fires — measured: the trace handler at $ee3c is never entered at either 1M or 20M
instructions. But that was MUSASHI'S UPSTREAM DEFAULT, and oracle/musashi/ is
gitignored and cloned `--depth 1` from HEAD at build time, so the CPU our entire
ground truth runs on was untracked, unpinned and asserted by nothing. Now:
-DM68K_EMULATE_TRACE=0 in kit.mk's OCFLAGS, an `#error` gate in shim.c, kit.mk
made a prerequisite of $(ORACLE) so flipping the flag cannot leave make reporting
"up to date", and a behavioural test that arms the T bit against a marking
handler (mutation-checked against a real -D=1 build: marker 0xff vs 0x00).
liboracle.so is BYTE-IDENTICAL before and after (sha256 c19d73ff…) because the
-D reproduces the header default exactly — verified by a forced rebuild.
BuggyBoy and Joust are unaffected: a sweep of all four shipped PRGs found the
Copylock's own `move.l a0,$24.l` as the workspace's only trace-vector install.

THE UNLOCK IS SMALLER THAN "+3 FUNCTIONS / +236 BYTES" READS. Of those 236 bytes
96 is copylock_entry's own replaced body (tautological) and 36 is
copylock_key_check, which has no incoming call edge at all — leaving 104 bytes,
one function, load_resource_by_index. Both roots stay unrunnable: T5 -> T4 is
"no source text" -> "the run is refused", and 8 of the 10 functions the stub
frees were never blocked only by the protection. Their new blocker is the sound
module's PSG read-modify-write. The stub's value is SUPERADDITIVE — alone
+236 B, psg:read alone +2,694 B, both +4,078 B, an interaction term of +1,148 B.
~83% of the stub's eventual value is locked behind the PSG read model.

Also measured, and the false green in its exact shape: a DISARM run entered AT an
arming site does come back — to $e7c8 in 184,997 instructions with 2,053 bytes of
the protection scrambled. "An unstubbed run never comes back" is true of the
guard entry only.

Defects the gate found in the fix itself, all in: `stub_pokes` had no type check,
so passing a dict positionally as `mechanism` stubbed nothing and came back green;
the poke/stub merge did not actually apply the stub last; the stop_pc guard was a
bare `assert` and vanished under -O.

KNOWINGLY UNPINNED: the Copylock's own effects (save area, three vector installs,
decrypt cursor, the d0 key) never happen, so a reconstruction verified under the
stub is verified for the DISARMED steady state — loads 2..n, not the first.
disk_check_signature, the four wipe-table pointers and the $f89a/$f89c readers
stay reachable only from ciphertext. The guards sit on copylock.run()/
stubbed_image()'s door, so a caller building its own image and witnessing it gets
no vetting; harness.differential() is that shape and has reachability ZERO today
(recreate/src/ is empty and no test calls it). The identified fix — differential()
returning the oracle's final image, NOT a write-set veto, which would false-
positive on the relocator — is recorded, not built.

Suites: kit 91, Wonder Boy 77 (was 57), Joust 4368, BuggyBoy 292,
portability_predictions 14, rad_differential 45. Mutation sweep 17/17.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: measure the wall — 47% of the code is even in scope
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: measure the wall — 47% of the code is even in scope

STATUS.md's blocker 2 said the game's I/O is all direct hardware, the oracle
models almost none of it, and how much of the game sits behind that wall had
never been measured. This measures it.

The tiers restate the shim's own behaviour per function: T0 no off-image access;
T1 captured by a modeled write ledger; T2 write silently dropped (memory effect
verified, hardware effect untested); T3 read returns 0 on BOTH sides — falsely
green if a branch depends on it; T4 the run is refused; T5 the code cannot be
read at all. Tiers are then closed over the call graph.

THE ANSWER, with its denominator, which is the part that matters:

Ghidra has recovered 252 functions / 25,696 of the ~54,854 bytes the region
table calls CODE. 21,534 bytes run end-to-end under the oracle — 83.8% of what
is MEASURED, but 39.3% of the program's believed code. 29,158 bytes are in no
tier at all because they are in no function body.

The gameplay logic is portable today: 136 of 138 game-logic functions touch no
hardware (the exceptions are the two PRNGs, which seed from the video address
counter), and 128 of them run end-to-end. But it is also the subsystem this
measurement covers LEAST — game logic 36.0% covered, against sound 68.9%, boot
56.0%, video 97-100%, disk 99.7%. Three of the four subsystems the report calls
blocked are measured BETTER than the code it calls portable; only the Copylock,
unreadable by construction, is worse. So a reconstruction started now proves
about 31% of the game-logic code believed to exist — a good place to start, but
not "the gameplay logic".

Findings:
- T1 IS EMPTY. All three PSG writers also read the PSG, so nothing reaches the
  write-ledger path. The music replay/drain path is unverifiable — but 62% of
  the sound module is verifiable now, including snd_trigger_effect, because
  triggers write RAM channel state and only snd_music_tick drains it to the chip.
- THE FDC POLL SUCCEEDS INSTANTLY. `btst #5,$fffa01 / bne` loops while the bit is
  SET, and the MFP line is active low, so the oracle's permanent 0 reads as
  "already done": fdc_wait_irq returns success in 107 instructions having moved
  no bytes. But the layer above rejects the fabricated status — the command
  entries return $fffb/$fffd and DO mutate driver state. "The driver reports
  success" is true of the polls and false of the driver.
- BUGGYBOY'S DEFECT IS PRESENT: snd_music_tick picks its tempo from
  `btst #1,$ff820a`, the same register that was invisible to BuggyBoy's entire
  differential and only surfaced on hardware. It reads 0, so the mono-monitor
  branch is taken unconditionally.

A SECOND BLIT FAMILY was found and named. $8366 is a 16-entry longword table
whose targets tile $83b6..$8dfe exactly (2,632 bytes) — the per-frame background
scroll blitter, entered through `jmp (a2)`, which Ghidra cannot follow, so it sat
in no function at all. Each variant splits its unrolled 30x `move.l (a0)+,(a1)+`
where the source byte offset wraps a 128-byte row. Naming it moved coverage
42.0% -> 46.8%, functions 236 -> 252, runnable 82.0% -> 83.8%.

That is the same trap that caught this project once before at $8fce, but a
harder form of it: the region table was RIGHT — the region was always CODE.
docs/methodology.md gains the sharper rule: a correct CODE verdict is not
coverage; ask which parts of a CODE region the disassembler actually reaches.

Tooling, game-agnostic: HwPortabilityScan.java (Ghidra's reference model, not an
operand scan — 15% of this game's hardware accesses are register-indirect and an
operand scan sees none of them), hw_scan.sh, hw_portability.py (tiers, closure,
and --stub/--model to price a capability).

Priced capabilities: a PSG read model is the biggest "can it run" lever
(+18 functions / +2,694 bytes); an MFP+FDC read model is the biggest "is the
green real" lever (false-green risk 29 -> 10 functions). The PSG model needs a
SEEDED register file, not just the write ledger: all three read-modify-writes
preserve bits the game never writes, so a ledger-only model recreates the very
false-green class this measures.

Empirically validated, not asserted: portability_predictions.py runs 14 cases
under the oracle and checks the predicted outcome actually happens, with
positive controls — mutation-tested so a bare `rts`, a wrong error code, a wrong
retry PC and a patched rewind instruction are each caught.

Honest limits, stated in the document rather than implied away: the tiers
describe 46.8% of believed code; 22,984 bytes of CODE-region address space carry
no disassembly at all; the steering analysis is intra-procedural and stops at
calls, so the false-green count (29 fns / 3,362 B) is a LOWER bound — $6470's
value really is branched on two frames up; 22 of 252 functions have an
unresolved indirect site in their subtree; and the answer box's coverage table
is the one table no tool produces.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: the game's own .RAD/.CRU cruncher, pinned by a differential
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: the game's own .RAD/.CRU cruncher, pinned by a differential

The data files are packed by a cruncher the game carries, so the depacker is IN
the binary and the format is provable rather than guessable. Found by grepping
the disassembly for roxl/roxr: the routine is 216 bytes at text $596a (runtime
$5d62), reached from five call sites that all do lea buf,a0 / lea dst,a1 /
jsr $5d62.w.

Container — no magic, because the game reaches these files only through its own
40-entry index table:
  +0  be32  packed length = filesize - 12   (the only thing that locates EOF)
  +4  be32  unpacked length
  +8  be32  checksum: XOR of every longword of the stream
  +12 ...   stream, consumed BACKWARDS from EOF down to +12

Bits leave a LONGWORD buffer LSB-first, refilled from decreasing addresses;
each refilled longword carries its own end marker rotated into bit 31 via
move #$10,ccr / roxr.l #1, so it yields exactly 32 data bits. Six token forms;
output is written backwards too. A correct decode closes three invariants at
once — output exactly full, stream pointer back at +12, checksum back to 0.

Pinned: notes/rad_differential.py runs the ORIGINAL routine under the kit's
Musashi oracle and diffs it against tools/depack_rad.py over the whole corpus —
45 files, 0 failures. It binds through recreate_kit.project.load() and keeps an
assertion on the bootstrap stub's bytes, plus two the earlier version only
assumed: that load_base + 8 == the runtime base, and that no relocation fixup
lands inside the copied body.

WHAT THE GREEN RESULT DOES NOT PROVE, found by an independent review and now
stated in the harness rather than implied away: the four protection-damaged
overlays were claimed to be the only way the corpus reaches the checksum gate.
That is true of the 68000 and FALSE of the Python, which refuses them earlier
on guards the original does not have — deleting `if stream.checksum:` left the
differential green. The damaged check now asserts WHICH guard fired on each
side, so "both refused" can no longer hide "for different reasons", and a
KNOWINGLY UNPINNED note names the unit test as the only thing holding that
branch. The general trap is written up in docs/binary-formats.md.

Two guards documented as catching a desync "one step earlier" than the checksum
turned out to be strictly STRONGER gates, not early forms of it: a stream padded
with an unread longword closes with a clean checksum, and the 68000 ACCEPTS
such a file where depack_rad refuses it — verified under Musashi. A third,
undocumented deviation (the match-past-end guard) is the one real damage
actually reaches. All three are now labelled and pinned.

Ten mutations that previously survived are caught (the checksum gate, the
stream-position gate, MAX_UNPACKED, _require_room, LSD_MAGIC, the stored-form
and MIN_FILE_LEN gates, and more); _refused() now asserts the NAMED guard
rather than only the exception type, which is what let three of them hide
behind an overlapping guard.

SPRITES.CRU is the container's STORED form — both length fields equal, never
passed to the depacker, loaded raw. Its 64-byte header holds a valid 16-entry
ST palette at +$20; the body at +$40 does not, correcting a claim that put the
palette in the body.

Corpus: the 41 intact files come from disk1/ and disk2_repaired/, and each row
names its corpus. bin/disk2/ was extracted from the UNREPAIRED image and four
of its overlays are still missing the 1779 bytes the copy protection cost —
they stay as the primary record of what the physical disk gave up, while the
repaired hybrid is used only where a hole must be filled. All four repaired
files decode with checksum residue 0 and the stream pointer landing exactly on
+12, which independently corroborates the repair.

Also resolved: VAPOUR2.PRG is 52,423 bytes carrying an LSD! stream that inflates
to 136,979 bytes — the crack's patched SWB.PRG, 89 bytes different, with this
depack routine byte-identical inside it. The earlier note claimed the routine
was absent from VAPOUR2; it is there, packed, which is exactly why an
lsl.b/roxl.b signature search missed a longword-buffered cruncher.

Housekeeping: the CLI both depackers duplicated verbatim moved to
tools/depack_common.py (depack_lsd.py shrinks 60 lines); depack_rad.py is
registered in CLAUDE.md and docs/README.md; the differential now poisons its
destination buffer so an offset-0 match could not agree by accident.

Left for later: rad_differential.py and lsd_differential.py still duplicate
_check_layout/run_original/_label, and run_original has diverged in return
arity under one name. Deconflicting needs lsd_differential.py, which has an
uncommitted local edit.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: bind the differential harness — and close a false green
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: bind the differential harness — and close a false green

projects/wonderboy/recreate/ binds the shared kit to SWB.PRG, so from here any
reconstructed function can be proven byte-for-byte against the original 68000
code. Nothing is reconstructed yet: STATUS.md is 0/? by design, and a row
appears when a function is green.

Binding:
- load_base = 0x3f8, so load_base + 8 == 0x400 and the LOADED image IS the
  RUNTIME image — the program's self-relocation becomes an identity copy and
  its absolute operands address the loaded image directly. Asserted, not
  assumed: none of the three relocation fixups (0x3fc, 0x217da, 0x217f0) lands
  inside the copied body [0x400, 0x217d8).
- image_size = 0x100000, forced equal to os.h's OS_IMAGE_SIZE. The game's own
  ceiling is bounded by evidence at 0x80000 — two `movea.l #$80000,a7` sites, a
  screen clear covering exactly 0x70000..0x7fd00, and no address-like longword
  constant at or above 0x80000. The caveat travels with the number: that is a
  scan of the SHIPPED image, and the Copylock body is encrypted.
- tos_malloc_unused, on much stronger evidence than Joust's: one trap
  instruction in the whole image, and it is a Super.

37 cases, and they are load-bearing rather than decorative — proven by
corrupting the inputs. Flipping the relocator's copy count fails 2; moving the
entry jmp target raises; setting load_base back to 0x10000 fails 4; 15 further
header and binary mutations were all caught, including a `trap #N` planted
INSIDE an ASCII string, which the classification heuristic alone would miss.
The trap census is also re-run over the RELOCATED image, since the scan reads
the file but the CPU runs the fixed-up bytes.

THE KIT CHANGE, and the defect it started as:

Wonder Boy runs at the fixed address 0x400, so its load_base is below the kit's
poked-input floor (0x620) and cannot be otherwise — everything under 0x400 is
the 68000 vector page. That needed a second project.toml waiver,
tos_poked_input_unused, built like tos_malloc_unused and off by default.

As first written the waiver documented itself as "the same shape as the Malloc
waiver's per-run re-check". It was not. The Malloc guard enforces a claim about
the GAME; the new one only fired when a TEST called one of two builders. An
independent review built the false green that gap allows: a Bconin in code that
exists only after a depack reads OS_CON_PENDING — the program's own nonzero
instruction bytes — so the model reports a keystroke pending, hands back four
bytes of game code as the key, and zeroes four bytes of code. Both sides do it
identically from the same os.h, so the diff is clean and the case proves
nothing.

Both halves are now enforced, and both key on the OVERLAP rather than on the
flag:
- shim.c tallies traps that reach the block (Bconstat, Bconin, Crawio's read
  direction only, Random, Giaccess, Kbdvbase); emu.run() refuses the run when
  that tally is nonzero and the block lies inside the program. This is the half
  that watches the game, and it is the half that matters, because a trap that
  exists only after a depack is invisible to any scan of the shipped file.
- harness.make_image() refuses any poke whose byte range lands in the block, at
  the layer pokes are APPLIED — so a hand-written {OS_RANDOM_VALUE: ...} dict
  is caught exactly like a console_key() one. That mattered more than its
  documentation admitted: the kit ships two builders for three kinds of poked
  state, so hand-writing the dict is the ONLY way to stage an XBIOS Random, and
  Joust already does it in three places.
- console_key()/psg_regs() still refuse, demoted to a friendlier early error.

Both are pinned, including a negative control that disarms the run guard and
MEASURES the corruption it prevents. The block's Python mirror moved to
recreate_kit/os_map.py, which imports nothing, so the kit's own suite can pin
the geometry — previously deleting both guards left it 57/57 green.

Deliberately NOT fixed, and recorded rather than smoothed over: OS_SCREEN_BASE
(0x8000, what Physbase/Logbase return) is also inside this program and is
tallied by nothing. The guard's predicate is the poked block's overlap, which
is the wrong question for 0x8000; doing it properly needs its own predicate.
A kit test now holds the list of unvetted regions so a third cannot join
quietly.

Absent flag means byte-identical behaviour for the other two games, verified in
the code and not only from green suites. All four suites re-run green: kit 86
(was 57), Joust 4368, BuggyBoy 292, Wonder Boy 37.

Blockers recorded in STATUS.md, in the order they will be hit: the kit's Super
model refuses this game's Super(program_end); all of the game's I/O is raw
hardware and the kit rejects direct PSG reads outright, and how much of the
game sits behind that wall is UNMEASURED; and the Copylock at $ecca runs on
the first resource load.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: the program runs at $400 — Stage 1 at the right base
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: the program runs at $400 — Stage 1 at the right base

SWB.PRG is position-DEPENDENT. Its entry trampolines to a 48-byte stub at
text $213e0 which does Super(), masks interrupts, copies 0x213d8 bytes from
image+8 to the absolute address $400 and jumps there. The three relocation
entries are at text $4/$213e2/$213f8; the `lea $400` and `jmp $400` are
deliberately NOT among them. So runtime = image offset + 0x3F8, and the body
lives at $400..$217D8.

Loaded at the workspace default 0x10000 every absolute operand in the body
dangles outside the loaded block, so Ghidra's flow analysis cannot follow one.
That — not packing, not jump tables — is why a first bootstrap found 57
functions in 136 KB and the image looked full of unexplained gaps. At 0x3F8
the same binary yields 186 before any naming, 238 after this sweep.

Stage 1:
- run.sh/reapply.sh bootstrap at 0x3f8; names.txt carries the base in its
  header so a later reader cannot miss it.
- names.txt: 96 fn, 57 var, 118 cmt, 9 proto — all applied, 0 failures.
  97 of 238 functions named.
- notes/architecture.md: the region table tiles $3F8..$218D0 with no gaps or
  overlaps (verified programmatically, sums to 136,408) — CODE 54,854 (40.2%),
  DATA 81,554 (59.8%), UNKNOWN 0.

Two findings that reshape the project:
- ONE trap instruction in the whole image, the Super above. No BIOS, no XBIOS,
  no GEMDOS file I/O, no Malloc. The game drives the WD1772 and DMA directly
  with its own FAT12 layer ($5e3e..$64f0), reading 10 sectors/track in one
  multi-record command — which is what leaves room for the protection's
  out-of-band sector IDs 11 and 12 on cylinders 0-4.
- $ed2a..$f89e is a Rob Northen-style COPYLOCK, and it is live:
  load_resource_by_index calls it at $e7bc on the first resource load. It
  installs handlers on the illegal/privilege/trace vectors, executes `illegal`
  instructions that vector to the following instruction, and single-steps
  itself while XOR-decrypting its own instruction stream. A differential
  harness will hit `jsr $ecca` immediately and must model or stub it; the
  fuzzy-byte check inside cannot be pinned because the code performing it
  cannot be read at all.

Corrections from the independent verification pass, all re-derived from the
bodies before applying: a 2,254-byte region classified DATA is CODE (12
unrolled planar blitters reached only through three jump tables — the exact
blind spot of a byte-idiom classifier, which also scores 78 false "bsr" in the
dialogue block); $6408 is not the protection check but a WD1772
Restore-with-verify; ~10 names and comments were wrong, including the comment
on load_resource_by_index that omitted the Copylock call and so hid the answer
to the unknown region. Five further proposed corrections were REJECTED after
reading the bodies and the reasons are recorded.

Tooling:
- ApplyNames.java clears a bogus auto-analysis data item lying across an `fn`
  address before disassembling. Ghidra had guessed a 4-byte pointer over $714,
  which silently made `fn 0x716 vbl_handler` a no-op. Fires only where the
  directive previously failed outright.
- prg_dis.py gains --base (default 0, output byte-identical without it) so a
  listing can be generated in runtime addresses. out/wonderboy_dis.txt at base
  0 was off by 0x3F8 on every line against names.txt.

Docs:
- docs/methodology.md: entropy does not imply packing. The Copylock region was
  left UNKNOWN partly on a 7.73 bits/byte reading whose source turned out to be
  a PLAINTEXT table of 2i mod 256 — a byte permutation is maximally entropic by
  construction.

Knowingly unpinned: ~2,000 bytes of Copylock ciphertext are unreadable by
construction; the $a271 dialogue block's indexer is untraced; $6bb8 is defined
only to stop Ghidra folding it into the key check, and its meaning is unknown.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: repair disk 2's protection holes from the crack
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: repair disk 2's protection holes from the crack

The Pasti dump of disk 2 lost 1779 bytes to the copy protection — four
overlay files with sectors that were never formatted, plus 31 bad bytes in
the one CRC-flagged sector that could be read back. A cracked release of the
same game has that content. crack_differential.py already attributed every
differing byte to its .ST sector and to why that sector was wrong; it can
now act on the attribution.

Repair:
- --patch OUT.ST writes a repaired image: authentic dump everywhere it read
  cleanly, crack bytes only where the dump had a hole. Result verified
  byte-identical to the crack for all four overlays, 36 of 40 files
  untouched, and the boot sector, FATs and root directory never written.
- THE SAFETY RULE: a byte may be taken only from a ZERO-FILLED or UNVERIFIED
  sector. A byte differing inside a cleanly-read sector means the crack
  altered the game — it is refused by name and the run exits 3. Proven by
  seeding one: the byte does not reach the output. The four real overlays
  hold none, so the crack did not touch overlay content.
- The output is a REPAIRED HYBRID and says so on every write. It is an
  artefact, never a source of truth about the physical disk.

Findings from the independent review, all fixed:
- DATA LOSS: the overwrite guard compared resolved path strings, so an
  uppercase extension (which the usage text itself invites) or a hard link
  aliased an input and --patch truncated it in place, exit 0, silently. Now
  compares inode identity for all three inputs.
- A hole the patch never filled still exited 0 under a 'PATCHED' banner. A
  ledger now reconciles every in-volume hole against what was answered for
  and exits 4 naming what is still lost.
- Fat12Image appends chain-integrity warnings lazily during file_bytes(), so
  draining them once at load discarded them all — a broken cluster chain was
  reported as 'not the same file'. Warnings are now re-checked after the
  compare and affect the exit status.
- The Pasti image was located only by swapping the .ST's extension, via a
  gitignored symlink, so the committed tool could not run for anyone else —
  and that silently-chosen file is the sole authority on which sectors may
  be overwritten. Added --stx, and the source is now proven to be this .ST's
  by comparing every cleanly-read sector before a byte is written.
- The crack's path-keyed file map was re-keyed by 8.3 base name, so a
  duplicate name in a second directory would bind arbitrarily and write a
  namesake's bytes where the safety rule cannot see. Refused on both sides.

Two further defects the gate found in the fixes themselves are also in:
an UNVERIFIED sector that read back correctly was counted as still missing,
and the ledger walks chains, so it raised warnings after they were reported.

Docs: docs/binary-formats.md records the repair and its hybrid status.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: Pasti .stx reader — the original, uncracked disks
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: Pasti .stx reader — the original, uncracked disks

The two .stx images are the original 1989 Activision release, not a crack:
Pasti keeps the flux detail the copy protection lives in, and underneath
sits a plain FAT12 filesystem.

Tooling:
- tools/stx_extract.py: game-agnostic Pasti/STX reader. Reports protection
  (fuzzy bytes, FDC-flagged sectors, address fields that lie about their
  track, duplicate IDs, unformatted tracks) and converts to a clean .ST for
  st_extract.py. Geometry is derived, never assumed: sectors/track is voted
  on well-formed descriptors, so read damage cannot shift the LBA stride,
  and the vote is cross-checked against the boot sector's BPB.
- A damaged-but-recorded sector is placed by default with a per-sector
  WARNING ('content unverified'); --strict zero-fills it instead. Zero-fill
  is reserved for sectors that were never formatted.
- tools/st_extract.py: cluster_start_sector() extracted (no behaviour change,
  shared with the new reader).

Findings on the two disks:
- Both: tracks 0-4 carry sectors 11/12 with 1024 fuzzy bytes and CRC errors,
  outside the 1..10 numbering — pure protection, no filesystem cost.
- Disk 2 also has the real teeth: cylinders 7-11 formatted with one sector
  deliberately absent, walking down 10/8/6/4/2, plus a cylinder 12 whose
  sectors claim to be on track 4 and whose ID 3 appears twice. Those holes
  sit inside allocated clusters, so 4 overlay files lose data.
- Recovering the CRC-flagged sector 7 of cylinder 12 gives OVALAY9A back
  481 of its 512 missing bytes (the last 31 are genuinely corrupt — which
  is why the CRC failed). The rest of the loss, 1748 B across OVALAY4B/5B/
  6A/9A, was never on the disk: the diagonal has no address field at all.
- projects/wonderboy/notes/crack_differential.py measures exactly that,
  against an extracted copy of the crack release (external data, no baked
  path). 35 of 39 overlays are byte-identical to the crack.
- Disk 1's AUTO/SWB.PRG is the uncracked original: header arithmetic exact
  at 136,979 B, the Psygnosis intro string intact, and the protection branch
  at 0xe8f6 still 'bra.s' where the crack had patched an 'rts'.

Docs:
- docs/binary-formats.md: '.stx / Pasti images' subsection — layout, the
  two-step pipeline, the sector-selection rule, and what protection cannot
  survive conversion.
- CLAUDE.md + README.md tool trees; notes/lsd_differential.py records that
  its corpus (the crack disk) is no longer the project's basis.

Review: author self-review, then an INDEPENDENT gate found 7 further
confirmed defects it had missed — a damage-sensitive geometry vote, an
unformatted track inside the volume silently zero-filled, silent last-wins
on conflicting duplicate sectors, fuzzy-only sectors discarded whole, a
bounds check keyed off a display string, and two factually wrong doc claims
about the disk. All fixed, each with a synthetic-STX regression (37 checks),
plus 14/14 negative and 6/6 seeded-mutation sweeps.

events.title: fix: four encoder/category bugs from the August 2026 audit (#18)
events.message:
fix: four encoder/category bugs from the August 2026 audit (#18)

A systematic review — EA categories against the PRM tables, decoder
pattern coverage, pass-1/pass-2 divergence across all directives, plus a
sweep over ~100 instruction forms — turned up four real bugs. Two of them
produced silently wrong output rather than an error.

* MOVE from CCR had no dispatch arm at all. The CCR marker fell through
  to the generic MOVE path, which read it as an ordinary immediate:
  `MOVE.W CCR,D0` assembled to 303C FFFF (`MOVE.W #-1,D0`) instead of
  42C0, with no diagnostic. Now encoded correctly and gated to 68010+.

* CONTROL_ALT aliased ALTERABLE_MEMORY and so included (An)+ and -(An).
  Those are not control modes — they have no fixed effective address —
  so "control alterable" cannot contain them. The bitfield instructions
  accepted `BFCLR (A0)+{0:8}` and emitted bytes for an instruction the
  CPU does not have. Callers that legitimately allow predecrement
  (FMOVEM/FSAVE/FRESTORE) already OR in APREDEC explicitly and are
  unaffected.

* `FSINCOS <ea>,FPc:FPs` — the colon spelling every Motorola assembler
  uses — was rejected; only a three-operand form existed that no
  assembler writes that way. Parses as a RegPair now.

* `PFLUSH #fc,#mask` (no EA) was rejected; only the three-operand form
  existed. The two-operand form has a different extension word: mode 100
  at bits 12-10 rather than 110, and no EA field in the opword.

All four verified byte-for-byte against a reference assembler. Byte
parity is unchanged (12/12 and 13/13 across both corpora), 600 tests
passing (was 595), 330k fuzz iterations clean.

plan.md records the full audit, including two reported findings that did
NOT hold up on verification: nine decoder patterns that are formally
shadowed but decode correctly anyway (decode_next retries on a failed
operand parse), and a suspected pass-1/pass-2 divergence in CNOP that
computes identical values in both passes. Both are documented so they
are not re-investigated.

events.message:
Allow loading KFS raw files from an archive (7z, zip, ...)
Unlike other supported floppy images where an image is made of only one file,
KFS dump are made of as many .raw files as there're tracks and side in the floppy.
We need to provide KFS_Insert() with the path in the archive for accessing the .raw
files and we load all these .raw files using Archive_ReadDisk() instead of File_Read()
NOTE : with .7z archives this can be quite slow because .raw files are sometimes
packed together in a single "block", requiring to unpack a big part of the archive
to access just one raw file

events.title: wonderboy/atari: LSD! cruncher solved — depacker pinned by a differential
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: LSD! cruncher solved — depacker pinned by a differential

Tooling:
- tools/depack_lsd.py: static depacker for the 'LSD!' backwards-LZ cruncher
  (bitstream read backwards from EOF, self-marking bit buffer, tiered
  literal/length/offset codes). Stream end comes from the header's EOF field
  like the ROM does, so embedded/cluster-rounded slices with trailing slack
  depack too. CLI + exit codes match st_extract.py.
- tools/recreate_kit/test/test_depack_lsd.py: header-bounds and padded-slack
  regression cases (5 tests).

Ground truth:
- projects/wonderboy/notes/lsd_depacker.asm: faithful transcription of the
  routine at VAPOUR2.PRG text $7ec (copied to $200 at boot), register map,
  the $ffff8240 loading-flash noted as knowingly unpinned.
- projects/wonderboy/notes/lsd_differential.py: original 68k routine under
  the recreate-kit Musashi oracle vs the Python depacker, byte-for-byte —
  96/96 files identical (largest: SPRITES.CRU 136k->279k, 5.2M insns).
  Mutation sweep over 9 decode constants: all caught. Refuses to report
  green on an empty corpus; layout invariants asserted.

Findings on the disk (bin/ stays untracked):
- Main Wonder Boy binary = LSD! block embedded at VAPOUR2 text $94c ->
  VAPOUR2.payload.bin, 50,006 -> 136,979 B GEMDOS PRG (game code, overlay
  name table, all dialogue). Loader depacks it over its own text and jumps.
- The 61 hex-named root files are a second game: Thalion's Seven Gates of
  Jambala — the disk is a two-game compilation. Its loader is not VAPOUR2.
- 37 .RAD/.CRU resources are doubly packed: inside the LSD! wrap sits the
  game's own container (packed_len/unpacked/stream) — a second cruncher,
  its depacker not in VAPOUR2. Unsolved, tracked as the next blocker.

Docs:
- docs/packed-executables.md: LSD section with invocation + the EOF-field
  lesson; CLAUDE.md + README.md tools trees (st_extract.py line added to
  README, missed in a22586a).

Review: my-code-review at high — 10 confirmed findings fixed (CLI crashes,
unbounded header alloc, len(data)-vs-EOF-field stream end, empty-corpus
false green, layout asserts, kit reuse); one finding's premise corrected by
measurement ($ffff8240 does not trip the PSG counters).

events.title: feat(fdc): port de MSA_WriteDisk/DIM_WriteDisk — les .msa/.dim redeviennent inscriptibles
events.message:
feat(fdc): port de MSA_WriteDisk/DIM_WriteDisk — les .msa/.dim redeviennent inscriptibles

Divergence D0 relevée à l'audit pré-release. Toute image .msa/.dim était montée
en LECTURE SEULE, et ce drapeau ne bloquait pas que la recopie hôte : il pilote
le bit WPRT du WD1772 vu par le programme émulé (updateWriteSectors,
updateWriteTrack, statut type I). Sauvegardes en jeu, tables de high-scores,
écritures depuis le bureau TOS et protections « écrit puis relit » échouaient
donc « disque protégé » sur ces formats, alors que la même disquette en .st
fonctionnait. Hatari ne dérive WPRT que du réglage et de stat() — JAMAIS du
format d'image (floppy.c:205-225 Floppy_IsWriteProtected) — et ré-encode le
fichier (MSA_WriteDisk, DIM_WriteDisk).

Portage :
- encodeMsa + msaFindRun : port de MSA_WriteDisk / MSA_FindRunOfBytes
  (msa.c:275-420), y compris l'échappement du marqueur $E5 même isolé et le
  repli « piste stockée brute » quand la compression n'y gagne rien.
- FloppyDisk::imgFormat (FMT_ST / FMT_MSA / FMT_DIM) : writeBack dispatche
  dessus — écriture partielle in situ pour le .ST, idem décalée de l'en-tête
  32 o pour le .DIM (en-tête existant PRÉSERVÉ, comme dim.c:134-149), et
  ré-encodage complet pour le .MSA, qui n'a aucune correspondance offset↔fichier.
- Le ré-encodage .msa est ATOMIQUE (tmp + rename) : réécrire un .msa, c'est le
  reconstruire entièrement, et une coupure à mi-course laisserait une disquette
  définitivement illisible là où le .st ne perdrait qu'un secteur.
- writeProtect ne vient plus que de stat(). `!raw` ne subsiste que là où l'on ne
  SAIT PAS ré-encoder (STX, ou en-tête .msa/.dim reconnu mais indécodable) : y
  écrire détruirait le fichier de l'utilisateur.
- raw/imgFormat sont remis à l'état « .ST inscriptible » à CHAQUE montage : `dk`
  est réutilisé, et sans ça un précédent STX ou .dim léguait son format.

NeoST reste en write-through là où Hatari n'écrit qu'à l'éjection (une coupure y
perd la sauvegarde) — écart assumé, en faveur de la durabilité.

Couverture : nouvel auto-test `neost-headless --msa-selftest`, enregistré comme
étalon `msa_selftest` dans le palier *fast* (donc dans la garde de release).
44 cas : aller-retour byte-exact sur 6 géométries (720 Ko, simple face, 820 Ko,
HD, ED, une seule piste) × 7 motifs (dont $E5 isolé, $E5 en run, alternance sans
run possible, et un motif incompressible qui force la piste brute), PLUS deux cas
de bout en bout montage → écriture → remontage sur fichiers .msa et .dim réels,
qui vérifient aussi que le montage n'est plus protégé en écriture.

Vérifié en plus : suite --tier full verte, aucun disque d'étalon suivi par git
modifié par un run complet, les .msa tronquées restent en lecture seule, et
l'auto-test comme les 51 images corrompues passent sous ASan/UBSan sans détection.

events.title: buggyboy/atari: audit vs the observable surfaces — a live bus error found
events.message:
buggyboy/atari: audit vs the observable surfaces — a live bus error found

The Joust lessons applied to the first game, as the retro's item 5
required. Headline: the SMOKE build's own teardown was BUS-ERRORING on
$454 after every dump — SYS_NVBLS = 0 from user mode in a build whose
VBL install is #ifndef SMOKE (nothing to detach, no Super) — and every
run printed OK, because game_smoke.py piped Hatari's output and never
read a byte, then killed the emulator the moment SCREEN.BIN appeared.
Joust's half-blind exit detector and its teardown class, compounded.

Fixed here (verified by injected-fault control — reverting the C fix
makes the new gate print the exact measured bus-error line):
- game_main.c: the detach gated on hw_ready, like every other
  supervisor-only poke in the file; the false 'image is 256-aligned'
  comment corrected (the code below it was already right).
- game_smoke.py: check_machine() — merged stream, banner tripwire so
  the vacuity cannot return, fault/halt scan with the benign ROM probe
  pinned by the same two exact PCs Joust pins (never 'PC is in ROM').
- run_hatari.py: a DIFF now exits 1 (it printed and exited 0 — a
  byte-compare that cannot fail its caller).

Audit result, both builds: memory is the ONLY surface either has
(golden byte-compares); trap ledger / hardware vector / rendered
pixels / timelines / exit-status are absent. Cleared: the class-8
video-base bug is NOT present (both builds round at runtime — though
nothing reads it back, and recreate pokes the shifter directly so
Physbase() would be the WRONG read-back there); no class-6 codegen
shape in either ELF; the remaster teardown measured correct over
12000 vblanks past Pterm — correct and entirely unpinned.

Recorded follow-ups, not folded in: the remaster's shared run_hatari
gate (one edit covers six runners; drop the unconditional kill so
exit status means something); a read-back sweep in both shims
(conterm is already un-restored in both — measured 0x00 after exit);
bound-assert the one data-derived hardware address (reg_sel from
COURSES.DAT can reach $ffff8260); require_fresh on the recreate
runners; a surfaces row in remaster/STATUS.md.

recreate gate: 292 passed, unchanged (game_main.c is PRG-only).
Remaster untouched: 732 stands.

events.title: joust/atari: harness hardening 2/2 — read-backs, timelines, and the rule
events.message:
joust/atari: harness hardening 2/2 — read-backs, timelines, and the rule

Retro item 3 — read back everything you write: 15 assertions over every
shim hardware/OS write (KBDVBASE vectors, VBL queue + nvbls, conterm,
_colorptr, Setscreen, the IKBD's write-only commands by proxy), surfaced
as two STATS words asserted as failed==0 AND attempted==exact mask — a
check that silently stops running is itself a failure. Bit names parsed
from the C and validated before any boot; the ISR half has its own
volatile pair. The sweep bit on its first run: TDRE is clear when
Ikbdws returns (it waits for room BEFORE each byte), so teardown ran
Pterm with the IKBD reset still shifting at 7812.5 baud — now drained,
with the one-byte shift-register residual stated, not rounded up.

Retro item 4 — the timeline surface: per-phase palette-load shape and
PSG-write prefix compared against the shipped binary, structural
inequalities pinned AS the designed pairs (push-on-change latency;
our-quit-vs-their-kill), redundancy counted over all program loads so
a phase boundary cannot hide it, and the two sides' desktop TABLES
cross-checked (a count check is silent exactly when the split anchors
on the wrong load). The fault control is the whole argument: _colorptr
re-armed every vblank -> 766-780 redundant loads while frames, palette,
hardware vector AND rendered picture all still report IDENTICAL — the
773-stomps class, caught by the surface built for it.

Retro item 5 — institutionalized: docs/on-target-execution.md gains
'The observable surfaces' (six surfaces, what each cannot see, the four
escapes as evidence) and the rule — every on-target change names the
surface that would catch its failure; naming none IS the finding. One
gate bullet in CLAUDE.md, a kit README pointer, and STATUS gains
'Unpinned on target, and why' — seven honest entries including the
review's find that the hand-back ORDER is state-asserted, not
sequence-pinned. The play/GUI build joins the matrix: boot read-backs
+ hardware vector asserted at the title (the resolution check now
actually fails on ST-high — its first version masked the wrong byte
half and could not fail, the exact class this slice eliminates).

24/24 smoke modes green on EmuTOS + TOS 1.04 (independently
corroborated 12/12 by the review's own sweep); make test: 4368 passed.
Deferred, recorded: the read-back mechanism is game-agnostic and
belongs in the kit once a second game needs it.
